stories.title: Toronto-Quebec high-speed rail project could cost more than Ottawa’s estimate, PBO says
stories.summary: Parliamentary watchdog projects construction could cost up to $113-billion, higher than Alto’s preliminary figure
stories.author: Bill Curry
stories.content:
The construction cost of building a dedicated high-speed rail line between Toronto and Quebec City could be between $75-billion and $113-billion, according to a new report from Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan.

The Pbo’s range is higher than the one regularly cited by Alto, the Crown corporation responsible for the project, which has said it will be between $60-billion and $90-billion.

Alto has said its range is a preliminary estimate that will be further refined and updated next year.

The PBO report released Thursday is based on a review of international examples of the per-kilometre cost of building high speed rail.

Both the Pbo’s figures and Alto’s estimates only include the cost of building the new line.

The PBO report does not attempt to estimate the operational cost of the project. It says operational costs and whether the project’s ridership revenue will cover those costs will be addressed in a future report.

The Globe and Mail reported in August that an internal document from 2023 it obtained shows that operating and maintaining the line is estimated to cost between $62.6-billion and $67-billion over 40 years. That is in addition to the cost of construction. When construction and operational costs are combined with rolling stock purchases, the internal report said the total price tag over 40 years would be around $150-billion.

That 2023 internal report also said total projected revenue for the high-speed rail system is $105-billion over the 40-year period, meaning ridership revenue would more than cover operational costs and would offset some of the construction cost.

The next PBO report will focus on the issue of ridership revenue and operational costs.

Alto estimates that ridership will reach 24 million passengers a year by 2055 and up to 43 million by 2084.

That would be a significant increase in comparison to current ridership levels on the existing Via Rail service, which has declined from eight million passengers a year in the 1980s to about 4.4 million in 2025, according to Alto.

Via Rail has long said it is hindered from offering faster and more reliable service because it shares track with slower freight traffic, which is given priority.

That is one of the government’s main arguments for why a new line exclusively dedicated to passenger rail services is needed in the corridor.

While Alto says the project will cover 1,000 kilometres, the PBO analysis uses 850 kilometres for its assumptions. The PBO says the driving distance from Toronto to Quebec City via Montreal and Ottawa is less than 850 kilometres and a high-speed rail line is likely to be more direct than driving because such lines require fewer and broader curves.

The PBO report lists parts of the line that carry the highest risks of cost overruns. This includes plans for a 15-kilometre tunnel under Mount Royal linking Laval and downtown Montreal.

The government has not officially decided whether the route between Peterborough, Ont., and Ottawa will run north through the Canadian Shield or south near Kingston.

The PBO says rock blasting through the Canadian Shield carries risks of higher costs.

The southern route also presents cost risks, as it could cut through sensitive ecological terrain as well as more densely populated areas.

The PBO report says recent legislation related to large federal project approvals, such as the Building Canada Act, and the High-Speed Rail Network Act, which deals with expropriation processes, could help accelerate the project and avoid cost overruns experienced in other jurisdictions.

“While Canada’s legislative framework is intended to avoid the major cost-overrun drivers we’ve seen in comparable American and British projects, Canada’s route geography has some significant cost escalators – most notably tunnelling in and around Montreal, and the complexities of the Canadian Shield portion,” Ms. Ryan said in a statement.

She said that the report offers Parliament an independent assessment of the potential costs and economic effects associated with the project, noting it’s the " one of the largest infrastructure projects ever proposed in Canada.”

Philippe Archambault, a spokesperson for Alto, said the Pbo’s analysis places the construction cost within a range “that is similar to and consistent with Alto’s working estimate,” despite using different methodology.

“This independent report also suggests that some of the more pessimistic scenarios raised in the public debate are not supported by international experience. The development phase is ongoing and will confirm the route, refine cost estimates and finalize a rigorous business case before any final investment decision is made,” he said in a statement.

He said Alto expects to release an initial version of the business case in the first half of 2027.

stories.title: AI optimism is fueling tech stocks amid rising oil prices and bond yields
stories.summary: Strength for artificial-intelligence stocks is helping the U.S. market to hold firmer on Thursday, even as pressure from the bond market continues to rattle financial markets.
stories.author: Stan Choe, Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman
stories.content:
Strength for artificial-intelligence stocks is helping the U.S. market to hold firmer on Thursday, even as pressure from the bond market continues to rattle financial markets worldwide.

The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and was on track to break a three-day losing streak. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 211 points, or 0.4 per cent , as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.5 per cent higher.

Technology stocks helped lead the way after Micron Technology delivered a stronger profit report for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The maker of memory chips for computers also said growth is strengthening, and it gave forecasts for upcoming profit and revenue that topped analysts’ estimates.

CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said it’s benefiting from the AI boom, which is driving demand for memory.

Micron’s stock edged down by 0.1 per cent , which analysts attributed to how much its stock had already jumped before the profit report. It came into the day with a gain of more than 270 per cent for the year so far, towering over the less than 12 per cent rise for the overall S&P 500.

But other AI stocks benefited from Micron’s optimism about continued demand related to AI. Nvidia rose 0.6 per cent , and Alphabet climbed 1.5 per cent after Google released its latest AI model, Gemini 4 Argon.

The gains came despite more swings in the bond market, where fast-rising yields have been rattling financial markets worldwide.

The 10-year Treasury edged up to 5.30 per cent from 5.29 per cent late Wednesday. That’s near its highest level since 2002, but any kind of plateau would count as relief when the 10-year yield has been jumping from less than 5 per cent roughly a week ago and from less than four per cent before the war with Iran began.

High yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, while undercutting prices for stocks and other investments.

Yields are on the rise for a range of reasons, including worries about high inflation and oil prices, signals that the U.S. economy remains solid and Washington’s insistence to continue to spend much more money than it brings in.

Those worries don’t look to be going away anytime soon, and oil prices climbed again Thursday to keep the pressure up on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 1.9 per cent to US$99.88, continuing its swings on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global oil industry to return to normal.

Another report also signaled the U.S. economy is powering through its many challenges. Fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could mean fewer layoffs. That followed a report on Wednesday that said the U.S. economy’s overall growth was even stronger in the spring than earlier thought.

Canada’s main stock index, the Toronto Stock Exchange, dipped slightly at the open by about 0.1 per cent, as gains for some technology stocks were offset by losses concentrated in the financial and banking sector. Shares of Shopify were up 2.3 per cent, Blackberry’s stock gained 2.5 per cent and Constellation Software was up close to four per cent, while shares of some of Canada’s largest banks were down between roughly 0.75 and 1.5 per cent each.

In stock markets abroad, London’s FTSE 100 dropped 0.8 per cent after the 10-year U.K. government bond’s yield briefly jumped to 5.53 per cent before pulling back to 5.42 per cent . The CAC 40 in Paris fell 0.6 per cent following a similar, early-morning leap for the 10-year French government bond yield.

In Asia, stock indexes finished stronger thanks to optimism around AI following Micron’s profit report. Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 3.3 per cent , and South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.9 per cent.

paragraphs: Strength for artificial-intelligence stocks is helping the U.S. market to hold firmer on Thursday, even as pressure from the bond market continues to rattle financial markets worldwide.

The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent and was on track to break a three-day losing streak. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 211 points, or 0.4 per cent , as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.5 per cent higher.

Technology stocks helped lead the way after Micron Technology delivered a stronger profit report for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The maker of memory chips for computers also said growth is strengthening, and it gave forecasts for upcoming profit and revenue that topped analysts’ estimates.
CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said it’s benefiting from the AI boom, which is driving demand for memory.

Micron’s stock edged down by 0.1 per cent , which analysts attributed to how much its stock had already jumped before the profit report. It came into the day with a gain of more than 270 per cent for the year so far, towering over the less than 12 per cent rise for the overall S&P 500.

But other AI stocks benefited from Micron’s optimism about continued demand related to AI. Nvidia rose 0.6 per cent , and Alphabet climbed 1.5 per cent after Google released its latest AI model, Gemini 4 Argon.
The gains came despite more swings in the bond market, where fast-rising yields have been rattling financial markets worldwide.

The 10-year Treasury edged up to 5.30 per cent from 5.29 per cent late Wednesday. That’s near its highest level since 2002, but any kind of plateau would count as relief when the 10-year yield has been jumping from less than 5 per cent roughly a week ago and from less than four per cent before the war with Iran began.
High yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, while undercutting prices for stocks and other investments.

Yields are on the rise for a range of reasons, including worries about high inflation and oil prices, signals that the U.S. economy remains solid and Washington’s insistence to continue to spend much more money than it brings in.

Those worries don’t look to be going away anytime soon, and oil prices climbed again Thursday to keep the pressure up on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 1.9 per cent to US$99.88, continuing its swings on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global oil industry to return to normal.

Another report also signaled the U.S. economy is powering through its many challenges. Fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could mean fewer layoffs. That followed a report on Wednesday that said the U.S. economy’s overall growth was even stronger in the spring than earlier thought.

stories.title: Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith’s sexual assault trial dismissed
stories.summary: Judge dismissed the case after Crown lawyers said they would not be presenting any evidence
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The sexual assault case against the Nova Scotia-based actor best known for playing Bubbles on the TV comedy Trailer Park Boys has been dismissed.

Mike Smith’s three-day trial was supposed to start in Dartmouth, N.S., this morning.

Judge Jill Hartlen dismissed the case after Crown lawyers said they would not be presenting any evidence.

Smith had pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault stemming from an alleged incident in 2017. The actor was charged on Oct. 2, 2025, but court documents did not provide details about the allegations.

Smith’s lawyer, Stan MacDonald, said outside the courtroom that his client was pleased with the case’s dismissal and wants to put the matter behind him.

Nova Scotia-based Trailer Park Boys Inc., where Smith is listed as a director, issued a statement saying he will resume his responsibilities with the company.

Other company directors include John Paul Tremblay, who plays Julian on the show, and Robert Wells, who plays Ricky.

stories.title: ‘Trailer Park Boys’ actor Mike Smith has sexual assault charge dismissed
stories.summary: known for playing Bubbles on the show, has had a sexual assault charge against him dismissed in a Nova Scotia court.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
known for playing Bubbles on the show, has had a sexual assault charge against him dismissed in a Nova Scotia court.

A three-day trial was set to begin Thursday, after he pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault in connection to an incident alleged to have taken place on Dec. 30, 2017.

Media packed the Dartmouth, N.S., provincial courthouse Thursday morning, expecting Smith to appear.

Smith’s defence lawyer, Stan MacDonald appeared on his behalf. The Crown told the judge they would be submitting no evidence in the matter, and the defence motioned for the charge to be dismissed, which was granted.

“Smith is happy to put this behind him,” MacDonald told the media outside the courtroom.

In a statement, Trailer Park Boys Incorporated, which handles the business operations of the TV franchise, stated Smith will be “resuming his responsibilities.”

“The court has dismissed the charge against Michael Smith, concluding the legal proceedings that began in October 2025 regarding an allegation dating to December 2017,” the statement read.

“Now that he is cleared of this matter, Mike is resuming his responsibilities with Trailer Park Boys Incorporated.”

The company added it will provide no further comment.

stories.title: Ontario Liberal leadership candidate Eric Lombardi drops out
stories.summary: He endorsed legislature member Lee Fairclough, whom he called substantive and pragmatic
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
There are four people left in the running to lead Ontario’s Liberal party.

Eric Lombardi ended his campaign on Wednesday and endorsed legislature member Lee Fairclough, whom he called substantive and pragmatic.

Lombardi says he knew running as a young, unelected candidate would be a “tough sell,” and that he did not have enough confidence in fundraising to reach the end without taking on debt.

Former federal cabinet minister Navdeep Bains, legislature member Stephanie Bowman and former political staffer Dylan Marando are the other remaining candidates.

Bonnie Crombie stepped down as leader this year after receiving lukewarm support at the party’s 2025 annual general meeting, following a provincial election in which she failed to win a seat in the legislature.

The next leader is set to be announced Nov. 21.

stories.title: AI agent attempted to hack Library and Archives Canada, says U.S. research group
stories.summary: Ottawa — The website for Library and Archives Canada was one of the targets of a failed hacking attempt by an artificial intelligence agent, says a San Francisco-based lab that monitors AI activity.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — The website for Library and Archives Canada was one of the targets of a failed hacking attempt by an artificial intelligence agent, says a San Francisco-based lab that monitors AI activity.

Transluce posted an incident report Wednesday detailing what it describes as “aggressive attempts” to access public data on Canadian and U.S. government web pages.

The report says the attempted hacks occurred on May 28 and June 9 and involved 899 search queries into divorce records between 1905 and 1911.

Thirteen of the requests involved “attack payloads” seeking vulnerabilities in the search parameters, the report says.

Transluce says it does not “confidently attribute” the attempt to OpenAI-powered agents but notes this episode was consistent with similar incidents attributed to OpenAI in a similar time frame.

Transluce says the incident was reported to the Canadian government on Monday, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security issued a statement Tuesday saying it’s aware of possible suspicious AI agent activity and there is no indication systems were breached.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Founder of Russia's largest cargo airline escalates fight with Ottawa over sanctions as jet racks up fees at Pearson
stories.summary: The world’s largest cargo jet remains stranded at a Toronto airport since landing shortly before Canada closed its skies to Russian aircraft.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The Russian founder of Russia’s largest private cargo airline group stepped up his battle with Ottawa over Canada’s sanctions against him in retaliation for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Aleksey Isaykin lost his court challenge seeking his removal from Canada’s sanctions list targeting Russia in August but on Tuesday he filed a notice of appeal in the Federal Court of Appeal in Ottawa.

Appealing sanctions alongside Isaykin is the airline he founded, which owns a massive cargo jet — the world’s largest — that remains stranded at Toronto’s Pearson airport since landing shortly before Canada closed its skies to Russian aircraft in 2022 after Russia’s attack on Ukraine.

Isaykin and Volga-Dnepr Airlines were both put on Canada’s sanctions list in 2023 under regulations allowing Ottawa to list a person or corporation on reasonable grounds to believe they have directly or indirectly helped or supported Russia’s “violation or attempted violation of the sovereignty or territorial integrity of Ukraine.”

He said that information could have changed the decision. The government argued that while the specific documents weren’t given to Joly, the information in them was summarized for her.

Similar arguments were made by the airline in its motion for a judicial review and the two cases were heard together at a five-hour hearing in April.

Justice Ann Marie McDonald ruled in August on both cases that the procedural fairness protection required in such government decisions was minimal and that Parliament granted the minister wide latitude when passing the sanction regulations.

As for the documentation complaints, McDonald said missing information would have to have been completely omitted from the record to have an impact, but in these cases information from the documents was summarized in the government’s memorandum to Joly and in Isaykin’s delisting application.

“Mr. Isaykin has not identified any errors or misinformation in the summaries that were before the Minister,” her judgment said.

McDonald dismissed both requests for judicial appeals.

Her decisions are now being appealed.

Vincent DeRose, a managing partner of the Ottawa law firm Tereposky & DeRose LLP, declined to comment on the August judgments or the decision to file appeals, saying he had no instructions on it from his clients.

stories.title: CPP Investments selling Australian toll road assets for $4.5-billion
stories.summary: Deal includes 10.5% stake in WestConnex, 25% interest in NorthWestern Roads Group
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada Pension Plan Investment Board has signed a deal to sell its Australian toll road assets to Transurban for a total of about $4.5 billion.

The deal includes CPP Investments’ 10.5 per cent stake in WestConnex and its 25 per cent interest in NorthWestern Roads Group, which includes the Westlink M7 and NorthConnex roadways.

James Bryce, head of infrastructure at CPP Investments, says the sale allows the investment manager to realize value from mature assets.

CPP Investments first invested in Westlink M7 in 2010, followed by investments to develop NorthConnex in 2014. It invested in WestConnex in 2018.

The deal will see Transurban increase its interest in NorthWestern Roads Group to 75 per cent and 60.5 per cent for WestConnex.

The transaction is subject to closing conditions, including regulatory approvals.

stories.title: Canada Life merges IPC and Quadrus as part of wider integration plan
stories.summary: The merger of Canada Life’s mutual fund dealers is part of a three-phase integration
stories.author: Rudy Mezzetta
stories.content:
Canada Life is amalgamating mutual fund dealers IPC Investment Corp. and Quadrus Investment Services Ltd. into one platform called IPC Wealth Inc., with plans to merge that new platform with its investment securities business by late next year.

Blaine Shewchuk, executive vice-president of wealth and advice for Canada Life, says the merger is part of a three-phase integration.

“We’re going to get our feet beneath us [...] with this amalgamation, but that’s our plan,” he says.

In July, the company completed the first phase of that integration by combining Canada Life Securities Ltd. and IPC Securities Corp. under the IPC Securities name.

As a result of the fund dealers’ merger, IPC Wealth will have 2,500 advisors in 1,300 offices across Canada with $141-billion in assets under administration (as of Aug. 31). The new firm is headquartered in Mississauga.

IPC Securities, which has 216 advisors, is also taking the trade name IPC Wealth, but remains a separate entity from the amalgamated mutual fund dealers.

Both the merged securities firm and merged dealer are headed by James McKay, president and CEO of IPC Wealth.

Amalgamating the mutual fund dealerships gives the company scale to invest and to attract and keep advisors, Mr. Shewchuk says.

“I’m really excited [about the mutual fund dealers’ merger] because we can land the plane on the integration and the common brand,” he says. “We have the conviction now to grow, retain [advisors] and be confident about our value proposition, which is high payout and customizable support.”

Mr. Shewchuk says it was always Canada Life’s strategy to combine the wealth businesses it acquired when it bought IPC from IGM Financial Inc. , a sister firm under the Power Corp. of Canada group of companies.

“It was about the wealth capabilities that IPC offered – the mutual fund platform, the securities platform, the discretionary portfolio management platform that came with it and the wealth-focused advisor [as well],” he says. “The intent of bringing it over was to integrate it into one dealer.”

Integrating the businesses in stages before combining them next year was the most efficient way to build out new technology, Mr. Shewchuk says. The company is rolling out workflow integration technology, including a new advisor desktop, portal and app.

Canada Life chose the IPC name for the merged entity because of its brand recognition built over three decades.

“IPC was a company built by advisors for advisors,” he says. “It’s really important for us to maintain that entrepreneurial spirit and culture that came with IPC.”

stories.title: What to watch this weekend: Tip Toe, a dark comedy-thriller, will stick with you
stories.summary: Also catch Florence Pugh in an TV adaption of John Steinbeck’s classic tome East of Eden
stories.author: Amber Dowling
stories.content:
Reality game show The Traitors has catapulted Alan Cumming from Broadway star to household name over the past few years, but that doesn’t mean he’s given up scripted material altogether. This week he makes his debut in the U.K. dark comedy and thriller Tip Toe , written by Russell T. Davies and co-starring David Morrissey. The miniseries revolves around two neighbours whose lives unravel over social tensions in their Manchester suburb, to the point where they can no longer tip toe around the issues. It’s a brilliant and intense watch that’s only bolstered by the stellar acting, with scenes that will stay on your mind long after you’ve switched off the telly.

There’s no denying Catherine Zeta-Jones is one of Hollywood’s most charming leads, and it’s that persona that makes this new thriller worth the watch. Here she plays the title role of Jackie Price, a former drug smuggler turned art dealer. When the people she angered in her past life hire an assassin to get even, not even the assassin (played by Christine Adams) can resist her sparkling personality. The eight-episode offering features creators with past credits including John Wick , Killing Eve and Gangs of London , and could be described as a love child between the three. It’s convoluted and full of adrenalin, but somehow Zeta-Jones keeps it all together.

If you’re in the mood for something comforting on Sunday night then the public broadcaster has you covered with the 10th-season debut of this delicious competition series. The show still features the same wholesome competitors and heartwarming moments we’ve come to expect, and Season 10’s new home bakers from across the country are just as eager to share their stories as they are to show off their talent. Hosts Alan Shane Lewis and Ann Pornel return alongside judges Bruno Feldeisen and Kyla Kennaley to helm the chaos under the tent, and find the next competitor who will take home the coveted cake plate.

Whether you think of John Steinbeck’s classic tome as a literary masterpiece or a melodramatic mess, Netflix is taking a crack at the story with this incoming miniseries starring Florence Pugh. It’s already causing controversy among book lovers who aren’t sure how the actor’s anti-hero take on Cathy Ames will land, particularly since she was far from a hero in the source material. Regardless, this is a new spin on a character you thought you knew, with a lauded actor at the helm. Creator Zoe Kazan, whose grandfather Elia Kazan directed the original film adaptation, has publicly promised this story is still rooted in the book, so the hope is that it doesn’t veer too far. If you’ve always thought Cathy was misunderstood, this project May become your thesis.

It’s hard to imagine Nicole (Snooki) Polizzi trading in the Jersey Shore for creepy Ontario haunts, but that’s exactly what the reality star does in the Friday night debut of this paranormal series. Polizzi joins psychic medium Kevin Whitaker, occult expert and historian Missy Morrow and paranormal tech specialist Todd Thomas for eight Crave-produced episodes. The action kicks off in Hamilton at the Tuckett Mansion before moving to Goderich’s Huron Historic Gaol in Episode 2. While Polizzi has matured since her Shore days, she’s still entertaining to watch, but the real stars are the locations and stories she and her team uncover. If you’re into the unknown, you May even be inspired to start planning your own road trip.

stories.title: Canadian government website targeted in AI hacking attempt, research firm says
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence agents tried to hack into a Canadian government site, researchers said, adding to the growing list of AI incidents.
stories.author: Washington Post
stories.content:
Canada

AI research nonprofit Transluce said the rogue agents attempted to access Library and Archives Canada

Author of the article:

View of the Parliament Hill during sunset in Ottawa from Gatineau, Quebec on Friday, Aug. 14, 2026.Photo by Hyungcheol Park /Postmedia

SAN Francisco — Artificial intelligence agents tried to hack into a Canadian government site, researchers said, adding to the growing list of incidents in which AI agents, many of them associated with ChatGPT maker OpenAI, probed or hacked corporate and government computer systems without being told to do so.

The agents, which can take actions on computers and the internet, attempted to access Library and Archives Canada, the Canadian equivalent of the Library of Congress, according to AI research nonprofit Transluce.

The researchers could not confirm that the agents were built by OpenAI, but they said their behaviour was similar to that of agents that have been confirmed as coming from the company. The attempted hack did not appear to be successful, Transluce said.

The researchers said they notified the Canadian government Wednesday. Canada’s federal cyber agency said it was aware of reports of suspicious AI activity but that there was no indication that government systems had been compromised.

“We’re aware of reports of OpenAI models attempting to access publicly available information from Canadian government websites,” a spokesperson for OpenAI said. “We’re reviewing these findings and have provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials conducting the government’s review.”

The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.

The new finding comes days after OpenAI said its agents had hacked into an Australian government health care website and also probed but did not break into websites run by the U.S. Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The company confirmed the incidents after they were first flagged by Transluce, which has been scouring the internet for evidence of misbehaving AI agents. OpenAI has said it is investigating another of Transluce’s findings, which suggests its AI agents attempted to hack into the U.S. Education Department.

Researchers at Transluce and other organizations have been searching for new evidence of errant AI since OpenAI disclosed in July that some of its AI agents had escaped an internal computer system, accessed the internet and hacked into another AI company.

OpenAI initially did not notice the activity and took weeks to get it under control. The Transluce disclosures, as well as findings from other independent AI researchers, show that OpenAI’s agents engaged in a much broader pattern of activity across the web.

In the Hugging Face hack, the company was targeted by OpenAI agents that were attempting to work together to find solutions to tests of their cybersecurity skills.

In other incidents, OpenAI’s agents used obscure online message boards to communicate with each other and hijacked internet services so they could pass computer code to one another.

The company has said it is still investigating the full scope of the agent activity and has paused training of advanced new AI models to avoid further incidents.

stories.title: Carney set to make West Coast pipeline announcement in Fort McMurray
stories.summary: Carney is in Fort McMurray with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to make a major announcement about the proposed West Coast pipeline.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

Carney and Smith are set to speak at 11 a.m. ET

Last updated 1 hour ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/mark-carney-danielle-smith-west-coast-pipeline#comments-area)

Premier Danielle Smith was joined by Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Red Deer, north of Calgary on Wednesday, July 29, 2026.Photo by Brent Calver /Postmedia

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Fort McMurray, Alta. with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Thursday to make a major announcement about the proposed West Coast pipeline.

The announcement comes on Oct. 1, the deadline for the project to be designated a project in the national interest, which would fast-track the pipeline’s regulatory journey. The pipeline is expected to carry up to a million barrels of crude from Alberta to B.C.’s coast.

The government says the pipeline will create 150,000 jobs and, with the announcement coming less than three weeks before an Alberta referendum about separating from Canada, Carney and Smith are hoping it helps make the case for federalism.

stories.title: Police seek answers in crash that killed 2 elders, hurt 2 others on BC First Nation
stories.summary: Police in Delta, BC, said it's believed the driver of a pickup had a medical emergency near one of the mall's entrances and drove into a group.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Community members on the Tsawwassen First Nation lined the road, drummed and sang as the bodies of two elders were loaded into coroners’ vehicles outside a shopping center near the nation’s reserve south of Vancouver.

They were killed and two others were injured by a vehicle outside the Tsawwassen Mills shopping center Wednesday while taking part in a walk to mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Police in Delta, BC, said it’s believed the driver of a pickup had a medical emergency near one of the mall’s entrances and drove into a group.

Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed his condolences on social media to those who lost loved ones or who were injured, saying the accident happened on a day already heavy with grievance.

The Provincial Health Services Authority said it sent 12 ground ambulances and two helicopters to respond to the crash.

Police spent much of the day with witnesses and nation members in a restaurant at the scene where the black pickup came to rest against a brick wall.

stories.title: Employees in Manitoba no longer need sick notes for short absences
stories.summary: Doctors Manitoba has welcomed the change, noting the province has gone from having no limits on sick notes to having the clearest and strongest rules in Canada.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Employees in Manitoba no longer need to provide a sick note when missing work for a minor illness or injury.

Under the new rules, which come into effect Thursday, employers can’t ask for medical documentation when an employee misses a week or less of work, or 10 days or fewer over a calendar year.

The government says it made the change to both support workers and reduce the burden on the health-care system.

Doctors Manitoba has welcomed the change, noting the province has gone from having no limits on sick notes to having the clearest and strongest rules in Canada.

The group says many employers still ask for sick notes where rules are in place, and it has urged companies to update their policies.

Employers can still ask for medical documentation for long-term absences, including maternity leave or serious injury.

stories.title: Small caps to watch: Ag Growth shares soar on ‘encouraging’ update, plus news from Primaris Reit, AutoCanda and more
stories.summary: A look at some small-cap stocks making news - or about to.
stories.author: Brenda Bouw
stories.content:
A look at some small-cap stocks making news - or about to. This file will be updated throughout the day on Thursday.

Canada’s S&P/TSX Small Cap Index ( Txtw-I ) is up by about 30 per cent over the past 52 weeks. It hit a record 1,496.55 on June 2. The Russell 2000 in the U.S. is up about 15 per cent over the past 52 weeks and reached a high of 3,069.71 on Aug. 14.

Ag Growth International Inc. ( AFN-T ) stock shot up on Wednesday after the company updated investors on its capital strategy, balance sheet improvement initiatives, strategic review process and outlook, which at least one analyst described as “encouraging.”

“As AGI enters 2027, the company is seeing positive market signals across many of its core businesses which support increasing confidence in its outlook,” it stated in a release before markets opened. “Farm markets have strengthened with a notable pick-up in order intake over recent months and commercial quoting activity is rising across key global regions. Overall, AGI continues to benefit from leading market positions across a range of geographies including North America, Emea, India, and Brazil.”

The company said the outlook, combined with more than $30-million of expected annualized cost savings and approximately $50-million of identified surplus real estate monetization opportunities, makes it “well positioned to improve earnings, strengthen cash flow, and accelerate balance sheet deleveraging.”

Ag Growth said it has secured covenant relief under its senior credit facilities through the second quarter of 2027, giving it extra operating and execution flexibility. It also said it has earmarked about $50-million of “excess, non-core real estate” to sell and plans to put the proceeds towards paying down debt.

“The real estate program is one component of a broader non-core asset monetization initiative and does not include potential proceeds from other non-core businesses or assets currently being evaluated by the company and the board’s strategic review committee,” it added. “Management is focused on using internally generated cash and proceeds from non-core asset monetization to reduce senior indebtedness and progressively strengthen the balance sheet.”

Ag Growth also said its targeted $30-million in annualized savings has so far included closing its Naperville office, restructuring underperforming North American business units, and an “overhaul of the senior executive team, among other actions.”

It also said its previously announced review of strategic alternatives is ongoing.

TD analyst Michael Tupholme said in a note that the update “contains some encouraging incremental items (i.e., now expects a higher level of proceeds from excess/non-core real estate monetization initiatives), while certain other items included in the update have been previously disclosed/are not new.”

Pulse Seismic Inc. ( PSD-T ) reported preliminary third-quarter results, including a 400-per-cent increase in revenue versus the same period last year.

After markets closed on Wednesday, the Calgary company that provides seismic data to the Western Canadian energy sector, said it generated approximately $17.3-million in seismic data licensing revenue, bringing expected total revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30 to about $22.8-million.

It said third quarter revenue increased more than 400 per cent compared to the third quarter of 2025, while revenue for the first nine months of 2026 decreased by 49 per cent compared to the “near-record revenue” for the first nine months of 2025. The company didn’t provide more specific data in the release.

“Consistent with previous disclosure, the timing of new seismic data licensing is impacted by a variety of factors affecting industry activity and is subject to significant fluctuations,” the company stated.

“These strong third-quarter sales results demonstrate the continued value and strategic importance of our extensive seismic data library to our clients,” said CEO Pamela Wicks in a release. “While our market experiences natural fluctuations tied to broader energy sector activity, we remain confident in our competitive position and the long-term value of our asset base.”

The company said the data is preliminary and has not been audited or reviewed by its auditors. It said final results for the period are expected to be released on Oct. 21

Primaris Reit ( PMN-UN-T ) announced a deal to buy a 100-per-cent interest in Upper Canada Mall in Newmarket, Ont. for $411-million in cash.

“The acquisition further advances Primaris’ strategy of acquiring market-leading enclosed shopping centres in growing Canadian markets, where the Reit can deploy its full-service operating platform to drive income growth and long-term per unit value creation,” it stated.

It said Upper Canada Mall will become its fourth-largest shopping centre by total commercial retail unit (CRU) sales volume.

“Upper Canada Mall is a dominant GTA shopping centre with strong demographics, an exceptional tenant mix and significant embedded growth potential,” said president Patrick Sullivan,

The company also lowered its fiscal 2026 funds from operations guidance to $1.83 to $1.88 from $1.85 to $1.90 based on an assumed transaction closing date of Oct. 31.

RioCan Reit ( REI-UN-T ) announced on Wednesday that Dennis Blasutti will resume his duties as chief financial officer, effective Oct. 1, following a temporary medical leave.

Franca Smith, who served as interim CFO from March to September, will continue as senior vice-president of finance.

Dye & Durham Ltd. ( DND-T ) reported mixed results for its fourth quarter ended June 30.

Before markets opened on Tuesday, the legal software company reported revenue of $104.2-million, down 1 per cent from the same period a year ago. Excluding the impact of the disposal of Credas Technologies Ltd. from all periods, revenue increased by 4 per cent year over year, the company stated. The expectation was for revenue of $94.9-million, according to S&P Capital IQ estimates.

Its net loss was $21.9-million or 32 cents per share, compared to a net loss of $29.6-million or 44 cents a year ago. The expectation was for a loss of 21 cents.

Adjusted Ebitda was $55.1 million up from $47.7-million a year ago. Excluding the impact of the disposal of Credas, adjusted Ebitda increased 18 per cent, it stated. The expectation was for adjusted Ebitda of $44-million.

AutoCanada Inc. ( ACQ-T ) said this week that it’s initiating a strategic review of its collision operations, including a potential sale.

On Tuesday, the Edmonton-based company said its board has set up a special committee of independent directors to analyze and evaluate “a range of strategic alternatives intended to maximize value for AutoCanada and its shareholders and to support the continued growth of its collision operations.”

The company said the alternatives May include, but are not limited to, separating the business from AutoCanada and potentially selling all or part of the business.

“The board believes the value and growth potential of the company’s collision operations May not be fully reflected in AutoCanada’s current public market valuation,” the release stated.

National Bank analyst Maxim Sytchev said the announcement was “somewhat of a surprise” in a note.

“Bottom line – announcement wasn’t expected; value-creation initiatives are appreciated, but macro needs to cooperate for the stock to really work; exit multiple of course can make a bigger swing,” he wrote. “From an accretion/shareholder value perspective, the impact of a potential monetization of the Collision business remains relatively value-neutral, in our view. ”

Slate Grocery Reit ( SGR-UN-T ), a Canadian-listed company that owns grocery-anchored retail centres in the United States, capped a volatile bout of trading with news of its acquisition by two American buyers.

On Monday, Slate announced its sale to Brixmor Property Group Inc., a publicly listed company, and Everview Partners, L.P., which is privately owned. Together, the buyers are paying US$13 in cash per unit, amounting to an equity value close to US$800-million. (Slate Grocery trades in U.S. dollars on the Toronto Stock Exchange.)

The sale itself wasn’t necessarily a surprise, because Slate launched a strategic review in May. However, the timing caught investors and analysts off guard.

Read the full story from the Globe’s Tim Kiladze here

Sangoma Technologies Corp. ( STC-T ) announced a deal to be bought by BRC Holdings, Inc. ( RLY-Q) in a deal valued at about US$204-million, or $289-million Canadian, or roughly $7.40 per share.

On Monday, the company said shareholders will receive US$4.925 in cash for each Sangoma share they own and 0.04767 of a share of common stock of BRC. “The consideration payable under the transaction represents a premium of approximately 47 per cent and 51 per cent to Sangoma’s closing price and 10-day Vwap, respectively, ON the TSX for the period ending on September 28, 2026,” the company stated.

It said officers and directors of Sangoma, collectively holding approximately 27 per cent of the issued and outstanding Sangoma shares, have agreed to vote in favour of the deal. The deal requires approval by two-thirds of votes cast by Sangoma shareholders at an upcoming special meeting, as well as regulatory approvals.

Stifel analyst Suthan Sukumar said the takeover offer follows a strategic review announced last quarter.

“A takeout was the optionality we flagged, and while the price sits at a discount to our C$9 target, the premium does capture value following Stc’s business transformation,” he wrote. “Net/net - we view this as a clean, credible outcome for a name that had run out of catalysts as a standalone public company. We see little risk of a higher bid, given a comprehensive sale process run since May 2026 that assessed other proposals, 27 per cent of shares locked up in voting support, and a 3-per-cent break fee.”

Oct. 21: Pulse Seismic Inc. ( PSD-T )

Oct. 22: Mullen Group Ltd. ( MTL-T )

Oct. 28 : Canada Packers Inc. ( Cpkr-T) , Cogeco Communications Inc. ( CCA-T )

Oct. 29: Aecon Group Inc. ( ARE-T ), Enerflex Ltd. ( EFX-T ), Centerra Gold Inc. ( CG-T ), Spin Master Corp. ( TOY-T )

Nov. 2 : RioCan Reit ( REI-UN-T )

Nov. 3: Curaleaf Holdings Inc.( Cura-T )

Nov. 5: Western Forest Products Inc. ( WEF-T )

Nov. 6 : NFI Group Inc. ( NFI-T ), Cineplex Inc. ( CGX-T )

Nov. 10: Superior Plus Corp. ( SPB-T )

stories.title: Minimum wage hikes set to begin across 5 provinces
stories.summary: The bumps of between 25 and 40 cents come in Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The minimum wage is going up in five provinces.

The bumps of between 25 and 40 cents come in Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

Like other government announcements, Ontario has tied the increase to the rising cost of living.

It’s moving its minimum wage up to $17.95 an hour, while P.E.I. is boosting it to $17.30 and Nova Scotia moves it to $17.

In Manitoba, the wage goes up to $16.40, and in Saskatchewan to $15.70.

The changes mean all provinces and territories will have raised their rates this year with the exception of Alberta, which hasn’t increased its minimum wage since 2019.

Alberta maintains the country’s lowest minimum wage at $15 an hour.

Nunavut lifted its minimum wage at the beginning of September and leads the country at just over $20 an hour.

The changes mean all provinces and territories will have raised their rates this year with the exception of Alberta, which hasn’t increased its minimum wage since 2019.
Alberta maintains the country’s lowest minimum wage at $15 an hour.
Nunavut lifted its minimum wage at the beginning of September and leads the country at just over $20 an hour.

stories.title: Toronto board of trade calls for regulatory reforms to spur housing growth
stories.summary: The Toronto Region Board of Trade is urging the province to amend zoning and building code rules as it says Ontario is on pace to fall well short of its new home goal.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
The Toronto Region Board of Trade is urging the province to amend zoning and building code rules as it says Ontario is on pace to fall well short of its goal of getting at least 1.5 million new homes built by 2031.

In a report published Thursday, the board said the target is unachievable by the current deadline, which was set by the provincial government in 2022, even if housing production increases over the next five years. Based on budget forecasts, Ontario is projected to fall more than 550,000 homes short of the pace needed by 2029, according to the analysis.

“We already had a massive gap. It was called the housing crisis for a reason,” said board president and CEO Giles Gherson in an interview.

“There’s been a lot of effort and a lot of work gone into, ‘How do we close this housing gap? How do we build houses faster?’ But the disappointing part of it is that the gap remains very, very large.”

The board said that even if ambitious reforms were adopted immediately, municipalities would need to update plans, amend zoning bylaws, align infrastructure investments, service land, and process applications. Those steps could take years, making the 2031 goal unrealistic.

Gherson said the key to unlocking new development at a quicker pace is through regulatory changes.

He described rules around zoning and building codes as “very fragmented” across the province, and “out of date.” In Toronto alone, builders face dozens of different requirements across the city, which makes it difficult to standardize production.

“It really adds a huge amount of cost and delay to housing development and that impacts the ability for the city to attract and retain our workforce that we need,” he said.

“But also, we know it is impacting the social fabric as the next generation sees home ownership as really a pipe dream, and that’s a really big problem.”

The report said Ontario should develop a provincial zoning code that provides every municipality the same framework and terminology.

That code could set a baseline of what housing types can move forward without special approval, starting with townhouses and multiplexes. The standard could also establish provincewide limits on the rules that most often block housing, such as parking, setbacks, lot coverage, height, density, and how far upper storeys must step back.

Meanwhile, it recommended key changes around building codes, saying there should be an assessment of every requirement for the cost it imposes to build, run and maintain over the life of the building. The report also proposed allowing single-stair buildings up to six storeys, along with smaller elevators in smaller buildings, as long as safety and accessibility are still prioritized.

Gherson said other cities in Canada are proof that a less patchy model can lead to meaningful housing growth. He pointed to Edmonton, where he said it’s more common see multiplexes in different types of neighbourhoods.

“Where we’ll have single-family dwellings on major roads, they’ll have a lot of these multiplexes and the reason is they have more flexible permissive zoning and they don’t have as many zoning codes,” he said. “There’s a city that’s been a fast-growth city for the last five decades … so we need to look to other places that have been successful.”

The call for action comes as affordability challenges persist for Toronto’s housing market, even as prices have been on the decline over the past year.

Last month, the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board said the average selling price in the Greater Toronto Area stood at $993,410 for August, down 2.7 per cent year-over-year, while the composite benchmark price, meant to represent the typical home, was down 4.5 per cent.

But the trade board’s report said housing remains out of reach for many residents, especially compared with past decades. It said that between 2006 and 2025, Toronto-area home prices, as measured by the composite price, increased by around 187 per cent. That significantly outpaced the cumulative increase for inflation over that time, which was around 51 per cent.

“Durable affordability depends on increasing the supply of homes,” the report said.

“Without continued housing construction, recent affordability gains are likely to prove temporary.”

stories.title: An AI agent tried to hack Canadian government website, researchers say
stories.summary: Transluce said it informed the Canadian government on Monday, Sept. 28, following which the Canadian Centre for Cybersecurity issued a statement on Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
A rogue artificial intelligence agent attempted to hack a Canadian government website earlier this year, an incident report by an AI research group revealed.

Two attempted hacks took place, one on May 28 and another on June 9 on a Canadian government website, the report by Transluce, an independent, nonprofit research lab dedicated to public oversight of AI, said on Wednesday evening.

The group observed 899 requests hitting the “collection-search” service of Library and Archives Canada, the group said, calling the attempted hack “rudimentary.”

The requests were associated with retrieving data on divorce records in Canada between 1905 and 1911.

Transluce said it informed the Canadian government on Monday, Sept. 28, following which the Canadian Centre for Cybersecurity issued a statement on Tuesday.

“We are aware of reports identifying suspicious activity, including suspected AI agent activity, targeting publicly accessible websites, such as the Government of Canada. There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time,” a statement from Canadian Centre for Cyber Security read.

It is not yet clear whose AI agent attempted the hack, but the report suggested the “tactic” are similar to those that OpenAI has used in previous hacks.

“We do not confidently attribute these attempts to OpenAI, but they exhibit tactics consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe,” Transluce said.

The group added, however, that they “do not believe that these probes were successful.”

The report also detailed the hacks of several U.S. federal and state government websites, including a failed attempt on the U.S. Department of Education.

An OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and targeted Medicare, Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan, Australia’s prime minister said last month.

More to come

stories.title: Hydro-Québec to face off against industry actors like Google in data centre hearing
stories.summary: A Hydro-Québec proposal that could double the cost of energy for data centres is being put to the test at a public hearing.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
A Hydro-Québec proposal that could double the cost of energy for data centres is being put to the test at a public hearing.

The hearing in Montreal will pit tech industry actors like Google against the provincial utility.

Hydro-Québec is asking the Régie de l’énergie, the provincial energy regulator, to consider a new electricity rate for data centres that require a capacity of over five megawatts.

The proposal would raise energy prices to an average of 13 cents per kilowatt hour.

The utility says this is around twice as much as what data centres pay as large‑power customers.

The hearing is scheduled to last until Oct. 9 and will involve actors from several industries, including the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.

Hydro-Québec says that higher rates for the sector could limit the impacts of growing data centre energy demand on residential rates.

Energy costs for data centres in Quebec are currently around six cents per kWh, which is much lower than in most other jurisdictions, said energy analyst Jean-François Blain.

“It creates an exceptional draw that benefits Quebec, as long as they can supply those companies,” he said.

With energy demand and costs increasing, Blain said Hydro-Québec might not be able to afford giving data centres the same advantageous price for long. The new rate would bring their rates closer to those of other areas.

Hydro-Québec said data centres that would be subject to the new rate currently consume 190 MW at peak consumption and could reach 1,000 MW by 2035.

The provincial energy regulator will be reviewing whether a new rate for data centres is fair and sustainable.

stories.title: Highway 401 closure following crash
stories.summary: Police, and fire crews are on scene with no details available as of publishing time on possible injuries or the cause of the crash.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A section of Highway 401 is closed Thursday morning following a crash between a transport truck and a passenger vehicle.

OPP say traffic is at a standstill in the eastbound lanes between Union Road and Colonel Talbot Road.

An OPP spokesperson told CTV News that one person was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

A tow truck is on its way to the scene to remove the car that is blocking traffic and police hope to have a lane opened soon.

More information will be provided as it becomes available.

stories.title: Large, corner unit sells in the overcrowded Toronto market
stories.summary: The unit’s layout, with the living room separating two bedrooms, convinced the buyers to make the deal
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
300 Balliol St., No. 612, Toronto

Asking price: $789,000 (May, 2026)

Selling price: $745,000 (June, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $340,000 (August, 2006); $191,328 (December, 1999)

Taxes: $3,845 (2025)

Days on the market: 36

Listing and buyers’ agents: Robert Greenberg and Amir Kiabi, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

Potential buyers toured this two-bedroom condo almost every day for five weeks this spring, but none returned with an offer to purchase. Many potential buyers liked its relatively large footprint and prime views from one corner of a boutique building siding onto Mount Pleasant Road.

“This unit had approximately 945 square feet [of living space], it was a corner unit, and it had southwest exposure, which is very desirable because it gets a lot of sun,” agent Amir Kiabi said. “That all adds to the scarcity factor. Looking at units 900 square feet and up, there were only six units that transacted in that building since 2022.”

By coincidence, Mr. Kiabi was showing different clients other large units nearby. The unit’s layout, with the living room separating the bedrooms, convinced them to buy it.

“They chose this one, No. 1, because of the layout,” Mr. Kiabi said.

This 27-year-old unit has windows in both bedrooms and a balcony wrapping around the living room.

There is a kitchen with an island, two full bathrooms and laundry machines.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $842 cover water, heating and use of a gym and party room.

“The building has a good reputation; it’s well-managed and was recently improved,” Mr. Kiabi said.

“It’s in a very popular school district, and to get into that school district, you usually need to have a house.”

stories.title: Collapse of an affordable housing dream
stories.summary: Assembly Corp. was seen as a leader in the sprint toward factory-built housing. Now, its projects are in limbo after it filed for bankruptcy protection
stories.author: John Lorinc
stories.content:
It was, and May still be, the home-building industry’s version of the chicken-and-egg quandary.

When Leith Moore, an architect and infill developer, in 2021 decided to take a run at constructing modular housing, his firm tapped into a stream of small-scale affordable projects backed by governments or non-profits aiming to build quickly. Their “volumetric” components – rooms, effectively – could be built in a factory, then assembled on site.

Yet after Mr. Moore and his Assembly Corp. partners began scaling up in anticipation of a surge of new factory-built projects promised to flow through Ottawa’s new Build Canada Homes (BCH), as well as the massive planned redevelopment of the former Downsview Airport lands, actual orders simply didn’t come fast enough to sustain their capital investment.

“I feel we were early for what we thought would happen with the federal government and off-site fabrication,” he said in an interview. “That is going to come about a year after when we needed it. There’s a lot of good things happening, but they didn’t happen in time for us.”

A spokesperson for Build Canada Homes – which is the centrepiece of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s effort to drive affordable housing construction using factory-based automation, dubbed “modern methods of construction” (MMC) – said the agency “is focused on creating a predictable pipeline of housing opportunities that can support manufacturers, suppliers and builders.”

“Roughly 50 per cent of the units committed by BCH,” the spokesperson added, “incorporate MMC approaches, including modular, panelized, prefabricated and factory-built housing.”

Assembly Corp., founded in 2018 and formerly known as R-Hauz, sent shock waves through Toronto’s affordable housing circles this summer when it was forced to declare bankruptcy, just months after entering receivership in May. “We’d given [the creditors] a proposal because we thought we could do it more cost-effectively and help wind them up at a lesser cost and faster. But after many lawyers and many meetings, that didn’t really transpire.”

Several of its mass timber or modular projects, for partners such as WoodGreen, the Ymca and the Elizabeth Fry Society, are in limbo.

“The City of Toronto has actively engaged with the non-profit housing providers impacted by these proceedings,” Aviva Levy, housing development office director, said in a statement. “This includes working closely with the court-appointed receiver and non-profits to develop a path forward for completing the projects.”

According to filings posted by receiver GlassRatner , seven nearly finished housing projects with a total of 153 affordable and deeply affordable units and a combined value of almost $70-million have been affected by the bankruptcy. Three involve First Nations. Mr. Moore and several investors, including former Evergreen CEO Geoff Cape, had invested $4-million in equity and debt in the firm since 2001, according to court records. The firm had 26 employees when it applied for creditor protection.

Creditors include numerous general contractors and suppliers, most of whom have registered liens against Assembly’s projects, as well as PaceZero Capital Partners, which had provided Assembly with $5-million in financing.

Besides these projects, the company last year purchased automated fabrication equipment from a Swedish firm and was negotiating a lease with Canada Lands to build a 124,000-square-foot factory next to the 370-acre Downsview site, a cquired in 2018 by the real estate arm of PSP Investments, Northcrest . A spokesperson for Northcrest declined to comment.

“We had assigned a lease at Downsview to build a plant there supposedly this year,” said Mr. Leith. “There [are] plans for 63,000 housing units up at Downsview,” Mr. Cape said in an interview with The Globe last year. “If we can secure 5 per cent of that, that’s a billion and a half dollars [of] work that helps us become a viable company.”

Mr. Moore said he couldn’t comment on the state of the automated equipment, which is currently subject to the bankruptcy proceedings.

Both Mr. Cape and Mr. Moore hoped to see more progress in the policy environment, including more financing to sustain the factories where the components for this kind of housing could be mass produced. Mr. Cape last year fronted a lobbying effort by other modular builders while Mr. Moore was hoping for movement as part of a broader reform effort driven by Canada’s wood products sector, which released a 60-page report in the spring.

Among other things, the Canadian Forest Sector Transformation Task Force recommended a range of policies to kick-start the MMC industry, such as accelerating Bch’s procurement activities and promoting the use of Canadian wood in mass timber products.

Task force co-chair Ken Kalesnikoff , principal a B.C.-based producer of factory-based modular components made from wood, says that boosting this market involves a range of policy fixes – among them, making more land available for logging and streamlining the permitting process. U.S. tariffs and procurement restrictions are also cramping the industry. But, he adds, “Build Canada Homes really has to get their act together and get that building started.”

Mr. Moore added that the challenge was finding suppliers interested in selling Assembly the kind of specialized cross-laminated timber products it needed for its modular projects. “The issue has been that there are so few fabricators [so] there is not a lot of incentive for change.”

In the end, Assembly was unable to figure out how to create both a reliable supply chain and an order book with enough business to justify the cost of building the kind of factory required to churn out easy-to-assemble housing. “Just timing,” Mr. Moore said with a sigh. “Everything didn’t work, and so it all came crashing together, with a whole bunch of contractors and liens and financing guys and lack of patience. It was a real lesson.”

Special to The Globe and Mail

stories.title: AI agents tried and failed to hack a Canadian government website, research firm says
stories.summary: Agents attempted to access Library and Archives Canada on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said
stories.author: Kanishka Singh, Christian Martinez and Deepa Seetharaman
stories.content:
An artificial intelligence research firm said on Wednesday AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, casting the effort as a failed hacking attempt, while Canada said there were no indications its systems were compromised.

AI research firm Transluce said the attempts exhibited tactics “consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe.” But it added that it was not confidently attributing these attempts to OpenAI.

The agents attempted to access Library and Archives Canada on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said in a blog post. Transluce said it disclosed the action to the Canadian government on Monday.

AI agents repurposed a University of Toronto link-sharing tool to communicate with each other

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said on Tuesday it was aware of reports of suspected AI agent activity. “There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time,” it said in a statement.

“We do not confidently attribute these attempts to OpenAI, but they exhibit tactics consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe,” Transluce said.

OpenAI said it was “aware of reports of OpenAI models attempting to access publicly available information from Canadian government websites.” A spokesperson said OpenAI was reviewing the reported findings and had provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials conducting the government’s review.

The world’s leading AI companies have warned of the risks posed by AI to humanity, appealing for governments to work together to manage the increasingly powerful technology. Governments around the world have struggled to keep pace with rapid advances in AI.

Free online service arquivo.pt, the national Portuguese web archive that is operated by the Portuguese Foundation for Science and Technology, captured 899 requests hitting the “collection-search” service of the Library and Archives Canada, including a series of apparently failed rudimentary hacking attempts, ON May 28 and June 9, Transluce said.

Australia says OpenAI agent hacked government website, accessed files

Several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents have alarmed governments and companies.

Last week, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, in what was the first known instance of an AI agent hacking into a government website.

OpenAI apologized on Tuesday for the hacking of the Australian government website by the rogue AI agent.

stories.title: Improved team and arena renovations make it ‘a great time to be a Sting fan’
stories.summary: When Sarnia Sting fans arrive for the home opener Friday against Sault Ste. Marie, they are going to see much more than a first-place hockey club.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
When Sarnia Sting fans arrive for the home opener Friday against Sault Ste. Marie, they are going to see much more than a first-place hockey club.

Massive renovations have taken place at Progressive Auto Sales Arena in Sarnia, Ont. during the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) offseason.

“We’re really excited to launch District 94,” said Jake Bourrie, vice president of business operations for the Sting.

“It lives in the heart of Progressive Auto Sales Arena. We’re thrilled to have ownership here with the Sting from Ryan Finch, David Legwand and Mark Guy who have made a significant investment into the food and beverage experience here and it starts here in the restaurant.”

“Whether we win or lose, we want our fans to leave saying, ‘I had a great time, and I’m looking forward to the next game.’”

On the ice, the Sting are off to a great start. They played all four of their games on the road as the arena renovations are ongoing and won three of four including their first victory in Ottawa in nearly two decades.

“I think you don’t want to look too far ahead,” said Sting captain Alessandro Di Iorio.

“You want to play hard and you want to play tough and fast. I think we’ve done on the first three games and if we keep playing, I think we’ll be very successful.”

The Sting have missed the playoffs for three consecutive seasons. After undergoing an ownership change last year, they brought in head coach Mathieu Turcotte in November 2025, replacing Alan Letang.

“The biggest thing is kind of gaining that respect back overall is pretty much the theme this year,” said Turcotte.

“With the past few years, we want to make sure that we shift things, we turn things around and make sure that we fight for that division every year.”

There have been a lot of roster turnover and new faces, with the new owners striving for a winning culture on and off the ice.

“They are making the investments but also the commitment and the sweat equity that they’re putting in,” said Bourrie.

“They’re here rolling up their sleeves and helping support in all aspects of our business. It’s a great time to be a Sting fan.”

“Our ownership group put a lot of time and effort and obviously money into all the renovations here so it’s a great fan experience,” said Turcotte.

stories.title: Toronto board of trade urges Ontario to amend zoning and building code rules to spur housing growth
stories.summary: Province is on pace to fall well short of its goal of getting at least 1.5 million new homes built by 2031
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
The Toronto Region Board of Trade is urging the province to amend zoning and building code rules as it says Ontario is on pace to fall well short of its goal of getting at least 1.5 million new homes built by 2031.

In a report published Thursday, the board said the target is unachievable by the current deadline, which was set by the provincial government in 2022, even if housing production increases over the next five years. Based on budget forecasts, Ontario is projected to fall more than 550,000 homes short of the pace needed by 2029, according to the analysis.

“We already had a massive gap. It was called the housing crisis for a reason,” said board president and CEO Giles Gherson in an interview.

“There’s been a lot of effort and a lot of work gone into, ‘How do we close this housing gap? How do we build houses faster?’ But the disappointing part of it is that the gap remains very, very large.”

The board said that even if ambitious reforms were adopted immediately, municipalities would need to update plans, amend zoning bylaws, align infrastructure investments, service land, and process applications. Those steps could take years, making the 2031 goal unrealistic.

Gherson said the key to unlocking new development at a quicker pace is through regulatory changes.

Annual pace of housing starts dips in August, Cmhc says

He described rules around zoning and building codes as “very fragmented” across the province, and “out of date.” In Toronto alone, builders face dozens of different requirements across the city, which makes it difficult to standardize production.

“It really adds a huge amount of cost and delay to housing development and that impacts the ability for the city to attract and retain our work force that we need,” he said.

“But also, we know it is impacting the social fabric as the next generation sees home ownership as really a pipe dream, and that’s a really big problem.”

The report also proposed allowing single-stair buildings up to six storeys, along with smaller elevators in smaller buildings, as long as safety and accessibility are still prioritized.

Gherson said other cities in Canada are proof that a less patchy model can lead to meaningful housing growth. He pointed to Edmonton, where he said it’s more common see multiplexes in different types of neighbourhoods.

Realtors predicted a modest housing comeback this year. Rising mortgage rates are now dashing those hopes

“Where we’ll have single-family dwellings on major roads, they’ll have a lot of these multiplexes and the reason is they have more flexible permissive zoning and they don’t have as many zoning codes,” he said. “There’s a city that’s been a fast-growth city for the last five decades ... so we need to look to other places that have been successful.”

The call for action comes as affordability challenges persist for Toronto’s housing market, even as prices have been on the decline over the past year.

Last month, the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board said the average selling price in the Greater Toronto Area stood at $993,410 for August, down 2.7 per cent year-over-year, while the composite benchmark price, meant to represent the typical home, was down 4.5 per cent.

But the trade board’s report said housing remains out of reach for many residents, especially compared with past decades. It said that between 2006 and 2025, Toronto-area home prices, as measured by the composite price, increased by around 187 per cent. That significantly outpaced the cumulative increase for inflation over that time, which was around 51 per cent.

“Durable affordability depends on increasing the supply of homes,” the report said.

“Without continued housing construction, recent affordability gains are likely to prove temporary.”

stories.title: Cyclist dies after being struck by vehicle in Thames Centre
stories.summary: A 34-year-old Thames Centre resident has died after being struck by a vehicle on Richmond Street, east of London, provincial police say.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A 34-year-old Thames Centre resident has died after being struck by a vehicle on Richmond Street, east of London, provincial police say.
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 7:18 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Middlesex County say a cyclist has died after being hit by a vehicle in Thames Centre.(Ontario Provincial Police)
A 34-year-old cyclist has died after being struck by a vehicle in Thames Centre, east of London, according to provincial police.
Emergency crews were called to Richmond Street, between Gore Road and Marion Street, at about 12:22 p.m. Wednesday.
The cyclist, a Thames Centre resident, was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died, police said.
The driver of the vehicle was not injured.
Middlesex County OPP Const. Jeff Hare said in a video posted to social media that police, paramedics and Thames Centre firefighters responded to the crash.
“Our thoughts go out to the families and everybody else involved in today's events,” Hare said.
Richmond Street in the area was closed while emergency crews responded but has since reopened.
Police are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has information about what happened to contact Middlesex County OPP.

stories.title: New rules for short-term rentals in London start today
stories.summary: As part of the changes through the city, hosts will be limited to one short-term rental and one short-term rental licence.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
take effect today. As part of the changes through the city, hosts will be limited to one short-term rental and one short-term rental licence. Hosts also cannot own or partly own more than one home or unit used as a short-term rental.

“These changes help protect housing in London and support responsible hosting in our neighbourhoods,” says Amanda Pfeffer, director of municipal compliance. “Hosts are responsible for making sure their rentals are licensed and follow City rules.

That includes being ready for the new limits on Oct. 1.” Short-term rentals include homes or rooms rented for stays of 28 days or less. Hosts already need a City business licence before advertising a rental or welcoming guests.

The rental must be at the address where the host lives. The licence number must be included in all ads and listings. Residents can check whether a rental is licensed on the City’s website. To report concerns about an unlicensed rental or nuisance issues, call Municipal Compliance at 519-930-3515 or email licensing@London.CA.
