stories.title: Foundation proposes national policy agenda on menopause
stories.summary: Menopause Foundation of Canada is calling for more training among health providers and increased research funding
stories.author: Tavia Grant
stories.content:
A new national campaign is calling on governments to boost support for Canadian women experiencing menopause, laying out what it says is a blueprint to help Canada become a world leader for care.

The Menopause Foundation of Canada, with backing from other groups, including the Society of Obstetricians and Gynecologists of Canada, is releasing a menopause policy agenda on Thursday. It calls for more training of health providers, more funding for research and expanded access to treatment.

“Menopause isn’t just a women’s health issue. It’s a matter of public policy, workforce sustainability and economic resilience,” Janet Ko, the foundation’s president and co-founder, said in an interview.

Unmanaged symptoms of menopause cost the Canadian economy $3.5-billion a year, the foundation has estimated. Women older than 40 make up a quarter of the country’s paid workforce, and most will reach menopause between the ages of 45 and 55. Many will experience symptoms that range from difficulty sleeping to night sweats, brain fog, migraines, heart palpitations and anxiety.

Those symptoms May cause some to reduce their hours, turn down promotions, or step into lesser roles, denting incomes in their peak earning years, the foundation said.

What the menopause gap in the labour force is costing Canada

As The Globe and Mail has previously reported, Canada doesn’t have a national strategy on menopause. It hasn’t had a national health campaign (Australia currently has one underway). And funding for dedicated research is still scarce.

In a paper to be released Thursday, the non-profit organization sets out seven priorities for provincial, territorial and federal governments. These include mandating menopause education for all physicians and nurse practitioners, adjusting fee structures so that physicians are adequately compensated for care, and ensuring menopause medications are accessible and affordable.

“Despite more conversation about menopause, systemic barriers are keeping women from getting the care they deserve,” Ms. Ko said.

“This is an urgent call to action for government to transform menopause care, support and research in Canada,” she said. The policy priorities provide a blueprint for decision-makers, and “an opportunity for Canada to lead the world in equitable menopause care and support.”

The foundation’s surveys have found that one in two women feel unprepared for menopause and perimenopause, a transition period where the body prepares to stop having periods. Two in five feel their symptoms were undertreated by their health care provider.

Menopause symptoms aren’t just disruptive, they’re costly

This is the first-ever proposed national policy agenda on menopause in Canada, and was two years in the making, the foundation says.

Access to menopause care is not equal, the report says, citing research , and many women are having difficulty finding help. The gaps are widest for Black, Indigenous, and racialized women, as well as for newcomers, those living in rural and remote communities, gender-diverse people, and those with lower incomes. A lack of access is forcing some to pay out of pocket – or go without care.

“Access to safe, evidence-based menopause care should never depend on a person’s ability to pay,” Ms. Ko said, adding that public menopause clinics and publicly funded virtual care can help fill the gap.

Other recommendations include policies that support women in the workplace, and more training for doctors. Currently, there is no standardized menopause curriculum for healthcare providers in Canada.

Nnamdi Ndubuka, president of Black Physicians of Canada, is among those supporting the initiative. “Better menopause education for healthcare providers is essential to ensuring that every patient receives the care they deserve,” he said in a release.

Menopause awareness is growing, but patients still face barriers to evidence-based care

The foundation also named Sophie Grégoire Trudeau, an author, advocate and public speaker, as its first ambassador.

Perimenopause can last for eight years or longer and brings varying experiences. For some, symptoms are mild, while for others, they can be debilitating.

“Too many women are suffering through this transition without ever being told that menopause is at the root of their experience,” Ms. Grégoire Trudeau said in the report. “They are dismissed, misdiagnosed, or left to figure it out alone. Failing half our population comes at a cost we all share.”

Research on the health of half of the population is scant. One 2025 study found that just 7 per cent of all funded grants went to female-specific research over a 15-year period; of that small pool, little went to menopause research.

This research gap has consequences, the report said, as health care providers and policy-makers lack the data to support women through midlife transitions that have a lasting impact on heart, bone and brain health.

stories.title: Minimum wage hike is now in effect across five provinces
stories.summary: Bumps of between 25 and 40 cents come in Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The minimum wage is going up in five provinces.

The bumps of between 25 and 40 cents come in Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

Like other government announcements, Ontario has tied the increase to the rising cost of living.

It’s moving its minimum wage up to $17.95 an hour, while P.E.I. is boosting it to $17.30 and Nova Scotia moves it to $17.

In Manitoba, the wage goes up to $16.40, and in Saskatchewan to $15.70.

The changes mean all provinces and territories will have raised their rates this year with the exception of Alberta, which hasn’t increased its minimum wage since 2019.

Alberta maintains the country’s lowest minimum wage at $15 an hour.

Nunavut lifted its minimum wage at the beginning of September and leads the country at just over $20 an hour.

Like other government announcements, Ontario has tied the increase to the rising cost of living.
It’s moving its minimum wage up to $17.95 an hour, while P.E.I. is boosting it to $17.30 and Nova Scotia moves it to $17.
In Manitoba, the wage goes up to $16.40, and in Saskatchewan to $15.70.
The changes mean all provinces and territories will have raised their rates this year with the exception of Alberta, which hasn’t increased its minimum wage since 2019.
Alberta maintains the country’s lowest minimum wage at $15 an hour.
Nunavut lifted its minimum wage at the beginning of September and leads the country at just over $20 an hour.

stories.title: Saskatchewan mayor who clashed with ‘Queen of Canada’ cult to step down
stories.summary: Village of Richmound says Brad Miller’s resignation takes effect Oct. 14 and that information about a by-election will be shared once a date is set
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The mayor of a southwestern Saskatchewan village that spent two years bedevilled by the Kingdom of Canada cult is stepping down.

A brief social media post from the Village of Richmound says Brad Miller’s resignation takes effect Oct. 14 and that information about a by-election will be shared once a date is set.

The village first made headlines in 2023 when the so-called “Queen of Canada” Romana Didulo and her followers set up a compound in a former school and soon began badgering residents.

Crown prosecutors stay charges against Saskatchewan cult leader Romana Didulo

The school had its sewer and water access cut off and was later closed for health reasons, as open sewage could be seen bubbling on the grounds.

Didulo, who rose to prominence from the 2022 “Freedom Convoy” in Ottawa, was among 16 arrested in a police raid of the compound in September, 2025, though charges against her were stayed in March.

Miller said at the time that he hoped Didulo and her followers would leave Saskatchewan.

stories.title: B.C.’s major parties on track to field candidates in all ridings as deadline looms
stories.summary: Smaller parties are struggling ahead of the Oct. 3 nomination deadline
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
The major parties running in British Columbia’s election appear to be on track to fill each of the 93 ridings, but smaller parties are struggling ahead of the Oct. 3 nomination deadline.

Elections BC lists 43 official candidates for the B.C. New Democrats, while there are 32 on the list for the Conservatives as of Sept. 30.

Both parties say on their websites that those numbers are much higher, but candidate figures for those running in the smaller parties remain in the single digits.

CentreBC and OneBC have one official candidate each, while seven Greens candidates have been registered with Elections BC.

All three parties say their candidate count is higher than that, but all are under 20 each.

Neither CentreBC nor OneBC existed during the last election in 2024, but emerged as the fledgling B.C. Conservative Party splintered amid disagreements shortly after coming within a few seats of forming government.

stories.title: Canada’s role in space exploration
stories.summary: Alberta-native Joshua Kutryk will be on his way this week for a six-month visit to the International Space Station.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is shown at the Kennedy Space Center on Merritt Island, Florida on Monday March 30, 2026. Kutryk says Canada's space industry is playing a key role in the upcoming Artemis II mission, which is sending humans near the moon for the first time since 1972. THE Canadian Press/Kelly Malone

By Analysis by The Big Story podcast

Posted October 1, 2026 6:32 am.

In today’s The Big Story podcast, another Canadian is heading to space! Alberta-native Joshua Kutryk will be on his way this week for a six-month visit to the International Space Station, alongside three other crew members onboard Nasa’s SpaceX Crew 13 mission. They plan on conducting research, maintenance, as well as experiments as they orbit the Earth.

Host Catherine Jetté speaks to Major Erin Edwards, Nasa Deputy Branch Chief for Crew Operation and ISS Capcom instructor. They discuss Kutryk’s mission, and Canadian impacts on space exploration and advancement at large.

stories.title: New bill should help prevent strikes in the 'centre of the economy,' think tank report says
stories.summary: The Carney government’s recent legislation designed to avoid crippling strikes was an important response, a new think tank report says.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Carney government’s recent legislation designed to avoid crippling strikes in the transportation sector was an important response to a growing trend that had the potential to cause serious economic damage, a new think tank report says.

In a report to be released Thursday, the Montreal Economic Institute (MEI) writes that Ottawa is justified in stepping in when the two sides in a labour dispute are not “remotely close to reaching common ground” and millions Canadians are paying the price.

The report cited recent lockouts at the ports of Montreal and Vancouver in 2024 and a labour strike a year later at Air Canada as examples of work stoppages that threatened major swaths of the Canadian economy and thousands of jobs. Airlines, ports and rail services are considered key parts of national infrastructure and are relied on by miners, manufacturers, farmers and many other economic sectors.

In August, 2024, for example, the simultaneous shutdowns of rail services at CN and Cpkc threatened the transport of about $1-billion of goods a day, the report says.

Gabriel Giguère, a senior policy analyst at MEI and the report’s author, said these types of transportation companies are different than most other employers and warrant unique legislation to help keep them in operation.

“It’s at the centre of the economy,” Giguère said of the transportation sector.

Christopher Monette, a spokesman with Teamsters Canada, whose members include truck drivers and dock workers, said the Canadian economy can withstand limited disruptions much more than “anti-union voices” suggest. More than 95 per cent of collective agreements are resolved without a work stoppage, he said.

“Claiming that few remaining cases are enough to cripple our economy is factually baseless and sells Canada short.”

Ottawa’s response to the sector’s stoppage threat was Bill C-39, more commonly known as the Building Canada Strong Act, an omnibus bill that was introduced last week. The proposed legislation is designed, among many other things, to make it easier to resolve labour disputes in federally regulated transportation industries by clarifying the process for government intervention.

The bill’s measures include an increase in the conciliation period before a strike or lockout and the explicit ability for the labour minister to intervene in the event of a “significant adverse national impact.”

The MEI says the problem of work stoppages in these important sectors has been on the rise. There were 22 recorded work stoppages in the transport sector between 2024 and 2025, an annual average almost three times the four work stoppages in those sectors in 2016.

The government was able to force resolutions to some work stoppages in the industry but its legislative authority was sometimes called into question. This legislation clarifies Ottawa’s ability to take action, as well as the process for doing so.

Monette said the number of referrals have been on the rise because employers lobby the government to use the existing legislation, then point to its frequent use as proof of its importance.

Workers’ rights to strike and to collective bargaining are protected in the Canadian constitution, Monette added, and those rights can’t be ignored because of an alleged economic disruption.

stories.title: How a couple with vastly different financial attitudes managed a $1-million inheritance
stories.summary: A free spender who came into money had a what’s-mine-is-yours mentality, but her frugal spouse wasn’t convinced the funds should be communal
stories.author: Rosemary Counter
stories.content:
The beneficiaries: “Christopher” and his wife “Jacqueline” are government workers in the Toronto with good (but not great) pensions in their future. They’re both on the cusp of 50, and have a university-aged daughter. Like many couples, Christopher and his wife – one money-minded saver and one a laissez-faire spender – have very different approaches to money and finances.

The inheritance: A few years ago, Jacqueline’s well-off parents died in short succession, bequeathing Jacqueline an impressive inheritance she always knew was coming her way: After taxes and red tape, it was almost a million dollars cash. “She came right to me and said, ‘What should we do with it?!’,” says Christopher. He was relieved and grateful for her generous what’s-mine-is-yours mentality, but wasn’t quite convinced the money should be communal after all.

What they learned: Firstly, some important context: “We come from two very different families,” he says. “I grew up lower-middle-class and my parents divorced when I was a kid. They worked long hours and double jobs, and I put myself through school with loans.” Christopher came into their marriage with plenty of debt he’s since worked diligently to pay off. All of it’s been paid off except the mortgage, which they got after getting married with some help from his in-laws, but still Christopher monitors their money very closely.

How a sister managed a sizeable inheritance while also navigating her brother’s addiction

Jacqueline enjoyed a far more privileged upbringing in a nuclear family. “They were both professionals, very comfortable with their house being paid off completely, and they’d received family money as well,” says Christopher. His wife therefore never had to rely on loans from banks, indeed never learned much about managing or budgeting money and spends freely most of the time, be it on Uber Eats or arts-and-crafts supplies. “She’s a retail therapy kind of person,” he says. “If she sees something she wants, she buys it.”

Despite their different spending habits, newlyweds Christopher and Jacqueline pooled their money together and have been navigating life via joint account ever since (That’s the approach taken by about a quarter of Canadian couples, according to a new study by personal finance website MooseMoney, though thanks to younger demographics, that percentage is shrinking). Jacqueline agreed to discuss any purchase she makes that’s more than a couple hundred dollars in advance; Christopher agreed to relax a bit and stop asking permission from his wife for every little purchase he makes. Their strategy works well to balance the other out, he notes.

But for reasons he can’t quite articulate, Christopher didn’t and doesn’t feel comfortable casually tossing a million dollars into the joint pot. It doesn’t relate to his parents’ divorce, he says, although he agrees that the psychology of money runs deep. “Yes, we’re married, and yes, it’s a partnership, but it doesn’t feel like my money. It’s her money and if she wants to spend it freely, I wouldn’t fight her. I might try to nudge her in another direction, but no fighting.”

Opinion: What an early inheritance could buy your kids

What they did with it: Luckily, the couple’s first big decision was almost made for them. “My father-in-law had told us that when he went, he wanted us to pay off the mortgage. He wanted us to have that sense of comfort that they had,” says Christopher. A large lump sum paid off the principal a decade earlier than anticipated.

Jacqueline’s neglected TFSAs were then topped up to the max, and for both pragmatic tax reasons and because she insisted, Christopher’s were, too. Since those accounts are filled, they next opened a spousal Rrsp and rejigged the timeline so that Jacqueline can retire early if she wants. To their daughter who’s about to enter the working world, they gifted $10,000 to ease the tough transition. “We want her to have a bit of a safety net and something to learn to build on,” Christopher says.

The couple hundred thousand that was left over is currently sitting in an investment account in his wife’s name. “It’s the only separation we have in terms of finances, but I want her to have something that’s just hers,” he says. If she spends it all on vacations and takeout, that’ll have to be fine by him, though he’ll do whatever he can to mitigate the damage from any spending he feels is frivolous.

“Her money’s under her name, but I have the account passwords to double-check dividends and reinvest wisely,” he says. Now she can spend and he can save so everyone’s happy in their element.

stories.title: Right? Left? Blue? Red? How do I choose a side when no party reflects all my values?
stories.summary: An ethicist answers a Globe reader’s question on how to balance concerns about climate change and free speech
stories.author: Shawna Cohen
stories.content:
Divisive political debates are a constant these days, with or without a federal election campaign on the horizon. For some Canadians, it can be hard to decide who to support when more than one party has policies they agree (or disagree) with.

In the first instalment of Conscience Call – a new series exploring everyday ethical, moral and philosophical dilemmas – we pose a reader’s question about voting strategies to an expert for advice.

Do you have a dilemma you’d like some guidance on? Tell us about it here .

Our reader Shane from Toronto writes:

I am someone who is deeply concerned about the climate crisis. At the same time, during the last three federal elections, I voted for the Conservative Party of Canada, even though I do not agree with its policies when it comes to protecting the environment.

Although I worry about what a Conservative government would mean for Canada’s fight against climate change, I would also never vote for the Liberal Party of Canada because, in my opinion, it has become increasingly illiberal through abandoning classically liberal values such as free speech, the rights of the individual and equality under the law.

I feel stuck between a rock and a hard place, because each of the two major political parties have ideas and policies that I strongly agree with, as well as those that I disagree with. How can I find a way to fight climate change while safeguarding classically liberal values?

From the ethicist: Arthur Schafer, professor and founding director of the Centre for Professional and Applied Ethics at the University of Manitoba

In Canada, with our electoral system, we have just a few major parties and each is a big tent. They include people with very different interests and priorities, all working together under one banner.

Each party represents policies on a broad range of issues, and if you’re looking for one that exactly represents your preferences and values on several different matters, you’re likely not going to find it. You’re never going to find a perfect match.

Most of us have several fundamental values, and we somehow weigh and balance those against the policies of a particular party. The question is: Which of your values should trump the others or be given the heaviest weight?

The weight you give those values can also change. In different circumstances, one value might deserve a higher priority. If we’re having a crisis in our health care system, a party that’s going to protect universal health care might become my priority. That May not ordinarily be at the top of my list – it might be the environment. But if universal coverage is threatened with collapse, I might vote for a party that has the best policy on protecting it, even though I disagree with them on other issues.

So ask yourself: At this time in Canadian history, and at this point in my life, what matters more to me, my family and my fellow citizens?

But how do you weigh two things that are both extremely important to you at the same time? Here’s an analogy: You’re trying to decide if you should take a job where the work is really satisfying but the pay is kind of poor, or one where the work is not fulfilling, but it pays really well.

The competing values aren’t commensurable. They’re apples and oranges. How do you weigh salary against work satisfaction? Yet, we do it all the time, such as when we’re choosing a job, a life partner or where to live. We somehow commensurate the incommensurable, but it’s mostly intuitive. There isn’t an easy way.

In your case, there is another question worth asking: Are the two values you’ve identified really as separate as they appear? The issues aren’t in silos. I would urge you to think about how your commitment to climate change is related to your commitment to freedom of expression. Look at the way the different policies you care about interact with one another. They May overlap and reinforce each other, or they May cut against each other.

Next, consider what you want your vote to accomplish. Ask yourself: Do I vote for the party whose policies and values are second-best because it’s the most likely to form government? Or do I vote on principle for the party that embodies the values I care about, even if I know it’s extremely unlikely to win the election?

You might vote for a party, even though you believe it’s not likely to win. The purpose might be to send a message that you’re someone who has this set of values. Or should you go for the second-best to minimize the harm done by another party you feel most opposed to?

There’s a cost regardless of the strategy you adopt. By voting pragmatically, you May be voting for policies that you don’t really agree with, in order to prevent even worse policies. But you’re also reinforcing the likelihood that the best policies will never be on the agenda, because the people who favour them haven’t sent a strong enough message.

I don’t think there’s any once-and-for-all best answer. It’s going to depend on the circumstances. It’s going to depend on you as a person. The question is what matters most to you under the circumstances you are facing now.

In the first instalment of Conscience Call – a new series exploring everyday ethical, moral and philosophical dilemmas – we pose a reader’s question about voting strategies to an expert for advice.
Do you have a dilemma you’d like some guidance on? Tell us about it here .
Our reader Shane from Toronto writes:

I am someone who is deeply concerned about the climate crisis. At the same time, during the last three federal elections, I voted for the Conservative Party of Canada, even though I do not agree with its policies when it comes to protecting the environment.

Although I worry about what a Conservative government would mean for Canada’s fight against climate change, I would also never vote for the Liberal Party of Canada because, in my opinion, it has become increasingly illiberal through abandoning classically liberal values such as free speech, the rights of the individual and equality under the law.

I feel stuck between a rock and a hard place, because each of the two major political parties have ideas and policies that I strongly agree with, as well as those that I disagree with. How can I find a way to fight climate change while safeguarding classically liberal values?
From the ethicist: Arthur Schafer, professor and founding director of the Centre for Professional and Applied Ethics at the University of Manitoba
In Canada, with our electoral system, we have just a few major parties and each is a big tent. They include people with very different interests and priorities, all working together under one banner.

Each party represents policies on a broad range of issues, and if you’re looking for one that exactly represents your preferences and values on several different matters, you’re likely not going to find it. You’re never going to find a perfect match.

Most of us have several fundamental values, and we somehow weigh and balance those against the policies of a particular party. The question is: Which of your values should trump the others or be given the heaviest weight?

The weight you give those values can also change. In different circumstances, one value might deserve a higher priority. If we’re having a crisis in our health care system, a party that’s going to protect universal health care might become my priority. That May not ordinarily be at the top of my list – it might be the environment. But if universal coverage is threatened with collapse, I might vote for a party that has the best policy on protecting it, even though I disagree with them on other issues.
So ask yourself: At this time in Canadian history, and at this point in my life, what matters more to me, my family and my fellow citizens?

But how do you weigh two things that are both extremely important to you at the same time? Here’s an analogy: You’re trying to decide if you should take a job where the work is really satisfying but the pay is kind of poor, or one where the work is not fulfilling, but it pays really well.

The competing values aren’t commensurable. They’re apples and oranges. How do you weigh salary against work satisfaction? Yet, we do it all the time, such as when we’re choosing a job, a life partner or where to live. We somehow commensurate the incommensurable, but it’s mostly intuitive. There isn’t an easy way.

In your case, there is another question worth asking: Are the two values you’ve identified really as separate as they appear? The issues aren’t in silos. I would urge you to think about how your commitment to climate change is related to your commitment to freedom of expression. Look at the way the different policies you care about interact with one another. They May overlap and reinforce each other, or they May cut against each other.

Next, consider what you want your vote to accomplish. Ask yourself: Do I vote for the party whose policies and values are second-best because it’s the most likely to form government? Or do I vote on principle for the party that embodies the values I care about, even if I know it’s extremely unlikely to win the election?

You might vote for a party, even though you believe it’s not likely to win. The purpose might be to send a message that you’re someone who has this set of values. Or should you go for the second-best to minimize the harm done by another party you feel most opposed to?

There’s a cost regardless of the strategy you adopt. By voting pragmatically, you May be voting for policies that you don’t really agree with, in order to prevent even worse policies. But you’re also reinforcing the likelihood that the best policies will never be on the agenda, because the people who favour them haven’t sent a strong enough message.

I don’t think there’s any once-and-for-all best answer. It’s going to depend on the circumstances. It’s going to depend on you as a person. The question is what matters most to you under the circumstances you are facing now.
As told to Shawna Cohen. Responses have been edited and condensed.

stories.title: Cybersecurity vendor Field Effect growing fast with new tool targeting ‘shadow AI’ at companies
stories.summary: Ottawa company’s customer base has jumped 33 per cent since launching AI detection and response tool in June
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Matt Holland started his career with Canada’s cybersecurity espionage agency, writing code for offensive security missions and breaking into information technology systems of the country’s enemies following the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

The cyberspy-turned-cybersecurity entrepreneur is still targeting threats, but he’s no longer going after al-Qaeda. His new pursuit is artificial intelligence – specifically, AI that lurks undetected within companies or is misused by employees.

In June, Mr. Holland’s company, Field Effect Software Inc., introduced an AI detection-and-response tool to help its small and medium business clientele. It prevents employees from unwittingly uploading sensitive corporate data to platforms like Claude or ChatGPT, blocking use that violates corporate policies, and will soon track prompts – the instructions users provide to generate AI content.

The program also stops so-called “shadow AI” programs operating within corporations – such as AI features added to cloud software they’ve used for years – from unknowingly accessing and transmitting their data to places they aren’t supposed to go. Mr. Holland, Field Effect’s chief executive officer, said in an interview his AI tool is “like a chaperone with a grimace and a large stick to smack the AI when it’s gone off the rails.”

That is what many companies want. In less than four months, privately-held Field Effect has seen its user base jump by about one-third, to 12,000 companies from about 9,000, largely driven by demand for its AI-targeting tool. The Ottawa-based company’s annualized revenues are approaching $50-million, up from $26-million last year.

Bell, Cohere release AI model designed to aid cybersecurity investigations

Mr. Holland estimates Field Effect will add 3,000 more customers this year and aims to raise US$100-million in 2027 to fuel expansion. Field Effect also plans to launch the AI tool this fall as a stand-alone product for companies of all sizes.

“Once we start to put that money to use on the commercial side, I will be shocked if we don’t grow 80 per cent to 100 per cent a year for the next five years,” he said. Recent stories that AI bosses themselves worry their tools are dangerous “are creating the business case for us in real time.”

Field Effect is one of several companies offering digital nannies to help organizations ensure the proliferation of AI applications within their operations won’t cause harm.

Toronto’s Signal 1 has developed an AI management system for health-care organizations to oversee all the new tools and making sure, for example, that AI-generated draft e-mails from doctors to patients conform to hospital standards. Teramind Inc. of Aventura, Fla., polices employee activity on computers, networks and other digital “end points” to ensure they aren’t using unapproved AI tools or uploading corporate data. Nvidia Corp. Nvda-Q this week announced a security platform that will set boundaries it says could stop rogue activity by AI.

“A lot of organizations haven’t figured out how to utilize AI correctly, let alone what is it being given access to, and there’s virtually no real controls around it,” said CEO Jeff Farr of Dallas-based Sera Brynn LLC, which manages cybersecurity services for companies and deploys Field Effect products to customers. Its new AI tool, he said, “has been eye-opening for several of our customers when they actually look” at the issue. “The light bulbs are going off in a big way, because almost nobody has a clue.”

Rob Schenk, chief strategy officer with Las Vegas-based Intelligent Technical Solutions, another third-party cybersecurity services provider that deploys Field Effect to about 800 clients, said “AI is becoming a driver of additional revenue for companies like ours.” Field Effect’s AI tool, he said “complements the direction that clients need to go. It’s accelerating the conversation.”

Canada’s plan to counter the U.S. and China in AI is taking shape. Will it work?

Mr. Holland joined the federal Communications Security Establishment’s Tailored Access Operations (TAO) group in 2000 after studying computer science at University of New Brunswick, earning a reputation as one of the best in the trade at understanding operating systems, and how to defend and exploit them.

After the Sept. 11 attacks. Tao’s profile within the cyberespionage unit swelled. Mr. Holland left in 2007 to start Linchpin Labs, which built software for Canada and its “Five Eyes” intelligence-sharing allies – the U.S., Britain, Australia and New Zealand – to run cyberintelligence operations. He self-funded the company and sold it to defence giant L3 Technologies in 2018 for US$200-million.

Mr. Holland decided to focus next on helping small companies protect against threats from cyberattacks. With Field Effect he set out to create an all-encompassing, affordable and simple product for small businesses offering the kind of protection large companies get. That platform combines a range of internally built capabilities to comprehensively monitor a client’s vulnerable digital assets, including network, computing devices, connected sensors and cloud operations.

Mr. Holland believed its holistic approach and “zero trust” modus operandi (as in never trust, always verify) would serve Field Effect well as it developed its AI detection tool. Now, he said, “We have the technology that guards against AI going off the rails.”

stories.title: West Coast pipeline deadline day: Carney, Smith to make announcement in Fort McMurray
stories.summary: Thursday marks Ottawa's deadline to decide whether to designate a proposed pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia's south coast as a project of national interest.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
It’s pipeline deadline day and Prime Minister Mark Carney and Premier Danielle Smith are set to make an announcement in the heartland of Alberta’s oil and gas industry.

The Prime Minister’s Office said the two will reveal the next step to accelerate a “major infrastructure project.”

The two are set to speak Thursday morning in Fort McMurray , where the Alberta government said they’ll be joined by Pembina Pipeline Corporation president and CEO Scott Burrows.

This story will be updated after the 9 a.m. MT news conference.

Oct. 1 marks Ottawa’s deadline to officially designate a proposed West Coast pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia’s south coast as a project of national interest.

Being designated is a regulatory step that would place the proposal within Ottawa’s accelerated major-projects framework — but is not final construction approval.

If that happens, the pipeline would be owned by Trans Mountain, the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission and Pembina Pipeline Corp.

Trans Mountain Corporation would be responsible for planning and construction, while Pembina Pipelines will act as a private sector partner.

It has a 10 per cent ownership stake in the construction , with an option to purchase an additional 10 per cent once the line is operational.

The pipeline is estimated to cost between $35.2 billion and $43.7 billion, according to the project submission package, and would run almost entirely along the same path as the current Trans Mountain Expansion pipeline (TMX).

The roughly 1,250-kilometre route would carry upwards of one million barrels of crude oil from Bruderheim, Alta. near Edmonton, to a port south of Vancouver near Delta, B.C., for shipment to international markets.

The proposed pipeline is a central component of an energy agreement between the federal and Alberta governments.

Oil and gas is Alberta’s biggest industry and global energy prices have a significant impact on provincial coffers , but the landlocked Prairie province has been hampered for decades by a lack of shipping capacity to get product to tidewater.

Smith has previously said Carney has acted constructively with Alberta in coming up with an Alberta-Ottawa energy agreement and working toward a new West Coast pipeline.

Carney has adjusted some policies to make the project more likely.

Bill C-39, the “ Building Canada Strong Act ,” proposes giving the federal government new powers to fast-track major infrastructure projects.

In August, Ottawa moved to list a West Coast pipeline as a national interest project . A notice published in the Canada Gazette on Aug. 1 sets a Sept. 18 deadline to submit comments on the national interest designation.

The proposed pipeline project was referred to the government’s major projects office, with the Alberta government listed as the proponent.

The government’s notice said Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Dominic LeBlanc would work with the Alberta and B.C. governments on the project while consultations with Indigenous communities were underway.

Ottawa has moved several other large projects toward national interest designation already, including the Grays Bay road and port project in Nunavut, the Mackenzie Valley Highway in the Northwest Territories and the Nuclear Waste Management Organization’s deep geological repository in northern Ontario.

On Tuesday, Carney announced $1.2 billion in federal funding for ocean protections as the country moved toward decisions on a new pipeline and expansion of a major port in Metro Vancouver.

Carney has said the proposed pipeline would avoid “highly sensitive areas” and the tanker ban along B.C.’s north coast will remain in effect.

Carney has previously backed a proposed expansion of the Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank terminal, telling reporters during a visit to the facility in July that his government was looking to provide about $10 billion for the project, part of Ottawa’s effort to “grow our exports away from the United States.”

A report from TD Economics released this summer said a new West Coast pipeline would boost Canada’s oil exports by 20 per cent and more than double what currently goes overseas on tankers to Asia.

With files from The Canadian Press and Ariel Rabinovitch, Global News

Pipelines faced key challenges in the past. Can Alberta’s overcome them?

stories.title: 5 candidates are running in London's Ward 5. here's what they say they're focused on
stories.summary: Five candidates are running for London's Ward 5 council seat in the 2026 municipal election. Affordability, property taxes, public safety, construction and transportation are among the issues they say they hear about from residents.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Five candidates are running for London's Ward 5 council seat in the 2026 municipal election. Affordability, property taxes, public safety, construction and transportation are among the issues they say they hear about from residents.
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 41 minutes ago
The new Ward 5 boundaries in London's 2026 municipal election.(City of London)
With five candidates vying for a seat on London City Council, the race for Ward 5 is largely focused on concerns over affordability and property taxes, public safety and construction.
The candidates are Corrine Rahman, Charles Spina, Abid Raza, Simon Sabeesh Karikkassery and Mary Blake Rose. One councillor will be elected.
Voting Day is October 26, with advanced voting begining on Thursday, Oct. 1.
This will be the first election with Ward 5's new boundaries. It saw significant changes following the 2024 review of ward boundaries, now shifting westward from Wonderland Road to Adelaide Street.
The boundary changes also mean current Ward 7 Coun. Corrine Rahman is running for re-election in Ward 5.
Rahman said the changes have required candidates to explain the new boundaries to residents while door-knocking.

“It's really been candidates in the election that have had to push the message of why the boundaries have changed and inform the residents of the change,” she said. “So that's definitely been part of the script when you're door knocking.”
As a result of the latest ward boundary review, incumbent Ward 7 Coun. Corrine Rahman is now running in Ward 5. (Corrine Rahman/Facebook)
Rahman said residents she's spoken with are looking for what she described as an "effective" city government.
If elected, she said she would focus on fiscal responsibility, more local police presence and support for vulnerable communities, including addressing upcoming funding pressures for services.
She also wants to see continued investment in infrastructure, including parks, facilities and trail connections, as well as a new community centre in northwest London.
Rahman said her experience on council is an asset.

“I'm able to really point to the fact that I've been a very active member of council,” she said. “I have a record for being somebody that is approachable, somebody that you can reach and talk with and engage with, but also that provides communication and feedback.”
Charles Spina is also looking to show residents that City Hall can work efficiently.
Ward 5 candidate Charles Spina comes from a corporate and consulting background. (Submitted by Charles Spina)

Spina comes from a corporate and consulting background, having held executive-level roles in multiple companies. He also spent 18 years on the Board of Directors at L'Arche and 11 years on the investment committee for the Catholic Diocese of London.
In his consulting work, he said he has gained a strong understanding of the operational workings of municipalities. If elected, he said will oppose any tax increases in the first year.
"I understand our financial statements," he said. "We have resources, we don't need money next year."
"I can tell you right now we probably wouldn't have to cut anything."
His campaign slogan is: "the good, the better, and less." Spina said it refers to appreciating the good things London has to offer, pushing for improvements, and reducing inefficiencies.
Abid Raza has lived in London for 10 years and has a background in logistics and supply chain management, he said.
He believes Londoners are paying too much property tax, while not getting enough services in return.
Abid Raza is running for London City Council in Ward 5. (Submitted by Abid Raza)

One issue he wants to tackle is construction, he said, pointing to multiple closures impacting residents in the ward, including projects on Sunningdale Road and one of Fanshawe Park Road, which he believes are impeding both residents and emergency services.
Raza wants to see construction projects completed faster, with crews avoiding work during rush hours and continuing work later into the day.
"Taxpayers are paying for these workers, so we should get it done, " he said.

Simon Sabeesh Karikkassery also indentified construction is a major issue in Ward 5.Karikkassery moved to London from the Greater Toronto Area in 2018 and has a background in supply chain management. He currently works as a personal support worker, he said.
He said construction projects should be planned and scheduled in a way that gets roads reopened more quickly.
"I see only one shift is happening for road construction," he said. "I know it will increase some expenditures, but it has to be two shifts, at least, so that it can be done fast."
Simon Sabeesh Karikkassery is running for London City Council in Ward 5. He wants to push for changes to construction planning and garbage collection. (Submitted by Simon Sabeesh Karikkassery)
Karikkassery also wants to change the city's garbage collection schedule, proposing weekly garbage pickup while collecting recycling every two weeks.

"Those who have small kids and elderly people at home, they're not happy," he said. "So instead of collecting (recycling) every week, you can do it every two weeks and you can collect the garbage every week."
Mary Blake Rose is making the environment front and centre in her campaign.
After moving to London in 2012 to pursue a degree in music, Rose went on to work for the national office of Citizens' Climate Lobby, a non-profit environmental advocacy organization.
"We need to protect things that we can't just rebuild, and I think that the planet is the most flagrant example of that," she said.
Ward 5 candidate Mary Blake Rose is putting the environment front and centre in her campaign. (Submitted by Mary Blake Rose)
She said she wants a city that is "fairer, greener and undaunted."

She said that includes improving transportation, including expanding the network of protected cycling infrastructure. She also sees transportation policy as a way for London to work toward the targets in its Climate Emergency Action Plan.
Rose said she believes London has sometimes taken a cautious approach to major projects.
She pointed to the city's Bus Rapid Transit system as an example, saying she believes it could have been expanded further with additional funding from other levels of government.
Advance voting begins Thursday, with additional advance voting opportunities on Oct. 3 and from Oct. 5 through Oct. 10.
Voting Day is Monday, Oct. 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Because ward boundaries have changed, voters can use the City of London's online election tool to check which ward they live in and find their assigned Voting Day location.

stories.summary: Advance voting for London's 2026 municipal election begins Thursday, giving voters several opportunities to cast their ballots before election day.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Advance voting for London's 2026 municipal election begins Thursday, giving voters several opportunities to cast their ballots before election day.
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 41 minutes ago
Advance voting begins in London, Ont., on Thursday, Oct. 1.(Paula Duhatschek)
Advance voting for London's municipal election begins Thursday, giving voters several opportunities to cast their ballots before Voting Day on Oct. 26.
There are advance voting locations across the city between Oct. 1 and Oct. 10, with all locations open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Unlike on Voting Day, Londoners can vote at any advance voting location that's open on the date they choose, regardless of which ward they live in.
Here are the dates and locations:
Two locations will be open:
Fanshawe College, Alumni Lounge (SC2013), 1001 Fanshawe College Blvd.
Western University, UCC 269C, 1151 Richmond St.
These seven locations will be open:
Beacock Library, 1280 Huron St.
Cherryhill Library, 301 Oxford St. W.
East Lions Community Centre, 1731 Churchill Ave.
Masonville Library, 30 North Centre Rd.
Sherwood Library, 1225 Wonderland Rd. N.
South London Community Centre, 1119 Jalna Blvd.
StarTech.com Community Centre, 501 Southdale Rd. W.
City Hall, second floor, Committee Room 5, 300 Dufferin Ave.
City Hall, second floor, Committee Room 5, at 300 Dufferin Ave., will be open for advance voting on:
Saturday, Oct. 3
Monday, Oct. 5, through Saturday, Oct. 10
The city is encouraging voters to check the Voters' List before heading to the polls.
Voters can use the city's online election tool to check or update their information, add themselves to the Voters' List, find their ward and find out where they will vote.
If you are registering online, you'll need identification showing your name, date of birth and London address.
You can also be added to the Voters' List when you go to vote, but checking your information ahead of time can make the process quicker.
Bring your voter notification card if you've received one. The card identifies your assigned Voting Day location.
You can still vote without the card, but you will need acceptable identification showing your name and address.
London's ward boundaries have changed for the 2026 election, so you may now be in a different ward than you were during the last municipal election.
The city has an online ward map where voters can check their ward before voting.
Slide the vertical bar to see changes to ward boundaries for the 2026 election:
Voting Day is Monday, Oct. 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Unlike advance voting, voters must go to their assigned voting location on Oct. 26. That location will be listed on their voter notification card or available through the city's online voter information tool.

stories.title: Former deans of medicine call on Ottawa to intervene in Alberta’s dual-practice health care model
stories.summary: In a letter to Carney, deans from the University of Calgary and the University of Alberta assert public-private model violates the Canada Health Act
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Four former deans of medicine in Alberta have joined a growing chorus of critics asking Ottawa to intervene in the province’s dual-practice health care model, which allows eligible doctors to toggle between the public and private systems.

Tom Feasby, Jon Meddings and Eldon Smith, all formerly with the University of Calgary, and Tom Marrie, who was with the University of Alberta – sent a letter on the contentious issue to Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday. They expressed “deep concern” about the public-private model and assert it violates the Canada Health Act.

“It is clear that the Alberta government is not going to change course and, therefore, we strongly request that you and the federal government step in and defend the principles of the Canada Health Act,” said the letter, which was also sent to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

Opinion: Mark Carney has said nothing about Alberta’s health care reforms. That’s a good thing

Alberta’s model is unlike any other in Canada, allowing some surgical specialists to bill the public purse while also privately charging patients for their services. The legislation, which took effect Sept. 1, covers such procedures as hip and knee replacements, cataract surgery and dermatology.

There is intense debate about whether it contravenes federal law.

The model has come under widespread scrutiny, including from the Canadian Medical Association and its Alberta counterpart, which argue it could create a two-tier system where people who can afford to pay out of pocket receive faster care. In March, 23 health and labour organizations across the country called on Mr. Carney to take action.

Dr. Meddings, in an interview on Wednesday, said there are other countries where a similar model has worked, but Alberta’s health care system is not conducive for a marriage between public and private care.

“I have nothing against dual practice per se, or some sort of private practice, in the same way as I don’t have anything against somebody paying extra money to fly business class on an airplane,” he said.

“The difference in Alberta is, because we have such a restricted number of both beds and physicians, that when somebody pays for this, it’s not an extra spot that wouldn’t have been used. It is taking it away from somebody who would have needed that spot.”

The Prime Minister has been largely silent on the issue, but federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel has expressed concern about how the policy will co-exist with the Canada Health Act.

Alexandre Bergeron, press secretary to Ms. Michel, did not address the letter directly in a statement on Wednesday but said the minister is in conversation with Adriana LaGrange, Alberta’s Minister of Hospital and Surgical Health Services.

“Minister Michel is engaged in ongoing, targeted discussions with her Alberta counterpart focused on ensuring access to medically necessary care and the core principles of the public system are protected while respecting Alberta’s jurisdiction,” he said.

Maddison McKee, press secretary to Ms. LaGrange, said in a statement that Ottawa must respect Alberta’s jurisdiction to determine how health care is delivered. She also reiterated the government position that dual practice does not contravene the Canada Health Act.

“Our priority is a strong public system and ensuring Albertans never have to pay out of pocket for medically necessary care,” Ms. McKee said. “Expanding access through dual practice does not take away from that. It adds to it. This is not an either/or debate. It is about giving Albertans more choice.”

Public-private health care model coming to Alberta breaches Canada Health Act, legal expert argues

The former deans said dual practice will harm patients by allowing those who can afford private care to jump to the front of the line, rather than providing care to the sickest first. This, they stressed in the letter, is what the Canada Health Act was designed to prevent.

Alberta has defended the dual-practice model as a way to reduce strain on the public system. The signatories argue that there is no evidence that shows a parallel public-private system will have that effect. Rather, they said, it will cause patients to wait longer in the public stream.

The province has said 400 expressions of interest were received over the summer to join the dual-practice system. As of mid-September, physicians were able to formally apply. Surgeries are expected to begin later this fall when the application process is complete.

While the letter did not specify what Ottawa should do, Dr. Meddings sees two ways in which the federal government could address the Alberta practice.

He said Mr. Carney and Ms. Michel can use the power of “moral suasion” with their counterparts in Alberta to push for changes to the legislation.

There is also what Dr. Meddings described as the “nuclear option,” where the federal government withholds or deducts health transfer payments to Alberta, which is permitted if a province violates the Canada Health Act.

stories.title: A country with its elbows up faces separation threats on two fronts
stories.summary: In Alberta and Quebec, Canada’s national unity paradox hits home
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
When Barry Cooper was six years old, he and his mother were stopped at a level crossing while a train passed.

“There goes the goddamn-CPR,” he chirped.

His mother reached into the back seat and slapped him. Stop blaspheming, she said.

Young Barry was puzzled. He thought goddamn-CPR was just what the company was called. Growing up in the Western Canada of the early 1950s, he’d only ever known the railway as a source of bitter resentment. Freight rates designed to help business in the east meant that it was cheaper for the Coopers to buy apples from Nova Scotia than the nearby Okanagan.

The goddamn-CPR, with its headquarters near Montreal’s Golden Square Mile, represented the almost colonial arrogance of the Laurentian elites, who seemed to view Alberta and Saskatchewan as provinces “in the Roman sense” – breadbaskets to be exploited and kept passive.

As a child, Barry May not have reached for that classical allusion, but it comes to his lips easily now, at the age of 83, sitting in his office at the University of Calgary department of political science.

All these years later, Prof. Cooper has emerged as the intellectual godfather of the Alberta separatist movement. His mother’s slap didn’t have the desired effect: He has continued to blaspheme against Canada’s sacred institutions, from equalization payments to official bilingualism to Confederation itself.

For the West, and especially for Alberta, the Canadian federation has been a terrible misadventure, Prof. Cooper believes.

“One hundred and twenty years of history have been 120 years of economic exploitation,” he said in his dimly lit office, decorated with taxidermied deer and pheasant, during a long interview this summer.

Few separatists have so many copies of Virgil and Thucydides in their libraries, but a significant percentage of Albertans share Prof. Cooper’s worldview. The province is about to embark on its first independence referendum, of sorts – really a vote about holding a vote on independence.

Leaving Canada is effectively on the ballot in not one but two provinces. Alberta’s referendum will come just two weeks after a provincial election in Quebec on Oct. 5, where the Parti Québécois is leading the polls with a promise to hold a third “popular consultation” on independence.

This could hardly be more alarming to many Canadians. They see national unity being attacked from within at the most dangerous time, when American threats to our sovereignty have bred existential anxiety about our closest neighbour as well. It can seem like Canada is battling for survival on three fronts, apparently out of nowhere.

But there is more to the story. The anger and alienation endangering Confederation run centuries deep. Canada has too much geography for it to be otherwise: With population and resources scattered across an expanse of 5,500 kilometres as if by some spiteful Greek god, and more languages than the Habsburg Empire, it is no wonder we have always had separatist movements. They are a case of chronic inflammation in the Canadian body politic, not a sudden infection.

The reassuring news for federalists is that the current separatist fever May be breaking. The same upsurge in elbows-up patriotism that has rallied Canadians against the American threat has the potential to undermine the drives for secession in Alberta and Quebec.

But this is not an argument for complacency: Support for independence in both provinces hovers around 30 per cent. If that sounds high, it has become the norm in Wild Rose country and is well below average in la belle province .

In the future, these movements could flare up again, more severely than before.

Separatist movements are as old as Confederation and as authentically Canadian as maple syrup. From the beginning, from Victoria to St. John’s, the virtues of coming together as a country were far from obvious.

Nova Scotia was dragged into the Dominion reluctantly; separatists dominated the first provincial legislature in Halifax. Many British Columbians wanted to leave when the pace of railway construction slowed. Manitoban farmers threatened to break away partly because of, yes, CPR freight rates.

Alberta, too, was born angry – a baby with teeth. Carved out of the former North-West Territories in 1905, some of its leaders hoped to remain conjoined with Saskatchewan in a bigger province, to be called Buffalo.

The federal government rejected the idea – it had a vision of the West as an inland empire, supplying grain for the rest of the country and a captive market for Central Canadian manufacturers.

Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were denied control of their natural resources, unlike other provinces, a power grab that was only reversed in 1930.

Newspapers such as the Calgary Herald raged against Ottawa’s treatment of the West from the beginning. “Can Albertans be forced to eat dirt and say they like it?” one editorial thundered. The first book floating the idea of Alberta independence was published as early as 1911.

Alberta was developing its own identity, influenced by American immigrants who constituted the largest group of newcomers. “The Yankee province” was recognized for its swaggering, democratic personality and its entrepreneurial spirit. It was the U.S. promoter Guy Weadick who organized the first Calgary Stampede in 1912, an enduring embodiment of that culture. A member of the Cooper ranching dynasty, Barry’s uncle, called the annual rodeo for decades.

Barry’s father bucked the family trend and became a doctor in B.C., raising his son to be a proud Canadian who revered the Red Ensign. The unifying force of the Second World War had defanged Western alienation for a generation.

So it was a shock for the young Prof. Cooper, living in Central Canada as a novice academic in the 1970s, to find all was not well with the federation. It wasn’t just meeting Quebec separatists for the first time and finding them surprisingly persuasive. It was also the sheer “parochialism” of his students from Southern Ontario, the only Canadian region that doesn’t consider itself a region. They couldn’t have known or cared less about Western Canada, he found. For the boy with Alberta in his blood, who used to sit on the chutes at the Calgary Stampede and pet the roughstock, this was hard to stomach.

Hugh MacLennan’s novel Two Solitudes was a popular metaphor for the gulf between English and French Canada at the time, but Prof. Cooper was beginning to feel that Canada contains “many more solitudes.”

The angriest part of Alberta May very well be the rural corridor between Edmonton and Calgary, where billboards made from converted trucking containers wage a culture war on the side of the highways. Signs for ABforAbortion and Flat Earth Canada compete with more recent referendum ads: “Send them a message they’ll never forget – Vote Yes in October,” reads one, with Justin Trudeau’s and Mark Carney’s faces set against a dark, sinister background.

It was also here – no coincidence – that a gusher of crude burst out of the Leduc No. 1 oil well in February, 1947, and permanently changed life in Western Canada. It was the beginning of Alberta’s energy boom; from then on, the province would be not only angry, but rich, and its identity would be intimately bound up with a single industry.

Leduc has become part of the Alberta vernacular, like heavy sour, wildcat, roughneck and tidewater, the oil jargon that trips off the tongue with total fluency here. But if Leduc represents the blessings of Alberta’s natural bounty, another bit of provincial shorthand, the NEP, represents the dark side. In Alberta, the phrase NEP captures with remarkable efficiency the province’s sense of having had its good fortune exploited by undeserving outsiders.

Prof. Cooper was back in his ancestral province teaching at the University of Calgary when the National Energy Program was hitting Alberta hardest. An attempt to Canadianize the oil industry, it siphoned off billions in revenue to the federal government, capped prices for consumers and contributed to a harsh recession in the province.

It was in this environment that Alberta separatism emerged as an organized force, most notably with a 1982 by-election victory by Gordon Kesler of the Western Canada Concept, still the only separatist party to sit in the provincial legislature.

That independence movement quickly fizzled, but even pro-Canadian Albertans recall the NEP with horror; Senator Paula Simons watched as her father lost his businesses in Fort McMurray and some of his friends died by suicide during the downturn.

This was also the climate in which Prof. Cooper became politically active, providing intellectual ammunition to the nascent Reform Party, Preston Manning’s vessel for channelling Western Canadian rage. In retrospect, its demands look relatively quaint. The party called for Senate reform to improve regional representation in Ottawa and a hands-off approach to resource development; its explicitly non-separatist slogan was “The West Wants In.” In a very Albertan metaphor, Mr. Manning called his movement a “relief well” designed to intercept an out-of-control oil strike.

For a time, he succeeded. Reform and the Bloc Québécois put regional discontent at the forefront of federal politics through much of the 1990s. It is easy to forget that two parties rooted in grievances with Canadian federalism took turns as the Official Opposition. The old Reform crusader Stephen Harper brought Mr. Manning’s ideas even further into the mainstream when he became prime minister in 2006.

But the old Alberta anger continued to bubble like sour crude beneath the country’s surface, waiting for a wildcatter to tap into it.

Red Deer is almost exactly halfway between Edmonton and Calgary, right in the beating heart of separatist country. It was settled by homesteaders in the late 19th-century and then boomed along with the province as a hub for servicing the oil-and-gas industry.

It was a natural location for the Alberta Prosperity Project, a leading independence organization, to host its Pulpit and Politics event in August.

Pickups filled the parking lot outside a sprawling event hall on a sunny Wednesday evening, including one bearing a placard that read, “Saving My Grandkids from Carney’s New World Order.”

It was the first hint of how much time the speakers inside would devote not to defending Alberta oil and autonomy but to the prevailing cultural tide of the country.

For every reference to equalization payments, there was one to the “plandemic;” for every allusion to Senate reform, a smear on “illegal immigrants.” For every complaint about pipelines, speakers added another about drag queen story hour. Extended discussions of constitutional issues and budget math seemed to bore the audience.

It was another sign of the overlooked cultural dimension of Alberta separatism. In conversations with leaders and foot soldiers of the movement, it becomes clear that the progressive drift of the country under Justin Trudeau – with its strict COVID measures, increased immigration and “wokeness” – convinced many conservative Albertans that they didn’t belong in Canada anymore. Separatists often say that Canada seceded from them, not the other way around.

When comparing the Alberta and Quebec separatist movements, it’s common to say Alberta’s isn’t about culture, but that’s wrong, said the Calgary-based pollster Janet Brown. The single most predictive factor in determining support for Alberta independence is not working in the energy industry, but the salience of religion in a person’s life, she noted. Breaking away from Canada has become as much about the prominence of right-wing evangelical Christianity in Alberta – part of its original American flavour – as about oil and gas.

“It is about culture,” Ms. Brown said. “Grievance with the federal government is only the starting point.”

The Trudeau government’s environmental policies clearly outraged many Albertans; they are often cited as a major reason for the current flare-up of separatism in the province. But it is notable that gestures toward reversing those policies have not stopped the independence movement in its tracks. When Mr. Carney reached a memorandum of understanding with Alberta in November, 2025, promising to support the construction of a new pipeline to B.C. and peel back environmental regulations, many separatists dismissed it as mere verbiage. The feeling of broken trust and cultural alienation was too deep for quick repair.

Like many in his movement, the good professor has lost faith with Canada on a more elemental level, beyond the reach of policy fixes. His alienation goes far deeper than the Trudeau government’s climate-change agenda, all the way back to CPR freight rates, the loss of the Red Ensign and the NEP – issues that are obscure to most people outside of his province but deeply ingrained in Albertan culture.

His father served proudly in the Royal Canadian Air Force during the Second World War, he said, but those ties of patriotic sentiment have been broken for him.

“That Canada was the Canada of our parents, and it’s not here anymore.”

The elbows-up nationalism sweeping the country under Mr. Carney fills him with contempt, even though – or especially because – it has made headway in Alberta. Pro-Canadian activists in the province gleefully report more Maple Leaf flags flying from rural barns than they’ve ever seen before; personal identification with Canada has increased in recent polls.

It is perhaps no wonder the current Prime Minister is such a hateful figure to Prof. Cooper and others committed to Albertan independence. Separatists often refer to Mr. Carney and his acolytes as “elbozos.”

When the subject of the PM comes up, the erudite professor drops his references to Leo Strauss and Plato and reverts to a blaspheming six-year-old in the back of his mother’s car.

“How stupid do you have to be to trust that son of a bitch?” he said.

Alberta and Quebec, 3,000 kilometres apart, are in some ways very different beasts. The contrast is visible in Red Deer County’s gleaming new megachurches with names such as CrossRoads and Impact Life on the one hand, and the century-old stone churches and seminaries of Chicoutimi, Que., their copper roofs rusted green, that haven’t seen a Catholic service in years.

These are places with very different histories and worldviews, like the movements they have nurtured. Where Alberta separatism is entirely right-wing with a strong evangelical bent, Quebec’s is aggressively secularist. The first is nominally about oil money, the second nominally about language. One is a populist insurgency with little institutional support, the other backed by the province’s largest media empire, Quebecor.

Because this is a land of paradox, however, it’s also true that both movements, for all their differences, emerge from the same wellspring of regional alienation that has always troubled the country. And if there’s one thing many residents of Red Deer and Chicoutimi can agree on, it’s that they would be better off outside of Canada.

No region voted more overwhelmingly for the Yes side of the 1995 sovereignty referendum than Chicoutimi’s Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean, two hours north of Quebec City, with an average of about 70 per cent. It’s an area that bleeds péquiste blue.

Just as the steakhouses, oil money and rolling parkland around Red Deer incarnate certain clichés about Alberta, so too does Saguenay exude le Québec profond . It’s a land of lumber camps where the smell of pine trees wafts through closed car windows. The farmland is dominated by dairy concerns that crank out delicious cheese curds. Local factories harness the region’s ample hydro power to zap bauxite into aluminum.

The retired city councillor Jean-Marc Crevier is a classic Saguenay man. He owns a little piece of property with friends on Lac Saint-Jean where he sails a catamaran. Like Prof. Cooper, he blasphemes colourfully and often, preferring an old religious curse that is antiquated even by Quebec standards: simonaque , meaning one who is guilty of simony, or trading in sacred things.

Like his father, he worked for decades in the Alcan aluminum plant in Arvida, a company town built by an eccentric American tycoon in the 1920s. The English-speaking managers who bossed him around were commonly called têtes carrées , a pejorative term for anglophones.

Mr. Crevier rose to be a union leader, first in the aluminum industry, then with the provincewide Fédération des travailleurs et travailleuses du Quebec. As sure as night followed day, he voted for the Parti Québécois. It was an identity as much as a choice.

The dialectic of federalism and separatism is centuries old in Quebec, older in a way than Canada itself. The British victory on the Plains of Abraham in 1759 produced an enduring desire to reclaim self-government and self-esteem. Nearly every generation saw violent eruptions of national pride: the Patriotes rebellion of 1837-38; riots against conscription in the First World War; the terrorist campaign of the Front de libération du Québec.

By the time the PQ emerged as a democratic force calling for political independence from Canada in the 1970s, the separatist impulse was part of Quebec’s DNA. The insouciant confidence of René Lévesque helped convince enough of his fellow citizens that “Quebec would be stronger on its own,” as Mr. Crevier put it. There was an undeniable flush of pride in imagining a Québécois head of state meeting the Canadian Prime Minister on an equal footing and finally earning his people the respect they deserved.

In a literal sense, Mr. Parizeau was right. Sixty per cent of francophones voted to leave that day, feeling burned by successive failed attempts to reform the constitution. Even long-time Canadian patriots such as André Pratte, future editor of the federalist La Presse newspaper and later a Canadian senator, felt the impasse was serious enough to vote Yes.

When Mr. Parizeau spoke those notorious words, many Quebeckers were ashamed of his outburst. Mr. Pratte recalls feeling revulsion and immediate regret for his Yes vote.

Others, felt a deep sense of recognition in Mr. Parizeau’s assertion of a French-Canadian nous , set apart from a sea of others. Cultural survival has always been a primal goal of French Canada, surrounded as it is by hundreds of millions of English-speakers in North America. Now, as Quebec’s own population becomes more diverse thanks to declining birth rates and increased immigration, the challenge can seem to come from within.

This siege mentality has an undeniable resonance for some Quebeckers. Ninety-eight per cent of Saguenay residents have French as a mother tongue, according to the most recent census, yet it’s still common to hear that immigrants there imperil French. Appealing to voters like these, who feel left behind by a changing Quebec, turned out to be a dead-end for the PQ. The party dropped to an all-time low of three National Assembly seats in 2022 as François Legault and his Coalition Avenir Québec promised to protect Quebec interests and culture without the upheaval of another independence vote.

Even then, as the PQ drifted further and further to his right, Mr. Crevier stayed true to his sovereigntist faith. This election, with his party leading in the polls and promising a third referendum, he should have been ecstatic. You might have expected to find him knocking on doors for the local PQ candidate, Jimmy Bouchard, an old friend and colleague on the Saguenay city council.

But in a country of contradictions and cross-hatched loyalties, perhaps nowhere is shaded with more subtlety than the mind of a Quebec voter. And sure enough, this hard man of the labour movement, with a granite face, salt-and-pepper hair and a navy-blue windbreaker, finds himself politically “ shaké ” this election season. He is rattled for a simple but powerful reason: “Everything that’s happening with the United States.”

In the current trade war with the U.S., American tariffs or demands have targeted virtually everything the Saguenay holds dear: aluminum, dairy and lumber, to say nothing of protections for the French language and culture. From where Mr. Crevier is sitting, the U.S. President looks like a far bigger threat to his nation and his region than Canadian federalism.

Like everything in Quebec, this is an old story. When Americans threaten, Quebeckers choose the ambivalent embrace of the British Crown and the Canadian federation. Benjamin Franklin came to Montreal as an emissary of the American Revolution and was firmly rebuffed. During the War of 1812, French-Canadian heroes such as the fur trader Dominique Ducharme helped fight off the Yankee invasion. The former patriote rebel George-Étienne Cartier became a Father of Confederation in part because he dreaded American annexation.

Quebeckers have always believed their distinct society was better protected within the Canadian mosaic than as a stray ingredient in the American melting pot. It is this existential belief, as much as the pain of tariffs, that has rallied the province to the Maple Leaf during this trade war.

On Aug. 31, another minor chapter of this story was written when Daniel Gobeil, the Liberal candidate in Chicoutimi–Le Fjord, won a landslide victory over the Bloc Québécois in a federal by-election. His face was still Liberal red after a night of celebration and speech-giving when he credited his victory to a hunger – even in deep-blue Saguenay – for “Canadian unity.”

Meanwhile, the PQ’s popularity has flatlined. They sit atop the polls because of voter fatigue with the CAQ and disarray within the provincial Liberal party. But the party has failed to reach out beyond the slightly under 30 per cent of Quebeckers who want independence, a historically low level for the province. If the PQ forms government, it will arguably be because the other parties split the federalist vote, not because voters want to leave Canada. And yet, the PQ almost certainly will form the next Quebec government, and hold a referendum if they secure a majority.

These days he is prone to delivering the pained soliloquy of a wavering separatist, one who is considering throwing in his lot with the CAQ and even – simonaque – the federal Liberals.

The independence drives in Alberta and Quebec May be stalling, but they are showing little sign of going away; Prof. Cooper’s profane rage and Mr. Crevier’s profane ambivalence both give voice to permanent doubts about their provinces’ place in Canada.
