I’m listening to what Carney has to say … I’ve never voted Liberal in my goddamn life. I’m shaken on every side, provincially and federally … Simonaque …”
paragraphs: When Barry Cooper was six years old, he and his mother were stopped at a level crossing while a train passed.
“There goes the goddamn-CPR,” he chirped.
His mother reached into the back seat and slapped him. Stop blaspheming, she said.

Young Barry was puzzled. He thought goddamn-CPR was just what the company was called. Growing up in the Western Canada of the early 1950s, he’d only ever known the railway as a source of bitter resentment. Freight rates designed to help business in the east meant that it was cheaper for the Coopers to buy apples from Nova Scotia than the nearby Okanagan.

The goddamn-CPR, with its headquarters near Montreal’s Golden Square Mile, represented the almost colonial arrogance of the Laurentian elites, who seemed to view Alberta and Saskatchewan as provinces “in the Roman sense” – breadbaskets to be exploited and kept passive.

As a child, Barry May not have reached for that classical allusion, but it comes to his lips easily now, at the age of 83, sitting in his office at the University of Calgary department of political science.

All these years later, Prof. Cooper has emerged as the intellectual godfather of the Alberta separatist movement. His mother’s slap didn’t have the desired effect: He has continued to blaspheme against Canada’s sacred institutions, from equalization payments to official bilingualism to Confederation itself.
For the West, and especially for Alberta, the Canadian federation has been a terrible misadventure, Prof. Cooper believes.

“One hundred and twenty years of history have been 120 years of economic exploitation,” he said in his dimly lit office, decorated with taxidermied deer and pheasant, during a long interview this summer.

Few separatists have so many copies of Virgil and Thucydides in their libraries, but a significant percentage of Albertans share Prof. Cooper’s worldview. The province is about to embark on its first independence referendum, of sorts – really a vote about holding a vote on independence.

Leaving Canada is effectively on the ballot in not one but two provinces. Alberta’s referendum will come just two weeks after a provincial election in Quebec on Oct. 5, where the Parti Québécois is leading the polls with a promise to hold a third “popular consultation” on independence.

This could hardly be more alarming to many Canadians. They see national unity being attacked from within at the most dangerous time, when American threats to our sovereignty have bred existential anxiety about our closest neighbour as well. It can seem like Canada is battling for survival on three fronts, apparently out of nowhere.

But there is more to the story. The anger and alienation endangering Confederation run centuries deep. Canada has too much geography for it to be otherwise: With population and resources scattered across an expanse of 5,500 kilometres as if by some spiteful Greek god, and more languages than the Habsburg Empire, it is no wonder we have always had separatist movements. They are a case of chronic inflammation in the Canadian body politic, not a sudden infection.

The reassuring news for federalists is that the current separatist fever May be breaking. The same upsurge in elbows-up patriotism that has rallied Canadians against the American threat has the potential to undermine the drives for secession in Alberta and Quebec.

But this is not an argument for complacency: Support for independence in both provinces hovers around 30 per cent. If that sounds high, it has become the norm in Wild Rose country and is well below average in la belle province .
In the future, these movements could flare up again, more severely than before.

Separatist movements are as old as Confederation and as authentically Canadian as maple syrup. From the beginning, from Victoria to St. John’s, the virtues of coming together as a country were far from obvious.

Nova Scotia was dragged into the Dominion reluctantly; separatists dominated the first provincial legislature in Halifax. Many British Columbians wanted to leave when the pace of railway construction slowed. Manitoban farmers threatened to break away partly because of, yes, CPR freight rates.

Alberta, too, was born angry – a baby with teeth. Carved out of the former North-West Territories in 1905, some of its leaders hoped to remain conjoined with Saskatchewan in a bigger province, to be called Buffalo.
The federal government rejected the idea – it had a vision of the West as an inland empire, supplying grain for the rest of the country and a captive market for Central Canadian manufacturers.
Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were denied control of their natural resources, unlike other provinces, a power grab that was only reversed in 1930.

Newspapers such as the Calgary Herald raged against Ottawa’s treatment of the West from the beginning. “Can Albertans be forced to eat dirt and say they like it?” one editorial thundered. The first book floating the idea of Alberta independence was published as early as 1911.

Alberta was developing its own identity, influenced by American immigrants who constituted the largest group of newcomers. “The Yankee province” was recognized for its swaggering, democratic personality and its entrepreneurial spirit. It was the U.S. promoter Guy Weadick who organized the first Calgary Stampede in 1912, an enduring embodiment of that culture. A member of the Cooper ranching dynasty, Barry’s uncle, called the annual rodeo for decades.

Barry’s father bucked the family trend and became a doctor in B.C., raising his son to be a proud Canadian who revered the Red Ensign. The unifying force of the Second World War had defanged Western alienation for a generation.

So it was a shock for the young Prof. Cooper, living in Central Canada as a novice academic in the 1970s, to find all was not well with the federation. It wasn’t just meeting Quebec separatists for the first time and finding them surprisingly persuasive. It was also the sheer “parochialism” of his students from Southern Ontario, the only Canadian region that doesn’t consider itself a region. They couldn’t have known or cared less about Western Canada, he found. For the boy with Alberta in his blood, who used to sit on the chutes at the Calgary Stampede and pet the roughstock, this was hard to stomach.

Hugh MacLennan’s novel Two Solitudes was a popular metaphor for the gulf between English and French Canada at the time, but Prof. Cooper was beginning to feel that Canada contains “many more solitudes.”

The angriest part of Alberta May very well be the rural corridor between Edmonton and Calgary, where billboards made from converted trucking containers wage a culture war on the side of the highways. Signs for ABforAbortion and Flat Earth Canada compete with more recent referendum ads: “Send them a message they’ll never forget – Vote Yes in October,” reads one, with Justin Trudeau’s and Mark Carney’s faces set against a dark, sinister background.

It was also here – no coincidence – that a gusher of crude burst out of the Leduc No. 1 oil well in February, 1947, and permanently changed life in Western Canada. It was the beginning of Alberta’s energy boom; from then on, the province would be not only angry, but rich, and its identity would be intimately bound up with a single industry.

Leduc has become part of the Alberta vernacular, like heavy sour, wildcat, roughneck and tidewater, the oil jargon that trips off the tongue with total fluency here. But if Leduc represents the blessings of Alberta’s natural bounty, another bit of provincial shorthand, the NEP, represents the dark side. In Alberta, the phrase NEP captures with remarkable efficiency the province’s sense of having had its good fortune exploited by undeserving outsiders.

Prof. Cooper was back in his ancestral province teaching at the University of Calgary when the National Energy Program was hitting Alberta hardest. An attempt to Canadianize the oil industry, it siphoned off billions in revenue to the federal government, capped prices for consumers and contributed to a harsh recession in the province.

It was in this environment that Alberta separatism emerged as an organized force, most notably with a 1982 by-election victory by Gordon Kesler of the Western Canada Concept, still the only separatist party to sit in the provincial legislature.

That independence movement quickly fizzled, but even pro-Canadian Albertans recall the NEP with horror; Senator Paula Simons watched as her father lost his businesses in Fort McMurray and some of his friends died by suicide during the downturn.

This was also the climate in which Prof. Cooper became politically active, providing intellectual ammunition to the nascent Reform Party, Preston Manning’s vessel for channelling Western Canadian rage. In retrospect, its demands look relatively quaint. The party called for Senate reform to improve regional representation in Ottawa and a hands-off approach to resource development; its explicitly non-separatist slogan was “The West Wants In.” In a very Albertan metaphor, Mr. Manning called his movement a “relief well” designed to intercept an out-of-control oil strike.

For a time, he succeeded. Reform and the Bloc Québécois put regional discontent at the forefront of federal politics through much of the 1990s. It is easy to forget that two parties rooted in grievances with Canadian federalism took turns as the Official Opposition. The old Reform crusader Stephen Harper brought Mr. Manning’s ideas even further into the mainstream when he became prime minister in 2006.
But the old Alberta anger continued to bubble like sour crude beneath the country’s surface, waiting for a wildcatter to tap into it.

Red Deer is almost exactly halfway between Edmonton and Calgary, right in the beating heart of separatist country. It was settled by homesteaders in the late 19th-century and then boomed along with the province as a hub for servicing the oil-and-gas industry.
It was a natural location for the Alberta Prosperity Project, a leading independence organization, to host its Pulpit and Politics event in August.

It was the first hint of how much time the speakers inside would devote not to defending Alberta oil and autonomy but to the prevailing cultural tide of the country.

For every reference to equalization payments, there was one to the “plandemic;” for every allusion to Senate reform, a smear on “illegal immigrants.” For every complaint about pipelines, speakers added another about drag queen story hour. Extended discussions of constitutional issues and budget math seemed to bore the audience.

It was another sign of the overlooked cultural dimension of Alberta separatism. In conversations with leaders and foot soldiers of the movement, it becomes clear that the progressive drift of the country under Justin Trudeau – with its strict COVID measures, increased immigration and “wokeness” – convinced many conservative Albertans that they didn’t belong in Canada anymore. “That Canada was the Canada of our parents, and it’s not here anymore.”

The elbows-up nationalism sweeping the country under Mr. Carney fills him with contempt, even though – or especially because – it has made headway in Alberta. When the subject of the PM comes up, the erudite professor drops his references to Leo Strauss and Plato and reverts to a blaspheming six-year-old in the back of his mother’s car.

The goddamn-CPR, with its headquarters near Montreal’s Golden Square Mile, represented the almost colonial arrogance of the Laurentian elites, who seemed to view Alberta and Saskatchewan as provinces “in the Roman sense” – breadbaskets to be exploited and kept passive.

content_blocks.caption: Barry Cooper, a professor at the University of Calgary, spoke with The Globe about his journey to the Alberta separatist cause. Chris MacArthur/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: As a child, Barry May not have reached for that classical allusion, but it comes to his lips easily now, at the age of 83, sitting in his office at the University of Calgary department of political science.

All these years later, Prof. Cooper has emerged as the intellectual godfather of the Alberta separatist movement. His mother’s slap didn’t have the desired effect: He has continued to blaspheme against Canada’s sacred institutions, from equalization payments to official bilingualism to Confederation itself.
For the West, and especially for Alberta, the Canadian federation has been a terrible misadventure, Prof. Cooper believes.

“One hundred and twenty years of history have been 120 years of economic exploitation,” he said in his dimly lit office, decorated with taxidermied deer and pheasant, during a long interview this summer.

Few separatists have so many copies of Virgil and Thucydides in their libraries, but a significant percentage of Albertans share Prof. Cooper’s worldview. The province is about to embark on its first independence referendum, of sorts – really a vote about holding a vote on independence.

content_blocks.caption: These Albertans turned out recently to hear a town hall from the Alberta Prosperity Project, one of the separatist groups. Chris MacArthur/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Leaving Canada is effectively on the ballot in not one but two provinces. Alberta’s referendum will come just two weeks after a provincial election in Quebec on Oct. 5, where the Parti Québécois is leading the polls with a promise to hold a third “popular consultation” on independence.

This could hardly be more alarming to many Canadians. They see national unity being attacked from within at the most dangerous time, when American threats to our sovereignty have bred existential anxiety about our closest neighbour as well. It can seem like Canada is battling for survival on three fronts, apparently out of nowhere.

But there is more to the story. The anger and alienation endangering Confederation run centuries deep. Canada has too much geography for it to be otherwise: With population and resources scattered across an expanse of 5,500 kilometres as if by some spiteful Greek god, and more languages than the Habsburg Empire, it is no wonder we have always had separatist movements. They are a case of chronic inflammation in the Canadian body politic, not a sudden infection.

The reassuring news for federalists is that the current separatist fever May be breaking. The same upsurge in elbows-up patriotism that has rallied Canadians against the American threat has the potential to undermine the drives for secession in Alberta and Quebec.

But this is not an argument for complacency: Support for independence in both provinces hovers around 30 per cent. If that sounds high, it has become the norm in Wild Rose country and is well below average in la belle province .
In the future, these movements could flare up again, more severely than before.

content_blocks.caption: Blue is a popular colour at separatist gatherings in 2026, from this PQ rally in Quebec City to a pro-independence protest in Edmonton. But judging by opinion polls, most of those who live under the blue provincial flags of Quebec and Alberta support remaining in a united Canada. Jacques Boissinot and Amanda Erickson/…

Mr. Cooper grew up disparaging the Canadian Pacific Railway, completed in 1885 by the Last Spike. Many key actors at that B.C. ceremony were from Quebec: Lord Strathcona, who hammered in the spike, was a Montrealer, as was William Cornelius Van Horne, the black-bearded rail baron with a hand in his pocket. The Canadia…

Mr. Cooper’s collection includes a ‘republic of Western Canada’ map that unites Alberta, Saskatchewan and northern B.C. Creating one Prairie province instead of two was a favoured option for some westerners, but they were overruled. Chris MacArthur/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Separatist movements are as old as Confederation and as authentically Canadian as maple syrup. From the beginning, from Victoria to St. John’s, the virtues of coming together as a country were far from obvious.

Nova Scotia was dragged into the Dominion reluctantly; separatists dominated the first provincial legislature in Halifax. Many British Columbians wanted to leave when the pace of railway construction slowed. Manitoban farmers threatened to break away partly because of, yes, CPR freight rates.

Alberta, too, was born angry – a baby with teeth. Carved out of the former North-West Territories in 1905, some of its leaders hoped to remain conjoined with Saskatchewan in a bigger province, to be called Buffalo.
The federal government rejected the idea – it had a vision of the West as an inland empire, supplying grain for the rest of the country and a captive market for Central Canadian manufacturers.
Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were denied control of their natural resources, unlike other provinces, a power grab that was only reversed in 1930.

Newspapers such as the Calgary Herald raged against Ottawa’s treatment of the West from the beginning. “Can Albertans be forced to eat dirt and say they like it?” one editorial thundered. The first book floating the idea of Alberta independence was published as early as 1911.

content_blocks.caption: An American promoter got the Calgary Stampede up and running in 1912.

content_blocks.text: Alberta was developing its own identity, influenced by American immigrants who constituted the largest group of newcomers. “The Yankee province” was recognized for its swaggering, democratic personality and its entrepreneurial spirit. It was the U.S. promoter Guy Weadick who organized the first Calgary Stampede in 1912, an enduring embodiment of that culture. A member of the Cooper ranching dynasty, Barry’s uncle, called the annual rodeo for decades.

Barry’s father bucked the family trend and became a doctor in B.C., raising his son to be a proud Canadian who revered the Red Ensign. The unifying force of the Second World War had defanged Western alienation for a generation.

So it was a shock for the young Prof. Cooper, living in Central Canada as a novice academic in the 1970s, to find all was not well with the federation. It wasn’t just meeting Quebec separatists for the first time and finding them surprisingly persuasive. It was also the sheer “parochialism” of his students from Southern Ontario, the only Canadian region that doesn’t consider itself a region. They couldn’t have known or cared less about Western Canada, he found. For the boy with Alberta in his blood, who used to sit on the chutes at the Calgary Stampede and pet the roughstock, this was hard to stomach.

Hugh MacLennan’s novel Two Solitudes was a popular metaphor for the gulf between English and French Canada at the time, but Prof. Cooper was beginning to feel that Canada contains “many more solitudes.”

content_blocks.caption: Canada’s regional rifts widened further in the 1970s, the political heyday of Peter Lougheed in Alberta and René Lévesque in Quebec. Both clashed with Pierre Trudeau over his vision of Confederation. The Canadian Press; Globe and Mail archives, 1976
The 1970s also brought the first screen version of Hugh MacLennan’s novel Two Solitudes. Globe film critic Jay Scott panned it. Globe and Mail archives, 1978

content_blocks.text: The angriest part of Alberta May very well be the rural corridor between Edmonton and Calgary, where billboards made from converted trucking containers wage a culture war on the side of the highways. Signs for ABforAbortion and Flat Earth Canada compete with more recent referendum ads: “Send them a message they’ll never forget – Vote Yes in October,” reads one, with Justin Trudeau’s and Mark Carney’s faces set against a dark, sinister background.

It was also here – no coincidence – that a gusher of crude burst out of the Leduc No. 1 oil well in February, 1947, and permanently changed life in Western Canada. It was the beginning of Alberta’s energy boom; from then on, the province would be not only angry, but rich, and its identity would be intimately bound up with a single industry.

content_blocks.caption: The Leduc oil gusher helped ignite Alberta's energy boom, and debates about who should benefit from the wealth. The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Leduc has become part of the Alberta vernacular, like heavy sour, wildcat, roughneck and tidewater, the oil jargon that trips off the tongue with total fluency here. But if Leduc represents the blessings of Alberta’s natural bounty, another bit of provincial shorthand, the NEP, represents the dark side. In Alberta, the phrase NEP captures with remarkable efficiency the province’s sense of having had its good fortune exploited by undeserving outsiders.

Prof. Cooper was back in his ancestral province teaching at the University of Calgary when the National Energy Program was hitting Alberta hardest. An attempt to Canadianize the oil industry, it siphoned off billions in revenue to the federal government, capped prices for consumers and contributed to a harsh recession in the province.

It was in this environment that Alberta separatism emerged as an organized force, most notably with a 1982 by-election victory by Gordon Kesler of the Western Canada Concept, still the only separatist party to sit in the provincial legislature.

That independence movement quickly fizzled, but even pro-Canadian Albertans recall the NEP with horror; Senator Paula Simons watched as her father lost his businesses in Fort McMurray and some of his friends died by suicide during the downturn.

This was also the climate in which Prof. Cooper became politically active, providing intellectual ammunition to the nascent Reform Party, Preston Manning’s vessel for channelling Western Canadian rage. In retrospect, its demands look relatively quaint. The party called for Senate reform to improve regional representation in Ottawa and a hands-off approach to resource development; its explicitly non-separatist slogan was “The West Wants In.” In a very Albertan metaphor, Mr. Manning called his movement a “relief well” designed to intercept an out-of-control oil strike.

For a time, he succeeded. Reform and the Bloc Québécois put regional discontent at the forefront of federal politics through much of the 1990s. It is easy to forget that two parties rooted in grievances with Canadian federalism took turns as the Official Opposition. The old Reform crusader Stephen Harper brought Mr. Manning’s ideas even further into the mainstream when he became prime minister in 2006.
But the old Alberta anger continued to bubble like sour crude beneath the country’s surface, waiting for a wildcatter to tap into it.

content_blocks.caption: Preston Manning built his Reform Party on the slogan ‘the West wants in.’ More recently, he’s co-chaired public forums about Alberta’s grievances with Ottawa. Chris MacArthur/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Red Deer is almost exactly halfway between Edmonton and Calgary, right in the beating heart of separatist country. It was settled by homesteaders in the late 19th-century and then boomed along with the province as a hub for servicing the oil-and-gas industry.
It was a natural location for the Alberta Prosperity Project, a leading independence organization, to host its Pulpit and Politics event in August.
Pickups filled the parking lot outside a sprawling event hall on a sunny Wednesday evening, including one bearing a placard that read, “Saving My Grandkids from Carney’s New World Order.”
It was the first hint of how much time the speakers inside would devote not to defending Alberta oil and autonomy but to the prevailing cultural tide of the country.

For every reference to equalization payments, there was one to the “plandemic;” for every allusion to Senate reform, a smear on “illegal immigrants.” For every complaint about pipelines, speakers added another about drag queen story hour. Extended discussions of constitutional issues and budget math seemed to bore the audience.

content_blocks.caption: Alberta’s debates in recent years over trans rights, COVID-19 and other issues have spilled over into this year’s referendum campaign. Artur Widak via Reuters connect/Reuters

content_blocks.text: It was another sign of the overlooked cultural dimension of Alberta separatism. In conversations with leaders and foot soldiers of the movement, it becomes clear that the progressive drift of the country under Justin Trudeau – with its strict COVID measures, increased immigration and “wokeness” – convinced many conservative Albertans that they didn’t belong in Canada anymore. Separatists often say that Canada seceded from them, not the other way around.

When comparing the Alberta and Quebec separatist movements, it’s common to say Alberta’s isn’t about culture, but that’s wrong, said the Calgary-based pollster Janet Brown. The single most predictive factor in determining support for Alberta independence is not working in the energy industry, but the salience of religion in a person’s life, she noted. Breaking away from Canada has become as much about the prominence of right-wing evangelical Christianity in Alberta – part of its original American flavour – as about oil and gas.
“It is about culture,” Ms. Brown said. “Grievance with the federal government is only the starting point.”

content_blocks.caption: When Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Red Deer this summer, joining Alberta Premier Danielle Smith for a housing announcement, several protesters rallied outside. Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: The Trudeau government’s environmental policies clearly outraged many Albertans; they are often cited as a major reason for the current flare-up of separatism in the province. But it is notable that gestures toward reversing those policies have not stopped the independence movement in its tracks. When Mr. Carney reached a memorandum of understanding with Alberta in November, 2025, promising to support the construction of a new pipeline to B.C. and peel back environmental regulations, many separatists dismissed it as mere verbiage. The feeling of broken trust and cultural alienation was too deep for quick repair.

Like many in his movement, the good professor has lost faith with Canada on a more elemental level, beyond the reach of policy fixes. His alienation goes far deeper than the Trudeau government’s climate-change agenda, all the way back to CPR freight rates, the loss of the Red Ensign and the NEP – issues that are obscure to most people outside of his province but deeply ingrained in Albertan culture.
His father served proudly in the Royal Canadian Air Force during the Second World War, he said, but those ties of patriotic sentiment have been broken for him.
“That Canada was the Canada of our parents, and it’s not here anymore.”

The elbows-up nationalism sweeping the country under Mr. Carney fills him with contempt, even though – or especially because – it has made headway in Alberta. Pro-Canadian activists in the province gleefully report more Maple Leaf flags flying from rural barns than they’ve ever seen before; personal identification with Canada has increased in recent polls.

It is perhaps no wonder the current Prime Minister is such a hateful figure to Prof. Cooper and others committed to Albertan independence. Separatists often refer to Mr. Carney and his acolytes as “elbozos.”
When the subject of the PM comes up, the erudite professor drops his references to Leo Strauss and Plato and reverts to a blaspheming six-year-old in the back of his mother’s car.
“How stupid do you have to be to trust that son of a bitch?” he said.

content_blocks.caption: From the Arvida aluminum plant to the farms near the river, the Saguenay region has held on to Quebec’s traditional industries. Support for the PQ runs deep here. Charles-Frederick Ouellet/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Alberta and Quebec, 3,000 kilometres apart, are in some ways very different beasts. The contrast is visible in Red Deer County’s gleaming new megachurches with names such as CrossRoads and Impact Life on the one hand, and the century-old stone churches and seminaries of Chicoutimi, Que., their copper roofs rusted green, that haven’t seen a Catholic service in years.

These are places with very different histories and worldviews, like the movements they have nurtured. Where Alberta separatism is entirely right-wing with a strong evangelical bent, Quebec’s is aggressively secularist. The first is nominally about oil money, the second nominally about language. One is a populist insurgency with little institutional support, the other backed by the province’s largest media empire, Quebecor.

Because this is a land of paradox, however, it’s also true that both movements, for all their differences, emerge from the same wellspring of regional alienation that has always troubled the country. And if there’s one thing many residents of Red Deer and Chicoutimi can agree on, it’s that they would be better off outside of Canada.

No region voted more overwhelmingly for the Yes side of the 1995 sovereignty referendum than Chicoutimi’s Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean, two hours north of Quebec City, with an average of about 70 per cent. It’s an area that bleeds péquiste blue.

Just as the steakhouses, oil money and rolling parkland around Red Deer incarnate certain clichés about Alberta, so too does Saguenay exude le Québec profond . It’s a land of lumber camps where the smell of pine trees wafts through closed car windows. The farmland is dominated by dairy concerns that crank out delicious cheese curds. Local factories harness the region’s ample hydro power to zap bauxite into aluminum.

The retired city councillor Jean-Marc Crevier is a classic Saguenay man. He owns a little piece of property with friends on Lac Saint-Jean where he sails a catamaran. Like Prof. Cooper, he blasphemes colourfully and often, preferring an old religious curse that is antiquated even by Quebec standards: simonaque , meaning one who is guilty of simony, or trading in sacred things.

content_blocks.caption: ‘Quebec would be stronger on its own,’ says Jean-Marc Crevier, a union leader at the aluminum plant in Saguenay. Charles-Frederick Ouellet/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Like his father, he worked for decades in the Alcan aluminum plant in Arvida, a company town built by an eccentric American tycoon in the 1920s. The English-speaking managers who bossed him around were commonly called têtes carrées , a pejorative term for anglophones.

Mr. Crevier rose to be a union leader, first in the aluminum industry, then with the provincewide Fédération des travailleurs et travailleuses du Quebec. As sure as night followed day, he voted for the Parti Québécois. It was an identity as much as a choice.

The dialectic of federalism and separatism is centuries old in Quebec, older in a way than Canada itself. The British victory on the Plains of Abraham in 1759 produced an enduring desire to reclaim self-government and self-esteem. Nearly every generation saw violent eruptions of national pride: the Patriotes rebellion of 1837-38; riots against conscription in the First World War; the terrorist campaign of the Front de libération du Québec.

By the time the PQ emerged as a democratic force calling for political independence from Canada in the 1970s, the separatist impulse was part of Quebec’s DNA. The insouciant confidence of René Lévesque helped convince enough of his fellow citizens that “Quebec would be stronger on its own,” as Mr. Crevier put it. There was an undeniable flush of pride in imagining a Québécois head of state meeting the Canadian Prime Minister on an equal footing and finally earning his people the respect they deserved.

Ahead of the 1976 election, Mr. Crevier bet his fellow aluminum workers $50 that the underdog PQ would win, and sure enough they did. It was a no-brainer when the party held referendums in 1980 and 1995: He proudly voted Yes both times. Premier Bernard Landry even tried to recruit the charismatic union boss to succeed Lucien Bouchard as a local PQ candidate in the early 2000s. He declined mainly because it would mean spending less time in Saguenay.
The party had been in power for almost a decade by then. Especially in the Saguenay, separatism was a default ideology, the wallpaper of political life.
“If people talked politics in the dining room, it was PQ,” Mr. Crevier recalled. “If someone was Liberal, they were hiding in the corner.”

content_blocks.caption: It’s been more than 30 years since the big referendum showdown between federalists, led by prime minister Jean Chrétien, and Quebec separatists allied with premier Jacques Parizeau. Andy Clark/Reuters
Bloc Québécois leader Lucien Bouchard conceded defeat on the 1995 referendum, but vowed to continue the fight in other areas. He took over Mr. Parizeau’s job in 1996.

content_blocks.text: When premier Jacques Parizeau took the stage at Montreal’s Palais des Congrès on the night of Oct. 30, 1995, he was expecting to give a victory speech. Instead he blamed “money and ethnic votes” for his narrow referendum defeat, and his movement was permanently changed.

In a literal sense, Mr. Parizeau was right. Sixty per cent of francophones voted to leave that day, feeling burned by successive failed attempts to reform the constitution. Even long-time Canadian patriots such as André Pratte, future editor of the federalist La Presse newspaper and later a Canadian senator, felt the impasse was serious enough to vote Yes.
When Mr. Parizeau spoke those notorious words, many Quebeckers were ashamed of his outburst. Mr. Pratte recalls feeling revulsion and immediate regret for his Yes vote.

Others, felt a deep sense of recognition in Mr. Parizeau’s assertion of a French-Canadian nous , set apart from a sea of others. Cultural survival has always been a primal goal of French Canada, surrounded as it is by hundreds of millions of English-speakers in North America. Now, as Quebec’s own population becomes more diverse thanks to declining birth rates and increased immigration, the challenge can seem to come from within.

content_blocks.caption: ‘Where is my free Quebec?’ reads this protest flag at a Montreal rally against secularism laws, a contentious subject in a province home to many faiths and cultures. Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: This siege mentality has an undeniable resonance for some Quebeckers. Ninety-eight per cent of Saguenay residents have French as a mother tongue, according to the most recent census, yet it’s still common to hear that immigrants there imperil French. In Quebec, language and culture can seem precarious even in their most impenetrable fortresses.

Appealing to voters like these, who feel left behind by a changing Quebec, turned out to be a dead-end for the PQ. The party dropped to an all-time low of three National Assembly seats in 2022 as François Legault and his Coalition Avenir Québec promised to protect Quebec interests and culture without the upheaval of another independence vote.

Even then, as the PQ drifted further and further to his right, Mr. Crevier stayed true to his sovereigntist faith. This election, with his party leading in the polls and promising a third referendum, he should have been ecstatic. You might have expected to find him knocking on doors for the local PQ candidate, Jimmy Bouchard, an old friend and colleague on the Saguenay city council.

But in a country of contradictions and cross-hatched loyalties, perhaps nowhere is shaded with more subtlety than the mind of a Quebec voter. And sure enough, this hard man of the labour movement, with a granite face, salt-and-pepper hair and a navy-blue windbreaker, finds himself politically “ shaké ” this election season. He is rattled for a simple but powerful reason: “Everything that’s happening with the United States.”

content_blocks.caption: Saguenay’s industrial neighbourhoods kept a careful eye on this summer’s Canada-U.S. trade talks, whose collapse was partly due to disagreements over French language laws. Charles-Frederick Ouellet/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: In the current trade war with the U.S., American tariffs or demands have targeted virtually everything the Saguenay holds dear: aluminum, dairy and lumber, to say nothing of protections for the French language and culture. From where Mr. Crevier is sitting, the U.S. President looks like a far bigger threat to his nation and his region than Canadian federalism.

Like everything in Quebec, this is an old story. When Americans threaten, Quebeckers choose the ambivalent embrace of the British Crown and the Canadian federation. Benjamin Franklin came to Montreal as an emissary of the American Revolution and was firmly rebuffed. During the War of 1812, French-Canadian heroes such as the fur trader Dominique Ducharme helped fight off the Yankee invasion. The former patriote rebel George-Étienne Cartier became a Father of Confederation in part because he dreaded American annexation.

Quebeckers have always believed their distinct society was better protected within the Canadian mosaic than as a stray ingredient in the American melting pot. It is this existential belief, as much as the pain of tariffs, that has rallied the province to the Maple Leaf during this trade war.

On Aug. 31, another minor chapter of this story was written when Daniel Gobeil, the Liberal candidate in Chicoutimi–Le Fjord, won a landslide victory over the Bloc Québécois in a federal by-election. His face was still Liberal red after a night of celebration and speech-giving when he credited his victory to a hunger – even in deep-blue Saguenay – for “Canadian unity.”

content_blocks.caption: Mr. Carney recently introduced the House to a new MP, Daniel Gobeil from Chicoutimi–Le Fjord. Tatiana Auguste from Terrebonne made her debut a few months earlier. Adrian Wyld/CP; Peter McCabe/Reuters

content_blocks.text: Meanwhile, the PQ’s popularity has flatlined. They sit atop the polls because of voter fatigue with the CAQ and disarray within the provincial Liberal party. But the party has failed to reach out beyond the slightly under 30 per cent of Quebeckers who want independence, a historically low level for the province. If the PQ forms government, it will arguably be because the other parties split the federalist vote, not because voters want to leave Canada. And yet, the PQ almost certainly will form the next Quebec government, and hold a referendum if they secure a majority.

All this weighs heavily on Mr. Crevier, someone who has always believed in the sovereigntist catechism but is having his faith tested like never before. These days he is prone to delivering the pained soliloquy of a wavering separatist, one who is considering throwing in his lot with the CAQ and even – simonaque – the federal Liberals.

It is an uncertain time for the country as a whole. A generational upsurge of Canadian nationalism is coinciding with a generational threat to national unity. The independence drives in Alberta and Quebec May be stalling, but they are showing little sign of going away; Prof. Cooper’s profane rage and Mr. Crevier’s profane ambivalence both give voice to permanent doubts about their provinces’ place in Canada.

In the coming years, our leaders will have to find creative ways of renewing the Canadian contract, especially when the American threat isn’t there to unite us. This country is vast and varied enough to contain the oil wealth and donut shops of Red Deer, along with the aluminum plants and casse-croûtes of Chicoutimi. That kind of diversity can be a source of bounty or vulnerability, depending on how it’s managed.

Over bottomless cups of coffee at a chain diner two days after the Chicoutimi by-election, the anxious words tumbled out of Mr. Crevier like they were being spoken through the brass latticework of a parish church confessional.

“People are saying, better to improve it then break it down … In a referendum, we tear our shirts in the public square, we spit in each other’s faces, then, when we have our independence, we’ll go say to Ontario, ‘Hey let’s work together against the U.S.’ They’ll say, ‘Hey, go eat crap’... It’s made me change my mentality personally, me who’s voted PQ since 1976. People feel less embarrassed to say, ‘Let’s vote for the CAQ’ … I have more confidence in the CAQ to work with Canada right now … If you look around the world, who’s standing up to Trump? I’m listening to what Carney has to say … I’ve never voted Liberal in my goddamn life. I’m shaken on every side, provincially and federally … Simonaque …”

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk set to launch to International Space Station
stories.summary: Merritt Island - As the sun rises over Florida's iconic Kennedy Space Center on Thursday morning, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk will be making the final preparations to fulfil his lifelong dream of blasting off into space.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MERRITT ISLAND - As the sun rises over Florida’s iconic Kennedy Space Center on Thursday morning, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk will be making the final preparations to fulfil his lifelong dream of blasting off into space.

JR[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/canadian-astronaut-joshua-kutryk-set-to-launch-to-international-space-station/article_4938267d-c61b-5cd8-8146-b2335117afaa.html)

By Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press

If the weather holds, the 44-year-old will be among NASA’s SpaceX Crew 13 launching at 11:10 a.m. ET to the International Space Station for a six-month mission.

From the ground, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly will be watching. It will be the first space launch she’s ever attended and Joly said it’s not lost on her that Kutryk will be on board with a Russian and two Americans.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

“It’s happening at a time where there is this trade war going on, there is geopolitical tensions,” Joly said at nearby Cocoa Beach on Wednesday. “I think it’s important that we are able to show that we can co-operate as human beings on space exploration.”

Joly has been on the front lines of U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, first as foreign minister and now with her current portfolio that’s in charge of mitigating many of the effects of the tariffs at home.

Space exploration remains an area of ongoing co-operation, Joly said, and she is scheduled to meet with NASA administrator Jared Isaacman while in Florida for the launch.

She said the International Space Station is a symbol of how countries can and must work together, noting essential Canadian robotics contributions to the facility such as the well-known Canadarm and its followup Dextre.

The tensions between Canada and the United States even came up during NASA’s prelaunch news conference on Wednesday.

Mathieu Caron, director of astronauts, life sciences and space medicine at the Canadian Space Agency, was asked whether some of the rhetoric directed at Canada was a distraction.

Caron responded that in his three-decade-long career working on the International Space Station project, the focus has always been on the safety of the crew and success of the mission.

“That commitment was true 27 years ago and it’s still true to this day,” he said. “So I’m happy to report that we’re happy to continue to work with our partners.”

That doesn’t mean Canada isn’t looking to diversify its space partnerships, as it has its economy, Joly said. She said NASA is changing its operating model and Canada “has to take stock of that” and reach out to other partners for partnerships and innovation.

That means working closer with the European and Japanese space industries, as well as other middle-power countries.

“We believe that space is important for Canada and is important for us as an industrial power, as a country that needs that sovereign capability of space launch,” she said, pointing to Spaceport Nova Scotia, a new commercial orbital launch site.

Joly said Canada’s defence industrial plan has recognized the importance of the space sector and new funds are also dedicated to the Canadian Space Agency. She said Canada needs to embrace the industrial part of space investment to create domestic jobs while also doubling down on the importance of science and civilian research.

A new Canadian Space Agency president will be announced in the coming weeks, Joly said. A new space strategy will be unveiled in the coming months, which will promote Canada’s goals of creating opportunities, playing a larger role in the sector and sending more astronauts off Earth, she added.

For now, Joly said she’s very excited to see Kutryk launch to space. She said he’s a great representation of Canada: humble, intelligent and dedicated to the mission.

At the NASA news conference, Caron said Canadian Space Agency members had spoken with Kutryk earlier Wednesday and the astronaut was in high spirits and ready for the launch.

While on the deployment, Kutryk will be taking part in some long-term Canadian research projects but he will also be essential to documenting new science around how the human body responds to space travel.

Kutryk will also be dealing with a unique situation during his months-long deployment off of Earth — his wife is set to give birth to the family’s third child.

Caron said the Canadian Space Agency and NASA are working together to provide Kutryk with support and to ensure some video calls with his growing family while in space.

“These are exciting times,” Caron said with a beaming smile.

stories.title: Advocates say Quebec rules keep unhoused voters from polls as election nears
stories.summary: Montreal - Marcel Dionne Jr. says he won’t let homelessness stop him from voting.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Marcel Dionne Jr. says he won’t let homelessness stop him from voting.

The 66-year-old has been living in transitional housing for the last four months, and plans to list the address of that facility as his residence when he casts his ballot in the Oct. 5 Quebec election.

“I don’t want to be forgotten, I want to be heard,” he said.

Dionne Jr. has followed the campaign closely. He said he has been worried about escalating costs for rent and hasn’t heard any promises that would address his concerns. Still, he said participating in the democratic process is important.

But while the challenges faced by Dionne Jr., and other unhoused people have dominated the campaign’s final weeks, it will likely be difficult for many of them to cast their ballots.

Quebec’s rules for voters without a fixed address are more restrictive than federal rules, and advocates say the gap is disenfranchising a population that has grown to over 12,000 people, increasing by nearly 20 per cent in four years.

Scarlett Martinez of the community group Tapaj Québec wants the provincial government to change election voting rules to eliminate the barriers that make it harder for unhoused people to vote.

She estimates that less than one per cent of those experiencing homelessness cast a ballot.

“For people who live in situations where there May be fewer options, it can be more restrictive,” she said. “At the federal level, it’s much simpler.”

Elections Canada has long allowed polling stations to be set up inside community organizations, like shelters and soup kitchens.

Élections Québec asked the national assembly to approve a pilot project to make voting more accessible to those experiencing homelessness. But PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon objected to the proposal in the legislature last spring, citing concerns about “electoral fraud.”

“If third parties approach certain groups and say, ‘Go vote,’ … we’re opening the door to possibilities that, in my opinion, need to be considered more seriously,” the PQ leader told journalists last March, when his party voted against the proposal.

That objection contrasts with the PQ’s platform in the current campaign. The party has said homelessness was its “top priority,” with St-Pierre Plamondon pledging to make himself the homelessness superminister if elected.

In Quebec, unhoused voters can confirm their identity with a statement signed by a community organization where they receive services. However, Élections Québec acknowledged in an email that this measure “May not be suitable for everyone experiencing homelessness,” since many would not have access to community support.

At the Old Brewery Mission, a shelter in downtown Montreal, about a dozen people gathered in the cafeteria to watch the final debate of the campaign Sept. 23. Some were scanning the local newspaper waiting for the debate to start. Others scoffed or nodded along as the five leaders presented their visions for the province.

A handful said they planned to cast a ballot.

There are posters around the shelter with information related to the election, and staff are trained to accompany residents to the nearest polling station.

Supervisor Marie-France Chauvin says staff make sure residents feel that they can be heard and affect change. While some are very politically engaged, others are disillusioned, she says.

“Some feel so neglected by politicians that they’ve lost faith in politics,” said Chauvin.

stories.title: Carney's electoral Trump card is falling flat in B.C., Quebec elections
stories.summary: With the opposition in disarray, Eby never mentioned the new interim Conservative leader, but referenced Donald Trump at least 20 times.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — When British Columbia Premier David Eby took the risky step last week of calling an election with almost exactly half of his mandate left, he didn’t seem too clear why he was doing so.

But there was no doubt who he wanted to run against.

With the opposition conservatives in disarray, Eby never mentioned the new interim B.C. Conservative leader in his Sept. 22 campaign-opening speech. But he referenced U.S. President Donald Trump at least 20 times, saying it was an “existential moment” and that the New Democratic government would erect a “firebreak” against the American threat.

Less than a month earlier, Québec Premier Christine Fréchette opened her campaign by making it clear that she wanted Trump on the ballot too. Fréchette called the unpopular U.S. leader “her main opponent.”

In both cases, the two premiers seemed to be following the path created by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who won big in the 2025 federal election because he presented himself as the best defender of Canadian interests against Trump’s threats to the country’s economy and sovereignty.

And in both provincial cases, the plan, at least so far, has failed.

“(Voters are) not looking for a rhetorical opposition to Trump,” said Stewart Prest, a political scientist at the University of British Columbia.

That viewed is backed up by the polls. Both Eby and Fréchette’s numbers have plunged and are now at risk of being tossed out of office.

So what happened to playing the Trump card? Has that move lost its potency for incumbents in Canadian politics?

Or is there something unique to Carney — or his job as prime minister — that makes it work?

Analysts say voters seem to have made a distinction in this case that international trade and dealing with Washington are not the provinces’ jobs, so they’re not buying the effort to play the Trump card.

In Eby’s case, they say it was a gross miscalculation to call the election early and to emphasize the province’s need to stand up to Trump, instead of waiting to hold the vote and then focusing on more traditional provincial matters such as health care, education and B.C.’s economic development. The province’s large deficit under Eby is expected to be an election issue at either time, analysts say.

Prest said Eby’s effort to link the election call to Trump might have worked if the Conservatives hadn’t switched leaders just a couple of days earlier.

The previous leader, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, resigned Sept. 20 following a caucus revolt and other internal strife. The former federal MP was seen as more sympathetic to Trump’s Maga movement and therefore, more vulnerable to the NDP charge that she wouldn’t defend B.C.’s interests against him.

The party’s new interim leader is Lorne Doerkson, a more moderate figure who is also more critical of Trump. He will lead the party into the Oct. 24 election.

Sanjay Jeram, a political scientist at Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, said voters aren’t usually very good at distinguishing between the responsibilities of the different levels of government, but seemed to have sussed out almost immediately this time that the New Democrats’ election call and efforts to play the Trump card were “disingenuous.”

“It’s a little far-fetched,” said Jeram.

And recent polls reflect that view. When the election was called, Eby’s New Democrats had a solid lead of between four and 10 percentage points over the Conservatives. Since then, depending on the poll, the NDP had fallen as many as six to eight percentage points, with those votes seeming to go straight to the Conservatives. Some recent polls in recent days have the Tory lead down to just a couple of points.

The Ndp’s fall should be seen as a “ballot backlash,” said Shachi Kurl, president of the Angus Reid Institute. “There’s a lot of unhappiness with this government.”

Unlike B.C., Quebec has fixed elections, leaving Fréchette and her Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) party no choice but to face voters. With the Oct. 5 election less than a week away, Caq’s polling numbers have fallen five to seven points since the election call.

André Lecours, a political science professor at the University of Ottawa, said Fréchette also had little choice but to play the Trump card because she’s the leader of an unpopular CAQ government that had been in power for almost eight years.

“There was no other card to play,” said Lecours. “She had to play it.”

Analysts are divided over whether the potency of the Trump card has faded in Canadian politics or just won’t work as well at the provincial level.

Lecours said Canadian voters are getting used to the Trump threats and rhetoric and their impact is fading.

Recent polls have Carney’s Liberals with the support of almost half of Canadian voters and the Conservatives almost 20 percentage points behind. If the Trump factor has faded, Carney May be attracting support more for his plan and policies, analysts say, not just his defence of Canada.

If the Trump card has faded as a weapon for incumbents in Canada, some Conservatives acknowledge their challenge May have grown. Carney maintains a big lead without the full boost that he earned last year from his defence against Trump, many voters May now be buying into his policies and plan for the country.

“I think we have to start looking more at Carney for Carney’s success,” says Jeram.

So what happened to playing the Trump card? Has that move lost its potency for incumbents in Canadian politics?
Or is there something unique to Carney — or his job as prime minister — that makes it work?

Analysts say voters seem to have made a distinction in this case that international trade and dealing with Washington are not the provinces’ jobs, so they’re not buying the effort to play the Trump card.
content_blocks.html: Analysts say voters seem to have made a distinction in this case that international trade and dealing with Washington are not the provinces’ jobs, so they’re not buying the effort to play the Trump card.

content_blocks.text: In Eby’s case, they say it was a gross miscalculation to call the election early and to emphasize the province’s need to stand up to Trump, instead of waiting to hold the vote and then focusing on more traditional provincial matters such as health care, education and B.C.’s economic development. The province’s large deficit under Eby is expected to be an election issue at either time, analysts say.
Prest said Eby’s effort to link the election call to Trump might have worked if the Conservatives hadn’t switched leaders just a couple of days earlier.

content_blocks.alt: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with Prime Minister Mark Carney at a working lunch with leaders of G7 and the Middle East on June 16 in Evian-les-Bains, France.
content_blocks.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with Prime Minister Mark Carney at a working lunch with leaders of G7 and the Middle East on June 16 in Evian-les-Bains, France. Photo by Evelyn Hockstein/Pool/Getty Images files

content_blocks.text: The previous leader, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, resigned Sept. 20 following a caucus revolt and other internal strife. The former federal MP was seen as more sympathetic to Trump’s Maga movement and therefore, more vulnerable to the NDP charge that she wouldn’t defend B.C.’s interests against him.
The party’s new interim leader is Lorne Doerkson, a more moderate figure who is also more critical of Trump. He will lead the party into the Oct. 24 election.

Sanjay Jeram, a political scientist at Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, said voters aren’t usually very good at distinguishing between the responsibilities of the different levels of government, but seemed to have sussed out almost immediately this time that the New Democrats’ election call and efforts to play the Trump card were “disingenuous.”
“It’s a little far-fetched,” said Jeram.

And recent polls reflect that view. When the election was called, Eby’s New Democrats had a solid lead of between four and 10 percentage points over the Conservatives. Since then, depending on the poll, the NDP had fallen as many as six to eight percentage points, with those votes seeming to go straight to the Conservatives. Some recent polls in recent days have the Tory lead down to just a couple of points.
The Ndp’s fall should be seen as a “ballot backlash,” said Shachi Kurl, president of the Angus Reid Institute. “There’s a lot of unhappiness with this government.”

Unlike B.C., Quebec has fixed elections, leaving Fréchette and her Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) party no choice but to face voters. With the Oct. 5 election less than a week away, Caq’s polling numbers have fallen five to seven points since the election call.

content_blocks.alt: Kerry-Lynne Findlay
content_blocks.caption: Kerry-Lynne Findlay, resigned Sept. 20 following a caucus revolt and other internal strife. The former federal MP was seen as more sympathetic to Trump’s MAGA movement. Photo by NICK PROCAYLO / PNG

content_blocks.text: André Lecours, a political science professor at the University of Ottawa, said Fréchette also had little choice but to play the Trump card because she’s the leader of an unpopular CAQ government that had been in power for almost eight years.
“There was no other card to play,” said Lecours. “She had to play it.”
Analysts are divided over whether the potency of the Trump card has faded in Canadian politics or just won’t work as well at the provincial level.
Lecours said Canadian voters are getting used to the Trump threats and rhetoric and their impact is fading.

Recent polls have Carney’s Liberals with the support of almost half of Canadian voters and the Conservatives almost 20 percentage points behind. If the Trump factor has faded, Carney May be attracting support more for his plan and policies, analysts say, not just his defence of Canada.

If the Trump card has faded as a weapon for incumbents in Canada, some Conservatives acknowledge their challenge May have grown. Carney maintains a big lead without the full boost that he earned last year from his defence against Trump, many voters May now be buying into his policies and plan for the country.
“I think we have to start looking more at Carney for Carney’s success,” says Jeram.

stories.title: Albertans could save cash at the pumps as gas tax holiday begins
stories.summary: Edmonton - Albertans filling their tanks May soon be saving cash as the province's gas tax holiday starts today.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Albertans filling their tanks May soon be saving cash as the province’s gas tax holiday starts today.

Premier Danielle Smith’s government is pausing its tax of 13 cents per litre on gasoline and diesel until the end of the year to ease the pressure of high everyday costs.

It comes as the oil-rich province’s treasury reaps the benefit of steep global energy prices.

Eligible adults also have until the end of October to apply online for $100 fuel tax rebates that started rolling out in July.

Smith had said the province went with payments out of concern that tax cuts don’t always get passed on to consumers.

Smith later acknowledged Albertans weren’t happy with the rebate program.

The online application portal was criticized by some as invasive and onerous, although the government tweaked the process to try to make it smoother.

On the heals of a projected $2-billion budget surplus, Smith ditched the rebate, and reverted to cutting the fuel tax until the end of the year.

Alberta’s fuel tax suspension will cost government coffers far more than the rebate. The province estimates it will forego $350 million in revenue in the coming three months.

Nearly 3.4 million adult Albertans are eligible for the rebate, but Finance Minister Jason Nixon said Wednesday only about 1.5 million people have applied.

Nixon previously said he’s not entirely confident the tax cut will be passed on to consumers.

But he has said the low number of rebate applications made it clear the government couldn’t dole out the cash efficiently.

The federal government has also stepped up to try to help Canadians dealing with the high cost of living.

It has extended its fuel excise tax relief until the end of January, which is expected to save drivers up to 10 cents a litre on gas, or four cents per litre on diesel.

Albertans are already paying less, ON average, than drivers across the country.

On Wednesday, the Canadian Automobile Association pegged the average price of gas in Canada at $1.77 per litre. The gas price tracking website GasBuddy, as of Wednesday afternoon, estimated Alberta’s average to be $1.67 per litre.

Fuel prices have soared since the U.S. war on Iran began in late February, choking the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane at the mouth of the Persian Gulf.

The impact has turned Alberta’s finances around.

Its budget is heavily dependent on oil exports, and before the conflict in the Middle East, was predicting a $9.4-billion deficit this fiscal year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

stories.title: News Alert: Sexual assault trial for ‘Trailer Park Boys’ actor Mike Smith dismissed
stories.summary: A three-day sexual assault trial is scheduled to begin today for Nova Scotia-based actor Mike Smith, best known for playing Bubbles on the TV comedy "Trailer Park Boys."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Mike Smith, the actor behind the character Bubbles from the "Trailer Park Boys," poses for photos at the 24th Annual Gemini Awards in Calgary on Nov. 14, 2009. THE Canadian Press/Larry MacDougal

By The Canadian Press

Posted October 1, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated October 1, 2026 10:09 am.

Dartmouth — The sexual assault case against the Nova Scotia-based actor best known for playing Bubbles on the TV comedy “Trailer Park Boys” has been dismissed.

Mike Smith’s three-day trial was supposed to start in Dartmouth, N.S., this morning.

Judge Jill Hartlen dismissed the case after Crown lawyers said they would not be presenting any evidence.

Smith had pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault stemming from an alleged incident in 2017. The actor was charged on Oct. 2, 2025, but court documents did not provide details about the allegations.

Smith’s lawyer, Stan MacDonald, said outside the courtroom that his client was pleased with the case’s dismissal and wants to put the matter behind him.

Nova Scotia-based Trailer Park Boys Inc., where Smith is listed as a director, issued a statement saying he will resume his responsibilities with the company.

Other company directors include John Paul Tremblay, who plays Julian on the show, and Robert Wells, who plays Ricky.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

The Canadian Press

Smith’s lawyer, Stan MacDonald, said outside the courtroom that his client was pleased with the case’s dismissal and wants to put the matter behind him.
Nova Scotia-based Trailer Park Boys Inc., where Smith is listed as a director, issued a statement saying he will resume his responsibilities with the company.
Other company directors include John Paul Tremblay, who plays Julian on the show, and Robert Wells, who plays Ricky.

stories.title: Margaret Atwood donates $1M to Western for migratory bird research
stories.summary: Margaret Atwood has donated $1 million to Western University to support research into migratory birds. The gift will create a research chair named after her late partner, author and bird advocate Graeme Gibson.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Margaret Atwood has donated $1 million to Western University to support research into migratory birds. The gift will create a research chair named after her late partner, author and bird advocate Graeme Gibson.
· Posted: Sep 30, 2026 9:31 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Canadian literary icon Margaret Atwood has donated $1 million to Western University to support research into migratory birds.
The gift will create the Graeme Gibson Chair for Avian Biology, named after Atwood's late partner, who shared her passion for birds and co-founded the Pelee Island Bird Observatory.
Gibson, who died in 2019, also wrote The Bedside Book of Birds, which was published in 2005.
Speaking on The Current in 2021, Atwood recalled how Gibson was a "late-life convert" to bird watching.

"He had one of those light bulb experiences in one of the Don Valley ravines when he saw a large bird, and he didn't know what it was," she said. "So he found out it was a red-tailed hawk, and from that moment on, he was a bird-er, as we say."
The new chair will support research into how birds move, behave and adapt to changes in their environment, according to Western.

Chris Guglielmo, a biology professor and director of Western's Centre for Animals on the Move, said he was asked to sit down before being told about the donation during an emotional phone call this summer.
"We're very, very excited and grateful for this gift," he said.
"To get a gift like this is just such a boost for all of us. It tells us we're on the right track, and great people are interested in what we're doing."
Guglielmo said there are numerous unanswered questions about migratory birds and he's excited about what the new chair could bring to the university.

Western is already a leader in avian migration studies, housing not only the Centre for Animals on the Move, but also the Advanced Facility for Avian Research, which houses the world’s only hypobaric climatic wind tunnel designed for bird flight.
The faculty also had a longstanding connection to Atwood and Gibson through the Pelee Island Bird Observatory on Lake Erie, which the couple founded in 2003.
Southwestern Ontario is a major hub for migratory birds, according to Guglielmo, adding that the huge boreal forests to the north are "the nursery for hundreds of millions of birds."

When it's time to move, he said they tend to avoid the Great Lakes. and the birds are then funneled through the relatively small area of land and tend to especially pile up along the coasts of Lake Ontario and Lake Erie.
According to Chris Guglielmo, the woods around Long Point in southwestern Ontario are full of different species of warbler during peak migration time. (Jayne Gulbrand / Shutterstock)
"Places like Point Pelee, Pelee Island, Long Point, and Rondeau Park become havens for these birds, and people come from all over the world to birdwatch," he said.
Guglielmo said he does a lot of his own research around Long Point during the peak of migration, adding that it's "an amazing thing to witness."
"It's like walking through this jeweled forest in the spring where the woods can be so full of these small warblers that are all different colors," he said.
"They can be down near eye level, so you're walking along, and it's just everywhere you look, it's a different species."

stories.title: Marking National Day for Truth and Reconciliation at Fort Edmonton Park
stories.summary: Edmonton's oldest historic site served as a place to remember the history of Canada's Indigenous people on the sixth annual National Day of Truth and Reconciliation.
stories.author: Joel Gotlib, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Edmonton’s oldest historic site served as a place to remember the history of Canada’s Indigenous people on the sixth annual National Day of Truth and Reconciliation .

The day is a sombre remembrance of 150,000 Indigenous children who suffered malnutrition and abuse over decades in Canada’s residential school system.

“Days like today are not necessarily happy days for us — they’re actually quite sad and heavy,” said Jasmine Hannig, an Indigenous social worker who took in the commemorative event at Fort Edmonton Park.

Many at the gathering wore bright orange shirts, the symbol for the children who attended residential schools. Some ate bannock and sipped on warm beverages on the chilly autumn morning.

The Federal statutory holiday was established after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission called on the Canadian government to recognize the impact residential schools had on survivors, their families and their communities.

In 2015, the commission concluded the schools were central to a state-backed policy of cultural genocide.

“Truth and reconciliation, definitely for Indigenous people, is not just one day. It’s a life that we live,” said Chief Desmond Bull from the Louis Bull First Nation in Maskwacis. “More importantly, the acknowledgement of our ancestors that went through residential school.”

Experts and First Nations advocates have cited the violence and abuse inflicted upon several generations of Indigenous children at the schools as the reason why Indigenous communities experience disproportionately higher rates of violence, psychological distress and substance use and abuse.

The trauma was compounded by events like the Sixties Scoop — a government policy that forcibly removed Indigenous children from their birth parents and sent to foster homes and other families for adoption.

Hannig wants people to know the day commemorates more than just Canada’s dark history with residential school.

“Not only residential schooling had an impact, but so did the Sixties Scoop, day schools, boarding schools, the 90s scoop and many other colonial aspects,” she said of the intergenerational trauma First Nations people have suffered.

“I think it’s really important we talk about the impact of all that harm collectively, and the echoes that has had within our community.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I think it's really important we talk about the impact of all that harm collectively, and the echoes that has had within our community."

The day is full of mixed feelings for Hannig.

“In one way, it’s really emotional because it’s so beautiful that we’re having this conversation — finally. But another way, I feel like there’s a lot of conversations that we’re not having collectively.”

On Wednesday, about 2,000 people were expected to walk through the Indigenous People’s Experience at Fort Edmonton Park, which is opened year-round.

“The immersive experience in here is really about the fact that you’re learning about us in a broader sense,” Evert Poor, an event manager at Fort Edmonton Park, said of the exhibit.

“A lot of people have a lot of myths and stereotypes about Indigenous people.

“This space basically teaches you the true history of our people.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "This space basically teaches you the true history of our people."

Chief Bull said listening to those whose lives were impacted is also encouraged.

“There’s much more you can learn from sitting down with a person of Indigenous background and hearing their story of where they are now, and how they came about where they are,” Bull said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre, Mayor Andrew Knack, leaders from First Nations near Edmonton and other officials took part in a commemorative ceremony at the interactive historical site.

Carney, who was born in the Northwest Territories and raised in Edmonton, recalled in his speech the numerous visits to Fort Edmonton in his youth.

Carney said the ceremony urged everyone to hear the stories of those affected by the residential school system and “reflect on a dark chapter in Canada’s past and to commit to move forward together.”

“This is not a distant chapter in Canada’s past, but a truth that endures,” said Carney, who wore an orange tie and a pin of a beaded orange T-shirt on his lapel.

“Reconciliation is a journey, not a destination. It’s an attitude, not an achievement. Our job is to move together as far and as fast down the path as we can.”

Alberta’s Minister of Indigenous Relations released a statement about the day.

“Reconciliation is about more than a single day,” the statement from Rajan Sawhney said. “Reconciliation takes time, care and sustained effort. It is shaped by relationships built on listening, respect and a willingness to learn, and by supporting Indigenous-led knowledge, perspectives and priorities.”

Anyone experiencing pain or distress as a result of their residential school experience can access this 24-hour, toll-free and confidential National Indian Residential School Crisis Line at 1-866-925-4419.

paragraphs: Edmonton’s oldest historic site served as a place to remember the history of Canada’s Indigenous people on the sixth annual National Day of Truth and Reconciliation .
The day is a sombre remembrance of 150,000 Indigenous children who suffered malnutrition and abuse over decades in Canada’s residential school system.

“Days like today are not necessarily happy days for us — they’re actually quite sad and heavy,” said Jasmine Hannig, an Indigenous social worker who took in the commemorative event at Fort Edmonton Park.
Many at the gathering wore bright orange shirts, the symbol for the children who attended residential schools. Some ate bannock and sipped on warm beverages on the chilly autumn morning.

The Federal statutory holiday was established after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission called on the Canadian government to recognize the impact residential schools had on survivors, their families and their communities.
In 2015, the commission concluded the schools were central to a state-backed policy of cultural genocide.

“Truth and reconciliation, definitely for Indigenous people, is not just one day. It’s a life that we live,” said Chief Desmond Bull from the Louis Bull First Nation in Maskwacis. “More importantly, the acknowledgement of our ancestors that went through residential school.”

Experts and First Nations advocates have cited the violence and abuse inflicted upon several generations of Indigenous children at the schools as the reason why Indigenous communities experience disproportionately higher rates of violence, psychological distress and substance use and abuse.

The trauma was compounded by events like the Sixties Scoop — a government policy that forcibly removed Indigenous children from their birth parents and sent to foster homes and other families for adoption.

“Not only residential schooling had an impact, but so did the Sixties Scoop, day schools, boarding schools, the 90s scoop and many other colonial aspects,” she said of the intergenerational trauma First Nations people have suffered.

stories.title: Fanshawe raises awareness on Truth and Reconcilliation day.
stories.summary: Fanshawe's students are honouring Indigenous students on Truth and Reconciliation day through many ways. Inclu...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
Fanshawe’s students are honouring Indigenous students on Truth and Reconciliation day through many ways. Included are an art gallery displaying artwork created by Indigenous students, an Artisan market to support Indigenous businesses, and a speaking event where Ray John Jr, an Indigenous educator, and Pam Tobin, the CEO of the Canadian Mental Health Association, Thames Valley Addiction and Mental Health Services. Tobin and John Jr discussed the importance of women in Indigenous communities. “I salute the women in my life,” said John Jr. “Thank you for giving us that life and for giving us a chance.”

Kristen Longdo, the Indigenous Strategic Learning Guide for the Institute of Indigenous Learning at Fanshawe, said that art plays a major role in how many Indigenous people express themselves. “ It’s important to highlight the wonderful parts of Indigenous cultures ,” said Longdo. “We wanted to utilize September 30 th to highlight Indigenous artisans from our surrounding communities and give them a platform to display their work.”

Longdo also discussed how Truth and Reconciliation day has changed over the years, being officially recognized in as a statutory holiday by Canada in 2021, but according to Longdo, was celebrated across Indigenous communities since 2015.

“Truth and Reconciliation day has continued to change and evolve over time the more truth has come out.” said Longdo. “Each year we see more people showing up and more people engaging in reconciliation efforts.”

This year has seen many students at Fanshawe wearing an orange shirt to show their support and raise awareness for Indigenous communities, the design of which was made by Fanshawe student Robin Cornelius.

“ I am Indigenous and recently I just got a job working for the Indigenous Center,” said one Fanshawe student. “I’m supporting my culture and all my friends, my family, stuff like that. “

“ I think we need to have more non-indigenous people showing up to these types of events,” said another student.

Longdo agrees that more non-indigenous people should show up for these events. “ Non-Indigenous people need to continue to educate themselves on our truths. Listen, learn, show up and support your local indigenous communities,” said Longdo. “A great way of doing this is giving Indigenous people a platform to speak about their truths, to buy from local Indigenous artists, to use your social media platforms to give Indigenous people, stories, and businesses a voice.”
