stories.title: Canadian astronaut set to take off for six-month stay on space station
stories.summary: Joshua Kutryk is part of a four-person crew scheduled to blast off from the Kennedy Space Center on Thursday
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Canada’s next space traveller is fast approaching his scheduled departure – but the weather May have other ideas.

On Wednesday afternoon, officials at Nasa’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida said there was a 55 per cent chance of favourable conditions for the launch of a four-person crew heading to the International Space Station for half a year.

The group includes Joshua Kutryk, a native of Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., and an air force pilot who was selected to be an astronaut by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.

Colonel Kutyrk is scheduled to fly with Jessica Watkins, crew commander, and Luke Delaney both of the United States, as well as Sergey Teteryatnikov of Russia. The team is set to lift off aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket Thursday at 11:10 a.m. ET and dock with the space station about eight hours later.

“I’m excited to do the science, I’m excited to look at the Earth, but I’m also excited to do it as a Canadian,” Col. Kutryk said during a press conference after he and his crewmates arrived on Sunday in advance of their launch.

He also stressed the value of the partnership that has enabled Canadians to work together with Nasa colleagues.

Col. Kutryk’s planned six-month stint on the ISS is another example of how active that partnership has been this year.

In April, Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen and his U.S. crewmates captured the world’s attention with Artemis II, the first mission to take humans around the moon and back in more than half a century.

Now, it’s Col. Kutryk’s turn to begin his nearer but far longer residency in Earth’s orbit.

During that time he will conduct a wide range of science experiments and help keep the station running in whatever way is needed.

And while it’s tempting to call the mission a marathon – especially when compared with Col. Hansen’s 9½ day lunar sprint – there is a more apt comparison.

“It’s a Tour de France,” said Robert Thirsk, a retired astronaut and physician who became the first Canadian to spend multiple months in space in 2009. “You get up and you go hard every day.”

Dr. Thirsk said he picked up the metaphor from Gennady Padalka, a seasoned Russian cosmonaut who was the station’s commander when he first arrived there for a 188-day stay.

“Gennady was a master at what I had to learn,” Dr. Thirsk said. “Every mission is going to have contingencies and inevitable malfunctions. So you need to have the physiological, but also the psychological reserves to deal with that.”

He said that while astronauts on short duration missions tend to train for specific tasks they need to complete on a tight timeline, those who expect to spend many months in orbit instead focus on skills that May be required to deal with the unexpected and maintain their physical and mental capacity over the long haul.

Dr. Thirsk said that Col. Kutryk was well suited for the challenge.

“During the fifth month of his expedition, he is going to need as much energy and enthusiasm to perform his tasks and his experiments as he will during this first week,” Dr. Thirsk said.

Col. Kutryk is set to become the fourth Canadian to undertake a long duration mission in space. Besides Dr. Thirsk, only Chris Hadfield and David Saint-Jacques have had comparably long flights aboard the ISS.

Jeremy Hansen and fellow Artemis II crew receive Congressional Space Medal of Honor

One way that Col. Kutryk’s mission differs is in how he will reach the station. Unlike his predecessors who were all launched from Kazakhstan in Soyuz spacecraft, Col. Kutryk will be transported in a SpaceX Dragon capsule as part of Nasa’s commercial crew program.

Because it is the 13 th regular flight under the program that relies on industrial partners to take astronauts to and from the station, the mission is referred to as Crew-13.

The flight was originally scheduled for mid-September, but was held up when engineers detected an oxidizer leak and decided to investigate. This led to the replacement of a valve – a delicate operation while the rocket was in its vertically stacked configuration.

During a call with reporters last week, Col. Kutryk said the problem was a minor one, but the decision to delay “makes us all feel that much more confident” in the safety of the vehicle.

Another way that Col. Kutryk’s trip is likely to be unique among Canadian astronauts is the fact that he and his wife Heather are expecting their third child to be born later this year while he is still in space.

Mathieu Caron, director of astronauts, life sciences and space medicine with the Canadian Space Agency said that Col. Kutryk would have access to enhanced communications with his family during his time on orbit.

“We have a team that’s dedicated to making sure that we support Josh and that the Kutryk family will receive whatever support is needed during the mission,” he said.

“I’m excited to do the science, I’m excited to look at the Earth, but I’m also excited to do it as a Canadian,” Col. Kutryk said during a press conference after he and his crewmates arrived on Sunday in advance of their launch.
He also stressed the value of the partnership that has enabled Canadians to work together with Nasa colleagues.
Col. Kutryk’s planned six-month stint on the ISS is another example of how active that partnership has been this year.

In April, Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen and his U.S. crewmates captured the world’s attention with Artemis II, the first mission to take humans around the moon and back in more than half a century.
Now, it’s Col. Kutryk’s turn to begin his nearer but far longer residency in Earth’s orbit.
During that time he will conduct a wide range of science experiments and help keep the station running in whatever way is needed.
And while it’s tempting to call the mission a marathon – especially when compared with Col. Hansen’s 9½ day lunar sprint – there is a more apt comparison.
“It’s a Tour de France,” said Robert Thirsk, a retired astronaut and physician who became the first Canadian to spend multiple months in space in 2009. “You get up and you go hard every day.”
Dr. Thirsk said he picked up the metaphor from Gennady Padalka, a seasoned Russian cosmonaut who was the station’s commander when he first arrived there for a 188-day stay.

“Gennady was a master at what I had to learn,” Dr. Thirsk said. “Every mission is going to have contingencies and inevitable malfunctions. So you need to have the physiological, but also the psychological reserves to deal with that.”

He said that while astronauts on short duration missions tend to train for specific tasks they need to complete on a tight timeline, those who expect to spend many months in orbit instead focus on skills that May be required to deal with the unexpected and maintain their physical and mental capacity over the long haul.
Dr. Thirsk said that Col. Kutryk was well suited for the challenge.
“During the fifth month of his expedition, he is going to need as much energy and enthusiasm to perform his tasks and his experiments as he will during this first week,” Dr. Thirsk said.

Col. Kutryk is set to become the fourth Canadian to undertake a long duration mission in space. Besides Dr. Thirsk, only Chris Hadfield and David Saint-Jacques have had comparably long flights aboard the ISS.
Jeremy Hansen and fellow Artemis II crew receive Congressional Space Medal of Honor

One way that Col. Kutryk’s mission differs is in how he will reach the station. Unlike his predecessors who were all launched from Kazakhstan in Soyuz spacecraft, Col. Kutryk will be transported in a SpaceX Dragon capsule as part of Nasa’s commercial crew program.
Because it is the 13 th regular flight under the program that relies on industrial partners to take astronauts to and from the station, the mission is referred to as Crew-13.

The flight was originally scheduled for mid-September, but was held up when engineers detected an oxidizer leak and decided to investigate. This led to the replacement of a valve – a delicate operation while the rocket was in its vertically stacked configuration.
During a call with reporters last week, Col. Kutryk said the problem was a minor one, but the decision to delay “makes us all feel that much more confident” in the safety of the vehicle.

Another way that Col. Kutryk’s trip is likely to be unique among Canadian astronauts is the fact that he and his wife Heather are expecting their third child to be born later this year while he is still in space.

Mathieu Caron, director of astronauts, life sciences and space medicine with the Canadian Space Agency said that Col. Kutryk would have access to enhanced communications with his family during his time on orbit.
“We have a team that’s dedicated to making sure that we support Josh and that the Kutryk family will receive whatever support is needed during the mission,” he said.

stories.title: Survey of candidates in municipal elections show differences between London politicians and voters
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/8bFKBD9DAgc Researchers at Western University recently published the results of a recent surv...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
Researchers at Western University recently published the results of a recent survey of candidates running in municipal elections across Ontario, and with it came a variety of potential differences between candidates and voters that one candidate said he has seen for himself.

According to its media release, the survey was conducted by the Local Democracy Project at Western, and surveyed close to 900 candidates running in municipal elections across Ontario. The stated purpose of the survey was to learn what drives candidates in terms that included their campaigns, demographics and what they think about local politics.

“It’s actually a national project,” said political science professor and the survey’s co-lead Zachary Taylor. “The goal is to look for trends across the entire country.”

The media release stated that the project has just sent out surveys to B.C., which is undergoing snap elections.

Because of the broad scope of the survey, finding data points about specific regions can be difficult. Taylor said that while the survey’s results May not be able to determine how London can deal problems like its lack of youth voter engagement , he believes it is linked to how candidates wage their campaigns, which the survey does examine.

However, Ward 12 candidate and Western student Ribal Zebian believes that the differences between candidates and the voting public can reflect on who tries to run in elections.

“When it’s … very hard to get by, you won’t really find the average voter going in,” he said. “You’ll find someone who doesn’t really represent them.”

Taylor said the survey data he collected showed that plenty of people are already showing up to run for elections, and that the barriers for running are very low.

“In the vast majority of races you have 2, 3, 4 candidates running, so I suppose that means things are working,” he said.

London City Hall. The survey conducted by Western researchers seems to point to financial and age differences between municipal politicians and the voting public. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

The survey also speaks to how money can be a barrier in municipal politics. The survey results showed that the average Ontario candidate has a yearly income over $100,000, that the average cost of a campaign is $2,600 and that campaigns are mostly self-funded.

“As places get bigger, the game changes,” said Taylor. “It is true that the people who run for office are generally better off financially … than the public they would seek to represent.”

Zebian said he has seen financial obstacles reflected in campaigns around Ward 5, where Western is located.

“They’re spending significantly beyond [$2,600],” he said. “When you look and you see some of the candidates … they have a lot more resources and a lot more to take advantage of.”

Money is only one characteristic of what the survey found was a part of the average candidate. It also found that the average age of candidates was 56, they are mostly men, they have a university degree and they own a home.

“There’s lots of examples of people in their late teens and 20s running for office and they often get picked up in the media because they’re such a novelty,” said Taylor.

Zebian, who is 19 years old, sees this for himself as well.

“If you look at the current mayor, you look at some of the councilors … [they are] in the age of 40s, 50s, have a degree whether it’s a bachelor’s or a master’s, they have an established career, all those types of things,” he said.

At the same time, Zebian believes he’s seeing a change in some of the survey’s averages. He says as well that candidates with less money May try to engage more directly with voters by knocking on doors and exchanging ideas, and that even if they don’t win their first election they can build a strong voter base for the future.

“You’ll see candidates who don’t have too too much, but they’ll still get themselves in,” he said. “And as we’re going through the years we’re seeing more people just getting themselves together, getting a little bit more brave … and eventually that leads you a very long way.”

stories.title: Man banned from future London Comic Cons after allegedly taking upskirt photos
stories.summary: A man was removed from London Comic Con last weekend after event staff received reports he was allegedly taking upskirt photos of women. The organizer says he is now banned from future events, while London police say they have not received a report about the incident.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A man was removed from London Comic Con last weekend after event staff received reports he was allegedly taking upskirt photos of women. The organizer says he is now banned from future events, while London police say they have not received a report about the incident.
· Posted: Sep 30, 2026 8:17 PM EDT | Last Updated: 43 minutes ago
A man has been banned from future London Comic Con events after staff received reports he was allegedly taking upskirt photos of women at the event.
The organizer confirmed the attendee was asked to leave the event, which took place at the Western Fair District J-AAR Expo Centre on Sept. 26 and 27.

“Following a review of the circumstances, London Comic Con has determined that the individual will not be permitted to attend future London Comic Con events,” the organizer said in an email to CBC News.
“This decision is consistent with the event’s policies and is intended to help maintain a safe, respectful, and comfortable environment for attendees, guests, exhibitors, and cosplayers.”
Neither event security nor the organizer contacted police about the incident.
London police said Tuesday they had not received a report related to the alleged incident.

“Under section 162 of the Criminal Code of Canada, it is an offence to secretly observe or record a person in circumstances where they have a reasonable expectation of privacy, including situations involving nudity, sexual activity, or where the observation or recording is made for a sexual purpose,” according to a statement from London police.
Police are encouraging anyone who May have been affected, witnessed the alleged behaviour or has information about the incident to contact them.
Jennifer Dunn, executive director at the London Abused Women's Centre, said people should be able to attend public events without having to worry about this type of behaviour.
“Safety is not just the absence of physical violence,” Dunn said. “Women have to be able to go to an event, or anywhere we want to go without having to worry about somebody else's behaviour.”
She was told 'upskirting' was not a crime in England and Wales — so she made it one
Dunn said preventing violence against women requires education and action from the broader community.
“There are a lot of people that definitely think that this is a woman's issue when really we need men standing up and saying this is not how we treat people,” she said.
Anyone who needs support can contact the London Abused Women's Centre at 519-432-2204.
Anyone with information about the alleged incident can contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or submit an anonymous tip through Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: ‘We come here for healing’: Saskatoon holds fifth annual truth and reconciliation powwow
stories.summary: Hundreds of orange shirts dotted the SaskTel centre on Wednesday to mark a day filled with reflection to honour residential school survivors.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Irene Nippi sees National Truth and Reconciliation Day as a way to show pride in a culture she was once told to abandon.

The elder from Kinistin Saulteaux First Nation was six years old when she was first sent to a residential school, an experience that compels her to take part in reconciliation ceremonies.

“I went to a residential school for a long time, and there are a lot of things that happened like sexual abuse, physical abuse, emotional abuse and spiritual abuse,” said Nippi.

Beginning in the 19th century, over 150,000 Indigenous children were separated from their families and communities and sent to church-run, government-funded residential schools where abuse, malnutrition and inadequate health care were rampant.

For Nippi, the schools stripped away more than family.

“It was taken away from us to be proud of who we are,” Nippi said, adding that the loss also extended to her culture, traditions, belief system and ceremonies.

On Wednesday, Nippi was among hundreds of others who donned an orange shirt and lined the inner bowl of the SaskTel Centre in Saskatoon for the Saskatoon Tribal Council’s fifth annual Truth and Reconciliation Powwow — a day marked by dancing, singing and reflection.

“All of them who went to the school are slowly getting their lives back but are still not ready to talk about what they experienced at the residential school,” she said, adding that she hopes events like Wednesday’s powwow can help start conversations.

Travis Toto, a drummer from Whitefish River First Nation, said he and his fellow members of the Eagle Boys Singers come for healing.

“It warms our hearts,” Toto said. “Just being around the drum and being around each other, it’s a good day.”

The federal government officially established Sept. 30 as the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in 2021 following recommendations in a report commissioned by the federal Truth and Reconciliation Commission six years earlier.

For some, attending the powwow in Saskatoon has already become a tradition.

“The grand entry always makes me weep. Even just talking about it makes me teary,” said Koreen Geres, an attendee at the powwow.

“I believe we need to get to know each other, that’s the best way for reconciliation,” Geres added.

Walking through the crowded concourse minutes before the grand entry, attendees of all ages could be seen meandering about. For some, the powwow marks a learning opportunity for future generations.

“My kids are extremely young, so the fact that they can come out to this particular event is quite special,” said Jordan Baptiste, adding he wants to show his kids to be proud of who they are.

In 2015, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission put forward 94 Calls to Action.

Since then, only 14 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 calls to action have been completed in the last 11 years, according to the independent monitor Indigenous Watchdog.

Another 41 recommendations are considered in progress, while 24 are stalled and 15 have not been started.

Saskatoon Tribal Chief Mark Arcand said reconciliation remains an ongoing process, and that progress is not coming fast enough.

“There’s still a lot of outstanding calls to action, and it’s been a few years, and that’s where we talk about accountability,” Arcand said. “It’s good to have them, but if we’re not enacting them, we have major problems.”

Arcand said the real measure of reconciliation is what happens beyond the one day set aside to mark it.

“Let’s start making a change together as a city, as a province, as a country, to be the leaders of working together because it’s tough when people don’t recognize the negative things that happen to First Nations people, and we have to have some hard, uncomfortable discussions,” he said.

paragraphs: Irene Nippi sees National Truth and Reconciliation Day as a way to show pride in a culture she was once told to abandon.
The elder from Kinistin Saulteaux First Nation was six years old when she was first sent to a residential school, an experience that compels her to take part in reconciliation ceremonies.
“I went to a residential school for a long time, and there are a lot of things that happened like sexual abuse, physical abuse, emotional abuse and spiritual abuse,” said Nippi.

Beginning in the 19th century, over 150,000 Indigenous children were separated from their families and communities and sent to church-run, government-funded residential schools where abuse, malnutrition and inadequate health care were rampant.
For Nippi, the schools stripped away more than family.
“It was taken away from us to be proud of who we are,” Nippi said, adding that the loss also extended to her culture, traditions, belief system and ceremonies.

On Wednesday, Nippi was among hundreds of others who donned an orange shirt and lined the inner bowl of the SaskTel Centre in Saskatoon for the Saskatoon Tribal Council’s fifth annual Truth and Reconciliation Powwow — a day marked by dancing, singing and reflection.

“All of them who went to the school are slowly getting their lives back but are still not ready to talk about what they experienced at the residential school,” she said, adding that she hopes events like Wednesday’s powwow can help start conversations.
Travis Toto, a drummer from Whitefish River First Nation, said he and his fellow members of the Eagle Boys Singers come for healing.
“It warms our hearts,” Toto said. “Just being around the drum and being around each other, it’s a good day.”

The federal government officially established Sept. 30 as the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in 2021 following recommendations in a report commissioned by the federal Truth and Reconciliation Commission six years earlier.
For some, attending the powwow in Saskatoon has already become a tradition.
“The grand entry always makes me weep. Even just talking about it makes me teary,” said Koreen Geres, an attendee at the powwow.
“I believe we need to get to know each other, that’s the best way for reconciliation,” Geres added.
Walking through the crowded concourse minutes before the grand entry, attendees of all ages could be seen meandering about. For some, the powwow marks a learning opportunity for future generations.
“My kids are extremely young, so the fact that they can come out to this particular event is quite special,” said Jordan Baptiste, adding he wants to show his kids to be proud of who they are.
In 2015, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission put forward 94 Calls to Action.
Since then, only 14 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 calls to action have been completed in the last 11 years, according to the independent monitor Indigenous Watchdog.
Another 41 recommendations are considered in progress, while 24 are stalled and 15 have not been started.
Saskatoon Tribal Chief Mark Arcand said reconciliation remains an ongoing process, and that progress is not coming fast enough.

“There’s still a lot of outstanding calls to action, and it’s been a few years, and that’s where we talk about accountability,” Arcand said. “It’s good to have them, but if we’re not enacting them, we have major problems.”
Arcand said the real measure of reconciliation is what happens beyond the one day set aside to mark it.

“Let’s start making a change together as a city, as a province, as a country, to be the leaders of working together because it’s tough when people don’t recognize the negative things that happen to First Nations people, and we have to have some hard, uncomfortable discussions,” he said.
— with files from Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney vows ‘true partnership’ with Indigenous people on major infrastructure projects
stories.summary: PM spoke at National Truth and Reconciliation Day event in Fort Edmonton Park on eve of expected West Coast oil pipeline announcement
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to create a true partnership with Indigenous people, including on operating and owning major infrastructure projects, as he marked the sixth annual National Truth and Reconciliation Day.

Mr. Carney’s comments at a commemorative event in Fort Edmonton Park Wednesday were made on the eve of an expected announcement to designate a West Coast oil pipeline as a project of national interest.

The pipeline is a key part of Mr. Carney’s suite of policy changes that aim to reset federal relations with Alberta and diversify Canadian exports away from the United States. But some First Nations have accused his government of a lack of meaningful consultation.

The Prime Minister, wearing an orange tie on what is known as “Orange Shirt Day,” addressed his government’s desire to build major projects across the country, but to do so sustainably.

“Sustainably means embedding Indigenous knowledge and leadership in our conservation efforts, and it means building in true partnership with Indigenous peoples,” Mr. Carney said.

New West Coast pipeline expected to be designated project of national interest by Thursday

He added that involves “meaningful opportunities to develop, operate and own major infrastructure, to share truly in the prosperity that’s created.”

“My point is, we are making some progress, but we know the work of reconciliation is far, far from finished,” Mr. Carney said.

“The wounds are still too deep, the gaps are still too wide. Reconciliation is a journey, not a destination. It’s an attitude, not an achievement. Our job is to move together as far and as fast down the path as we can.”

The Assembly of First Nations declined to comment on Mr. Carney’s remarks but said it would respond on Thursday.

In May, Mr. Carney’s government said it would designate the proposed pipeline a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act by Oct. 1. That process is being led by the federal Major Projects Office, headquartered in Calgary.

Indigenous leaders strike resolute tone as Canada marks sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation

One of the groups opposing the fast timeline for the process is the Coldwater Indian Band, in British Columbia. The group also opposed the Trans Mountain Expansion Project owing to concerns about risks to the community’s aquifer.

On behalf of the band, Vice-Chief Michael Smithers said in an e-mail earlier this week that there has been a lack of meaningful consultation between the community and the Major Projects Office about the new pipeline.

In his speech Wednesday, Mr. Carney called residential schools a “dark chapter” and said it’s the government’s responsibility to respond to the findings uncovered by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which documented the stories of residential-school survivors and the historical inequities faced by Indigenous people.

Beginning in the 1800s, more than 150,000 Indigenous children in Canada were sent to church-run residential schools, where abuse and malnutrition were rampant.

In 2015, the TRC concluded the schools were central to a state-backed policy of attempted cultural genocide.

Mr. Carney said that while the “gaps are still large,” the government is responding, including by improving opportunities in education to ensure children on reserve have access to high-quality learning that respects and embraces their culture.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said it's important to reflect on a 'dark chapter' in Canada's history and honour the children who survived residential schools and those who never made it home. He made the comment Wednesday on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation at an event in Fort Edmonton Park.

The Canadian Press

He said the government is building homes for families on reserve and throughout the country, improving access to drinking water, as well as placing an emphasis on mental wellness, primary care and culturally relevant care for First Nations.

NDP MP Leah Gazan, her party’s critic for Indigenous affairs, said in an interview that Mr. Carney’s comments on a day dedicated to residential-school survivors, who were removed from their families in the name of “nation-building,” show “how out of touch this government [is], and how uncommitted this government is to true reconciliation.”

She pointed to the release Wednesday of a report from the Permanent Peoples’ Tribunal, a human-rights organization, that called on the government to rescind the Building Canada Act, which allows it to accelerate projects designated in the national interest. The report said the law “uses ‘projects of national interest’ to justify the persistent land dispossession of Indigenous Peoples.”

Ms. Gazan also noted that the government in its June legislation removed language stating that those living on First Nations have a “human right” to clean drinking water, instead focusing on furthering progress toward that goal.

“As an Indigenous person – but not even as an Indigenous person, as a human being – I feel deeply hurt by the ongoing human-rights violations of the Carney Liberal government,” said Ms. Gazan, a member of Wood Mountain Lakota Nation in Saskatchewan.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s office did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday. But in a statement posted to X, he said residential schools “were a massive intrusion of government coercion imposed on Indigenous families.”

“On the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, we honour these children, their families and their communities, and recommit to reconciliation built on self-determination, opportunity, and true partnership,” he wrote.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.summary: Claims have spread online this week that a white nationalist group's demonstration at a First Nation in British Columbia, which has been denounced by authorities as "disgusting" and "cowardly," was in fact a false flag operation. The claims say the action was the work of government agents with purported goals ranging from stifling free speech to influencing…
stories.author: Timon Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada

Claims have spread online this week that a white nationalist group’s demonstration at a First Nation in British Columbia, which has been denounced by authorities as “disgusting” and “cowardly,” was in fact a false flag operation. The claims say the action was the work of government agents with purported goals ranging from stifling free speech to influencing the upcoming provincial election. But a number of elements, including statements by prominent members of the organization, point to the action being carried out by white nationalists.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Flu season off to an early start in these parts of Canada
stories.summary: Sniffles, coughs and an early start to flu season are showing up in several parts of the country.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown, P.E.I. – Sniffles, coughs and an early start to flu season are showing up in several parts of the country.

While respiratory illnesses typically ramp up in the fall, particularly in October, health authorities on P.E.I. are already reporting confirmed cases and hospitalizations. Alberta , B.C . and southwestern Ontario are also reporting an earlier-than-usual rise in illnesses, with increases beginning as early as September. Farther west, Yukon’s chief medical officer said lab-confirmed cases of influenza A have been identified since mid-August.

“This is the beginning of the beginning of the respiratory virus season,” said infectious diseases specialist Dr. Isaac Bogoch.

Nationally, circulation of COVID-19, influenza and RSV has been low , Bogoch said, though there is a slight uptick in the surveillance data. An official Canadian respiratory virus surveillance report update is set for Friday.

Vaccines and vulnerability

Provinces are beginning to roll out their vaccination programs, with some prioritizing high-risk people first.

Bogoch said anyone can develop a severe COVID-19 infection, but older adults are more vulnerable, with hospitalizations disproportionately concentrated in seniors 75 and older.

Among those who should be vaccinated, according to recommendations from the National Advisory Committee on Immunization, are people 65 and over, living in long-term care homes, or have underlying health conditions that put them at greater risk.

“Everyone else May be vaccinated. Some people will choose to do so. Some people May choose not to,” he said.

Influenza vaccines are recommended for everyone six months and older.

The flu most significantly impacts the oldest and youngest, Bogoch said, while chronic health conditions can also raise the risk. The same is true for RSV.

RSV protection remains a patchwork across Canada. Several provinces, including P.E.I., Ontario and Nova Scotia, cover infants under eight months, certain higher-risk groups and adults 75 and older.

What could be ahead

Outside a Shoppers Drug Mart in Charlottetown on Wednesday, some were seeking relief.

“Actually, I have a little cold right now,” Puga said. “I’m outside the pharmacy because we were looking for some stuff to help with this.”

“It’s the change of weather, so it can happen anytime,” said Ransford Adomah.

Experts look to the Southern Hemisphere for clues about what the colder months could look like, but Bogoch says respiratory viruses are “predictably unpredictable.”

Getting vaccinated, staying home when sick, masking and improving indoor air quality are among the tried-and-true ways to reduce the risk of infection and transmission, he said.

“We’ll get through it just like we’ve gone through every (cold season) before it.”

stories.title: ‘It was like a bomb’: Laval overpass collapse still haunts, 20 years later
stories.summary: It's been 20 years since the De la Concorde overpass collapsed, killing five people, but retired firefighter Guy Archambault can still recall arriving at the chaotic scene.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea, Dan Spector
stories.content:
Guy Archambault still has nightmares about the De la Concorde overpass collapse.

Twenty years since the Laval, Que., overpass collapsed on Highway 19 on Sept. 30, 2006, Archambault can still picture what it was like as one of the first responders to arrive at the scene.

“It was like a bomb explode,” the retired firefighter told Global News.

“They had a car with people trapped in the car. It was really bad to discover that.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "They had a car with people trapped in the car. It was really bad to discover that."

Five people were killed that day, including the parents of an eight-year-old boy and a couple that was expecting a baby. Six others were injured.

There had been warnings from drivers and an inspector who looked at the span just an hour before a 20-metre section of the overpass disintegrated.

But for a tragedy that scarred Quebec, Archambault is one of many who feel it’s not given the respect it deserves.

“It’s time to have something to commemorate the event,” he said.

The area’s outgoing MNA and Liberal candidate, Virginie Dufour, said the disaster deserves an annual remembrance ceremony like how the province does for other tragedies.

“For the families it’s very important, they need that to complete their grief,” Dufour said.

Dufour and the head of the Laval Historical Society have been in touch with the families of the victims, and even had a plaque made that everyone agrees on.

That plaque will be unveiled Wednesday, but the problem is – they can’t get permission to install it anywhere.

“I wrote to different ministers, and I just never got any reply whatsoever,” Dufour said.

“The advocates hope whoever the next government is they install some sort of monument to the victims, so families can get some closure.”

Transports Quebec told Global News though it’s sensitive to the families’ mourning, it’s not within the ministry’s practice to erect plaques or monuments.

A spokesperson added it’s not a safe place for pedestrians and motorists to stop and look at a plaque.

“History is not just about the grand narrative. It’s also about people,” said Jasmin Miville-Allard of the Laval Historical Society.

“I think they try to forget.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I think they try to forget."

A year-long inquiry headed by former Quebec premier Pierre-Marc Johnson didn’t lay any specific blame but called the collapse the result of a sequential chain of events.

However, the commission that investigated the accident did blame the Quebec Transport Ministry for failing to take the necessary steps to fix the structure.

The ministry now inspects overpasses and bridges every two or three years, instead of every five to six years.

stories.title: Mayor Josh Morgan blasts Susan Stevenson for campaign announcement on Truth and Reconciliation Day
stories.summary: Susan Stevenson called a campaign platform announcement Wednesday morning behind city hall to propose changes to council oversight, improved access to the Mayor’s office and to scrutinize senior administration.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Susan Stevenson called a campaign platform announcement Wednesday morning behind city hall to propose changes to council oversight, improved access to the Mayor’s office and to scrutinize senior administration.

Mayor Josh Morgan responded by blasting Stevenson for doing in on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

“Today is not a day for political campaign announcements,” Morgan told CTV News.

“This day belongs to survivors, their families and Indigenous communities.”

During Stevenson’s announcement she says she would not use strong mayor veto in the budget, she would like earlier access to agenda materials and financial information and would like significant spending decisions to go to council.

“it’s bringing back the decisions that are made here at council to the elected officials,” said Stevenson.

“Right now, many of the decisions are being made by civic administration and coming through for an approval, rather than being presented with the alternatives and being asked to make a decision.”

She added she would set up a finance committee to review financials quarterly, bring forward an independent municipal Auditor General and a confidential fraud and waste hotline, and review senior management which could then present a restructuring plan to reduce the size and cost of the top administration while protecting front-line service delivery.

“I don’t believe senior administration is being held accountable at all,” said Stevenson.

“We’re delegating the authority to make the decisions and then fulfill whatever the projects are without any oversight or report back. In many instances, even when the amounts go up into the hundreds of millions. So that’s an issue. The province took over the hospital and the school board, but they can’t take over council. That’s up to the people to do that. If people want their elected representatives to see the $1.4 billion budget line by line, if they want them to see an oversight and reports back on half $1 billion projects like BRT, then they need to elect a council that’s going to ask for that.”

stories.title: Ottawa is shifting its stance on ‘anti-Zionism’ — and the reactions so far are mixed
stories.summary: The federal government has identified "anti-Zionism" as a driver of anti-Jewish hate — a major policy shift that has prompted a range of reactions.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 5:14 pm.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 5:28 pm.

OTTAWA — The federal government has identified “anti-Zionism” as a driver of anti-Jewish hate — a major policy shift that has prompted a range of reactions.

The change took place on Sept. 24 when Public Safety Canada published a progress report on federal efforts promised in January to combat antisemitism.

The report said Ottawa sought to do a better job of recognizing and responding to “contemporary manifestations of antisemitism, including anti-Zionism.”

Here’s a closer look at the terminology, why it’s being used now and what it all means for free speech.

What is Zionism?

The Canadian Oxford Dictionary defines Zionism as “a movement originally for the re-establishment and now the development of a Jewish nation in what is now Israel.”

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, which identifies itself as a Zionist organization, says it means supporting the idea that “the Jewish people have the right to self-determination in their ancestral homeland.”

Opponents of Zionism argue the term has come to embody a colonial mentality that allows the Israeli government to subjugate Palestinians and seek to expand its borders.

The State of Israel was declared founded in May 1948, after the end of British rule over Palestine.

The founding of the state saw Zionist paramilitaries violently disperse Palestinians who were living there, while Arab states around the region responded by deporting Jews to Israel.

Carleton University political scientist Mira Sucharov surveyed American Jews on their views of Zionism and anti-Zionism in 2022.

“Self-proclaimed Zionists (Jewish or otherwise) and anti-Zionists (Jewish or otherwise) are talking about completely different things,” she wrote in a commentary in Haaretz.

She concluded that Jews embrace Zionism when it’s defined as “a belief in a Jewish and democratic state” and reject the term when it’s defined as “the belief in privileging Jewish rights over non-Jewish rights in Israel.”

What is anti-Zionism?

For decades, Jews in Canada and around the world have debated how Israel should operate and whether it amounts to a colonial project.

Independent Jewish Voices identifies as an anti-Zionist organization. It defines anti-Zionism as “the rejection of Jewish settler-colonialism in Palestine and belief that Palestinians deserve dignity and safety like all other people.”

The Association for Canadian Studies offered its own definition, which has prompted criticism from left-leaning groups.

“Anti-Zionism refers to a movement that calls for the erasure of Israel and denies the Jewish people the right to self-determination in part of their ancestral homeland,” the association wrote in a report Ottawa commissioned.

The Network of Engaged Canadian Academics, a group of mostly Jewish academics, argues “the latest incarnation of Jew hatred is anti-Zionism (which) relies on libel and distortion to claim that the Jewish collective, Israel, rather than the individual Jew, is uniquely evil.”

That ideology, the group argues, claims Jews have fabricated a claim to their ancestral land.

“Anti-Zionists dismiss Jews as nefarious settlers who have usurped the rights of the true Indigenous people, Palestinians,” the group wrote in a brief to senators.

stories.title: St. Thomas business owner shares emotional personal story on Truth and Reconciliation Day
stories.summary: Chris Patriquin had planned to take the microphone and continue to advocate for clean drinking water on Oneida Nation of the Thames during Truth and Reconciliation Day festivities.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Chris Patriquin had planned to take the microphone and continue to advocate for clean drinking water on Oneida Nation of the Thames during Truth and Reconciliation Day festivities.

The St. Thomas, Ont. man owns a water business and makes multiple deliveries every week to serve local First Nation communities.

“Sadly, this is a yearly reminder for all of you that our closest indigenous neighbors are still without clean, safe drinking water,” said Patriquin.

“The boil water advisory in Oneida Nation of the Thames continues to this day, seven years after it was initially announced. As I’ve stated before, in my opinion, the conversation around Truth and Reconciliation cannot truly start until all indigenous communities have clean, safe drinking water.”

However, his speech quickly pivoted to a very personal story after seeing a protest against Orange Shirt Day by Second Sons Canada this week.

“These cowardly, masked protesters were holding a sign that said, ‘Got Bones?’ similar to the ‘Got Milk?’ campaign,” said Patriquin.

“They were trying to deny the trauma of residential schools and the conversation around Truth and Reconciliation unless someone or anyone could produce the remains of dead children as proof, the residential school system was designed to take the Indian out of the child. It did not need to leave a body in every field to succeed. The evidence is in the families that are still healing, three and four generations later. Every indigenous person you meet is a survivor of this system.”

Patriquin said every Indigenous person is a survivor whether or not they ever set foot in a residential school.He went into detail about how when he was 23 years old, he tried to end his life.

He is grateful to have woken up 48 hours after taking pills and alcohol.Ten years later, his cousin took his life. He said they were both abused as young boys and after being told to keep it a secret, they did.

“Anger, insecurity, substance abuse, broken relationships, that’s what intergenerational trauma looks like,” he added.

“When there are no graves to dig and no bodies to count, it lives in the living. It shows up in the suicide rates, the addiction rates, the incarceration rates, the broken trust and the silence that still sits at so many kitchen tables.”

He says this day is about remembering a six-year-old named Phyllis Webster who had her orange shirt taken from her.

“That same system took the language, culture and safety from thousands of kids, some of those kids never came home,” said Patriquin.

“Many more came home carrying wounds that they are still passing down. The damage is real. The trauma is real. You do not need a body to prove it. You only need to listen to the living.”

The microphone was then handed to grass dancer Jonas Phillips.

He spoke about years of trauma leading to a family which used alcohol and drugs. He proudly told of his ability to get clean and sober and bringing his grandchildren to be in attendance to support teachings about the past.

“I heard someone today say the world reconciliation,” said Phillips.

“It should be Truth and Action. People like me have to be strong and get away from drugs and alcohol and do what they have to do to survive.”

He added that all Indigenous people are lucky to be alive.

“We all survived,” said Phillips.

“A very small percentage of people survived a very big genocide. I would like to show other people what I’m doing better, why I’m doing better, and how I could do better. If I can do it, anyone else can do it.”

The ceremony featured performances by Black Ops singers drum group, Indigenous hip hop artist Braeden Rickwood, Jingle Dress Dancers and guest speakers.

It did not need to leave a body in every field to succeed. The evidence is in the families that are still healing, three and four generations later. Every indigenous person you meet is a survivor of this system.”

content_blocks.alt: Chris Patriquin
content_blocks.caption: Chris Patriquin hugs his wife Jame during the Truth and Reconciliation Day ceremony in St. Thomas, Ont. on September 30, 2026 (Source: Brent Lale/CTV London)

content_blocks.text: Patriquin said every Indigenous person is a survivor whether or not they ever set foot in a residential school.He went into detail about how when he was 23 years old, he tried to end his life.

He is grateful to have woken up 48 hours after taking pills and alcohol.Ten years later, his cousin took his life. He said they were both abused as young boys and after being told to keep it a secret, they did.
“Anger, insecurity, substance abuse, broken relationships, that’s what intergenerational trauma looks like,” he added.

“When there are no graves to dig and no bodies to count, it lives in the living. It shows up in the suicide rates, the addiction rates, the incarceration rates, the broken trust and the silence that still sits at so many kitchen tables.”
He says this day is about remembering a six-year-old named Phyllis Webster who had her orange shirt taken from her.
“That same system took the language, culture and safety from thousands of kids, some of those kids never came home,” said Patriquin.
“Many more came home carrying wounds that they are still passing down. The damage is real. The trauma is real. You do not need a body to prove it. You only need to listen to the living.”

content_blocks.alt: Indigenous dancer Jonas Phillips
content_blocks.caption: Indigenous dancer Jonas Phillips poses at the end of his performance during the Truth and Reconciliation Day ceremony in St. Thomas, Ont. on September 30, 2026 (Source: Brent Lale/CTV London)

content_blocks.text: The microphone was then handed to grass dancer Jonas Phillips.

He spoke about years of trauma leading to a family which used alcohol and drugs. He proudly told of his ability to get clean and sober and bringing his grandchildren to be in attendance to support teachings about the past.
“I heard someone today say the world reconciliation,” said Phillips.
“It should be Truth and Action. People like me have to be strong and get away from drugs and alcohol and do what they have to do to survive.”
He added that all Indigenous people are lucky to be alive.
“We all survived,” said Phillips.

“A very small percentage of people survived a very big genocide. I would like to show other people what I’m doing better, why I’m doing better, and how I could do better. If I can do it, anyone else can do it.”
The ceremony featured performances by Black Ops singers drum group, Indigenous hip hop artist Braeden Rickwood, Jingle Dress Dancers and guest speakers.

stories.title: Young Canadians less hopeful about future of democracy: Statistics Canada
stories.summary: Prairie provinces, including Alberta, had the highest percentage of respondents who felt no hope at all about democracy while British Columbia led with those who felt very hopeful.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
A study released Tuesday suggests young Canadians are more likely to feel hopeless about the future of democracy in Canada than older residents.

The Statistics Canada study found about a quarter of respondents aged 25 to 44 were “not at all hopeful” when asked to think about the future and about how democracy works in Canada.

In comparison, those 65 and older were more likely to feel very hopeful (about 18 per cent) than not at all (about 10 per cent) about democracy’s functions.

The vast majority of those 15 and older were a little or somewhat hopeful about democracy in the country.

The study used data from a survey series conducted from 2022 to 2024 with a targeted sample size of about 70,000 people about democracy, their confidence in institutions and information, as well as their voting behaviour.

The response rate of the fifth and final panel, where the question was asked about hopefulness in democracy, was about 24 per cent.

Respondents were asked to respond to how hopeful they were about certain topics when thinking about the future in Canada, including “the way democracy works in Canada.”

They were asked to rate their feelings in one of four categories, ranging from not at all hopeful to very hopeful.

They were also asked about their confidence in institutions and information sources, voting behaviours and political participation.

The report comes as three major votes are set to be held in Canada in October — provincial elections in Quebec and British Columbia and a referendum in Alberta with a question on separation.

The Prairie provinces, including Alberta, had the highest percentage of respondents who felt no hope at all about democracy, about 25 per cent. British Columbia led with those who felt very hopeful, about 15 per cent.

The study didn’t find a link between faith in democracy and voter turnout but says those with no hope were more likely to participate in political activity.

The report also details how non-immigrants reported a less hopeful view on democracy than immigrants and non-permanent residents.

And it suggested that people with better mental health were more likely to feel very hopeful than those who reported poor mental health.

Respondents who said they were not hopeful at all about democracy reported lower trust in scientific experts and civic institutions, like Canadian news media and the justice system, and instead placed their trust in local businesses and police services.

Overall, the more faith respondents had in democracy, the more trust they said they placed on civic institutions, including Parliament and the school system.

stories.title: Cyclist dies after crash in Middlesex County
stories.summary: Middlesex OPP say a cyclist has died after a crash in Thames Centre.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Middlesex OPP say a cyclist has died after a crash in Thames Centre.

OPP, paramedics and firefighters responded to Richmond Street for a collision involving the cyclist around 12:22 p.m. on Wednesday.

Police say the cyclist was taken to hospital with life-threatening-injuries, but later died as a result of those injuries.

Richmond is expected to be closed for about three hours for the investigation.

stories.title: Federal Indigenous spending quadrupled to $40.8B under Trudeau, with 'negligible' improvement to communities
stories.summary: From 2014/15 to 2024/25, federal Indigenous spending increased to $40.8 billion, growing seven times faster than overall federal spending.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
In the decade leading up to 2024/25, inflation-adjusted federal Indigenous spending jumped from $10.3 billion to $40.8 billion, growing seven times faster than overall federal spending, according to a new study published by the Fraser Institute .

The independent think tank found that inflation-adjusted federal Indigenous spending increased by an average of 4.3 per cent per year from 1969/70 to 2014/15. But from 2014/15 to 2024/25, average annual Indigenous spending increased 17.1 per cent, not including the “substantial” spending on lawsuits and court settlement payouts.

Broken down by federal spending per province, annual federal Indigenous spending ranges from a low of $73 million in P.E.I. to a high of $8.8 billion in Ontario.

In B.C. in 2024/25, the federal government spent approximately $6.3 billion on program benefits for Indigenous people in the province — an average expenditure of $20,306 per Indigenous person, according to the study.

“Ottawa’s Indigenous spending has skyrocketed in recent years, even more so than general federal spending, which itself has increased substantially,” said Tom Flanagan, co-author of the study and senior fellow at the Fraser Institute.

“Canadians need to understand the magnitude of Ottawa’s Indigenous spending in recent years if they’re ever to properly assess what that additional spending is achieving in terms of results for Indigenous people.”

In former prime minster Justin Trudeau’s first major promise as part of his 2015 election campaign, he said that a Liberal government would invest a total of $2.6 billion in First Nations education .

Meanwhile, previous Fraser Institute research from 2024 found that federal Indigenous spending almost tripled under Trudeau, from $11 billion in 2015 to a projected $32 billion.

And in the spring economic update in April, the Carney government announced $601 million for culturally relevant elementary and secondary education on reserve, and $700 million over six years to support Indigenous communities implementing jurisdiction for child and family services.

However, Statistics Canada’s Community Well-Being index (CWB), which gauges the socio-economic health of Canadian communities, suggests the spending increases have led to little improvement for Indigenous communities.

The Fraser Institute’s analysis found that in 1981, the difference in the index between First Nations communities and other Canadian communities was 19.5 points. In 2016, the gap was 19.1 points, showing essentially no change after 35 years.

In 2021, the most recent year for which the data is available, that gap had shrunk somewhat to 16.3, but the Fraser Institute study argues that “closer analysis shows that improvement was due to an increase in the Canada Child Benefit, which is a general family support measure not included in Indigenous program spending.”

It adds that the positive impact of these spending increases on First Nations’ reserve communities “has been negligible.”

The Fraser Institute study, published on Tuesday, comes as Canada marks the sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, which honours residential school survivors and their families.

It is not the first report to suggest that the government is failing to improve the lives of First Nations people. In October 2025, an Auditor General follow-up on First Nations programs found that Indigenous Services Canada had made “unsatisfactory progress” in implementing recommendations made in six audits completed from 2015 to 2022.

The report said: “Despite an 84 per cent increase in the department’s spending on programs since the 2019-20 fiscal year, significant challenges remained in improving services and program outcomes for First Nations communities.”

paragraphs: In the decade leading up to 2024/25, inflation-adjusted federal Indigenous spending jumped from $10.3 billion to $40.8 billion, growing seven times faster than overall federal spending, according to a new study published by the Fraser Institute .

The independent think tank found that inflation-adjusted federal Indigenous spending increased by an average of 4.3 per cent per year from 1969/70 to 2014/15. But from 2014/15 to 2024/25, average annual Indigenous spending increased 17.1 per cent, not including the “substantial” spending on lawsuits and court settlement payouts.
Broken down by federal spending per province, annual federal Indigenous spending ranges from a low of $73 million in P.E.I. to a high of $8.8 billion in Ontario.

In B.C. in 2024/25, the federal government spent approximately $6.3 billion on program benefits for Indigenous people in the province — an average expenditure of $20,306 per Indigenous person, according to the study.

“Ottawa’s Indigenous spending has skyrocketed in recent years, even more so than general federal spending, which itself has increased substantially,” said Tom Flanagan, co-author of the study and senior fellow at the Fraser Institute.

“Canadians need to understand the magnitude of Ottawa’s Indigenous spending in recent years if they’re ever to properly assess what that additional spending is achieving in terms of results for Indigenous people.”
In former prime minster Justin Trudeau’s first major promise as part of his 2015 election campaign, he said that a Liberal government would invest a total of $2.6 billion in First Nations education .
Meanwhile, previous Fraser Institute research from 2024 found that federal Indigenous spending almost tripled under Trudeau, from $11 billion in 2015 to a projected $32 billion.

And in the spring economic update in April, the Carney government announced $601 million for culturally relevant elementary and secondary education on reserve, and $700 million over six years to support Indigenous communities implementing jurisdiction for child and family services.

However, Statistics Canada’s Community Well-Being index (CWB), which gauges the socio-economic health of Canadian communities, suggests the spending increases have led to little improvement for Indigenous communities.

The Fraser Institute’s analysis found that in 1981, the difference in the index between First Nations communities and other Canadian communities was 19.5 points. In 2016, the gap was 19.1 points, showing essentially no change after 35 years.

In 2021, the most recent year for which the data is available, that gap had shrunk somewhat to 16.3, but the Fraser Institute study argues that “closer analysis shows that improvement was due to an increase in the Canada Child Benefit, which is a general family support measure not included in Indigenous program spending.”
It adds that the positive impact of these spending increases on First Nations’ reserve communities “has been negligible.”
The Fraser Institute study, published on Tuesday, comes as Canada marks the sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, which honours residential school survivors and their families.

It is not the first report to suggest that the government is failing to improve the lives of First Nations people. In October 2025, an Auditor General follow-up on First Nations programs found that Indigenous Services Canada had made “unsatisfactory progress” in implementing recommendations made in six audits completed from 2015 to 2022.

The report said: “Despite an 84 per cent increase in the department’s spending on programs since the 2019-20 fiscal year, significant challenges remained in improving services and program outcomes for First Nations communities.”

Elsewhere, a 2022 analysis carried out by the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer found that while financial resources allocated to providing Indigenous services had “increased significantly” for the 2015/2016 to 2022/2023 period, it hadn’t resulted in an improvement in the ability of the organizations to achieve their goals.
In fact, the document said, “the ability to achieve the targets specified has declined.”

stories.title: Riders host Stamps in important division showdown
stories.summary: It's another important West Division contest for Trevor Harris and the Saskatchewan Roughriders.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
It’s another important West Division contest for Trevor Harris and the Saskatchewan Roughriders.

Saskatchewan (8-6) hosts the Calgary Stampeders (7-8) on Friday night. The Riders can sweep the season series 2-0 with a win after earning a 40-37 overtime decision back in June.

Conversely, a win by four or more points would not only move Calgary into a tie with Saskatchewan in the standings but give it the season series — and the tiebreaker if the two teams ended the year with identical records.

The defending Grey Cup champions are coming off a 31-24 road loss to B.C. (8-6) that gave the Lions the tiebreaker in that series.

The Stampeders are coming off a home-and-home sweep of the Ottawa Redblacks. Vernon Adams Jr. threw for 422 yards and three TDs in last week’s 45-31 victory while Jalen Philpot (six catches, 127 yards), Tevin Jones (eight catches, 122 yards, TD) and Clark Barnes (three catches, 109 yards, TD) all cracked the century mark in receiving.

Saskatchewan has dropped its last two contests. Harris completed 26 of 33 passes for 297 yards and a TD last week versus B.C., and the Riders’ offence had the ball for almost 34 minutes in the contest.

But Lions’ starter Nathan Rourke finished 22 of 28 passing for 375 yards and four TDs.

Calgary comes in leading the CFL in offensive points per game (33.1) and offensive TDs (53) and stands second in passing TDs (31). But the Riders should present an interesting matchup with a defence that’s allowed a league-low 35 offensive touchdowns and is second in fewest offensive points (25.5 per game) surrendered.

The Stampeders have allowed 34 sacks this season, behind only Winnipeg (36). Saskatchewan’s defence has 32 sacks, second-most behind Toronto (37).

Pick: Saskatchewan.

Hamilton Tiger-Cats vs Ottawa Redblacks (Friday night)

At Ottawa, two teams eliminated from playoff contention look to snap long losing streaks. Hamilton (4-11) has dropped five straight, including last week’s 37-35 overtime decision in Edmonton that ended its playoff hopes. Harrison Frost completed 17 of 34 passes for 214 yards with two TDs and two interceptions. McLeod Bethel-Thompson is expected to remain the starter for the Redblacks (0-14) after passing for 418 yards and two TDs last week versus Calgary. The offence had 475 net yards, but the Stamps rolled up 520 yards. However, the Ticats are last in offensive yards (330.4) and passing (253.3) and just ahead of last-place Ottawa (23.6) in offensive points scored (23.7).

B.C. Lions vs Toronto Argonauts (Saturday afternoon)

At Toronto, the Argos (9-6) chase a fifth straight win, having already clinched second in the East. Chad Kelly leads the CFL in passing yards (5,067), TDs (33) and interceptions (24) and was limited in practice Wednesday (hand) after not practising at all Tuesday. If he can’t go, veteran Nick Arbuckle will look to improve the team’s record at BMO Field to 5-0. B.C. comes off its big win over Saskatchewan and is looking for a third straight victory and eighth in nine games. Rourke is the offensive catalyst, but Zander Horvath has a CFL-best 16 rushing TDs and is within striking distance of the league records for most rushing touchdowns (19) and total touchdowns (23) in a season.

Winnipeg Blue Bombers vs Montreal Alouettes (Saturday night)

At Montreal, the Alouettes (11-3) come off a bye week with a chance to clinch first in the East with a win and a Toronto loss to B.C. The Als are 9-2 coming off a bye under head coach Jason Maas, who’s in his fourth season at the helm. They’re also 7-0 at home thus far. Dru Brown starts again for Winnipeg (7-7) with incumbent Zach Collaros (head) out. Brown completed 16 of 28 passes for 193 yards with two TDs and two interceptions in last week’s 30-28 home loss to Toronto. The West Division team did earn a 44-28 win in the last meeting between the two squads in August, although Alexander also had four TD strikes in that contest.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Breaking: Four pedestrians struck during Truth and Reconciliation Day walk near Tsawwassen Mills, B.C.
stories.summary: Delta police are asking people to stay away from Tsawwassen First Nation lands in South Delta after 4 pedestrians were struck by a vehicle.
stories.author: David Carrigg
stories.content:
Two pedestrians were killed outside an entrance to the Tsawwassen Mills mall in South Delta on Wednesday morning.

According to the Delta Police Department, the driver of the vehicle that hit the pair May have experienced a medical emergency before the collision. Two other pedestrians were injured.

“Four pedestrians were struck and, tragically, two people have died as a result of their injuries,” the police statement said.

“The remaining injured individuals were treated at the scene by B.C. Emergency Health Services and transported to hospital.”

Police said the incident was not related to the Truth and Reconciliation Walk that was taking place nearby on Tsawwassen First Nation lands at the time. The mall is also on the First Nation’s lands.

However, images from the scene show many people affected by the tragedy were wearing orange Truth and Reconciliation Day T-shirts.

The Tsawwassen First Nation confirmed that the incident had occurred at the same time as their Truth and Reconciliation Day walk was underway.

“Out of respect for Tsawwassen First Nation families and ongoing response efforts, we will not be providing additional details at this time. Further information will be shared when appropriate,” the TFN statement read.

“Tsawwassen First Nation extends its sincere gratitude to the Delta Police Department, emergency responders, and community members who assisted during the incident.”

“Tsawwassen First Nation is in our hearts today. To lose two beloved elders — in such a terrifying accident and on a day already so heavy with grief — is devastating,” he said. “My thoughts are with the loved ones of those who died, those who were injured, and the entire community who are in grief and shock.”

The black truck that appeared to have struck the pedestrians was towing a trailer and was marked Alpine Services. Alpine Services has had a cleaning contract at the mall since 2019.

The incident occurred close to the No. 3 south entrance to the mall. It appears that the truck was being driven close to the entrance when it crashed through an awning in front of Boston Pizza, then struck a brick wall.

An air ambulance and several road ambulances were dispatched to the scene.

B.C. Premier David Eby said he was awaiting more information on the incident.

“On a day already set aside for solemn reflection, a tragedy during the Tsawwassen First Nation Truth and Reconciliation event has shocked and saddened us all,” he wrote on social media.

“Police say it appears the driver of the vehicle experienced a medical event before the collision. As we wait for more details, our thoughts are with the families, with those injured, and with everyone at Tsawwassen First Nation.”

stories.title: Police in Delta, B.C., say four hurt in crash involving medical emergency
stories.summary: Delta — Police in Delta, B.C., say four pedestrians have been struck and hurt by a vehicle in what appears to have been a medical incident.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Police in Delta, B.C., say two people have been killed in a crash at the Tsawwassen Mills mall and two others are injured.

They say early information indicates the driver of the vehicle May have experienced a medical emergency before the collision.

Police say the injured were treated at the scene by ambulance teams and transported to hospital.

“The incident is not related to the Truth and Reconciliation Walk that was taking place on Tsawwassen First Nation lands at the time,” police said in an updated news release on Wednesday.

“There is no ongoing risk to public safety.”

Video posted online from the scene at the Tsawwassen Mills shopping centre shows a truck against the mall’s exterior and police tape surrounding the area, along with ambulances and a helicopter in the parking lot.

A statement from Tsawwassen First Nation says it is deeply saddened to confirm the incident, which occurred during its walk for truth and reconciliation.

The Nation says it would not share additional details at this time out of respect for families and ongoing response efforts.

Both police and the Nation have asked people to avoid the area.

stories.title: Two dead, two injured after vehicle hits pedestrians at B.C.’s Tsawwassen Mills mall
stories.summary: The driver May have experienced a medical emergency prior to the crash, police say
stories.author: Alanna Smith, Zosia Bielski
stories.content:
Two people were killed after being struck by a vehicle on the Tsawwassen First Nation in British Columbia on Wednesday, according to police.

Delta Police, in a statement, said the collision took place at approximately 10:25 a.m. local time. Four pedestrians were hit, two of whom have died as a result of their injuries. The two injured victims have been transported to hospital.

“Preliminary information indicates the driver of the involved vehicle May have experienced a medical emergency prior to the collision,” said the police service. “Our thoughts are with the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic incident.”

The collision occurred in the parking lot at Tsawwassen Mills mall. It was not related to the event marking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation and there is no ongoing risk to public safety, said police.

“The investigation remains in its early stages as officers work to determine all of the circumstances surrounding the collision.”

Tsawwassen First Nation, in a statement, said it is “deeply saddened” by the incident, which they said occurred during Wednesday’s Truth and Reconciliation walk.

The nation said it will not be providing any additional information at this time out of respect for the affected families and ongoing response efforts. Tsawwassen thanked the police, emergency responders and community members for their efforts.

People are being asked to avoid the area.

stories.title: U.S. trade court scrutinizes Trump’s forced labour tariffs
stories.summary: Four small businesses and 25 Democratic-led states argue that the tariffs, applied to imports from 60 trading partners, including Canada, far exceed the president's authority.
stories.author: Dietrich Knauth
stories.content:
The U.S. Court of International Trade on Wednesday scrutinized the legal and factual underpinnings of U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest global tariffs , which were imposed on nearly all U.S. imports over allegations trading partners aren’t doing enough to stop forced labour.

A panel of three judges appointed by Presidents Trump, Barack Obama and Joe Biden heard arguments in Manhattan over lawsuits alleging that the latest tariffs are an attempt to revive the unchecked tariff power the Supreme Court struck down in February.

Four small businesses and 25 Democratic-led states argue that the tariffs, applied to imports from 60 trading partners including Canada, the EU and China, far exceed the president’s authority.

Pratik Shah, an attorney representing small businesses that sued over the tariffs, told the court that the Trump administration has misused a law that offers only a “carefully constrained” tariff authority.

In its rush to impose new tariffs, the Trump administration skipped the legal requirements to make country-specific findings that each of the tariffs was justified, Shah said. Shah contrasted the tariffs with duties imposed under the same law during Trump’s first term, when the US Trade Representative produced country-by-country reports and imposed tariffs tailored to each economy.

“If you’re going to do it at breakneck speed and try to cover the entire globe, you still have to satisfy the statutory requirements,” Shah said.

Eric Hamilton, representing the U.S. Department of Justice, said the U.S. Trade Representative had thoroughly evaluated the prevalence of goods produced with forced labour in international commerce. The government did not need to show “with metaphysical certainty” that forced labour was a “burden” on US commerce before imposing tariffs, he said.

The panel is expected to issue a written ruling in the coming weeks.

The plaintiffs asked the court to throw out the tariffs entirely. The court could also issue a more limited ruling that asks the government to re-do its investigation to provide more detail and justifications for the tariffs, as the court did with some of Trump’s tariffs in his first term.

The judges interrupted attorneys for both sides soon after they began their arguments, peppering them with questions about the level of detail required in the government’s investigation into forced labour in other countries before deciding to apply tariffs.

They asked Shah whether he was simply asking for “more paper” from the government, and they asked Hamilton whether the government was ignoring more detailed statutory requirements that dealt specifically with forced labour, rather than relying on broader authority about “unreasonable” trade practices.

Trump has made tariffs a central pillar of his foreign policy, using them as leverage to negotiate trade deals around the globe. But the Supreme Court ruled against most of Trump’s widest-ranging tariffs on February 20, finding that the president cannot use emergency economic powers to unilaterally impose tariffs on all US trading partners.

Trump responded by immediately imposing a temporary 10 per cent global tariff under a different U.S. law. When those temporary tariffs expired, he invoked another legal authority to impose in July the forced labour tariffs now being challenged, which range from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent.

The plaintiffs’ lawsuits, consolidated before the court, argue the administration failed to satisfy the legal requirements for imposing the tariffs and is using concerns about forced labour as a pretext to revive a broad tariff authority that U.S. courts have repeatedly rejected.

The Trump administration argued in court papers that it had conducted real investigations into other nations’ failure to prevent imports of goods produced with forced labour, and concluded that tariffs were warranted for each of the 60 investigated trading partners.
