stories.title: Staying the course: why some Fanshawe students switch programs
stories.summary: For some Fanshawe students, the program they start in isn't always the program they finish. Interests, career ...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
For some Fanshawe students, the program they start in isn’t always the program they finish. Interests, career goals and new experiences can all play a role in deciding whether to stay or make a change.

Human resources student Sahar Yousefi said her original program pre-health didn’t meet her long-term goals.

“I decided to switch because I kind of realized that the program didn’t really fit my long-term goals. I had kind of like a switch desire and career path. So I kind of wanted to take a different route with my career,” she said.

She said that her original program wasn’t what she expected and why she switched.

“No, it was kind of odd that I expected a lot of math, science and whatnot, just wasn’t really aligning with what I had envisioned for my future,” she said.

She said that switching has affected her, and caused a set back.

“It’s set me back in some time, that’s for sure. I don’t really pay attention to the cost, which maybe I should, but I’m kind of putting that in the back of my mind for now and kind of focusing on what I need to get done and what feels comfortable for me,” she said.

She said students can decide to switch their programs for a lot of reasons.

“This could be a lot of reasons. It varies from person to person. Sometimes people kind of like, have a change in mind or like they get a feel of their program and realize its not really what they’re looking for, and that’s totally okay and it happens. That’s what college is for,” she said.

“Its one of those kind of things where you have to kind of jump in and see what its like to really see if its a right fit for you or not,” she said.

Cited federal national center for education statistics (Nces) longitudinal estimate found about 30 per cent of U.S. undergraduates switch their programs at least once according to [Research.com].

Robyn Naylor, co-operative education consultant employment and student entrepreneurial services at Fanshawe College said that she thinks there’s a variety of reasons why students switch.

“I think a lot of times they find out that the program wasn’t the right fit for them. They might have learned a little bit about some of the career pathways and those aren’t aligning with what they want to be doing. Or they might find that the courses are either too challenging or aren’t challenging enough and don’t fit what they kind of signed up for,” she said.

“It could end up costing you more in the end because you would have maybe already paid for a program and hadn’t made the decision in time and then have to sign up again to enroll into a new one,” she said.

Fanshawe human resources student Dansea Steckly said that she wanted to stay in her program because she likes business, and she loves the environment.

“I really like business and it was the cheapest option,” she said.

“I really love all the classes I have and all the teachers are so friendly,” she said.

“Its been pretty much exactly what I’ve expected, like a mix of all the business courses, and I find it all very interesting and I love it,” she said.

“I was kind of considering switching into marketing, but I’m not sure yet because its only been a month, but we’ll see,” she said.

“I took a bunch of marketing classes in high school, so I have already like, know a bunch of boat marketing and I think its like the most interesting thing ever. And I would love to do that, but as of right now, I’m in human resources,” she said.

She said that she does not feel confident yet if she chose the right program for her future.

“Not yet, because I haven’t actually taken like an actual human resources course yet. But I’ve taken like all the other business ones and I’m confident that I want to be in business,” she said.

Naylor said that Fanshawe has many supportive resources for students who are considering the switch.

(Torey Joseph Legarrie)

“Absolutely, they can speak to program coordinators, academic advisors, pathway coordinators, career consultants, any folks in the student services area to get some support there,” she said.

“I think talk to your faculty, make sure that you’re taking the time to thoughtfully make the decision, do research in the new program that you’re looking for. Whether that would be looking at different career paths, different outcomes of employment on the Canada Job Bank, to really make sure you’re making a thoughtful decision around it,” she said.

“It’s set me back in some time, that’s for sure. I don’t really pay attention to the cost, which maybe I should, but I’m kind of putting that in the back of my mind for now and kind of focusing on what I need to get done and what feels comfortable for me,” she said.
She said students can decide to switch their programs for a lot of reasons.

“This could be a lot of reasons. It varies from person to person. Sometimes people kind of like, have a change in mind or like they get a feel of their program and realize its not really what they’re looking for, and that’s totally okay and it happens. That’s what college is for,” she said.
“Its one of those kind of things where you have to kind of jump in and see what its like to really see if its a right fit for you or not,” she said.

stories.title: Sharia law 'religious divorce' fails to fly with Immigration and Refugee Board
stories.summary: "Honesty is not the prerogative of educated people," said the Immigration and Refugee Board panel in its decision.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Canadian Muslim who tried to sponsor his Ethiopian wife for a permanent resident visa is out of luck because her “religious divorce” from her first husband under Sharia law isn’t recognized here.

Fetno Umer Kemo appealed a visa officer’s decision to deny Rahama Adem Abdi the document that allows foreign nationals to live, work and study anywhere in Canada indefinitely to the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada. But the panel concluded that Kemo failed to establish that Abdi was “free to marry” when they wed in 2021.

“Mr. Kemo has not shown that Ms. Abdi’s religious divorce in 2017 was valid under Canadian law,” the panel said in a decision published in June in French and this month in an English translation.

“As a result, the officer’s decision not to issue his wife a visa is valid in law. The couple’s marriage is not valid, and Ms. Abdi is therefore not a member of the family class. The panel does not have jurisdiction to consider humanitarian and compassionate considerations in this case. The appeal is dismissed.”

The visa officer further determined that the couple’s relationship was not genuine and that their marriage was entered into primarily for immigration purposes.

The panel said it didn’t have to consider “the issues of the genuineness of the couple’s relationship or their intent at the time of their marriage” because their marriage isn’t “valid under Canadian law.”

Canada’s Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations “state that a foreign national shall not be considered the sponsor’s spouse if the foreign national was, at the time of their marriage, the spouse of another person,” said the decision.

During her immigration interview last year, Abdi said her divorce was carried out verbally by religious authorities in Ethiopia. Her ex-husband took part remotely by telephone, she said.

In the same interview, Abdi didn’t “submit any official document attesting to her divorce,” said the decision.

That led the visa officer to conclude that, “at the time of her marriage to Mr. Kemo, Ms. Abdi was still legally married to her first husband, contrary to the requirements of the regulations.”

Kemo argued that Abdi’s first marriage and divorce “took place in Ethiopia in a rural context where issuing and registering official documents is the exception, not the rule,” said the decision.

Kemo gave the panel a document attesting to Abdi’s divorce. “It is a judgment issued by Ethiopian judicial authorities recognizing Ms. Abdi’s divorce. The judgment was rendered on January 1, 2026.”

The panel sided with the visa officer, finding that Abdi’s first marriage was not legally dissolved in 2021, and she was therefore still married to her first husband when she married Kemo.

Abdi is approximately 38, but she doesn’t know her exact age. “At the hearing, she described herself as someone who could not read or write.”

Canadian immigration authorities interviewed her in April 2023 in Canada, and again in June 2025 in Ethiopia.

At her first interview, Abdi said her first marriage to Abdulasit Aman “lasted approximately one and a half years.”

They had a child, according to the decision.

“When the officer asked why her first marriage and child had not been disclosed in the immigration forms, Ms. Abdi gave contradictory answers. Ms. Abdi initially stated that she had argued with her ex-husband about whether or not to include her child in the immigration documents. Ms. Abdi then stated that she and Mr. Kemo had agreed not to include this information in the sponsorship application.”

At the end of the 2023 interview, the visa officer told Abdi “that he was refusing the sponsorship application and that she had to leave Canada, given her misrepresentations,” said the decision, noting that Adbi had the right to try again.

Kemo submitted a second application to sponsor Abdi in August 2023. “At her second interview, in 2025, Ms. Abdi stated that she had been abducted and forced into marriage. Ms. Abdi recounted how two days after her abduction, her marriage to her first husband was celebrated and validated at a Nikah ceremony attended by the elders of both families.”

Abdi went on to say “that her first marriage was not legal because she had been forced to marry her first husband.”

The panel noted Abdi “said nothing about a forced marriage” at her first hearing.

“Ms. Abdi instead explained that her mother had wanted her to marry and that she agreed to do so. That explanation directly contradicts Ms. Abdi’s statements at her second interview and at the hearing,” said the decision.

The panel gave “more weight” to her first explanation, “in accordance with the principle that ‘a person’s first story is usually the most genuine and, therefore, the one to be most believed.’”

But the officers who interviewed her in 2023 and 2025 “both concluded that Ms. Abdi had not answered their questions truthfully.”

The officer who interviewed her last year “confronted Ms. Abdi, who had stated that she spoke little Amharic and did not understand. Ms. Abdi defended herself by stating that she did not talk much at the 2023 interview. When the officer pointed out to her that the recording of the 2023 interview shows she spoke throughout it in Amharic, Ms. Abdi gave no explanation.” The panel noted the 2023 interview lasted more than three hours.

The panel “does not find” Abdi credible, said the decision.

“Throughout the sponsorship application process, Ms. Abdi had a duty of candour and truthfulness,” it said.

“Ms. Abdi cannot discharge this duty by pointing to her illiteracy. Honesty is not the prerogative of educated people.”

stories.title: Indigenous constable designs uniform patch for Western officers to signal safety, support
stories.summary: Indigenous officer Jonathan Jamieson designed a new patch for Western Special Constable Service uniforms to open dialogue and promote safety.
stories.author: Megan Stacey
stories.content:
An idea that came to Jonathan Jamieson in the middle of an overnight shift is now being implemented across the Western Special Constable Service, with a new addition to uniforms during Truth and Reconciliation Week.

Jamieson designed a patch for Wscs members to show support and open dialogue with Indigenous communities. His concept was inspired by the Medicine Wheel, a teaching framework used and adapted across many Indigenous communities. In this patch, the Medicine Wheel is represented by four quadrants of white, yellow, red and black.

“It’s surreal that this is happening. It’s so cool to know my patch is going to be worn by our team,” said Jamieson, an Indigenous special constable who joined Wscs in 2024.

“I want to promote open and honest communication that fosters the positive interaction between our service and the Indigenous community. Normalizing positive interactions with those in the uniform is one of my priorities, because I know the barriers can be big and deep. I hope this design helps to signal ‘yes, I’m wearing a vest, but I’m a human being still,’” he said.

Jonathan Jamieson with the Western Special Constable Service designed a patch to be worn on uniforms during days of recognition for Indigenous communities, including National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Jamieson said he understands the trauma and uncertainty many Indigenous people carry and feel toward law enforcement.

He hopes the new patch – which will be worn during special days and times of year, including National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Treaty Week in November, National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Women, Girls, and Two- Spirited people (Red Dress Day)on May 5 and Indigenous History Month in June – will highlight special constables as a supportive force for all on campus.

“I want to help build understanding and trust. We know there are some who won’t report concerns to us because there’s mistrust. We want you to come to us when you have troubles,” he said of Western constables.

Bill Chantler, director of Campus Safety and Emergency Services at Western, said he was pleased to see Jamieson’s vision come to fruition.

“We are very proud of Jonathan and this initiative towards building a stronger community. Jonathan is very thoughtful and genuine, and he truly makes a difference with our campus community through his service as a member of the Western Special Constable Service,” Chantler said.

‘Help someone through a tough time’

Joining Wscs showed Jamieson the possibilities that come with community-focused approaches to policing, from clothing drives to supporting those in mental health crises.

“We’re always seeking genuine engagement. Not just our patrol division, but the community resources team as well. It’s inspiring to be here and be part of that,” he said.“I want to be that person who can help someone through a tough time. I want to make their life a little bit easier, a little bit better.”

Jamieson is no stranger to facing challenges.

Raised by his grandmother, who died when he was 16, Jamieson navigated significant instability, including bouts of homelessness.

“I focused on how I could pick myself back up. I managed to get back on my feet after having nothing. I got my security licence and started building connections.”

It led him to the world of policing, starting at Fanshawe College with the police foundations program. He started to dream of a world where he could make a difference.

After working for campus and hospital security teams, Jamieson applied to work with Wscs. Two years into his role at Western, he sees himself staying long-term, now setting goals to becoming a coach officer and sergeant.

Colleagues and mentors have demonstrated the importance of prioritizing relationships and human interactions, whether that’s responding to students in crisis or addressing emergencies on campus.

“There’s always an emphasis on support first – how can we make this better, make life easier? I don’t think I would be in this position today if I hadn’t gone through what I went through. I base it on my own experience.”

It’s also what inspired the new patch.

Jamieson is excited to see his idea turned from dream to reality, and eager to see the design worn by Wscs members throughout the year.

“This wasn’t for profit or to give me an advantage; that was never my mindset. I did it for change, for hope, for building new trust within the community,” Jamieson said.

“Sometimes people see us and they don’t see the people behind the vest. I’m hopeful this patch eventually fosters this change.”

stories.title: Ksi Lisims LNG signs long-term supply deal with Centrica
stories.summary: Under the agreement, the parent company behind British Gas will buy one million tonnes of LNG per year for 20 years
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ksi Lisims LNG LP has signed a long-term supply deal with Centrica Energy for its proposed liquefied natural gas export facility.

Under the agreement, the parent company behind British Gas will buy one million tonnes of LNG per year for 20 years.

Ksi Lisims LNG has proposed a floating export facility located on the northwest coast of B.C. with capacity for 12 million tonnes of LNG per year.

With the Centrica commitment, the company says it has signed agreements covering nine million tonnes per year of its planned capacity.

Houston-based Western LNG is the lead developer and future operator of Ksi Lisims alongside Rockies LNG, a consortium of Canadian natural gas producers, and the Nisga’a Nation, ON whose lands the project is planned.

First shipments from the project, which is still subject to a final investment decision, are expected in the early 2030s.

stories.title: You Had to Be There review: Godspell documentary is a holy lot of fun
stories.summary: Nick Davis’s film tells the story of the stage musical’s cultural impact
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
You Had to Be There

Directed by Nick Davis

Written by Nick Davis and Jane Mendelsohn Davis

Starring Martin Short, Dave Thomas, Stephen Schwartz

Classification NR; 98 minutes

Opens in Toronto, Kingston and Ottawa Oct. 2, with further screenings to follow

When the hippie musical Godspell opened in 1972 in Toronto, Globe and Mail theatre critic Herbert Whittaker wrote, “Things are certainly starting to happen over at the Royal Alexandra Theatre.”

Wasn’t that the truth.

Nick Davis’s engaging and upbeat documentary You Had to Be There tells the story of the stage musical’s cultural impact and of the nascent, mostly Canadian ensemble cast of Godspell , which went on to achieve so much in show business. Among them were Martin Short, Gilda Radner, Eugene Levy, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Jayne Eastwood, Dave Thomas and musical director Paul Shaffer.

The Toronto comedic scene at the time also included Dan Aykroyd, Catherine O’Hara and John Candy. The collective talent helped stock the early Second City Toronto troupes (which led to television’s Sctv ) and the casts of Saturday Night Live (produced by Toronto’s Lorne Michaels).

Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty! movie review: The best Sundance movie that 2004 never delivered

Terry Fox documentary Run Terry Run proves just how long a legacy can last

Godspell , a clown-happy musical from Stephen Schwartz and John-Michael Tebelak based on the Gospel of Matthew, opened off-Broadway in 1971. The hit staging spawned numerous productions elsewhere but none that took off like the Toronto production in 1972 and ‘73.

Davis’s film attempts to explain why the Canadian staging was such a phenomenon − why, as the documentary poses, it was responsible for a “good chunk of the comedy royalty who would go on to blaze unprecedented careers in the world of entertainment.”

Composer-lyricist Schwartz says it came down to timing. The talent came of age in a culturally tumultuous time when cornball comedy began to give way to zanier humour. As the film puts it, “ Godspell seemed to be the joy that the world needed.”

American director Davis had most of the cast members at his disposal. Their delight in reminiscing is the film’s heartbeat. What Davis didn’t have was much in the way of video or audio from the production. Only because of a bootleg tape made by Short are we able to hear the cast in action. (Radner saw the tiny microphones Short set up at the rear of the stage and purposely sang into them. Other cast members guided her back to the rest of the group.)

The animation used to recreate onstage and off-stage memories adds to the film’s zip. Not that the doc was lacking it otherwise − Short, Levy, Thomas, Eastwood and Shaffer are talking heads worth their weight in storytelling gold.

On the other hand, the random use of commentators such as SNL ’s Heidi Gardner and James Austin Johnson is mysterious and unrewarding. Johnson, 37, is a gifted comedian but not on firm footing as a cultural anthropologist. “There was an interest in growing your hair out and growing your beard out, and Jesus just kind of slides right in there,” he says in an attempt to explain the popularity of a musical with the son of God as the star character.

Mind you, it’s the director’s fault, not Johnson’s, that the popularity of religion at the time was not explored more deeply as context. In an archival news clip from outside the Royal Alex on opening night, a woman says the musical was a “real Christian experience.”

There was a sudden surge in the early 1970s of young people adopting Christian faith. A Time magazine cover story in 1971 coined the phrase “the Jesus Revolution.” I mean, the Doobie Brothers had a hit single with the gospel song Jesus Is Just Alright at the same time Godspell was playing to sold-out crowds in Toronto.

After the 14 month-run was over, the cast scattered. Garber had already left the Toronto production after three months to star in David Greene’s film version of the musical. (Though Titanic’ s Gerber is a fine actor, he is less than convincing with his claim to have been “heartbroken” when he was picked for the Godspell movie in New York.)

As for the documentary’s title, it comes from Sctv ’s Thomas. He joined the Godspell cast as replacement but watched the Canadian premiere as an audience member.

“I don’t think you can capture the spirit of what I saw on opening night at the Royal Alex in Toronto,” he says. “I think that that’s one of those experiences where you had to be there.”

When the hippie musical Godspell opened in 1972 in Toronto, Globe and Mail theatre critic Herbert Whittaker wrote, “Things are certainly starting to happen over at the Royal Alexandra Theatre.”
Wasn’t that the truth.

Nick Davis’s engaging and upbeat documentary You Had to Be There tells the story of the stage musical’s cultural impact and of the nascent, mostly Canadian ensemble cast of Godspell , which went on to achieve so much in show business. Among them were Martin Short, Gilda Radner, Eugene Levy, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Jayne Eastwood, Dave Thomas and musical director Paul Shaffer.

The Toronto comedic scene at the time also included Dan Aykroyd, Catherine O’Hara and John Candy. The collective talent helped stock the early Second City Toronto troupes (which led to television’s Sctv ) and the casts of Saturday Night Live (produced by Toronto’s Lorne Michaels).
Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty! movie review: The best Sundance movie that 2004 never delivered
Terry Fox documentary Run Terry Run proves just how long a legacy can last

Godspell , a clown-happy musical from Stephen Schwartz and John-Michael Tebelak based on the Gospel of Matthew, opened off-Broadway in 1971. The hit staging spawned numerous productions elsewhere but none that took off like the Toronto production in 1972 and ‘73.

Davis’s film attempts to explain why the Canadian staging was such a phenomenon − why, as the documentary poses, it was responsible for a “good chunk of the comedy royalty who would go on to blaze unprecedented careers in the world of entertainment.”

Composer-lyricist Schwartz says it came down to timing. The talent came of age in a culturally tumultuous time when cornball comedy began to give way to zanier humour. As the film puts it, “ Godspell seemed to be the joy that the world needed.”

American director Davis had most of the cast members at his disposal. Their delight in reminiscing is the film’s heartbeat. What Davis didn’t have was much in the way of video or audio from the production. Only because of a bootleg tape made by Short are we able to hear the cast in action. (Radner saw the tiny microphones Short set up at the rear of the stage and purposely sang into them. Other cast members guided her back to the rest of the group.)

The animation used to recreate onstage and off-stage memories adds to the film’s zip. Not that the doc was lacking it otherwise − Short, Levy, Thomas, Eastwood and Shaffer are talking heads worth their weight in storytelling gold.

On the other hand, the random use of commentators such as SNL ’s Heidi Gardner and James Austin Johnson is mysterious and unrewarding. Johnson, 37, is a gifted comedian but not on firm footing as a cultural anthropologist. “There was an interest in growing your hair out and growing your beard out, and Jesus just kind of slides right in there,” he says in an attempt to explain the popularity of a musical with the son of God as the star character.

content_blocks.caption: A still from Godspell, showing Victor Garber in striped pants. Supplied

content_blocks.text: Mind you, it’s the director’s fault, not Johnson’s, that the popularity of religion at the time was not explored more deeply as context. In an archival news clip from outside the Royal Alex on opening night, a woman says the musical was a “real Christian experience.”

There was a sudden surge in the early 1970s of young people adopting Christian faith. A Time magazine cover story in 1971 coined the phrase “the Jesus Revolution.” I mean, the Doobie Brothers had a hit single with the gospel song Jesus Is Just Alright at the same time Godspell was playing to sold-out crowds in Toronto.

After the 14 month-run was over, the cast scattered. Garber had already left the Toronto production after three months to star in David Greene’s film version of the musical. (Though Titanic’ s Gerber is a fine actor, he is less than convincing with his claim to have been “heartbroken” when he was picked for the Godspell movie in New York.)
As for the documentary’s title, it comes from Sctv ’s Thomas. He joined the Godspell cast as replacement but watched the Canadian premiere as an audience member.
“I don’t think you can capture the spirit of what I saw on opening night at the Royal Alex in Toronto,” he says. “I think that that’s one of those experiences where you had to be there.”

stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Middlesex OPP say a cyclist has been taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries after a crash.

OPP, paramedics and firefighters have closed Richmond Street between Marion and Gore as a result of the collision involving a cyclist on Wednesday.

Police say the cyclist has been transported with hospital with life-threatening-injuries and updates will be provided when available.

stories.title: Trump trade adviser outburst makes Carney laugh: 'I take note of both comments. How’s that?'
stories.summary: U.S. trade adviser Peter Navarro said Canadian lobbyists should "get the hell out" of America as president predicted an apology from Canada.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Canada

Peter Navarro said Canadian lobbyists should 'get the hell out' of the U.S. as Donald Trump predicted an apology from Canada

Last updated 52 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/carney-laughs-off-trump-trade-adviser-telling-canadian-lobbyists-to-get-the-hell-out-of-u-s#comments-area)

Prime Minister Mark Carney speaking at a press conference on ocean conservation in Vancouver on Sept. 29.

Prime Minister Mark Carney laughed out loud when asked to comment on remarks by U.S. trade adviser Peter Navarro that Canadian lobbyists should “get the hell out” of the U.S. and stop interfering in the upcoming midterm elections there.

Carney also appeared amused by the U.S. president’s prediction that Canada would apologize and roll back its counter-tariffs on U.S. goods.

Navarro’s comments came yesterday during a summit on American economic growth hosted by Widehall, a public policy consulting firm in Washington, DC. “Do you really want to spend any time on Canada?” he said. “Because Canada economically is a rowboat. We’re an aircraft carrier. How’s that going to end?”

He continued: “Any Canadians here, please, if you’re on K Street, get the hell out of our country, because the problem you have is you lobby this country, and you’ve been successful in the past, and you think you can keep doing that.”

The world gets it now: tariffs bring countries to the table. Everyone lined up to negotiate. Canada? They showed up with lobbyists. Message to them? Get the hell out. pic.twitter.com/JES6qaHZZl — Peter Navarro (@RealPNavarro) September 29, 2026

K Street, a major avenue in Washington, DC, is home to law firms, think tanks, trade associations and advocacy groups, and has become synonymous with lobbying in the U.S. capital.

“Memo to Canada,” Navarro continued: “You cannot do that. OK? That game is up, and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly.”

The comments in some way recalled remarks by Canadian Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who posted to social media on Election Day in April 2025: “President Trump, stay out of our election. The only people who will decide the future of Canada are Canadians at the ballot box.”

Trump had earlier that day posted to Truth Social: “Good luck to the Great people of Canada.” He had added: “Elect the man who has the strength and wisdom to cut your taxes in half, increase your military power, for free, to the highest level in the World,” suggesting all this and more would come if Canada became the 51st state.

This week at the White House, Trump told reporters his latest prediction on Canada: “I think what’s going to happen is, over the next three or four weeks, they’re going to come to us and they’re going to say, ‘We’re going to get rid of all the tariffs.’ We’re going to win everything.”

He added: “They’re going to come in and they’re going to say, ‘Sir, we are sorry.'”

"They're going to come in and they're going to say, 'Sir, we are sorry.'" President Trump weighs in on how the trade dispute with Canada could end, predicting Canadian officials will come back to the U.S. within the next "3 or 4 weeks" looking to drop tariffs and reach an… pic.twitter.com/3hm9qhM9rC — Fox News (@FoxNews) September 28, 2026

Carney was asked about both comments yesterday at a press conference in Vancouver on the topic of ocean protection. He broke into laughter even before the question was complete.

Composing himself, he replied: “I take note of both comments. How’s that? No response to either.”

Before the next question was posed, he added: “I’ll just say this on trade. It continues to be the case that Canada stands ready to negotiate in good faith (on) a mutually advantageous trade arrangement that respects both our countries’ sovereignty.”

Carney was asked later in the event if he was considering “applying new trade pressure” with the U.S. midterms just weeks away.

“Never rule anything out,” he said. “I’ll stand by my earlier comments, and the position of the government, which is — look the reality is that the cost of living is very high in the United States. And there’s things that Canada can do to help lower that cost of living.”

He spoke of cooperation between Canada and the U.S. on issues including energy security, food security, information security and financial security.

“Those are fundamental issues that are best addressed through reliable partnerships. Canada is a reliable partner and we’re ready to work in any or all of those areas.”

He added: “Our timing isn’t dictated by any specific aspect of the U.S. calendar.”

stories.title: Blue Jays’ Shapiro backs Guerrero Jr. after comments: ‘I know how much he cares’
stories.summary: Guerrero's down year saw his OPS drop to .688 over 144 games as he hit a full-season career-low nine home runs.
stories.author: Sportsnet
stories.content:
Posted September 30, 2026 12:45 pm.

Mark Shapiro’s belief in Vladimir Guerrero Jr. hasn’t wavered.

Despite a disappointing season from the Toronto Blue Jays first baseman, which ended with Guerrero issuing an apology for comments that surfaced in a Spanish-language interview before the club’s final series, Shapiro reiterated his belief in the six-time all-star while meeting with reporters on Wednesday at Rogers Centre.

“The comments are what he was with us and how he responded to us, and that his feelings were authentic and genuine,” Shapiro said. “There have been players that have reacted and said similar things in the past when they’ve struggled and faced frustration. It’s a tough stage for a 27-year-old to be on and deal with that level of pressure and anxiety.

“But again, I doubled down on the fact that I believe in Vlad as a player and a person, and I know how much he cares. And that’s how I interpret those comments, that they weren’t a reflection of how much he cares.”

In a clip posted to social media from an upcoming podcast with Veronica Batista of Noticias Telemicro, Guerrero said he received his $500-million, 14-year contract not “for what I’m going to do, it was for what I already did, they didn’t pay me because I’m going to hit 40 every year, they paid me for what I already accomplished.”

Those comments created a firestorm on social media and led to the pre-game apology on Sept. 25.

“I probably didn’t understand what I was trying to say, or maybe I didn’t explain what I wanted to say,” Guerrero said through interpreter Hector Lebron. “I’m here to apologize to everyone and letting them know that I am going to go into the off-season, I’m going to work very hard, I am going to be ready, I will be focused to make that contract a great one.”

Guerrero’s down year saw his OPS drop to .688 over 144 games as he hit a full-season career-low nine home runs, contributing to the Blue Jays’ fall from AL East champions to last in the division.

“We’ve obviously been talking about that all year,” Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins said Wednesday. “I’m encouraged now that we will have a better canvas to work with without the pressures of having to compete on a nightly basis, not only against his competition, but with the pressure of performance and what it means to win and lose in front of a fan base and an industry.”

As for the mechanics of Guerrero’s swing, Atkins said the two-time Silver Slugger “lost a little bit of (his) rhythm and timing pretty early in the season.”

“It started to impact his confidence, and once it impacted his confidence, the in-game adjustments and in-season adjustments became very difficult.”

Both Atkins and Shapiro spoke about the Blue Jays’ plan for Guerrero this off-season in hopes of returning the franchise pillar to peak form going forward.

“We need to make sure that we’ve considered all stakeholders and as much information as possible,” Atkins said of what that plan involves. “We’ve been doing that over the year, but want to consolidate it again and present our thoughts to him, download his (thoughts), and then allow him some time to breathe and reconnect.”

content_blocks.text: Posted September 30, 2026 12:45 pm.
Mark Shapiro’s belief in Vladimir Guerrero Jr. hasn’t wavered.

Despite a disappointing season from the Toronto Blue Jays first baseman, which ended with Guerrero issuing an apology for comments that surfaced in a Spanish-language interview before the club’s final series, Shapiro reiterated his belief in the six-time all-star while meeting with reporters on Wednesday at Rogers Centre.

“The comments are what he was with us and how he responded to us, and that his feelings were authentic and genuine,” Shapiro said. “There have been players that have reacted and said similar things in the past when they’ve struggled and faced frustration. It’s a tough stage for a 27-year-old to be on and deal with that level of pressure and anxiety.

“But again, I doubled down on the fact that I believe in Vlad as a player and a person, and I know how much he cares. And that’s how I interpret those comments, that they weren’t a reflection of how much he cares.”

In a clip posted to social media from an upcoming podcast with Veronica Batista of Noticias Telemicro, Guerrero said he received his $500-million, 14-year contract not “for what I’m going to do, it was for what I already did, they didn’t pay me because I’m going to hit 40 every year, they paid me for what I already accomplished.”
Those comments created a firestorm on social media and led to the pre-game apology on Sept. 25.

“I probably didn’t understand what I was trying to say, or maybe I didn’t explain what I wanted to say,” Guerrero said through interpreter Hector Lebron. “I’m here to apologize to everyone and letting them know that I am going to go into the off-season, I’m going to work very hard, I am going to be ready, I will be focused to make that contract a great one.”
Guerrero’s down year saw his OPS drop to .688 over 144 games as he hit a full-season career-low nine home runs, contributing to the Blue Jays’ fall from AL East champions to last in the division.

“We’ve obviously been talking about that all year,” Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins said Wednesday. “I’m encouraged now that we will have a better canvas to work with without the pressures of having to compete on a nightly basis, not only against his competition, but with the pressure of performance and what it means to win and lose in front of a fan base and an industry.”
As for the mechanics of Guerrero’s swing, Atkins said the two-time Silver Slugger “lost a little bit of (his) rhythm and timing pretty early in the season.”
“It started to impact his confidence, and once it impacted his confidence, the in-game adjustments and in-season adjustments became very difficult.”
Both Atkins and Shapiro spoke about the Blue Jays’ plan for Guerrero this off-season in hopes of returning the franchise pillar to peak form going forward.

“We need to make sure that we’ve considered all stakeholders and as much information as possible,” Atkins said of what that plan involves. “We’ve been doing that over the year, but want to consolidate it again and present our thoughts to him, download his (thoughts), and then allow him some time to breathe and reconnect.”

stories.title: Conservative MP Scott Aitchison to resign at end of year
stories.summary: MP for Parry Sound-Muskoka is set to become the 12th to resign since January
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Ontario Conservative MP Scott Aitchison has announced he will resign his seat of Parry Sound-Muskoka at the end of the current fall parliamentary sitting.

In a letter released to constituents today, Aitchison says that after 30 years of public life, he plans to explore other opportunities.

Aitchison ran for the party leadership in 2022 and has served as the opposition’s housing critic.

He is set to become the 12th MP to resign since January.

The exiting MP says it has been the “honour of his lifetime” to serve the people of his community and he hopes he made them proud.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre issued a statement thanking Aitchison for his public service and wishing him all the best in his next chapter.

stories.title: Showers persist in London forecast, sunny weekend ahead
stories.summary: Environment Canada says London, Ont., residents can expect a transition from wet weather to clear skies this week.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Environment Canada says London, Ont., residents can expect a transition from wet weather to clear skies this week.

Showers are likely to continue through Friday before giving way to a pleasant, sunny weekend.

Here’s the extended forecast:

Wednesday: Increasing clouds and a high of 22C, followed by a cloudy night with showers and a low of 15C.

Thursday: Showers ending to cloudy skies with a high of 23C, with a cloudy night and a 60% chance of showers and a low of 13C.

Friday: Cloudy with a 40% chance of showers and a high of 19C, clearing to a low of 7C overnight.

Saturday: Sunny with a high of 18C, followed by clear skies and a low of 6C overnight.

Sunday: Sunny with a high of 21C, transitioning to cloudy periods overnight with a low of 8C.

Monday: A mix of sun and cloud with a high of 13C, followed by cloudy periods and a low of plus 2C overnight.

Tuesday: A mix of sun and cloud with a high of 15C.

stories.title: Ontario Conservative MP Aitchison to resign when fall sitting ends
stories.summary: Ottawa — Ontario Conservative MP Scott Aitchison has announced he will resign his seat of Parry Sound-Muskoka at the end of the current fall parliamentary sitting.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
MP for Parry Sound-Muskoka Scott Aitchisonrises during question period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Thursday, June 18, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Adrian Wyld

By David Baxter, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 12:16 pm.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 12:22 pm.

Ontario Conservative MP Scott Aitchison has announced he will resign his seat of Parry Sound-Muskoka at the end of the current fall parliamentary sitting.

In a letter released to constituents today, Aitchison says that after 30 years of public life, he plans to explore other opportunities.

“From being elected to Huntsville Town Council and Muskoka District Council at the age of 21, to serving as Mayor of Huntsville and, for the past seven years, as your Member of Parliament, it has been the honour of my lifetime to serve you and represent our community,” Aitchison’s statement read, which he shared to X.

“Whether it was in the council chambers, or the halls of Ottawa, I worked to build consensus, cut through the bureaucracy, and make life better for the people who placed their trust in me. I carried myself with the same values of the town that raised me: respect, decency, and looking out for your neighbour.”

Aitchison ran for the party leadership in 2022 and has served as the opposition’s housing critic.

He is set to become the 12th MP to resign since January.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre issued a statement thanking Aitchison for his public service and wishing him all the best in his next chapter.

paragraphs: MP for Parry Sound-Muskoka Scott Aitchisonrises during question period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Thursday, June 18, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Adrian Wyld
By David Baxter, The Canadian Press
Posted September 30, 2026 12:16 pm.
Last Updated September 30, 2026 12:22 pm.
Ontario Conservative MP Scott Aitchison has announced he will resign his seat of Parry Sound-Muskoka at the end of the current fall parliamentary sitting.
In a letter released to constituents today, Aitchison says that after 30 years of public life, he plans to explore other opportunities.

“From being elected to Huntsville Town Council and Muskoka District Council at the age of 21, to serving as Mayor of Huntsville and, for the past seven years, as your Member of Parliament, it has been the honour of my lifetime to serve you and represent our community,” Aitchison’s statement read, which he shared to X.

“Whether it was in the council chambers, or the halls of Ottawa, I worked to build consensus, cut through the bureaucracy, and make life better for the people who placed their trust in me. I carried myself with the same values of the town that raised me: respect, decency, and looking out for your neighbour.”
Aitchison ran for the party leadership in 2022 and has served as the opposition’s housing critic.
He is set to become the 12th MP to resign since January.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre issued a statement thanking Aitchison for his public service and wishing him all the best in his next chapter.

stories.title: London and District Labour Council recognizes National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
stories.summary: The London and District Labour Council (Ldlc) is recognizing the importance of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation Day for labour and the broader community.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
The London and District Labour Council (Ldlc) is recognizing the importance of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation Day for labour and the broader community.

Ldlc officials say they understand the truth of the history and they re-commit to reconciliation to ensure that the tragic history and ongoing legacy of residential schools is never forgotten.

“Authentic reconciliation requires continuous reflection, action, and consideration throughout the year. However, ON the National Day for Truth Reconciliation, it is important that we make time to commemorate the lost children and the survivors of residential schools, their families, and communities,” states a news release from the Ldlc.

The Residential School Survivors’ Flag is raised on Sept. 30 as an expression of remembrance to honour survivors and all lives affected, includes elements selected by First Nations across this country including Métis peoples.

“It is crucial to reflect on what all of us can do to identify and to eliminate structural and overt racism, as well as other forms of discrimination in our workplaces and communities,” said Patti Dalton, Ldlc President.

“This Day is a time to acknowledge the truth of our collective history, and the inequities faced by Indigenous peoples across the country. We must, as a collective labour movement, resolve to work for a better, more equitable future, and to pursue implementation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 Calls to Action and the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (Undrip), and also to seek justice for missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls.”

The labour council encourages the community to take part in some of the significant events taking place on Sept. 30.

stories.title: Roughriders reacquire kicker Lauther in trade with Redblacks
stories.summary: The Roughriders acquired Brett Lauther from the Ottawa Redblacks on Wednesday for a fifth-round pick in the 2027 CFL draft.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Saskatchewan has brought veteran kicker Brett Lauther back into the fold.

The Roughriders acquired Lauther from the Ottawa Redblacks on Wednesday for a fifth-round pick in the 2027 CFL draft.

The 35-year-old Lauther has made 32 of 34 field-goal attempts this season, including all three of his tries from beyond 50 yards.

The native of Truro, N.S., signed with Ottawa in the off-season after spending the previous eight seasons with Saskatchewan, helping the Roughriders win the Grey Cup last year.

Saskatchewan is 8-6 and tied with B.C. for second in the West Division, while Ottawa has lost all 14 of its games and sits last in the East.

Both teams are in action Friday, with Ottawa hosting Hamilton and Saskatchewan welcoming Calgary.

Saskatchewan began the ‘season with Canadian rookie Alex Hale, who made 24-of-32 field goals (75 per cent) and 32-of-35 converts (91.4 per cent) in 12 games before landing on the practice roster.

Dawson Hodge, another rookie from Coquitlam, B.C., had made all five of his field-goal attempts.

The ‘Super El Nino’ is upon us. What does that mean for Ontario’s fall colours?

‘We owe them action,’ Carney says on Truth and Reconciliation Day

stories.title: Trade Minister Sidhu set to speak with U.S. trade rep at G20 meeting in Wisconsin
stories.summary: Ottawa — International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu is expected to speak with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during the G20 trade ministers' meeting in Wisconsin this week.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canada's Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu speaks at a press conference in Toronto, ON Friday, July 24, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Sammy Kogan The Canadian Press

By David Baxter, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 11:31 am.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 11:46 am.

Ottawa — International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu is expected to speak with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during the G20 trade ministers’ meeting in Wisconsin this week.

Sidhu’s spokesperson says a specific time and format for that conversation have not been set.

Sidhu also has bilateral meetings scheduled for today with the trade ministers for France, Australia and Turkey, and is meeting with India’s representative on Thursday.

The two-day meeting of trade ministers from the world’s biggest economies is being held in Milwaukee amid a global trade disruption caused in large part by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade agenda.

Canada is looking to reduce its economic reliance on the United States in response to Washington repeatedly targeting Canadian goods with tariffs.

In a statement, Sidhu says Canada’s key priorities for the meeting include advancing a digital trade agreement with the European Union, advancing talks with the South American trade bloc Mercosur, and working on an economic partnership agreement with India.

stories.title: TD Bank to buy back up to $10-billion of its shares
stories.summary: Bank says the plan is to repurchase up to 61 million of its shares under a program it expects to complete by July next year
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TD Bank Group TD-T says it plans to buy back up to $10-billion worth of its shares.

The bank says the plan is to repurchase up to 61 million of its shares under a program it expects to complete by July next year.

The new buyback, which is subject to the approval by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Canada, will represent up to 3.74 per cent of the bank’s issued and outstanding shares as of Aug. 31.

TD says it plans to cancel all of the purchased shares.

The move comes after TD spent $7-billion to buy back 47.2 million of its shares as of Sept. 25 in a program that began on Jan. 20.

By buying back its shares, the bank reduces its equity base, spreading profits over fewer shares, increasing its return on equity and earnings per share, two key ratios used to assess its financial health.

stories.title: Quebec election 2026: What to know about the major parties, their platforms and where to vote
stories.summary: From the PQ, CAQ and QS to the Liberals and Conservatives, here’s your guide ahead of Oct. 5’s provincial vote
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
Election day is approaching in Quebec , where a crowded race could make winning a majority of the 127 seats up for grabs challenging for any party on the ballot.

None of the five main parties have polled higher than 30 per cent, but in a divided political landscape, the Parti Québécois now appears likely to form government – and potentially even a majority – despite a promise of a sovereignty referendum most Quebeckers don’t want.

Which parties are in the running, who are their leaders and what do they stand for? Here’s a breakdown of what you need to know before Quebeckers head to the polls next week.

The Quebec provincial election will take place on Monday, Oct. 5.

Polling stations will be open from 9:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET on election day. To find the closest polling station, enter your address on Elections Quebec’s website.

Advanced polls ended on Monday, but voters can still cast their ballots early at the office of the returning officer in their riding at the following times:

Wednesday, Sept. 30, from 9:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET

Thursday, Oct. 1, from 9:30 a.m. to 2 p.m. ET

There are 127 members of the National Assembly of Quebec, meaning a party must win 64 seats to form a majority government.

Leader: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon

Primary base: Sovereigntists

Four years ago, the Parti Québécois was on the verge of extinction when it won just three seats in the legislature. Though the party has now been leading in the polls for the better part of three years, its support has been limited by its promise to hold a referendum on Quebec sovereignty that most people don’t want. Still, the separatist party could now be on the cusp of winning a majority government .

That’s not because there’s been a groundswell of separatist sentiment, but because the sovereignty question hasn’t played a large role in this election. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a third referendum on independence in a first mandate – but not until U.S. President Donald Trump is out of office – and tamped down his separatist rhetoric for an electorate nervous about the trade war.

Profile: The persistence of Paul St-Pierre Plamondon

Neither of the three main parties that oppose a separation vote have managed to rally the anti-referendum forces behind them, and regional divisions favour the PQ. Vote-splitting could mean Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s party wins a majority without ever having polled above 30 per cent during the campaign, the lowest vote share in Quebec history for a majority government.

Leader: Christine Fréchette

Primary base: Older francophones who don’t want a separation referendum

In the weeks after the election was called in August, the governing Coalition Avenir Québec seemed to be making a comeback under the leadership of Christine Fréchette , who positioned herself as a safe bet during an escalating trade war with the United States. But weak debate performances and a change-hungry electorate have taken the wind out of her sails. Three polls early this week showed support for the CAQ slipping below 20 per cent, and the party seems to be fighting for survival instead of a third mandate.

Profile: Christine Fréchette's fresh start withers in the end

The CAQ won its first government in 2018, promising a new brand of nationalism that didn’t include a referendum on separation, and blowing up a political landscape defined for decades by the sovereignty debate. But now, the baggage of the Caq’s eight years in power is weighing on the campaign, and Ms. Fréchette has struggled to distance herself from former Premier François Legault, who stepped down earlier this year after his support collapsed .

Leader: Charles Milliard

Primary base: Non-francophone federalists, largely in and around Montreal

The opposition Liberals were once the only viable choice for Quebeckers who didn’t wish to separate, but since the emergence of the nationalist CAQ in 2018, the party has had stiff competition for its federalist base. The centre-right party is unlikely to win this election, but could retain its Official Opposition status. Leader Charles Milliard has been trying to make a comeback since inheriting the party from Pablo Rodriguez in February, but the Liberals remain stubbornly unpopular among francophones, particularly outside Montreal.

Mr. Milliard has cast his party as the only federalist option, attacked the Caq’s record and warned the PQ’s separation referendum promise is “risky” given the trade war. But the anti-Trump campaign playbook that proved so successful for the federal Liberals hasn’t found the same traction in Quebec.

Mr. Milliard also hasn’t come out too strongly on questions of nationalism and identity, and has been hesitant to criticize the Caq’s Bill 21 – which restricts public servants from wearing religious symbols at work – or to rock the boat on minority language rights, of which the party has traditionally been a staunch defender.

Leader: Éric Duhaime

Current seats: 1 (crossed floor from CAQ)

Primary base: Right-leaning voters, particularly around Quebec City

After capturing 13 per cent of the popular vote last election, the Conservatives are now looking to win seats in the legislature for the first time. Led by Éric Duhaime, the newcomer party drummed up support by railing against pandemic public-health restrictions in 2022. Today, Mr. Duhaime has recast his party as a sober watchdog fighting to protect taxpayers from state overspending, promising “historic” tax cuts , more private health care and an end to Quebec’s carbon price.

Mr. Duhaime is hoping to hold the balance of power and has promised that he would “block any referendum project” if his party succeeds. His strong campaign has mostly focused on the Quebec City region, where there is at least some genuine excitement about the prospect of a Conservative caucus in the National Assembly for the first time.

Leader: Ruba Ghazal and Sol Zanetti (co-spokespersons)

Primary base: Urban progressives

The left-leaning Québec Solidaire is working to hold on to the handful of seats it holds in urban ridings and control the balance of power if another party fails to win a majority. Formed in 2006, the sovereigntist party hopes that its progressive policy proposals can still gain traction with federalist voters at a challenging time for left-wing parties.

Co-spokespersons Ruba Ghazal and Sol Zanetti have touted their signature promises – a wealth tax and publicly-run grocery stores – during this campaign, and the party is expected to win a handful of seats. But QS will likely be limited to urban ridings in Montreal and Quebec City.

With reports from Maura Forrest and Eric Andrew-Gee.

stories.title: After 27 parties shut down in Ontario, police watching N.S. university homecomings
stories.summary: Homecoming celebrations at the University of Guelph in Ontario saw student parties spill into the streets leading to a massive police response and numerous charges.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - Homecoming celebrations at the University of Guelph in Ontario saw student parties spill into the streets leading to a massive police response and numerous charges.

In Halifax, Dalhousie University’s homecoming weekend featured 27 unsanctioned parties shut down by police and 36 tickets were issued under the Liquor Control Act.

Police in the city now have a simple and strict message as Saint Mary’s University prepares for its homecoming this weekend.

Bear spray discharged, thousands gather during homecoming: Guelph police

“If something larger, such as what happened at Guelph was to occur, we are prepared and we are always ready for something like that,” said Const. Martin Cromwell of the Halifax Regional Police.

He said community response officers are educating students on potential consequences and that there will be an increased police presence around the university.

“First and foremost, we stress safety for the students, and we ask them to consider their alcohol consumption,” said Cromwell, adding “it could lead to a night in our cells, and people could be arrested for public intoxication.”

The president of the Saint Mary’s University Students’ Association (Smusa) Liza Zahid said homecoming is an event that often transforms into a celebration for students as they begin a new school year.

“I would just reiterate that students are welcome to have the best time that they want to have, but to do it in a safe and respectful manner and we also want to give the students a good time,” said Zahid.

“I think homecoming is one of the best weekends throughout the year, and every student looks forward to it, and every student knows how to have a good time and be respectful of our neighbours.”

Guelph streets show the aftermath of Homecoming festivities, with the cleanup underway following a day of celebrations and large crowds.

Saint Mary’s will feature alcohol-free homecoming activities planned over the three-day period, starting this Friday.

“We have the SMU Huskies football game against Acadia, we have a homecoming brunch that is happening and we also have a family skate night,” said Zahid. “And, we have activities for students who want to celebrate and have that high-energy homecoming feel.”

Zahid also pointed out Saint Mary’s University homecoming events will take place on campus, which is contained within a city block. Organizers hope the compact setting of the university will help keep the festivities safe and under control during homecoming weekend.

CTV reached out to Saint Mary’s University for an interview, but they did not provide a response.

stories.title: How this farmer, chef and sommelier preps and stocks up for Thanksgiving
stories.summary: Given his expertise in preparing feasts both big and small, The Globe asked Zach Littlejohn for advice on how to put together a Thanksgiving dinner
stories.author: Daniel Reale-Chin
stories.content:
To call Littlejohn Farm in Prince Edward County, Ont., quaint May seem cliché, but how else do you describe a house, a barn, a pumpkin patch and even a wooden treehouse all tucked onto a few acres of land just off the shores of Lake Ontario?

Home to chef, sommelier and farmer Zach Littlejohn, his wife Luhana, and their two children, the farm seems like the perfect setting for Thanksgiving: tables under the gazebo set for a feast, apple cider served by the firepit and pumpkin patch, and a few turkeys gobbling in the pen.

“We also like to have squash on display, all of autumn,” says Littlejohn.

Since the couple purchased the property in 2017, they have been raising their children alongside a farm full of heritage pigs, chickens, sheep, ducks and, of course, some turkeys.

Here, the couple also hosts culinary events curated by Luhana, the farm’s co-founder and CEO, including collaborations with chefs such as Toronto’s Ron McKinlay, multi-course lunches and a classic Thanksgiving Sunday dinner that features produce grown on the farm. With each ticketed event, the couple hopes to teach people where their food comes from through wholesome, healthy and sustainable culinary experiences.

How four roommates save money by grocery shopping together

The Littlejohns also host their own personal Thanksgiving lunch with their family and sometimes neighbours, who pop in for an afternoon on the farm.

Given his expertise in preparing Thanksgiving feasts both big and small, The Globe and Mail asked Littlejohn for advice on how to put together a Thanksgiving dinner – and, of course, what’s in his cart?

What’s on the table: I typically host 15 to 25 people. Our table always has a seasonal bounty of vegetables including squash varieties such as delicata, butternut and acorn, Brussels sprouts, autumn greens, cabbages and potatoes. The brassicas and gourds are always roasted, potatoes mashed with a generous amount of cream and butter and we always have a couple autumn-inspired salads with greens, beets, dried fruits, apples, pear and high-fat yogurt and cheese.

Tips to save some time: It can be kind of daunting because the goal is to not spend the entire time cooking, and instead, spend more time with your guests. For this reason, I typically plan a menu that allows us to go heavy on the prep leading up and easier on the day of execution. I give myself one or two days ahead of time to debone the thighs of the turkey and tie it; I also brine the beast ahead of time to make it juicier. You can purchase items such as cranberry sauce to save time, but I recommend cooking your own vegetables so you can control the oil, salt and tenderness.

How a lobster fisherman and professional Strongman shops for groceries

How I make the perfect bird: For a successful turkey, I always opt for two smaller birds over one large bird, depending on the size of the group. It’s difficult to get a big bird evenly cooked in a small household oven.

I cook it at 350 degrees Fahrenheit and stuff the cavity with savoury herbs, a sliced whole head of garlic and two halved shallots (I often leave the skin on). I cook my trussed bird in an All-Clad roasting pan on a bed of mirepoix (onions, carrots and celery) and add one cup of dry white cooking wine and a litre of cold water to the bottom of the roasting pan, which creates some stock in the bottom of the pan from drippings.

I cook the turkey until the internal temperature comes to 160 degrees Fahrenheit, and rest it for half an hour before carving (the internal temperature will continue to rise). Take the roasting pan and strain the liquid into a sauce pot to make a pan gravy and reserve the vegetables to add to a stock pot with the bones and cold water to make a soup for the next few days. After I carve my turkey, I always place it on a platter and drizzle it with olive oil and Maldon salt for extra flavour, and place the platter under the broiler for one minute.

How I save : Buying old-fashioned dinner rolls and pumpkin pies. I have made pumpkin pies and dinner rolls many times, but I feel that you can get pretty good premade options that don’t cost a lot or take a lot of time to make.

How I splurge : On good-quality dairy products such as a good brie that I can turn into an appetizer. I also splurge on the turkey. Get a fresh, free-range or pasture-raised turkey and support your local butcher or farm when you can.

How this Nunavut grandfather grocery shops for his 12-person family

The hardest shopping habit to keep up: Avoiding hidden sugar in packaged foods. It’s important to read labels and inform yourself about ingredients.

How I’ve changed my eating habits recently: With us being a Brazilian/Canadian household, a new tradition that I have embraced is eating rice and beans as side dishes.

Five items always in my cart:

Cranberries – Springbrook Cranberry – $3.99 a pack: I buy these fresh throughout the season, and I’ll often buy extra to freeze so we can use them for the holidays as well.

Sea salt flakes – Maldon – $10.99 per box: This salt is the best for finishing your turkey with and adding on top of the butter that you will spread on your bread rolls.

Maple syrup – Edwin County Farms – $13 per bottle: I enjoy this drizzled on top of my pumpkin pie. I May save a bit on a pie, but I spend those savings on great maple syrup.

Brie wheel – Alex de Portneuf Brise du Matin – $16: This makes a great little appetizer inside of puff pastry baked with the brie cheese and fruit compote, with a drizzle of honey. This cheese costs around $16 a wheel, so with the puff pastry, fruit, honey and baguette, you can expect to spend $24 to feed 12 people.

Vanilla ice cream – Kawartha Lakes – $8.99 per tub: This is a must to go with the pumpkin pie and maple syrup. A tub can easily feed about 12 people.

Home to chef, sommelier and farmer Zach Littlejohn, his wife Luhana, and their two children, the farm seems like the perfect setting for Thanksgiving: tables under the gazebo set for a feast, apple cider served by the firepit and pumpkin patch, and a few turkeys gobbling in the pen.
“We also like to have squash on display, all of autumn,” says Littlejohn.
Since the couple purchased the property in 2017, they have been raising their children alongside a farm full of heritage pigs, chickens, sheep, ducks and, of course, some turkeys.

Here, the couple also hosts culinary events curated by Luhana, the farm’s co-founder and CEO, including collaborations with chefs such as Toronto’s Ron McKinlay, multi-course lunches and a classic Thanksgiving Sunday dinner that features produce grown on the farm. With each ticketed event, the couple hopes to teach people where their food comes from through wholesome, healthy and sustainable culinary experiences.
How four roommates save money by grocery shopping together
The Littlejohns also host their own personal Thanksgiving lunch with their family and sometimes neighbours, who pop in for an afternoon on the farm.

Given his expertise in preparing Thanksgiving feasts both big and small, The Globe and Mail asked Littlejohn for advice on how to put together a Thanksgiving dinner – and, of course, what’s in his cart?

What’s on the table: I typically host 15 to 25 people. Our table always has a seasonal bounty of vegetables including squash varieties such as delicata, butternut and acorn, Brussels sprouts, autumn greens, cabbages and potatoes. The brassicas and gourds are always roasted, potatoes mashed with a generous amount of cream and butter and we always have a couple autumn-inspired salads with greens, beets, dried fruits, apples, pear and high-fat yogurt and cheese.

Tips to save some time: It can be kind of daunting because the goal is to not spend the entire time cooking, and instead, spend more time with your guests. For this reason, I typically plan a menu that allows us to go heavy on the prep leading up and easier on the day of execution. I give myself one or two days ahead of time to debone the thighs of the turkey and tie it; I also brine the beast ahead of time to make it juicier. You can purchase items such as cranberry sauce to save time, but I recommend cooking your own vegetables so you can control the oil, salt and tenderness.
How a lobster fisherman and professional Strongman shops for groceries

How I make the perfect bird: For a successful turkey, I always opt for two smaller birds over one large bird, depending on the size of the group. It’s difficult to get a big bird evenly cooked in a small household oven.

I cook it at 350 degrees Fahrenheit and stuff the cavity with savoury herbs, a sliced whole head of garlic and two halved shallots (I often leave the skin on). I cook my trussed bird in an All-Clad roasting pan on a bed of mirepoix (onions, carrots and celery) and add one cup of dry white cooking wine and a litre of cold water to the bottom of the roasting pan, which creates some stock in the bottom of the pan from drippings.

I cook the turkey until the internal temperature comes to 160 degrees Fahrenheit, and rest it for half an hour before carving (the internal temperature will continue to rise). Take the roasting pan and strain the liquid into a sauce pot to make a pan gravy and reserve the vegetables to add to a stock pot with the bones and cold water to make a soup for the next few days. After I carve my turkey, I always place it on a platter and drizzle it with olive oil and Maldon salt for extra flavour, and place the platter under the broiler for one minute.

How I save : Buying old-fashioned dinner rolls and pumpkin pies. I have made pumpkin pies and dinner rolls many times, but I feel that you can get pretty good premade options that don’t cost a lot or take a lot of time to make.

How I splurge : On good-quality dairy products such as a good brie that I can turn into an appetizer. I also splurge on the turkey. Get a fresh, free-range or pasture-raised turkey and support your local butcher or farm when you can.
How this Nunavut grandfather grocery shops for his 12-person family
The hardest shopping habit to keep up: Avoiding hidden sugar in packaged foods. It’s important to read labels and inform yourself about ingredients.
How I’ve changed my eating habits recently: With us being a Brazilian/Canadian household, a new tradition that I have embraced is eating rice and beans as side dishes.
Five items always in my cart:

items: Cranberries – Springbrook Cranberry – $3.99 a pack: I buy these fresh throughout the season, and I’ll often buy extra to freeze so we can use them for the holidays as well.
Sea salt flakes – Maldon – $10.99 per box: This salt is the best for finishing your turkey with and adding on top of the butter that you will spread on your bread rolls.
Maple syrup – Edwin County Farms – $13 per bottle: I enjoy this drizzled on top of my pumpkin pie. I May save a bit on a pie, but I spend those savings on great maple syrup.

Brie wheel – Alex de Portneuf Brise du Matin – $16: This makes a great little appetizer inside of puff pastry baked with the brie cheese and fruit compote, with a drizzle of honey. This cheese costs around $16 a wheel, so with the puff pastry, fruit, honey and baguette, you can expect to spend $24 to feed 12 people.
Vanilla ice cream – Kawartha Lakes – $8.99 per tub: This is a must to go with the pumpkin pie and maple syrup. A tub can easily feed about 12 people.

stories.title: A Trump adviser's outburst and a new poll suggest Canada’s tariff strategy is landing
stories.summary: A new U.S. survey suggests Canada’s tariff strategy and the trade war May be raising the political cost for Trump and Republicans.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — If Canada is betting that Trump’s tariff fight and Ottawa’s retaliation will exact political costs on U.S. President Donald Trump and Republicans in November’s midterms, it May be onto something: a senior Trump adviser just signalled that the White House sees the Canada-U.S. trade spat as politically sensitive.

Speaking at an economic conference in Washington on Tuesday, Trump trade adviser Peter Navarro had a few choice words for Canada. He likened the country to a rowboat and the U.S. to an aircraft carrier before asking whether any Canadians were in the room.

Addressing them, Navarro said: “If you’re on K Street, get the hell out of our country because the problem you have is you lobby this country, and you’ve been successful in the past, and you think you can keep doing that.”

“Memo to Canada: You cannot do that. OK, the game is up, and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan , you will pay even more dearly.”

Navarro offered no evidence that Canadian lobbying or retaliatory tariffs amounted to election interference. But by naming the Pine Tree and Great Lake States, both of which have close economic ties to Canada and consequential Senate races, he underscored the administration’s apparent concern about the dispute’s political effects.

The administration May have reason to be concerned. In a newly released survey , the Cato Institute and Morning Consult found that 75 per cent of registered U.S. voters said tariffs, defined in the poll as a U.S. tax imposed on imported products, would be important to their vote.

While few issues draw bipartisan backing these days in the United States, Democrats were not alone in feeling hard done by by tariffs. According to Emily Ekins, vice president for policy and society and the director of polling at the Cato Institute, nearly two-thirds of Republicans also said tariffs imposed under Trump had increased prices.

“We were very clear in asking, ‘Are tariffs affecting the prices of things you buy at the store?’” she explained.

“Seventy-four percent of all Americans agree with that, and nearly two-thirds of Republicans did too,” she said (as did 73 per cent of independents and 84 per cent of Democrats).

Andrew Hale, senior fellow at Advancing American Freedom, says the price effect could become especially potent in working-class regions where Trump won former Democratic voters by promising economic relief. Based on recent conversations with Republican campaign staffers, he said voter anger over tariffs is registering.

“The campaign is being won or lost on tariffs, which is seen to be raising prices,” Hale said.

Pollsters, however, are less convinced that tariffs alone will lead to specific voting decisions.

Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball, a nonpartisan election forecasting newsletter, says it has more to do with the economy overall.

“I would just view it as sort of a subset of the larger affordability issue,” said Kondik.

Andrew Smith, director of the UNH Survey Center, agrees.

“Tariffs are, I think, one factor in that, but it’s really just the state of the economy,” he said.

He said tariffs are less of a standalone trade-policy issue than a shorthand for voters’ broader anxiety about the cost of living. He also doubts Americans really understand tariffs.

“I don’t think that people could frankly tell you what a tariff is or what it does,” he said.

But on this, Ekins pushed back, inferring that Trump has been using his favourite word, “tariffs,” a lot over the past two years.

“Ordinarily, trade and tariffs have very little to do with people’s vote. But here’s the difference: Donald Trump has made trade and tariffs his signature economic policy,” she said.

“This year, tariffs are on the ballot because now people think of tariffs as being, ‘You’re raising my prices.’”

While Hale believes some working-class people who were once Democrats and voted for Trump will go back to voting Democrat, the pollsters disagree. They say no matter how frustrated they are by higher prices, most Republicans are about as likely to vote for Democrats as Maple Leafs fans are to start cheering for the Canadiens.

Instead, how Republicans fare will come down to one thing: turnout.

Will Republicans show up on election day? “The hardcore ones will, but the more modestly Republican are the ones that are least likely to show up,” Smith said.

Ekins echoed this. “I don’t expect them all to rush to the Democrats. They’re going to sit at home and not turn out to vote in the midterms.”

Americans still like the idea of using tariffs to support domestic manufacturing, Ekins said, but they are far less enthusiastic about paying higher prices for it.

That reluctance is especially pronounced when the target is Canada. In the Cato/Morning Consult survey, 56 per cent opposed tariffs on Canadian goods — the strongest opposition among the countries tested. Meanwhile, majorities of 57 and 60 per cent, respectively, supported tariffs on China and Russia.

Ekins explained that U.S. voters seemed willing to accept tariffs when the duties are framed as a national-security tool against adversaries, not in trade with close allies.

“Canada is the one country Americans do not want to put tariffs on,” Ekins said, noting that Britain was a close second.

Kondik agrees, noting, “It’s a lot easier to point the pitchfork at China than it is to point the pitchfork at Canada.”

“Most Americans don’t understand why we’re having a trade war with Canada,” Hale pointed out.

He also noted that Navarro’s stark comments amounted to an effort to blame Canada for voter frustration with the administration’s tariff policy, rather than acknowledging the policy’s political cost.

As for election results, pollsters and trade watchers expect the Democrats to win a majority in the House of Representatives, while the Senate remains a closer call. Kondik puts it at 50/50 for now, but Smith expects the Democrats to also win that chamber.

Hale believes the administration is seriously underestimating how severe a midterm defeat Republicans could be facing.

“I think they’re in for a real pasting,” he said, adding, “I don’t think, quite frankly, this administration has tuned into how potentially horrific this could be for them.”
