Orange shirts with Williams’ design will be sold year-round at the Dellelce Family Bookstore in Western’s University Community Centre. Proceeds will support the Save the Barn campaign, a project to preserve the last remaining building from Mount Elgin Industrial Institute, a residential school on what is now Chippewas of the Thames First Nation, near London, Ont.
Preserving Indigenous history and language at former Mount Elgin residential school

Mount Elgin, one of the first residential schools in Canada, operated until 1946. It included a farm where children were forced into labour tending livestock and growing crops, though the harvest was rarely used to supplement their meagre diets. A barn bearing inscriptions students left on the walls is the only structure still standing. The First Nation has been fundraising to restore it as an interpretive centre to document local history and help revitalize the community’s language and culture.

“Our communities did so much work to keep our language, culture and people alive in a time when everything was against them,” Williams said. “It’s a big part of why the Save the Barn campaign is such a vital part of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation here in London. While this city was being developed, the trauma of residential schools was happening just a half hour away to local First Nations children.”

Western supports National Day for Truth and Reconciliation by designating September 30 as a non-instructional day with no regular classes, allowing the campus community to participate in educational and commemorative events. Attendees are encouraged to wear orange. Williams said she hopes her design prompts meaningful reflection on the ongoing responsibility to remember the past, learn from it and carry those lessons forward.
“When people put on an orange shirt, I hope they have reconciliation in mind and put it into action in their daily lives when thinking about and interacting with any Indigenous Peoples.”

stories.title: CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette’s fresh start withers in the end
stories.summary: François Legault’s successor tried to set herself apart, and it seemed to be paying off. But she and the Coalition Avenir Québec are now fighting for survival in Monday’s election
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Christine Fréchette has done her best to outrun her own party.

Since taking over the Coalition Avenir Québec and becoming Premier in April, she has tried less to rehabilitate a tarnished brand than to erase it.

Her strategy was on display at the launch of the Quebec election campaign in late August, when observers quickly noticed that her bus and election signs did not feature her party’s name. “ Avançons ,” her campaign slogan read. Let’s move forward.

Ms. Fréchette, 56, began the first debate of the campaign by declaring that she is not her predecessor, François Legault.

As she faces a restive electorate looking for change, she has attempted to shed the baggage of her party’s eight years in government. In this election, she is selling herself.

For a moment, voters were buying in. Early in the campaign, which began days after trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart, Ms. Fréchette invited comparisons to Prime Minister Mark Carney. Like him, she embodied the sort of unflappable technocrat that seemed a welcome contrast to the erratic and hostile behaviour of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Though the Coalition Avenir Québec had spent months circling the drain, Ms. Fréchette, who declined an interview request from The Globe and Mail, orchestrated an unlikely comeback.

It seemed possible she could achieve what Mr. Carney had done in last year’s federal election and turn near-certain defeat into an improbable victory. If she was a touch bland, well, perhaps that was exactly what Quebeckers were looking for.

But then it went away. Days ahead of the vote on Oct. 5, Ms. Fréchette’s campaign has lost its momentum. The winds of change are blowing in the direction of a Parti Québécois government, regardless of Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s unpopular promise to hold a third referendum on independence.

Despite Ms. Fréchette’s best efforts, the legacy of the CAQ has caught up to her. Now, she is fighting for the survival of the party she would prefer not to name.

Christine Fréchette is not the kind of politician who delivers thunderous oratory or inspires breathless excitement, but in a way, that’s what her supporters like about her.

She has had the unenviable task of reshaping a party built in the image of Mr. Legault, who co-founded the CAQ in 2011 and led it to form government in 2018.

Mr. Legault, who announced his resignation in January after more than seven years as premier, had a folksy, plainspoken style and a hair-trigger reaction to negative press. Though he walked on water during the COVID-19 pandemic, a series of controversies and questionable financial decisions had made him one of the least popular politicians in the country by the time he made his exit.

At a September campaign event on Montreal’s South Shore, supporters told The Globe and Mail they’d joined the party specifically because of Ms. Fréchette.

Marie-France Bilodeau, 69, said she previously voted for the CAQ but grew disenchanted with Mr. Legault’s performance. She became a party member to support Ms. Fréchette’s bid for the leadership earlier this year. “She’s really smart. I think she takes the time to think things through before making decisions,” Ms. Bilodeau said. “She’s calm.”

As the room emptied out after the event, she approached the CAQ Leader. “The only thing that brought me back was you,” she told her.

Ms. Fréchette doesn’t stand out as the type of person who would want to be premier, though she showed an interest in public policy and civic life from a young age.

The cut and thrust of partisan politics appealed less to her, said Vicky Trépanier, a long-time friend. “She wants to have in-depth debates.”

Ms. Trépanier, who is not involved in politics, met the future Premier when they were both part of the student movement of the 1990s. Ms. Fréchette earned a Master’s degree in international relations from Laval University in 1994, and went on to work for a provincewide student union.

In those early years, she rubbed shoulders with a group of future politicos, including Martin Koskinen, who would become Mr. Legault’s long-time chief of staff. “She wasn’t someone who wanted to be the centre of attention,” Mr. Koskinen recalled in an interview.

Several years after completing her studies, Ms. Fréchette began organizing annual simulations of a North American parliament attended by university students from Canada, the United States and Mexico.

It was an impressive achievement, said Ms. Trépanier, who helped out with the paperwork and grew close to Ms. Fréchette during that time. “She created an institution that didn’t exist.”

Starting in 2007, Ms. Fréchette worked at a centre for international studies at the University of Montreal, where she met Jean-François Lisée, a future leader of the separatist Parti Québécois. When Mr. Lisée was elected to the National Assembly in 2012 and named minister of international relations, he hired her to work in his office.

Ms. Fréchette had voted “yes” in 1995, but she was never a “militant sovereigntist,” said Ms. Trépanier, her friend.

Her career with the PQ would be short-lived, however. She left the minister’s office in 2014, unable to accept the government’s proposed charter of values, which would have banned religious symbols for many public servants.

Ms. Fréchette would go on to spend nearly five years as the head of the chamber of commerce of eastern Montreal. But there were signs she was looking for a new political home. Ms. Trépanier recalled that after Ms. Fréchette left the PQ, the two of them attended a meeting of a group of so-called “orphelins politiques” (political orphans) organized by none other than Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who would seek the PQ leadership for the first time in 2016.

As the CAQ gained prominence, Mr. Legault, who had moved in the same circles as Ms. Fréchette in her younger years, tried to recruit her to the party multiple times, according to her partner, businessman Guy Nadeau. She declined his invitation to run for the CAQ in 2018, having started her position at the chamber of commerce not long before.

But when he came calling again four years later, she was ready to take the plunge. Among other things, she was impressed by how Mr. Legault had handled the pandemic, Mr. Nadeau said. “It took shape slowly in her mind,” he said. “She’s not an opportunist.”

Ms. Fréchette won a seat in the National Assembly as the CAQ formed its second majority government. She was named immigration minister, before being moved to the high-stakes energy and economy portfolio in 2024.

In the fall of 2025, after the Caq’s support had collapsed, colleagues told Ms. Fréchette she should consider running to replace Mr. Legault if he resigned, her partner said. She felt it might be a “unique opportunity” that wouldn’t come along again, he added.

Mr. Koskinen, Mr. Legault’s chief of staff, hadn’t expected the reserved Ms. Fréchette would want the job.

But he now believes her restraint was part of her appeal to party members. “Quebeckers weren’t going to choose a François Legault 2.0.”

After being sworn in as the province’s second-ever female premier in April, Ms. Fréchette hit the ground running.

Political observers suggested the best she could hope for was to save her party from devastation. But ahead of an election set for October that would hinge partly on the question of sovereignty, she took steps to prove she could work within Canada.

While Mr. Legault had an often adversarial relationship with Ottawa, Ms. Fréchette arranged a meeting with Mr. Carney two days after her swearing-in. The two leaders have since made several joint announcements, and the CAQ enjoyed a modest bump in the polls.

Ms. Fréchette kicked off her campaign in late August as a new round of U.S. tariffs loomed, naming Mr. Trump as her prime adversary. Her party’s fortunes rose again, with one survey putting the CAQ neck-and-neck with the PQ.

But the Trump effect didn’t last, said political analyst Antonine Yaccarini. “People have gotten somewhat used to the tariff crisis.”

Ms. Fréchette has proven less adept at campaigning than at being Premier, Ms. Yaccarini said, and her debate performances were underwhelming. She is also an easy mark for her opponents, given the eight years of unpopular CAQ decisions that are all too easy to dredge up.

The CAQ Leader has also prevaricated repeatedly when asked for her personal position on sovereignty, despite her promise not to hold a referendum.

Back in April, before anyone was comparing Ms. Fréchette to Mr. Carney, some were drawing parallels to a different Canadian prime minister. Kim Campbell, who took over from Brian Mulroney in June, 1993, led the Progressive Conservatives to a devastating defeat in an election that November, from which the party never really recovered.

Ms. Fréchette May share the same fate. Quebec’s governing party is once again looking to save the furniture, with projections suggesting it could lose every one of its 79 seats. A majority May be in reach for the PQ.

In the months since becoming Premier, Ms. Fréchette has made it very clear who she is not. She is not François Legault. She is certainly not Donald Trump. And she is not Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

But it is less clear who she is, and that could be her downfall. “The problem is she herself, despite her impressive demeanour, is a bit of an empty shell,” journalist and author Francine Pelletier said in an interview. “What’s the new dream?”

How do today’s young Quebec sovereigntists differ from other generations since the Quiet Revolution? Reporter Maura Forrest spoke with The Decibel about how age and ideology shape Quebec politics, and could decide this year’s provincial election. Subscribe for more episodes.

In the months since becoming Premier, Ms. Fréchette has made it very clear who she is not. She is not François Legault. She is certainly not Donald Trump. And she is not Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

But it is less clear who she is, and that could be her downfall. “The problem is she herself, despite her impressive demeanour, is a bit of an empty shell,” journalist and author Francine Pelletier said in an interview. “What’s the new dream?”

How do today’s young Quebec sovereigntists differ from other generations since the Quiet Revolution? Reporter Maura Forrest spoke with The Decibel about how age and ideology shape Quebec politics, and could decide this year’s provincial election. Subscribe for more episodes.

stories.title: Canadians mark fifth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canadians across the country will mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday for the fifth consecutive year, honouring the survivors of residential schools and those who never made it home.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Indigenous leaders struck a resolute tone Wednesday as the country marked the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation following reports of a white supremacist demonstration in a First Nations community in the B.C. interior.

“Survivors have fought for decades to defend their truths and confront the distortion of history, while our legal system still fails to recognize denialism for what it is — hatred disguised as free speech,” Stephanie Scott, executive director of the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, told a gathering on Parliament Hill.

“All of you hold the power to honour survivors and demand accountability, not only from our leaders but from one another. Truth and reconciliation is an ongoing responsibility, a human rights obligation and a sacred commitment.”

Roseanne Casimir, chief of Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc First Nation, said on Sunday a group of masked individuals dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops, B.C. The banner — bearing the words “Got bones?” — appeared to be questioning reports of human burials at the former sites of residential schools.

In May 2021, the First Nation announced ground-penetrating radar had uncovered what were believed to be 215 unmarked graves at the site of the former Kamloops Indian Residential School. That news made international headlines and led to the community being attacked online.

Some outside individuals reportedly brought shovels to the community and the First Nation was forced to increase security around the site of the former school.

Researchers at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation have identified 63 children who died at the former Kamloops Indian Residential School. Their names and dates of death are listed by the organization.

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak visited the community on Wednesday in an act of solidarity.

Beginning in the 19th century, more than 150,000 Indigenous children were separated from their families and communities and sent to church-run residential schools where abuse, malnutrition and inadequate health care were rampant.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission concluded in its landmark 2015 final report that the school system was a central element of a state-backed policy of cultural genocide.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission initially documented the deaths of 3,200 children at residential schools. Experts at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation — who continue to comb through millions of records — say the actual number could be much higher.

The establishment of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Sept. 30 was among the recommendations in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s report. It’s meant to honour the survivors of residential schools and those who never made it home.

A First Nation in B.C. was forced to end its memorial walk early on Wednesday after two people were killed in a crash at the Tsawwassen Mills mall in Delta.

Police said early information indicates the driver of the vehicle May have experienced a medical emergency before the collision. Police reported no ongoing public safety risk and said the crash was not related to the community walk to mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation that was taking place nearby.

The incident prompted the Tsawwassen First Nation to end the event.

“Tsawwassen First Nation is deeply saddened to confirm that an incident occurred during today’s Truth and Reconciliation Walk,” it said in a media statement.

CBC/Radio-Canada, Aptn and the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation hosted the annual Remembering the Children event on Parliament Hill.

Bernard Andreason, a survivor who has written a book describing how he and two friends fled the Stringer Hall Residential School in Inuvik, told the crowd in Ottawa that it was inspiring to hear from survivors who speak their own languages.

“‘Take the Indian from the child.’ You can’t do that. It’s next to impossible,” he said.

Andreason said many communities today are “working towards a better education for our children” so they can be at home while they go to school.

Jacquie Bouvier, a third-generation survivor and a member of the survivors circle at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, told Indigenous youth in the crowd they carry the strength and love of previous generations.

“Every time we speak our languages, share our teachings, gather with one another as Indigenous Peoples, we reclaim something that was meant to be taken from us,” she said.

Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour told the gathering Canada must “confront all forms of denialism that persist, despite extensive historical records.”

“Remembering is only one step. It must be accompanied by a commitment to ensuring that injustices are never, ever repeated,” Arbour said.

Guests and participants at the Parliament Hill event were encouraged to bring a pair of children’s shoes to place at the front of the stage to honour those who attended residential schools.

Arbour added a small pair of orange moccasins to the display as a 60-metre-long cloth bearing the names of children who died as a result of residential schools was carried through the crowd.

A number of people in attendance held one another and wiped away tears as the memorial cloth was presented.

Separate events to mark the day took place across the country, including in Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary and Iqaluit.

Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke at an event in Edmonton.

He issued a statement before the event in English, French and nine Indigenous languages, including Algonquin, Denesuline, Innu-Aimun, Inuktitut (Northern Baffin), Mi’kmaq, Michif, Oji-Cree, Plains Cree, and Western Ojibway.

In his speech, Carney said we shouldn’t choose which parts of history we remember.

“We shouldn’t admire the beadwork and forget the children that were forced into uniforms. We shouldn’t honour the drum and ignore the years that it was made to fall silent,” he said. “And we should not hear the truth of residential schools and fail to act on it.”

Only 14 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 calls to action have been completed in the last 11 years, according to independent monitor Indigenous Watchdog. Another 41 recommendations are considered in progress, while 24 are stalled and 15 have not been started.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also attended the event in Edmonton. He wrote on social media that residential schools were a “massive intrusion of government coercion imposed on Indigenous families.”

“They removed children from their parents and communities, while attempting to break their connection to their very identity,” he said.

“On the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, we honour these children, their families and their communities, and recommit to reconciliation built on self-determination, opportunity and true partnership.”

Scott said people around the world are looking to Canada for guidance, but the country still has a very long way to go.

“We are seeing a rising wave of residential school denialism, racist diatribe that tries to dehumanize us and incite violence,” Scott said.

“But we are better than that, and we are stronger than that because we know our own power.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume and Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Mark Carney is banking on economic reconciliation but critics say he’s not on track
stories.summary: Ottawa — When Wilton Littlechild was co-chairing the landmark Truth and Reconciliation Commission more than a decade ago, he thought a lot about the idea of economic reconciliation and how it could help transform Indigenous communities.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 6:01 am.

Ottawa — When Wilton Littlechild was co-chairing the landmark Truth and Reconciliation Commission more than a decade ago, he thought a lot about the idea of economic reconciliation and how it could help transform Indigenous communities.

“You May have the best ideas in the world but without a fundamental grounding and foundation to self-determination, you’re missing a very important part,” Littlechild said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

Littlechild said economic reconciliation is still the key to achieving reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians — but not in the way Prime Minister Mark Carney sees it.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, launched out of a legal settlement between the federal government and survivors of residential schools, was tasked with researching the history and legacy of those institutions. It was chaired by Littlechild, Murray Sinclair and Marie Wilson.

Between 1857 and 1996, 150,000 Indigenous children were forced to attend church-run, government-funded schools. They were barred from speaking their languages in institutions often rife with abuse and located far away from their families and communities.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission initially documented the deaths of 3,200 children attending residential schools. Experts at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation — who continue to comb through millions of records — say the actual number could be much higher.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission concluded in 2015 the goal of the schools was to erase Indigenous cultures. MPs unanimously voted to recognize residential schools as a form of genocide in 2022.

Economic reconciliation is mentioned twice in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 Calls to Action. They call on the corporate sector to engage in meaningful consultations before proceeding with economic development projects, and to ensure Indigenous people have equitable access to jobs in those projects.

The federal government under Carney has made economic reconciliation the focus of its efforts to rebuild relations with Indigenous Peoples as it pushes forward an aggressive major projects agenda in the face of U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Littlechild said that while Carney has been focused on securing overseas investments, he’s ignoring the rights of Indigenous Peoples at home and sidelining their traditional economies by fast-tracking legislation that would allow for quicker project approvals and environmental reviews.

He said Carney’s approach risks alienating Indigenous communities and the federal government’s idea of economic reconciliation falls short of the efforts industry is making to work in partnership with communities. He said he also fears traditional economies — hunting, fishing, trapping — could be damaged by an aggressive approach to resource development.

“Right now, it’s like a four-legged stool with one leg missing,” Littlechild said. That missing leg, he said, is true respect for Indigenous rights.

The federal government’s Bill C-39, known as the Building Canada Strong Act, seeks to approve projects within one year. First Nations chiefs say they worry that will severely compress the timeline for their communities to complete land-use assessments and consultations.

Similar legislation introduced by Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s government is being challenged by Indigenous and environmental groups in court.

And while Ottawa’s focus has shifted to economic reconciliation, the Trc’s Calls to Action that touch more on social issues are languishing, Littlechild said.

“(Carney is) approaching things by violating treaty rights, by violating the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and just steamrolling on national interest strategies that completely exclude us by way of disrespect,” he said.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty disagreed with the suggestion that Carney does not prioritize Indigenous rights or the social issues faced by communities.

“There is a lot of institutional reconciliation that’s happening,” Gull-Masty told The Canadian Press, citing work on reforming child and family services.

“And to me, that institutional reconciliation is maybe not language people are familiar with, but it is in progress and it is occurring.”

Hayden King, executive director of the Yellowhead Institute, said he wonders what those institutional commitments are — since First Nations are still waiting for the government to pass clean drinking water legislation, improve their access to health care, address the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, and reduce incarceration and over-policing in their communities.

“All I’ve heard Carney talk about is resource development,” King said.

“You can look at all of the proposals to improve the relationship, institutionally or otherwise, and it’s just a record of neglect.”

Yellowhead released a report last year on major projects and the conflicts that could arise from Indigenous participation — including the prospect of one First Nation violating the rights of another in order to invest in a controversial project.

King said Carney’s approach to relations with Indigenous communities puts him more in line with former prime minister Stephen Harper than with Justin Trudeau. Harper’s government also introduced legislation to speed up project approvals, leading to the Idle No More movement that staged protests across the country in 2012.

“Where Harper was the stick, Carney is the carrot,” King said.

The “carrot” approach can be seen in how Carney’s cabinet is encouraging First Nations to back the Trans Mountain pipeline through a low-cost loan and a $2.5 million payment for willing investors that some are comparing to a bribe.

“The discourse around (economic reconciliation) is most definitely that Indigenous people are going to be formal partners and this is going to breathe life into Indigenous sovereignty,” King said.

“But it’s the reverse of the process that the TRC advocated for — it was, ‘Let’s get this relationship right, and then we can talk about partnerships.'”

King said economic reconciliation can’t be achieved until Indigenous groups no longer have to fight for their rights and their land in court.

“If we’re really interested in holding up sovereignty and jurisdiction, then we have to insist on consent, and consent means knowing all the details before we make decisions.”

Stephanie Scott heads the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, which works to preserve the historical record of residential schools and educate Canadians about what happened in the institutions.

She said while economic reconciliation can help create opportunities, strengthen communities and support Indigenous governance, reconciliation is about people — the survivors, their families, communities and future generations.

She pointed to the growing tide of residential school denialism — which scholars have warned risks unwinding decades of progress in the relationship between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Peoples.

“In a time when truth is being challenged and distorted, the need for trusted institutions to preserve, protect and share the historical record has never been greater,” Scott said.

NDP MP Leah Gazan has put legislation to criminalize residential school denialism before the House of Commons, but the Liberals have not indicated they will support it.

Calls for its passage grew louder this week after a group linked with white nationalism reportedly staged a demonstration in the B.C. interior.

Roseanne Casimir, chief of Tk̓emlups te Secwepemc First Nation, said on Sunday a group of masked individuals dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops, B.C. The banner — bearing the words “Got bones?” — appeared to be questioning reports of human burials at the former sites of residential schools.

The demonstration happened just days ahead of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, a day to honour the children who attended residential schools and to remember the ones who never came home.

Scott said that while Canada’s future depends on trust, justice and shared prosperity, those things can’t exist without truth.

“Residential school denialism is not harmless dialogue or a difference of opinion. It is a deliberate misinterpretation of the history and is an ongoing source of harm to Indigenous Peoples,” Scott said.

Littlechild said the way forward is to work together — both on the economy and on the social issues that have afflicted Indigenous communities for decades.

“We’re not taking advantage of opportunities because they’re still building a fence between us by not including us,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: From chocolate to coin purses, Lake Ontario merchandise proves a hit with consumers
stories.summary: Toronto — After Tareq Hadhad and his family moved to Antigonish, N.S., as Syrian refugees in 2016, they built a business on the premise that chocolate was so uniting it could create peace.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 6:01 am.

Toronto — After Tareq Hadhad and his family moved to Antigonish, N.S., as Syrian refugees in 2016, they built a business on the premise that chocolate was so uniting it could create peace.

So when U.S. President Donald Trump renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America in late August, the chief executive of Peace by Chocolate felt he couldn’t ignore the antagonism.

Within a day, his company had created the Lake Ontario bar — 92 grams of milk chocolate and maple cream, made partially with Ontario ingredients, packaged in a Canadian flag wrapper and emblazoned with the body of water’s name and information about its Indigenous origins.

“We wanted to be there for our country, no matter how odd that it sounded,” Hadhad said. “If you showed me a Lake Ontario chocolate bar, even a year ago, I would say, why would we even create one because we have so many great lakes all across Canada? But it meant a big deal.”

The treat quickly became one of the company’s five bestselling bars, generating interest from coast to coast and a flurry of emails from south of the border, where Peace by Chocolate has paused sales because of tariffs on exports to the United States.

The reaction has been just as strong at many other Canadian companies selling Lake Ontario products, ranging from candles and caps to cottage decor and more. One month after the body of water entered the president’s crosshairs, businesses say interest in Lake Ontario merchandise remains high.

Teresa Paul, owner of Rockwood, Ont., leather goods company Hides in Hand, said the Lake Ontario coin purses she started making and selling recently are a “pretty hot” commodity.

Customers have been buying them from a store in Erin, Ont., or craft fairs she participates in, often picking up extra for family members.

“People are like, ‘Yep, I want it. Yep, I’ll take two,'” Paul said. “They love them.”

The zippered pouches come in red or blue leather and are embroidered with the outline of Lake Ontario and the body of water’s name. They’re made with Canadian components and embroidered in Ontario.

Paul designed the pouch in no time after Trump’s lake renaming “rubbed me the wrong way,” she said.

“Because I’m a leather designer, my way of responding was to actually make something. I thought why not put Lake Ontario right there on something that we’re making here in Ontario?” she said.

“It’s that little expression of Lake Ontario and Canadian pride. Nothing angry, nothing over political. Just something practical, something that meant home to me.”

Unlike Paul, when the name swap first bubbled up, Province of Canada wasn’t sure it would wade into the moment. There was no shortage of patriotism in the Toronto-based apparel company’s collections — Le Canadien T-shirts, “Made in Canada” sweatshirts and “I was Canadian before it was cool” crop tops.

“But it really became, I think, a movement and we felt that as a Canadian brand who makes their products in Canada, we really did need to become part of the conversation in some way,” said product and operations manager Alli Piccininni.

The company had been selling prints of the Great Lakes for a few years but decided that wasn’t enough.

It designed a grey fleece sweatshirt with “Lake Ontario” in navy and offered it through preorder with 15 per cent of each purchase being sent to Indspire, an Indigenous education charity.

The sweater sold out “really, really quickly,” Piccininni said.

Another round was made and availability has dwindled down to just a few sizes, so the company prepared a third batch shipping in December and fourth featuring a new colourway scheduled to reach buyers before Christmas.

Piccininni couldn’t be happier with that reception.

“When customers get behind us and support us … it’s a really good feeling,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Mark Carney’s stand against Trump leads to Nobel Peace Prize and Time Person of the Year buzz
stories.summary: Toronto (AP) — Mark Carney built a global profile in 2026 by standing up to U.S. President Donald Trump. If some prediction-market traders and prominent admirers are right, the Canadian prime minister could end the year with the Nobel Peace Prize and Time magazine’s Person of the Year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Rob Gillies, The Associated Press,

Posted September 30, 2026 3:17 am.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 6:01 am.

Toronto (AP) — Mark Carney built a global profile in 2026 by standing up to U.S. President Donald Trump. If some prediction-market traders and prominent admirers are right, the Canadian prime minister could end the year with the Nobel Peace Prize and Time magazine’s Person of the Year.

Carney briefly became the favorite Monday for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Kalshi , a U.S.-based prediction market, when traders on the exchange put his chances at 14%. His odds later fell, illustrating the highly speculative nature of the wagering.

There is no public evidence Carney is on the Nobel Committee’s secret shortlist for the prize that will be announced Oct. 9 in Oslo, Norway.

But the buzz about the Canadian leader possibly winning the esteemed peace prize reflects the message that has raised his profile: Middle powers should band together to defend sovereignty as great powers increasingly use economic and military leverage.

Whether that position resonates with the Nobel Committee is impossible to know. One thing is certain, though: the Nobel and Time’s annual award happen to be two honors Trump covets .

Trump believes he deserves Nobel honor

Carney and Trump are locked in an escalating trade war , with 50% U.S. tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods and Canadian retaliation. Trump also has told Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far Worse” than existing tariffs.

Trump, who has twice been Time’s Person of the Year, has repeatedly complained about not receiving the Nobel, saying in July that he “should have won that award more than anybody.”

“President Trump would be furious, of course,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. “If this ever happens, I would love to be a fly on the wall of the Oval Office to see the president’s face when he learns about it.”

Trump already possesses a Nobel medal, just not one awarded to him.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 Nobel laureate, presented Trump with her medal at the White House in January. Trump accepted it, while the Nobel Committee stressed the prize itself remains hers.

“Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel,” said Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto. “If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are.”

Carney has strong case for Time award

Time already named Carney one of its 100 most influential people of 2026 and specifically noted his popularity increased as he stood up to Trump.

On Tuesday, Carney was the second choice on major prediction markets for Time’s Person of the Year, behind New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The winner will be announced Dec. 10.

There is no public evidence Carney is on the Nobel Committee’s secret shortlist for the prize that will be announced Oct. 9 in Oslo, Norway.

But the buzz about the Canadian leader possibly winning the esteemed peace prize reflects the message that has raised his profile: Middle powers should band together to defend sovereignty as great powers increasingly use economic and military leverage.

stories.title: Mary Louie recalls leaving residential school and why her band marks Orange Shirt Day a day early
stories.summary: When Mary Louie was at Residential school she remembers wanting only one thing when she was a young girl at residential school: to get home.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
Mary Louie remembers wanting only one thing when she was a young girl at residential school: to get home.

Louie says she did not understand everything happening around her, but she noticed changes in the friends and became increasingly uneasy.

“Well, I did go to residential school, but what I seen, I didn’t quite understand what was happening,” Louie said.

She eventually escaped the school late one night.

“I stayed off the road. I stayed in the mountains and crossed the highway at night. Walked back and walked home” Louie said.

She says fear did not stop her from making the journey.

“I just walked and I wasn’t afraid or anything, so I just wanted to get home,” she said.

Louie’s story was among those remembered Tuesday as the Lower Similkameen Indian Band (Lsib) held its Community Walk close to Keremeos for Truth and Reconciliation, one day before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Organizers wanted the community to come together for a collective remembrance on Sept. 29, leaving the actual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation for people to commemorate in their own way. Darian Ueusta-Che-Peone, who works with the band, says the group activity is meant to happen beforehand so people can spend Sept. 30 reflecting individually.

“That actual day we can kind of rest and like you know think about what happened and today we celebrate it so we have that kind of rest in between of the day,” he said.

For Lsib elder Herman Edward, residential schools took far more than childhoods from Indigenous families.

“We all lost something. It’s not always the orange shirts, but it was our culture, language, way of life,” Edward said.

But the national day of remembrance has also become a point of controversy.

In Kamloops, masked men were seen protesting Truth and Reconciliation events, drawing condemnation and an RCMP investigation.

Janet Cherbaskin, an Lsib council member, says demonstrations like that cannot erase the experiences of residential school survivors.

“You can’t erase history. It doesn’t matter what you say and how you dress. You can be in masks and and try and prove a point. But to our people, we know what the truth is,” Cherbaskin said.

When Louie finally made it home, she never wanted to return to school. Instead, she stayed home to look after her younger siblings and learned from her grandmother.

“Ever since I got home, my place was to take care of my siblings, so I didn’t go back to school. A lot of the things I’ve learned was from my grandmother and the teaching she gave me,” Louie said.

For Louie, seeing children take part carries particular meaning after her own experience at residential school.

“Well, it’s good to see the children and to know and I pray that the parents love their children and start teaching them,” she said.

After walking home from residential school as a young girl, Louie now sees children walking together as a community

stories.title: Fatal shooting investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (September 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section are investigating a fatal shooting in the downtown core.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (September 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section are investigating a fatal shooting in the downtown core.

At approximately 5:45 p.m. on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, police responded to the area of Central Avenue and Richmond Street after receiving reports of a possible shooting.

An adult male was located with life-threatening injuries and transported to hospital by paramedic services, where he was later pronounced deceased.

A suspect male has been arrested and the investigation is ongoing.

Officers are actively investigating this matter and will maintain a visible presence in the area as the investigation continues.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 5:30 p.m. and 6 p.m., and who May have information, dash-cam footage, or residential or business video surveillance, to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670.

The investigation is in its early stages, and more information will be provided as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .
paragraphs: London, ON (September 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section are investigating a fatal shooting in the downtown core.
At approximately 5:45 p.m. on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, police responded to the area of Central Avenue and Richmond Street after receiving reports of a possible shooting.
An adult male was located with life-threatening injuries and transported to hospital by paramedic services, where he was later pronounced deceased.
A suspect male has been arrested and the investigation is ongoing.
Officers are actively investigating this matter and will maintain a visible presence in the area as the investigation continues.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 5:30 p.m. and 6 p.m., and who May have information, dash-cam footage, or residential or business video surveillance, to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670.
The investigation is in its early stages, and more information will be provided as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Good medicine: LHSC’s Visiting Elders program brings culture, connection, and healing to patients
stories.summary: September 30, 2026
stories.content:
September 30, 2026

At London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), the Visiting Elders program is helping First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous patients access cultural and spiritual support as part of their care journeys. Through the program, patients, families, staff, and care teams can meet with Elders from local First Nations communities, who provide teachings, ceremony, Traditional medicines, counselling, and cultural support.

Elders are respected Knowledge Keepers, cultural advisors, and spiritual guides from local First Nations communities. Many have spent decades practicing Traditional healing and ceremonies, and carry languages, knowledge, and teachings passed down through generations. They help patients reconnect with culture, find comfort during difficult moments, and navigate challenges that extend beyond physical illness.

For Chantel Antone, LHSC’s Director of Indigenous Health, the Visiting Elders program is an essential step in ensuring Indigenous patients and families can access care that reflects their needs, traditions, and values.

“This program was initially launched in 2022 to support patients with their mental, spiritual, and physical well-being,” says Antone. “Over the years, we have seen countless stories where the wisdom, lived experience, and knowledge that our Elders offer has been invaluable to the healing process.”

The program exists alongside LHSC’s Indigenous Healing and Cultural Practices Policy , which helps ensure these services are available as part of a patient’s healing journey. Patients and families who would like to access the Visiting Elders program or Indigenous healing and cultural supports can speak with a member of their care team, who can help connect them with the service.

Elder Tracey Whiteye visits LHSC from Elunaapéwii Lahkéewiit (Delaware Nation of the Thames) and is a regular presence in LHSC’s Mental Health Indigenous Healing Space . For Whiteye, healing begins when people reconnect with themselves, their culture, and the world around them.

“Everything has spirit,” she explains. “The land has spirit, the plants have spirit, everything is alive. When we connect these spirits together, it also connects our spirit. And with that, healing happens.”

Whiteye says some Indigenous patients carry the impacts of colonization, Residential Schools, and historic trauma with them when they come to the hospital for care. For many, reconnecting with ceremony, medicines, songs, language, or teachings can awaken what she calls “blood memory” and remind people where they come from.

Her vision for health-care is one where Indigenous and Western approaches work side by side.

“Let's put our Indigenous lens and our Western lens together,” she says. “That way, we can focus on our strengths, our wisdom, and our knowledge. Ultimately, we're here for the patients.”

Elder Mike Hopkins also visits LHSC from Elunaapéwii Lahkéewiit (Delaware Nation of the Thames). He believes that healing requires caring for the whole person.

As an Elder, Hopkins has spent more than four decades learning Traditional teachings. He often reminds patients, families, and staff that every healing journey is unique.

“Everyone that comes in, they're all different,” he says. “They have to be treated differently.”

Through ceremony, prayer, Traditional medicines, and spiritual guidance, Hopkins helps patients care for the needs of the spirit as well as their physical wellness.

“When we have a patient in the Healing Space, and their body and spirit are disconnected, we do the best we can to take care of that,” he explains. “We also take care of the spirit so it can become one that will heal itself.”

His work extends beyond patients, as Hopkins routinely supports LHSC staff by teaching cultural knowledge, sharing Indigenous values, and helping people navigate personal and professional challenges.

Elder Wendy Hill visits LHSC from Six Nations of the Grand River Territory and feels the need for cultural healing is deeply connected to history.

“For too long Indigenous Peoples have been deprived of it,” she says. “The knowledge, teachings, history, ceremonies, and languages have been hidden from us.”

She recalls supporting an Indigenous woman nearing the end of her life who had become estranged from her family after experiencing the impacts of Residential Schools. Through conversations grounded in compassion, understanding, and cultural teachings, Hill helped the patient begin forgiving herself and repairing damaged relationships.

“It was just a real healing moment that I saw with her,” Hill remembers. “I don't know if she would have gotten that from anywhere else.”

For Hill, stories like these demonstrate why cultural support belongs in health-care.

“Sometimes just smelling the sage or tobacco, or hearing the prayers and the language, is what really heals their spirit.”

Elder Myeengun Henry visits LHSC from Deshkan Zibing (Chippewas of the Thames First Nation). He states that the future of health care lies in bringing together the strengths of Indigenous and Western approaches.

“For generations, many of us were discouraged from practicing Traditional ceremonies or accessing cultural supports within health-care settings,” says Henry. “There’s still a fear of coming to hospitals because of the treatment that we’ve had over the years.”

LHSC’s Visiting Elders program helps remove those barriers by creating safe spaces for Indigenous patients to access care that aligns with their identity, beliefs, and healing traditions.

“We have to build it so that everybody can feel the wealth of healing, which they're entitled to,” says Henry.

He sees hope in the growing number of young people learning their languages, ceremonies, and cultural teachings, and in health-care organizations willing to walk alongside Indigenous communities on the path toward Reconciliation.

Elder Chris George also visits LHSC from Deshkan Zibing (Chippewas of the Thames First Nation), and brings teachings rooted in Traditional medicine, public speaking, and knowledge passed down from the Elders who came before him. He believes that being an Elder means carrying those teachings forward and sharing them in ways that support healing, understanding, and connection.

For George, meaningful Truth and Reconciliation in health-care settings requires hospitals and care providers to better understand the different histories, teachings, and worldviews that Indigenous and non-Indigenous people can bring into a shared experience.

Traditional ways of healing carry deep spiritual teachings and cultural knowledge, while Western medicine is shaped by its own philosophy and systems. To George, Reconciliation means making room for both, so Indigenous patients can receive care that respects their identity, honours their healing traditions, and helps rebuild trust.

“People need to know there are two understandings when it comes to Reconciliation,” says George, reflecting on the relationship between Indigenous spiritual teachings and Western philosophy. "Knowing this is essential for us to create a future where Indigenous patients feel that their culture, spirit, and medicines are embraced as part of their healing.”

Looking ahead, George finds hope in seeing more Indigenous communities become strong and healthy through Traditional healing and cultural practices. It is a vision where Reconciliation is actively lived through care that honours the individual and helps build a stronger future for generations to come.

The Visiting Elders program is part of a broader Indigenous Health strategy underway at LHSC, positioning the organization as a leader in advancing culturally safe, Indigenous-led care within hospital settings.

Over the past several years, the hospital has worked closely with Indigenous communities, Elders, Knowledge Keepers, patients, and leaders to build culturally safer care environments. Those partnerships have helped shape LHSC’s Indigenous Healing and Cultural Practices Policy, which affirms Indigenous patients’ right to access ceremony, traditional medicines, healing spaces, and Elder support as part of their care.

For Antone, this work is ultimately about building trust.

“This program represents another positive step in our efforts to build trust with Indigenous patients, families, and communities, and create a hospital environment where they feel seen, heard, and supported in every aspect of their healing.”

At London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), the Visiting Elders program is helping First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous patients access cultural and spiritual support as part of their care journeys. Through the program, patients, families, staff, and care teams can meet with Elders from local First Nations communities, who provide teachings, ceremony, Traditional medicines, counselling, and cultural support.

Elders are respected Knowledge Keepers, cultural advisors, and spiritual guides from local First Nations communities. Many have spent decades practicing Traditional healing and ceremonies, and carry languages, knowledge, and teachings passed down through generations. They help patients reconnect with culture, find comfort during difficult moments, and navigate challenges that extend beyond physical illness.

For Chantel Antone, LHSC’s Director of Indigenous Health, the Visiting Elders program is an essential step in ensuring Indigenous patients and families can access care that reflects their needs, traditions, and values.

“This program was initially launched in 2022 to support patients with their mental, spiritual, and physical well-being,” says Antone. “Over the years, we have seen countless stories where the wisdom, lived experience, and knowledge that our Elders offer has been invaluable to the healing process.”

The program exists alongside LHSC’s Indigenous Healing and Cultural Practices Policy , which helps ensure these services are available as part of a patient’s healing journey. Patients and families who would like to access the Visiting Elders program or Indigenous healing and cultural supports can speak with a member of their care team, who can help connect them with the service.

Elder Tracey Whiteye visits LHSC from Elunaapéwii Lahkéewiit (Delaware Nation of the Thames) and is a regular presence in LHSC’s Mental Health Indigenous Healing Space . For Whiteye, healing begins when people reconnect with themselves, their culture, and the world around them.

“Everything has spirit,” she explains. “The land has spirit, the plants have spirit, everything is alive. When we connect these spirits together, it also connects our spirit. And with that, healing happens.”

Whiteye says some Indigenous patients carry the impacts of colonization, Residential Schools, and historic trauma with them when they come to the hospital for care. For many, reconnecting with ceremony, medicines, songs, language, or teachings can awaken what she calls “blood memory” and remind people where they come from.
Her vision for health-care is one where Indigenous and Western approaches work side by side.
“Let's put our Indigenous lens and our Western lens together,” she says. “That way, we can focus on our strengths, our wisdom, and our knowledge. Ultimately, we're here for the patients.”
Elder Mike Hopkins also visits LHSC from Elunaapéwii Lahkéewiit (Delaware Nation of the Thames). He believes that healing requires caring for the whole person.
As an Elder, Hopkins has spent more than four decades learning Traditional teachings. He often reminds patients, families, and staff that every healing journey is unique.
“Everyone that comes in, they're all different,” he says. “They have to be treated differently.”
Through ceremony, prayer, Traditional medicines, and spiritual guidance, Hopkins helps patients care for the needs of the spirit as well as their physical wellness.

“When we have a patient in the Healing Space, and their body and spirit are disconnected, we do the best we can to take care of that,” he explains. “We also take care of the spirit so it can become one that will heal itself.”
His work extends beyond patients, as Hopkins routinely supports LHSC staff by teaching cultural knowledge, sharing Indigenous values, and helping people navigate personal and professional challenges.

“For too long Indigenous Peoples have been deprived of it,” she says. “The knowledge, teachings, history, ceremonies, and languages have been hidden from us.”

Through conversations grounded in compassion, understanding, and cultural teachings, Hill helped the patient begin forgiving herself and repairing damaged relationships.
“It was just a real healing moment that I saw with her,” Hill remembers. “I don't know if she would have gotten that from anywhere else.”

“Sometimes just smelling the sage or tobacco, or hearing the prayers and the language, is what really heals their spirit.”

stories.title: Expert insight: Local journalism faces growing crisis in Canada – is government support part of the solution?
stories.summary: Western journalism professor Chris Arsenault examines whether government funding impacts journalists' freedom to report.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
In defending an independent press, American founding father Thomas Jefferson famously remarked that he would prefer “newspapers without a government” to a “government without newspapers.” So it’s doubtful the third president of the United States would approve of a program for the government to pay reporters’ salaries.

But desperate times for Canadian media, where newspapers are closing and journalists are losing their jobs, especially at the local level, May call for desperate measures.

At least one-third of journalism jobs in Canada have simply disappeared since 2010, according to government data, as news outlets collectively lost some $4.9 billion.

Canada has faced a net loss of at least 343 local news outlets since 2008, according to the Local News Research Project. It doesn’t require an investigative reporter to determine this is a crisis.

Against this backdrop, the federal government has spent $128.8 million since 2019 to support the hiring of more than 400 journalists under the Local Journalism Initiative(LJI) at newsrooms across the country.

The goal? Quality coverage in communities where the free market alone cannot support reporting, particularly news on local governments and civic affairs.

The money is doled out by administrator organizations – such as News Media Canada – representing different sections of the media industry and at arm’s length from the government of the day. Politicians don’t pick which reporters get funded.

News outlets apply to these organizations to hire reporters; individual journalists or content creators can’t apply on their own. All stories produced under the initiative are published under a Creative Commons licence on The Canadian Press news wire, meaning other media outlets are free to republish them, expanding the pool of local information available to everyone.

The program has been controversial. Journalists have a responsibility to hold powerful entities, including the government, to account. Critics, including some leading journalists, argue “taking money from the people we cover will place us in a permanent and inescapable conflict of interest,” producing “newspapers concerned less with appealing to readers than to grantsmen.”

Audiences don’t like how this smells either. Two polls came to similar conclusions, one commissioned by Toronto-based news outlet The Hub, which has been critical of the LJI, and the other commissioned by journalism support organizations. More than 70 per cent of Canadians believe news outlets could struggle to hold the government accountable while taking its money.

LJI critics also contend this infusion of government cash won’t do much to make the local news business sustainable over the long term.

On this last point, a majority of reporters funded under the initiative agree, according to my new research published in the journal Journalism Practice.

But the study, based on interviews with 22 LJI-funded reporters, paints a more complicated picture of conflict of interest.

Two-thirds of respondents expressed at least some concern with the appearance of a conflict of interest.

Yet no one could point to a specific story they were unable to cover assertively or that editors or grantors pressured them to change or drop as a result of the funding. Several of the same journalists, in contrast, offered clear examples of malign local advertiser influence earlier in their careers.

One now-veteran reporter was chasing tips that a grocery store in British Columbia was selling rotten meat to customers, exactly the kind of local accountability story audiences want. He recounted:

“I was told in no uncertain terms I was to stop working on the story, as the grocery store was the biggest advertiser for the paper. I had to do what I was told. The guys I worked with would have thrown me right off the bridge for the advertising money … I am sure most people who work in news could tell you a similar situation.”

No one described anything comparable involving LJI funding.

This isn’t to say the program is perfect. Many reporters complained about the sheer volume of stories they were expected to produce. Some said their LJI contracts stipulated they needed to write 12-15 stories each week. Under that kind of pressure, it’s nearly impossible to do serious investigative work holding governments, or anyone else, to account.

It’s much easier to rewrite a simple news release under those workload demands than to dig through campaign donations for local city councillors, analyze zoning board reports or engage in genuine investigative journalism.

These kinds of complaints about volume over value will be familiar to anyone who has worked in a newsroom. Still, many reporters financed by the initiative said they wouldn’t have a job without it, meaning no one would be keeping an eye on local officials, covering community events or writing the first draft of history in small-town Canada.

In years past, many viewed government control or censorship as the biggest threat to a free press. Today, that might not be the choice.

Of the options facing an industry in crisis, some targeted, arms-length government support might be the least bad option available. The audience, however, is right to be concerned. Journalists, like the people we cover, deserve scrutiny for our financial choices.

The key will be ensuring government cash isn’t the only option. In the U.S., non-profit foundations have increased their funding for journalism amid the industry’s business crisis.

Media Impact Funders, a network of grantors, estimates that the 25 largest journalism funders gave US$1.1 billion to journalism grantees globally between 2018 and 2022, based on 2024 data.

Smaller news outlets in Canada and elsewhere are trying new business models beyond selling advertising, including printing services, website hosting and even online gambling, in the case of Torstar, the company behind the Toronto Star.

Perfection shouldn’t get in the way of progress – or even risky experimentation – when it comes to saving the news industry.

The future of journalism May look like a loot bag following a kid’s birthday party – a little advertising money, subscription funds from loyal audience members, some entrepreneurial activities outside of the standard news business, and yes, perhaps some government support.

Today, the “government without newspapers” Jefferson feared is closer than ever. In some communities, it’s already here.

Ironically, some taxpayer assistance might be what the industry needs if we are to keep both our local news and some level of government accountability.Image 1: The Conversation

Chris Arsenault, Chair of the Master of Media in Journalism and Communication Program (Mmjc) and assistant professor of journalism, Western University

stories.title: Government overreach the true motivation behind Alberta separatism, not Canada itself, Poilievre says
stories.summary: In an Edmonton speech, the Conservative leader set aside Liberal attacks in favour of a more neutral takedown of Ottawa's relentless excesses
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre urged Albertans to vote to stay in Canada in the province’s upcoming referendum, arguing that Alberta’s resentments are best addressed by doubling down on the values that the Canadian Constitution was originally meant to uphold.

At a keynote speech in Edmonton, Poilievre made a classical conservative case for why the province’s deep resentments toward confederation are actually due to years of relentless government overreach rather than issues with the country itself.

“What Albertans are complaining about is not Canada,” he told a gathering of Conservative supporters. “It is the government policies that are actually inconsistent with how Canada was meant to work in the first place.”

At the root of the problem, Poilievre said, is that Ottawa has continued to expand its reach into areas of public life that it was never mandated to preside over, while trampling on the personal freedoms of citizens for political gain.

“Simply put, the last decade the federal government has done terribly at the things that are actually its job: immigration, crime, military spending, borders, while intruding into things that are not its job: regulating our resources, going after hunting rifles which are private property, just to name a few examples.”

“The problem with all of these things is not Canada,” he said. “Separation will not solve those problems.”

Poilievre’s address comes as more pro-federalist voices have started to make the case for keeping Alberta within confederation just weeks ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum. The federal Conservatives have long opposed Alberta’s separation, and earlier this month launched a “Conservatives for Canada” campaign in an effort to sway public opinion.

Support for separation on the Canadian prairies has reached new highs in the last few years, spurred on by frustration over everything from Ottawa’s over-regulation of its oil and gas sector to the federal government’s COVID-19 vaccine mandates during the pandemic.

Notably, Poilievre’s speech never once mentioned the federal Liberal Party or Prime Minister Mark Carney, leaving aside politically-charged attacks in favour of a more statesmanlike appeal to the problem of government excess.

The Canadian project was explicitly intended to give Alberta and other provinces control over its own affairs, Poilievre said as part of his address, with governments expected to intervene only within narrow and specified areas of public life. That means provincial governments sticking to matters like health care and education, and Ottawa focusing on matters like borders, national defence and criminal law.

Canada’s founding constitutional document, the British North America Act, gives governments direct instructions to “mind your own business,” the Conservative leader said.

Poilievre also made a more practical case for Alberta staying in Canada, saying the province ought to “lock arms” with the rest of the country under a shared border and common military.

“Simply put, Alberta has had more independence in the past, and we’ll have more independence in the future as part of a united Canada as part of that gigantic country, sharing a military and borders with millions of other Canadians than we would ever have if we were isolated and alone.”

Poilievre, who is from Calgary but spent much of his political life in Ottawa before losing his seat in the city in the 2025 federal election, also made an emotional plea on behalf of Alberta’s unique identity and the shared traits of its people.

“I love Alberta,” he said. “I love what it represents — hard work, generosity, unpretentiousness, resilience, common sense. I love the grit of the people.”

The Conservative leader also called on the rest of Canada to listen to the anger among some Albertans over its treatment within the federation, saying that efforts to appease that anger would likely benefit the broader country.

“If you listen carefully to what Albertans are asking for, they don’t want to take away anything from anyone else. In fact, their demands would not only make Alberta better off, it would make all of us better off.”

content_blocks.text: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre urged Albertans to vote to stay in Canada in the province’s upcoming referendum, arguing that Alberta’s resentments are best addressed by doubling down on the values that the Canadian Constitution was originally meant to uphold.

At a keynote speech in Edmonton, Poilievre made a classical conservative case for why the province’s deep resentments toward confederation are actually due to years of relentless government overreach rather than issues with the country itself.

“What Albertans are complaining about is not Canada,” he told a gathering of Conservative supporters. “It is the government policies that are actually inconsistent with how Canada was meant to work in the first place.”

At the root of the problem, Poilievre said, is that Ottawa has continued to expand its reach into areas of public life that it was never mandated to preside over, while trampling on the personal freedoms of citizens for political gain.

“Simply put, the last decade the federal government has done terribly at the things that are actually its job: immigration, crime, military spending, borders, while intruding into things that are not its job: regulating our resources, going after hunting rifles which are private property, just to name a few examples.”
“The problem with all of these things is not Canada,” he said. “Separation will not solve those problems.”

Poilievre’s address comes as more pro-federalist voices have started to make the case for keeping Alberta within confederation just weeks ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum. The federal Conservatives have long opposed Alberta’s separation, and earlier this month launched a “Conservatives for Canada” campaign in an effort to sway public opinion.

Support for separation on the Canadian prairies has reached new highs in the last few years, spurred on by frustration over everything from Ottawa’s over-regulation of its oil and gas sector to the federal government’s COVID-19 vaccine mandates during the pandemic.

Notably, Poilievre’s speech never once mentioned the federal Liberal Party or Prime Minister Mark Carney, leaving aside politically-charged attacks in favour of a more statesmanlike appeal to the problem of government excess.

The Canadian project was explicitly intended to give Alberta and other provinces control over its own affairs, Poilievre said as part of his address, with governments expected to intervene only within narrow and specified areas of public life. That means provincial governments sticking to matters like health care and education, and Ottawa focusing on matters like borders, national defence and criminal law.
Canada’s founding constitutional document, the British North America Act, gives governments direct instructions to “mind your own business,” the Conservative leader said.
Poilievre also made a more practical case for Alberta staying in Canada, saying the province ought to “lock arms” with the rest of the country under a shared border and common military.

“Simply put, Alberta has had more independence in the past, and we’ll have more independence in the future as part of a united Canada as part of that gigantic country, sharing a military and borders with millions of other Canadians than we would ever have if we were isolated and alone.”

Poilievre, who is from Calgary but spent much of his political life in Ottawa before losing his seat in the city in the 2025 federal election, also made an emotional plea on behalf of Alberta’s unique identity and the shared traits of its people.
“I love Alberta,” he said. “I love what it represents — hard work, generosity, unpretentiousness, resilience, common sense. I love the grit of the people.”

The Conservative leader also called on the rest of Canada to listen to the anger among some Albertans over its treatment within the federation, saying that efforts to appease that anger would likely benefit the broader country.

“If you listen carefully to what Albertans are asking for, they don’t want to take away anything from anyone else. In fact, their demands would not only make Alberta better off, it would make all of us better off.”

stories.title: Sentencing hearing for man who randomly stabbed elderly woman
stories.summary: Elizabeth O’Loughlin who was out for a walk with her dog along Brydges Street in Aug. 2024 when she was viciously attacked by a man who stabbed her six times.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Elizabeth O’Loughlin who was out for a walk with her dog along Brydges Street in Aug. 2024 when she was viciously attacked by a man who stabbed her six times.

The 78-year-old was rushed to hospital at the time and received dozens of stitches for her wounds.

The senior has since passed away from issues not related to the attack.

Last December, Cristefer Young-Hough, 33, plead guilty to aggravated assault in connection to the incident. He also plead guilty to assault causing bodily harm after he attacked a corrections officer while in custody at the Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre.

The court has heard that Young-Hough has suffered a lifetime of mental health issues.

At his sentencing hearing on Tuesday, the Crown asked that he receive a total of nine years behind bars with the defence asking for time already served.

Before wrapping up Justice Michael Carnegie told the court, “This is a very difficult proceeding.”

Justice Carnegie is expected to hand down his sentencing decision on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Truth and Reconciliation includes promoting women to leadership positions: Indigenous knowledge sharer
stories.summary: With National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday, a local Indigenous Knowledge Sharer says women should be at the forefront of leadership in our communities.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
With National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday, a local Indigenous Knowledge Sharer says women should be at the forefront of leadership in our communities. “There’s 94 calls to action, but they always focus on one.

We need to focus on other aspects that really get overlooked. So, we’re focusing on the importance of women,” said Ray John Jr. of Oneida First Nation near London. John will speak at “Approachable Conversations with an Indigenous Man” Wednesday at Fanshawe College in London from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. at Canada Village Square at Fanshawe.

An event co-hosted by Fanshawe and Canada Life Innovation Village. John says his message is about how promoting women into positions of leadership is one way to fulfill Truth and Reconciliation commitments. “It starts in your home.

Then it goes into your community. Then it goes into the nation. So, when they’re speaking on behalf of the nation, it’s because they came straight from here, right from the beginning. And then so, we have doctors, we have lawyers, we have people in positions of power.

But we need to hear them more,” he stated.

stories.title: Nearly dozen of Winnipeg school trustees acclaimed ahead of election
stories.summary: Eleven school trustees have been acclaimed ahead of election day, which is nearly three times more acclaimed races than last election.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Eleven school trustees have been acclaimed ahead of election day, which is nearly three times more acclaimed races than last election.

Four candidates were acclaimed in the previous election, according to official election results in 2022. The Winnipeg School Division had the most, five, uncontested school trustee seats this election.

“It feels different. To win by acclamation is I guess a relief, but it feels a bit weird, because you’re winning a race you didn’t run,” said Tamara Kuly, an acclaimed school trustee in the Winnipeg School Division.

Kuly was contested when she ran for school trustee in 2022, according to official election results.

“There’s two reasons why trustees get acclaimed, one is they do a great job, and the other reason is democracy is tired,” said Laura Reimer, a former school trustee at the St. Boniface and Louis Riel School Division in the early 2000s.

stories.title: Edmonton condo owners accuse investment firms of ‘predatory’ takeovers
stories.summary: Some Edmonton condo owners say investment firms are making individual offers on multiple units at the same time, in order to gain enough control to turn the property into rentals.
stories.author: Erik Bay
stories.content:
Condominium owners in Edmonton are trying to stop what they’re calling a ‘hostile takeover’ of their buildings.

They say investment firms are making individual offers on multiple units at the same time, in order to gain enough control to turn private homes into rentals.

“They can start taking control of the board of directors and issuing special assessments and levies that the other owners maybe can’t afford,” explained Darlene Reid with the Realtors Association of Edmonton.

“Now these people are being forced out of their homes and forced to sell.”

Condominium owners and board members at The Berkeley near 101 Avenue and 116 Street say they are being inundated with letters from companies offering to buy their units.

The letters promote the idea of converting the condominium building into rental housing through a process known as deconversion, while promising owners above-market prices for their units.

Some owners say they are concerned companies could acquire a majority voting stake in the building, leaving remaining owners with limited options if they choose not to sell.

One of the companies identified by owners provided a statement to Global News.

Harmani Investments said its goal is to create long-term rental housing, but acknowledged that not everyone supports condominium deconversion.

The company said it respects those views, makes voluntary offers to purchase units and exercises the rights associated with any units it owns.

Darlene Reid said the takeover approach is happening at several buildings in Edmonton.

“It is totally legit and legal — I just don’t think it’s very ethical.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It is totally legit and legal — I just don't think it's very ethical."
