stories.title: One of two teens charged in sexual assault involving mini hockey stick in Nova Scotia pleads guilty
stories.summary: Sentencing and the case of the second teen, who has pleaded not guilty, are expected to be heard next year
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
A teenaged boy pleaded guilty to sexual assault with a weapon in a Nova Scotia youth court Tuesday after a violent hockey hazing incident last fall.

A second boy, who is facing four charges related to the assault and who has pleaded not guilty, is scheduled to go to trial next February.

In the Truro courtroom, the first teen, now aged 15, stood with his hands on the front of his slacks, rocking slightly as Judge Brian Warcop read out the charge. The boy’s father sat next to him in the front row, his head down, his elbows on his knees. Dozens of supporters of the three victims listened intently on the opposite side of the courtroom as the details of the violent sexual assault at a team sleepover party were read aloud from the agreed statement of facts.

The identities of the victims and accused cannot be named under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

News of the assault struck a chord nationwide as hockey, and the sports bodies that regulate them, has faced a reckoning in recent years for a culture of silence and toxic masculinity. Hockey Canada, which governs amateur hockey in the country, opened an investigation into the Nova Scotia incident, but the sports body said it is confidential.

In a Nova Scotia town, parents and students rally behind those accusing hockey teammates of sexual assault

The court heard that on the evening of Oct. 3, 2025, the under-15 boys hockey team gathered at a teammate’s house for a team party and sleepover at or around Colchester County. The gathering had been organized so the more senior players could get to know the rookies.

The players’ parents gathered downstairs, while the boys socialized upstairs in two rooms. In one room, a 13-year-old rookie player was laying down on his stomach on a bed, scrolling on his phone, when two older players, who were 14 at the time, pinned him down, pulled down his pants and underwear and exposed his buttocks. The boy who has pleaded not guilty allegedly pushed a mini hockey stick between the younger boy’s buttocks. The rookie shouted for them to stop and started crying, later telling authorities that the assault lasted 15 to 20 seconds, but it “felt like forever.”

The court heard that he always planned to tell his parents but didn’t know how to raise the subject and he didn’t want to get anyone in trouble.

After the assault, the two older boys went after two other rookies and removed their pants, but were unsuccessful in taking off their underwear. The younger boys kicked themselves free of their attackers.

The victim’s father eventually heard about the incident, went to the RCMP on Jan. 30 and filed a complaint, according to the statement of facts.

In court, it was agreed that a psychological and psychiatric study on the boy who pleaded guilty would be presented to the court prior to sentencing, which is expected to take place in the new year. The defence and the Crown attorney told the court they would be recommending a joint sentencing submission for the boy’s case.

The sentence for sexual assault with a weapon for a youth can range from an absolute discharge to a period of secure custody and community supervision, senior Crown attorney Patrick Young said after the hearing.

Mr. Young told reporters he couldn’t disclose the discussions that took place ahead of the guilty plea, but he said that the agreement, sentence and statement of facts can all be negotiated by counsel. “Because they’re privileged it would be inappropriate for me to comment on that.”

The teen is also facing two other charges of sexual assault. Those charges will carry over to sentencing and be disposed of at that time, Mr. Young said.

His guilty plea also impacts the case against the second teen because he now potentially becomes a compellable witness for the Crown, Mr. Young said. The trial of the second teen is scheduled to begin Feb. 22. That boy, who is also now 15, has pleaded not guilty to charges of sexual assault with a weapon, two counts of sexual assault and one count of assault.

Hockey Canada to extend suspensions of four 2018 world junior players, lifts one

Hockey Canada has been embroiled in controversy over its handling of sexual assault allegations made against five members of the 2018 national junior team (they were found not guilty in a criminal court last year), and for quietly using registration fees from players across the country to settle such cases.

In response to that scandal, Hockey Canada launched an independent third party (ITP) process in 2022 for confidentially handling hockey-related maltreatment complaints and to ensure possible Criminal Code offences are reported to law enforcement and child protection services.

Hockey Nova Scotia, a branch of Hockey Canada and the organization that governs the sport in the province, initially suspended and later disbanded the team involved in last year’s hazing incident. The Globe and Mail is not naming the team to protect the identities of the victims and accused.

The incidents of sexual violence involving the team were reported to Hockey Canada’s ITP and an investigation was launched earlier this year, Hockey Canada chief of staff Jeremy Knight said, adding he couldn’t comment on the status or outcome of the process, which is confidential.

The ITP has the power to make their decision public. They did not immediately respond to The Globe’s query about what they plan to do.

stories.title: Plane pull at London airport takes flight, fundraises with a unique experience
stories.summary: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mJ67EM0lyWU On the tarmac of the London International Airport, the only specta...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
On the tarmac of the London International Airport, the only spectacle that could match the sound of jet engines idling and loudspeakers blaring Mamma Mia by Abba, was the sight of groups of 10-15 people pulling a small jet airliner across the runway.

And many of those people said they couldn’t be happier to be there.

The Elgin Middlesex United Way hosted its second annual Plane Pull event on Tuesday, a fundraiser where groups of people will come to the airport and pull one of two jet aircraft which, despite being small by airliner standards, respectively weighed 19 and 27 metric tonnes.

“Some of our United Way friends from across the country have done this … and we said ‘nobody’s doing this in London, let’s try this’,” said Elgin Middlesex United Way director of m arketing and communications Chris McInnis when asked how the event came to be.

McInnis also explained that the money raised at the event will fund 35 United Way agencies across Elgin Middlesex in providing assistance such as food, toiletries, housing stability and youth mentorship.

“We’re basically just trying to build a better community any way we can,” he said.

Other organizations besides United Way were also there in hopes of making a difference. Western University’s commercial aviation program

A Girls in Aviation kiosk at the event. The Plane Pull offered opportunities for other organizations to reach out to people alongside the United Way fundraiser. Photo by: Curtis Stokman was one of several different kiosks set up along the edge of the runway, offering brochures and speaking to people about the program.

“We always like to come to events that involve the community and involve students,” said Sebastian Fredrich Yap, one of the people manning the kiosk.

Western’s kiosk sat underneath a tent emblazoned with a Girls in Aviation logo, and Yap believes what the kiosk was doing helps to promote an otherwise male-dominated industry to women.

“The more we can introduce young girls to aviation and show them that’s a legitimate career path for them, I think is beneficial long-term,” he said.

The primary showcase of the event, though, was the people hauling the aircraft through a combination of teamwork, effort, and very large ropes.

The London Community Foundation team trying to pull a 19-tonne jet aircraft. Many of the teams at the event were excited for the experience, even if it wasn’t like anything they’d done before. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

“None of us have ever done anything like this before and it’s such an amazing opportunity,” said London Community Foundation director of philanthropy Jennifer Cahill.

Many teams tried different strategies to pull their plane. Lerners Law Firm team leader Andrew Johnson admitted that his team’s preparations amounted to “sitting at our desks”, while the RBC Bank Rollers said they stretched beforehand and selected their members carefully.

“We set up the best absolute team to do a great job here today,” said Steven Mattis, the Bank Rollers’ team leader.

Some teams were even comprised of high school students. Maiyar Altawil was a part of a team from Westminster Secondary School in London, and was cheered on by her friend Teniola Olaoye. They, like many other teams, found pulling a plane to be a unique experience.

“It was actually … easier than I expected,” said Altawil. “You actually have a whole team backing you up, and that’s what I feel like is just so beautiful and meaningful about this whole thing.”

In the end, after many teams had put their backs into hauling a passenger jet and gone to adjacent kiosks for pizza and ice cream, they agreed it was all for a worthy cause. Several also believed they would be back next year.

“[United Way] are really the backbone of the community,” said Cahill. “They bring all of the organizations together, whether they be for-profit or public or agencies themselves.”

stories.title: Canada seeking mediators to help rescue Ukrainian children
stories.summary: In many cases, Russian officials have changed the children’s personal information, making positive identification difficult
stories.author: Geoffrey York, Janice Dickson
stories.content:
The international campaign to rescue Ukrainian children from Russian control has been complicated by identity verification issues and the search for intermediaries to negotiate the return of the children, officials say.

Canada, Ukraine and Norway led a conference in Toronto this week to seek progress on the return of the estimated 20,650 Ukrainian children in Russian hands in occupied Ukrainian territory or in Russia itself. But the effort will need to rely on countries with closer ties to Moscow to serve as mediators, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand acknowledged.

Ms. Anand said 83 countries and international organizations attended the conference, of which 54 signed a “Toronto pledge” to help recover the children, along with detained civilians and prisoners of war. This exceeds the number who signed a similar commitment at a Montreal conference two years ago.

Under the new pledge, the countries expressed grave concern at the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children by Russia. They called for global efforts to identify, trace and locate the children and verify information about each case.

“We have pledged to bring them back, knowing that it can be dangerous, complex, difficult, but above all necessary,” Ms. Anand told the conference.

How two Ukrainian children fought their way back home

She cited India, Germany and the United States as countries that could be mediators on the issue, since they have better relations with Moscow. The conference participants agreed on the need for “sustained and expanded diplomatic efforts” to find “additional states that could act as intermediaries,” Latvian official Dace Melbarde told the closing session.

Alexandra Chyczij, the president of the Ukrainian Canadian Congress, said “back channels” are crucial for the release of the children because Moscow won’t talk to those who openly support Ukraine. “I think we need to continue to use every possible channel we have,” she told journalists.

Another potential mediator is South Africa, a longtime friend of Moscow, which is working with Qatar on a parallel initiative to seek the return of the children. South Africa has been “engaging with the Russians,” but the process “has not been easy,” said Zane Dangor, director-general of South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation (Dirco).

Disagreements on how to verify the identities of the children – whose personal information has often been changed by Russian officials – are among the obstacles on the issue, the South African government says.

“That has been a sticky point,” said Chrispin Phiri, a spokesperson for Dirco. “There is a dispute about what verification process can be used to ascertain the identity of the kids amongst others.”

South Africa sees itself practising “shuttle diplomacy” between Ukraine and Russia, including on the issue of the Ukrainian children, Mr. Phiri told The Globe and Mail. But it hoped the Toronto conference would help clarify the process for verifying their identities, he said.

In Depth: The children’s gulag

Ms. Anand, speaking at the opening of the Toronto conference, noted that Russia has “altered children’s identities and personal information” as part of its efforts to erase their Ukrainian identity.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , in a visit to Pretoria last year, handed South African President Cyril Ramaphosa a list of 400 Ukrainian children and asked him to help secure their return.

Asked whether South Africa had made any progress on the list, Mr. Phiri said the effort was stalled by technical issues, including verification and safe passage mechanisms.

Mr. Ramaphosa raised the issue directly with Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this month in New Delhi at the annual conference of Brics countries (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and five others).

South Africa was grateful to be invited to the Toronto conference, but “we will want to hear your views on that as well, because we would like to attend, to see how best we can continue advancing our relations,” Mr. Ramaphosa told Mr. Putin in their Sept. 11 meeting. It was unclear if the two leaders discussed the issue further.

South Africa has declined to join the 51-member International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, which was founded in 2024 and is co-chaired by Canada and Ukraine. It reportedly made the decision because the coalition is dominated by Western countries that are perceived as enemies of Moscow.

Instead it has been working with Qatar and the Vatican – two other states that declined to join the coalition or sign the “Toronto pledge” Tuesday − in a separate initiative to seek the children’s return. Qatar told the conference that it has helped rescue and return 87 Ukrainian children since 2023.

Mr. Ramaphosa first raised the issue of the children with Mr. Putin in 2023 when he led a delegation of African leaders to Moscow to seek peace in Ukraine, but Mr. Putin brushed off the issue and insisted that Russia was merely ensuring the safety of the children.

South Africa describes itself as a “non-aligned” country and has abstained on most United Nations votes about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. But last December it broke from this stand to vote in favour of a UN General Assembly resolution calling for the immediate return of the children.

stories.title: Judge dismisses injunction over Saskatoon homeless encampment
stories.summary: Justice Richard Danyliuk issued a written decision Tuesday, ruling the plaintiffs who brought forward the injunction request had no standing to do so.
stories.author: Chris Vandenbreekel
stories.content:
A Court of King’s Bench judge in Saskatoon has dismissed an emergency injunction request to prevent the City of Saskatoon from clearing an encampment located in the Pleasant Hill neighbourhood.

Justice Richard Danyliuk issued a written decision Tuesday, ruling the plaintiffs who brought forward the injunction request had no standing to do so.

The 46-page decision details several uses of hearsay and opinion contained in submissions from the plaintiffs, lawyer Crystal Fafard and Sheela McLean, while citing several documented warnings provided to the encampment occupants by the City of Saskatoon.

Fafard filed for an injunction last Wednesday to prevent the clearing of an encampment at 301 Avenue K South and two other nearby sites at 1112 and 1202 19th Street West until those living there can find shelter.

The Saskatoon Fire Department had plans to clear the two encampment sites on 19th Street West last Thursday, but paused its operations after being met with “aggressive protestors,” according to the city.

All efforts to remove the camps were then paused while the injunction matter was before the courts.

In response to the decision, the City of Saskatoon said in a statement that it “remains committed” to working with its community partners and plans to continue following its established encampment response processes to provide support to those who need it.

“The City’s approach to the encampment has consistently focused on connecting individuals with available supports and services while addressing significant health and safety concerns for people staying at the site, the nearby school, neighbouring residents, businesses and the broader community,” the statement said.

It is unclear whether the city will move ahead with encampment clearing in the days ahead, with the city’s lawyers telling the court Monday it will decide next steps following a court decision or an emergency situation requiring its intervention.

In the decision, Danyliuk says the city was responding to a serious issue, given the various health and safety concerns of the camp, and that the city was not seeking an “eviction” as argued by the applicants, since the land is owned by the city with there being no termination of occupation rights.

Fafard identified herself as an Indigenous advocate in a Court of King’s Bench courtroom Monday afternoon, filing the application on behalf of encampment residents seeking temporary relief until the status quo can be restored for them.

But the judge noted in his decision that this raised a procedural issue in the case, as Fafard appeared in court Monday as an applicant, lawyer, and witness simultaneously, which is prohibited in a Saskatchewan court.

Fafard told reporters outside the courthouse Monday that she had “very short time” to pull the application together and hoped the judge would look at the issue at hand rather than the rules of the court.

Danyliuk also acknowledged in his decision a worsening homelessness situation in Saskatoon, but says it is a matter that should be solved through policy rather than in a courtroom.

Both applicants are also ordered to pay the City $250 in costs for the case, with Danyliuk noting that costs that are “too high” could discourage future litigation.

Saskatchewan’s Attorney General was an intervenor in the case because it raised constitutional concerns.

The city says it started noticing the encampments around 20th Street growing in size earlier this month, noting dozens of structures stretching to nearby lots and an escalating number of complaints from nearby residents, businesses and an elementary school.

With files from Chris Vandenbreekel

stories.summary: On the eve of National Truth and Reconciliation Day across the country, the province and the City of Brandon have bought a burial site linked to a former residential school, and they have plans to dedicate a memorial at the site. The school opened in 1895, and historical records show a cemetery was used there […]

The Manitoba Government is acquiring Turtle Crossing Campground in Brandon to protect a confirmed burial site connected to the former Brandon Indian Residential School. Justin Hardy Reports.

Posted September 29, 2026 6:54 pm.

On the eve of National Truth and Reconciliation Day across the country, the province and the City of Brandon have bought a burial site linked to a former residential school, and they have plans to dedicate a memorial at the site.

The school opened in 1895, and historical records show a cemetery was used there between 1895 and 1912.

The burial ground was later developed into a park, and eventually became Turtle Crossing Campground in 2001.

The province says historical records and family knowledge indicate unmarked graves are still located within parts of the campground.

“This land contains the buried remains of children who attended the Brandon Indian Residential School and their existence has been documented for more than 100 years,” said Premier Wab Kinew. “These graves have been known about since long before the invention of ground-penetrating radar.”

Future decisions about the site will be guided by survivors and affected First Nations, including Sioux Valley Dakota Nation, which has stepped up as steward of the land.

“This is important work for our nation and for Indigenous peoples across Canada,” said Chief Jennifer Bone, Sioux Valley Dakota Nation. “Sioux Valley Dakota Nation’s investigation is Indigenous-led, with specialized support for a careful, non-invasive search. Technical expertise and community knowledge will guide the work, with respect for the children, their families and this sacred site at every stage.”

Manitoba Keewatinowi Okimakinak will also be involved. The organization says the site includes 56 children from eight of its communities.

The province says acquiring the land is part of its work to protect residential school burial sites and support truth and reconciliation.

The Manitoba government is acquiring the campground where students who died at a residential school were buried. Every Child Matters flag during the second annual South Island Powwow at Royal Athletic Park in Victoria, Saturday, Sept. 30, 2023. THE Canadian Press/Chad Hipolito

stories.title: More than 70,000 visit International Plowing Match near Walkerton
stories.summary: Thousands of people walked the dirt roads of the International Plowing Match (IPM) near Walkerton last week.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Thousands of people walked the dirt roads of the International Plowing Match (IPM) near Walkerton last week.

71,300 is the official attendance figure, according to the Ontario Plowmen’s Association.

That number is on par with previous Ipm’s, but below the 100,000 visitors, Bruce County organizers were aiming for.

Bruce County has hosted the IPM, four times in the past 50 years. At the first match in 1976, nearly 200,000 took in the tented city. In 2008, at the match in Teeswater, nearly 95,000 took in the event.

Organizers are still calling the 5 day event “a success”, drawing in visitors to farmer’s fields near Walkerton, from around the world for an agricultural showcase.

stories.author: Laura Stone

Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

There will be no newsletter tomorrow as The Globe recognizes the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. However, our website will be staffed so please visit theglobeandmail.com for the latest news. We will be back in your inbox on Thursday.

It was double duty for Prime Minister Mark Carney in Vancouver today: first energy, then oceans.

First there was the announcement that LNG Canada is going ahead with the $30-billion Phase 2 expansion project at its liquefied natural gas export terminal in Kitimat, B.C.

“The speed of this project shows that now when Canadians want something built, we get it built,” Carney said.

As Jeffrey Jones reports, Shell and its partners are banking on decades of rising demand for liquefied natural gas, predicated on a longer-term transition away from more carbon-intensive fossil fuels, according to LNG Canada chief executive officer Chris Cooper.

Later in the day, the Prime Minister’s Office acknowledged that expanding strategic infrastructure along the West Coast will help diversify trade, but also “place increased pressure on our ocean ecosystem.” To that end, Carney announced $1.2-billion for ocean safety, protecting marine wildlife and strengthening front-line conservation enforcement.

“We inherited these oceans, and it’s our obligation to pass them on better than we found them,” Carney said during his remarks at his second public appearance of the day.

Environmentalists are not impressed. Reacting to the LNG news, activists said the investment in the project runs counter to what they predict will be a worldwide transition to fossil-fuel-free energy, and that the LNG Canada expansion will double greenhouse gas emissions from the facility and from increased drilling activity in northeast B.C. to supply the plant.

Anand sidesteps calls for Havana Syndrome inquiry

The unexplained health ailments experienced by Canadian diplomats stationed in Cuba almost a decade ago are a human-resources concern, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said.

The promise of a referendum puts Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on centre stage

Days ahead of the Quebec election, he seems destined to become the province’s 34th premier and could eke out a majority win that would pave the way for him to hold the third referendum on independence he has promised since taking over the party.

Economist warns Brexit was ‘cakewalk’ compared with what Alberta separation would entail

The years-long trade wrangling and uncertainty that faced Britain in the wake of the Brexit vote was a “cakewalk” compared with what Alberta’s separation from Canada would involve, according to the author of a new report.

The House of Commons is on a break this week, but there’s plenty going on.

Prime Minister’s Day: Mark Carney held two major announcements today in Vancouver: LNG Canada’s Phase 2 expansion, and new measures for ocean protection. Party Leaders: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is holding a fundraiser tonight in Alberta in a bid to bolster efforts to mount a paid campaign against separation. NDP Leader Avi Lewis continues his tour of Atlantic Canada. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May is campaigning in British Columbia with the Leader of the province’s Green Party, Emily Lowan. The Manitoba PCs have a new interim leader : Konrad Narth is the new interim leader of the Manitoba Progressive Conservatives, after Obby Khan abruptly stepped down and quit caucus.

“Any Canadians here? Please, if you’re on K Street, get the hell out of our country.” - Donald Trump adviser Peter Navarro, at a conference in Washington today, in reference to an area of the city where lobbyists work, as he warned Canadians not to interfere in next month’s U.S. midterm election.

The new U.S. import ban hit Canada at 12:01 a.m. today - affecting Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and some dairy products. Approximately how much alcohol (in dollars) was exported to the U.S. last year?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

The ugly reckoning coming for Danielle Smith

Everything about this referendum on separation and the other nine questions on the ballot – among other things they attempt to scapegoat immigrants for many of the province’s problems – is contemptible. It’s a phony, illegitimate exercise Ms. Smith has lent credibility to in order to save her job. — Gary Mason

Why Trumpenomics will outlive its author

A president can do a lot of governing without Congress, especially when it comes to foreign affairs – as Mr. Trump has spent the last 20 months demonstrating. — Tony Keller

When weighing Alberta’s future, trust the experts

It’s probably true that Alberta and Canada, were separation to occur, would figure out a separation agreement and then life would go on on both sides of the border. But that it could happen smoothly is no guarantee that it will, and that it could be a success is even less of an argument in favour of separation than you might think. — Tyler Dawson

The answer to today’s question: Canada exported about $1.4-billion in alcohol products to the U.S. last year, with more than $740-million in spirits coming from Ontario.

stories.title: Conservative MP Scott Aitchison expected to resign by the end of the year
stories.summary: Conservative MP and former leadership contender Scott Aitchison is expected to resign from the House of Commons by the end of the year.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi, Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

Poll aggregator 338Canada suggests that Parry Sound—Muskoka could flip to the Liberals if a byelection were held today speaks at a Foyer of the House of Commons at the West Block on Parliament Hill before Question Period in Ottawa on Monday, June 15, 2026.Photo by Hyungcheol Park /Postmedia

Ottawa — Conservative MP and former leadership contender Scott Aitchison is expected to resign from the House of Commons by the end of the year, becoming the eighth party member to leave the caucus since last election.

Aitchison represents Parry Sound—Muskoka, a large rural Ontario riding a few hours north of Toronto and was first elected for the Conservatives in 2019 after serving for decades on Huntsville Town Council, where he was mayor from 2014 to 2019.

He also ran for Conservative leadership against Pierre Poilievre in 2022, where he finished fourth in a pool of four candidates.

His resignation was first reported by CTV News.

Aitchison’s resignation will spark a new political test for Poilievre as poll aggregator 338Canada suggests that Parry Sound—Muskoka could flip to the Liberals if a byelection were held today. Aitchison won the riding in 2025 with a 10 point lead over the Liberals.

This summer, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals won the Quebec riding of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord from the Tories during a by-election sparked by Conservative MP Richard Martel’s appointment to the Senate.

Poilievre will also eventually have to fight to maintain the Ontario riding of Brantford—Brant South left vacant after the recent resignation of Conservative MP Larry Brock, who returned to his previous job as Crown prosecutor.

National Post cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: Police file criminal, provincial charges over University of Guelph homecoming party
stories.summary: Off-campus party results in objects thrown, people climbing buildings, shoplifting and vandalism, Guelph police say
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi
stories.content:
After an off-campus University of Guelph homecoming party descended into chaos last weekend, other Ontario universities say they are working to minimize the impacts of similar upcoming events.

The unsanctioned party in Guelph on Saturday risked the safety of students and neighbours, university president Rene Van Acker said in a statement.

Videos circulating online show massive crowds of young people filling the streets, and some of them throwing bottles and other items as police officers tried to control the situation. The videos also show police putting some people in handcuffs.

“The University of Guelph is deeply disappointed by what occurred, and we are clear that this cannot happen again,” Van Acker said, adding that the school will review the incident.

He said the people who got involved in property damage and other disruptive behaviour also included those who do not attend the university.

Guelph police said the gathering was “significantly larger” than similar events in recent years and officers were dealing with objects being thrown, people climbing buildings, as well as shoplifting and vandalism at nearby businesses.

They said officers laid several criminal and provincial charges, including causing a disturbance and numerous alcohol-related offences.

“Homecoming is an opportunity for students, residents and visitors to celebrate together. Most people enjoyed the day responsibly, but behaviour that puts others at risk cannot be accepted,” said Guelph police Chief Gord Cobey.

Guelph is not the only university town that has at times struggled to contain rowdy off-campus parties in the fall.

In Ottawa, the annual Panda Game between Carleton University and the University of Ottawa football teams is taking place this weekend and Carleton said it recognizes the event can affect nearby communities.

Post-game misbehaviour in recent years included people flipping a car and stealing street signs, and has sent several people to the hospital.

University of Guelph pledges action after out-of-control homecoming parties

Carleton University spokesperson Steven Reid said the school is working closely with the University of Ottawa, the city, Ottawa Police and others to ensure safety for everyone this year.

“We are taking steps before, during and after the game to minimize those impacts,” he said. “We are also continuing to communicate with students about their responsibilities, the importance of being good neighbours and the consequences of unlawful or disruptive behaviour.”

Another homecoming party is scheduled in Kingston, Ont., starting on Oct. 16 for Queen’s University students and alumni.

A spokesperson for the school said preparations for the event include planning and co-ordination with the city, police, student leaders and groups across the university.

Students are reminded of local bylaws and potential fines, as well as responsible behaviour, the university said.

“Those found in violation of nuisance party regulations, noise bylaws, or open liquor laws can face fines from $50 to $2,000 and sanctions under the Queen’s University Non-Academic Misconduct system,” it said.

The institution said Kingston police will focus on community outreach on campus and in the near-campus neighbourhoods leading up to the event.

Back in Guelph, Mayor Cam Guthrie said police are working to find those responsible for putting residents, businesses, and emergency responders in danger.

“We all must agree that this type of reckless behaviour can never be allowed to happen in our city again,” he said.

stories.title: Carney says workers have been 'betrayed' by steelmaker Stelco's layoffs
stories.summary: Carney expressed his disappointment with steelmaker Stelco's decision to lay off hundreds of workers at its plant in Hamilton, Ont.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

Stelco is owned by Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., an American steel manufacturer based in Ohio

Prime Minister Mark Carney in Vancouver, B.C., September 29, 2026. Photo by Arlen Redekop /PNG

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed his disappointment with steelmaker Stelco’s decision to lay off hundreds of workers at its plant in Hamilton, Ont., while also promising his government will explore legal options to oppose what he described as the company’s betrayal of Canadian workers.

“We were very disappointed at this decision by Stelco,” said Carney, during a press conference in Vancouver on Tuesday. “Our thoughts are with the workers and the families who have been betrayed by the company.”

Stelco is owned by Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., an American steel manufacturer based in Ohio. The chairman and CEO of the company, Lourenco C. Goncalves, has previously expressed support for U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

“I would just take note that this situation is caused by the U.S. tariffs, and…the CEO of the ultimate owner of Stelco, Cleveland Cliffs, applauded President Trump for putting those tariffs on,” said Carney.

Cleveland-Cliffs acquired the Hamilton-based Stelco in 2024 for $3.4 billion, after former industry minister François-Philippe Champagne approved the investment with several binding conditions.

One of those conditions was to maintain the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees that were employed when the transaction was announced for a period of five years.

Carney said his government intends to hold Cleveland-Cliffs to those binding obligations that were set out in the approval of the acquisition.

“The company made representations and has legal obligations for employment,” he said. “We intend to use all powers that we have and pursue them to the full extent of the law.”

The layoffs at Stelco come on the heels of trade talks between Canada and the United States breaking down last month. There are currently no scheduled meetings to resume negotiations between both parties, although Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said communication continues with his American counterparts. Section 232 tariffs amounting to 50 per cent remain on Canadian steel and aluminum.

On Monday, Trump said he believes he can strike a trade deal with Canada in the coming weeks and anticipates an apology from Canadian officials.

“They’re going to come in, and they’re going to say, ‘Sir, we are sorry’,” he told reporters.

On Tuesday, Trump’s trade adviser Peter Navarro said Canadian lobbyists in Washington should “get the hell out of our country” when he was asked about the Canada trade dispute at an economic conference in Washington.

Prime Minister Mark Carney in Vancouver, B.C., September 29, 2026. Photo by Arlen Redekop /PNG

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed his disappointment with steelmaker Stelco’s decision to lay off hundreds of workers at its plant in Hamilton, Ont., while also promising his government will explore legal options to oppose what he described as the company’s betrayal of Canadian workers.

“We were very disappointed at this decision by Stelco,” said Carney, during a press conference in Vancouver on Tuesday. “Our thoughts are with the workers and the families who have been betrayed by the company.”

Stelco is owned by Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., an American steel manufacturer based in Ohio. The chairman and CEO of the company, Lourenco C. Goncalves, has previously expressed support for U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

“I would just take note that this situation is caused by the U.S. tariffs, and…the CEO of the ultimate owner of Stelco, Cleveland Cliffs, applauded President Trump for putting those tariffs on,” said Carney.
Cleveland-Cliffs acquired the Hamilton-based Stelco in 2024 for $3.4 billion, after former industry minister François-Philippe Champagne approved the investment with several binding conditions.

One of those conditions was to maintain the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees that were employed when the transaction was announced for a period of five years.
Carney said his government intends to hold Cleveland-Cliffs to those binding obligations that were set out in the approval of the acquisition.
“The company made representations and has legal obligations for employment,” he said. “We intend to use all powers that we have and pursue them to the full extent of the law.”

The layoffs at Stelco come on the heels of trade talks between Canada and the United States breaking down last month. There are currently no scheduled meetings to resume negotiations between both parties, although Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said communication continues with his American counterparts. Section 232 tariffs amounting to 50 per cent remain on Canadian steel and aluminum.
On Monday, Trump said he believes he can strike a trade deal with Canada in the coming weeks and anticipates an apology from Canadian officials.
“They’re going to come in, and they’re going to say, ‘Sir, we are sorry’,” he told reporters.

On Tuesday, Trump’s trade adviser Peter Navarro said Canadian lobbyists in Washington should “get the hell out of our country” when he was asked about the Canada trade dispute at an economic conference in Washington.
Carney declined to comment on Tuesday about Trump and Navarro’s remarks.

“It continues to be the case that Canada stands ready to negotiate in good faith what is there, which is a mutually advantageous trade arrangement that respects both our country’s sovereignty,” the prime minister said.

stories.title: Sean Ward's death during synagogue attack should not taint COVID-19 lawsuit he and other ex-soldiers filed, his lawyer says
stories.summary: Ward was one of 128 Canadian Forces members and ex-members who claim their careers were damaged or destroyed by COVID-19 vaccination mandate
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The shocking death of Sean Ward in a shootout with police protecting a Belleville synagogue from his “hate-motivated” attack should not taint the public’s view of a large lawsuit he was part of against the Canadian military’s COVID-19 mandate, says his lawyer.

“There is an obvious risk that intense public attention focused on one plaintiff May obscure the experiences of the many other military members and veterans involved in these proceedings,” Catherine Christensen, the lawyer for dozens of Canadian soldiers and former soldiers named in the lawsuit, told National Post.

“The events in Belleville involving Sean Ward and police outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue were extremely serious. Our thoughts are with the injured police officer, the members of the congregation, and everyone affected,” she said.

“Sean Ward was one individual claimant among a large number of serving and former CAF members who have sought legal remedies arising from the vaccination directives, the exemption and accommodation process, administrative measures, releases, and resulting career consequences.

“The litigation did not originate with Mr. Ward, and its factual and legal foundation does not depend upon him.”

Ward, 29, was involuntarily discharged from the Canadian Armed Forces in 2022 when he was deemed “unsuitable for further service” after defying the military’s vaccine mandate during the pandemic, according to court documents. He was seeking $1.5 million in general damages and additional compensation for a financial loss of $140,000.

He was one of 128 members and former members of the Canadian Forces who claimed their military careers were damaged or destroyed by a mandatory COVID-19 vaccination mandate.

The lawsuit describes Sean Douglas Reginald Ward as holding the rank of corporal in the infantry with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based at Canadian Forces Base Edmonton. The lawsuit claims Ward refused to be vaccinated “on religious grounds” but his exemption was denied by military officials.

“Beyond information contained in that (court) record, we will not discuss confidential communications relating to Mr. Ward or any other client,” Christensen said.

“The circumstances surrounding Mr. Ward’s death remain the subject of investigation. Police have publicly stated their conclusions concerning the nature and apparent motive of the incident. Mr. Ward is deceased, those allegations will not be tested through a criminal trial, and it would be inappropriate to speculate about his intentions or state of mind,” she said.

Belleville’s Chief of Police, Murray Rodd, said Ward came heavily armed with a shotgun, other undisclosed firearms, a significant amount of ammunition, containers of gasoline and additional resources in a planned attack on the synagogue where about 25 people had gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Rodd said during a firefight with two police constables outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue Ward yelled, “You are going to die for the Jews.” One officer was seriously injured when ambushed by Ward, who was shot and killed by police. “This was a targeted attack against the Jewish community. The suspect had the means, the motive and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue,” Rodd said.

“It is equally important that the public understand the much broader history of the litigation,” Christensen said of the ongoing COVID lawsuit.

“The present proceeding is not the first large civil action brought by CAF members arising from the COVID-19 vaccination directives. An earlier Federal Court mass tort proceeding was commenced on behalf of approximately 330 serving and former members and advanced constitutional and civil claims arising from the mandate and its enforcement.

“That earlier proceeding was struck at the pleadings stage on a technical issue. The underlying allegations concerning the CAF vaccination policy were therefore not determined following a trial on the evidence.

“The claims raise questions concerning the legality of those measures, the accommodation framework, the administrative and career consequences imposed on members, and the constitutional and other legal obligations of the Canadian Armed Forces and the Government of Canada,” she said.

She said those issues need to be heard and considered separately from the circumstances of Ward’s death and the attack at the synagogue.

“Hundreds of serving and former CAF members have pursued grievances or litigation arising from the vaccination policy over a period of several years. They have different service histories, different circumstances and different experiences under the policy. Their claims should be understood on their own facts.”

In a statement of defence filed in court by Department of Justice lawyers, the Canadian government and military “deny each and every allegation” in the lawsuit.

The government defended the vaccine mandates in a court filing as having a primary objective of protecting the “readiness, health, and safety of the Force, the entire Defence Team, as well as members of the public they May be called upon to serve.” The government says “a member’s failure to comply with the Directives demonstrates an unwillingness to obey and support lawful authority.”

stories.title: Stelco layoffs highlight domino effect of U.S. tariffs: industry experts
stories.summary: The job cuts are the latest in a string of tariff-linked layoffs in the province and come after plans for more than 1,000 job cuts at Algoma Steel.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
The latest round of layoffs in Ontario’s steel belt highlights the ripple effects of U.S. tariffs as their impact reverberates through Canada’s manufacturing supply chain, industry experts say.

Stelco Holdings Inc. on Monday said it was laying off up to 500 workers at its Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, with the company citing the ongoing trade crisis, weak demand and continued import pressure.

The job cuts are the latest in a string of tariff-linked layoffs in the province and come after plans for more than 1,000 job cuts at Algoma Steel in Sault Ste. Marie and the closure of ArcelorMittal’s Hamilton wire-drawing mill.

Alan Arcand, chief economist at Canadian Manufacturers and Exporters, said the decline in Canadian steel demand reflects the way tariffs are working their way through highly integrated manufacturing supply chains.

Companies that use steel are losing U.S. sales and cutting production, which in turn reduces the amount of steel they buy from Canadian producers, he said.

“Supply chains have been optimized on the assumption that we would have free trade with the U.S. and you yank that away suddenly without warning and these are the consequences,” Arcand said.

“You have impacts within the firm being directly hit by the tariff and the firms within the broader supply chain.”

Stelco called the layoffs “unfortunate but necessary” to ensure its survival, noting U.S. tariffs have significantly shrunk the market for its cold-rolled and galvanized products.

The end users for those products can include automotive and parts manufacturers, machinery and fabricated metal producers, appliance makers, and construction and electrical equipment manufacturers.

Those manufacturers are facing U.S. tariffs of up to 50 per cent on steel-intensive and derivative products, while automakers face separate trade barriers, weighing on exports and production.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, which represents workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant, said the union is disappointed in the situation and wants the ongoing tariff issues settled.

“We’re hoping this trade situation resolves itself so our members can get back to work,” he said.

Wells said Lourenco Goncalves, the chief executive of U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which acquired Stelco in 2024, said on a recent earnings call that coated steel prices in Canada are significantly lower than in the United States.

“He’s blaming this on Canada not tariffing steel being imported into Canada, which drives down the price,” Wells said of Goncalves’ comments. “They’re claiming they can’t make any money selling coated products.”

Arcand said there is “significant overproduction” of steel globally.

“There’s a lot more steel being produced than consumed,” he said. “It’s mainly a China story and that’s been a long-running issue.”

Arcand said that while the government has responded with anti-dumping duties and other measures, it needs to keep monitoring steel import volumes and adjust its policies as needed.

Meanwhile, Brendan Sweeney with the Pacific Manufacturing Association of Canada said Honda and Toyota are still producing at steady levels in Canada and continue to buy significant volumes of Canadian steel, suggesting the weakness in Stelco’s domestic demand May be coming from other manufacturers or different parts of the auto sector.

“Production is not down,” said Sweeney, president and chief executive of the trade association, which was launched by the two major Japanese automakers last April. “Production is pretty stable despite the tariffs.”

He said Honda and Toyota are among the top consumers of Canadian-made steel from southern Ontario and “it’s important for us to have steel mills around.”

Sweeney added: “We don’t see an immediate impact on our operations as the result of this (Stelco) announcement … I don’t know what the lasting effects are going to be.”

stories.title: Carney announces $1.2B for ocean conservation ahead of pipeline decision
stories.summary: Ottawa faces a Thursday deadline to decide whether to designate a proposed pipeline from Alberta to the southern B.C. coast as a project of national interest.
stories.author: Breanna Owen
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says the government is making a new $1.2 billion investment in ocean conservation as the country inches toward a decision on a new West Coast pipeline.

Speaking in Vancouver today, Carney said the funds will go to several new measures, including an expansion of the Canadian Coast Guard’s capacity to monitor marine traffic and a national marine mammal oil spill response plan.

Ottawa faces a Thursday deadline to decide whether to designate a proposed pipeline from Alberta to the southern B.C. coast as a project of national interest.

Albertans will also head to the polls in a matter of weeks to vote in a referendum on separating from Canada.

Carney said that as more ships enter the Port of Vancouver, the government must bolster systems for protecting marine life.

Earlier in the day, LNG Canada said it will proceed with a Phase 2 expansion of its facility in Kitimat, B.C., a project that would double its capacity.

stories.title: Jury watches victim’s final moments before fatal shooting in east London
stories.summary: As the Crown’s case got underway at the second degree murder trial of Zachary McDermott on Tuesday two Agreed Statement of Facts were read to the jury.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
As the Crown’s case got underway at the second degree murder trial of Zachary McDermott on Tuesday two Agreed Statement of Facts were read to the jury.

In one it stated, “On Sept. 12, 2018 Zachary McDermott fatally shot Christopher Clements-Card in the parking lot of Tim Hortons at 2094 Dundas Street... it is admitted that the accused before the court shot the deceased.”

After that the Crown proceeded to show surveillance camera footage from various nearby locations.

London police Det.-Sgt. Jon Pain testified that in one you can see the accused pull up to where Clements-Card’s girlfriend lives off of Bonaventure Drive in East London.

Then minutes later the victim is seen showing up to the same location and he is seen to be visibly upset with the woman, with the officer saying, “You see Mr. Clements-Card smashing something to the ground...it did not seem positive.”

Then cameras track Clements-Card, 21, leaving the area and going to a nearby coffee shop with his brother. Moments later a car identified as the same Silver Chevy driven by McDermott, 26, pulls up and goes towards the victim. Within seconds the car is seen taking off down Dundas Street.

Emergency crew rush to the scene and Clements-Card is taken to hospital where he would be pronounced dead after suffering two gunshot wounds to the back.

McDermott who was 18 years old at the time would be arrested days later on Sept. 21, 2018 and he has plead not guilty to second degree murder.

The trial and the Crown’s case resumes on Thursday.

stories.title: Cleveland-Cliffs could face legal action for layoffs at Stelco
stories.summary: Job cuts fall afoul of pledges made when U.S. company acquired Canadian steelmaker, union says
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
U.S. steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N could face legal action from Ottawa for violating job commitments stemming from its 2024 acquisition of Stelco Holdings Inc. after announcing hundreds of layoffs in Canada on Monday, but the devil will be in the details, a legal expert told The Globe and Mail.

In 2024, the Cleveland-based company announced its intentions to buy Stelco for $3.4-billion. The federal government approved the transaction, but only after imposing a series of legally-binding conditions on Cliffs.

Those included Cliffs promising to maintain for five years at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees.

Cliffs on Monday said it was laying off a total of up to 500 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant and its Lake Erie Works operation in Nanticoke, Ont. The company said the layoffs were necessary to ensure the company’s survival during the trade war with the United States.

Some of the workers affected by the layoffs will be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works, but the number won’t be nearly enough to fill the void left by the cuts.

Trump expects Canada to cave in trade war as Stelco cites tariffs for layoffs

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said that there are only 46 openings at Nanticoke and he is now pushing for Ottawa to hold Cliffs to its promise to maintain employment levels.

“We’re hopeful that the Canadian government enforces the Investment Canada Act,” he said. That act stipulates that major investments into Canada by foreign companies should benefit the domestic economy.

The Globe asked the office of Industry Minister Mélanie Joly whether the government considers Cliffs to be in violation of its commitments, and whether it is intending to sue the steelmaker.

“Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs have made significant commitments to Canadian steelworkers,” Gabrielle Landry, deputy director, media relations with the office of Ms. Joly wrote in an e-mail.

“We will use every lever possible to defend Canadian industry, protect jobs, and secure our supply chain.”

Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

Six charts that explain Canada’s countertariffs on U.S. goods

Subrata Bhattacharjee, national chair of the competition and foreign investment review group with Borden Ladner Gervais LLP, said that without knowing the details of the legal agreement between the company and Ottawa it is impossible to know with certainty whether Cliffs is offside.

“Until you actually see the agreement, you can’t really say for sure,” he said.

At the very least, however, he believes Ms. Joly will be having a conversation with the company around the promises it made in the agreement.

“Cleveland Cliffs will likely be trying to explain how the tariff situation is out of its control, and that it will need either some other deal, or have to be released from the undertaking, and then we’ll see what happens,” Mr. Bhattacharjee said.

“The process now includes the opportunity to renegotiate or mediate another solution, and I suspect that in the current environment, it’s quite likely the government May try to seek some other type of assurance.”

Trump’s attacks on Canada keep colliding with U.S. interests

There is precedent for the government to act and it revolves around the same Canadian steelmaker. After U.S. Steel acquired Stelco in 2007, it made commitments under the Investment Canada Act around jobs and production levels. After the financial crisis hit in 2008, U.S. Steel laid off workers in Canada. The federal government later sued the company for allegedly reneging on its legally-binding commitments. A settlement was reached in 2011 with U.S. Steel agreeing to a new set of commitments , including around production levels and investment in Canada.

Canada’s steel sector has been throttled by 50-per-cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last year. The federal and provincial governments have rolled out multiple initiatives to help the industry, including providing hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, cracking down on the dumping of foreign steel into Canada and mandating that publicly funded projects use Canadian steel wherever possible.

Ms. Landry said that financial aid has been offered by Ottawa to Stelco to keep its operations going during the trade war in order to maintain employment levels, but it was turned down.

“For some time, o ur government has made clear to the company that we are ready and willing to provide financial support to sustain operations and protect jobs,” she said.

“Its decision to reject these practical proposals and continue with layoffs is extremely disappointing.”

After the financial crisis hit in 2008, U.S. Steel laid off workers in Canada. The federal government later sued the company for allegedly reneging on its legally-binding commitments. A settlement was reached in 2011 with U.S. Steel agreeing to a new set of commitments , including around production levels and investment in Canada.

Canada’s steel sector has been throttled by 50-per-cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last year. The federal and provincial governments have rolled out multiple initiatives to help the industry, including providing hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, cracking down on the dumping of foreign steel into Canada and mandating that publicly funded projects use Canadian steel wherever possible.
Ms. Landry said that financial aid has been offered by Ottawa to Stelco to keep its operations going during the trade war in order to maintain employment levels, but it was turned down.
“For some time, o ur government has made clear to the company that we are ready and willing to provide financial support to sustain operations and protect jobs,” she said.
“Its decision to reject these practical proposals and continue with layoffs is extremely disappointing.”

Winnipeggers will see some service changes and opportunities to take part in reconciliation events as the city marks the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday, Sept. 30.

Southern Chiefs Organization Healing Walk & Pow Wow

Several streets (which are listed below) will be closed between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m.

Hargrave Street from St Mary Avenue to Portage Avenue

Additionally, northbound Main Street between York Avenue and Portage Avenue will close for periods of time.

stories.title: Canada’s military seeking anti-drone defences for bases, facilities
stories.summary: The Department of National Defence says they need anti-drone defences to protect personnel, equipment and facilities across Canada.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The Department of National Defence (DND) is looking to purchase anti-drone defences for military installations within Canada, federal procurement documents show.

In a short notice posted online Monday, DND said they need a system that can defend personnel, equipment and facilities from drone attacks at locations across Canada. The details of what DND is looking to buy — including what threats the system is meant to defend against — is only being made available to qualified suppliers.

DND did not respond to Global News’ request for information Monday or Tuesday.

The Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) has spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars bolstering its drone defences for personnel deployed as part of Operation Reassurance in Latvia — part of Nato’s efforts to bolster its eastern flank as Russia continues its invasion of Ukraine.

The deployment in Latvia has offered a front-row seat to Canadian and allied forces for the evolution of drone warfare tactics since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.

Canadian military installations at home, though, are far from the threat of direct combat with advanced drone warfare technology — but that doesn’t mean there is no threat, experts say.

Stephanie Carvin, a professor at the Norman Paterson School of International Relations and former intelligence analyst, said the CAF is likely more concerned about hostile powers hiring help within Canada.

Carvin pointed to the recent spate of hired gunman in Canada, allegedly working under the direction of nation states or their proxies.

“It’s very, very hard to sneak operatives across borders. So the model really is just to find people on social media and convince them to engage in this. And it is becoming a major focus of not just the CAF, but the RCMP (which) has a counter-drone unit,” Carvin said in an interview.

“Obviously (the RCMP are) worried about drugs, but I also think they’re worried about public events and policing.”

Carvin noted that Canada already has deployed counter-drone systems to protect critical infrastructure, such as nuclear power plants.

“I would say that the use of counter-drone technology around critical infrastructure is becoming the norm,” Carvin said.

The CAF previously budgeted between $100 million and $249 million for a vehicle-mounted anti-drone system to be used by soldiers deployed in Latvia. That system includes detectors and jammers for radio frequencies and global navigation systems used in drone targeting.

Separately, the federal government launched the Defence Drone Initiative in July 2026 to scale Canada’s ability to produce low-cost uncrewed and autonomous systems at home.

“Recent conflicts have shown that drone technology evolves rapidly,” a statement announcing the initiative read.

“The DDI will help build a more responsive and scalable Canadian ecosystem and it reflects the Government of Canada’s commitment to provide the CAF and (Canadian Coast Guard) with access to Canadian-developed technologies that enhance operational readiness while supporting Canadian innovation, skilled jobs and long-term economic growth.”

The DDI program is intended to study both drone combat systems — including the ability to launch long-range precision strikes — as well as drone interceptor systems meant to defend against hostile uncrewed vehicles.

stories.title: Council committee votes down proposal for 2 towers at Wellington and High street
stories.summary: Council's planning committee has voted down a proposal to build two large apartment towers on Wellington Road just south of the Thames River following concerns flagged by city staff and neighbours.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Council's planning committee has voted down a proposal to build two large apartment towers on Wellington Road just south of the Thames River following concerns flagged by city staff and neighbours.
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 4:58 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
A rendering of two apartment towers proposed for 60-68 High St. and 57-75 Wellington Rd. in London.(Goodplace Design)
Ascity staff and neighbours flag concerns, council's planning committee has voted down a proposal to build two large apartment towers on Wellington Road just south of the Thames River.

An investment group called Foundation Development Fund submitted planning applications for properties at 60-68 High St. and 57-75 Wellington Rd. Together, the projects would include 1,000 apartments beside the city's rapid transit corridor currently under construction.
The High Street proposal included a 32-storey apartment building with 540 units, while the Wellington Road building proposal included a 22-storey high building with 440 units.
2-tower proposal would bring more than 1,000 apartments to London's Wellington Gateway

City staff recommended both proposals be refused, saying it would result in over-intensification of the site and would require setback amendments that would crowd the Wellington Road corridor. Staff also flagged concerns about the request to reduce required bicycle storage.

The building plans also had no underground parking, which is allowed in proposals along transit corridors. However, some neighbours who spoke at Tuesday's meeting expressed concern that parking and traffic from the two large buildings would spillover into the neighbourhood.
"We feel that the proposed towers are stark and out-of-character with the surrounding Old South neighbourhood," said Old South resident Patrick Clancy.
Renee Borg, who lives on nearby Grand Avenue, called the two towers "Lego-like developments."
"It is the design and size and height of these buildings that everybody is against," she said.

Michael Nemanic, representing the developer of the Wellington Road proposal, said the building will deliver much-needed affordable housing — with some of the units set at 80 per cent average market rent. Nemanic said rents in 98 of the units across both properties would be $850 for a studio unit and $1,100 for a one-bedroom unit.

Nemanic said the building's design elements — including the elimination of some balconies, the lack of underground parking and planned use of concrete poured off-site — are all aimed at keeping the building cost and rents low.
"We don't expect many of our tenants will own vehicles," said Nemanic. "That's not our target market."

Renderings submitted by the developer show the two tower proposals from High Street. Planning committee voted to follow a city staff recommendation that the proposed towers be voted down. (Foundation Development Fund)

Coun. Skylar Franke, who represents the area, said there was a strong community response against the proposal. She said most were not opposed to added density, but instead want something that's a better fit with the area.

"They accept there will be infill here, they understand it will probably be substantial, but they want something that adds to the neighbourhood and not feel like it's taking away from it," she said. "We're talking about two very large towers on a very constrained site."
The staff recommendation against both buildings was voted down by a 3-0 vote. It will next go to the Oct. 14 council meeting for consideration.

stories.title: Former Montreal synagogue lead rabbi Leigh Lerner advocated for ‘radical inclusivity’
stories.summary: He performed a groundbreaking interfaith wedding in Minnesota in the 1970s and continued that practice in Montreal, where he also presided over same-sex civil unions and later same-sex marriages
stories.author: Lisa Fitterman
stories.content:
Rabbi Leigh Lerner’s catchphrase was “Go do it,” no matter if the goal was to start a food bank, combat human trafficking, fight for Lgbtq rights or overcome opposition to interfaith marriage. As a university student in the United States in the mid-1960s, he was steeped in the tradition of social justice advocacy, with a finely honed sense of right and wrong and the quiet determination to get things done, even if others disagreed with him.

As the long-time lead rabbi of the reform Temple Emanu-El-Beth-Sholom in Westmount, Que. (upon his retirement in 2012, he became the synagogue’s “Rabbi Emeritus”), he saw the job as something that was rooted in tradition but needed to change to respond to the times. Like the Talmudic scholars of yore, he believed that issues needed to be discussed openly, not only within the confines of the Jewish community, and that faith should encompass everyone who wanted to participate, even in the most peripheral of ways.

In 1977, when Mr. Lerner was the senior rabbi at the Mount Zion Temple in St. Paul, Minn., he officiated over what the state’s historical society calls the first interfaith wedding in any Minnesota house of worship. He continued that practice in Montreal, where he also regularly presided over same-sex civil unions and then same-sex marriages when they became legal.

“If you spend 23 years leading one congregation and over 50 years in the rabbinate, like Leigh did, you don’t do it well without perseverance and a commitment to who you are and what you do,” said Rabbi Lisa Grushcow, his successor at Temple Emanu-El-Beth-Sholom. “He left a strong and healthy community in a city where we are the only Reform congregation with all the unique pressures that entails. And he did it by bringing us to the table with a radical inclusivity.”

Mr. Lerner died in Las Vegas on Sept. 5 from complications due to a stroke. He was 81 years old, a tall, lean, polyvalent man who learned French when he moved to Montreal in 1989 in order to better understand the city at large, and who was given to striding the streets in a deerstalker hat, his hands folded behind his back.

His friend, Rabbi Bob Alper, with whom he studied at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati, said their relationship really began a few years after they had both graduated. That was when Mr. Lerner returned class notes he had borrowed from Mr. Alper in their final year.

“I had asked for the notes to be returned but Leigh insisted he had no idea what I was talking about,” Mr. Alper recalled. “Then, as he was going through old boxes in St. Paul, he found them, sent them to me with an apologetic note.

“That was a spark for me. He was a man of quality and modesty, with great strength of character.”

It demonstrated what his friend was so good at, Mr. Alper continued: creating sparks of kindness and understanding day by day, year by year, that represented the highest form of Judaism.

For 22 years, Mr. Lerner marched in Montreal pride parades, while he was a member of the advisory council of the now-defunct Across Boundaries Multifaith Institute in Montreal, a past president of the Montreal Christian Jewish Dialogue and a supporter of the Montreal Muslim Jewish Dialogue. He was wont to say that it was through such dialogues that people learned of the diversity that thrives on the other side of the table.

“Is inter-religious dialogue realistic? Is it practical? Yes, and it is very necessary,” he once said during a panel discussion in November 2003. “It is remarkable for me to see how people who have been in dialogue for some time are discovering that others are coming to them and saying, ‘Can we get in on it?’

“They realize that there is a gap, there is something missing in the quality of our understanding of one another, and that only dialogue is a viable and safe way for people of different faiths to understand each other.”

At a time when anti-Semitism is on the rise, including a firebombing of the Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom earlier this year, Mr. Alper said that his friend’s message is more important than ever.

“As grief-stricken we all are, as upset, angry at what the world has come to, Leigh would have been consoling and strengthening people where he could, encouraging people to be strong,” he noted.

Leigh Lerner was born in a military hospital in Fort Snelling, Minn., ON March 3, 1945, the first of David and Edith Lerner’s two children. At the time, his father was overseas with the army in the final months of the Second World War; when he came back, he worked as a car salesman. The family lived in St. Louis Park, a suburban community just west of Minneapolis before moving to Atlanta for about a decade, then to Chicago. Perhaps because of the moves, Leigh and his little sister, Trudie, were close; when they fought, as siblings will do, it was always the brother who would approach his sister later, hand outstretched and asking for them to be friends again.

Neither parent wanted their son to enter the rabbinate. Indeed, his mom pushed for him to become a doctor. Wanting to please her, he took premed classes at Duke University in Durham, N.C., but was drawn more to English and writing, eventually getting his undergraduate degree in English literature.

While he was at Duke, his mother became gravely ill. As she lay dying, she gave her son her blessing to become a rabbi. In 1972, he was ordained by the Hebrew Union College-Jewish Institute of Religion in Cincinnati and embarked on a career that would take him from St. Paul to Montreal and, upon his official retirement, to minister to congregations during stints in Italy, for which he learned Italian. As much as he loved Montreal, he was happy to leave snow and ice storms behind, so he established a new home in Las Vegas.

Among the highlights was a trip he took with Mr. Alper in 1983 to Moscow and Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg) to meet with Soviet refuseniks, the term for Jewish citizens who were denied visas to emigrate.

“It was one week of an amazing, dangerous, scary, spiritually uplifting experience, the most important week of my life as a Jew,” said Mr. Alper. “We met in the Frankfurt Airport, where we walked around and around, coding our notes, memorizing them, then throwing them out because we knew the last thing the KGB wanted was for nosy American rabbis encouraging dissidents.

“I have this memory of Leigh standing tall and straight in Moscow next to a woman we’d hired as our tour guide for a day, laughing delightedly when I told them to smile and say ‘visa’,” he continued. “His smile was just one of the innumerable sparks he lit that will continue to light our way into the future.”

Mr. Lerner was awarded the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal in 2012 for his contributions to the community and to Canada. He leaves his wife, Loren Lerner; his sister, Trudie Lerner; a half-brother, Terry Brashem; his daughters, Meredith Bloom and Sasha Lerner; his stepsons, Sam and Daniel Singer; and four grandchildren.

Perhaps because of the moves, Leigh and his little sister, Trudie, were close; when they fought, as siblings will do, it was always the brother who would approach his sister later, hand outstretched and asking for them to be friends again.

Neither parent wanted their son to enter the rabbinate. Indeed, his mom pushed for him to become a doctor. Wanting to please her, he took premed classes at Duke University in Durham, N.C., but was drawn more to English and writing, eventually getting his undergraduate degree in English literature.

While he was at Duke, his mother became gravely ill. As she lay dying, she gave her son her blessing to become a rabbi. In 1972, he was ordained by the Hebrew Union College-Jewish Institute of Religion in Cincinnati and embarked on a career that would take him from St. Paul to Montreal and, upon his official retirement, to minister to congregations during stints in Italy, for which he learned Italian. As much as he loved Montreal, he was happy to leave snow and ice storms behind, so he established a new home in Las Vegas.

Among the highlights was a trip he took with Mr. Alper in 1983 to Moscow and Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg) to meet with Soviet refuseniks, the term for Jewish citizens who were denied visas to emigrate.

“It was one week of an amazing, dangerous, scary, spiritually uplifting experience, the most important week of my life as a Jew,” said Mr. Alper. “We met in the Frankfurt Airport, where we walked around and around, coding our notes, memorizing them, then throwing them out because we knew the last thing the KGB wanted was for nosy American rabbis encouraging dissidents.

“I have this memory of Leigh standing tall and straight in Moscow next to a woman we’d hired as our tour guide for a day, laughing delightedly when I told them to smile and say ‘visa’,” he continued. “His smile was just one of the innumerable sparks he lit that will continue to light our way into the future.”

Mr. Lerner was awarded the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal in 2012 for his contributions to the community and to Canada. He leaves his wife, Loren Lerner; his sister, Trudie Lerner; a half-brother, Terry Brashem; his daughters, Meredith Bloom and Sasha Lerner; his stepsons, Sam and Daniel Singer; and four grandchildren.

stories.title: Rush frontman Geddy Lee endorses Brad Bradford for Toronto mayor
stories.summary: Lee says he fears for future of city with current leadership
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Canadian rockstar Geddy Lee has endorsed candidate Brad Bradford for Toronto mayor. The frontman for the legendary band Rush posted his approval for the centre-right municipal politician on Instagram.

“I was born in Toronto and have built a life with my family here,” Lee wrote in his post on Monday. “It was always a place I’ve been proud to call home. But it’s changing, and not for the better. I’m not one to make public statements about politicians, but I truly fear for the future of Toronto with its current leadership, and believe that Brad has energy, fresh ideas and really cares about ALL of this city’s communities.”

Holding his Norwich terrier Dottie Wasserman, the Working Man singer posed with Bradford, who lost to Olivia Chow in 2023, coming in eighth place. He is thought to be Chow’s strongest challenger in the municipal election set for Oct. 26.

Lee, the 73-year-old son of Jewish Holocaust survivors from Poland, grew up in the suburban Willowdale area of Toronto. He once had a home in the Upper Beaches neighbourhood, which Bradford has represented on Toronto City Council since 2018.

Marcus Gee: In polarized times, Ford and Chow have an unusual partnership

Rush is currently on a wildly successful international tour after being inactive since 2015. Lee and guitarist Alex Lifeson, along with two touring musicians, sold out four concerts at Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena in August.

Though Rush is not known to be a political band, the lyrics penned by the late drummer Neil Peart were influenced by Russian-born American author and philosopher Ayn Rand. Singer-bassist Lee wrote in his 2023 memoir My Effin’ Life that it was in Rand’s The Fountainhead that he found “moral reinforcement” in the band’s early struggles with its management and record label.

“In the novel her protagonist Howard Roark stands up defiantly for the rights of the individual, and passionately against the concept of artistic compromise,” Lee wrote in his book.

Lee has endorsed Bradford at a time when Canadian musicians are increasingly flexing their political muscles. Two days before Canada Day, B.C.-based Bryan Adams released the single 51st State , a rocking protest song directed at U.S. President Donald Trump: “So let me give you some advice, mister. You might have too much on your plate. Go and load us up with tariffs, but we’ll never be the 51st state.”

In April, Toronto-born Neil Young, who has a summer residence in Ontario, implored Prime Minister Mark Carney to fight what he described as a threat to Canada’s “very existence” from the United States.

“They want our resources, they want our land, they want our fisheries, they want our water, they want our Arctic, maybe they want our souls,” the Rockin’ in the Free World musician wrote in an open letter on his news site, NYA Times-Contrarian.
