stories.title: 'Not in the public interest': Liberals won't try to recoup $34 million paid by 'green slush fund' to ineligible projects
stories.summary: The Liberals says they will not try to recover any of the $34 million in ineligible funding paid out by the so-called "green slush fund".
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberal government says it will not try to recover any of the at least $34 million in ineligible funding paid out by the so-called “green slush fund,” saying such efforts would not be in the public interest.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly quietly made the revelation in a response tabled last week to questions by Conservative MP Luc Berthold on the now defunct Sustainable Development Technology Canada (Sdtc).

Sdtc was a scandal-plagued cleantech fund derogatively referred to as the “green slush fund” by Conservative MP. It was dissolved in 2024 by then industry minister François-Philippe Champagne after a scathing report by the Auditor General on the organization.

In the response, Joly said roughly $34 million was paid out by Sdtc to ineligible recipients who applied and performed “in good faith.”

“Therefore, as a matter of fairness and sound stewardship of public funds, it was determined that further pursuit of recoveries was not likely to be successful, and not in the public interest,” reads the document.

In a statement, Berthold and colleague Aaron Gunn lambasted the decision, which they said flies in the face of the will of MPs of all political stripes. In 2024, the Commons Public Accounts committee unanimously expressed “ extreme concern with the blatant disregard of taxpayer funds” called on the government to recoup them.

In her 2024 report, Auditor General Karen Hogan found that of the 58 Sdtc-funded projects she audited, 10 were ineligible for such funding totalling $59 million.

Furthermore, she found 90 cases where an Sdtc board member participated and voted in a discussion about a contract despite being in a conflict of interest.

Hogan also found the organization had serious governance issues.

“It’s not always clear that funding decisions made on behalf of Canadian taxpayers were appropriate and justified,” she wrote of Sdtc.

At the time, Sdtc leadership only partially agreed with some of the key findings in Hogan’s report. It disagreed with some of her findings on funded project eligibility.

The report not only led to the dissolution of Sdtc (whose activities were folded into the National Research Council), it also sparked multiple parliamentary committee studies, a call by Conservatives for an RCMP investigation and a months-long logjam in the House of Commons over access to documents.

Joly’s response tabled last week sheds new light on what happened to Sdtc after Hogan’s report.

It reveals that Sdtc decided to conduct its own review of 158 projects it funded, including those audited by Hogan. The review included “three independent third-parties,” which are not identified.

Despite reviewing three times more projects than Hogan, the foundation concluded that only five (compared to Hogan’s 10) were ineligible for the funding they received.

Those projects received $34 million in total funding from Sdtc since 2017. The document does not identify them.

Joly’s response said the review found the five funding recipients negotiated and performed “in good faith,” suggesting blame for the error lied entirely with Sdtc.

Innovation, Science and Economic Development (Ised), the National Research Council and the auditor general’s office did not immediately respond to questions about the findings by print deadline.

stories.title: Goderich family paying it forward with “Fun-dation” in memory of son
stories.summary: Ken Costello will never forget how Goderich and area supported him and his family, while their son Hunter was fighting leukemia.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Ken Costello will never forget how Goderich and area supported him and his family while their son Hunter was fighting leukemia.

“The community was huge for us. The amount of support they did, the amount of fundraisers that were done for us. It was a big inspiration for why we started what we do. We wanted to pay it forward and, you know, start the charity and give back to the community that gave to us,” said Ken Costello, Hunter’s father.

Sadly, Hunter died in 2016. A year later, his family started the Hunter Costello Memorial Fun-dation, to help Huron County families with expenses around ill or special needs children.

“Whether it’s they have a hospital stay, or even if it’s just stuff at home, that we’ve helped out with. Chairlifts and, special beds and stuff like that, just to make life easier for kids with special needs,” said Ken.

Since 2017, the Hunter Costello Memorial Fun-dation has given $110,000 to more than 25 families, to help them during their darkest days.

“We’ll tell a family, all you need to do is give us your email address. That’s it. And then we’ll send you an e-transfer. And if you need more help, you have our contact information and get a hold of us. So, it’s been for me, almost therapeutic to be part of,” said Joe Hallam, family friend, and Hunter Costello Fun-dation board member.

One of those families the Fun-dation helped was Roo Fox’s. A couple of years ago, Fox’s family needed help after she went blind during pregnancy, her son was very premature and had trouble breathing, and her husband was laid off, all at the same time.

“We wouldn’t really have been able to do it, if we didn’t have that foundation supporting us, not only just financially, but, you know, as a community. Like, we’re here for you. We see you. You’re not alone. So, that that was really nice. And I’m sure other families feel the same way too,” said Fox.

“The community helped us. It feels good to help others that need it, and they appreciate it. And we appreciate the fact that they appreciate it,” said Ken.

The Fun-dation is holding a wrestling fundraiser Oct. 17 in Goderich to raise funds to help more Huron County families, as well as improve the playground bearing Hunter’s name.

“We always want to keep helping families. That’s the number one goal. But, the next goal is to improve upon this wonderful playground behind me. We’re looking at getting some rubber matting put on it. Maybe a pavilion nearby, all sorts of other stuff,” said Ken.

“For the fundraiser, if you can afford to put some money in the bin, that’d be great. We can give that to a family in need, and if you can’t, then just enjoy the show and have some fun,” said Hallam.

stories.title: London mom questions school response after children injured in violent altercation
stories.summary: A London, Ont., mom says she and her children were let down by school officials after a schoolyard fight, she says, resulted in both of her children being hurt and her son suffering a concussion.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A London, Ont., mom says she and her children were let down by school officials after a schoolyard fight, she says, resulted in both of her children being hurt and her son suffering a concussion.
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 4:28 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
London police and the Thames Valley District School Board are investigating after a video of a fight at CC Carrothers Public School was shared on social media on Sept. 24.(Google Maps)

A London, Ont., mother says she and her children were let down by school officials after a schoolyard fight she says left both children injured, including her son, who was diagnosed with a concussion.
Samantha Riley shared a video on social media of a fight involving her daughter and son at C.C. Carrothers Public School in southeast London on Sept. 24.
Riley said both children were struck multiple times while on the ground and were later suspended for one day.

"My kids should be able to feel safe going to school. Any child should. It's not even my own," said Riley. "I'm speaking for all these kids that get bullied at this point now, because that's not fair to those kids. "
The video reviewed by CBC News shows Riley’s daughter being held by another student while the two exchange punches. Riley’s son then appears to intervene.
A separate video posted to social media shows Riley’s daughter sitting on the ground surrounded by several students. One student appears to stomp on her leg while another kicks her.

The video also shows a student bringing Riley’s son to the ground and punching him before dragging him toward a nearby wall. The student is then seen punching the boy several times and kicking him in the face.
Riley said she was appalled by what she saw.
"It feels like the teachers just stood there and did nothing about it," she said. "I'm upset. I'm sad that this happened."
Following the incident and a visit to the hospital, Riley's son was diagnosed with a mild concussion.
LISTEN | Concerns around violence in Ontario schools :
Ontario Morning 8:23 Concerns around violence in Ontario schools

While starting a new school year brings excitement, it can also bring considerable stress. Data from the Ontario Secondary School Teachers' Federation reveals a sharp surge in school violence across Ontario, with reported incidents climbing 77% between 2018 and 2025. Simcoe County school trustee Mike Foley is bringing his concerns directly to Premier Doug Ford and the Ministry of Education. He joins us to discuss why he felt compelled to take urgent action and shares the outcomes of these discussions.
London police told CBC News they are aware of the altercation and have been investigating since Sept. 24.
"At this time, we can confirm that all individuals involved are youths," police said in a statement.
Riley said she was shocked when she saw the videos of the fight, but she wasn't surprised that her children were involved in an incident at the school.
“Over the past three years, I have asked the school to help me transfer my children out because they do not feel safe,” Riley said.
She said the school board denied her requests to move her children to different schools. She now plans to try to move them into the Catholic school system.
The Thames Valley District School Board told CBC News an investigation into the incident is underway.
"The school board takes incidents like these very seriously, and there is no place for violence inside or outside of TVDSB classrooms," board officials said.
Riley said school officials suspended all of the students involved for one day, including her children.
“Everybody knows that my children were just trying to defend themselves from an attack,” Riley said.
After videos of the incident began circulating on social media, Riley said the response has been mixed. Some people have blamed her children, she said, while others have offered overwhelming support.
Riley said the divide in public reaction highlights the need for parents to take responsibility for their children's behaviour.
“Parents need to take accountability for their children's actions, stop defending abusive behaviour, and work together to teach children not to bully,” she said.

stories.title: All in the classroom: how artificial intelligence is changing education
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), is changing the way students approach schoolwork, with some using it regularly, ...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI), is changing the way students approach schoolwork, with some using it regularly, while other refuse to use it.

Jada Kaasti, London Christian High student, said that AI has changed the way she completes assignments, and that teachers are vague on telling the rules of AI use.

“It makes it so much easier. Now it feels like there’s less effort I have to put into it. It’s not as hard to keep my grades up,” she said.

Jada Kaasti, London Christian High, grade 12, photo: (Torey Joseph Legarrie)

“Sometimes, but not always. Usually it’s vague,” she said.

The growing use of AI is making professors rethink how they create and grade assignments, while raising questions about it’s potential impact on student learning and critical-thinking skills.

Jeff Miles, associate dean, school of arts and language at Fanshawe College said that it’s trickier now.

“So for example, a lot of our online courses used to be essay-based. So students would write their essay and then put them in a submissions folder. That’s a little bit tricker now because we can’t be certain who actually did the work,” he said.

Jeff Miles, associate dean, school of arts and language, photo: (LinkedIn)

“It’s created a lot of difficulty in students submitting essays because we’re not sure if they’ve actually done the work or not, or if it’s just the writing has been done by ChatGPT,” he said.

“There’s AI detectors out there, of course. But the AI detectors are not very reliable. So sometimes professors will use a high AI detection score,” he said.

He said the rules are clear if you are allowed or not allowed to use AI.

“Absolutely. So one of the college requirements is that we need to indicate on assignments what level of AI is acceptable,” he said.

In 2026, over half of U.S students aged 13 – 17 use it. 57 per cent searching information, 54 per cent in education, and 47 per cent for entertainment.

AI use is rising. For example, 19.2 per cent of Canadian businesses reported the use of AI to produce goods and deliver services in 2026.

Fanshawe College student Josh Dinkel said that he will never use AI because it is prone to be inaccurate, and can provide false information.

“AI is prone to many mistakes and hallucinates a bunch of random things that don’t happen, and it brings up random sources that don’t involve the thing that you May look up,” he said.

Josh Dinkel, electrical engineering technology, year 1, photo: (Torey Joseph Legarrie)

Dinkel said that he students who do use AI don’t have an advantage.

“No, not really, because it could mess something up and it could bring their grades down. Or they could get something wrong and put it down,” he said.

Dr. David Bourget, associate professor of philosophy and Matcha developer at Western University said that using AI negatively affects students’ learning.

“It obviously can affect their learning negatively if they don’t learn, because they’re doing everything with AI, which you know, when measures are not taken, that can happen,” he said.

He said that because AI is so intelligent, it has affected people getting hired for entry level jobs as they are not needed anymore, but universities and colleges are on top of it.

“AI can do a lot of what people do in their desk jobs, and that creates a situation where effectively entry level jobs are not needed anymore. AI right now can replace entry level programmers very well. For example, that’s probably the field that’s the most affected at this time,” he said.

Dr. David Bourget, associate professor of philosophy and Matcha developer, photo: (The Globe and Mail)

“Right now universities and colleges are geared towards training people for the entry level positions for those positions of disappearing, so they need to start aiming higher. They need to provide more training,” he said.

He said that he predicts that the future with AI will be not only be more strict on the rules for using it, but students will also be prepared on how they can use it.

“I think probably we’re gonna be systematically, holding back AI in some ways. But also, of course, trying to prepare students to use it in other ways,” he said.

stories.title: Canada’s peacekeeping myth ‘needs to fade away,’ retired general writes in memoir
stories.summary: Canada's former top soldier says the country's "persistent myth" about being a nation of peacekeepers hasn't kept up with a changing world and it "needs to fade away."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 4:10 pm.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 4:21 pm.

Ottawa — Canada’s former top soldier says the country’s “persistent myth” about being a nation of peacekeepers hasn’t kept up with a changing world and it “needs to fade away.”

In a new memoir, retired general Wayne Eyre says traditional, UN-style peacekeeping is not only dead, it has been a ghost for decades. He says he knows because he was there when it died — at Medak Pocket in 1993.

Eyre details his experiences in peacekeeping in Croatia, Bosnia and Cyprus — along with his later time in Afghanistan and eventual rise to the top of the Canadian Armed Forces — in his book Into the Breach: A Soldier’s Journey, which comes out on Oct. 6.

In it, he describes in great detail his experiences in the Battle of Medak Pocket in the former Yugoslavia, where he was deployed as a captain in the 2nd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. He calls it a “turning point that saw the death of traditional UN peacekeeping.”

Canadian Forces in the former Yugoslavia faced artillery and heavy machine-gun fire in the neutral zone but ultimately drove back Croatian forces. In the book, Eyre describes his battalion pushing past a roadblock into the village of Lički Čitluk, where they found evidence of ethnic cleansing among the burning buildings.

A traditional peacekeeping operation deploys a minimally armed force to separate combatants and act as a buffer. Eyre writes that multiple sides in the former Yugoslavia made targets of the under-resourced peacekeepers and the mission failed to prevent a brutal escalation of the violence.

“The only thing that the belligerents respected was force,” Eyre said in an interview with The Canadian Press, adding the wider United Nations Protection Force mission was unable to provide enough of that force.

He said peacekeeping was “an era for the Canadian military” that lasted decades and ended in the early 1990s. Modern missions, he said, are set against a very different geopolitical backdrop.

“Take a look now at where most peacekeeping operations are — Africa, where there is an extreme local reluctance to have large Western forces on the ground there, for various historical reasons, to keep the peace,” he said. “And the utility of many of those missions are in question.”

Medak Pocket was a formative experience for Eyre and many of his colleagues. He writes about the overpowering smells of smoke and death hanging over the field and how, for many years afterward, he could not “smell a campfire without being taken back” to that moment.

His book, which runs to just over 400 pages, covers the ups and downs of his career, from the battlefield to top command.

Eyre said he felt the need to describe history as he saw it from his front-row seat.

“In the Canadian military, we don’t have a tradition of senior military officers or generals and admirals capturing history,” he said in the interview.

Eyre said as chief of the defence staff, he frequently fielded requests from politicians who didn’t always understand the potential impacts of their decisions — or how thinly spread the Canadian Armed Forces had become after decades of underfunding and the launch of the Russian deterrence mission in Latvia.

“I know I irritated some in government. I was told at one point I was being seen as obstructionist, but it’s the reality of what we had on the shelf,” he said.

Eyre said Canada’s future in a shifting international order depends on strong alliances and selectively deploying military power on very specific operations.

He called Latvia — where Canada leads a battalion on Nato’s eastern flank and has stationed 2,000 troops — the most “geopolitically significant deployment that Canada has undertaken since the end of the Cold War.”

Eyre’s own time and experiences in the military were shaped by major turning points, starting with the end of the Cold War and continuing through the 9/11 terror attacks and the start of the Afghanistan war. In Afghanistan, Eyre commanded Canada’s largest combat advisory mission up to that point.

Eyre stepped into the role of chief of the defence staff somewhat reluctantly just five years ago, when Admiral Art McDonald stepped aside in the face of a sexual misconduct allegation. The allegation did not lead to charges.

Eyre said he initially thought he would only be in the job for weeks as acting chief — and soon after considered resigning on principle.

He said he wondered whether cabinet had lost trust in him when then-deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland openly criticized his decision not to fire Navy commander Vice-Admiral Craig Baines amid a scandal.

“The lesson here is just the messiness of political-military relations,” he said, adding the book is not meant to be a political “tell-all.”

He said he felt he had the confidence of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau but it took “a while to develop” at a time when, thanks to the pandemic, meetings were all being conducted by video.

Eyre helmed the forces from 2021 to 2024, a tenure he writes was consumed by “crisis stacked upon crisis.”

On top of the series of sexual misconduct allegations against top brass that rocked the armed forces, Eyre’s time in the top job also coincided with a global pandemic, the evacuation of Canadians from Afghanistan in 2021, the start of the war Ukraine, the “Freedom Convoy” that occupied Ottawa, chaotic gang violence in Haiti and forest fires and floods at home.

He said he fielded nearly two dozen requests for international disaster response and upwards of 100 for help with managing the COVID-19 crisis, in addition to other domestic requests.

“My observation was all of these crises stacked upon each other was really limiting the bandwidth of our decision makers,” the retired general said in the interview.

“That’s where something like understanding and having clearly articulated national security interests and objectives can provide you guardrails so that when the pressure is on, when time is tight, you have something to help you make those decisions.”

He said that while he empathizes with elected officials, he struggled with the slow pace of government peacetime processes.

Eyre said in one instance, he worried he had he overstepped his authority by committing Canada to training Ukrainians in Latvia at a time when Ottawa was not giving him “decisions at the speed of war.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

Ottawa — Canada’s former top soldier says the country’s “persistent myth” about being a nation of peacekeepers hasn’t kept up with a changing world and it “needs to fade away.”

In a new memoir, retired general Wayne Eyre says traditional, UN-style peacekeeping is not only dead, it has been a ghost for decades. He says he knows because he was there when it died — at Medak Pocket in 1993.

Eyre details his experiences in peacekeeping in Croatia, Bosnia and Cyprus — along with his later time in Afghanistan and eventual rise to the top of the Canadian Armed Forces — in his book Into the Breach: A Soldier’s Journey, which comes out on Oct. 6.

In it, he describes in great detail his experiences in the Battle of Medak Pocket in the former Yugoslavia, where he was deployed as a captain in the 2nd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. He calls it a “turning point that saw the death of traditional UN peacekeeping.”

Canadian Forces in the former Yugoslavia faced artillery and heavy machine-gun fire in the neutral zone but ultimately drove back Croatian forces. In the book, Eyre describes his battalion pushing past a roadblock into the village of Lički Čitluk, where they found evidence of ethnic cleansing among the burning buildings.

A traditional peacekeeping operation deploys a minimally armed force to separate combatants and act as a buffer. Eyre writes that multiple sides in the former Yugoslavia made targets of the under-resourced peacekeepers and the mission failed to prevent a brutal escalation of the violence.

“The only thing that the belligerents respected was force,” Eyre said in an interview with The Canadian Press, adding the wider United Nations Protection Force mission was unable to provide enough of that force.
He said peacekeeping was “an era for the Canadian military” that lasted decades and ended in the early 1990s. Modern missions, he said, are set against a very different geopolitical backdrop.

“Take a look now at where most peacekeeping operations are — Africa, where there is an extreme local reluctance to have large Western forces on the ground there, for various historical reasons, to keep the peace,” he said. “And the utility of many of those missions are in question.”

Medak Pocket was a formative experience for Eyre and many of his colleagues. He writes about the overpowering smells of smoke and death hanging over the field and how, for many years afterward, he could not “smell a campfire without being taken back” to that moment.
His book, which runs to just over 400 pages, covers the ups and downs of his career, from the battlefield to top command.
Eyre said he felt the need to describe history as he saw it from his front-row seat.
“In the Canadian military, we don’t have a tradition of senior military officers or generals and admirals capturing history,” he said in the interview.

Eyre said as chief of the defence staff, he frequently fielded requests from politicians who didn’t always understand the potential impacts of their decisions — or how thinly spread the Canadian Armed Forces had become after decades of underfunding and the launch of the Russian deterrence mission in Latvia.
“I know I irritated some in government. I was told at one point I was being seen as obstructionist, but it’s the reality of what we had on the shelf,” he said.
Eyre said Canada’s future in a shifting international order depends on strong alliances and selectively deploying military power on very specific operations.

He called Latvia — where Canada leads a battalion on Nato’s eastern flank and has stationed 2,000 troops — the most “geopolitically significant deployment that Canada has undertaken since the end of the Cold War.”

Eyre’s own time and experiences in the military were shaped by major turning points, starting with the end of the Cold War and continuing through the 9/11 terror attacks and the start of the Afghanistan war. In Afghanistan, Eyre commanded Canada’s largest combat advisory mission up to that point.

Eyre stepped into the role of chief of the defence staff somewhat reluctantly just five years ago, when Admiral Art McDonald stepped aside in the face of a sexual misconduct allegation. The allegation did not lead to charges.
Eyre said he initially thought he would only be in the job for weeks as acting chief — and soon after considered resigning on principle.

He said he wondered whether cabinet had lost trust in him when then-deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland openly criticized his decision not to fire Navy commander Vice-Admiral Craig Baines amid a scandal.
“The lesson here is just the messiness of political-military relations,” he said, adding the book is not meant to be a political “tell-all.”
He said he felt he had the confidence of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau but it took “a while to develop” at a time when, thanks to the pandemic, meetings were all being conducted by video.
Eyre helmed the forces from 2021 to 2024, a tenure he writes was consumed by “crisis stacked upon crisis.”

On top of the series of sexual misconduct allegations against top brass that rocked the armed forces, Eyre’s time in the top job also coincided with a global pandemic, the evacuation of Canadians from Afghanistan in 2021, the start of the war Ukraine, the “Freedom Convoy” that occupied Ottawa, chaotic gang violence in Haiti and forest fires and floods at home.
He said he fielded nearly two dozen requests for international disaster response and upwards of 100 for help with managing the COVID-19 crisis, in addition to other domestic requests.
“My observation was all of these crises stacked upon each other was really limiting the bandwidth of our decision makers,” the retired general said in the interview.

“That’s where something like understanding and having clearly articulated national security interests and objectives can provide you guardrails so that when the pressure is on, when time is tight, you have something to help you make those decisions.”
He said that while he empathizes with elected officials, he struggled with the slow pace of government peacetime processes.

Eyre said in one instance, he worried he had he overstepped his authority by committing Canada to training Ukrainians in Latvia at a time when Ottawa was not giving him “decisions at the speed of war.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.
Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Little Debbie snacks make a comeback to Canada
stories.summary: Little Debbie snacks are back on Canadian shelves four years after leaving the Canadian market.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
Posted September 29, 2026 3:53 pm.

Little Debbie snacks are back on Canadian shelves four years after leaving the Canadian market.

McKee Foods Corporation tells CityNews the popular sweet treats brand has returned across Canada in Loblaws banner stores.

“While McKee Foods is excited to bring our products back to Canada and plans to reintroduce additional varieties, we do not yet have specific details on which products will launch or when,” Mike Gloekler, McKee’s Corporate Communications & PR Manager wrote in an email.

The company says they reintroduced four family pack varieties including: Swiss Rolls, Honey Buns, Oatmeal Creme Piesike Gloekler and Cosmic Brownies.

Little Debbie snacks were off Canadian shelves since 2022, after their sole Canadian distributor cut ties with McKee Foods.

McKee Foods, owner of the Little Debbie brand, is an American company based in Tennessee.

stories.title: Canada not going to apologize to Trump amid trade war, LeBlanc says
stories.summary: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc dismissed the idea that Canada would apologize to the U.S. in the coming weeks, as President Donald Trump stated.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc dismissed the idea that Canada could apologize to the U.S. in the coming weeks as the trade war stretches on, as President Donald Trump has said he expects.

Trump made the comments from the Oval Office on Monday while speaking to reporters after being asked how recent trade developments between Canada and the U.S. will end, and after multiple rounds of U.S. tariffs and Canada’s counter-tariff measures.

“They’re going to come in and they’re going to say, ‘sir we are sorry,'” Trump said in response.

The comments also came hours before a U.S. import ban went into effect Tuesday , which blocked all Canadian alcohol, as well as some dairy products and motorcycles from entering the U.S.

LeBlanc spoke at an event in New Brunswick Tuesday hours after that ban went into effect, and was asked by reporters if Canada would indeed apologize to the U.S., as Trump suggested.

“I’m not thinking that the government of Canada is going to apologize for standing up for Canadian workers, Canadian businesses, defending our economy,” LeBlanc said.

“The American government decided to apply a series of tariffs that violated a free-trade agreement that this administration signed six years ago.”

The U.S. import ban on some Canadian goods is the latest escalation in Trump’s trade war with Canada.

It follows a wave of updated 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods on Sept. 15, which were in response to Canada’s counter-tariff measures enacted on Sept. 8. Those counter-tariffs were Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s first round of 50 per cent tariffs launched on Aug. 22.

Those escalations came after Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled his trade negotiators out of Washington, and said that Canada was “walking away from a bad deal.”

There have been no formal trade negotiations since, but LeBlanc said Tuesday that “we are having conversations with our American counterparts.”

“We’re not negotiating detailed text as we were five, six weeks ago, but we remain in contact with them,” said LeBlanc.

“If the prime minister concludes at some point that there’s a deal possible that protects the sovereignty of our country, that would be in the economic interests of the country, then obviously we would be in a position to have that conversation.”

“But for the moment, we’re focusing on what we can control in Canada.”

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump’s senior council for trade and manufacturing, Peter Navarro, said his message for Canadian lobbyists in the United States is: “get the h— out of our country!”

The comments were made at a conference appearance, when Navarro criticized Canada’s attempts to lobby in the Washington – an expression sometimes referred to as “K Street.”

“Canada, economically, is like a row boat. We’re an aircraft carrier, how’s that going to end? Any Canadians here? Please, if you’re on K Street, get the h— out of our country,” said Navarro.

The world gets it now: tariffs bring countries to the table. Everyone lined up to negotiate. Canada? They showed up with lobbyists. Message to them? Get the hell out. pic.twitter.com/JES6qaHZZl — Peter Navarro (@RealPNavarro) September 29, 2026
paragraphs: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc dismissed the idea that Canada could apologize to the U.S. in the coming weeks as the trade war stretches on, as President Donald Trump has said he expects.

Trump made the comments from the Oval Office on Monday while speaking to reporters after being asked how recent trade developments between Canada and the U.S. will end, and after multiple rounds of U.S. tariffs and Canada’s counter-tariff measures.
“They’re going to come in and they’re going to say, ‘sir we are sorry,'” Trump said in response.
The comments also came hours before a U.S. import ban went into effect Tuesday , which blocked all Canadian alcohol, as well as some dairy products and motorcycles from entering the U.S.
LeBlanc spoke at an event in New Brunswick Tuesday hours after that ban went into effect, and was asked by reporters if Canada would indeed apologize to the U.S., as Trump suggested.
“I’m not thinking that the government of Canada is going to apologize for standing up for Canadian workers, Canadian businesses, defending our economy,” LeBlanc said.
“The American government decided to apply a series of tariffs that violated a free-trade agreement that this administration signed six years ago.”
The U.S. import ban on some Canadian goods is the latest escalation in Trump’s trade war with Canada.

It follows a wave of updated 50 per cent U.S. tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods on Sept. 15, which were in response to Canada’s counter-tariff measures enacted on Sept. 8. Those counter-tariffs were Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s first round of 50 per cent tariffs launched on Aug. 22.
Those escalations came after Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled his trade negotiators out of Washington, and said that Canada was “walking away from a bad deal.”
There have been no formal trade negotiations since, but LeBlanc said Tuesday that “we are having conversations with our American counterparts.”
“We’re not negotiating detailed text as we were five, six weeks ago, but we remain in contact with them,” said LeBlanc.

“If the prime minister concludes at some point that there’s a deal possible that protects the sovereignty of our country, that would be in the economic interests of the country, then obviously we would be in a position to have that conversation.”
“But for the moment, we’re focusing on what we can control in Canada.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Trump’s senior council for trade and manufacturing, Peter Navarro, said his message for Canadian lobbyists in the United States is: “get the h— out of our country!”
The comments were made at a conference appearance, when Navarro criticized Canada’s attempts to lobby in the Washington – an expression sometimes referred to as “K Street.”
“Canada, economically, is like a row boat. We’re an aircraft carrier, how’s that going to end? Any Canadians here? Please, if you’re on K Street, get the h— out of our country,” said Navarro.

The world gets it now: tariffs bring countries to the table. Everyone lined up to negotiate. Canada? They showed up with lobbyists. Message to them? Get the hell out. pic.twitter.com/JES6qaHZZl — Peter Navarro (@RealPNavarro) September 29, 2026

stories.title: Halifax gets nearly $2M in federal funding to prevent gun, gang violence
stories.summary: The federal government has announced nearly $2 million in funding for the Halifax area to help prevent gun and gang violence in the community.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
The federal government has announced nearly $2 million in funding for the Halifax area to help prevent gun and gang violence in the community.

“We’re giving them the tools to turn away from crime,” said Canada’s Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree in Dartmouth, N.S. Tuesday.

“This funding will support projects that address risk factors associated with gun and gang violence, specifically focusing on the underlying social conditions that lead young people to crime.”

The funds for Halifax Regional Municipality (HRM) will be delivered through the federal government’s Build Safer Communities Fund, which is part of a larger $157.5-million commitment nationwide over the next three years.

Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore says these measures will strengthen community groups and hopefully steer vulnerable youth away from crime.

“The best public safety work often begins much earlier. It begins when a young person finds a mentor or a program that they can believe in, a place where they belong,” said Fillmore.

Since 2022, the municipality has received more than $3 million during the federal program’s first installment. The city’s public safety advisor, Amy Siciliano, says the new funding will help expand crisis de-escalation supports for youth in need.

“We’ve really been able to build our internal capacity to better support community organizations as well as our own facilities like recreation centres, library work, to work alongside community to improve the conditions that create those safer places for everyone,” said Siciliano.

As well, officials say the support will improve spaces for youth to connect with a mentor and help them receive educational and mental health resources.

Some ideas include programs specific to anti-trafficking and sexual exploitation.

“We would like to develop tools and training to educate young people around healthy relationships and things to look out for online,” said Sylvia Ofunne, a social policy strategist with the municipality.

The federal government says funding was issued based on the severity of crime in a community. HRM data shows there were nine homicides and 30 shootings in 2025.

With these additional supports, officials say they hope those figures will be reduced.

“(We) want to counter that with off-ramps that will enable young people to not fall into that trap of the criminal justice system,” said Anandasangaree.

stories.title: Csis May have misused special powers when gathering information, says spy watchdog
stories.summary: Some Csis employees May have committed offences without required designation, review agency finds
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Canadian Security Intelligence Service May not have complied with the law when using special powers to gather information, a review by the national spy watchdog has found.

The Csis Act allows designated spy service employees to commit certain offences when collecting information – a measure intended to ensure Csis operations do not break the law.

A newly released National Security and Intelligence Review Agency report notes there are limitations and requirements tied to this authority to ensure legal curbs on Csis activities.

For instance, the authority does not permit Csis to wilfully obstruct justice, infringe on a Charter right or detain, torture or kill a person.

Employees committing offences or directing sources to do so must spell out why they believe the actions are reasonable and proportional in the circumstances.

Security experts call for inquiry into Havana Syndrome cases at Canada’s embassy in Cuba

The intelligence review agency looked at Csis’s use of the authority in operations in 2022 and 2023.

The review agency found some Csis employees May have committed offences without the required designation, and that direction May have been given to commit some acts without the authorization required by law.

The report also says Csis sometimes failed to adequately document the justifications for offences. In addition, it says, some required internal reporting and notifications to the review agency were not done.

The spy watchdog says Csis has a duty to ensure all of its operations respect the law, especially when those operations require activity that would otherwise be considered illegal.

Csis had no immediate comment on the report.

The Ottawa-based International Civil Liberties Monitoring Group called the findings “deeply disturbing.

“Once again, we see a case where Csis pushes the boundaries of the law and fails to abide by the rules and regulations meant to instill confidence that they can be trusted with such sensitive powers in the first place,” the group said in a statement.

stories.title: N.S. man sentenced to six years for killing ailing wife after they were evicted
stories.summary: Douglas Andrew Smith pleaded guilty in April to manslaughter in the death of his wife, Iris Dodd, in 2022.
stories.author: Global News
stories.content:
A Nova Scotia judge sentenced a man to six years in prison for killing his 72-year-old wife after promising to help her take her own life so she could avoid being hospitalized or sent to long-term care.

Iris Dodd and Douglas Andrew Smith had been married for nearly 33 years in 2022, when they found themselves facing eviction from their home in Kingsport, N.S., with nowhere else to go, according to an agreed statement of facts read aloud in provincial Supreme Court on Tuesday.

Dodd was nearly blind and could barely walk, and she asked her husband to lay out her pills and go for a drive, so he’d be free from any responsibility when she took them all and died, the court head.

Smith, then 71, agreed. But he worried the overdose would only make her sicker.

“In a singular moment, exhausted and confused about what was best for the victim, Mr. Smith resolved all these thoughts and fears in his head by getting up and holding a pillow over the victim’s face,” Crown prosecutor Daniel Rideout said, reading from the statement of facts.

A quiet cry can then be heard on the audio recording of Tuesday’s proceedings, and Rideout pauses for a few moments. The judge then asks the defence if Smith needs to take a break.

The couple’s relationship was caring and supportive and they’d lived together since they were married on Nov. 1, 1989, court heard. She had a stroke in 2018, which triggered a slow but progressive decline in her health. She began to use a wheelchair when she could no longer manage the stairs. Her vision deteriorated and fibromyalgia caused her daily pain.

When they were living in Kingsport, about 85 kilometres northwest of Halifax, their landlord said in July 2021 that they had to move out. A court ordered them to leave on May 1, 2022, Rideout said.

Taking care of Dodd hampered Smith’s search for a new home, and he couldn’t find a place they could afford that would suit their accessibility needs.

Dodd had been a nursing assistant in hospitals and long-term care and she was adamant that she never wanted to live in either setting, “blind and bound to her chair,” Rideout said.

Days before their eviction, she told Smith about her overdose plans and he promised he’d help lay out her pills, so she could see them. They decided to carry out the plan the next day. But after Dodd fell asleep, Smith began worrying that her medications wouldn’t kill her, and that she’d just become more incapacitated.

“Mr. Smith couldn’t stop thinking of the victim being alone at the time of death, as he did not want her to be alone, and he did not want her to experience any fear in those moments of passing,” Rideout read to the court.

“(He) was emotionally and physically exhausted from the pressure they were under to find a new home, preparing to vacate the home, caring for the victim, and now processing for the first time the victim’s expressed in clear desire to end her life and his agreement to help her in that plan.”

He killed Dodd on April 30, 2022, believing it was the “best way to ensure the victim would not suffer more pain or fear,” Rideout said.

Smith left the home and checked into a hotel, but he couldn’t sleep. He drove back to his house in the early morning hours and sat with his wife. He wrote emails to her family, their landlord and their realtor, to tell them she was dead, Rideout said. He then gathered up some belongings, sat one more time with Dodd before driving about 12 kilometres to the RCMP detachment in New Minas, N.S.

Sitting in his van in the parking lot, he called 911 and told the dispatcher what happened. An officer came out and arrested him.

In April, he was set to stand trial for a charge of second-degree murder. Instead, he pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of manslaughter, avoiding a trial.

A spokesperson for Nova Scotia’s public prosecution service said Tuesday that Smith’s six-year sentence worked out to five years and seven months, less two days, after accounting for the time he had already spent in custody.

stories.title: Ikea finally arrives in London
stories.summary: After years of anticipation, Swedish furniture retailer Ikea has opened its first store in London, Ont., welcoming hundreds of shoppers to White Oaks Mall on opening day.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
After years of anticipation, Swedish furniture retailer Ikea has opened its first store in London, Ont., welcoming hundreds of shoppers to White Oaks Mall on opening day.

The new location, a compact-store concept that is the first of its kind in Canada, opened Tuesday morning following a ribbon-cutting ceremony shortly before 10 a.m.

Customers began lining up hours before the opening. Among them was Western University student Micka Soria, who said she and her friends arrived around 2:30 a.m. to secure a spot near the front of the line.

“We had to wait for maybe more than four hours just to get in, and the weather, too, is really cold,” Soria said. “Growing up, I was always going to Ikea in Toronto. When I moved here, Ikea was nowhere.”

Ikea Canada CEO and chief sustainability officer Selwyn Crittendon said the company has long recognized demand for a location in London but noted that traditional Ikea stores require significantly more space.

“We know that it’s hard to plop down 300,000 square feet anywhere in the country, so now it’s about being more accessible,” Crittendon said.

The London store spans about 43,000 square feet and features curated room displays, more than 2,500 home furnishing and seasonal products, and a self-serve warehouse area with about 400 furniture items available for immediate purchase.

Ikea officials said the store’s product selection was tailored to local demand using purchasing data from the company’s Burlington location.

“We took a quite deep dive into what the London market has been buying and what the needs are,” said Danny Santana, deputy market manager for Ikea Burlington. “We really wanted to prioritize everyday essentials and convenience for the product assortment here.”

The opening follows a lengthy effort to bring Ikea to London. More than two decades ago, the company announced plans for a south London store but later abandoned the proposal amid changing market conditions.

Crittendon said the compact-store model is better suited to London’s market and allows the company to expand into communities where a traditional Ikea store May not be feasible.

Opening-day celebrations included giveaways, contests and special promotions, while shoppers also had access to Ikea’s food offerings, including its signature Swedish meatballs.

stories.title: Dangerous high-risk sex offender to live in Surrey, B.C. police say in a warning
stories.summary: Leonard Michael Ramstead is subject to a 10-year long-term supervision order and a host of bail conditions.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Police in Surrey, B.C., have taken the step of advising the public that a dangerous high-risk sex offender will be residing in the community.

In a press release and on posts to social media , Surrey Police Services (SPS) said it was issuing a Public Interest Disclosure after being notified that the offender, Leonard Michael Ramstead, will be residing in the city. Ramstead has previously been convicted of sexual offences involving children and is believed to continue to pose a risk for violent sexual offences against children, police said. Surrey is part of the metropolitan Vancouver region.

Police have released an image and a description, and say Ramstead is a 58-year-old white male, 5-foot-7 and approximately 235 lbs. He has brown hair, blue eyes, and normally has a beard.

Ramstead is the subject of a long-term supervision order, defined by the Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) as “a non-custodial sentencing option available to the courts to extend the length of time that the CSC will supervise and support an offender in the community.”

The order cannot exceed 10 years, and Ramstead has been given the maximum duration. He also has a long list of bail conditions, which include not consuming alcohol or drugs; avoiding all contact with past or present victims of offences for which he has been convicted, or any known members of their families; and having no contact or to be in the presence of any children under the age of 16.

This incudes a ban on being near day cares, elementary or secondary schools, parks and playgrounds, swimming pools, and recreational centres, or seeking any employment or voluntary work that involves being in a position of trust or authority towards someone under 16.

Anyone seeing Ramstead breaching his release conditions is asked to immediately call 911.

Surrey Police Services took over as the police of jurisdiction from the local RCMP detachment in 2024. However, the RCMP has also announced it will be partnering to surveil Ramstead via traditional police methods, as well as through electronic monitoring.

Ramstead was first convicted in 2019 for sexual interference with a person under age 16, and again in 2021 for the same charge with a person under 14. He is considered a high risk to young people and children.

He was given statutory release in April 2024 upon serving two-thirds of his fixed-term sentence. RCMP at the time warned the community of his release, which concluded this month with the transition to the long-term supervision order.

Ramstead’s statutory release in 2024 coincided with that of another dangerous sex offender, prompting consternation from Surrey’s mayor, Brenda Locke.

“I am absolutely appalled and outraged that not one, but two dangerous sex offenders have been released into our community in a mere two-week span,” Locke told Vancouver Sun .

“It is beyond comprehension why several high-risk offenders are being unleashed into our city, which has the largest youth population in B.C.,” she said. “This is utterly unacceptable. The blatant disregard for the safety and security of our community, particularly our most vulnerable individuals, is a grave injustice that cannot be overlooked.”

stories.title: Alberta CEOs join ‘stay’ camp as Calgary Chamber warns of separatism economic fallout
stories.summary: A University of Calgary study estimates trade costs would rise by five to eight per cent and Alberta could see up to 175,000 jobs cut and a $62-billion annual hit to the economy.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Alberta business leaders have signed on to an open letter from the Calgary Chamber of Commerce warning of the dire economic consequences if the province were to separate from Canada .

“We must remain at the table and prioritize relationships, opportunities and stability that have helped make this province and this country prosperous,” reads the letter released Tuesday along with an analysis into the trade, labour and fiscal implications of separation.

“Alberta can be proud of Its identity while remaining confident in its future within Canada.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Alberta can be proud of Its identity while remaining confident in its future within Canada."

Among the signatories to the letter are the heads of AltaGas, Atco, AltaLink, Capital Power, Keyera, BHE Transmission and Chirp Foods Inc., Canada’s largest McDonald’s franchise business. Tourism Calgary and Calgary Economic Development have also signed, as well as a former CEO of Trans Mountain Corp.

The chamber said more are expected to join.

In three weeks, Albertans vote on 10 referendum questions, including one on whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the process of holding another referendum on separation.

The study by University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimates trade costs would rise by five to eight per cent — the range the United Kingdom has seen since its withdrawal from the European Union.

It said Alberta is the most trade-exposed jurisdiction in the country, with nearly one in three workers having jobs in sectors significantly vulnerable to such disruptions.

The higher trade costs would translate into to job reductions of up to 175,000 in Alberta and an up to $62-billion annual hit to the economy, the report said.

Alberta would also find itself with a $9-billion fiscal shortfall if it were to separate, Tombe concluded. Closing the gap would require a 13 per cent sales tax, a 10 per cent corporate income tax hike or a 40 per cent cut in the transfers Alberta businesses and individuals now receive, like the Canada Child Benefit and old age security.

“When you hear something like GDP contracting, it seems like an abstract statistical notion, but this translates directly into real incomes and wages. How much goods and services can you afford to purchase with an hour of work?” Tombe told reporters.

Chamber president and CEO Deborah Yedlin said Alberta splitting from Canada would be like scoring on its own net, just to send a message.

“I grew up with this notion of the Alberta advantage — no sales tax, low taxes, good education, health care, social services. All of that would disappear and we would not be able to sustain that level of support for Albertans,” she told reporters.

“That, in turn, turns into a negative feedback loop, and you don’t get the investment, you don’t generate the tax revenue, you can’t provide the services unless you change how you operate, and that’s just not something anybody really wants to see.”

The vote also comes as “we stand on the doorstep of some significant opportunity,” Yedlin added.

The world is clamouring for stable supplies of energy as wars rage in the Middle East and Russia. And the federal government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has made a raft of policy shifts embraced by businesses while demonstrating an eagerness to build new energy infrastructure.

Some people might be looking to send a message with a pro-separation-referendum vote after 10 years of former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s less oilpatch-friendly approach, Yedlin said.

“It’s easy to look in the rear-view mirror and it’s easy to be aggrieved and to focus on that. It’s much harder to be an optimist, but we’re at a point in time where we need to have that optimism.

paragraphs: Alberta business leaders have signed on to an open letter from the Calgary Chamber of Commerce warning of the dire economic consequences if the province were to separate from Canada .

“We must remain at the table and prioritize relationships, opportunities and stability that have helped make this province and this country prosperous,” reads the letter released Tuesday along with an analysis into the trade, labour and fiscal implications of separation.

“Alberta can be proud of Its identity while remaining confident in its future within Canada.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Alberta can be proud of Its identity while remaining confident in its future within Canada."

Among the signatories to the letter are the heads of AltaGas, Atco, AltaLink, Capital Power, Keyera, BHE Transmission and Chirp Foods Inc., Canada’s largest McDonald’s franchise business. Tourism Calgary and Calgary Economic Development have also signed, as well as a former CEO of Trans Mountain Corp.
The chamber said more are expected to join.
In three weeks, Albertans vote on 10 referendum questions, including one on whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the process of holding another referendum on separation.

The study by University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimates trade costs would rise by five to eight per cent — the range the United Kingdom has seen since its withdrawal from the European Union.
It said Alberta is the most trade-exposed jurisdiction in the country, with nearly one in three workers having jobs in sectors significantly vulnerable to such disruptions.
The higher trade costs would translate into to job reductions of up to 175,000 in Alberta and an up to $62-billion annual hit to the economy, the report said.

Alberta would also find itself with a $9-billion fiscal shortfall if it were to separate, Tombe concluded. Closing the gap would require a 13 per cent sales tax, a 10 per cent corporate income tax hike or a 40 per cent cut in the transfers Alberta businesses and individuals now receive, like the Canada Child Benefit and old age security.

“When you hear something like GDP contracting, it seems like an abstract statistical notion, but this translates directly into real incomes and wages. How much goods and services can you afford to purchase with an hour of work?” Tombe told reporters.

stories.title: ‘Separation will not solve problems’: Poilievre speaks in Alberta ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton — Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre tried Tuesday to convince Albertans to vote to stay in Canada with less than three weeks to go until a provincial vote on separation.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre delivers a speech on national unity in Calgary, Monday, June 8, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Jeff McIntosh THE Canadian Press

By Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 2:01 pm.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 11:16 pm.

Edmonton — Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre tried Tuesday to convince Albertans to vote to stay in Canada with less than three weeks to go until a provincial vote on separation.

His speech at a downtown Edmonton hotel was among others he has given or plans to give in the province as part of his efforts to convince Conservative voters that Alberta is stronger within a united Canada.

Poilievre, who is from Alberta, said separatists have a problem with the federal Liberal government — not with Canada.

“Many Albertans are legitimately frustrated that a costly and controlling, big and bossy government has gone far beyond its jurisdictional boundaries,” he told a crowd of supporters holding Canadian flags and “Conservatives for Canada” signs.

Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party government has called a 10-question referendum for Oct. 19. The 10th and final question asks Albertans whether they want to stay in Canada or have a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Smith has said she supports Alberta staying a part of Canada and plans to vote that way in the referendum, but that hundreds of thousands have signed petitions for and against separation, and it’s time to put the issue to rest.

Critics, pointing to long-standing opinion polls indicating massive support for Alberta staying in Canada, have accused Smith of calling the vote to appease restive separatist hardliners in her party.

Poilievre said Liberal government policies have left Canadians struggling to make ends meet, everywhere from the gas pump and the grocery store to buying a house.

“Our businesses and workers are frustrated that our oil and gas is left in the ground and our opportunities are left there with it,” he said Tuesday.

The solution to those problems is not an independent Alberta, he said.

those problems. Becoming even more Canadian will,” Poilievre said.

“The solution is to double down on the way the country was always meant to work.”

He said Albertans should keep fighting by, for example, forcing Ottawa to unlock the power of Alberta’s oil and gas industry.

Earlier in the day, Poilievre attended a fundraiser for Conservatives for Canada, a group of federal politicians making the case for Alberta to stay in Confederation.

He has tapped Dane Lloyd, a member of Parliament who represents an Alberta riding, to lead that effort.

On Tuesday night, Lloyd gave a shout-out to the Conservative MPs in the room who have campaigned for the federalist side of the separation debate.

“Conservatives are patriots,” Lloyd said. “We love our country. We love our home province of Alberta.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

On Tuesday night, Lloyd gave a shout-out to the Conservative MPs in the room who have campaigned for the federalist side of the separation debate.
“Conservatives are patriots,” Lloyd said. “We love our country. We love our home province of Alberta.”

stories.title: Csis can break the law. They need to document it better, watchdog warns
stories.summary: The National Security and Intelligence Review Agency (Nsira) said Csis did not properly document justifications for illegal activities as required.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada’s spy agency needs more oversight into operations that include illegal activities in order to gain intelligence, a new watchdog report suggests.

The Canadian Security and Intelligence Service (Csis) is authorized in certain circumstances to take actions that would ordinarily break Canadian law in its pursuit of information about national security threats.

But while the National Security and Intelligence Review Agency (Csira) found that Csis stayed within the bounds of the illegal activities they’re permitted to use, the spy agency lacked documented justifications and rationale for taking those actions.

“Csis has a duty to ensure that all of its operations respect the rule of law, even more so when those operations require activity that would otherwise be considered illegal,” the review body wrote in a report released publicly Tuesday.

The review body examined operations from 2022 and 2023 where Csis operations involved actions or omissions that would normally break Canadian laws. The powers were granted to the agency by the Liberals’ 2017 national security reforms, which also placed limitations on what illegal actions the spy agency can engage in.

According to Csis 2025 report, the powers were authorized 173 times in 2022-23 and 178 times in 2023-24.

Csis is still prohibited from certain activities, such as causing bodily harm, obstructing justice, violating someone’s sexual integrity and torture. Instead, eight “classes” of illegal activities have been approved by both the minister of public safety and the independent intelligence commissioner — although each instance requires authorization and written justification and explanation after the fact.

It’s the documentation that Nsira found issue with.

In some cases, the review agency said, Csis operatives failed to document the nature of the threat that led them to believe illegal activities were justified. In others, Csis employees did not document the nature of the illegal activities or their negative consequences.

In other operations, the agency didn’t detail what alternatives were considered before engaging in illegal activity.

Nsira noted that the team within Csis tasked with oversight for these activities is under-resourced, and said increased internal guidance and review is needed to make sure Csis is following the rules.

“Many of the deficiencies … noted above can be attributed to confusion or lack of understanding of the requirements and the consequences of not meeting them,” the review agency wrote.

In a statement to Global News Tuesday afternoon, Csis welcomed the Nsira review — but suggested the agency May disagree with some of the review body’s findings. The agency said a full response to Nsira’s recommendations will be posted publicly in the future.

“While Csis May not agree with all Nsira’s findings, Csis holds the same strong commitment to transparency and accountability, and takes all potential non-compliance seriously,” the agency said in a statement.

“As such, Csis will take appropriate steps proposed by Nsira’s assessment, and will continue to collaborate effectively with Nsira, which includes notifying the review body as per its requirements in the Csis Act.”

While Csis May not agree with all of Nsira’s findings, Csis holds the same strong commitment to transparency and accountability, and takes all potential non-compliance seriously. As such, Csis will take appropriate steps proposed by Nsira’s assessment, and will continue to collaborate effectively with Nsira, which includes notifying the review body as per its requirements in the Csis Act.

stories.title: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe to lay out nuclear development plan
stories.summary: Countries across the globe are either building or promising to construct more nuclear power plants as many look for ways to reduce emissions.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
has unveiled the province’s nuclear energy plan, including a power production goal within 24 years.

Under the plan, the province aims to produce at least 2,600 megawatts of nuclear power by 2050. By comparison, Ontario’s Pickering Nuclear Generating Station produces 2,100 MW of electricity, powering 1.5 million homes annually, according to the Government of Canada

“Our future electricity mix in this province will include, yes, natural gas; it will include hydro, wind, solar as well as some thermal,” Moe said Tuesday. “But we must also invest in a future source of power that is reliable in every season. Available around the clock, is affordable for decades to come, affordable for us to continue to attract that investment, but also, most importantly, affordable for the families that live here.”

The province says its plan contains four priorities:

The first priority is focused on nuclear energy providing a reliable source of non-emitting electricity to strengthen the reliability of the power grid and meeting growing demand.

Incorporating large reactors will see SaskPower begin planning for the potential development of such structures in northwestern Saskatchewan.

Moe said more than 2,000 of that 2,600 megawatt goal will come from large-scale nuclear reactors, the first of which is planned to come online by 2042.

“To put that into perspective, 600 megawatts can power the equivalent of Saskatchewan’s two largest cities, Regina and Saskatoon,” Moe explained. “Twenty-six hundred megawatts could power the equivalent of 2.6 million homes.”

Consultations with local communities near the proposed reactors and Indigenous peoples would be part of SaskPower’s evaluation of potential locations.

Crown Investment Corporations Minister Jeremy Harrison told reporters that 2042 for the first large reactor was a “very realistic timeline.”

He said there have been “very good” discussions regarding long-term plans with the federal government, along with the governments of Alberta and the Northwest Territories.

“I’ve said publicly often that, you know, there’s a lot in Canada that pushes us apart. Nuclear is one of those things that really can bring the country together from Ontario to Western Canada to New Brunswick,” Harrison said Tuesday.

Saskatchewan has already been looking into the idea of nuclear energy, with the government and SaskPower in a multi-year planning phase of a proposed small modular reactor (SMR) by the mid-2030s.

Those SMRs are highlighted in the province’s plan, with the Rafferty site near Estevan selected to undergo further study for development of such a reactor. The utility plans to advance planning for potential SMR deployment with a goal of delivering at least 600 megawatts.

“This plan gives SaskPower a clear path to meet growing demand and support the investment and industries that keep our province strong,” said Crown Investments Corporation Minister Jeremy Harrison in a news release.

The final goal of Saskatchewan’s plan is focused on ensuring electricity supply keeps up with demand.

The province says it plans to engage with Indigenous rights holders, municipalities, industry stakeholders and other leaders as it makes further plans for nuclear energy.

Tim Gitzel, CEO of Cameco, one of the largest uranium mining companies in the world, said the plan recognizes the “essential role” nuclear power plays in supporting growth.

“We understand the economic, environmental and energy security benefits that safe, reliable and carbon-free nuclear power can provide for our people, communities, and industries,” Gitzel said in a news release. “We look forward to competing for the province’s business as it embarks on this transformative plan to build a reliable energy grid, utilizing nuclear energy to power Saskatchewan’s future.”

Nuclear energy will also provide more than just electricity, Moe said, it will provide opportunities for tradespeople, Indigenous businesses, technological companies, fabricators and suppliers.

He told reporters the Saskatoon-based mining company is working with the federal government on regulations and opportunities to expand its workforce. When asked by reporters about costs, he said the numbers “change over time.” Harrison said there was the potential for private sector financing to be “part of the conversation.”

stories.title: $22.4M investment to unlock 165 acres at Kelowna Airport
stories.summary: The federal government is providing up to $22.4 million for infrastructure that will open up the airport land for industrial and aerospace development.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
There is a lot of room to grow at Kelowna International Airport (YLW) and a major investment announced Monday is set to start unlocking it.

The federal government is providing up to $22.4 million for infrastructure that will open up 165 acres of airport land for industrial and aerospace development.

The funding will help pay for the water, sewer, electrical, communications and stormwater infrastructure needed to service the site.

Philip Elchitz, director of operations and innovation at Kelowna International Airport, says YLW already has a significant economic footprint, supporting about 9,000 jobs and generating roughly $2 billion in annual economic output.

The airport expects that footprint to grow as the East Lands are developed.

“If you add up the current and the future, we expect to go to 3 billion dollars in annual economic output per year and approximately 12,000 jobs per year, both direct and indirect.”

But the entire site will not be built out right away.

The first phase will service roughly one-third of the available land. That leaves two-thirds open for future investment.

Three aerospace companies, De Havilland Aircraft, Wildcat Helicopters and Fire Swarm, are already in talks with the airport about opportunities on the site.

For Wildcat Helicopters, a larger footprint could mean expanding its operations and workforce.

“Oh, absolutely. We’ll be hiring more people. Yeah, there’s no doubt about it,” says Mike Michaud, President, Wildcat Helicopters

The expansion is also being matched by investments in training.

Okanagan College’s new aerospace facility is expected to open in 2027. The college currently trains about 64 aircraft maintenance engineers, a number expected to rise to 144 once the new facility opens.

Most of the new infrastructure will be built on the east side of the runway. The airport says construction is expected to begin next spring, with the work scheduled to wrap up by the end of 2028.

For now, much of that side of the airport remains open space.

The plan is to turn it into a growing aerospace hub, with new taxiways, hangars, offices, companies and, ultimately, more people working at YLW.

stories.title: Immigration increase could be on the horizon, Carney suggests in interview
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney suggested a "controlled increase" in the country's population could be on the way in a recent interview with the New York Times.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says with Canada’s immigration system back under control, the question now is about when to begin a “controlled increase” of the country’s population.

Carney made the remark in a recent interview with the New York Times, just over a month before the government is required by law to release its immigration levels plan for the next three years.

The last three federal immigration plans focused on reducing the number of people coming to the country after a rapid post-pandemic population spike.

The government also started setting targets for annual temporary arrivals to reduce the number of short-term workers and students to five per cent of the population after they cracked seven per cent in October 2024.

The C.D. Howe Institute’s immigration targets council recommends the government continue to shrink the number of arrivals over the next three years.

That council includes several top academics who study immigration policy, a former deputy minister and former Alberta premier Jason Kenney.

stories.title: Carney set to make energy announcement in Vancouver
stories.summary: Carney's announcement comes after LNG Canada said earlier Tuesday that it will go ahead with the multibillion-dollar Phase 2 expansion of its liquefied natural gas export terminal.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney announced in Vancouver on Tuesday that LNG Canada is moving forward with the Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.

“Today’s $33 billion investment in LNG Canada 2 will make LNG Canada the second-largest facility of its kind in the world. It will create over thousands of new jobs,” Carney said.

“It will connect low-cost, low-carbon Canadian energy to global markets, providing the secure supply our partners in Asia and Europe need.”

The expansion comes as global energy markets have been in turmoil amid the war in the Middle East and the closures of the Strait of Hormuz over recent months, sending prices soaring.

Carney added that this is a “great” day for Canada.

“The scale of this investment shows it,” he said.

“The partnership proves it. The speed confirms it. Canada is working. Canada is building big again”

Carney said that this project represents Canada coming together on a bigger scale.

“It’s above and beyond this project,” he added.

“It’s the way it’s come together. It’s the way it’s being built. It’s the teamwork that’s here that teaches a lesson for all Canadians.”

BC NDP leader David Eby called the announcement a “big deal.”

“I want to recognize a few people who are very key to getting us here today,” Eby added.

“But I also want to take a moment to reflect on what it means to have the partners that we have committing to Phase 2 of this project in British Columbia and in Canada.

“We have very high standards, unapologetically. Workers have to be treated right. Indigenous partners need to be at the table. We need to ensure that when we build a project like this, that it has world-leading environmental standards and there has to be a fair return to Canadians and to British Columbians.”

Eby said he visited Kitimat and spoke to those working in Phase 1 and they wanted to know when Phase 2 would become a reality.

“This project means 4,000 in just the Phase 2 project, 4,000 high-paid jobs,” he added.

“It doesn’t talk about all the ancillary jobs that come with that. It means $28 billion over the life of the project in revenue for governments to pay for the services that people depend on.”

Former B.C. premier Christy Clark said she was thrilled by Tuesday’s announcement.

“I am so delighted,” she said.

“We started talking about LNG in 2011. Everybody made fun of us, and me in particular. And I think John Horgan and David Eby both said that I was like some kind of crazy dreamer just making stuff up. And I’m glad they both turned out to be so wrong.

“This is so good for workers and for our economy.”

Clark added that if B.C. had embraced LNG years ago, the province would not be in the position that Carney is now trying to fix.

“He says we don’t have diversified markets, we don’t have partners in Asia, we’re not selling enough of our natural resources,” she said.

“That was the whole point of LNG. Create jobs at home and diversify our market so that we’re no longer so dependent on the United States. If we’d been allowed to just, you know, by other levels of government, federal government in particular, but then subsequently the NDP governments of Horgan and Eby, we’d been allowed to go ahead, we would be way ahead of the game right now, much better protected from the aggressive moves from the American government against us on tariffs.”

BC Green Party Leader Emily Lowan was not excited, however, about the Phase 2 announcement. “LNG Canada is an entirely foreign-owned project,” she said in a statement.

“It is owned by Shell, one of the most profitable companies in history, several foreign state-owned oil companies, and U.S. private equity. LNG Canada’s owners also own the fracking operations in the Peace (region) that feed the project.

“The profits from LNG development flow directly to shareholders and governments abroad, while the costs stay here. ”

Lowan referred to the announcement as a “nation-draining” project.
