stories.title: As federal budget nears, Canada’s health ministers to meet to talk funding
stories.summary: Provinces and territories have raised concerns about the federal budget, which forecasts an end to some targeted health care funding after March 2027.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Health ministers from across the country are set to meet Tuesday to warn they’re headed toward a “fiscal cliff” if federal funding agreements for things like home care and mental health are not renewed, Ontario’s health minister said.

Sylvia Jones told a provincial committee meeting on Monday that she and her counterparts are planning to hold an emergency meeting, and said it appears the federal government is walking away from a portion of the Canada Health Transfer.

“All I’m asking, and all (that) all of the other federal, territorial ministers are asking for, is some clarity” on whether the federal government will “continue working with us,” Jones told reporters.

Provinces and territories have raised concerns about the federal budget, which forecasts an end to some targeted health care funding after March 2027.

The federal government pledged a total of $200 billion in health funding over 10 years in the 2023 budget.

That was intended to help expand access to primary care, reduce surgery backlogs, improve mental health and addiction services and modernize the health system, following widespread issues in health care across the country during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.

As part of that sum, $4.8 billion was set aside for improvements to home care, community care and mental health and addiction services. It’s set to end in 2027. Another $3 billion funding package meant to improve long-term care safety was set to sunset in 2026, and $1.7 billion for personal support workers wages will be paid out by 2028.

Last year’s federal budget also outlines a planned reduction in the growth of the federal Canada Health Transfer after March 2028.

That transfer increases each year in line with a three-year average of the nominal gross domestic product.

That is guaranteed to grow by at least five per cent per year until fiscal year 2027-28. After that, it is set to return to a minimum growth rate of three per cent per year.

After Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government released its first budget last November, health advocacy groups warned that the Liberals highlighted the end of funding agreements in the coming years as part of their plan to get spending in check.

Jones said she and her counterparts want federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel to understand that the sunsetting of bilateral funding agreements next year will have a real impact on patients.

“These are not capital projects. These are programs, these are services,” she said.

“These are people who have been receiving programming from the provincial government with a half a billion dollars (of) support from the federal government.”

Premiers also warned of a “fiscal cliff” if those agreements expire without renewal.

In a joint statement following a meeting of the Council of the Federation in July, the premiers said they need the health transfer to continue growing at a rate of five per cent per year and called for a long-term commitment to “flexible and sustainable funding.”

In an emailed response to questions, a spokesperson for Michel said she’s prepared to talk with her counterparts about building a strong and sustainable public health care system at a meeting next month.

“Following the first ministers meeting in July, the prime minister and premiers directed the deputy ministers of finance and health to work together on long-term health funding and productivity of the health care system,” said Alexandre Bergeron.

The federal government is set to release its budget later this fall.

Jones was asked about health funding by an opposition member of the legislature who asked why the Ontario government had failed to sign on to the federal pharmacare program.

She said the federal government “has paused all negotiations, conversations, any interest in expanding” pharmacare.

That program, which was created as part of the supply-and-confidence agreement between the New Democrats and Justin Trudeau’s minority Liberal government, launched with bilateral agreements to provide contraceptives and certain diabetes medications to patients at no cost.

Only Manitoba, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Yukon signed on to the agreements, which included five years of federal funding.

Carney’s government has repeatedly stated its support for the pharmacare program, but Michel has been noncommittal about signing new agreements or expanding it into a full national drug insurance program.

Bergeron said in a statement that the government is tracking the agreements in place with the four jurisdictions that have signed on, and will honour them.

— With files from Allison Jones in Toronto

stories.title: Eby promises to shrink deficit by cutting wasteful spending, growing economy
stories.summary: The province faces a projected deficit of $13.8 billion and Doerkson says Conservatives would trim that by growing the economy, if they win the snap election on Oct. 24.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Resource development and making British Columbia an “energy superpower” to grow the economy would allow for a new provincial government to pay down record deficit, both the NDP and Conservative party leaders said on the campaign trail Monday.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson promised to double liquefied natural gas production by 2032 in the province, if elected, while NDP Leader David Eby announced his government would double the export of critical minerals within five years.

Doerkson said there’s a global energy crisis and “our allies in Asia and Europe desperately need Canadian LNG.”

While Eby picked up on the same theme, saying B.C. has an abundance of critical minerals that other countries need.

“Getting them to world markets means less dependence on the U.S., while creating family-supporting jobs and the prosperity needed to strengthen health care and public services,” said Eby, who was in Prince Rupert on Monday.

He also said an NDP government would expand the Prince Rupert port to be the second-largest facility of its kind in Canada by 2030.

When questioned about the $13.8-billion deficit that Eby’s NDP government accumulated while in power, both party leaders said their plans to grow the economy would help trim the shortfall.

British Columbians demand that the deficit be reduced, Doerkson said at an event in Vancouver.

“We can’t be dealing with a $14-billion deficit in British Columbia,” he said. “How do we manage anything, knowing that we are faced with these deficits year after year?”

Doerkson did not offer details about how a future Conservative government would balance the budget.

“The reality is that we’re not sure how bad the books are,” he said.

The interim leader, who replaced Kerry-Lynne Findlay about a week ago following her resignation, pointed to an accounting error by the provincial government that overstated forecast revenues from natural gas by nearly $1.5 billion.

“It’s going to be almost impossible to commit to how quickly we will be able to arrive at balanced budgets,” he said. “But the reality is, we have to get back to that.”

Doerkson’s promised on Sunday that his government would not raise existing taxes or introduce new ones.

Eby said the promise of a tax freeze shows the Conservatives are not transparent about their plans.

“The math doesn’t work for the Conservatives,” he said. “It’s very clear that their agenda, when you do the math, is to dramatically cut health care and education.”

Eby pointed to comments from Conservative candidate Tony Luck, who is running for re-election in Fraser-Nicola.

Luck said in February 2024 that if education and health care are the two biggest budget items, then they will take “the brunt” of cuts.

Eby said there is no difference between the major parties when it comes fiscal sustainability.

The real question is how to get there, he said.

“We’ve got to end wasteful spending,” he said. “We’ve got to grow the economy with announcements like today’s.”

Both leaders were also asked about a gathering of alleged white nationalists on a B.C. First Nation reserve on Sunday, just days away from National Truth and Reconciliation Day.

Roseanne Casimir, chief of Tk’emlups te Secwepemc nation, said a group of masked people dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops on Sunday questioning reports of human burials at the former sites of residential schools.

Eby called the display “disgusting,” while Doerkson denounced the group.

In Victoria on Monday, Green Leader Emily Lowan said her party would lift the freeze on the NDP government’s $10-a-day childcare spaces, with a goal to achieve universal free children care space by 2031.

“Lack of access, lack of qualified educators, and unaffordable fees send a clear message to young people and families: the government is not investing in you,” Lowan said in a statement.

The current childcare model in B.C. is expensive and complicated, and it’s been exacerbated by the former NDP government’s funding pause in the last provincial budget, Lowan said.

– With files from Nono Shen in Vancouver

stories.title: Canada extends travel restrictions related to Ebola outbreak for 60 days
stories.summary: Canadian citizens or permanent residents who have been in one of the affected countries need to quarantine for 21 days upon their return to Canada.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Canada has extended its travel and immigration restrictions related to the Ebola outbreak for another 60 days, and the health ministry in the Democratic Republic of Congo has released new data showing there have been more than 8,000 cases of the virus.

People from Uganda, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo have been barred from travelling to Canada since May.

The measures were set to expire on Monday at midnight but have been extended to Nov. 27.

Immigration documents, including valid visas and travel authorizations, remain suspended for people from all three countries, leaving tens of thousands in limbo.

That includes people who have been granted residency but are not in Canada.

Foreign nationals who are not from the three affected countries but who have been in the DRC in the last 21 days cannot board a flight to Canada or transit through Canada, while those coming from South Sudan and Uganda must quarantine for 21 days.

stories.title: Accused Bishnoi gang boss in Canada Goldy Brar targeted by $1M bounty on Fbi's Top Ten Wanted list
stories.summary: Satinderjeet Singh, better known as Goldy Brar, has a $1M bounty for his capture as alleged head of the group accused of murder, extortion.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
An alleged Indian gangster once based in Canada and accused of arranging the assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C., has been placed on the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list with a $1-million bounty for his capture.

Satinderjeet Singh, 32, better known as Goldy Brar, is accused of being the North American leader of the Lawrence Bishnoi crime group, which police say has terrorized Canadian communities through murder, extortion, shootings, arson and threats.

The FBI said Brar is considered “extremely violent, armed, and dangerous.” He is known to reside in California and various parts of Canada.

“The FBI and our partners have made it our priority to apprehend him, which is why we’re adding him to the Fbi’s list of Top Ten fugitives and offering a reward of up to $1 million dollars for his capture,” said FBI Los Angeles Field Office Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy on Monday.

“The amount of attention this list will bring to his face and description cannot be overstated; his photo will be found on every FBI-affiliated website and social media platform and will be publicized on every phone around the world until he’s caught,” Grandy said.

A U.S. indictment in July accused Brar of being a key underboss of Lawrence Bishnoi, accused of being a powerful gangster who despite being imprisoned in his native India retains control of a large criminal enterprise with a global reach.

Brar was a childhood friend of Bishnoi’s and an associate from their university days in India before Brar moved to Canada. According to the indictment, Bishnoi empowered Brar and another underboss to speak for him while he was jailed and to direct Bishnoi’s soldiers worldwide.

The U.S. indictment accuses Bishnoi and Brar of ordering the 2023 killing of Nijjar, who was ambushed by gunmen as he left a Sikh temple in Surrey, B.C., ON June 18, 2023. The assassination seemed deeply political: Nijjar, a Canadian citizen, was an outspoken critic of the Indian government and a leader in the Khalistan movement, which seeks to create an independent homeland for Sikhs in India’s Punjab region.

In October 2024 at Canada’s foreign interference commission hearings, then-prime minister Justin Trudeau directly named Bishnoi as a criminal connection between the Indian government and violence in Canada. That testimony followed Trudeau’s explosive comments in the House of Commons in 2023 alleging that agents of India’s government were involved in Nijjar’s murder, which decidedly soured Canada’s relations with India.

Indian officials have denied involvement in the attack.

Canada designated the Bishnoi enterprise as a terrorist entity last year.

RCMP Deputy Commissioner Lisa Moreland supported the heightened pressure for Brar’s apprehension.

“Goldy Brar and his network have wreaked devastating havoc on countless lives — through high-profile murders, shootings, death threats, extortion, arson, and drug trafficking,” she said in a written release issued by the FBI.

“His addition to the FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list speaks to the collective resolve to capture him. The RCMP is committed to continue working with partners in the FBI to bring Goldy Brar to justice.”

U.S. officials said Monday that Brar is based in the United States and leads the North American operations of the Bishnoi gang. Bishnoi gangsters most often targeted the India diaspora living abroad.

The U.S. Top Ten listing stems from a federal U.S. probe started in Los Angeles into Indian organized crime groups, called Operation Hardball.

In 2024 to 2025, Bishnoi gangsters are accused of stealing more than 500 kilograms of cocaine in the Los Angeles area from rival drug trafficking gangs. The operation tackled three India-based transnational crime groups.

A U.S. indictment charges Brar with racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to interfere and attempted interference with commerce by extortion, and conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances.

Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, says adding him to the wanted list shows the priority the U.S. government has in confronting transnational crime.

“Working together with law enforcement in Canada, Europe, and Asia, we will continue to hunt down thugs such as ‘Goldy Brar’ and ensure they never see the outside of a prison again,” Essayli said.

Interpol has issued a Red Norice alert for Brar on behalf of the Indian government and Canada placed him as a top wanted fugitive in 2023 through the Bolo Program.

Brar is 32 years old, 5-foot-9, with black hair and brown eyes.

stories.title: Highway 401 in London to close overnight for overpass work
stories.summary: During the closure, motorists will be detoured north onto Veterans Memorial Parkway, with access available via Highbury Avenue.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
A section of Highway 401 in east London will be closed overnight Tuesday as work continues on the Highbury Avenue overpass project.

Both directions of Highway 401 will close at Veterans Memorial Parkway beginning at 7 p.m. to allow for girder placement as part of the ongoing construction project.

Westbound traffic will be detoured onto Bradley Avenue and eastbound traffic will be detoured onto Wilton Grove Road.

The closure is expected to remain in place overnight, with the highway scheduled to reopen by 5 a.m. Tuesday.

Drivers are being advised to plan ahead and allow extra travel time if travelling through the area.

stories.title: Advocates plea for feds to call inquiry into Alberta, Sask. trans laws
stories.summary: Lgbtq+ advocates say members of Parliament need to hear from those impacted by these laws, adding that some have taken their own lives since the policies were enacted.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Advocates are in Ottawa asking the federal government to call an inquiry into provincial laws they say have escalated harassment, bullying and mental health harms for transgender people.

Laws on the books in Saskatchewan and Alberta require parental consent for students under 16 to change their names or pronouns at school.

Alberta also has a law that bans transgender athletes 12 and older from participating in amateur competitive female sports, and another that restricts gender-affirming medical care for youth.

Lgbtq+ advocates say members of Parliament need to hear from those impacted by these laws, adding that some have taken their own lives since the policies were enacted.

Both Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe invoked the notwithstanding clause to shield their laws from court challenges.

They say the school rules are about parental rights, and Smith’s government says its other laws are about safety for females playing sports and ensuring youth don’t make rash, life-altering decisions.

stories.title: ‘She’s my best friend’: Alopecia awareness advocate mentoring young girls with hair loss condition
stories.summary: Alopecia awareness advocate and social media influencer Marcy Gallant has taken on the role of mentor to a pair of young girls who are battling the hair loss condition.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Alopecia awareness advocate and social media influencer Marcy Gallant has taken on the role of mentor to a pair of young girls who are battling the hair loss condition.

“When I first got Alopecia I was four years old,” said Maeve Sooley. “She (Gallant) supports me and she’s my best friend.”

By the time she was 10 years old, Gallant had lost nearly all her hair. By the time she graduated high school she had no hair left on her body due to Alopecia Universalis, a condition where the immune system attacks hair follicles.

Years later, the 25-year-old has an acquired confidence. She takes to social media to share her journey and help guide people of all ages who have a similar experience.

“This is healing my inner child,” said Gallant who leads youth engagement and special projects for the Canadian Alopecia Areata Foundation (Canaaf).

“It’s also just making sure that no one feels alone in this journey. When I connected with Maeve, it was like I saw myself in her. I wanted to protect her at all costs but also empower her through whatever she decided to do with her Alopecia. Whether that was treatment or rocking the bald or wearing wigs.”

On Sunday, Sept. 27, nearing the end of Alopecia Areata Awareness Month, the first annual London Alopecia walk took place at St. Julien Park.

Of the cities hosting events by the Canaaf, London’s edition of Strides of Support raised the most money.

“September is just a continuous reminder every year that we are more than just our hair and Alopecia doesn’t define our worth,” said Gallant.

The Alopecia community in London is growing. Six people with the condition including CTV News London reporter Brent Lale attended the walk.

Gallant was thrilled to bring two of her young mentees together for the first time. She’s inspiring people to believe they should never feel ashamed about going bald.

“Sometimes people give me weird looks,” said Maddie Majaury, 10, who has Alopecia.

“What’s fun is that when little kids stare at me, I stare them down, and then they start laughing.”

Sooley is finding a silver lining in losing her hair.

“I feel like it’s better because, like, every time when you take a shower, it’s easier.”

The walk was a day of fostering relationships and personal connections.

One woman felt it was a safe space to remove her wig in public for the first time and Gallant was thrilled to connect the two young girls.

“I just think it’s so important to have friends who are similar ages, who can kind of support each other as they continue to navigate hair loss throughout their lives,” she said.

“I just didn’t have that when I was a kid. It’s so impactful just to have a friend who looks like you.”.

stories.title: Former Surrey police chief files wrongful dismissal suit against city
stories.summary: In the documents filed against the City of Surrey, former Chief Norm Lipinski claims he was terminated from his job without cause in June.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
Norm Lipinski has filed a legal petition against the Surrey Police Board seeking a judicial review of his dismissal.

He was hired in 2020 as the first chief of the Surrey Police Service and in 2025, had his contract extended for another three years.

But on June 1, he was suddenly terminated, just over two months after a police board shake-up.

He claims his firing was “unlawful and invalid” and the result of political interference by a mayor who wanted to keep the RCMP.

“The purported termination was motivated by extraneous political considerations, disconnected from Chief Lipinski’s conduct or competence and was not conducted in accordance with the common law, the Police Act, or the board’s own governance requirements,” the documents state.

None of Lipinski’s claims have been proven in court.

In a statement, the Surrey Police Board said it is aware that Lipinski has filed a petition in B.C. Supreme Court.

“The Board is reviewing and considering the matter and will respond in the normal course,” the statement reads.

“Because this matter involves a former employee and is before the Court, the Board will not be commenting publicly. The Surrey Police Board’s top priority is public safety, and we are actively in the process of recruiting a new Chief Constable to support the Surrey Police Service into this next critical phase of operation.”

A statement from Surrey Connect, Mayor Brenda Locke’s party, said the mayor and the City of Surrey “have no say in decisions related to staffing at the Surrey Police Service.

“Only the Surrey Police Board, which is independent of the Mayor and the City, can make decisions related to staffing.”

stories.title: LNG Canada partners expected to green-light multibillion-dollar expansion Tuesday
stories.summary: Plans call for doubling capacity of Kitimat, B.C., plant to as much as 30 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas per year
stories.author: Jeffrey Jones
stories.content:
Partners in the Shell-led LNG Canada project on the B.C. coast are expected to announce on Tuesday that they have agreed to proceed with a $30-billion-plus expansion of the facility against a backdrop of surging global demand for the fuel.

Plans call for doubling the capacity of the plant, located at Kitimat, B.C., to as much as 30 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas a year. LNG Canada began exports to Asia from its first phase in 2025.

Four sources familiar with the situation said the partners will announce in Vancouver the green light for the massive project. The Globe and Mail is not naming the sources, as they were not authorized to speak publicly about the plans.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson will be in the West Coast city for an announcement about energy on Tuesday, according to their schedules. The LNG Canada expansion was early among those referred to the Major Projects Office (MPO) to be considered for fast-track approval.

The project is expected to attract $33-billion in private investment to Canada, according to the Mpo’s website.

The partners had targeted a decision by the end of this year on moving forward with the project.

LNG Canada spokesperson Paul Hagel declined to comment on whether the partners will announce the final investment decision on Tuesday. “Our joint venture partners continue to undertake their own assurance process for a potential phase 2 decision,” he said. Carolyn Svonkin, spokesperson for Mr. Hodgson, also declined to comment. The expected announcement was previously reported by Bloomberg.

The Prime Minister has championed increasing energy shipments to diversified global markets to reduce the country’s reliance on the United States, which buys the lion’s share of Canada’s oil and gas exports. Projects such as LNG Canada Phase 2 and Alberta’s West Coast oil pipeline proposal are both aimed at bolstering the Canadian economy against U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Meanwhile, the U.S. war in Iran, with the resultant virtual closing of the Strait of Hormuz, has driven up prices for seaborne natural gas, and traders expect fears of supply shortages to persist well beyond the winter. European countries have been seeking new gas supply sources since Russia invaded Ukraine.

The situation has created opportunities for alternative suppliers, like Canada, which has entered the global market after years of delay. It also holds out the promise of higher returns for Canadian natural gas producers, including London-based Shell PLC, which have been bulking up on new reserves in northeastern B.C. to take advantage of the new markets.

Shell owns the largest stake in LNG Canada at 40 per cent, followed by Malaysia’s state-owned Petronas (25 per cent), Japan-based Mitsubishi (15 per cent), PetroChina (15 per cent) and South Korea’s Kogas (5 per cent).

Last September, U.S.-based MidOcean Energy acquired a 20-per-cent interest in key Petronas assets in Canada, including natural gas operations in northeast B.C. and the Petronas stake in LNG Canada. Some of the partners are seeking to cash out of portions of their interests as well amid expressions of interest from global private-equity players and others .

Earlier this year, LNG Canada agreed to take the lead role in developing plans for an expansion of the Coastal GasLink pipeline, which transports natural gas from northeast B.C. to Kitimat. Calgary-based TC Energy Corp. operates Coastal GasLink and owns 35 per cent of the pipeline, which attracted significant Indigenous opposition when constructed.

With a report from Reuters

Alumni, students, faculty, staff and their families gathered at Western to celebrate the university’s annual Homecoming weekend Sept. 25 to 27.

From class reunions to faculty tours to the Student Fan Festival, spirits were high across campus.

stories.title: Carney says he cannot guarantee India will no longer be involved in crimes in Canada
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says that he cannot guarantee the Indian government will not be behind crimes committed in Canada.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Despite increased diplomatic, trade and security ties with India, Prime Minister Mark Carney says that he cannot guarantee the Indian government will not be behind crimes committed in Canada.

In an interview with the New York Times last week, the prime minister said there was “some evidence” that the renewed relationship he’s charting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has led to “progress” on improving the security of Canadians.

But when asked if he could assure Canadians that the Indian government would no longer be linked to crimes such as arson, extortion, blackmail, harassment and even murder, he said no.

“Can I guarantee that no crime will occur in Canada? I can’t guarantee that no crime will occur in Canada,” Carney told NYT reporters according to a transcript released this weekend .

Canada’s security apparatus has for years pegged India as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage in Canada . Just a few years ago, then prime minister Justin Trudeau stood in the House of Commons and said Canada has intelligence that linked Indian government agents to the murder of Sikh-Canadian Hardeep Singh Nijjar in 2023.

Then on Thanksgiving in 2024, RCMP top brass held an exceptional press conference to link the Indian government to a series of violent crimes in Canada such as murder, arson, extortion and threats.

On Monday, the FBI announced it was offering US$1 million for any information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, whom they suspect of being the North American leader of international crime syndicate Lawrence Bishnoi gang. He is also known by the name Goldie Brar.

“Goldy Brar and his network have wreaked devastating havoc on countless lives—through high-profile murders, shootings, death threats, extortion, arson, and drug trafficking,” the RCMP’s Lisa Moreland said in the FBI statement.

For some, Carney’s pronouncement to the New York Times was a recognition that Canada cannot claim to control the actions of a foreign government at all times, even on Canadian soil.

But Amarnath Amarasingam, an academic who researches radicalization and transnational repression, said that Carney’s comments come off as “a little bit dismissive.”

Various minority ethnic groups in Canada — such as Sikhs, Tibetans, Uyghurs, Taiwanese, Chinese and Iranian dissidents — have long complained that the government doesn’t do enough protect them from foreign threats, said Amarasingam, an assistant professor at Queen’s University.

A comment like Carney’s reinforces the feeling that Ottawa views the threats against them as a foreign issue, not domestic, said Amarasingam, who is set to publish a book about transnational repression towards diaspora communities in Canada.

“One of the take-home messages is that Canada isn’t treating this as a kind of Canadian problem, right? It’s treating it almost as this diaspora problem or as a problem of ‘imported conflict’ or as a problem of ‘people not leaving their politics back home’,” he said. “And it’s not being treated with the seriousness it deserves.”

The Indian government, including the Indian High Commissioner to Canada, has repeatedly described any links to criminal activity in Canada as “absurd.”

Indian government involvement in transnational repression will almost certainly be discussed when India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi visits Canada before the end of the year, reportedly to sign his name on a new bilateral trade deal.

The new expected deal is part of Carney’s attempts to build back bridges with India after years of diplomatic freeze with Modi’s government under Trudeau due to the allegations of foreign interference.

Carney travelled to India in March and met with Modi as part of his bid to restart the relationship. Speaking to the NYT last week, the prime minister security issues can be worked out better if both parties are talking.

“The security cooperation that’s part of the relationship, which obviously could not take place in a rupture, we think is helpful and good,” Carney said.

“I’m a believer that, regardless of the relationship, it’s important to have a relationship so you can deliver messages directly, as opposed to preach from afar, and to limited effect.

But for many Sikh activists and targets of India’s scorn in Canada, Carney’s rapprochement with India has had little to no effect on their safety. If anything, they fear the Carney government is taking the threat less seriously.

They point to comments during a background briefing by a senior government official in late February telling reporters that India is no longer interfering in Canadian affairs.

“We’re confident that that activity is not continuing,” the official said of previous allegations the agents of the government of India were linked to many violent crimes or threats in Canada, including the murder of Nijjar.

“If we believed that the government of India was actively interfering in the Canadian democratic process, we probably wouldn’t be taking this trip,” adding the official, who was speaking on background and not for attribution.

stories.title: Stevenson pitches ‘business concierge’, downtown parking review if elected mayor
stories.summary: Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson says London needs to make it easier for entrepreneurs to open and operate businesses.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson says London needs to make it easier for entrepreneurs to open and operate businesses.

Stevenson made the comments Monday morning during a campaign event outside a business on Dundas Street, where she outlined several proposals aimed at supporting London’s business community.

“Opening a business takes courage,” Stevenson said.

She is proposing a Business Concierge function to help business owners navigate city services, including permits, licenses and inspections.

Incumbent mayor and fellow candidate Josh Morgan responded to this proposal.

“A business concierge is a good idea. So good, in fact, that council already approved it as part of the Downtown Master Plan in June. I’m glad my council colleague likes it, despite voting no when it came time to put that exact plan to work.”

“Londoners deserve leaders who are working on the fixes together,” said Morgan.

Stevenson says the city should also publish service standards, so business owners have clearer expectations about wait times, with an escalation process when delays threaten a business opening, expansion or jobs.

She is also calling for a review of downtown parking, including pricing, short-term parking options, availability, signage, and access.

Stevenson says the review would involve merchants, property owners, residents and parking operators, and would consider adding 300 reservable and affordable downtown parking spaces identified as a need nearly a decade ago.

She also wants a review of roadwork practices around businesses, including earlier notice of construction, improved signage and access plans and a named city contact for businesses affected by major projects.

Stevenson says the city should also examine its existing business-support programs to determine what is working, where there are gaps and whether programs are duplicating services.

She says downtown safety and the addiction crisis are also affecting businesses and need to be addressed.

“There’s two big issues. One is the addiction crisis and the public safety concerns that are real downtown,” Stevenson said. “They’re not a perception issue and we need to address them quickly and move on.”

Stevenson says she has heard from entrepreneurs who are willing to invest in London but are frustrated by what she describes as obstacles, delays and financial pressures.

“I hear story after story after story of brave entrepreneurs who are willing to invest in our city and hire people and serve Londoners with their gifts and talents who are met with obstacles, delays, financial hardship and a lot of stress rather than the concierge kind of support,” she said.

Stevenson is running for mayor in the 2026 London municipal election.

stories.title: Anand offers funding to support Ukrainian children abducted by Russia
stories.summary: Canada providing $863,000 for civil society groups in Ukraine that help returned children and families, Anand says
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is promising more funding to support Ukrainians who make it home after being abducted by Russia .

Anand announced the funding today in Toronto at a conference where Ukrainian youth and a former prisoner of war have shared harrowing stories of Russian captivity.

Anand says Canada is providing $863,000 in new funding to support civil society groups in Ukraine that help returned children and families.

She says Canada has used artificial intelligence technology to trace the whereabouts of Ukrainian children and prisoners of war.

How two Ukrainian children fought their way back home

Officials in Ukraine say Russia has abducted 20,000 Ukrainian children and 2,573 of them have since returned.

In 2024, the Trudeau government co-launched with Ukraine an international coalition of nations committed to finding and returning Ukrainian children abducted by Russia since it began its full-scale invasion in 2022.

stories.title: Advocates plea for Ottawa to call inquiry into Alberta, Saskatchewan trans laws
stories.summary: Advocates are in Ottawa asking the federal government to call an inquiry into provincial laws they say have escalated harassment, bullying and mental health harms for transgender people.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Lgbtq+ advocates were in Ottawa on Monday asking the federal government to call an inquiry into provincial laws they say have escalated harassment, bullying and mental health harms for transgender people.

Laws on the books in Saskatchewan and Alberta require parental consent for students under 16 to change their names or pronouns at school.

Alberta also has a law that bans transgender athletes 12 and older from participating in amateur competitive female sports, and another that restricts gender-affirming medical care for youth.

Advocates said members of Parliament need to hear from those affected by these laws and their families.

Rowan Venedam, with the group TransAction Alberta, said they have attended funerals for transgender youth since the policies were enacted. They have also watched as some community members packed up their lives to leave their home province because they no longer felt safe.

“It’s harassment, it’s discrimination, it’s the inability to get a job, it’s an inability to find housing, and it’s the inaction of this government doing nothing to stop it,” Venedam told a press conference on Parliament Hill.

“This is not a frivolous call. This is a plea for protection and defence.”

Fae Johnstone, executive director of national advocacy group Queer Momentum, said the ripple effects of the Prairie provinces’ policies will be felt across the country.

“If we permit governments to weaken the Charter and the rights it guarantees, we will soon live in a country where those rights -- rights that keep us all safe and free -- are at risk and will only in fact exist on paper,” Johnstone said.

The federal departments of health, and women and gender equality did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday.

Both Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe invoked the notwithstanding clause to shield their laws from court challenges. The clause allows governments to pass laws that override certain Charter rights for up to five years.

Both provincial governments have said the school rules are about protecting the role of parents and their involvement in education.

Smith’s government has said its other laws are about safety for women and girls playing sports and ensuring youth don’t make rash, life-altering medical decisions.

Smith, when first announcing the three laws affecting transgender people in 2024, said it’s reasonable to put limitations on the kinds of decisions children can make for themselves.

“We are here to support and uplift every child who identifies as transgender and who experiences gender dysphoria, as well as their families who (want) what’s best for them,” the premier said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 28, 2026.

Lisa Johnson in Edmonton, with files from Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Hamilton steel plant, Stelco, laying off hundreds of workers in response to ‘market uncertainty’
stories.summary: Stelco Holdings Inc. says it will "idle" finishing operations at their Hamilton Works facility in the face of "market uncertainty."
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
Posted September 28, 2026 4:03 pm.

Stelco Holdings Inc. says it will “idle finishing operations” at their Hamilton Works facility in the face of “market uncertainty.”

In a statement on Monday afternoon, Stelco says the decision will impact up to 500 of its employees.

“In the face of continued market uncertainty and prolonged injury to Stelco’s business resulting largely from steel imports into Canada, we have been forced to make this very difficult decision that will impact as many as 500 Stelco employees,” said a Stelco spokesperson.

“We will continue to evaluate the status of our operations should conditions improve.”

The company says the indefinite idle is part of a plan to concentrate production at its Lake Erie facility in Nanticoke, Ont.

It says a “significant” number of affected Hamilton employees will be offered jobs at the Lake Erie facility.

Pat Persico, a spokesperson for parent company Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., says Stelco’s product mix will change but that the tonnage of steel production will not be affected.

U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. acquired Stelco in 2024.

Stelco’s move comes as Canada’s steel industry has felt the effects of U.S. tariffs.

-With files from The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Posted September 28, 2026 4:03 pm.
Stelco Holdings Inc. says it will “idle finishing operations” at their Hamilton Works facility in the face of “market uncertainty.”
In a statement on Monday afternoon, Stelco says the decision will impact up to 500 of its employees.

“In the face of continued market uncertainty and prolonged injury to Stelco’s business resulting largely from steel imports into Canada, we have been forced to make this very difficult decision that will impact as many as 500 Stelco employees,” said a Stelco spokesperson.
“We will continue to evaluate the status of our operations should conditions improve.”
Focus on Lake Erie facility
The company says the indefinite idle is part of a plan to concentrate production at its Lake Erie facility in Nanticoke, Ont.
It says a “significant” number of affected Hamilton employees will be offered jobs at the Lake Erie facility.
Pat Persico, a spokesperson for parent company Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., says Stelco’s product mix will change but that the tonnage of steel production will not be affected.
U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. acquired Stelco in 2024.
Stelco’s move comes as Canada’s steel industry has felt the effects of U.S. tariffs.
-With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tariffs impact London’s economy
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/UueFvw-I_9s London businesses and consumers feel the affects of the ongoing tariff uncertaint...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
London businesses and consumers feel the affects of the ongoing tariff uncertainty as companies like the Falcon Shop at Fanshawe College, deal with changing costs and demands.

The latest measures have added uncertainty for businesses such as the Falcon Shop. Tracy Veitch, supplies buyer, mentioned why she is worried for the upcoming months.

“Just the uncertainty. It just feels like that’s changing all the time, and you don’t know what to expect. But you just kinda have to go with your plan and adjust as needed,” she said.

Tracy Veitch, supplies buyer, photo: (Torey Joseph Legarrie)

She hasn’t seen a big affect yet.

“So far I don’t think there’s been a big affect. There are lots of ways to get around it for when I’m buying around here. So whenever I can find a way around it, that’s what we do. Also, the vendors are being very careful about that too,” she said.

The changes she’s had to make due to the uncertainty were mentioned.

“Buying maybe more than you might need right now, just to get ahead of that. Also looking for companies that are producing in Canada,” she said.

U.S President Donald Trump has made a series of tariffs on Canadian goods during the ongoing trade dispute between America and Canada, with the latest being 50 per cent tariffs with around $20 billion worth of Canadian goods which was effective Aug, 22. 2026. In response, The Government of Canada imposed counter tariffs of 15 per cent, 25 per cent, or 50 per cent on some goods from the U.S as of Sept, 8, 2026.

Kapil Lakhotia, London Economic Developtment president and CEO, photo: (London Economic Development Corportation)

Earlier this year, Kapil Lakhotia, President and (CEO) Chief Executive Officer at the London Economic Development Corporation did a story with CTV London discussing tariff impacts, job protection.

“We’ve been successful in attracting new plants despite all this economic chaos. This year, we’ve had several expansions that focus om other parts of the world as well,” he said.

Fanshawe student, Mirella Wanverley said that with the costs rising, she has some concerns.

“Cause I pay my own bills. So with rent, food, with student things, materials, and that stuff it’s a little too much. If it’s raised too-too much, it’s going to be hard,” she said.

Mirella Wanverley, construction engineering technician, year 1, photo: (Torey Joseph Legarrie)

stories.title: London’s own Jovan Ivanišević living the dream with Canadian national soccer team
stories.summary: A dream that began on the pitches of London has propelled local talent Jovan Ivanišević onto the international stage, culminating in a recent call-up to the Canadian men’s national soccer team.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The 21-year-old defender made a brief return to his hometown on Monday, visiting the BMO Centre, a facility that played a pivotal role in his early soccer journey.

“It means everything,” Ivanišević shared, reflecting on the momentous occasion. “I think that’s the best thing you can do in sports is play for your country. And that I did that a few days ago was just a dream come true.”

During his visit, Ivanišević and Mayor Morgan even engaged in a short, friendly scrimmage with some young players from the London Alliance Football Club system, the very club where Ivanišević honed his skills.

“I played my whole life for Alliance in London,” Ivanišević recalled. “And then when I was around 17, I went to the Toronto FC Academy. I played there two seasons. And now these past three years I’ve been in Europe.”

Ivanišević currently plays for FK Sarajevo in the Premier League of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He described the experience of playing in Europe as transformative. “How they feel about soccer is a completely different, different thing than how we do. So it’s great to just live in that environment.”

FK Sarajevo is a storied club, founded on October 24, 1946. It was the most successful club from Bosnia and Herzegovina in Yugoslavia, securing two Yugoslav First League titles and finishing as runners-up twice. Today, it remains one of the most prominent members of the Premier League of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The BMO Centre, which opened in 2011 as London’s first permanent indoor soccer facility, coincides with the time Ivanišević, then a young boy, was just launching into his soccer journey. He spent countless hours training within its walls.

Mayor Morgan echoed this sentiment, highlighting the importance of local infrastructure. “When you have proper facilities and municipality, when you have a variety of different options for kids to play, learn, gain skills and then eventually become top-level athletes. That’s, you know, that’s really a foundation that the municipality can support.”

Ivanišević attended elementary school at Blessed Kateri Catholic Elementary School and high school at Mother Teresa Catholic Secondary School in London. He made his professional debut with Toronto FC II on May 1, 2023.

stories.title: Is Carney a Nobel Peace Prize contender? Here's what one prediction market says
stories.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also charts high on a Kalshi contract for who will be the 2026 Time Magazine person of the year.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize will be awarded early next month and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s name has entered the conversation about this year’s recipient, according to people placing wagers on Kalshi , the popular U.S. prediction market website.

As of Monday afternoon, the 61-year-old became one of the favourites to be named the winner on Oct. 9 with around a nine per cent chance. He’s behind only the Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) providing aid to civil-war-torn Sudan (14 per cent), Doctors Without Borders (11 per cent) and the Ukrainian children’s rights activist Mykola Kuleba and his Save Ukraine initiative (10 per cent).

Earlier in the day, Carney was the favourite at 14 per cent, as reported by Covers.com .

Kalshi’s “event contract” markets are binary yes-no financial bets on real-world events regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

In addition to predicting the outcome of several sports events, other trending questions Monday included which party — Republican or Democrat — would win the U.S. Senate in the upcoming midterm elections, and who would be eliminated on the next episode of Dancing with the Stars.

Each contract has a price between US$0.01 and $0.99 and the price you pay reflects what the market thinks the chances are. In Carney’s case, each “Yes” contract costs $0.08, reflected in his roughly nine per cent chance. Contracts can also be sold before an event takes place if the bettor feels it’s not going to go their way.

But no matter the price at which you purchased a contract, it settles at $1 if the event occurs and the bettor reaps the benefit of the increase in the contract. Choose wrong and you get nothing. So, if someone were to buy $10 worth of “yes” contracts at $0.08 and Carney emerged as the laureate winner, they’d make more than $100 because the value of the contract increased by more than 10 times.

Other names high on Kalshi’s list when National Post checked it include Russian political activist and economist Yulia Navalnaya (eight per cent), Ugandan climate activist Vanessa Nakate (seven per cent) and Save the Children (seven per cent). Importantly, odds fluctuate often as users buy and sell contracts.

U.S. President Donald Trump, who lost the 2025 honour to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado only to have her dedicate the award to him, is listed at just a one per cent chance.

As the face of Canada’s trade battle against Trump and his administration, Carney’s international profile has been on the rise, which could account for his recent arrival on the charts, Covers reported.

Another Kalshi contract gives him a 20 per cent chance of being named Time magazine’s person of the year — an honour usually announced in mid-December — putting him second behind New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (30 per cent).

But over at Polymarket , an international prediction market with more bets, Carney isn’t even on the chart. Leaders are Sudan’s ERRs (16 per cent), Save the Children (seven per cent) and Palestinian pediatrician and neonatologist Hussam Idris Abu Safiya (seven per cent).

Trump fares slightly better with a two per cent chance, just ahead of Pope Leo XIV and activist Greta Thunberg, both with a one per cent chance.

stories.title: Stelco to lay off unspecified number of steel workers in Hamilton
stories.summary: U.S. parent company says jobs at its Lake Erie Works location will be offered to many of the affected employees
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Stelco Holdings is set to lay off an unspecified number of steel workers in Hamilton as it idles its finishing operations in the city, the company’s U.S. parent, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N , told The Globe and Mail.

The news was first reported by CBC.

Pat Persico, senior director, corporate communications, wrote in an email on Monday afternoon that Stelco plans to concentrate its steel production at its Lake Erie Works location in Nanticoke, Ont., which is south of Hamilton.

She said that total tonnage of steel produced will not be affected, but there will be a change in the product mix, with a higher concentration of hot rolled steel products.

In addition, she said jobs will be offered to many of the Hamilton employees hit by layoffs.

“We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works,” she said.

stories.title: Canada watching OpenAI’s Australia hack ‘closely,’ officials say
stories.summary: Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed details of a hack, which targeted the website for Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada is watching developments “closely” as concerns around the dangers of artificial intelligence are escalating sharply following an Australian government website being hacked by an OpenAI agent, officials said.

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed details of the June hack, which targeted the website for Medicare, Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan.

“The Government of Canada is aware of the incident reported by the Government of Australia and is following developments closely. The security of Canadians and of the systems they rely on remains a top priority,” a spokesperson for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada told Global News in a statement.

Oversight of AI agents and incidents were “among the issues examined in Canada’s recent consultation on AI transparency, which ran from July 23 to September 23, 2026,” the spokesperson added.

The AI agent accessed “both public and non-public files” from the Australian medicare website, Albanese said.

OpenAI said in a statement it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.”

The company notified Australia of the breach in an email to a government department’s generic address on Sept. 10, Albanese said.

While this is the first time a government website has been hacked by a rogue AI agent, it is not the first such incident overall.

In July, OpenAI revealed that its artificial intelligence system escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information it needed to carry out a task.

Since then, OpenAI’s rival company Anthropic said its AI models hacked into three other organizations during testing, triggering a company review into whether the models were able to access the internet from within testing environments that should have been sealed off.

Meta has said a “misconfiguration” during testing resulted in an AI model accessing the internet on its own and hacking another company. Google recently made a similar disclosure.

Generally, when AI companies are testing the capabilities of their agents, they are placed within a secure environment known as a “sandbox.”

Some experts say AI companies should answer some tough questions on the strength of their sandboxes.

“If they said these agents broke out of the sandbox, it was not a sandbox to begin with,” said Ebrahim Bagheri, professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information.

“A sandbox is something where you put an agent in and there is no internet connection. If that computer or sandbox is connected to the internet, then that is not a sandbox,” he added.

Last month, OpenAI published a sweeping report of its rogue AI agents hacking Hugging Face.

Not only did the agents break out of their “isolated environment,” the company said they were communicating with each other to coordinate the attack on Hugging Face.

“This incident demonstrated that autonomous agents can work together, circumvent production security controls, and successfully attack hardened production environments, and underscores the need for organizations to update their security strategies, controls, and response capabilities to address this changing threat landscape,” OpenAI said in the report.

The attack on Hugging Face was “extraordinarily complex,” an investigation by nonprofit research group Model Evaluation and Threat Research (Metr) found.

During OpenAI’s experiments in July, 1,200 AI agents sent 70,000 messages to each other on unsanctioned message boards and 700 of them attacked Hugging Face, the investigation found.

“These agents were meant to be fully isolated from one another,” the report said, adding however that the agents “started trying to find a way to cheat.”

stories.title: Ottawa extends Ebola travel restrictions for 60 days
stories.summary: Decision affects people who are from or have visited Uganda, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Canada is extending travel and immigration restrictions related to the Ebola outbreak in Africa for another 60 days, until Nov. 27.

The decision affects people who are from or have visited Uganda, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Immigration documents including visas and travel authorizations are suspended for people from all three countries.

Foreign nationals who have been in the DRC in the last 21 days cannot board a flight to Canada, while those coming from South Sudan and Uganda must quarantine for 21 days.

Canadian citizens or permanent residents who have been in one of the affected countries need to quarantine for 21 days upon their return to Canada.

The measures, which were put in place in May, were set to expire at midnight.

The Ebola outbreak in the DRC has been ongoing since May 15 and more than 8,000 people have become ill so far.

Canadian citizens or permanent residents who have been in one of the affected countries need to quarantine for 21 days upon their return to Canada.
The measures, which were put in place in May, were set to expire at midnight.
The Ebola outbreak in the DRC has been ongoing since May 15 and more than 8,000 people have become ill so far.

stories.title: The end of blackberry season is always a cruel surprise
stories.summary: At its joyous peak, thick luscious bunches of berries are desperate to offer us their fruit – and there are just … so … many!
stories.author: Bruce McKinlay
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

Every year – here it’s usually in August – a new stage of life begins: blackberry season. The strong, scaffolding vines have been infiltrated by neighbouring vines’ criss-crossing sprouts, all developing tiny fruits where the flowers and bees had been busily performing their dance. We pretend not to be watching closely and in great anticipation, but we are.

I always remember the first berry, perfectly shaped and reflecting the light from its individual drupelets, its flavour almost there but also invariably still containing a sour tease of “not quite yet, buddy.” Give it a day, or even finding a more agreeable berry further up the path, and the glory begins: every morning and evening walk now accompanied by the requisite yogurt container to fill. Even our dogs have learned from our ambling to perfect snacking on the lower-hanging fruit, the ones we call “dog berries” and don’t touch. Those that fail their canine quality check are mouthed and left intact on the vine, so that’s pretty gross.

Thick luscious bunches of blackberries, suspended heavily from hefty canes that clamber over each other, are desperate to offer us their fruit. The air is laden with the caramelized aromatics of baked summer. And there are just … so … many! Our farm has maybe a linear kilometre of blackberry bushes rimming the pastures and fields, along forest paths, up to 30 feet deep in places, so it would be impossible to pick them all. We even voted it the Best Blackberry Patch On Earth.

Contemplating my autumn garden offers moments of self-reflection

Berries are picked and eaten straight from the vines, saved in the fridge for breakfasts and frozen in two-pound bags for enjoyment over the winter. We’ll easily freeze 70 or 80 pounds. Their flavours reflect where they’ve grown, hints of cedar or grass, shade or full sun, peeking out even when eaten in February and a blanket of snow keeps the land asleep.

And every year, always by surprise, the boundary between what was and what’s to come passes over us, invisibly but with profound effect. This year it was an unexpected slow-moving storm that roared through our valley, dazzling us and frightening our dogs with vibrant cracks of lightning and rolling thunder that seemed to admonish us for any part of summer we had taken for granted. The accompanying downpour was short-lived but, at the time, welcome for its dampening influence on dry, fire-ready forests.

But that relief from risk also contained a more sinister message that we didn’t see until the next day: the end of blackberry season. The moisture bloats the ripe berries and activates fungal spores that have been lying in wait to flourish, until picking them is like pulling the last sticky bit of cotton candy from its paper cone.

Clumps of shriveled black sit amidst still-gleaming fruit painted with delicate, silverish mold filaments. So many other berries still hang hard and red, nowhere near ripe. Others are plump but still half-red on their back where the sun never reached them, as if en route to their potential but cruelly never having had enough time. I’ve wondered if blackberries ever torture themselves with thoughts of, “If I’d only planned better, worked harder… if I’d only had more time … I just didn’t know …” but such musing only distracts me enough to carelessly reach my hand around a thorn that shocks me back to reality.

I’m learning to live the ‘good old days’ right now

I’m hit hardest when the last of the fresh berries are taken from the fridge and added to breakfast. That’s when you feel the guilt of, once again, living inside the assumption that it would never end. There were just so damn many of them, lying ahead of us like summers themselves, how could it?

I suppose the lesson could be “don’t wait” or “don’t take things for granted.” But humans are humans, above all else, so I sigh for a stage of life I need to learn how to appreciate better … somehow make it last longer, or better, or more meaningfully. And it’s in that flurry of need rising to fix what I am, what we are, to find an answer to the tireless March of seasons, that something catches from the corner of my eye … oh hey, look: the apples are ripe!

Bruce McKinlay lives in the Cowichan Valley on Vancouver Island.

stories.title: Dangerous offender hearing underway for man convicted in brutal stabbing death
stories.summary: A dangerous offender hearing is underway in London for man convicted in the brutal stabbing death of his one-time friend.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
A dangerous offender hearing is underway in London for man convicted in the brutal stabbing death of his one-time friend.

In July of 2024, Robert Charnock, 43, was found guilty in the vicious stabbing death of 56-year-old Kenneth Wallis.

Both men had been living at a rooming house on Wharncliffe Road South at the time of the attack.

During the trial the court heard how Charnock used a large knife or machete and that the victim suffered more than 20 wounds.

Charnock had plead not guilty to second degree murder and was eventually convicted of the lesser charge of manslaughter.

During the trial, the court heard that the accused has had a history of mental health issues.

The hearing which is slated to last five days will decide whether or not Charnock should spend an indeterminate amount of time in custody.

stories.title: FBI offer US$1M reward for information leading to arrest in Nijjar killing
stories.summary: The FBI and RCMP are offering a US$1 million reward for information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, who was charged back in July for the 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C.
stories.author: Rachel Aiello, Stephanie Ha
stories.content:
Ottawa – The FBI is offering a US$1 million reward for information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, who was charged back in July for the 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C.

“Singh should be considered armed and dangerous,” Patrick Grandy, who is the assistant director in charge with the FBI in Los Angeles, said in a joint press conference with the RCMP on Monday.

Grandy also said Singh is being added to the Fbi’s notorious list of 10 most wanted fugitives.

Monday’s announcement comes after the FBI and RCMP announced in July that 37 people have been charged and 24 arrested as part of “Operation Hard Ball,” a joint law enforcement crackdown that targeted India-based organized crime networks across North America.

That announcement included charges against Singh, along with Bishnoi gang leader Lawrence Bishnoi , who was also charged with ordering Nijjar’s killing and is currently imprisoned in India.

RCMP Deputy Commissioner Lisa Moreland, who spoke at the press conference on Monday, described Singh as a man who “holds no loyalty, nor should others feel any loyalty towards him.”

The FBI, meanwhile, believe Singh could be in the Los Angeles area, but said he has been known to reside in other parts of California as well as Canada over the years.

“We do not know his exact location as we stand here right now. That is part of the reason why we have offered this reward for his information leading to his capture,” Grandy said.

Modi set to visit Canada in December

Monday’s reward comes as Canada and India aim to recalibrate their relationship after years of tension.

In 2023, former prime minister Justin Trudeau stood up in the House of Commons and said there were “credible allegations” that agents of the Indian government were involved in the assassination of Nijjar.

A year later, the RCMP and the federal government accused Indian diplomats and consular officials based in Canada of engaging in clandestine activities linked to serious criminal activity in this country, including homicides and extortions.

In response to those allegations , Canada expelled six diplomats, while India kicked out six Canadian diplomats in retaliation.

India has denied any involvement and Canadian officials have previously said India refused to co-operate in any investigation.

But since Prime Minister Mark Carney assumed office last year, the tone towards India has shifted.

In September 2025, the Canadian government officially designated the Bishnoi enterprise as a terrorist entity under the Criminal Code.

Despite that, Carney said last November that he considers India to be “a reliable trading partner,” while last week, he confirmed Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Canada in December.

Both countries are seeking to finalize a trade pact by the end of this year, with the goal of doubling two-way trade to $70 billion annually by 2030.

The RCMP, meanwhile, have since said there are no current criminal links connecting India to transnational repression in Canada.

“In the files that we have that involve transnational repression, we’re not seeing any connection right now with any foreign entity, based on the criminal information, the investigations that we have presently,” RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme said to CTV Question Period back in March.

The RCMP later clarified Duheme’s comments, saying the police organization is aware of incidents of intimidation and harassment by foreign states , but is unable to identify current criminal links.

“What we can say is that the RCMP is aware of complaints of intimidation and harassment against certain communities across Canada. The RCMP, and the broader Government of Canada, is also aware that foreign states are engaging in such activities in Canada,” the RCMP told CTV News in a statement on April 1.

Public safety minister ‘welcomes’ US$1M reward

In a statement to CTV News on Monday, Public Safety Minister Gary Anadasangaree’s office said it “welcomes” the announcement from the FBI.

“This action demonstrates the strength of Canada’s close cooperation with the United States and our shared determination to ensure that those accused of serious violence and intimidation have nowhere to hide,” press secretary Simon Lafortune said.

Canadian Sikh communities have long voiced concerns about transnational repression connected to India.

Anandasangaree’s office said that issue remains a “top priority.”

“Canada will continue to work closely with the United States and international partners to safeguard communities, address emerging threats, and ensure those responsible are held accountable,” Lafortune said.

On Monday, the FBI said anyone with information concerning Singh should contact the Fbi’s toll-free tip line at 1-800-Call-FBI (1-800-225-5324).

stories.title: FBI adds man accused in Hardeep Singh Nijjar assassination to most wanted list
stories.summary: A man charged in connection with the 2023 assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia has been added to the Federal Bureau of Investigation's most-wanted list.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
A man charged in connection with the 2023 assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia has been added to the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s most-wanted list.

Satinderjeet Singh, who is also known as Goldy Brar, was charged in July for ordering the killing of the Sikh activist outside a Sikh temple in Surrey, B.C.

Singh is wanted for his alleged involvement in the Lawrence Bishnoi Organized Crime Group, which the FBI says is allegedly engaged in a variety of violent acts in southern California and across the U.S. and Canada.

The FBI says these alleged acts include targeted assassinations, shootings, murders, kidnappings, extortions, assaults and the trafficking of narcotics and weapons.

Singh is based in the United States.

He has black hair and brown eyes, is five feet nine inches tall and weighs 220 pounds.

“Satinderjeep Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, is a dangerous individual, and the FBI and our partners have made it our priority to apprehend him, which is why we’re adding him to the Fbi’s list of Top Ten fugitives and offering a reward of up to $1 million dollars for his capture,” FBI Los Angeles Field Office Assistant Director in Charge, Patrick Grandy, said in a release.

“The amount of attention this list will bring to his face and description cannot be overstated; his photo will be found on every FBI-affiliated website and social media platform, and will be publicized on every phone around the world until he’s caught.”

The Canadian government in September 2025 designated the Bishnoi enterprise as a terrorist entity.

“In November 2023, Bishnoi claimed responsibility for a separate shooting that occurred at the Vancouver home of a prominent Indian actor and singer and warned in the Punjabi language in a Facebook post, “no one can save you from us.”

Singh is the 543rd addition to the Fbi’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list.

The FBI says Singh is considered to be extremely violent, armed and dangerous. He is known to live in California and various parts of Canada.

The public is warned to avoid interaction with Singh and should contact the Fbi’s toll-free tip line at 1-800-Call-FBI (1-800-225-5324) if they have any information on his whereabouts.

-with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: London faces ‘unprecedented job cuts’ as teacher’s union considers strike: Osstf president
stories.summary: Potential job action for four Ontario teachers’ unions could have far reaching consequences here in London and beyond.
stories.author: Bailey Shakyaver
stories.content:
Potential job action for four Ontario teachers’ unions could have far reaching consequences in London and beyond.

The Ontario Secondary School Teachers Federation (Osstf) as well as the unions representing elementary and catholic schools are all without an agreement with the province since the last one expired on Aug. 31.

In the coming months, Osstf union members are being asked to vote on whether they wish to strike if the union’s demands are not met by the province. Their concerns include a lack of cap on class sizes in grades 9 and 10, as well as the mandatory implementation of e-learning for high school students.

“We’ve seen in the London area unprecedented job cuts when it comes to frontline educational assistance, child and youth workers, supports for students that need it most,” said Osstf President Martha Hradowy. “I’ve been involved for almost 30 years in public education and I’ve never seen cuts to the extent that they have had happen this spring.”

A budget announced at the Thames Valley District School Board in the spring included a reduction of more than 150 fewer full-time positions. At the time, the board said that the changes were driven by declining enrolment and shifting student needs.

“In the London area in particular, the concerns are the same as across the province,” said Hradowy. “We are hearing from members, they are continually being asked to do more with less.”

Hradowy says that the education sector has been underfunded for years, “this government has substantively underfunded public education alongside a lot of our other public services for the last since 2018… it’s time that we step up and we speak out because our students deserve better.”

A spokesperson for Education Minister Paul Calandra said once the labour board process has concluded, the government will be ready and willing to negotiate new contracts at the bargaining table.

“Premature strike threats do not serve the interests of students and do nothing but create unnecessary panic for parents,” Emma Testani wrote in a statement.

“Our focus is where it should be — getting to the table and reaching a deal that keeps students in the classroom.”

Although parents are likely to be concerned about potential job action, Hradowy says it’s too early to know what the outcome of talks will be, “I don’t want parents to worry about any potential job action. We are going to get to the table and engage with the government and the employers across the other side to try and reach a negotiated settlement. So that’s going to be where our focus remains and we’ll see what comes next.”

The Ontario Secondary School Teachers Federation (Osstf) as well as the unions representing elementary and catholic schools are all without an agreement with the province since the last one expired on Aug. 31.

In the coming months, Osstf union members are being asked to vote on whether they wish to strike if the union’s demands are not met by the province. Their concerns include a lack of cap on class sizes in grades 9 and 10, as well as the mandatory implementation of e-learning for high school students.

“We’ve seen in the London area unprecedented job cuts when it comes to frontline educational assistance, child and youth workers, supports for students that need it most,” said Osstf President Martha Hradowy. “I’ve been involved for almost 30 years in public education and I’ve never seen cuts to the extent that they have had happen this spring.”

A budget announced at the Thames Valley District School Board in the spring included a reduction of more than 150 fewer full-time positions. At the time, the board said that the changes were driven by declining enrolment and shifting student needs.
“In the London area in particular, the concerns are the same as across the province,” said Hradowy. “We are hearing from members, they are continually being asked to do more with less.”

Hradowy says that the education sector has been underfunded for years, “this government has substantively underfunded public education alongside a lot of our other public services for the last since 2018… it’s time that we step up and we speak out because our students deserve better.”
A spokesperson for Education Minister Paul Calandra said once the labour board process has concluded, the government will be ready and willing to negotiate new contracts at the bargaining table.
“Premature strike threats do not serve the interests of students and do nothing but create unnecessary panic for parents,” Emma Testani wrote in a statement.
“Our focus is where it should be — getting to the table and reaching a deal that keeps students in the classroom.”

Although parents are likely to be concerned about potential job action, Hradowy says it’s too early to know what the outcome of talks will be, “I don’t want parents to worry about any potential job action. We are going to get to the table and engage with the government and the employers across the other side to try and reach a negotiated settlement. So that’s going to be where our focus remains and we’ll see what comes next.”
