stories.title: Fantasy, cosplayers, and celebrities at London Comic Con
stories.summary: Pop culture fans packed the Western Fair Agriplex for two days of cosplay, fantasy, and celebrity meet and greets.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Pop culture fans packed the Western Fair Agriplex for two days of cosplay, fantasy, and celebrity meet and greets.

“We’re going on year 14 now and the excitement just keeps growing,” said Andrew Kitt, president of London Comic Con.

“Our numbers are up and fans are happy with our change to the Western Fair. It’s a new venue; more space and just has more attractions. We were able to expand to have three stages of entertainment constantly rotating. We have live wrestling taking place and we even have Nuggie Con, which is a whole new thing within Comic Con.”

Among the celebrities in attendance were WWE legend D’Lo Brown, movie actors, voice actors, and television stars including actors from Crave shows Heated Rivalry and Letterkenny.

“I love coming to conventions and getting to meet the fans,” said Dylan Playfair, who plays Reilly on the show Letterkenny.

“We don’t get to do what we do without fans watching the show, so it’s always a treat to come and meet people and hang out and make some good memories.”

Playfair was taking photos and signing autographs. He said he gets about an equal split from fans from his show Letterkenny and roles in the Descendants film franchise.

“The wildest thing is that I did a show called Some Assembly Required, which was in 2014,” added Playfair.

“It was a show meant for kids, age five to 10, and now they’ve grown up and now they’re attending the conventions, which is really cool to see kids who have grown up watching a show that I was on a couple of years ago. I’m very fortunate in the sense that I’ve got a pretty broad spectrum of fans in the in the age range anywhere from nine-to-10-year-old kids, all up to grown adults who like Letterkenny.”

Thousands of people dressed in costume were shopping with local vendors, watching shows on stage and soaking in everything organizers brought to the table.

“This is a place to find what you love and really celebrate it,” said Kitt.

“If you’re a pop culture fan of Star Trek, Star Wars or Pokemon, anything in between. You will find your people and live your fandom here.”

stories.title: BC Conservatives makes 1st policy announcement of election campaign
stories.summary: The BC Conservatives are leading in the polls as the snap election campaign gets underway, but Sunday is leader Lorne Doerkson's first official campaign announcement.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
B.C. Conservative Interim Leader Lorne Doerkson is set to make a campaign announcement as the provincial snap election nears the end of its first week.

Doerkson is expected to unveil the party’s first policy announcement as it kicks off the campaign.

It’s also Doerkson’s first official campaign appearance since the election began.

Days after the election was called on Tuesday, Doerkson’s party leads the way with a new poll suggesting 43 per cent of leaning and decided voters intend to vote for the Conservatives. The number is up six points in just 11 days.

The BC NDP are now down six points at 35 per cent, dropping from a slim four-point advantage they held 12 days earlier.

stories.title: Poilievre urges tax cuts to make diesel fuel more affordable, ensure future supplies
stories.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is pitching a plan to cut federal taxes on diesel fuel and help ensure Canada has affordable supplies of the fuel in the future.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is pitching a plan to cut federal taxes on diesel fuel and help ensure Canada has affordable supplies of the fuel in the future.

The Conservatives say Canada already produces enough diesel to meet national demand, but transportation bottlenecks leave some regions dependent on U.S. imports.

In April, as global fuel prices rose, Ottawa introduced a temporary suspension of the federal fuel excise tax. It has extended the suspension through January, and will collect 50 per cent of the regular excise tax rate from Feb. 1 through March 31, 2027.

Poilievre proposes eliminating all tax on diesel sales until at least Canada Day by extending the full fuel excise tax cut until July 1 of next year and removing the GST from the purchase of fuel.

“When farmers and truckers pay more, the price gets passed on to you,” Poilievre said Sunday at a suburban Ottawa gas station.

“Why aren’t we using our oil to power our people? We should be energy independent, and you, the Canadian family, should enjoy the price savings from that.”

Poilievre also advocates removing all diesel production taxes by permanently scrapping the federal industrial carbon tax and the Clean Fuel Standard, which he says adds costs to the production of diesel and discourages new investment in refineries.

The Conservatives want refineries to be excluded from the federal impact assessment process, saying this would not eliminate environmental protection. Refineries would still have to follow federal rules on pollution, wastewater, leaks and monitoring, as well as provincial environmental laws and permits, the party says.

The Conservatives say the overall plan would expand refining capacity, help refineries process more Canadian crude and build the transportation and storage infrastructure needed to supply every region.

The office of Prime Minister Mark Carney had no immediate response to a request for comment on Poilievre’s proposals.

Asked if he envisions Canada eventually transitioning away from diesel, Poilievre said the focus needs to be on affordability.

“Affordable fuel is one of the most important pillars to defeat poverty, enrich our middle class and make our country self-reliant,” he said.

“I do not want to phase out Canadian oil and gas. I want to produce more of it and at a lower price.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 27, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Former colleagues, allies defend Jewish CBC journalist facing reprimand over video, comments about anti-Israel protest
stories.summary: Neil Herland should be free to document and share his 'lived experience' outside a Yom Kippur service, say former CBC staffers and a Conservative MP.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Canada

Neil Herland should be free to document and share his 'lived experience' outside a Yom Kippur service, say former CBC staffers and Conservative MP Shuv Majumdar

An image from Neil Herland's video shows protesters outside the Meridian Arts Centre in Toronto.Photo by @NEILNews/X

Several friends and former colleagues of a Jewish CBC staffer reportedly facing “disciplinary action” after sharing a video on social media showing anti-Israel protesters outside a Yom Kippur event he was attending in Toronto last week are questioning and condemning the broadcaster’s decision.

“CBC’s own former Ombudsman said in a ruling a journalist’s lived experience can ‘rest comfortably within journalistic standards,” former CBC host Travis Dhanraj wrote on X.

“So explain this: Neil Herland attended a Yom Kippur service, he documented what he encountered. He talked about his lived experience. Now he’s under investigation, ripped off the air. The double standard is appalling.”

Herland, a veteran journalist and national newsreader, was “quietly pulled” from the airwaves after his video shot outside the Meridian Arts Centre at Yonge and Sheppard last Sunday evening piled up views on X, as reported byToronto Sun’s Warren Kinsella.

Dhanraj, whose July 2025 departure sparked a controversy over allegations of perceived bias in news coverage, was referring to Kinsella’s reporting that a CBC Ombudsman decreed that a Muslim journalist didn’t break any rules when she put forth a personal opinion on the 2021 murder of a Muslim family in London, Ont.

Dhanraj added that “CBC has spent years plastering ‘diversity’ and ‘lived experience’ on billboards, in commercials and throughout its corporate messaging” and said it’s not a principle that can be simply turned off “when it becomes uncomfortable.”

Conservative MP Shuv Majumdar also highlighted the “lived experience” clearance

“That standard apparently does not extend to Jewish journalists,” he wrote onX.

I'm a journalist. And I happen to be Jewish. On Yom Kippur I went to a synagogue service in Toronto and was met by protesters trying to taunt and intimidate me from entering the building. 1/5 pic.twitter.com/2eH3MaC9QB — Neil Herland (@NEWSneil) September 22, 2026

In Herland’s 52-second clip, he walks toward a small but vocal group of protesters outside the facility rented by The Song Shul synagogue. As he gets closer, a man’s voice is heard saying “Zionist alert” into a megaphone, prompting the journalist to pan his camera back to two individuals with a sign reading “Where’s your humanity?” The man shouts “Zionist alert” again before waving at the camera and flashing a peace sign.

“You’re going to hell,” one protester yells repeatedly at Herland as he walks through their ranks, while another calls him a “baby killer” over the sound of blaring horns and chants of “Free Palestine.”

“I’m a journalist. And I happen to be Jewish. On Yom Kippur I went to a synagogue service in Toronto and was met by protesters trying to taunt and intimidate me from entering the building,” he wrote in a thread on Monday.

Herland, whose father was a Holocaust survivor from Romania, said he got an Austrian passport last year, “in case Canada becomes unsafe” for him as a Jew.

“I fear that moment is approaching, here in Canada and elsewhere,” he wrote.

“Jewish Canadians are living in a parallel world. Where police stand guard with guns outside synagogues. And Jewish schools, religious sites and businesses are targeted with bullets. And most Canadians have no awareness or understanding.”

Asked about the reported punishment, a CBC spokesperson told National Post it doesn’t “comment on internal matters” for privacy reasons.

“However, we are aware of reporting on this matter that contains errors and mischaracterizations,” they wrote without elaborating, citing “the privacy of the situation.”

Former CBC investigative and political journalist Alison Crawford said she was “appalled at this ludicrous decision” and defended Herland, whom she counts as a friend.

“He wasn’t working,” shewrote on X. “He posted a POV video experience entering the space his synagogue had rented for Yom Kippur.”

Lawyer and former CBC political affairs reporterJennifer Dundas replied to his thread: “I support Neil Herland, and condemn CBC News for taking him off the air.”

Carole MacNeil, a former CBC journalist who left the broadcaster in 2021, said she was “confused about the treatment of Herland.”

“Normally when a journalist witnesses a news story live they are encouraged to record it. If there was an issue with how Neil subsequently posted or framed the material, surely a simple, ‘Next time, run it past an editor,’ could suffice,” shewrote on X, noting that overcautiousness around the Israel-Palestine issue “has consequences.”

“Too much CBC coverage of this extraordinarily important story has been light, or so carefully constructed that it ends up being neither particularly interesting nor enlightening. Or worse, distorts the actual story.”

Toronto lawyer Kathryn Marshall, who’s representing Dhanraj in hishuman rights complaint against the public broadcaster, offered her services for free.

Herland himself has not publicly commented on the unfolding controversy, but did share a photo on X of two lit candles and a Kiddush cup used in Jewish ceremonies on Saturday, the Jewish sabbath.

stories.title: ‘Part of my world flew away to heaven’: Tributes pour in as victims of helicopter crash outside Montreal identified
stories.summary: A day after a helicopter crash on Montreal’s South Shore killed four people, their identities were revealed by family members and friends paying their tributes on social media Sunday. According to the provincial police agency Sûreté du Québec (SQ), the incident happened Saturday around 2:30 p.m. in the Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville municipality, in the Montéré…
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By News Staff

Posted September 27, 2026 12:43 pm.

Last Updated September 27, 2026 2:37 pm.

A day after a helicopter crash on Montreal’s South Shore killed four people, their identities were revealed by family members and friends paying their tributes on social media Sunday.

According to the provincial police agency Sûreté du Québec (SQ), the incident happened Saturday around 2:30 p.m. in the Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville municipality, in the Montérégie, about 50 kilometres southeast of Montreal.

The three passengers were identified by Océane Perreault as her husband Gabriel Jasmin, mother Chantal Raymond and brother Loucas Perreault who were on a helicopter ride to celebrate Raymond’s birthday when the chopper tragically crashed and caught fire.

“On Sept. 26, a part of my world flew away to heaven,” Perreault wrote on Facebook.

“I don’t have the words to describe the pain, the shock, and the emptiness I feel. Three people I love more than anything were taken from me far too soon, right before my eyes.”

Jasmin was a host of a show at a Sherbrooke-based radio station 106.1 Énergie. He has a daughter with Perreault.

The pilot of the plane Suzanne Jutras, 50, was identified as the fourth victim in a tribute on Facebook by Syndicat UPA Haut-Richelieu, a regional farmers’ union. Jutras’ husband Yves Boulais, a field crop farmer and a former dairy farmer in the region, the syndicat said.

“During this difficult time, the board of directors of the Haut-Richelieu UPA, along with the entire farming community, would like to offer their most sincere condolences to Yves, their family, their loved ones, and everyone affected by this tragedy,” the union wrote.

An investigation by SQ’s Major Crimes Unit is underway. Investigators from the Transportation Safety Board were also on site Saturday.

stories.title: New U.S. bans to take effect Tuesday: Here’s what’s affected
stories.summary: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told Global News that Canada "maintains ongoing communications with our American counterparts."
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
U.S. import bans on select Canadian items are set to take effect this week, the latest salvo between the two countries in an ongoing trade war.

The ban is set to come into effect on Tuesday at 12:01 a.m., and will see a full import ban on Canadian-made cheese and other dairy products, as well as alcoholic beverages and Canadian-made motorcycles.

When he signed the executive orders implementing the bans on Sept. 8, Trump said the decision was in response to Canada’s own counter-tariff measures. Those Canadian tariffs went into effect earlier in the day on Sept. 8 and were in retaliation for the president’s 50 per cent tariffs on numerous Canadian goods.

Trump also said Canada hasn’t stopped discriminating against U.S. autos, dairy and vehicles so they can now block the import of certain products because it was “consistent with the interests of the United States and the public interests.”

Though a majority of alcohol in Canada is sold within the country, much of what is exported internationally is sent to the U.S.

According to a fact sheet released by the White House, dozens of products will be banned Tuesday including rye, whisky, wine, beer, vermouth, tequila, vodka and rum. Some of the products banned also include both packaged and unpackaged versions.

The Government of Canada’s Trade Commissioner Service reports Canada exported $1.36 billion in alcoholic beverages in 2023 and 90 per cent went to the U.S. Of that number, two-thirds were for spirits alone.

Wine Growers of Canada previously told Global News about $8.3 million of wine was exported to the U.S. in 2025, 57 per cent of which was represented by ice wine alone.

Beer Canada reported $28 million in beer products was exported out of the country last year, amounting to about 10 per cent of all beer produced. The organization said the U.S. is its number one partner for exports.

stories.title: 30th Fall Colour Ride raises thousands of dollars for Children’s Health Foundation
stories.summary: For three decades motorcycle riders have gathered in London, Ont. for a three-hour trek to raise money for the Children’s Health Foundation.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
For three decades motorcycle riders have gathered in London, Ont. for a three-hour trek to raise money for the Children’s Health Foundation.

Started by Randy and his wife Audrey Collins, the event was renamed the Randy Collins Memorial Fall Colour Ride after his passing in 2023.

“This was certainly a ride that Randy had a lot of passion for,” said Paul Goldsmith, sales consultant at Hully Gully.

Dozens of riders met at Hully Gully to register, then made their way around Southwestern Ontario before heading back to London. Each rider collected pledges and the total over the three decades is now well over $800,000 raised.

“It’s getting bigger and bigger,” said Scott Fortnum, CEO and President of the Children’s Health Foundation.

“That money translates oftentimes into specific pieces of equipment. We’ve got lots of things in the Nicu, in surgery and the pediatric critical care unit throughout the hospital, and it also supports the many programs. Our friend Ollie the therapeutic clown, they’re things like this wouldn’t exist without donor support and that comes through events like the Hully Gully Fall Colour Randy Collins Memorial ride.”

Among those riding was Wally Thibodeau, president of the 1st Ortona Unit of the Canadian Army Veterans Motorcycle Unit.

That group has been a big supporter of this ride because the Collins family has supported their endeavors.

“Whether you’re veterans or civilians, you look at people walking around and when they see bikes all together like this, they want to talk bikes,” said Thibodeau.

“Where you’re from? What you’re doing? I’ve never been anywhere without my bike that somebody hasn’t approached me. That’s the biker community. You see a bunch of bikers out on the road, you know they’re always out raising money for something.”

The Collins family has always been community supporters, and donated thousands of dollars from their family business. They built and funded seven playgrounds in London, including a fully accessible park in 2021 to mark Hully Gully’s 50th anniversary.

stories.title: This vegan snack has an undeclared ingredient that’s not vegan
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) is alerting Canadians about a vegan snack that has an undeclared milk ingredient.
stories.author: Elianna Lev
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) is alerting Canadians about a vegan snack that has an undeclared milk ingredient.

Smarter Snack brand Vegan Protein Puff Chili & Lime Flavored 50 g bags were sold nationally and online. It is not clear how many units of the product were sold across the country.

“The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) is warning people who are allergic or sensitive to the affected product not to consume the affected product because it contains milk which is not declared on the label,” the Cfia wrote in a recall alert on Saturday.

The agency advised Canadians with allergies or sensitivities to the product not to consume it, as it “May cause a serious or life-threatening reaction”.

It also advised not to “serve, use, sell or distribute affected products.”

Cfia said the warning was triggered by test results. So far there have been no reported reactions linked to the consumption of the recalled snack.

Cfia said it is conducting a food safety investigation, which could lead to the recall of this or other products.

The Cfia initially put out a similar recall warning for the snack on Sept. 5, after a consumer complaint.

Click here to learn more about the UPC and codes for the snack.

stories.title: North Atlantic right whales at greater risk of collision with boats at night: study
stories.summary: Halifax — A recent study has found that critically endangered North Atlantic right whales are feeding closer to the ocean’s surface at night, increasing their risk of being struck by boats.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Tori Fitzpatrick, The Canadian Press

Posted September 27, 2026 11:50 am.

Halifax — A recent study has found that critically endangered North Atlantic right whales are feeding closer to the ocean’s surface at night, increasing their risk of being struck by boats.

The study, published earlier this month in the peer-reviewed journal Plos One, documented nighttime surface feeding in North Atlantic right whales, providing new evidence that could be used to prevent deadly collisions between the whales and vessels.

The paper’s lead author, Jay Kirkham, a PhD student at Dalhousie University in Halifax, said the research team worked with U.S.-based non-profit Ocean Alliance to tag 23 right whales in the Shediac Valley, an underwater valley in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence.

A portion of the North Atlantic right whale population, which is estimated to be approximately 384 whales, gathers to feed in the Shediac Valley each summer.

Kirkham said the tags recorded video footage along with data on how the whales moved and in which direction they swam.

He said he used video footage to record right whale feeding behaviour during the day.

“When a right whale opens its mouth, it’s kind of like a big parachute opening on the front of their face … and that just slows them down an awful lot,” he said. “And so, they have to work harder, which they do by kicking their tail higher and faster.”

Kirkham said he used these observations to train a machine learning algorithm that could recognize a right whale feeding at night when he was unable to visually identify the behaviour.

This data revealed that whales are feeding within the same depth as large vessels at night, increasing the risk of collision, he said.

While right whales typically feed close to the seafloor during the day, Kirkham said the whales follow their food — zooplankton — higher up in the water column at night.

“These big ships that go through the gulf, they extend into the water maybe 10, maybe 15 metres,” he said. “The whales are in a sort of vertical overlap with that.”

He said collisions with vessels and entanglements in fishing gear are the leading causes of death in the population and this study May help inform conservation measures for the whales.

Transport Canada and Fisheries and Oceans Canada currently oversee protection measures for the population.

In a statement to The Canadian Press, Fisheries and Oceans Canada said its measures focus on preventing whale entanglements in fishing gear and enforcing seasonal fishing closures.

The department said the study can help it develop “tailored management measures to protect North Atlantic right whales.”

Transport Canada implements speed restrictions and enforces a vessel exclusion zone in the Shediac Valley during the summer to reduce the risk of collisions between boats and right whales in the area.

However, Kirkham said that the whales he and his team tagged spent approximately 25 per cent of their feeding time outside of the vessel exclusion zone, exposing them to ship traffic.

In a statement to The Canadian Press, Transport Canada said it has a right whale surveillance program to help protect the whales from collisions by using both visual and audio detection tools.

“Acoustic monitoring systems and other complementary technologies can support whale detection regardless of daylight conditions and help inform protective measures when whales are present,” the statement said.

The department also said it uses the latest scientific research, monitoring data and feedback from stakeholders to inform its protection measures.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 27, 2026.

Tori Fitzpatrick, The Canadian Press

stories.title: As Canada pivots to Arctic, experts wonder if Ottawa has enough regional diplomats
stories.summary: As Canada plans an ambitious expansion of defence and economic activity in the Arctic, regional experts are asking whether it has enough diplomats to build the ties it wants in the North.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — As Canada plans an ambitious expansion of defence and economic activity in the Arctic, regional experts are asking whether it has enough diplomats to build the ties it wants in the North.

“The Arctic is a geopolitical hot spot,” said Natan Obed, president of Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami. “The (Global Affairs) department does not have huge bench strength when it comes to Arctic diplomacy.”

Here’s a look at how the Liberals have both cut back and restaffed positions across the North in recent years.

Closing an expert centre

In 2023, the government of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau closed the Canadian International Arctic Centre, a hub for diplomacy across the region that had been operating within Canada’s embassy in Norway since 2009.

In a briefing note obtained by The Canadian Press, Global Affairs Canada cited “high costs in Oslo” and anticipated savings of $550,000 per year.

“The hybrid work model has demonstrated the department’s ability to engage worldwide through technology … diminishing the relative advantage of operational staff located in the field,” says the briefing note.

Artur Wilczynski, who served as Canada’s ambassador to Oslo from 2014 to 2018, said Ciac helped him prepare for the posting by registering him in conferences and introducing him to “key” Arctic contacts.

Wilczynski called the decision to close Ciac “incoherent.”

“You need to develop a cohort of people who actually have a deep understanding and knowledge of a very complex and diverse region,” he said. “You do not get that from a Zoom call.”

In December 2024, the Trudeau government released an Arctic foreign policy that committed to boosting domestic and international collaboration to face down emerging foreign threats.

The policy said the region was “no longer free from tension” because of increased geopolitical instability following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Ottawa appointed Virginia Mearns as Arctic ambassador last year and promised new consulates in Greenland and Alaska.

The government of Prime Minister Jean Chrétien created the role of Canadian ambassador for circumpolar affairs in 1994. The government of Prime Minister Stephen Harper shelved the role in 2004.

The policy’s release followed several incidents in the region, including a high-altitude balloon from China crossing into Canadian airspace in 2023.

Ottawa has since promised billions of dollars for defence and new infrastructure for northerners.

Wilczynski argues that buildup needs to be accompanied by a commensurate increase in the number of diplomats in order to build circumpolar contacts.

“I don’t think that there is a more immediate and proximate security, economic and political interest for Canada and Canadians than the Arctic,” said Wilczynski, who also worked as an executive in Canadian intelligence.

“Investing more in our diplomatic presence in the region is part of a strategy that recognizes the interests that Canada has in relationships with our Arctic partners.”

In February, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand opened Canada’s first consulate in Greenland’s capital, Nuuk. Due to the shortage of available buildings, the Canadian consulate operates out of the Icelandic consulate.

A briefing document obtained by The Canadian Press estimates the operating cost of the consulate at $8.76 million over five years — roughly $1.75 million annually. That includes staffing and the use of various services.

The consulate originally was intended to employ three full-time equivalents. But the consulate has only one staffer and it’s not clear if that is due to budget cuts.

“These figures were prepared for planning purposes … and May be temporarily higher than the actual costs incurred during implementation due to a number of factors, including employing fewer staff than originally planned,” Global Affairs Canada said in a media statement.

The department did not say when the consulate in Alaska will open or how many staffers it will have.

‘Key contacts’ lost

Part of Canada’s goal in Arctic diplomacy is to give northerners a voice in international platforms so that federal policies reflect their concerns.

Ottawa helps facilitate this through the Global Arctic Leadership Initiative, which connects Inuit and northern people with projects and conferences abroad and funds their travel.

An internal Global Affairs audit reported in May 2025 that closing the Canadian International Arctic Centre deprived the Global Arctic Leadership Initiative of “key contacts in the Arctic.”

“This led to a certain loss of expertise, outreach and support for the missions,” says the audit, adding that means fewer opportunities for “Indigenous and northern speakers.”

Obed said this shows the shortcomings in Ottawa’s approach to engagement with Inuit. Obed said there is “untapped” potential in the region and Inuit can help Canada make new contacts around the North Pole.

“These new times require greater administrative and political and policy footprints in order to do it right,” he said.

Marc Lanteigne, a political scientist from Montreal, is a professor at the Arctic University of Norway in the northern city of Tromso and teaches at the University of Greenland.

He said Canada has made itself more visible in Nordic capitals in recent years by sending larger and more varied delegations to the annual Arctic Circle assembly in Iceland.

Canadian foreign ministers have also met with their five Nordic counterparts in recent years.

“We have a lot to contribute, not only in our particular corner of the Arctic, but (across) the region as a whole,” Lanteigne said from Tromso, which sits on the same latitude as Yukon’s northern coast.

“Where I’m standing right now, everyone’s talking about the green transition and how we can balance that with the ongoing need for fossil fuels. These are really areas where I get asked, “Where’s Canada in all this?’”

How many diplomats are needed in the north?

Lanteigne said people in Greenland and Norway are troubled by the “very sudden” rise in international interest in the Arctic, driven by the prospect of new shipping routes and U.S. President Donald Trump’s talk of annexing Greenland, Canada and Iceland.

“A lot of the issues regarding sovereignty and regarding the livelihoods of the people of the Arctic sometimes get lost in the crush,” Lanteigne said.

He said Trump’s threats have elevated Canada’s status in the region as a partner in economic co-operation and education.

Lanteigne said Canada does not necessarily need a large diplomatic cohort in places like Nuuk and Anchorage — as long as those on the ground make connections for Indigenous communities, businesses, climate-change researchers and development experts.

He said this type of “para-diplomacy” is more important in an age of geopolitical tumult.

“Our capitals are right now in opposition, but we are facing a lot of similar concerns,” he said.

“What will need to be done with Anchorage is to basically identify areas of mutual concern — of which there are many — and try to stick to that particular menu, even though it is going to be a bit tricky.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 27, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Threats to Canada’s North have ‘shifted significantly,’ foreign minister says
stories.summary: The long-serving cabinet minister tells The West Block that Canada and the U.S. remain at the table to discuss Arctic security, sovereignty.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Threats to the Canadian Arctic have “shifted significantly” in recent years amidst Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and an upended geopolitical order, Canada’s foreign minister says.

But despite political tensions, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told The West Block ’s Jeff Semple that Canada and the United States remain in close coordination on Arctic security and sovereignty issues.

Anand said she attended a meeting of Arctic nations convened by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio last week and they “had a frank discussion about the collective need to work together on Arctic security.”

“So the United States is very much at the table in this conversation. And one of the ongoing dialogues that Secretary Rubio and I have had specifically … is in fact how can Canada and the United States ensure that our shared interests in the Arctic are advocated, are worked on within the confines of multilateral organizations including Nato.”

Anand, who formerly served as minister of national defence under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, pointed to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to ramp up defence spending and the impact that money will have on northern security. That includes a massive contract to German company Tkms to build a new fleet of as many as 12 submarines, as well as the federal governments still as-yet finalized decision to buy new fighter jets.

On the diplomatic front, Anand pointed to the newly-opened Canadian consulate in Nuuk, Greenland, and plans to open one in Anchorage, Alaska.

Anand said that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has changed thinking not only of the security environment in Europe, but in the Arctic as well.

“So while Canada has Operation Reassurance on the Eastern flank, we cannot forget that Nato, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, should have a view that is based on a strategic assessment of the North and the Arctic, in order to ensure that we are well defended and protected in terms of the Arctic, not only on the Eastern flank” Anand said.

The threat to Canada’s Arctic maybe be shifting, but so are northerners’ perceptions of Canada’s once-closest ally.

Global News reported last week that new polling suggested residents of Canada’s North — including Nunavut, the Northwest Territories, Yukon and Nunavik — view the United States as the greatest threat facing the region.

Nearly half of respondents (48 per cent) to a poll for the Observatoire de la politique et la sécurité de l’Arctique (Opsa) saw the U.S. has the greatest threat, followed distantly by Russia (30 per cent) and China (12 per cent).

“So while Canada has Operation Reassurance on the Eastern flank, we cannot forget that Nato, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, should have a view that is based on a strategic assessment of the North and the Arctic, in order to ensure that we are well defended and protected in terms of the Arctic, not only on the Eastern flank” Anand said.
The threat to Canada’s Arctic maybe be shifting, but so are northerners’ perceptions of Canada’s once-closest ally.

Global News reported last week that new polling suggested residents of Canada’s North — including Nunavut, the Northwest Territories, Yukon and Nunavik — view the United States as the greatest threat facing the region.

Nearly half of respondents (48 per cent) to a poll for the Observatoire de la politique et la sécurité de l’Arctique (Opsa) saw the U.S. has the greatest threat, followed distantly by Russia (30 per cent) and China (12 per cent).

stories.title: Voters in Quebec head to the first day of advance polling ahead of general election
stories.summary: Voters have the option of voting today and on Monday, from 9:30 a.m. to 8 p.m.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Polls are opening for the first day of advance polling in Quebec ahead of general elections.

Voters have the option of voting today and on Monday, from 9:30 a.m. to 8 p.m., ahead of the Oct. 5 election.

Five parties are expecting to win seats in the election – the Coalition Avenir Québec, the Parti Québécois, the Quebec Liberals, the Quebec Conservatives and Québec solidaire.

Claims of foreign interference dominated the campaign on Friday and Saturday.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette said she was concerned Americans might try to support the sovereigntist Parti Québécois to destabilize Canada.

Her rivals were skeptical about the warnings, and Fréchette also said that there was no indication of interference in the current campaign.

stories.title: Canada’s premiers tight-lipped on constitutional changes in Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Albertans will vote on several proposals, including three of which would likely require the support of more than half of Canada's legislatures.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s counterparts across the country are keeping their cards close to their chest on where they stand on the major constitutional reforms Smith is sending to a provincewide vote next month.

Smith’s four proposals, three of which would likely require the support of seven legislatures representing over half of Canada’s population (known as the 7/50 rule) and Parliament to implement, are among 10 questions she’s putting to Albertans on Oct. 19.

Her ideas, in brief, are: to abolish the Senate; let Alberta, not Ottawa, pick provincial King’s Bench and Court of Appeal judges; allow Alberta to opt out of federal programs without losing the associated funding; and to give provincial laws standing over Ottawa’s when jurisdictional disputes occur.

Smith’s government concedes on its referendum website that abolishing the Senate, which would require unanimous cross-country support and the support of the Senate itself, is going to be a non-starter for other political leaders.

But the premier’s office says there’s support for the other proposals and that “targeted” amendments to Canada’s legal and administrative spine are more likely to become reality, which is why it wants a mandate from Albertans to proceed.

“Provinces across the country are tired of federal overreach and want more authority within Confederation, not less,” said Ryan Fournier, a communications adviser to Smith.

“We believe this conversation is a vital step towards a fairer Confederation.”

The Canadian Press reached out to premiers across the country to ask whether they supported Smith’s proposals, but many did not respond to repeated requests.

Some, such as Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe’s office, said they wouldn’t be commenting, and those who did respond didn’t answer directly.

“This is a matter for Albertans to consider through their referendum process,” said a spokesperson for Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson.

Nunavut Premier John Main said the territory is be closely monitoring the results of the referendum.

“Like Alberta, Nunavut is rich in resources that benefit the rest of Canada and the world, and we need external supports to bring those resources to market,” Main said.

“We intend to make our mark in partnership with other governments and private industry, and support measures that build a stronger Canada.”

Yukon Premier Currie Dixon said he looked forward to “hearing what Albertans have to say” when it comes to the Constitution, but didn’t offer an opinion.

He did, however, voice his support for Alberta remaining in Canada, referring to the headlining question on succession.

“While I know Albertans have a number of grievances with the federal government, it’s my hope that Alberta will continue to stay in Confederation,” Dixon said.

“Canada, including the Yukon, would be negatively affected if Alberta were to leave.”

While they May not be saying so now, one constitutional law expert said Smith’s office is correct in saying there could be enough support from other provincial governments to take two of the proposals beyond the ballot — having provinces pick provincial judges and opting out of federal programs without financial punishment.

“It’s extra provincial power. Why wouldn’t they want it?” said Gerard Kennedy, a constitutional law professor at the University of Alberta.

“To me, the big problem is going to be getting the federal Parliament to agree, because the federal government would have to be agreeing to reduce its own power for nothing in return.”

Smith, Moe, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and former Quebec premier François Legault penned a letter to Ottawa in March asking that all provincial Appeal Court and Superior Court judges be appointed from a pre-approved list submitted by the provinces.

Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser quickly shut the issue down, saying Ottawa wasn’t considering changes to the judicial appointment process. He pointed to the advisory committees set up across the country that review and advise on judicial applications to say that provinces already have input, since each government appoints some of the committee’s members.

Kennedy said the proposal about giving provincial laws paramountcy over federal laws probably won’t go anywhere, adding that there was no federation in the world with that setup.

He said regardless of the support that May exist, Alberta could be opening a can of worms if it makes serious efforts at working with other provinces.

“The problem if you open up constitutional negotiations is that some other provinces are going to have their pet projects and they’ll say, ‘well, we won’t agree to amend the Constitution on terms favorable to Alberta unless they’re also amended on terms that are favorable to New Brunswick or Quebec,'” he said.

“And then you end up having a package and too many provinces won’t like some part of the package and then it doesn’t get through.”

He said there’s a third way Alberta could try to amend the Constitution.

Some changes can be made with only the support of Parliament and the province that is being affected by the amendment. An example was in 2001, when the Constitution was amended to change the name of Newfoundland to Newfoundland and Labrador.

Alberta could try to go that route, Kennedy said, but the effort would likely end up in court, as granting the province special privileges others don’t have would go against the presumption that all provinces are treated equally.

Despite the premier and her office hinting that they’re committed to lobbying other provinces should the four proposals get majority approval on Oct. 19, some doubt Smith is willing to put in the effort.

Smith framed her referendum questions as presenting Albertans with a plan to better the province’s standing within Confederation so that voters don’t resort to separatism. She’s also blamed federal immigration policy for Alberta’s overburdened health and education systems.

Calgary-based political scientist Duane Bratt said the constitutional questions feel like an afterthought for the referendum.

Bratt said he’d feel differently if the questions were a bigger part of the premier’s messaging or the government’s $4-million ad campaign, which he said are far more focused on Smith’s five immigration proposals that are also on the ballot.

“She’s not really talking about the Constitutional questions,” Bratt said in an interview, pointing to recent speeches the premier has made.

“It’s immigrants who are the scapegoats and the villains here.”

Bratt, a professor at Mount Royal University, said the lack of attention Smith has given the constitutional proposals, combined with the amount of work needed to actually move the issues forward, means he doesn’t think she will act after Oct. 19.

“Where is their energy? Is their energy (on) building pipelines, restructuring the health-care system, or constitutional change? Because I don’t think they could do all of that.”

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said this week that he thinks Smith is only trying to find new enemies to blame for Alberta getting a raw deal.

“She doesn’t want to get those things,” Nenshi told reporters Tuesday about the Constitution reforms.

“She wants to complain about not getting those things.

“She wants the other provinces to say no.”

stories.title: Corrections Canada to distribute items for 'safe snorting' in federal prisons
stories.summary: Corrections service says it also addresses the "introduction, trafficking, financing, and distribution of unauthorized substances."
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The Correctional Service of Canada has confirmed that paper straws will soon be distributed in federal prisons to facilitate safe snorting of drugs.

This week a social media post included photos of a memo distributed to Corrections staff stating that paper straws were being newly “introduced” for “safer snorting” and “intended for inhaling substances in powdered form or inhaling vapour from heated substances.”

The explanation provided was that paper straws will “reduce harm” by lessening the risk of internal nose cuts that could occur from homemade or plastic straws and reduce infections from diseases such as hepatitis B and C, while “recognizing that overdose and toxicity risk remain.”

Meanwhile, according to the memo, foil strips are to be distributed “for safer smoking.” So were drug-testing strips for fentanyl, benzodiazepine and xylazine.

The memo states that these items are being introduced “in response to increased inhalation, smoking and snorting substances among federal inmates” adding that “harm reduction must adapt to reduce overdose risks, prevent the transmission of infectious diseases and align with current evidence-based practices.”

The new harm reduction items if found on their own, should not result in criminal charges, but the memo states that if they are “found alongside illicit substances or unauthorized paraphernalia, standard operational procedures … must be followed.”

In a statement emailed to National Post by Correctional Service Canada communications officer Laurence Côté, the CSC confirmed that the document shown in the social media post is genuine and “was developed … to provide information to all employees regarding the expansion of harm reduction products.”

The CSC stated that its health services include “harm reduction measures” designed to prevent and minimize “harms related to substance use.”

Judge sends Hamilton fentanyl dealer to prison despite 'immigration consequences'

The 'King' sent to U.S. prison for 20 years for running cocaine and meth smuggling into Canada

It says its National Drugs and Substances Strategy recognizes substance use as a health issue, and therefore approved harm reduction supplies are not considered contraband.

However, the counterbalance to provide these “safe snorting” items seems to be that the CSC says it “maintains robust measures” to address “introduction, trafficking, financing, and distribution of unauthorized substances … within its institutions, and holds those involved accountable.”

Finally, the CSC stated that harm reduction interventions “are widely recognized as cost-effective because they help prevent the transmission of infectious diseases such as HIV and Hepatitis C, reducing the need for significantly more expensive medical treatment and long-term health care costs associated with these conditions.”

Training for Health Services staff responsible for distributing the supplies to inmates is set to begin on Oct, 1, ahead of planned implementation on Oct. 13. At that time, says the CSC, “Health Services staff will provide education and guidance to support informed and appropriate use of these supplies.”
paragraphs: The Correctional Service of Canada has confirmed that paper straws will soon be distributed in federal prisons to facilitate safe snorting of drugs.

This week a social media post included photos of a memo distributed to Corrections staff stating that paper straws were being newly “introduced” for “safer snorting” and “intended for inhaling substances in powdered form or inhaling vapour from heated substances.”

The explanation provided was that paper straws will “reduce harm” by lessening the risk of internal nose cuts that could occur from homemade or plastic straws and reduce infections from diseases such as hepatitis B and C, while “recognizing that overdose and toxicity risk remain.”
Meanwhile, according to the memo, foil strips are to be distributed “for safer smoking.” So were drug-testing strips for fentanyl, benzodiazepine and xylazine.

The memo states that these items are being introduced “in response to increased inhalation, smoking and snorting substances among federal inmates” adding that “harm reduction must adapt to reduce overdose risks, prevent the transmission of infectious diseases and align with current evidence-based practices.”

The new harm reduction items if found on their own, should not result in criminal charges, but the memo states that if they are “found alongside illicit substances or unauthorized paraphernalia, standard operational procedures … must be followed.”

In a statement emailed to National Post by Correctional Service Canada communications officer Laurence Côté, the CSC confirmed that the document shown in the social media post is genuine and “was developed … to provide information to all employees regarding the expansion of harm reduction products.”
The CSC stated that its health services include “harm reduction measures” designed to prevent and minimize “harms related to substance use.”
Judge sends Hamilton fentanyl dealer to prison despite 'immigration consequences'
The 'King' sent to U.S. prison for 20 years for running cocaine and meth smuggling into Canada
It says its National Drugs and Substances Strategy recognizes substance use as a health issue, and therefore approved harm reduction supplies are not considered contraband.

However, the counterbalance to provide these “safe snorting” items seems to be that the CSC says it “maintains robust measures” to address “introduction, trafficking, financing, and distribution of unauthorized substances … within its institutions, and holds those involved accountable.”

Finally, the CSC stated that harm reduction interventions “are widely recognized as cost-effective because they help prevent the transmission of infectious diseases such as HIV and Hepatitis C, reducing the need for significantly more expensive medical treatment and long-term health care costs associated with these conditions.”

Training for Health Services staff responsible for distributing the supplies to inmates is set to begin on Oct, 1, ahead of planned implementation on Oct. 13. At that time, says the CSC, “Health Services staff will provide education and guidance to support informed and appropriate use of these supplies.”

stories.title: One of Chile’s leading winemakers starts a new chapter in the Okanagan
stories.summary: Emily Faulconer embraces new role as technical director overseeing the Mark Anthony group’s Okanagan wineries
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Winemaker Emily Faulconer, who has produced some of Chile’s most iconic red wines, including Seña and Viñedo Chadwick, has embraced a new role as technical director overseeing the Mark Anthony group’s Okanagan wineries. Since starting in June, the 20-year veteran has worked with the winemaking and viticulturalist teams responsible for the company’s seven wineries, which include Mission Hill, Checkmate and Martin’s Lane, to map out plans.

Prior to her first visit to British Columbia’s largest wine region in February, Faulconer says she knew little about the Okanagan, but was quickly impressed by its potential. “The region is so beautiful,” she says. “It attracts a lot of tourists, and a lot of the wine is consumed here. That’s one of the reasons why the Okanagan isn’t well-known outside of this country. If you don’t come here, you won’t know about it.” Faulconer told The Globe and Mail what brought her to the Okanagan and how she is approaching her new role in Canada.

What is your approach to your first grape harvest in the Okanagan?

I think one has to be humble working as a winemaker. I am spending a lot of time in vineyards and with the winemakers to understand what can be done. I have a lot of ideas in my head that I am still validating. When it comes to viticulture and winemaking, I don’t believe in low intervention. Everything we do is intervention. The human factor, the decision making that leads to the final wine, is so important.

How has the recent wildfire in Summerland affected the harvest?

This is a challenging region. With the cold and the smoke, there isn’t much room for mistakes. Since the wildfire, it has rained and the smoke has cleared. Checkmate has picked most of its chardonnay grapes. We are optimistic about the white wines. We’re tasting the fermentations and don’t detect any smoke issues. This region has experienced smoke during harvest before. Few regions know better than this one how to manage that.

What attracted you to the Okanagan wine scene?

When I think of the types of wines that people are looking for today, there’s a huge opportunity here. I can see a balance between high acidity and good fruit ripeness that many consumers are looking for in wine. I am generally very, very interested in what the Okanagan can deliver. This should be a region that everyone is talking about. It’s very exciting. The Okanagan already has very nice wines, but I think there’s the opportunity now to put them on a global stage.

How can you help each in the Von Mandl Family Estates portfolio develop a distinct identity?

I always like to think that you’ve never made your best bottle of wine. There’s that challenge every year of how you fine-tune to get that precision, to achieve the best version of those vineyard sites in the glass. These winemakers are not aspiring to be Bordeaux, the Mosel or Burgundy, they aspire to be best version of the Okanagan. We might look to those historic regions for references, but this is a unique place. The wines, the grapes and the vineyards need to speak for themselves.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

stories.title: 24 Sussex Drive is getting renovated. Some think the National Capital Commission should be overhauled too
stories.summary: As he makes his way north through Ottawa's Strathcona Park, Peter Meggs walks along a multi-use pathway run by a federal crown corporation.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — As he makes his way north through Ottawa’s Strathcona Park, Peter Meggs walks across the Adawe Crossing Bridge, veering away from the connecting path that leads to a parking lot.

Both the connecting path and the pedestrian bridge are municipal jurisdiction. The bridge overlooks the Rideau River, which is provincial responsibility, although the Rideau River Conservation Authority is the river’s watershed agency, which means it manages things such as environmental and flood monitoring.

After crossing the 125-metre bridge, Meggs then hangs a right and joins a smattering of cyclists, dog walkers and step counters for the home stretch along the multi-use pathway of his regular, 5-kilometre loop around his Overbrook neighbourhood. That means he’s now on property run by the National Capital Commission (NCC), the under-the-radar federal body whose mission, according to the organization’s web site, is to help the national capital region be “a dynamic and inspiring source of pride for all Canadians, and a legacy for generations to come.”

Before being turned into a park 119 years ago, Strathcona Park was a swampy floodplain overrun by mud and swarms of mosquitoes. But as Meggs’ brief trek across the bridge suggests, the 15-acre park May now be overrun by swarms of government.

The difference in this regard between the national capital region and other Canadian cities is the NCC. The commission’s critics have for years been asking why the national capital region needs – or perhaps deserves – an extra layer of government and extra source of taxpayer dollars than other Canadian communities.

Those questions have re-emerged in recent months because the Ncc’s profile has jumped over its management of the prime minister’s official residence, uninhabited for more than a decade but now on a path to repair. Some NCC critics are also asking if it’s not time that the commission undergo its own renovation.

The NCC, unlike municipalities, is run by unelected officials who are not directly accountable to the public – and, according to critics, seem fine with it that way.

“You have to accept the good and bad of democracy,” said Meggs, a former town councillor in Cornwall, P.E.I.

But Franco Terrazzano, federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, said the NCC needs greater scrutiny and accountability, in part because it spends and wastes a lot of taxpayers’ money. For example, he said, the crown corporation spent $140,000 to study and design – not build – a staircase, and $1 million for a barn at Rideau Hall, the governor general’s official residence.

“It must be the most incompetent agency in all of Canada — which is saying a lot.”

With the Carney government presumably looking for more cuts in the bureaucracy to help pay for big spending hikes in defence, infrastructure and other priorities, could the NCC be a target for this fall’s upcoming budget?

John Fragos, a spokesman for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said it’s too early in the budget process to speak to any possible cutbacks.

Don Drummond, a former senior official at the Department of Finance and chief economist at TD Bank, said most of the discussions over the years about the NCC have been about democratic reform and transparency, not getting rid of it. For example, Drummond said, folding the NCC into a federal department that May have more experience writing cheques than running programs might be tempting but also might be a bad idea.

Supporters say the NCC, created through a House of Commons vote in 1959, is important because it helps make the National Capital Region – Ottawa and the city of Gatineau, Que. on the other side of the Ottawa River — a special region that all Canadians can be proud of. It brings a national perspective, they argue, to issues that would normally be local.

Results have included a protected Greenbelt on the outskirts of Ottawa, federal parklands and parkways including the popular Gatineau Park, and a wide range of recreational sites, such as cross-country ski trails, walkways, the Rideau Canal skating rink, and public swimming spots along local lakes and rivers — all considered attributes by local residents, and some visitors.

Supporters, such as former Ottawa city councillor Clive Doucet, say the NCC has made an excellent contribution towards presenting the national capital region as the country’s heart, not just another city, in a way that local governments likely wouldn’t.

“It’s been a great success in beautifying Ottawa.”

NCC defenders point out that Canada is by no means the only country that assigns a special government body to giving its capital extra care.

There’s no perfect comparison internationally, but India, France, Australia and Brazil are among those countries that have a federal body with a mandate similar to the NCC. In the U.S., the National Capital Planning Commission (Ncpc) serves as the federal government’s planning agency for Washington, D.C.

But in other ways, the District of Columbia is far from over-governed – or as governed as Canadians in the national capital area.

Unlike Ottawa-Gatineau, D.C. residents are less represented than those in any other part of the U.S. While the city of Washington has a mayor and council, the District is part of no state, which means that it has no governor or state legislature. It also means that D.C. also has just one non-voting representative in the U.S. House of Representatives and no representation in the influential U.S. Senate.

Doucet isn’t wrong that the Ncc’s job is to make the national capital region an enjoyable and attractive place to live or visit. In other words, the commission has goals that are often in line with most municipalities, even if the structures, and method of funding, are very different.

As a federal body, one key discrepancy is of course its source of money. The NCC, unlike municipalities, gets its funding from the federal government, which means taxpayers from across the country, not just those in Ottawa and Gatineau.

According to its annual report, the NCC received $164.3-million from Parliament in 2025, a 57 per cent increase from the previous year. While much of the Ncc’s annual budget is a function of the capital projects that it’s asked to manage during any given year, its operating budget has also been on the rise, a pace well above inflation.

By contrast, the crown corporation is now a larger organization by budget than the municipal governments in cities such as Maple Ridge, B.C., North Bay, Ont. and Moose Jaw, Sask.

Despite its low profile nationally, the NCC is a large organization by other metrics too.

According to its web site, the organization has 419 employees, although that figure doesn’t seem to have been updated since 2017.

And those pathways along the river at Strathcona Park are only a tiny fraction of the Ncc’s territory. It manages about 116,000 acres of land in the National Capital Region, about 11 per cent of the region’s land. That’s about eight times the size of Manhattan, more than double the size of Washington, D.C., and much larger than all of Vancouver.

The crown corporation, which reports directly to Parliament through Public Works Minister Joel Lightbound, is also responsible for management of 1,664 properties, including Rideau Hall (the governor general’s residence), Stornoway (the opposition leader’s residence), The Farm (the Speaker’s residence), 7 Rideau Gate (the government’s official guest house), and the prime minister’s two official residences: Harrington Lake, the prime minister’s cottage, and 24 Sussex, the prime minister’s dilapidated official residence.

With 24 Sussex Dr. uninhabited for more than a decade, there have also been fresh accusations that the NCC doesn’t do a good enough job of maintaining its properties.

The prime minister’s official residence has been vacant, in part, because of complaints about heating and cooling, asbestos, mould, and even rodents. The absence of a decision about what to do with the famous residence does not fall on the NCC, however, as the long-term pause can be traced back to the prime minister’s office.

Detractors have also pointed out that the organization makes important planning decisions about the national capital region, yet its board members are appointed, not elected. And related to that, the most frequent criticism of the NCC is likely that it lacks the transparency expected of other levels of government.

In 2023, when the Office of the Information Commissioner of Canada ruled that the NCC had improperly withheld information in response to an Atip request, it bolstered that case.

Neither NCC chief executive Tobi Nussbaum, nor a spokesperson, was available for interview.

Earlier this year, when asked for an interview about plans for the prime ministers’ official residence, an NCC spokesperson told National Post that that subject is one that the Crown corporation normally would only discuss after its board meetings. They’re held four times a year.

But are there not other models that would allow the capital region to get some extra care, without adding a layer of government that seems less transparent and accountable than our norm?

Jerald Sabin, a public policy specialist at Carleton University in Ottawa, called the NCC a “band-aid solution” designed to fix the fact that the Canadian constitution didn’t create a capital region structure.

In 1867, as the Canadian constitution was being drafted, Sabin said, there were more important issues that how to carve out special attention for the new country’s capital region. “They had bigger fish to fry.”

Beyond the cost to taxpayers, extra layers of government can also have other unintended consequences. During the 2022 truckers’ convoy protest in downtown Ottawa, for example, Ottawa police were tasked with enforcement, including on NCC property.

There have been no reports of a turf war at that time between the two organizations — the NCC has conservation officers, but no police force — but that doesn’t mean there wasn’t jurisdictional confusion, and more layers of communication required than otherwise would have been the case.

Andrew Sancton, a retired professor from Western University in London, Ont. who specializes in local government, said it’s “reasonable” to want a presentable national capital region for both foreign and domestic visitors.

He said he’s not sure why the NCC isn’t expected to be as open as municipal governments, but that getting rid of it would likely lead to a legal battle over which levels of government would inherit its land.

For the NCC, 24 Sussex represents perhaps its highest profile, and most politically sensitive, project in decades, even though the Carney government has limited the organization’s role in the process.

In April, the Auditor General of Canada reported that the Ncc’s systems and practices showed a “significant deficiency” in its handling of employee safety, and, among other things, that improvements were needed in its managing of assets and capital projects. While those findings likely didn’t help the Ncc’s case to play a bigger role in the 24 Sussex renovation project, Auditor General Karen Hogan also found there were “no significant deficiencies” elsewhere in the Ncc’s systems and operations.

Two months later, Carney announced a competition for the redesign and rebuild of the prime minister’s dilapidated official residence. That competition, which largely ends more than a decade of debate about where Canada’s prime ministers will live, will be led and largely judged by The Royal Architectural Institute of Canada — not the NCC. The institute, which has experience supporting architectural competitions, will review proposals and then make a recommendation to cabinet by July 1 of next year.

The residence, which sits on a 2.1-hectare property overlooking the Ottawa River, has been out of commission since the end of former prime minister Stephen Harper’s government years. The 35-room, 12,000-square-foot residence has suffered over the years from a range of problems. Both Carney and former prime minister Justin Trudeau have lived across the road at Rideau Cottage, ON the governor general’s grounds.

When he announced the competition in June, Carney also said the government will try to reduce the costs of the project by using a non-partisan charity, the Rideau Hall Foundation, to lead a national fundraising campaign to raise as much money as possible.

As of July 27, the fundraising effort, which has a $50-million cap, has received $735,000 in donations from 3,336 Canadians.

Despite being asked to play a limited role in the 24 Sussex reno, there’s little indication that the federal government is considering changing the Ncc’s role or reducing its budget.

Most Ottawa-Gatineau residents, living in a region where the federal government forms the economic base, are less concerned about jurisdictional divisions, and just happy to take advantage of the Ncc’s recreational sites, and other services.

Vino Bhindi, who grew up near Strathcona Park and crosses the pedestrian bridge to get to the Rideau Sports Club, also on NCC land, said the region seems to have a lot of government levels, but that never gets in the way of his tennis matches.

“I don’t feel the politics.”

paragraphs: Ottawa — As he makes his way north through Ottawa’s Strathcona Park, Peter Meggs walks across the Adawe Crossing Bridge, veering away from the connecting path that leads to a parking lot.

Both the connecting path and the pedestrian bridge are municipal jurisdiction. The bridge overlooks the Rideau River, which is provincial responsibility, although the Rideau River Conservation Authority is the river’s watershed agency, which means it manages things such as environmental and flood monitoring.

After crossing the 125-metre bridge, Meggs then hangs a right and joins a smattering of cyclists, dog walkers and step counters for the home stretch along the multi-use pathway of his regular, 5-kilometre loop around his Overbrook neighbourhood. That means he’s now on property run by the National Capital Commission (NCC), the under-the-radar federal body whose mission, according to the organization’s web site, is to help the national capital region be “a dynamic and inspiring source of pride for all Canadians, and a legacy for generations to come.”

Before being turned into a park 119 years ago, Strathcona Park was a swampy floodplain overrun by mud and swarms of mosquitoes. But as Meggs’ brief trek across the bridge suggests, the 15-acre park May now be overrun by swarms of government.

The difference in this regard between the national capital region and other Canadian cities is the NCC. The commission’s critics have for years been asking why the national capital region needs – or perhaps deserves – an extra layer of government and extra source of taxpayer dollars than other Canadian communities.

Those questions have re-emerged in recent months because the Ncc’s profile has jumped over its management of the prime minister’s official residence, uninhabited for more than a decade but now on a path to repair. Some NCC critics are also asking if it’s not time that the commission undergo its own renovation.
The NCC, unlike municipalities, is run by unelected officials who are not directly accountable to the public – and, according to critics, seem fine with it that way.
“You have to accept the good and bad of democracy,” said Meggs, a former town councillor in Cornwall, P.E.I.

But Franco Terrazzano, federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, said the NCC needs greater scrutiny and accountability, in part because it spends and wastes a lot of taxpayers’ money. For example, he said, the crown corporation spent $140,000 to study and design – not build – a staircase, and $1 million for a barn at Rideau Hall, the governor general’s official residence.
“It must be the most incompetent agency in all of Canada — which is saying a lot.”

With the Carney government presumably looking for more cuts in the bureaucracy to help pay for big spending hikes in defence, infrastructure and other priorities, could the NCC be a target for this fall’s upcoming budget?
John Fragos, a spokesman for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said it’s too early in the budget process to speak to any possible cutbacks.

Don Drummond, a former senior official at the Department of Finance and chief economist at TD Bank, said most of the discussions over the years about the NCC have been about democratic reform and transparency, not getting rid of it. For example, Drummond said, folding the NCC into a federal department that May have more experience writing cheques than running programs might be tempting but also might be a bad idea.

Supporters say the NCC, created through a House of Commons vote in 1959, is important because it helps make the National Capital Region – Ottawa and the city of Gatineau, Que. on the other side of the Ottawa River — a special region that all Canadians can be proud of. It brings a national perspective, they argue, to issues that would normally be local.

Results have included a protected Greenbelt on the outskirts of Ottawa, federal parklands and parkways including the popular Gatineau Park, and a wide range of recreational sites, such as cross-country ski trails, walkways, the Rideau Canal skating rink, and public swimming spots along local lakes and rivers — all considered attributes by local residents, and some visitors.

Supporters, such as former Ottawa city councillor Clive Doucet, say the NCC has made an excellent contribution towards presenting the national capital region as the country’s heart, not just another city, in a way that local governments likely wouldn’t.
“It’s been a great success in beautifying Ottawa.”
NCC defenders point out that Canada is by no means the only country that assigns a special government body to giving its capital extra care.

There’s no perfect comparison internationally, but India, France, Australia and Brazil are among those countries that have a federal body with a mandate similar to the NCC. In the U.S., the National Capital Planning Commission (Ncpc) serves as the federal government’s planning agency for Washington, D.C.
But in other ways, the District of Columbia is far from over-governed – or as governed as Canadians in the national capital area.

Unlike Ottawa-Gatineau, D.C. residents are less represented than those in any other part of the U.S. While the city of Washington has a mayor and council, the District is part of no state, which means that it has no governor or state legislature. It also means that D.C. also has just one non-voting representative in the U.S. House of Representatives and no representation in the influential U.S. Senate.

That competition, which largely ends more than a decade of debate about where Canada’s prime ministers will live, will be led and largely judged by The Royal Architectural Institute of Canada — not the NCC. The institute, which has experience supporting architectural competitions, will review proposals and then make a recommendation to cabinet by July 1 of next year.

content_blocks.alt: Mark Carney and Robert Prichard.
content_blocks.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, with board chair of the Rideau Hall Foundation Robert Prichard, leaves a news conference at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa on June 25, 2026. Photo by Blair Gable/Postmedia

content_blocks.text: The residence, which sits on a 2.1-hectare property overlooking the Ottawa River, has been out of commission since the end of former prime minister Stephen Harper’s government years. The 35-room, 12,000-square-foot residence has suffered over the years from a range of problems. Both Carney and former prime minister Justin Trudeau have lived across the road at Rideau Cottage, ON the governor general’s grounds.

When he announced the competition in June, Carney also said the government will try to reduce the costs of the project by using a non-partisan charity, the Rideau Hall Foundation, to lead a national fundraising campaign to raise as much money as possible.
As of July 27, the fundraising effort, which has a $50-million cap, has received $735,000 in donations from 3,336 Canadians.
Despite being asked to play a limited role in the 24 Sussex reno, there’s little indication that the federal government is considering changing the Ncc’s role or reducing its budget.

Most Ottawa-Gatineau residents, living in a region where the federal government forms the economic base, are less concerned about jurisdictional divisions, and just happy to take advantage of the Ncc’s recreational sites, and other services.

Vino Bhindi, who grew up near Strathcona Park and crosses the pedestrian bridge to get to the Rideau Sports Club, also on NCC land, said the region seems to have a lot of government levels, but that never gets in the way of his tennis matches.

stories.title: The troubled Nova Scotia ferry that had a massive comeback — but still might not survive
stories.summary: There is still no contract for 'The Cat' – the Yarmouth-based ferry that runs between Nova Scotia and Bar Harbor, Maine – to operate next year.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Yarmouth, N.S. – As the busy summer-fall tourism season winds down, there is still no contract for “The Cat” – the Yarmouth-based ferry that runs between Nova Scotia and Bar Harbor, Maine – to operate next year.

“I think it’s important that there are real signals to operators and the tourism industry at large, that the government, our province and the officials will have a deal in place,” said Yarmouth and Acadian Shores Tourism Association CEO Neil MacKenzie. “People who are booking travel need to know that the service will be here and they can plan their vacation ahead of time.”

The final crossing for the ferry will be Oct. 14. This year, through July, Mackenzie said ferry ridership is up nearly 30 per cent, compared to 2025.

The vessel is run by Bay Ferries Ltd., which is headquartered in Charlottetown and operates the ferry service through a contract with the U.S. Navy.

CTV News also reached out to the U.S. Navy, but they were unable to provide a response at this time.

Nova Scotia’s Public Works Minister Fred Tilley recently told reporters he is hopeful that a new long-term ferry contract could soon be signed, but did not offer any details related to the negotiations.

Sixteen years ago, Dalhousie University business professor Lorn Sheehan served on a panel that examined the Yarmouth ferry strategy.

“It was really a broad engagement of stakeholders around the economic realities of having that ferry,” said Sheehan, who speculated the trade tensions between Canada and the U.S. could be possibly slowing down contract negotiations.

“I think part of the reason that the delay is occurring, is because of the uncertainty in the trade environment,” said Sheehan. “Economically on balance, I think this ferry makes sense.”

According to the town’s mayor, the ferry is a job creator for Yarmouth.

“You’re talking about an entire season of folks going to the gas station, going to the restaurants, shopping in the shops,” said Yarmouth Mayor Pam Mood.

For those examining the overall financial viability of the ferry, Sheehan urged people to look at the economic impact for the entire province, not just Yarmouth and the surrounding area.

“It’s obviously important to Yarmouth, but it is also spread out throughout the whole province,” said Sheehan. “When Americans come across, it’s rare that they come to Yarmouth, and go back to Maine. They will go to the wine region in Nova Scotia, Halifax or visit Cape Breton and all these communities enjoy benefit from the ferry.”

MacKenzie said a new contract needs to be signed soon, or the province could lose a lot of tourism business in 2027.

“We know that visitors stay and travel around the province, we know that they are here on average seven or eight days, and we know they are spending more than $3,000 per party,” said MacKenzie.

There have been previous interruptions in the ferry crossings between Nova Scotia and Maine. The province cancelled its subsidy to Bay Ferries in 2009, which halted service until 2014. The ferry was also idle during the COVID-19 pandemic because of international travel restrictions.
