stories.title: The Stunt Driver is the latest film from London-born filmmaker Michael Dowse
stories.summary: The Stunt Driver tells the true story of daredevil Ken Carter, also known as "The Mad Canadian" and his rivalry with Evel Knievel.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: The Stunt Driver tells the true story of daredevil Ken Carter, also known as "The Mad Canadian" and his rivalry with Evel Knievel.
· Posted: Sep 27, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
The Toronto International Film Festival (Tiff) has wrapped up, and for those who missed out, some of those films are making their way to theatre screens across southwestern Ontario.
Among them is The Stunt Driver. It's the latest film from London, Ont.,-born filmmaker Michael Dowse, who is known for his work on Fubar and The F Word.

The Stunt Driver tells the true story of daredevil Ken Carter, also known as "The Mad Canadian," and his rivalry with Evel Knievel. In 1976, Carter set out to make a mile-long jump across the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered Lincoln Continental.
The film is coming to theatres on Friday and will be screened at the Forest City Film Festival in October.
Dowse spoke with Afternoon Drive guest host Josette Lafleur.
The following has been edited for length and clarity.
Josette Lafleur: What was it like seeing your film on the world stage at Tiff?
Michael Dowse: It was amazing. It was like a culmination of a 10- to 12-year journey of seeing the doc [The Devil at Your Heels] and falling in love with it, and then getting the rights.
A lot of work went into it, but it was really incredible to share it with the world, to screen it to a crowd, and to screen it to a lot of the people that helped me make it. Incredibly satisfying.
LISTEN | Michael Dowse discusses 'The Stunt Driver':
Afternoon Drive 6:59 The Stunt Drive: The Ken Carter Story

The Stunt Drive is a film telling the true story of The Mad Canadian, Ken Carter. Director Michael Dowse joins Afternoon Drive to share how he told the incredible daredevil story as it hits movie screens.
JL: What was it about Ken Carter's story that intrigued you so much?

MD: I think the first thing was just the physical scale of it. When you first even just look up the documentary, you see this massive ramp and this huge yellow car with wings, and you see something that looks impossible.

I was immediately intrigued by this crazy story that I'd never heard about that had happened in Canada — and this idea that when Evel Knievel was at the height of his fame, there was a Canadian guy that was sort of living in his shadow, trying to make his own mark. So that immediately spoke to me.

But then, when you watch the documentary that this film was based on, The Devil at Your Heels, and you get to know the real Ken Carter through that documentary. He's an incredible person. He's riddled with contradictions, like all of us. He's incredibly brave, optimistic, and just a real believer.

I think everybody has a bit of Ken Carter inside of them. Everybody has their own version of a 90-foot ramp and a two-tonne rocket car. I think people can get a lot out of this film and out of Ken's story.
JL: Through your research, what did you discover about Ken that drove him to this level of risk?
MD: I think he was a man who was obviously brave. He's a guy who comes from nothing and sort of fell into the mechanics' world. Then he joined the circus stunt team and travelled the world.

By the time this documentary captures him, he's around 37 years old. He's broken every bone in his body and still hasn't quite made his mark. So, he was a man who really wanted to prove to everybody what he could do — and for everybody to remember his name.

I think we can all understand that feeling, as you get older, that you wanna you wanna leave a legacy, and hopefully this film does a small part in terms of cementing his legacy and shining a spotlight on the story and who this man was.
JL: What does it mean to you to be able to bring these stories of lesser-known Canadians to the big screen?
MD: It's less about it being Canadian. It's just a great story.
Because it was Canadian, we knew we could raise some money to do it, so they sort of complemented each other beautifully. But for me, the story is universal.
I'm proud to tell a Canadian story, but it's never anything I try to lead with.
JL: This film is coming to the Forest City Film Festival in October. There will also be a theatrical release this Friday, is that right?
MD: Yes, it's coming out this Friday in Canada, and then in the United States. We're excited that it got a theatrical release. It's a rare thing these days and we think the film deserves it.
It's a really unique story driven by a fantastic performance by Jay Baruchel, who really puts the film on his back and and embodies the Ken Carter story.

I'm excited for everybody to see it and hopefully it gets some traction. Because of what's been happening right now, I think people are really hungry to support a Canadian-grown and Canadian-born story.

stories.title: Meet the London family who made libraries their must-see travel destination
stories.summary: A London, Ont., family has turned library visits into a travel tradition, visiting 50 libraries across Canada, the U.S. and India, and they aren't stopping there.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A London, Ont., family has turned library visits into a travel tradition, visiting 50 libraries across Canada, the U.S. and India, and they aren't stopping there.
· Posted: Sep 27, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
The Nagpal family visit a library in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia on a road trip to Eastern Canada.(Submitted)
For some, the perfect vacation means hunting down the best local coffee shops, exploring a new trail or checking out the nightlife.
For one London, Ont., family, it's all about libraries.
The Nagpal family has made a tradition of visiting libraries wherever they travel — and this summer, they reached a milestone: their 50th library.
Guneet Kaur Nagpal and her husband, Robin, first started visiting libraries together about two decades ago while they were studying in India.
When they moved to the U.S. for school and eventually to Canada in 2013, they kept seeking out libraries along the way.
"We had less money, less to do, but still the library [was] a lot of fun," he said. "It just feels home to us, like a second home."
London, Ont., family Robin, Avraj, Guneet and Nehmat Nagpal pose outside the Grand Falls Public Library in New Brunswick. (Submitted)
That tradition only grew after their children were born, Guneet said. Now, whenever the family travels, they look for local libraries and make sure to spend some time there.
"Naturally we both liked it, and it has also played a huge part in our lives," Robin said.
It wasn't until Guneet decided to make a list of all the libraries they had visited that she realized the number was already more than 40.
"That's when it occurred to me: let's make it a deal as a family and try to reach 50 as a number," she said.
This summer, the family took a 5,000-kilometre road trip through Eastern Canada, stopping at libraries in Quebec, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
They wanted their 50th stop to be something special.
They chose Maison de la littérature in Quebec City — or House of Literature — a library and cultural space housed in a renovated building filled with books and art installations.
The space is home to 25,000 works of Quebec literature and hosts cultural and creative programming, according to the library.
A crafted whale hangs from the ceiling of the children's section at the Bibliothèque de Montmagny in Montmagny, Que. (Submitted)
Back home in London, the family has visited almost every branch of the London Public Library.

One of Guneet's favourite spots is the reading garden at the Central Branch. The family has also visited libraries in St. Thomas and explored others across southern Ontario, from Paris to Wasaga Beach and Collingwood.
For eight-year-old Avraj, it's the books — especially graphic novels — that keep him coming back.
His six-year-old sister, Nehmat, also loves reading and spending time at libraries.
Robin said public libraries offer much more than books. He sees them as important community spaces for new parents, children, newcomers and anyone looking to learn something new.
"I think there are a lot of countries who could learn a lot about how Canada is using and maintaining its library infrastructure, which is providing benefits for so many people," he said.
And the Nagpals aren't stopping at 50.
They're already planning their next library visits, with stops around Parry Sound on the itinerary for an upcoming camping trip.
For this family, the library isn't just a place to visit, it's part of the journey.

Guneet Kaur Nagpal and her family love visiting libraries. They join Afternoon Drive after visiting their milestone 50th library to share their experience with guest host Josette Lafleur.

stories.title: Can you turn left from a lane with a straight arrow?
stories.summary: Those arrows at intersections aren’t just helpful pointers – they’re usually showing you your only option
stories.author: Jason Tchir
stories.content:
An intersection near my condo has three lanes: a left-turning lane, a lane for going straight and a right-turning lane. Each lane has a sign with an arrow showing what you should do. I was in a line of cars waiting to turn left in the left-turning lane on the green light when a car bypassed us on the right and made the left turn from the lane with the straight arrow. A car in front of me in the left-turn lane made a wide turn and the two cars nearly hit each other – there was a lot of honking. Don’t you have to do what the arrows on the signs say? – Ted, Mississauga

Those arrows at intersections aren’t just helpful pointers – they’re usually showing you your only option.

“If a lane is designated [as] straight through, that’s the movement drivers are expected to make from that lane,” said Sean Shapiro, a road safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop. “If there is a dedicated left-turning lane and you make the left turn from the through lane beside it, that can absolutely result in a charge.”

In Ontario, the law states that when there are designated lanes, drivers “shall obey the instructions on the official signs.”

But even if there aren’t signs for a designated turning lane – or lanes – you’re supposed to turn from the leftmost lane.

If you turn left from the wrong lane, you could face charges including making an improper left turn, Shapiro said. That comes with an $85 fine – $120 in a community safety zone – and two demerit points . With fees, that comes to $110 or $150.

If the move is dangerous, you could also be charged with careless driving, which comes with a $400 fine – $490 with fees – and six demerits.

Typically, when there are signs with arrows, there are also painted arrows on the pavement. Sometimes, the arrows May show that you can make more than one move – for example, they May show that you can go straight or turn left.

Also, if the lane has a straight arrow, you shouldn’t be turning right from it either.

While the rules vary by province, they generally require you to obey signs and to turn from a designated left-turning lane – or if there isn’t one, the leftmost lane.

But the law aside, making a left turn from the straight lane is confusing to other drivers around you.

“Signs, signals and pavement markings allow us to anticipate what another driver is going to do,” Angelo DiCicco, chief executive officer of the Ontario Safety League, a non-profit which focuses on driver education, said in an email. “If I’m beside you in a lane designated for a left turn and you’re in a lane designated to proceed straight, I’m making decisions based partly on the reasonable expectation that you’re going straight.”

So, for example, that driver turning left next to the lane that goes straight has no reason to expect that a car will be turning there – so they likely won’t be looking out for you.

“It creates a conflict that other drivers aren’t expecting,” Shapiro said.

It doesn’t matter why you’re turning from the wrong lane, he said. Maybe you’re trying to “bypass the lineup” of cars waiting to turn. Or maybe you just ended up in the wrong lane by mistake.

“Traffic law doesn’t give you a free pass because you missed your lane,” Shapiro said. “[But] if someone realizes late that they’re in the wrong lane, signals, safely changes completely into the turning lane and then makes the turn, that’s different. They May have poor planning skills, but they haven’t necessarily committed an improper turn.”

stories.title: The Tragically Hip, Feist to be inducted into Canadian Songwriters Hall of fame
stories.summary: The artists will be celebrated at a star-studded Toronto gala featuring tributes from Jeff Tweedy, Finneas, Our Lady Peace and others
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Toronto’s indie music scene mainstay Feist and Kingston, Ont., alt-rock legends The Tragically Hip are among the musical acts who will be inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame during a star-studded gala on Saturday night.

Feist, whose first name is Leslie but is more commonly known by her last name alone, says it was surreal to have her songwriting honoured especially because writing songs begins as such a private act.

She says ahead of the show held at Toronto’s Massey Hall that she doesn’t know of any other event that celebrates the “quiet part” of songwriting, so it “does mean a lot.”

Feist talks Heated Rivalry, iPod ads and hit covers ahead of induction into Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame

Wilco lead singer Jeff Tweedy and Los Angeles songwriter-producer Finneas are set to perform some of Feist’s music. Finneas, who is Billie Eilish’s brother and collaborator, will also induct the singer, known for the hits 1234 and You and I , an acoustic duet with Tweedy.

Meanwhile, Our Lady Peace and City and Colour are among the artists performing songs by The Hip, while actor and filmmaker Jay Baruchel will induct the band into the Hall of Fame.

The Hip bassist Gord Sinclair says it’s special to be inducted as a band.

“That group dynamic and the way we wrote together was the most important thing that we did,” he says while standing alongside bandmates Rob Baker and Paul Langlois on the red carpet.

“We literally went around in a circle and bounced ideas off of each other. To be recognized for that, obviously we’re missing a huge part of our circle. But yeah, it really, really does mean a lot.”

Band frontman Gord Downie died in 2017.

Baruchel says the opportunity to induct The Hip into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame is a unique honour.

“As someone that was raised to believe that this is the best country in the world, it was always pretty special to me to have a band, a group of artists that were unconditionally Canadian and didn’t have aspirations to be anything but that,” Baruchel says. “And that told me that I could be that, too.”

Fellow inductees also include the songwriting partners behind Loverboy, Mike Reno and Paul Dean, as well as French-Canadian singer-songwriter Roch Voisine.

Other performers scheduled to take the stage include Allison Russell, Charlotte Cornfield and Amanda Marshall, who walked the red carpet wearing a T-shirt with “Loverboy” written across the front. The Canadian singer-songwriter is set to perform the rock band’s 1980 hit Turn Me Loose .

“It seemed only fitting that a woman sing this song because this genre, this kind of music, is very kind of hyper-masculine,” Marshall says. “It seemed fitting that a woman sing it and that I be that woman.”

Longtime Drake producer Boi-1da is slated to make a special appearance to pay tribute to The Hip. Also on hand as inductors are songwriter Jim Vallance and Olympic hockey gold medallists Marie-Philip Poulin and Laura Stacey.

The ceremony will be hosted by broadcaster George Stroumboulopoulos and singer Marie-Mai.

It will also be live-streamed globally via the Amazon Music Twitch channel and on Prime Video in Canada.

stories.title: ‘We’re in a rush’: Ottawa businesses want Canada-U.S. trade war resolved
stories.summary: Businesses on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border are feeling the effects of an ongoing trade dispute, even as the Trump administration signals it is comfortable with the status quo.
stories.author: Jeremie Charron
stories.content:
Ottawa — Businesses on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border are feeling the effects of an ongoing trade dispute, even as the Trump administration signals it is comfortable with the status quo.

At Infinity Flooring in Ottawa, tariffs have hit a large portion of the carpet products the family-owned business sells.

“It’s all tariffed,” said Heidi Gagne, co-owner and managing director of the store as she pointed to a large display of products.

Products from major American suppliers are now facing tariffs ranging from 25 to 50 per cent, depending on the materials used, Gagne said.

Some orders have increased by thousands of dollars, while Canadian alternatives are limited and in high demand.

“We could run into shortages as this progresses,” said Gagne.

The uncertainty is adding pressure to businesses that rely on cross-border supply chains.

“We’re in a rush, we want to see it resolved,” said Gloria Beaucaire, a sales representative who has worked at the store for more than two decades.

“We have employees, we have people who depend on people coming into our store.”

But while Canadian businesses are eager for a resolution, the Trump administration has indicated there is little urgency to reach a new trade agreement.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week that there is no rush to reach a deal and that U.S. President Donald Trump is comfortable with the current situation.

Kelly Anne Shaw, a former senior White House trade adviser under Trump, said Canada and the U.S. appear to have very different views of the current state of the relationship.

“The United States and Canada seem to be living in two different alternative realities about what the politics are, what the situation is,” Shaw said.

Shaw said the Trump administration believes Prime Minister Mark Carney was the one who walked away from a potential agreement and that Canada would need to make the request to return to the negotiating table.

Communication between Canadian and U.S. officials continues, but formal trade negotiations remain paused.

“The relationship is not in a great place, there are no formal negotiations,” said William Pelerin, an international trade lawyer with McMillan LLP in Ottawa.

Back at Infinity Flooring, the uncertainty is one of the biggest concerns for Gagne, who only recently took over the family business.

“We would like to see this resolved,” Gagne said. “I think it’s ridiculous that what’s going on is going on.”

Washington is also set to impose its latest round of trade measures Tuesday, including an import ban affecting a list of Canadian goods ranging from alcohol and dairy products to motorcycles.

For businesses like Infinity Flooring, the hope is that the uncertainty won’t last much longer.

stories.title: P.E.I. joins Alberta with fuel-tax break amid high gas and diesel prices
stories.summary: Filling the tank cost a little less for Islanders Saturday, with a pause on the provincial fuel tax taking effect for the next four months.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Borden-Carleton, P.E.I. - Filling the tank cost a little less for Islanders Saturday, with a pause on the provincial fuel tax taking effect for the next four months.

The break comes days after Alberta announced its own fuel-tax suspension, as high-energy costs add to affordability pressures. P.E.I.’s suspension takes 8.47 cents per litre off gasoline and 14.15 cents per litre off diesel. Premier Rob Lantz announced the changes Friday.

“It’s a little bit lower than it was yesterday,” said Peter Mullins at a gas station in Borden-Carleton. “It’s about five dollars a tank difference, so I can buy a coffee or two with the extra.”

But there was still pain at the pump.

“This is the worst price of gas we’ve witnessed in a very long time,” said another customer. “You cannot save any money.”

Ottawa has introduced legislation to continue its fuel excise tax holiday through Jan. 31, which could keep 10 cents per litre off gasoline and four cents off diesel.

P.E.I.’s reprieve will last until the same date, before it returns at 50 per cent of its regular rate on Feb. 1, and then is fully restored April 1.

“Fuel costs touch almost everything on our Island, from the commute to work to the price of goods delivered to store shelves,” Finance and Affordability Minister Jill Burridge said in a release. “Global markets are driving prices up, and Islanders shouldn’t have to face that alone.”

Straining industries reliant on gas

The gasoline reduction will be felt by many, said Ian Lee, associate professor at Carleton University’s Sprott School of Business.

“You see the prices going up, and you’re reminded every time you fill up your car,” he said. “That’s what I think makes it so toxic to us the citizens and to the ministers who realize they are becoming the target of the anger.”

The strain is particularly acute for industries that depend on diesel.

Hundreds of dump-truck drivers convoyed into Vancouver on Friday to protest record-high diesel prices.

The Vancouver area has the highest fuel-tax rates in the country. According to Natural Resources Canada the provincial comparison is 27 cents per litre on gasoline and 27.5 cents per litre on diesel.

While tax cuts could mean lower expenses for truckers and their companies, in P.E.I., the impact will be “trivial” on the cost of goods Lee said.

“This is more symbolic and political so that the government can say look, people, we hear your pain, we care about you. We’re sensitive to your suffering and this is what we’re doing,” he said. “But it’s not going to move the needle on retail prices.”

That’s because the Island’s tax on diesel accounted for about five per cent of its retail price before the pause, he said. Freight, in turn, makes up only a small share of what consumers ultimately pay for a product.

Outside B.C., Quebec has the highest provincial fuel-tax rates, at 19.2 cents per litre on gasoline and 20.2 cents on diesel. Nova Scotia charges 15.5 cents and 15.4 cents respectively, while Saskatchewan charges 15 cents on both.

Alberta, meanwhile, will drop its 13-cent-per-litre fuel tax to zero starting Oct. 1.

stories.title: 4 killed after helicopter crashes in field near Montreal
stories.summary: Four people have died in a helicopter crash in Montérégie, Que., in the Rang des Écossais area. It crashed into a field in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Four people have died in a helicopter crash in Montérégie, Que., in the Rang des Écossais area.

A spokesperson for the Sûreté du Québec (SQ) says the incident happened just after 2:30 p.m. Saturday.

The helicopter crashed into a field in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, southeast of Montreal.

The chopper caught fire, but police say it’s unclear if the fire began in the air or as a result of the crash.

Fire crews had the blaze under control within an hour.

The SQ says four occupants were declared dead at the scene.

The force’s major crime unit is investigating the incident, and the Transportation Safety Board of Canada has been notified.

stories.title: Four dead in helicopter crash near Montreal
stories.summary: Crash happened in Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, 50 kilometres southeast of Montreal
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Four people have died in a helicopter crash in Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, 50 kilometres southeast of Montreal, according to provincial police.

A spokesperson says police were called to the scene around 2:30 p.m. on Saturday.

They found the crashed aircraft on fire and later discovered the bodies of the four occupants, who were declared dead at the scene.

The provincial police have not yet identified the victims nor the cause of the crash.

The spokesperson says the helicopter seems to have been a private aircraft.

She says the investigation is ongoing and the Transportation Safety Board of Canada has sent investigators to the crash site.

stories.title: Thousands of students party under watchful eye of police; Western beats McMaster during homecoming weekend
stories.summary: Thousands of students packed Broughdale Avenue and Huron Street under the watchful eye of London Police during Homecoming weekend at Western University.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Thousands of students packed Broughdale Avenue and Huron Street under the watchful eye of London Police during Homecoming weekend at Western University.

‘It’s like Christmas,” said Hunter Ellis, a fourth-year student who has lived on Broughdale for three years.

“It’s the biggest party school in Canada.”

The street is the epicentre of the weekend party.

“It’s the best holiday ever,” said roommate Douglas Bond.

“We try to keep the house a little tame, but it gets a little messed up. It’s fun to see the whole school come together.”

Members of the London Police Service (LPS) along with paramedics and firefighters were all stationed along Audrey Street between Broughdale and Huron.

“We have additional officers from Windsor, from Hamilton, as well as the OPP assisting us on the ground here in relation to any of the unsanctioned gatherings that take place,” said Sgt. Sandasha Bough of the LPS.

This year the City of London put up barricades along Richmond Street and closed one of the southbound lanes to keep students away from traffic.

“We’ve closed at least one of the lanes on Richmond to ensure public safety,” said Bough.

“We’ve put some additional closures in and around Broughdale and Audrey to ensure that everybody who is out here gathering stays off of the roadway to ensure public safety as well.”

Across campus a much more subdued party was being held outside Alumni Stadium. Current and former cheerleaders were gathering for a tailgate party.

“It really is just a purple and proud moment,” said former National Champion cheerleader Michelle Brock.

On the way into the stadium, London Mayor Josh Morgan – a Western University graduate – stopped to tell CTV News what Homecoming means to him.

“I came here in 1998, and actually, it was my reason for coming to the city and I never left,” said Morgan, who came from outside the Sarnia-area to attend school.

“I ended up becoming the mayor, so Homecoming is a nice reminder to see old friends and where my story in London really began.”

More than 10,000 people witnessed London, Ont. wide receiver Emmett Charles haul in three touchdowns in the second quarter as the Mustangs won to improve to 4-0 this year.

Back at Broughdale Avenue, LPS were keeping a close eye on the activity. Bough told CTV News that information on incidents will be released in the coming days.

“We will collect information from our community partners throughout the weekend and hopefully at the beginning of next week at some point, we’ll be able to share those numbers with you,” said Bough.

Just after 4 p.m., the London police declared the festivities on Broughdale Avenue a nuisance party. Partygoers were asked to clear the area by police.

More photos of the weekend are available in CTV London’s photo galleries .

stories.title: $1 million donation to expand LHSC’s cardiac care
stories.summary: Andy and Helen Spriet have donated $1 million to London Health Sciences Centre to expand cardiac care.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Andy and Helen Spriet have donated $1 million to London Health Sciences Centre to expand cardiac care. The funds will go towards bringing a third Electrophysiology (EP) Lab to University Hospital. The third lab is part of a $6.5 million campaign to expand and modernize cardiac care.

“We’ve been fortunate to call London home for so many years, and we know how important it is to have the right care available when you need it,” said the Spriets. “When we learned more about the need for a third EP Lab, it was a project we felt strongly about supporting.

Most importantly, it will help improve timely access to life-changing cardiac procedures, reduce wait times, and enhance the overall patient experience.”

stories.title: Lawyer wins case against multinational firm behind day school settlement
stories.summary: A First Nations lawyer who started the quest for justice for day school survivors has won a lawsuit against a firm regarding compensation for her work.
stories.author: Melissa Ridgen
stories.content:
A First Nations lawyer who launched the legal fight for day school survivors before the file was turned over to a larger law firm as a class-action, has won a lawsuit against that firm.

Joan Jack filed the statement of claim for a group of day school survivors in 2009.

Gowling WLG took over the file in 2016 using work Jack and other lawyers had done, including a database of 12,500 potential class action members.

Gowling got a $1.5 billion settlement for day school survivors and were paid $55 million in legal fees.

Manitoba Judge Shauna McCarthy in a 46-page ruling found Gowling “had a contractual and fiduciary duty to present the plaintiffs’ fees to the Federal Court for approval with respect to work asserted to have been done by the plaintiffs in advancing the day school claims” and that “Gowling breached their obligations to do so.”

The six-year David versus Goliath battle “was hard” says Jack, and she feels “vindicated” by the ruling.

“Every human being wants to be recognized for their contribution in life and for us as Indigenous people, so often our contributions are erased, changed, ignored,” Jack said. “And so in that space, I feel very joyful.”

Gowling managing partner Lorraine Mastersmith said “we have significant concerns with elements of the judgment and are reviewing the decision to determine our next steps.”

How much Gowling will pay will be determined at a later date.

Nearly 200,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children attended more than 700 Indian day schools beginning in the 1920s. Many endured physical and sexual abuse at the federally-run schools. Under the settlement agreement, Canada compensated each eligible survivor between $10,000 and $200,000.

stories.title: Suspect wanted in hit-and-run involving a cyclist
stories.summary: A suspect is wanted by the Owen Sound police in connection with a hit-and-run involving a cyclist.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A suspect is wanted by the Owen Sound police in connection with a hit-and-run involving a cyclist.

On Saturday around 7 a.m., police were called to the incident at the intersection of 10th Street East and 1st Avenue East.

Officers believe the car is a dark-coloured Cadillac sedan with damage to the front, passenger-side corner. That includes a broken headlight, and it is believed to be missing the passenger side mirror.

After the crash, the Osps said the vehicle did not try to stop and drove westbound on 10th Street West.

The cyclist was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Police are asking anyone with information or dash cam footage of the incident to contact Const. Kinal at 215@owensoundpolice.com

stories.title: Kids starting a fire, taking a vehicle set off warning from Mounties in B.C.
stories.summary: Police say a seven-year-old boy found a small blow torch in his home on Sept. 18, managed to connect it to a propane cylinder and started a fire inside his home.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Mounties in Mission, B.C., are reminding parents just how “resourceful” children can be after separate situations last week.

Police say a seven-year-old boy found a small blow torch in his home on Sept. 18, managed to connect it to a propane cylinder and started a fire inside his home.

The local fire department attended and put out what police say was a small blaze.

The second incident, which happened the same day, involved a four-year-old boy who took the keys to his parents’ Cadillac Escalade and climbed inside.

The RCMP says Cctv footage confirmed the boy started the Cadillac and drove it into two parked cars that were nearby.

No one was hurt, but police say in a news release that parents should look around their homes and consider what they could do in order to reduce the risks.

stories.title: 10 women Huron-Bruce women recognized for Rural Ontario Week
stories.summary: 10 women have been recognized by Huron-Bruce MPP Lisa Thompson for their contributions to agriculture in their communities, part of Rural Ontario Week.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
10 women have been recognized by Huron-Bruce MPP Lisa Thompson for their contributions to agriculture in their communities, part of Rural Ontario Week.

The women recognized were Tara Terpstra, Emily Morrison, Carol Leeming, Miranda Klaver, Margaret Vincent, Becky Maus, Kristie Gilchrist, Barb Zettler, Amanda Hammell, and Christine MacIntyre.

“Women have always been an integral part of agriculture and rural life here in Huron-Bruce, and this year provides a special opportunity to recognize the women who continue to strengthen our farms, businesses, and communities,” Thompson said.

“I am proud to recognize these 10 women for their leadership, dedication, and hard work they bring to our rural communities. Their contributions are helping build a strong future for agriculture and rural Ontario.”

Rural Ontario Week runs Sept. 20 to Sept. 26.

stories.title: 2 teens charged with murder in connection to pedestrian collision that killed 16-year-old
stories.summary: Two teens from Guelph, Ont. are facing second-degree murder charges in connection to a fatal pedestrian collision last weekend that claimed the life of 16-year-old boy.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Two teens from Guelph, Ont. are facing second-degree murder charges in connection with a fatal pedestrian collision last weekend that claimed the life of a 16-year-old boy.

Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and paramedics responded to the collision, which involved a minivan, ON Wellington Road 29, south of Eramosa-Garafraxa Town Line just after midnight last Saturday.

The victim has been identified as a teen from Puslinch Township, OPP said.

According to police, officers arrested two 17-year-old boys on Friday. Both were held in custody and are scheduled to appear in Ontario Court of Justice in Guelph on Saturday.

Their identities are protected under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

Anyone with information about this investigation is asked to contact the Wellington County OPP at 1-888-310-1122 or submit a tip anonymously through Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Parts of Nova Scotia national park closed temporarily after coyote bite: Parks Canada
stories.summary: In a social media post, the parks agency says the MacIntosh Brook area where the incident happened has been temporarily closed.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
Parts of a national park in northern Nova Scotia have been closed after a visitor was bitten by a coyote.

Parks Canada says the bite occurred in the Cape Breton Highlands National Park on Thursday evening.

In a social media post, the parks agency says the MacIntosh Brook area where the incident happened has been temporarily closed.

The post says the Lone Shieling trail and pull-offs in the surrounding area have also been closed as staff assess the situation.

Parks Canada says it will provide updates when more information is available.

Coyote attacks in the park are not uncommon but are rarely fatal.

stories.title: After Canada stopped using solitary confinement, it made an exception for these prisoners
stories.summary: Years after its segregation practices were supposedly halted, Canada still uses other forms of isolation on certain prisoners.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
It is Nov. 5, 2024. Over the course of half an hour, a hand-held camera follows Joey Toutsaint as prison guards forcibly remove him from a cell, then lead him through a hall, across a yard and into another building. The camera captures him pleading.

“I’m not going to the observation cell. No. You guys are making a mistake. Put me back in my cell.”

At one point, he weeps. “I won’t self-harm … I give you my word. On my mother’s grave. On my daughter’s life…. I don’t want to live like this no more.”

“I recognize you have mental health issues,” an officer says at one point.

The prison guards lead Toutsaint, wrapped in a blanket after a strip search, into the observation cell.

“As you can see on camera,” one of the officers says to the person filming before the camera is turned off, “we had some challenges with Mr. Toutsaint and wanting to submit to going into the observation cell.”

Observation cells are bare rooms subject to 24/7 surveillance in which prisoners such as Toutsaint are placed, dressed in a sleeveless, untearable smock and sometimes without a blanket or mattress, when they have tried to harm themselves or are suspected of intending to do so.

Another variant on these isolation cells is the “dry cell,” which is similarly bare but lacks plumbing or running water. It’s used when prison staff want someone to excrete something they are suspected of having swallowed or hidden in their body, such as drugs.

Canada does not call these cells solitary confinement.

But their use meets a definition of solitary under international rules — to which Canada has agreed — that are meant to minimize the use of such isolation.

What are known as the “Mandela Rules” define solitary confinement as 22 hours a day or more without meaningful human contact, and define prolonged solitary confinement as a period exceeding 15 consecutive days. The rules say solitary confinement should only be used “in exceptional cases as a last resort” and should be “prohibited in the case of prisoners with mental or physical disabilities when their conditions would be exacerbated by such measures.”

Yet the use of observation cells and dry cells has been rising, according to data obtained by the Investigative Journalism Bureau through access-to-information requests.

The number of times Canadian prisons used observation cells rose from 859 in 2018 to 1,316 in 2024 — a 53 per cent increase. In total, observation cells were used more than 8,000 times between 2018 and November 2025, CSC data show.

The number of times Canadian prisons used dry cells rose from 160 in 2022 to 291 in 2024 — an 82 per cent increase. Dry cells were used almost 700 times between 2022 and 2024.

Observation and dry cells can be used for indefinite periods in Canada. The prisoner has no immediate means of appeal.

“It doesn’t really matter what the correctional service calls these cells or units or ranges,” former correctional investigator and current Canadian Civil Liberties Association head Howard Sapers said. “The fact of the matter is they operate like segregation, where people are locked down, locked in their cells, often for 24 hours a day, sometimes for 23 or 22….

“The fact that we don’t have the words ‘solitary confinement’ in our law does not mean that solitary confinement does not, in fact, take place.”

In observation cells, and in other special sections of prisons reserved for people deemed unsafe in the general population, Sapers says, Canadian federal prisoners are “being dealt (with) in a way that’s off the books, frankly.”

It doesn't really matter what the correctional service calls these cells or units or ranges. The fact of the matter is they operate like segregation Howard Sapers, Canadian Civil Liberties Association head

Correctional Service Canada says placements like Toutsaint’s “must be used appropriately, humanely, and with strong oversight” and only “when less restrictive interventions cannot adequately manage an imminent risk of self-harm or suicide.” CSC spokesperson Laurence Côté said prisons conduct health team assessments and case reviews of these placements, but the head of the prison makes the final call.

Observation cells and dry cells are needed to keep prisons safe, says Frederick Lebeau, president of the federal correctional officers’ union.

“When an inmate is acting out and he’s trying to commit suicide, sometimes we’ve got to protect them from themselves.”

While dry cell use could be replaced by tools such as body scanners, he said, observation cells will continue to be necessary “to save lives.”

The IJB obtained 53 videos, about five hours’ worth of footage, shot in and around observation cells — videos legal aid organization Prisoners Legal Services obtained through federal Privacy Act requests.

The videos show how the cells are used and the force — tackling and handcuffing, pepper-spraying or tying down — employed to manage prisoners’ behaviour during transportation to and from these cells.

The IJB reviewed the Privacy Act request through which Prisoners Legal Services obtained the videos. Correctional Service Canada would not comment on their veracity.

Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada’s public safety minister, Gary Anandasangaree, did not respond to requests for an interview.

Sometimes we’ve got to protect them from themselves Frederick Lebeau, president of the federal correctional officers’ union

The IJB found that Indigenous prisoners like Toutsaint are more likely than white people to be put in an observation cell.

The number of Indigenous men placed in observation cells annually more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, to 674 from 284, a period during which the number of white men placed in observation cells increased by about 5.6 per cent, to 397 from 376.

“CSC regularly reviews trends in the use of observation measures, including among Indigenous offenders, and continues to strengthen culturally responsive mental health services and Indigenous-specific interventions,” said Côté, the agency’s spokesperson.

There are also significant disparities by institution. The prison with the highest use of observation cells is one designed to meet the needs of mentally ill inmates: Saskatoon’s Regional Psychiatric Centre.

“Enhanced observation May be used more frequently at the Regional Psychiatric Centre because it serves offenders with complex mental health needs,” Csc’s Côté said.

A federal policy directive authorizes the use of “enhanced observation” in cases of suicidality, self-harm or severe mental illness with a serious impairment. It is only to be used as a last resort, according to the federal directive and instructions to officers the IJB reviewed.

It's easier just to lock people in Catherine Latimer, head of the John Howard Society

In 2021, a Nova Scotia court deemed dry cells “a unique form of solitary confinement” after a woman spent more than 15 days in one, based on suspicions that she was smuggling contraband in her vagina. As a result of that ruling, the use of dry cells federally has been narrowed.

“(Dry cells) are only used as a last resort when there are reasonable grounds to believe that an inmate has ingested or is carrying contraband in either their digestive system or in their rectum, and not in an inmate’s vagina,” Côté said.

Since 2019-20, the CSC said, it has seized weapons or drugs more than 400 times following a dry cell placement.

The proliferation of unofficial forms of isolation, such as observation and dry cells, could be the result of a correctional mindset that seeks to deal with immediate security risks in the simplest way possible, Sapers said. Or, “it could very well be that it’s a system response to being overworked, overburdened, overcrowded, under-resourced.”

Catherine Latimer, head of the John Howard Society, a non-profit focused on humane responses to crime, wants to prohibit these kinds of isolation for people with serious mental illness.

Dedicating sections of prison to vulnerable people could be an alternative to putting them in isolation, Latimer said. But this could take additional staff and reserved space.

“It’s easier just to lock people in, lock them down.”

It’s dehumanizing Kenny Allen, former inmate

Kenny Allen remembers his first time in an observation cell, in December 2007.

He was 18 and had just arrived in Saskatchewan Penitentiary on an armed robbery conviction. He’d spent the previous 14 years in and out of foster homes and juvenile institutions.

He didn’t feel safe — he had just left a gang — and said he was suicidal, hoping to be placed somewhere out of harm’s way.

Instead, he got a bare cell, people watching him pee, and no soap to wash his hands. He lost his clothes in exchange for a sleeveless smock.

“Degrading” is the word he uses, repeatedly, to describe the experience, which took place several times over the course of 15 years in federal prisons. The IJB has reviewed multiple videos of Allen’s placements, including one during which he is strapped to a stretcher before being rolled into a cell where he appears to sleep on and off, periodically struggling against his restraints and attempting to hurt himself. “It’s dehumanizing,” he said.

In late May 2018, Joey Toutsaint returned to prison following nine days in hospital after trying to sever his jugular vein.

Standing in the observation cell, he picked at a suture on his neck. The guards pepper-sprayed him. Fish-eye surveillance video shows the orange-red spray filling the cell; according to his lawyer, in a human rights complaint filed three years later, he “felt like he couldn’t breathe.”

Guards then led Toutsaint to a shower, put a spit hood over his head to stop him from spitting or biting and tied him down to a stretcher that was itself tied down in another observation cell.

Years after that event, Toutsaint spoke with the IJB from a video visit room at Kent Institution, about 60 kilometres northwest of Agassiz, B.C. His last observation cell placement was October of last year, after he swallowed razor blades.

On camera, he showed the self-inflicted white scars worming their way up his tattooed left arm. His memories of his times in observation cells are uncomfortably vivid: no clothes, no bedding, no sound, no communication with the outside world.

“There’s no help there,” he said.

Toutsaint doesn’t think anyone should be held in these forms of solitary.

“They should shut it down. Permanently.… It’s torture.”

paragraphs: It is Nov. 5, 2024. Over the course of half an hour, a hand-held camera follows Joey Toutsaint as prison guards forcibly remove him from a cell, then lead him through a hall, across a yard and into another building. The camera captures him pleading.
“I’m not going to the observation cell. No. You guys are making a mistake. Put me back in my cell.”
At one point, he weeps. “I won’t self-harm … I give you my word. On my mother’s grave. On my daughter’s life…. I don’t want to live like this no more.”
“I recognize you have mental health issues,” an officer says at one point.
The prison guards lead Toutsaint, wrapped in a blanket after a strip search, into the observation cell.

“As you can see on camera,” one of the officers says to the person filming before the camera is turned off, “we had some challenges with Mr. Toutsaint and wanting to submit to going into the observation cell.”

Observation cells are bare rooms subject to 24/7 surveillance in which prisoners such as Toutsaint are placed, dressed in a sleeveless, untearable smock and sometimes without a blanket or mattress, when they have tried to harm themselves or are suspected of intending to do so.

Another variant on these isolation cells is the “dry cell,” which is similarly bare but lacks plumbing or running water. It’s used when prison staff want someone to excrete something they are suspected of having swallowed or hidden in their body, such as drugs.
Canada does not call these cells solitary confinement.
But their use meets a definition of solitary under international rules — to which Canada has agreed — that are meant to minimize the use of such isolation.

What are known as the “Mandela Rules” define solitary confinement as 22 hours a day or more without meaningful human contact, and define prolonged solitary confinement as a period exceeding 15 consecutive days. The rules say solitary confinement should only be used “in exceptional cases as a last resort” and should be “prohibited in the case of prisoners with mental or physical disabilities when their conditions would be exacerbated by such measures.”
Yet the use of observation cells and dry cells has been rising, according to data obtained by the Investigative Journalism Bureau through access-to-information requests.

The number of times Canadian prisons used observation cells rose from 859 in 2018 to 1,316 in 2024 — a 53 per cent increase. In total, observation cells were used more than 8,000 times between 2018 and November 2025, CSC data show.
The number of times Canadian prisons used dry cells rose from 160 in 2022 to 291 in 2024 — an 82 per cent increase. Dry cells were used almost 700 times between 2022 and 2024.
Observation and dry cells can be used for indefinite periods in Canada. The prisoner has no immediate means of appeal.

“It doesn’t really matter what the correctional service calls these cells or units or ranges,” former correctional investigator and current Canadian Civil Liberties Association head Howard Sapers said. “The fact of the matter is they operate like segregation, where people are locked down, locked in their cells, often for 24 hours a day, sometimes for 23 or 22….
“The fact that we don’t have the words ‘solitary confinement’ in our law does not mean that solitary confinement does not, in fact, take place.”

In observation cells, and in other special sections of prisons reserved for people deemed unsafe in the general population, Sapers says, Canadian federal prisoners are “being dealt (with) in a way that’s off the books, frankly.”

It doesn't really matter what the correctional service calls these cells or units or ranges. The fact of the matter is they operate like segregation Howard Sapers, Canadian Civil Liberties Association head

Correctional Service Canada says placements like Toutsaint’s “must be used appropriately, humanely, and with strong oversight” and only “when less restrictive interventions cannot adequately manage an imminent risk of self-harm or suicide.” CSC spokesperson Laurence Côté said prisons conduct health team assessments and case reviews of these placements, but the head of the prison makes the final call.
Observation cells and dry cells are needed to keep prisons safe, says Frederick Lebeau, president of the federal correctional officers’ union.
“When an inmate is acting out and he’s trying to commit suicide, sometimes we’ve got to protect them from themselves.”
While dry cell use could be replaced by tools such as body scanners, he said, observation cells will continue to be necessary “to save lives.”

The IJB obtained 53 videos, about five hours’ worth of footage, shot in and around observation cells — videos legal aid organization Prisoners Legal Services obtained through federal Privacy Act requests.
The videos show how the cells are used and the force — tackling and handcuffing, pepper-spraying or tying down — employed to manage prisoners’ behaviour during transportation to and from these cells.
The IJB reviewed the Privacy Act request through which Prisoners Legal Services obtained the videos. Correctional Service Canada would not comment on their veracity.
Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada’s public safety minister, Gary Anandasangaree, did not respond to requests for an interview.
Sometimes we’ve got to protect them from themselves Frederick Lebeau, president of the federal correctional officers’ union
The IJB found that Indigenous prisoners like Toutsaint are more likely than white people to be put in an observation cell.

The number of Indigenous men placed in observation cells annually more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, to 674 from 284, a period during which the number of white men placed in observation cells increased by about 5.6 per cent, to 397 from 376.

“CSC regularly reviews trends in the use of observation measures, including among Indigenous offenders, and continues to strengthen culturally responsive mental health services and Indigenous-specific interventions,” said Côté, the agency’s spokesperson.

There are also significant disparities by institution. The prison with the highest use of observation cells is one designed to meet the needs of mentally ill inmates: Saskatoon’s Regional Psychiatric Centre.
“Enhanced observation May be used more frequently at the Regional Psychiatric Centre because it serves offenders with complex mental health needs,” Csc’s Côté said.

A federal policy directive authorizes the use of “enhanced observation” in cases of suicidality, self-harm or severe mental illness with a serious impairment. It is only to be used as a last resort, according to the federal directive and instructions to officers the IJB reviewed.
It's easier just to lock people in Catherine Latimer, head of the John Howard Society

In 2021, a Nova Scotia court deemed dry cells “a unique form of solitary confinement” after a woman spent more than 15 days in one, based on suspicions that she was smuggling contraband in her vagina. As a result of that ruling, the use of dry cells federally has been narrowed.

“(Dry cells) are only used as a last resort when there are reasonable grounds to believe that an inmate has ingested or is carrying contraband in either their digestive system or in their rectum, and not in an inmate’s vagina,” Côté said.
Since 2019-20, the CSC said, it has seized weapons or drugs more than 400 times following a dry cell placement.

The proliferation of unofficial forms of isolation, such as observation and dry cells, could be the result of a correctional mindset that seeks to deal with immediate security risks in the simplest way possible, Sapers said. Or, “it could very well be that it’s a system response to being overworked, overburdened, overcrowded, under-resourced.”

stories.title: B.C. tribunal weighs in on who gets Walter the dog after women split
stories.summary: "When pet-owners separate and there is a dispute about the pet, the question is who owns the pet rather than who should have 'custody'."
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
When couples split up, who gets the family pooch is more about money than love, according to a civil resolution tribunal out of British Columbia.

The tribunal heard the case of former romantic partners Misty Donovan and Makenzie Jade Murray who ended their two-year relationship in April 2024. The two women shared their dog, Walter, for another 10 months while living apart. Then in February 2025, Murray kept Walter and refused to bring him to Donovan’s home, where he’d been spending weekends.

Donovan asked the tribunal for an order requiring Murray to return Walter, who appears to be a Boston Terrier in their social media photos of him.

“While she claims $2,500, it is clear Ms. Donovan wants the dog, not monetary compensation,” said tribunal member Alissa Reynolds in the Sept. 23 decision that declares a dog, though loved like a child, is not in fact a child.

The tribunal’s task was not to award custody, Reynolds said, but to divide property, albeit nothing like a sofa or an espresso maker.

“The courts have recognized that animals are a unique form of personal property because they are living creatures and not inanimate objects,” she wrote in the decision.

“This means when pet-owners separate and there is a dispute about the pet, the question is who owns the pet rather than who should have ‘custody’ of it.”

Relevant factors to consider, Reynolds said, include “who bought and selected the pet, who attended its veterinary appointments, who paid for the pet’s needs, who licensed it, and how the parties viewed ownership.”

Murray chose Walter, noted the adjudicator.

“She provided her messages to the breeder that show this. She says Ms. Donovan was not involved in selecting Walter, and Ms. Donovan did not deny that. So, I find this factor favours Ms. Murray.”

But Reynolds found that Donovan purchased the dog for $2,000, noting she “provided bank statements and e-transfer details that show she paid the breeder.”

That favours Donovan, said the adjudicator.

Text messages and veterinarian records show that before Murray refused Donovan access to Walter, both women “attended Walter’s vet appointments, together and individually,” said the decision.

“However, Ms. Donovan says she was the one who remembered to book Walter’s regular checkups and follow-ups and advised Ms. Murray when they were. Ms. Murray does not deny that.”

The evidence shows that Donovan attended more of Walter’s appointments without Murray, and that Murray only took Walter on one emergency vet visit this past February when she was caring for the dog.

“However, Ms. Donovan attended all the follow-up visits. For that reason, I find this factor favours Ms. Donovan slightly,” Reynolds said.

Both women “claimed that they paid for the majority of Walter’s needs,” said the decision.

“This is complicated by the fact that Ms. Murray had three other pets and often paid for their food and other supplies together.”

But after reviewing all the financial information both women provided, Reynolds said it shows that Donovan “paid nearly three times as much” as Murray for Walter’s vet bills, pet food and supplies. “I find this factor heavily favours Ms. Donovan.”

Murray testified that her “messages with the breeder show the parties always intended that she would own Walter,” said the decision.

“She relies on her first message that said, ‘I’m very interested in a puppy,’ and a later message when she said, ‘I have been hoping to find Pearl (another pet) a little friend.’ However, that same message thread shows she also referred to both parties adopting Walter, as follows: ‘We would like to proceed with adopting…,’ ‘A bit about us…,’ ‘We are going to be in Victoria…I was wondering if we could stop by quickly and meet Walter,’ and ‘Would we be able to come pick him up…we are so excited!’”

Reynolds found that the messages show that Murray “intended that the parties would own Walter jointly.”

That’s also supported by their “agreement to share Walter after they split up,” said the decision.

Reynolds found both women “care about Walter, spend a lot of time enriching his life, and both are capable of taking care of his needs and health. So, I find this factor does not favour either party.”

Reynolds concluded “that the balance of the factors favours Ms. Donovan.”

She ordered Murray to give Walter to Donovan within 30 days.

paragraphs: When couples split up, who gets the family pooch is more about money than love, according to a civil resolution tribunal out of British Columbia.

The tribunal heard the case of former romantic partners Misty Donovan and Makenzie Jade Murray who ended their two-year relationship in April 2024. The two women shared their dog, Walter, for another 10 months while living apart. Then in February 2025, Murray kept Walter and refused to bring him to Donovan’s home, where he’d been spending weekends.
Donovan asked the tribunal for an order requiring Murray to return Walter, who appears to be a Boston Terrier in their social media photos of him.

“While she claims $2,500, it is clear Ms. Donovan wants the dog, not monetary compensation,” said tribunal member Alissa Reynolds in the Sept. 23 decision that declares a dog, though loved like a child, is not in fact a child.
The tribunal’s task was not to award custody, Reynolds said, but to divide property, albeit nothing like a sofa or an espresso maker.
“The courts have recognized that animals are a unique form of personal property because they are living creatures and not inanimate objects,” she wrote in the decision.
“This means when pet-owners separate and there is a dispute about the pet, the question is who owns the pet rather than who should have ‘custody’ of it.”

Relevant factors to consider, Reynolds said, include “who bought and selected the pet, who attended its veterinary appointments, who paid for the pet’s needs, who licensed it, and how the parties viewed ownership.”
Murray chose Walter, noted the adjudicator.
“She provided her messages to the breeder that show this. She says Ms. Donovan was not involved in selecting Walter, and Ms. Donovan did not deny that. So, I find this factor favours Ms. Murray.”
But Reynolds found that Donovan purchased the dog for $2,000, noting she “provided bank statements and e-transfer details that show she paid the breeder.”
That favours Donovan, said the adjudicator.
Text messages and veterinarian records show that before Murray refused Donovan access to Walter, both women “attended Walter’s vet appointments, together and individually,” said the decision.
“However, Ms. Donovan says she was the one who remembered to book Walter’s regular checkups and follow-ups and advised Ms. Murray when they were. Ms. Murray does not deny that.”
The evidence shows that Donovan attended more of Walter’s appointments without Murray, and that Murray only took Walter on one emergency vet visit this past February when she was caring for the dog.
“However, Ms. Donovan attended all the follow-up visits. For that reason, I find this factor favours Ms. Donovan slightly,” Reynolds said.
Both women “claimed that they paid for the majority of Walter’s needs,” said the decision.
“This is complicated by the fact that Ms. Murray had three other pets and often paid for their food and other supplies together.”

But after reviewing all the financial information both women provided, Reynolds said it shows that Donovan “paid nearly three times as much” as Murray for Walter’s vet bills, pet food and supplies. “I find this factor heavily favours Ms. Donovan.”
Murray testified that her “messages with the breeder show the parties always intended that she would own Walter,” said the decision.

“She relies on her first message that said, ‘I’m very interested in a puppy,’ and a later message when she said, ‘I have been hoping to find Pearl (another pet) a little friend.’ However, that same message thread shows she also referred to both parties adopting Walter, as follows: ‘We would like to proceed with adopting…,’ ‘A bit about us…,’ ‘We are going to be in Victoria…I was wondering if we could stop by quickly and meet Walter,’ and ‘Would we be able to come pick him up…we are so excited!’”
Reynolds found that the messages show that Murray “intended that the parties would own Walter jointly.”
That’s also supported by their “agreement to share Walter after they split up,” said the decision.

Reynolds found both women “care about Walter, spend a lot of time enriching his life, and both are capable of taking care of his needs and health. So, I find this factor does not favour either party.”
Reynolds concluded “that the balance of the factors favours Ms. Donovan.”
She ordered Murray to give Walter to Donovan within 30 days.

stories.title: Say its name
stories.summary: Canada’s leaders need to denounce not just the crime but the ideology behind antisemitic attacks
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
Authorities have reacted to last Sunday’s antisemitic attack in Belleville, Ont., in all the usual and necessary ways: with stern expressions of abhorrence and promises to protect Canada’s shaken Jewish community. What they have failed to do is to identify or challenge the ideology that is feeding the wave of hate sweeping this country.

That ideology is anti-Zionism.

Zionism is the idea that the Jewish people have the right to a national homeland: Israel. Anti-Zionism, as it has evolved, is the idea that Israel is an alien, illegitimate, colonial state imposed by violence on the Middle East.

We don’t know whether the ex-soldier who opened fire on the Belleville synagogue held such beliefs or what other dark motivations he May have had. And of course anti-Zionists themselves insist that they deplore antisemitism and any kind of violence directed at Jews. But it is obvious by now that the bitter, hateful rhetoric they use is fueling both. Painting Israel as a malevolent force pours gasoline on the ever-flickering flame on antisemitism.

Belleville’s tiny Jewish community vows to carry on after attack

Anti-Zionism has a long history, going back at least to the foundation of Israel. Like its older cousin, antisemitism, it is both stubborn and mutable, expressed in many different ways. Israel is an “apartheid” state. Israel is a racist “ethno-state.” Israel is not a state at all, but a “Zionist entity.”

It is not the same as antisemitism – you can be anti-Zionist without hating all Jews – but the two share the idea that their target is the cause of great evil in the world.

The Israeli statesman Abba Eban put it this way in 1975, when the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution calling Zionism a form of racism. “Classical antisemitism denies the equal rights of Jews as citizens within society. Anti-Zionism denies the equal rights of the Jewish people to its lawful sovereignty within the community of nations. The common principle in the two cases is discrimination.”

Half a century later, this species of discrimination is booming. “ Globalize the intifada ” is its war cry. Pop stars spout it. Famous actors embrace it. That Israel is the principal bad guy of the Middle East, if not the world, is conventional wisdom on university campuses.

Even the head of a major Canadian political party, the NDP, feels free to accuse Israel of the worst crime in the world as if it were an established fact. Avi Lewis, who is Jewish, marked Yom Kippur by lecturing fellow Jews that “we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name.”

Since the Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel and the start of the Gaza war nearly three years ago, Jews have come under threat in just about every corner of the world.

It often seems as if nowhere is safe. Not a synagogue in Manchester. Not a bus stop in Jerusalem. Not a beach party in Sydney. Not even a little synagogue in Belleville. Only the heroism of two police officers prevented that attack from ending in another massacre of innocents. “You are going to die for the Jews,” the gunman shouted at one of the officers before opening fire.

Opinion: The Belleville attack was a warning shot for the antisemitic attacks Canada has let fester

The bullet holes left in the synagogue’s stained-glass windows show what a near thing this was. A night of broken glass in a quiet corner of Southern Ontario. This is where we are.

“Last year, over two-thirds of all religion-motivated hate crimes were directed at Jewish Canadians, who make up only one per cent of the population,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said recently.

In a major address on the issue, he quoted the Jewish prophets, condemned “the scourge of antisemitism” and listed all the things his government is doing to combat it, but said nothing about Oct. 7, nothing about the anti-Zionists who March chanting through quiet Jewish neighbourhoods and wave their Palestinian flags in front of synagogues.

It was as if the haters came out of nowhere. In fact, they spring directly from the notion that Israel is to blame for all the horrors that are happening in its troubled corner of the world. In the guise of criticizing Israel, they demonize it.

It is one thing to call out Israel’s government for abusing Palestinian prisoners, tolerating violence by West Bank settlers or bombing Gaza into rubble; it’s quite another to call it a bloodthirsty imperial juggernaut bent on conquest.

It is time for Canada’s leaders to denounce such lies. It is time for them to name the twisted ideology behind the wave of hate that found expression in Belleville this week. Its name is anti-Zionism.

Half a century later, this species of discrimination is booming. “ Globalize the intifada ” is its war cry. Pop stars spout it. Famous actors embrace it. That Israel is the principal bad guy of the Middle East, if not the world, is conventional wisdom on university campuses.

Even the head of a major Canadian political party, the NDP, feels free to accuse Israel of the worst crime in the world as if it were an established fact. Avi Lewis, who is Jewish, marked Yom Kippur by lecturing fellow Jews that “we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name.”
Since the Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel and the start of the Gaza war nearly three years ago, Jews have come under threat in just about every corner of the world.

It often seems as if nowhere is safe. Not a synagogue in Manchester. Not a bus stop in Jerusalem. Not a beach party in Sydney. Not even a little synagogue in Belleville. It is time for Canada’s leaders to denounce such lies. It is time for them to name the twisted ideology behind the wave of hate that found expression in Belleville this week. Its name is anti-Zionism.

stories.title: Anand to address UN on Arctic, Ukraine, Middle East
stories.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is set to address the United Nations General Assembly today.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa —Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says Canada’s foreign policy is guided by establishing autonomy in strategic fields to limit superpower coercion, along with aspirations to lead middle powers.

“Great powers are walking away from global economic co-operation, dismantling economic integration,” Anand said Saturday in Canada’s annual address to the United Nations General Assembly.

“In the face of this rupture, Canada’s goal is to achieve greater strategic autonomy,” she said at the green marble dais.

Anand’s speech did not directly mention American tariffs nor last month’s collapse of trade talks between Canada and Washington, and she instead mentioned work to diversify trade beyond North America.

Her speech echoed Prime Minister Mark Carney’s rhetoric over the past year about middle powers forging deeper ties and working with countries on shared goals, including states that aren’t close partners.

She said that involves emerging technologies, critical minerals, defence production and energy — as well as the rule of law and respect for sovereignty.

“We are facing serious challenges in the global order,” Anand said.

“We will lead other middle powers to act collectively and decisively, because middle powers are playing a key role in building the framework for the new international order — which is being established as we speak.”

Anand used an analogy that she said comes from her roots in rural Nova Scotia. “The tide does not wait; you must move with it.”

She suggested countries form “long-term partnerships” with Canada for security and prosperity.

“Rather than yearn for days gone by, let us together take this opportunity to do right by our people, and build together,” she said.

Anand said state sovereignty “has been treated with disdain” but that Canada will defend that principle, and work toward stability and common rules.

She said that is why Canada is calling for a just peace in Ukraine, self-determination for Palestinians and Israelis, and an end to hate-based violence.

“We were tragically reminded of the scourge of antisemitism again, when a gunman carried out an attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont.,” she told the UN.

“Canada is an open, pluralistic society, with a public square full of robust and civil debate. Our success is underpinned by this civility, by our democratic institutions, and by respect for our differences,” she said.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Anand of Canada speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Heather Khalifa)

For the second year in a row, Anand spoke instead of Carney, who was at the UN from Monday to Wednesday but whose officials said he could not deliver Canada’s address due to scheduling issues.

The UN schedules foreign ministers later in the rotation during the annual high-level week, with weekday, daytime speeches reserved for heads of state and government. Anand spoke late Saturday afternoon.

Anand also voiced support for the Nato alliance, amid an increase in warnings from European leaders about Russian hybrid attacks. She cited a recent defence agreement between Denmark, its autonomous territory Greenland and U.S. President Donald Trump.

“This agreement is yet another reminder that North America and Europe are stronger together. And as a founding member of Nato, our commitment to the transatlantic alliance is ironclad,” Anand said.

To that end, Anand reiterated work being done to better secure the Canadian Arctic, saying this is occurring in lockstep with Indigenous Peoples.

Anand said Canada supports the International Criminal Court amid Washington’s quest to dismantle the institution. Her comments come as Canadian critics argue Ottawa is not calling out American coercion, including the sanctioning of a Canadian judge for her work at the ICC.

She reiterated Canada’s bid for a seat on the UN Human Rights Council, through a vote expected in one year.

Anand said Ottawa is pursuing “values-based realism” while advocating for democracy in Iran, the return of Ukrainian children kidnapped by Russia and work to end Haiti’s gruesome gang crisis.

Rescue workers put out a fire on the roof of an office building damaged by a Russian drone strike, in Kyiv, Ukraine, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka)

Her speech mentioned gender equality, Lgbtq+ rights, Sudan’s civil war, Hamas attacks on Israel, Israeli settler violence against Palestinians and safe approaches to artificial intelligence.

Anand also said Canada is ready to work with whoever UN members elect as their next secretary-general, referring in French to the role in the masculine and feminine titles.

That comment followed the Trudeau government calling for a woman to be the next secretary-general, in September 2024. The Carney government has not repeated that call.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 26, 2026.
