ByJim Rankin Staff Reporter

Port Hope, Ont.—On a sticky summer day, there is relief in the shade of the foliage along the east bank of the Ganaraska River, though not from the mosquitoes. Mark Chard, a local firefighter, community theatre actor and musician, leads the way to a serene spot not far from the heart of a small town, where his daughter Madison was found dead four years ago.

The first time Mark visited this spot was days after the discovery of her body, accompanied by the lead Port Hope police detective probing Madison’s disappearance.

“He was afraid of what I might do to myself,” says Chard. “But I wasn’t thinking that.”

Article continues below

Project South unsealed court records explained

Image 36Image 37Image 38

The grieving father says he was looking to connect with his daughter somehow, when along came “a stupid giant bumblebee. It kind of landed on me, and I thought it was her.”

A search party located Madison, 29, ON May 19, 2022, a month after one of her last known messages — a late afternoon text exchange with her mother, Lori, who offered to arrange a ride home.

From left to right, Lori, Teigan, Madison and Mark Chard are seen in a family portrait in front of the family’s Port Hope home.

The Chard family filed a missing person report, and searches ensued, including around the very area where her body was ultimately found. The discovery finally came a day after Port Hope police floated the possibility in a news story that Madison had fallen prey to a human-trafficking operation.

Madison was lying flat on her back, clothed for cool spring weather. An autopsy and toxicology tests found she had died of hypothermia, with a lethal amount of fentanyl in her system, and some cocaine.

Four years on, a criminal investigation led by the Port Hope Police Service and directed by the Ontario Provincial Police is all but officially closed, leaving many questions unanswered and a family grappling with a grief that’s been compounded by the unknown. What happened to Madison? Did she die alone? Did police do enough to get to the bottom of it?

In a town where there is little local news coverage anymore, there remain plenty of rumours and speculation. One story the family has heard is that Madison overdosed and the people with her panicked and put her in a freezer, and later moved the body.

The Chard family believes people who use and sell illicit drugs know what happened.

“Somebody knows stuff,” says Lori, who still gets asked in the grocery store if there’s anything new in the case.

The OPP, in a statement to the Star on behalf of the OPP and the Port Hope Police Service, “acknowledge and sympathize with Madison Chard’s family as they continue to grieve their loss.” The statement said every avenue of inquiry was “thoroughly examined,” but ultimately no evidence was established to suggest foul play.

The Chards, who believe the police investigation was inadequate,filed a formal police complaint about the investigation, but it has since been informally resolved, with an agreement that police will consider any new leads passed their way by the family.

A story now, the family believes, May be among the Chards’ best chances to surface new information.

Madison Chard’s body discovered off a path along the Ganaraska River in the heart of Port Hope, Ontario.

Madison had come back to live with her parents in the Chard family’s two-storey home on Ward Street with an ivy-covered front porch. Life had not been easy. She had a brief, bad marriage, and Madison had worked hard to overcome mental health and substance use problems.

Born and raised in Port Hope, along with her younger brother, Teigan, Madison’s ashes now rest on the mantel in the living room in an urn, behind a white butterfly light, overlooked by an angel statue.

As a kid, Madison — Madi to those who loved her, and there are many — adored dance and took ballet lessons, but also did karate and played soccer, with her father as coach in the Timbits league.She was “right from the get go very outgoing and chatty and headstrong,” says Mark, and when brother Teigan came along, “she became a little mother to him.”

Madison was a “Swiftie,” and grew to love theatre and musicals through her father, beginning with his role in a production of “Jesus Christ Superstar.” Madison went to every performance, sitting in the front row and learning the words to every song. There were more productions, and Madison would hang out and eventually started filling in when people were sick.

She also modelled from a very young age and was signed in her teens by an agent in New York. It was fun — father and daughter spent a month there — but it “never came of anything,” says Lori.

Madison had to overcome a lot. There was a diagnosis in her teens of bipolar disorder — there was Madi A for “awesome” and Mabi B who was not, says Lori — and later a brief, bad marriage with an abusive, controlling partner, which her parents believe led to post-traumatic stress disorder and a heroin addiction.Madison would use cocaine when she was slipping to manage the urge for heroin, Lori says. Madison sought treatment at Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences, and obtained a diploma from Durham College, where she studied criminal psychology and behaviour. She had a job at Giant Tiger, but was out of work when she went missing.

One thing you would not get from looking at Madison was that inside she lacked confidence, says Mark.

Among the tattoos Madison had was a replica of a wire-art tree pendant Mark had made for her, a rendering of a family tree. She had it done on the back of her left hand.

“She used to say that the pain of getting a tattoo is better than, or masks, the pain that she felt in her heart, or in her existence,” Mark says.

After her death, the family held fundraising events for Ontario Shores, using the family tree as a symbol of Madison’s life, along with the slogan “Stronger Than the Storm.”It was a motto Madison lived by and wore on a necklace, a gift from her parents after one year of recovery.

Madison had been “85 per cent doing OK” for four years before she died, says Lori, but there were “slips.”

The necklace Madison was wearing when her body was found, bearing her motto: “Stronger than the Storm.”

On April 15, 2022, Madison celebrated her 29th birthday with her family but was headed for one of those “slips.”

Madison had bought cocaine in early April from a woman operating out of what the Chard family discovered was a drug “trap house,” and had a seizure, the family says. The house was not far from where Madison’s body would be found, and backs onto the Ganaraska ravine. At the time of Madison’s disappearance, the woman owed Madison $150, Mark discovered. He believes Madison started buying elsewhere because she thought the supply was bad.

According to her family, she never deliberately used fentanyl, the opioid responsible for an epidemic of deaths and accidental drug poisonings across North America. In 2022 in Ontario, an average of seven people a day were dying from opioid toxicity. In the Haliburton Kawartha Northumberland Peterborough Health Unit, which includes Port Hope, there were 153 emergency department visits from April to June of that year, and 19 deaths, related to opioid toxicity.

On Tuesday, April 19, Madison left home early afternoon and would not come back.

For 30 agonizing days, there were false sightings of Madison, and Mark and Lori became de facto detectives.

They later compiled, organized and analyzed binders full of police records obtained in freedom-of-information requests, and had help from Don Sellar — an editor and journalist, and former Toronto Star public editor — who lives in Port Hope and occasionally writes on local stories involving the police. What emerged was a cast of characters involved in the local drug scene. Police seemed quite aware of who was who in that scene as the connections emerged, the family says.

Madison was texting with Lori and a close friend in the late afternoon of April 19. Madison had plans to get together with the friend the following weekend to celebrate their mutual birthdays. A text from Lori sent at 5:51 p.m. was delivered, but not read — none after that ever would be.

Madison was seen that afternoon at a rooming house on Walton Street, where she bought cocaine from known drug dealers, and later with a man who was headed to the trap house; he maintained the two then went in different directions.

When Madison did not come home, the Chards started to worry.

Today, they believe Madison made another stop that evening.

5:49 p.m., April 19, 2022 —Madison sends a text to her mom. After that, incoming texts to Madison’s phone are marked as “delivered,” but not “read.”

April 19, 2022 —Madison is last seen near a Pharmasave store in Port Hope. Earlier that afternoon, she is seen at a downtown rooming house, where she bought cocaine.

April 21, 2022 —Mark Chard reports his daughter missing. Police conduct “pings” on Madison’s phone and find it is moving. Police issue a “Bolo” for officers to be on the lookout for Madison.

April 22, 2022 —Mark Chard receives a phone call from a woman living at a Port Hope “trap house” backing onto the Ganaraska River. The woman has Madison’s phone, and the SIM card has been removed. Mark retrieves the phone and advises police. Police speak to a “friendly,” who provides Mark the password.

May 18, 2022 —The Toronto Sun publishes a story on Madison’s disappearance; police tell the Sun they are concerned she May have fallen prey to a human-trafficking operation.

May 19, 2022 —A search and rescue team resumes a search of the Ganaraska River ravine. Madison’s body is discovered on the east side of the river, not far from where she was last seen. Missing for 30 days, Madison’s body shows no sign of animal scavenging; the OPP steps in to assist in the investigation.

June 13, 2022 —Police identify a man who provided Madison with fentanyl and consult with a Crown attorney about a manslaughter charge.

August 2026 —After four years, no arrests have been made in the case; police tell the Star they found no evidence of foul play.

With a missing persons report filed, Mark, the police and others set out looking for Madison and clues. On Friday, three days after Madison’s last texts, Mark got a phone call from the woman at the trap house. She had Madison’s phone at the house and said a certain person had dropped it off, and that the SIM card was missing. When Mark went to retrieve it the next day, the woman was not there, but about eight other people were.

Mark got Madison’s Samsung Galaxy phone later the next day. The SIM card was indeed missing, along with the phone’s case.

Police would discover that on the Thursday, two days after Madison’s last texts, Madison’s phone “pinged” off cell towers in three places: on Phillips Road in Port Hope; on Division St. in Cobourg; and in Baltimore, north of Cobourg. In other words, Madison’s phone was moving, then it stopped.

Police told the family the woman at the trap house was questioned several times, as were others. Though the trap house has a security camera on the front door, it did not show Madison. However, the house had a back patio door, which the Chards say was commonly used. There was no camera there.

Mark set about investigating what he could on Madison’s phone, which was password-protected. Mark mentioned that to the lead Port Hope detective, and in short order, the detective got back with a four-digit code from a “friendly.” It was 5683, or L-O-V-E. And it worked. It raised obvious questions: How and why would someone know the code? And who?

When the family obtained police notes from the investigation, names and identifying information were mostly redacted, which is expected for privacy reasons in freedom-of-information requests. But the family determined who this “friendly” was.

Police did not ask Mark for the phone for 11 days before picking it up and sending it off to the OPP for a forensic analysis.

Police did not answer any of the Star’s questions about the phone, which has been returned to the family. Mark is trying to find someone who can independently examine the phone for any location data.

In April, along the banks of Ganaraska River, the foliage is sparse. The ravine was searched, and police used a drone at one point. Nothing was found.

On May 18, 2022, the Toronto Sun posted an online story about Madison being missing for nearly a month. In it, Port Hope police said new information suggested Madison May have been taken in by a human trafficker and, according to the story, “May be in their control somewhere between Montreal and Windsor.” A police inspector was quoted as saying that traffickers often take their victim’s phone away.

(The Chards believe the trafficking story was a red herring, cooked up and passed along by local “criminals.”)

The next morning, ON May 19, the Sun story ran in print with a headline of “Where’s Madi?” Later that day, a search and rescue team returned to the ravine, and Madison’s body was located on the east side of the Ganaraska, where the river splits.

Paul Racine, 74, has lived nearby with his family for decades and knows the river well. Lately, he’s been keeping an eye on the beavers and their handiwork, bringing down aspen and ash trees. The river area is also frequented by turkey vultures and home to coyotes, foxes, raccoons, groundhogs, muskrats and “numerous dogs that are walked up and down there,” a lot off leash, says Racine.

“My contention,” says Racine, “is that there were Labs, there were setters, there were beagles, there were all kinds of dogs, and if (Madison) lay there for a month, there is absolutely no way that a dog wouldn’t have gone over and sniffed her out.”

Mark Chard believes there would have also been some wildlife interference if his daughter was there for so long.

According to weather records, Port Hope saw daytime high temperatures ranging from 10 to 21 C in the first seven days Madison was missing, and had climbed to highs of 26 to 27 C by the second week of May. Otherwise, temperatures were in the teens. Parts of Madison’s body showed “advanced” and moderate decompositional changes, according to a pathology report.

The police records obtained by the Chards indicate that police intended to consult with a Crown attorney about laying a manslaughter charge at one point.

One possible explanation is that police considered charging the person who sold or gave Madison tainted drugs.

A 2024 paper by York University graduate student Liam Michaud examined a “recent proliferation” of Canadian manslaughter charges and prosecutions of people involved in overdoses, who themselves use, share and sell drugs.

By looking at media reports and court decisions and through federal and provincial requests for information, Michaud found “the vast majority of those who face manslaughter charges are engaged in the lowest tiers of the drug trade, are themselves people who use drugs, and are often intimately known to the deceased.”

To date, no arrests have been made, and although police contemplated doing so, no search warrants were sought, according to police notes.

For years, the investigation remained open, and Mark passed along everything he discovered. Now, officers involved in the initial investigation are no longer on the case, and Port Hope has a new police chief.

The Star contacted the new chief, Tim Farquharson, to request an interview and shared a long list of questions about the investigation in writing in May. Following a couple of meetings Farquharson had with the OPP on the Star’s queries, the OPP responded by email with a statement on behalf of the two services.

“We are unable to comment on specific aspects of the investigation, including investigative processes, techniques, evidence-gathering methods or operational considerations,”Agata Czajkowski, Strategic Communications Advisor for the Ontario Provincial Police, said in the statement to the Star.

“Releasing such details could compromise investigative practices and operations.”

As for when to charge or not,Czajkowski said that in drug-related death cases “where investigators establish the necessary grounds, charges — including manslaughter, criminal negligence causing death or drug trafficking offences — will be pursued in accordance with the evidence.”

In police notes obtained by the Chards, a Port Hope officer references an unidentified male providing Madison with fentanyl and noted police will “need multiple witnesses to build manslaughter.”

The officer notes an OPP investigator on the case cautioning that if “witnesses are weak then we have nothing.”

Mark Chard, centre, played drums at the “Songs For Madi” concert.

Mark Chard holds a “Dad’s Walk” fundraising event for Ontario Shores annually in honour of his daughter. It takes place on the Port Hope Waterfront Trail along Lake Ontario, passing by a bench and tree with plaques bearing Madison’s name. He posts to Facebook on important anniversary dates, hoping they will get attention and maybe spark someone to speak up about what happened to a woman who is still very missed and loved.

Last August, more than 150 people turned out at the Port Hope United Church for “Songs for Madi” — a night of performances by friends and family, complete with drag performers — Mark was on drums with a band, including Mark’s older brother on guitar, playing “Day by Day” from the musical “Godspell.” Lori stood in a church pew, dancing. The event raised close to $5,000, again, for Ontario Shores, adding to $72,000 already raised.

“Madi is pissed that she’s not here,” said one of the emcee drag performers, prompting laughter.

Madison did make an appearance, however, when a video of her played on a large screen, made for her father’s 50th birthday. Accompanied by a guitar, Madison delivered a beautiful rendition of Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah.

“Love you, daddy,” said Madison, blowing a kiss to the camera at the end.

During an evening of songs for Madi, one by her brought tears.

Jim Rankin is a Star reporter based in Toronto. Reach him via email: jrankin@thestar.CA

Mark Chard, a local firefighter, community theatre actor and musician, leads the way to a serene spot not far from the heart of a small town, where his daughter Madison was found dead four years ago.
The first time Mark visited this spot was days after the discovery of her body, accompanied by the lead Port Hope police detective probing Madison’s disappearance.
“He was afraid of what I might do to myself,” says Chard. “But I wasn’t thinking that.”

The Chard family filed a missing person report, and searches ensued, including around the very area where her body was ultimately found. The discovery finally came a day after Port Hope police floated the possibility in a news story that Madison had fallen prey to a human-trafficking operation.

Madison was lying flat on her back, clothed for cool spring weather. An autopsy and toxicology tests found she had died of hypothermia, with a lethal amount of fentanyl in her system, and some cocaine.

Four years on, a criminal investigation led by the Port Hope Police Service and directed by the Ontario Provincial Police is all but officially closed, leaving many questions unanswered and a family grappling with a grief that’s been compounded by the unknown. What happened to Madison? Did she die alone? Did police do enough to get to the bottom of it?

In a town where there is little local news coverage anymore, there remain plenty of rumours and speculation. One story the family has heard is that Madison overdosed and the people with her panicked and put her in a freezer, and later moved the body.
The Chard family believes people who use and sell illicit drugs know what happened.
“Somebody knows stuff,” says Lori, who still gets asked in the grocery store if there’s anything new in the case.

The OPP, in a statement to the Star on behalf of the OPP and the Port Hope Police Service, “acknowledge and sympathize with Madison Chard’s family as they continue to grieve their loss.” The statement said every avenue of inquiry was “thoroughly examined,” but ultimately no evidence was established to suggest foul play.

Madison had come back to live with her parents in the Chard family’s two-storey home on Ward Street with an ivy-covered front porch. Life had not been easy. She had a brief, bad marriage, and Madison had worked hard to overcome mental health and substance use problems.

Born and raised in Port Hope, along with her younger brother, Teigan, Madison’s ashes now rest on the mantel in the living room in an urn, behind a white butterfly light, overlooked by an angel statue.

There were more productions, and Madison would hang out and eventually started filling in when people were sick.
She also modelled from a very young age and was signed in her teens by an agent in New York. It was fun — father and daughter spent a month there — but it “never came of anything,” says Lori.

Madison had to overcome a lot. She had a job at Giant Tiger, but was out of work when she went missing.
One thing you would not get from looking at Madison was that inside she lacked confidence, says Mark.

stories.title: Knights continue winning streak to start season
stories.summary: The London Knights remain undefeated to start the 2026-27 season after defeating the Owen Sound Attack in a back-and-forth affair Friday night at Canada Life Place.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The London Knights remain undefeated to start the 2026-27 season after defeating the Owen Sound Attack 7-4 in a back-and-forth affair Friday night at Canada Life Place.

London fell down 2-1 halfway through the second period, before storming back with three goals in the span of four minutes off the backs of Cooper McAsian, Eloan Le Gallic, and Carson Hammer.

The Knights would extend their lead into the third period, before the Attacks would make things interesting, making it a one-goal game with five minutes to play.

Newly acquired Knight Thomas Zocco scored his first as a Knight to regain the two goal lead with under three minutes to go, while Evan Van Gorp would get the empty netter to secure the win for London.

The Knights will be back in action next Friday when they host the North Bay Battalion at Canada Life Place.

stories.title: Western Homecoming brings football, festivities and heightened safety measures for weekend
stories.summary: Western University’s campus is buzzing as students and alumni prepare for a weekend of football, festivities and Homecoming traditions.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Western University’s campus is buzzing as students and alumni prepare for a weekend of football, festivities and Homecoming traditions.

The annual event is expected to bring large crowds to campus and surrounding areas, prompting police, emergency services and university officials to prepare for the weekend.

“We’re excited for the weekend,” said Western University Provost (Students) John Doerksen. “It’s a great opportunity for alumni and students to come back to campus, reconnect with old friends and celebrate.”

Alongside the celebrations, authorities are mounting a major safety operation and warning people against large, unsanctioned street parties.

London police Inspector David Pratt said officers have been planning for the weekend for months with London Fire Services, paramedics, the City of London, Western University, Fanshawe College and other community partners.

“We’ll be well prepared and out in the community to show a presence,” Pratt said.

Police say additional officers will be deployed throughout the weekend, including support from neighbouring police services.

Hamilton police, Windsor police and the Ontario Provincial Police are expected to assist London police with enforcement and patrols.

Officials are urging people to avoid large, unsanctioned street gatherings, warning that violations can result in fines or criminal charges.

Western is encouraging students to take part in organized events on campus.

The football game remains a major draw, while the university is also hosting a Fan Festival featuring free food and activities for students.

“We have really good programming for students,” said Doerksen. “We have the football game, of course, that’s always a big draw, and we have something we call Fan Festival. So that’s an opportunity for students to come. There’s free food there. There’s all kinds of activities.”

London Health Sciences Centre is also preparing for a potentially busy weekend.

Dr. Vico Dagnone, head of emergency medicine at LHSC, said staff want people to enjoy Homecoming while making responsible decisions.

“We just want to make sure that everybody is safe and responsible,” said Dagnone. “We don’t want Homecoming remembered for the wrong reasons. We want it to be memorable for all the right reasons. But if you do need our medical care, we’ll be there for you.”

Officials say the goal is not to prevent people from celebrating, but to encourage people to do so safely and responsibly.

stories.title: RCMP remind drivers to stop for school buses after two Kelowna students are struck by a vehicle
stories.summary: Both students were taken to hospital with what police describe as serious injuries. Arbor View Drive was closed for hours while police investigated.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Two elementary school students were seriously injured after being struck by a vehicle in Kelowna’s Upper Mission Thursday.

“I thought it was my own kid because he gets off that bus as well,” said witness Kevin Dalman.

The incident happened on Arbor View Drive after the students got off the bus.

“The school bus had just dropped off the students,” said Kelowna RCMP Col. Steven Lang. “They were in the process of crossing the street and that’s when they were struck by the SUV, which was coming head-on towards the school bus in an opposite direction.”

Both students were taken to hospital with what police describe as serious injuries.

Arbor View Drive was closed for hours while police investigated.

One person was taken into custody but has since been released.

Police say no charges have been laid at this point.

“Alcohol is not considered to be a contributing factor. The other part of the criminality or related factors are under investigation,” Lang said.

Police are also investigating whether the school bus had activated its flashing red lights at the time of the incident.

The collision is prompting RCMP to remind drivers of the law when approaching a school bus.

“Drivers are required by law to stop on both sides of the school bus, remain stopped until those stop sign and lights are turned off, at which point they can proceed,” Lang said.

Several other students were still on the bus and witnessed the incident.

Central Okanagan Public Schools Superintendent Jon Rever issued the following statement:

“We are deeply saddened at this incident, and our thoughts are with the family and all those affected. Currently, our focus is supporting students and families. Our Post-Critical Incident Response Team is supporting students, staff, and conversations at home and school to ensure the safety and well-being of students.”

stories.title: Elections Alberta pushes back against misleading online claims ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Officials are countering false claims about the Oct. 19 vote as hundreds of thousands of Albertans request mail-in ballots
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Elections Alberta is attempting to crack down on misleading information online that is swirling around the province’s coming referendum, emphasizing election integrity as hundreds of thousands of Albertans for the first time are expected to cast mail-in ballots.

The province’s elections agency has become increasingly active on social media in recent weeks, putting out regular notices and responding to posts – a large number of which have cast doubt on the vote.

“Albertans should expect misinformation and disinformation campaigns to increase leading up to the referendum,” Elections Alberta wrote in an August news release.

In the past week alone, the agency has called out certain social media posts as “the latest disinformation attempt” and accused accounts of deliberately misleading electors. It has disabused speculation of voter fraud and taken great lengths to explain its safeguards around mail-in voting.

The effort is just one component of the daunting task before Elections Alberta as it works toward pulling off the Oct. 19 referendum, which it says is one of the biggest electoral events in Canadian history.

Alberta independence ballot count expected to run deep into morning after vote

Elections Alberta has ordered 45 million ballots for the 10 separate referendum questions, more than twice the number of ballots cast in the 2025 federal election, and it’s still trying to reach its target of hiring at least 60,000 election workers.

Roughly 639,000 voters had requested mail-in ballots as of Friday – more than a fifth of Alberta’s electorate.

It is the first time that Albertans have unrestricted access to mail-in ballots for a provincial vote. Voters were previously required to prove that they couldn’t cast their ballot in person.

Massive interest in Alberta’s newly expanded mail-in voting process has added to the heavy lift for the electoral agency.

On Monday, Elections Alberta responded to a surge of online claims that ineligible electors living outside Alberta could be approved to receive a mail-in ballot.

Eva Chipiuk, a prominent independence advocate and lawyer, was among the voices asking the agency to clarify its rules after one poster said they registered a family member from the U.S.

Elections Alberta responded: “There is a difference between raising a potential issue with a process and deliberately misleading electors with faked confirmations and screens. We clarified many times: no valid Alberta address, no getting past screen 1. No valid voter record, no approval. No valid ID, no vote.”

Russian, U.S. actors are targeting Albertans with pro-separatist content, research shows

Some organizers in Alberta’s separatist movement have encouraged supporters to vote by mail. Keith Wilson, the lawyer behind Let Alberta Decide, said in an interview that he has promoted voting from home.

Mr. Wilson said some core independence supporters – farmers in the middle of harvest or remote camp workers, for example – May face roadblocks to voting on referendum day. He also fears long line-ups at the polls could discourage voters.

“We’ve encouraged them to vote by mail-in ballot so that their vote counts,” Mr. Wilson said.

Others in the pro-independence camp cite a deep mistrust with the voting method. Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said he has actively encouraged supporters to opt for in-person voting.

“My personal belief has always been that you should have to go vote in-person,” Mr. Sylvestre said.

“I have no faith in that system at all, and I don’t care how convenient it is.”

Pro-Canadian groups have roundly supported voting by mail, and on Friday fired off e-mails reminding voters that it was their last opportunity to register for a special ballot.

Observers say voters have likely been motivated to vote early out of convenience, and because of concerns around short-staffed polling booths and an unruly voting process.

Alberta executives urge business community to raise alarm over economic risks of separation

Elections Alberta has hired 32,000 elections officers for the referendum and received roughly 57,000 applications, it said in a Friday statement to The Globe and Mail. The agency says it needs at least 60,000 workers for the referendum to run smoothly. Observers also expect voting on 10 questions on separate ballots will slow down lines on voting day.

A handful of blunders by Elections Alberta have also fuelled concerns about referendum-day complications.

Despite Albertans’ unrestricted access to mail-in voting, swaths of ballots sent earlier this month accidentally included a section requiring signed testimony that they’re unable to vote in person – included with the threat of a $50,000 fine or prison time

Elections Alberta also found that 313 packages sent to electors were missing ballots, it said on Sept. 18.

Annalise Klingbeil, co-founder of Champion Communications and ex-staffer under former premier Rachel Notley, said Elections Alberta has been under pressure long before the referendum.

She pointed to the agency’s 2024-25 annual report that described an agency rife with chronic employee burnout. It referred to its operating model as “unreasonable and unsustainable” and said the electoral office had operated “for many years with an austerity approach.”

“I think it feels like the Elections Alberta machinery is being held together by chewing gum and duct tape at this point,” Ms. Klingbeil said. “It doesn’t give voters a lot of confidence, which is super concerning.”

In the past week alone, the agency has called out certain social media posts as “the latest disinformation attempt” and accused accounts of deliberately misleading electors. It has disabused speculation of voter fraud and taken great lengths to explain its safeguards around mail-in voting.

The effort is just one component of the daunting task before Elections Alberta as it works toward pulling off the Oct. 19 referendum, which it says is one of the biggest electoral events in Canadian history.
Alberta independence ballot count expected to run deep into morning after vote

Elections Alberta has ordered 45 million ballots for the 10 separate referendum questions, more than twice the number of ballots cast in the 2025 federal election, and it’s still trying to reach its target of hiring at least 60,000 election workers.
Roughly 639,000 voters had requested mail-in ballots as of Friday – more than a fifth of Alberta’s electorate.
It is the first time that Albertans have unrestricted access to mail-in ballots for a provincial vote. Voters were previously required to prove that they couldn’t cast their ballot in person.
Massive interest in Alberta’s newly expanded mail-in voting process has added to the heavy lift for the electoral agency.
On Monday, Elections Alberta responded to a surge of online claims that ineligible electors living outside Alberta could be approved to receive a mail-in ballot.
Eva Chipiuk, a prominent independence advocate and lawyer, was among the voices asking the agency to clarify its rules after one poster said they registered a family member from the U.S.

Elections Alberta responded: “There is a difference between raising a potential issue with a process and deliberately misleading electors with faked confirmations and screens. We clarified many times: no valid Alberta address, no getting past screen 1. No valid voter record, no approval. No valid ID, no vote.”
Russian, U.S. actors are targeting Albertans with pro-separatist content, research shows

Some organizers in Alberta’s separatist movement have encouraged supporters to vote by mail. Keith Wilson, the lawyer behind Let Alberta Decide, said in an interview that he has promoted voting from home.

Mr. Wilson said some core independence supporters – farmers in the middle of harvest or remote camp workers, for example – May face roadblocks to voting on referendum day. He also fears long line-ups at the polls could discourage voters.
“We’ve encouraged them to vote by mail-in ballot so that their vote counts,” Mr. Wilson said.

Others in the pro-independence camp cite a deep mistrust with the voting method. Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said he has actively encouraged supporters to opt for in-person voting.
“My personal belief has always been that you should have to go vote in-person,” Mr. Sylvestre said.
“I have no faith in that system at all, and I don’t care how convenient it is.”
Pro-Canadian groups have roundly supported voting by mail, and on Friday fired off e-mails reminding voters that it was their last opportunity to register for a special ballot.
Observers say voters have likely been motivated to vote early out of convenience, and because of concerns around short-staffed polling booths and an unruly voting process.
Alberta executives urge business community to raise alarm over economic risks of separation

Elections Alberta has hired 32,000 elections officers for the referendum and received roughly 57,000 applications, it said in a Friday statement to The Globe and Mail. The agency says it needs at least 60,000 workers for the referendum to run smoothly. Observers also expect voting on 10 questions on separate ballots will slow down lines on voting day.
A handful of blunders by Elections Alberta have also fuelled concerns about referendum-day complications.

Despite Albertans’ unrestricted access to mail-in voting, swaths of ballots sent earlier this month accidentally included a section requiring signed testimony that they’re unable to vote in person – included with the threat of a $50,000 fine or prison time
Elections Alberta also found that 313 packages sent to electors were missing ballots, it said on Sept. 18.
Annalise Klingbeil, co-founder of Champion Communications and ex-staffer under former premier Rachel Notley, said Elections Alberta has been under pressure long before the referendum.

She pointed to the agency’s 2024-25 annual report that described an agency rife with chronic employee burnout. It referred to its operating model as “unreasonable and unsustainable” and said the electoral office had operated “for many years with an austerity approach.”

“I think it feels like the Elections Alberta machinery is being held together by chewing gum and duct tape at this point,” Ms. Klingbeil said. “It doesn’t give voters a lot of confidence, which is super concerning.”

stories.title: Eby proposes 2-per-cent tax on unsold condos to encourage developers to sell
stories.summary: Government would impose tax on units left vacant for more than a year
stories.author: Rachelle Younglai
stories.content:
A new NDP government would slap a 2-per-cent tax on empty, unsold condos in British Columbia in a bid to force developers to cut prices and sell the units, party leader David Eby said on Friday.

There are nearly 4,000 newly built condos sitting empty in the Vancouver region, according to data from new-home research firm Zonda, as investors shun the units because they are no longer profitable.

At a Burnaby news conference during the first week of his re-election campaign, Mr. Eby said his government would impose the tax on newly built units that have been vacant for more than a year.

The tax would be on the assessed value of the condo unit, and the levy would increase by one percentage point for each additional year that the condo remained unsold.

That means if a new condo is empty for three years, the tax on the assessed value of the property would increase to 3 per cent.

Mr. Eby said that developers aren’t selling these units “at the price that people are willing to pay.” He said developers have deep pockets and can wait out the market downturn. “Families can’t wait. They need a place now.”

He cited an industry report that valued all the newly built and empty condos in the province at $4.5-billion.

B.C. Premier David Eby calls snap election

The development industry on Friday called the new tax proposal punitive.

“It would effectively be a penalty levied on developers for completing their projects at the wrong time in the housing market cycle,” said Ryan Berlin, chief economist with real-estate services company Rennie & Associates Realty Ltd.

“This adds risk and cost to future projects and creates yet another barrier to future construction,” he said in an e-mail.

Beau Jarvis, chief executive of B.C. developer Wesgroup, called the tax a “perfect example of the type of policy that results in the unintended consequence of homebuilders never wanting to build homes again.”

“To suggest that developers are purposefully sitting on empty condos and not trying to sell them is ridiculous,” he said. “The fact is there are no buyers, even at prices where developers are willing to take a significant loss.”

Mr. Eby also said Friday that a new NDP government would increase the province’s speculation and vacancy tax on empty homes. Canadians and permanent residents would see their tax on empty properties increase to 2 per cent from the current 1 per cent.

The tax has been in place since 2018 and was designed to push homeowners to rent out their homes. Each year, every B.C. homeowner must complete a declaration as to whether they’ve lived in their home for at least six months.

Value of unsold condos in Metro Vancouver put at $4.6-billion

At the news conference on Friday, Mr. Eby did not mention a previously announced proposal to buy $1.45-billion of unsold condos, which the province and Ottawa unveiled in the summer.

Under that proposal, the B.C. and federal governments would buy about 2,200 unsold new condos in the province and convert them to rentals for a rent-to-own scheme.

Asked about the status of the proposal, B.C. NDP campaign spokesperson Bhinder Sajan said in an e-mail on Friday: “There’s been no change.”

Industry officials have speculated the plan May have died, given that the Eby government has not provided details on how it would work.

The plan has been publicly derided as a bailout for developers, while developers have said they never wanted the government to buy their unsold units.

Vancouver and Toronto have been flooded with newly built condos as developers have completed constructing buildings while demand dropped.

The sales downturn is in part because of a lack of interest from investors, who used to account for the majority of purchasers. But a federal cap on temporary foreign workers and international students has also contributed to the slowdown in demand. And many prospective homebuyers simply cannot afford to buy, even though home prices have declined from their peak in 2022.

stories.title: Canada signs preliminary agreement buy six Saab GlobalEye radar planes
stories.summary: The GlobalEye radar systems will be constructed in Canada and used primarily for Arctic surveillance.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
Canada

The GlobalEye radar systems will be constructed in Canada and used primarily for Arctic surveillance

Author of the article:

A model of GlobalEye, Saab’s Airborne Early Warning & Control aircraft platform on display at Saab booth at Cansec defence trade show in Ottawa on May 27, 2026.Photo by Hyungcheol Park/Postmedia

Canada on Friday announced a preliminary agreement signed with Swedish arms giant Saab to acquire six GlobalEye radar aircraft.

The non-binding agreement “establishes the scope and foundation for detailed negotiations,” Canada’s Defence Investment Agency said in a press release. Prime Minister Mark Carney formed the agency last October to streamline the country’s military acquisitions.

Talks between the Canadian government and Saab began on May 27, with the original focus pertaining to the acquisition of at least 40 aircraft.

In addition to the six aircraft, Canada also seeks to acquire GlobalEye systems and training, although no timetable has been set for that.

“Together, we are advancing capabilities that will strengthen our security and deliver value for Canadians,” Defence Minister David McGuinty said in a statement.

Canada had been in talks to make deals with US companies, including L3Harris’s Aeris X and Boeing’s E7 Wedgetail, but the Saab agreement ultimately won out.

Canada has significantly increased its military defense spending, allocating $65 billion dollars.

Carney told The New York Times earlier this week that he needed to be prepared for the “extreme” scenario of a U.S. military intervention on Canadian soil.

stories.title: Quebec premier warns of U.S. attempts to sow division ahead of election
stories.summary: Document from U.S. think tank detailed a plan to support Quebec independence, including by helping the sovereigntist PQ party to power
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette is warning of U.S. attempts to sow division between the province and Canada less than two weeks from an election that could see the sovereigntist Parti Québécois come to power.

She was responding to media reports saying the federal government has warned Ms. Fréchette’s Coalition Avenir Québec government about possible U.S. interference in the Quebec election aiming to help elect sovereigntists.

The Premier also said on Friday that U.S. authorities sought a separate trade deal with Quebec around sensitive sectors such as aluminum earlier this year. Ms. Fréchette said she rejected the deal in order to maintain a common front with the rest of Canada amidst tense negotiations.

“There was an approach in the spring to attempt to have an agreement with us, Quebec,” Ms. Fréchette told reporters Friday. “When my team told me that, I closed the door right away. It’s not possible to think that Quebec would conclude an agreement with the U.S. on our own, and in any case it wouldn’t respond to the needs of Quebec. We need to have a comprehensive agreement. It’s important to keep a united front and to join our efforts.”

Quebec party leaders square off in final debate

In a separate statement also released Friday, Ms. Fréchette said there is no proof of interference in the province’s electoral process. She said her government became aware last Saturday of a U.S. think-tank document proposing to break up Canada by supporting Quebec independence, including by helping to elect the PQ and offering the province its own trade deal.

The relatively obscure think tank Defense Analyses and Research Corporation, or Darc, published the document in February.

She said her government met with the Canadian Security Intelligence Service about it on Wednesday, and that she was only addressing intelligence matters publicly because of the media reports.

Csis did not respond to requests for comment Friday afternoon.

The Premier told reporters she is seeking a meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney to shed light on the situation.

The Québécor media chain reported on Friday that the federal government informed the Quebec government about the think-tank publication earlier this month in a secret meeting.

In the document, a pseudonymous author suggests funding for the Parti Québécois, along with “behind-closed-doors trade negotiations with the PQ where the United States commits to offering lower tariffs on Quebec than on the rest of Canada.”

Crowded political landscape leaves Quebec voters lukewarm as election nears

On Friday, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon denied receiving any foreign assistance and questioned the timing of the media leaks, with his party leading in the polls shortly before election day on Oct. 5.

He told reporters he had “never heard of” Darc before Friday.

Canada’s Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said at a news conference in Ottawa that the federal government is taking the issue very seriously.

“Protecting our democracy is of the utmost importance to our country,” she said.

She added that she will speak with her U.S. counterpart, Marco Rubio, after reviewing evidence of the allegations.

“Right now I have not seen the evidence,” Ms. Anand said.

Thomas Juneau, a professor at the University of Ottawa’s Graduate School of Public and International Affairs, said it’s possible there is more to the federal warnings about election interference in Quebec than is publicly known.

“Given the irrelevance of that group, and the amateurishness of some of the recommendations in that report, it makes me wonder if there are other aspects to what was detected,” he said.

It is too early to draw clear parallels with the pro-separatist disinformation campaigns directed at the continuing Alberta referendum campaign, some of it from U.S. sources, he added.

“The one coherent element here, the one parallel, is that our assumptions are shattered,” said Prof. Juneau. “Whatever exactly is going on, the simple fact that we’re thinking about this should tell us, if anyone still had any doubts, that relations with the United States are not what they were.”

With reports from The Canadian Press, Mercedes Stephenson and Maura Forrest

She added that she will speak with her U.S. counterpart, Marco Rubio, after reviewing evidence of the allegations.
“Right now I have not seen the evidence,” Ms. Anand said.

Thomas Juneau, a professor at the University of Ottawa’s Graduate School of Public and International Affairs, said it’s possible there is more to the federal warnings about election interference in Quebec than is publicly known.
“Given the irrelevance of that group, and the amateurishness of some of the recommendations in that report, it makes me wonder if there are other aspects to what was detected,” he said.
It is too early to draw clear parallels with the pro-separatist disinformation campaigns directed at the continuing Alberta referendum campaign, some of it from U.S. sources, he added.

“The one coherent element here, the one parallel, is that our assumptions are shattered,” said Prof. Juneau. “Whatever exactly is going on, the simple fact that we’re thinking about this should tell us, if anyone still had any doubts, that relations with the United States are not what they were.”

stories.title: Encampment standoff in Saskatoon underscores growing municipal battles across Canada
stories.summary: Three homeless encampments on city-owned lots are raising safety concerns for those staying there and the residents that live in the neighbourhood.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Saskatoon – Three homeless encampments on city-owned lots are raising safety concerns for those staying there and the residents that live in the neighbourhood.

The City of Saskatoon had hoped to clear the areas by now, but officials say “aggressive” protests from advocacy groups and a court application have paused all efforts .

“There are two safety concerns here that have to be addressed equally,” lawyer Crystal Fafard told CTV News.

Fafard filed for an injunction that would prevent the city from clearing one of the encampments until the people staying there can find suitable shelter.

She will make her case at a hearing scheduled for Monday afternoon.

“I know so many Saskatoon residents are extremely concerned about these encampments. We all are. We don’t want them. We want security,” she said.

Until the people staying in the encampments can find secure housing, Fafard said more services need to be provided at the encampment, including water, washrooms and garbage bins.

“They need basic rights that every human is entitled to,” she said.

There are growing public health concerns related to the encampment, according to fire inspectors who have observed human waste and rotting food that are attracting insects and rodents in the area.

“The city’s goal is to always support the safety and well-being of people staying at the site, but also support the safety and well-being of neighbouring residents and businesses,” the city wrote in a statement.

A nearby school has also raised concerns about the encampment.

Thursday’s efforts to clear the site were met with resistance by a group of protesters, largely made up of community advocates not people living at the encampment, according to the city.

In the past, advocacy groups have helped protect encampments from being cleared.

In June, a Quebec judge made a ruling that blocked Montreal officials from dismantling an encampment, stating that the city failed to offer a suitable, safe alternative.

Encampment safety remains a complex issue, and a patchwork of policies exist across the country that determine how municipalities handle encampments.

The City of Regina adopted a support-focused approach to homeless encampments after dismantling previous ones in recent years.

Regina Mayor Chad Bachynski previously stated that moving people away from encampments does not solve the issue of homelessness.

Under the updated framework, officials work directly with people staying in encampments to assess their health and safety while connecting them to multiple services, including shelter, identification assistance and counselling.

The Saskatoon Fire Department says it is working with the Salvation Army to connect people at the encampment with housing, transportation, outreach and other supports.

Earlier this week, crews visited the site to serve notice of a clean up. At that time, no one accepted offers of support, according to the fire department.

Fafard said she is confident a “reasonable decision” will come from the court hearing.

The City of Saskatoon said it will act in good faith and refrain from clearing the encampment until the court hearing.

Officials are monitoring the sites and still deciding how to proceed with the other encampments.

stories.title: Planned driving safety training campus in Beaumont gets $38.5M from province
stories.summary: The Alberta Motor Transport Association Safety Campus, or Amta Safety Campus, will provide specialized, hands-on training for law enforcement and commercial drivers.
stories.author: Joel Gotlib
stories.content:
A long-term vision for City of Beaumont is a step closer to reality after the Alberta government announced funding for a new safety training campus in the community south of Edmonton.

The Alberta Motor Transport Association Safety Campus , or Amta Safety Campus, will provide specialized, hands-on training for law enforcement and commercial drivers.

“This is going to really, truly change the landscape of this community in a positive way that I think is gonna be groundbreaking, quite frankly,” said Public Safety and Emergency Services Minister Mike Ellis.

The City of Beaumont has secured 160 acres of land for the proposed campus in the planned Beaumont Innovation Park , which will be south of Highway 625, between Highway 814 and Range Road 241.

On Friday, the province said it will be providing $38.5 million to the City of Beaumont to build the infrastructure for the Innovation Park, including for the proposed safety campus.

“This funding is going to go to the City of Beaumont to support roads, utilities, servicing for a future development of an innovation park,” Ellis said.

“I’m so proud of Beaumont and I can’t wait to see this come to life,” said Brandon Lunty, MLA for Leduc and Beaumont.

Plans include an emergency vehicle operator track for high-speed and emergency driver training, a firearms range, scenario-based training areas and dedicated commercial vehicle training facilities.

The campus and construction of it is also seen as an economic boon for the bedroom community five minutes south of Edmonton.

“It’s also going to help us diversify our tax base so all of those are benefits in terms of creating opportunities, brining in skilled professionals as well as labourers,” said Beaumont Mayor Lisa Vanderkwaak.

“I see this as, once it gets started it’s just going to take off.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I see this as, once it gets started it's just going to take off."

The Alberta Motor Transport Association is responsible for financing, building and operating the safety campus. There’s no firm timeline yet on when it will open.

“It’s up to us to go roll up our sleeves and say, ‘How do we build it, when can we have it first occupied?’ and move forward and continue to grow,” said Tim Bennett, chair of the Amta.

Bringing these training opportunities together would build on the existing relationship between law enforcement and Alberta’s commercial transportation industry, the province said.

Alberta’s Sheriff highway patrol already works closely with the commercial sector on vehicle inspections, enforcement and safety standards.

“Strong public safety depends on well-trained professionals and the infrastructure needed to support them,” Ellis said.

“This investment will help create the foundation for a modern training facility that can serve Alberta’s public safety and commercial transportation sectors for years to come, while supporting economic growth and employment in the Beaumont region.”

stories.title: Former RCMP intelligence director convicted of violating secrets law granted day parole
stories.summary: Cameron Ortis, sentenced to 14 years for violating Canada’s secrecy laws, was deemed a low risk to reoffend by the Parole Board of Canada
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Cameron Ortis, a former RCMP intelligence official who was convicted of violating Canada’s secrecy laws, is no longer in prison after being granted day parole earlier this year to facilitate his return to society.

Mr. Ortis was sentenced to 14 years in 2024 after a jury found him guilty of multiple counts of violating Canada’s Security of Information Act. The 54-year-old former RCMP intelligence director was accused of trying to pass along highly sensitive police dossiers to transnational gangs.

His sentence was reduced by about half because of the time he spent in pre-trial custody. He was first granted day parole in a decision by the Parole Board of Canada in February and it was renewed in August. It was not publicly reported until this week.

Day parole means that he can be out on his own during the day but must return to a halfway house or jail at night.

In its February decision, the board said he completed electrical and environmental courses in prison and also submitted 26 letters from friends and family about his “positive qualities and good character.”

“You have no prior criminal history,” the February ruling reads. It adds that “you pose a low risk to re-offend.”

That was extended for another six months in August.

“The board finds that your risk to re-offend can be safely managed on a day parole,” says the Aug. 25 ruling, which tells Mr. Ortis that “your release will contribute to the protection of society by facilitating your reintegration into society as a law-abiding citizen.”

Mr. Ortis led an RCMP group that assembled secret information on cybercriminals, terror cells and transnational criminal networks.

He pleaded not guilty in court to all charges – including breaking the Security of Information Act by revealing classified information to three individuals of interest to police in 2015 and trying to do so in a fourth instance.

Mr. Ortis, who was born and raised in British Columbia, obtained a PhD in political science and international relations and completed a postdoctoral fellowship.

Mr. Ortis testified he did not betray the RCMP. Rather, he said, he offered secret material to targets in a bid to get them to use an online encryption service set up by an allied intelligence agency to spy on adversaries.

The Crown argued Mr. Ortis had no authority to disclose classified material and that he was not doing so as part of a legitimate undercover operation, though it could not pinpoint a motive.

Mr. Ortis is appealing his case. The Ontario Court of Appeal has scheduled a court date in November to hear Mr. Ortis’s arguments that he should never have been convicted in the first place.

“He maintains his innocence as he has throughout,” said Toronto lawyer Matthew Gourlay, who is representing Mr. Ortis, in an interview on Friday.

His parole conditions include a ban on using a cellphone without permission and from communicating with criminals. He has been ordered to surrender his electronic devices to searches upon demand and he must provide statements about how he handles money because he has been “debanked” – or cut off from Canadian financial institutions.

The board also told him that his crimes remain an enormous black eye for Canada.

“Your deceitfulness in willfully sharing this sensitive information resulted in detrimental impacts to your colleagues, Canadian law enforcement agencies and the Canadian public,” the Aug. 25 decision reads. “It will take many years to rebuild trust with international law enforcement partners.”

stories.title: Belleville’s tiny Jewish community vows to carry on after attack
stories.summary: ‘There has been some trauma from this. But we’re going to pick up the pieces,’ synagogue’s volunteer president says
stories.author: Greg Mercer, Photography by David LeClair
stories.content:
As the volunteer president of the only synagogue serving a rural stretch of mid-eastern Ontario, Norman Weddum is used to taking on a lot of job responsibilities. Fixing leaks in the roof. Mopping the floor. Mowing the lawn. Even cleaning the toilets if needed.

This week, he added a new, grim task to his to-do list: fix two dozen bullet holes in the large, technicolour stained glass window depicting the 12 Tribes of Israel, or the ancient lineage of the Jewish people.

“I need to find a craftsman who knows how to repair that type of stuff,” he told The Globe and Mail. “This place is a mess. I need to clean it up.”

At sundown on Sunday, the small congregation of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., was settling in for Yom Kippur services when gunfire erupted outside . At first, Mr. Weddum thought it was firecrackers or a car backfiring, and went into the lobby to look at the street.

Realizing what was happening, he ran back inside, slammed the doors behind him and told everyone to get on the floor of the sanctuary. Bullets began flying over their heads as police engaged in the fierce gun battle with Sean Ward, a former member of the Canadian military, who had come prepared to carry out a mass-casualty attack, armed with multiple firearms, ammunition and gasoline, investigators said.

The gunman, who was caught on video shouting “you are going to die for the Jews,” was killed in the firefight and a Belleville Police officer, Constable Jeff Smith, was critically injured.

Three days later, board members of Sons of Jacob gathered here for the first time since the shooting, shared hugs and got back to the business of running their synagogue during what’s normally the holiest time in the Jewish calendar. Though shaken by questions about what would have happened if the gunman had breached their door, they say they will continue to gather to celebrate their faith, just as they always have.

“There has been some trauma from this. But we’re going to pick up the pieces and we’re going to start over and we’re going to carry on. We will not be stopped by this person, or anybody else,” Mr. Weddum said.

Mr. Weddum, semi-retired at 70 and managing the synagogue in between shifts as an usher at the local hockey rink, says the threat of violence has become a reality for Jewish organizations in 2026, even in the smallest of communities in Canada.

With no paid staff, there is little money in the Sons of Jacob budget to hire off-duty police or private security, but those things have become essential, he said. Constable Smith was on-duty Sunday and assigned to protect the building as part of a long-running partnership with the Belleville police.

Sunday’s attack is a dramatic escalation of antisemitic incidents targeting Jewish people in Canada, and has fuelled calls for a national response.

More than two dozen reports of gunfire, arson, window-breaking and other types of vandalism have been documented at synagogues, Jewish schools and institutions across Canada in the past three years, according to the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs. While most of those have happened in larger urban centres, the Belleville shooting casts a spotlight on the vulnerability of the country’s smallest Jewish communities.

“We always have police protection,” Mr. Weddum said. “Every synagogue in North America on the high holidays has police protection. We’ve been doing it for years. Whenever there’s a large gathering of Jews in a synagogue, there’s police protection. That’s just a sign of the times.”

On Thursday, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said federal funds will be used to improve security at the synagogue, but didn’t elaborate. The synagogue has also started a $90,000 GoFundMe campaign to help rebuild and protect the building.

The members of Sons of Jacob, meanwhile, say they’re reflecting on their past this week, and the determination of previous generations of Jewish people who resettled in the Belleville area.

“When you’re Jewish, you look to the history of your people,” Shima Viggoda, Sons of Jacob’s vice-president, told The Globe. “The people who came here were Holocaust survivors. They escaped Czarist Russia. They came to make a better life in this country, just as every Jewish community across this country.”

has persevered for well over a century. In the late 1800s, this railway stop halfway between Toronto and Montreal attracted Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe, who faced barriers in traditional professions and trades but found work as furriers and peddlers. In 1905, a handful of families began holding religious ceremonies at a rooming house for travelling Jewish workers, laying the early roots for the Sons of Jacob congregation, according to the synagogue’s own historical records.

By 1956, when the current synagogue opened on a leafy residential street, the area’s Jewish community included some of its most prominent merchants, but also plenty of blue-collar families. They raised the money to build their new place of worship in part through bingo games, hosted at an ice cream parlour where the main attraction was two domesticated bears.

At its peak, the Sons of Jacob had a thriving congregation of more than 55 families, with its own Hebrew school, rabbi and shochet, a specially trained kosher butcher. The synagogue was a bustling hub for fundraising dances, bazaars, lectures and Bar Mitzvah ceremonies.

As many younger people left for larger cities, however, the membership dwindled. For years, Sons of Jacob didn’t have enough congregants to hold regular weekly services. On Sunday night, there was only 25 people inside the building, even though they’d used their limited budget to fly in a rabbi from Israel, and waived fees to attend.

They say they’ll continue their work to revive their congregation.

“We’re resilient, that’s why we keep going. We have to fight,” said Mary Cohen, a longtime congregant who sits on the synagogue’s board. “There was a time when we couldn’t have services and we didn’t have the people. But again, we built ourselves up, and we are standing on our feet now.”

Sunday’s shooting was not the first antisemitic incident experienced by members of the congregation. In 2023, a man smashed out the synagogue’s basement window in an act of vandalism some saw as targeted. As part of its history display, the congregation also has a letter to the editor published by a high school student in 2019, describing her experience with racism growing up Jewish in Prince Edward County.

There have been historical incidents here, too. In 1925, prominent businessman Harry Yanover, the son of Jewish immigrants from Poland, woke up to find a large cross burning on his front lawn, according to an account of Ku Klux Klan activity in the area by local historian Trevor Parsons.

Mr. Weddum said the synagogue will reopen its doors to the public soon, now that the building is no longer a crime scene. There’s still some unfinished business to follow Yom Kippur, the holy day of atonement when, according to the religious doctrine, God seals the fate of his people for the coming year, he said.

“For Jews, it’s kind of like, who’s going in the bad book? Who will not live through this year?” he said, pausing, then adding: “I guess we were all in the good book, because we survived.”

stories.title: Death of pregnant woman and her baby prompts call for Saskatchewan rural health changes
stories.summary: The NDP says the case of Chelsea Bear, a mom pregnant with twins who died with one of the babies after seeking care in Meadow Lake, was failed by the rural health-care system.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon, Grace Miller
stories.content:
Saskatchewan’s Opposition leader is calling on the province to investigate the death of a mother that Carla Beck claims was caused by lacking maternal care in rural areas.

The NDP leader said the death of Chelsea Bear, a mother-of-five who sought maternal care for pain in Meadow Lake , was caused by a lack of available services in non-urban parts of Saskatchewan.

Bear died while pregnant with twins, and only one of the infants survived. On Aug. 10 while experiencing pain and bleeding, Bear visited the Northwest Health Facility in Meadow Lake, located 300 kilometres northwest of Saskatoon — but was turned away, according to the Saskatchewan NDP.

At the time, she was 36 weeks pregnant with the twins, and it was considered a high-risk pregnancy.

Bear returned to the hospital the following day because her pain had intensified and was sent south to a hospital in Saskatoon. After waiting to be seen for hours, her placenta tore, which her family said caused a hemorrhage.

She died with one of the twins, who was stillborn, her family said.

“Now that my daughter’s gone and the baby, I just want things to change in hospitals and how they treat people,” said Debbie Bear, Chelsea’s mother.

As of Wednesday, the surviving twin named Gracie remained in critical condition at the Jim Pattison Children’s Hospital in Saskatoon.

Her family shared Bear’s story and is demanding an independent investigation into the care she received prior to her death – their request was backed at a news conference earlier this week by the Meadow Lake Tribal Council (Mltc).

Saskatchewan’s NDP amplified the family’s call Friday, when they issued a news release calling on the government to perform a full investigation and offer a public release of findings, including recommendations for improvement, in light of Bear’s treatment while in hospital.

“We have heard stories of mothers giving birth on the side of highways, and not able to access health care where and when they need it — as the minister claims he’s putting patients first,” Beck said in the release.

“He could truly demonstrate that by launching an investigation today, to ensure this never happens again.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "He could truly demonstrate that by launching an investigation today, to ensure this never happens again."

An email statement sent on behalf of Saskatchewan Health Minister Jeremy Cockrill extended condolences over the Bear’s death.

“Maternal care and providing access to high-quality health care services to patients in rural and northern communities are significant priorities for our government,” the statement said, adding a patient safety review is being conducted.

No other information was released.

“The Opposition knows it would be inappropriate and a violation of The Health Information Protection Act (Hipa) privacy laws for the province or the SHA to comment on a patient’s specific clinical details and circumstances with the media,” the ministry said.

On Friday, Beck referred to an earlier news conference where Mltc representatives spoke about the loss of Bear.

At that event, the tribal council said prior to her death, leaders were told “keep quiet” about the situation when they sought answers from the Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA).

“Basically, the concern was on ‘What’s the image going to look like?’ It wasn’t about answering or giving the family comfort,” alleged Mltc Tribal Chief Jeremy Norman.

The SHA confirmed to Global News it met with the tribal council, but did not confirm or deny whether those comments were made during that meeting.

“At the time of that meeting, the SHA had not received consent from the family to discuss the specifics of their case with Mltc,” the authority said in a statement for Global News.

“We have since received the family’s consent and will continue our discussions with Mltc in the coming days.

“We take Mltc’s concerns seriously and value their role as an important community partner as we continue this dialogue in a culturally respectful and responsive way.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We take Mltc's concerns seriously and value their role as an important community partner as we continue this dialogue in a culturally respectful and responsive way."

This is the second Indigenous woman to die during childbirth this year in Saskatchewan.

Jaali Weenie-Sutherland, 24, died in April after being transferred to two different hospitals in Saskatoon and waiting 13 hours after receiving a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia — a dangerous pregnancy complication causing high blood pressure.

content_blocks.text: Bear died while pregnant with twins, and only one of the infants survived. On Aug. 10 while experiencing pain and bleeding, Bear visited the Northwest Health Facility in Meadow Lake, located 300 kilometres northwest of Saskatoon — but was turned away, according to the Saskatchewan NDP.
content_blocks.html: Bear died while pregnant with twins, and only one of the infants survived. On Aug. 10 while experiencing pain and bleeding, Bear visited the Northwest Health Facility in Meadow Lake, located 300 kilometres northwest of Saskatoon — but was turned away, according to the Saskatchewan NDP.

content_blocks.text: At the time, she was 36 weeks pregnant with the twins, and it was considered a high-risk pregnancy.

Bear returned to the hospital the following day because her pain had intensified and was sent south to a hospital in Saskatoon. After waiting to be seen for hours, her placenta tore, which her family said caused a hemorrhage.
She died with one of the twins, who was stillborn, her family said.
“Now that my daughter’s gone and the baby, I just want things to change in hospitals and how they treat people,” said Debbie Bear, Chelsea’s mother.
As of Wednesday, the surviving twin named Gracie remained in critical condition at the Jim Pattison Children’s Hospital in Saskatoon.

content_blocks.text: Her family shared Bear’s story and is demanding an independent investigation into the care she received prior to her death – their request was backed at a news conference earlier this week by the Meadow Lake Tribal Council (Mltc).

Saskatchewan’s NDP amplified the family’s call Friday, when they issued a news release calling on the government to perform a full investigation and offer a public release of findings, including recommendations for improvement, in light of Bear’s treatment while in hospital.

“We have heard stories of mothers giving birth on the side of highways, and not able to access health care where and when they need it — as the minister claims he’s putting patients first,” Beck said in the release.

“He could truly demonstrate that by launching an investigation today, to ensure this never happens again.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "He could truly demonstrate that by launching an investigation today, to ensure this never happens again."

content_blocks.text: An email statement sent on behalf of Saskatchewan Health Minister Jeremy Cockrill extended condolences over the Bear’s death.

“Maternal care and providing access to high-quality health care services to patients in rural and northern communities are significant priorities for our government,” the statement said, adding a patient safety review is being conducted.
No other information was released.

“The Opposition knows it would be inappropriate and a violation of The Health Information Protection Act (Hipa) privacy laws for the province or the SHA to comment on a patient’s specific clinical details and circumstances with the media,” the ministry said.

content_blocks.text: On Friday, Beck referred to an earlier news conference where Mltc representatives spoke about the loss of Bear.
At that event, the tribal council said prior to her death, leaders were told “keep quiet” about the situation when they sought answers from the Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA).
“Basically, the concern was on ‘What’s the image going to look like?’ It wasn’t about answering or giving the family comfort,” alleged Mltc Tribal Chief Jeremy Norman.
The SHA confirmed to Global News it met with the tribal council, but did not confirm or deny whether those comments were made during that meeting.
“At the time of that meeting, the SHA had not received consent from the family to discuss the specifics of their case with Mltc,” the authority said in a statement for Global News.
“We have since received the family’s consent and will continue our discussions with Mltc in the coming days.
