stories.title: Fréchette warns of U.S. interference risk in Quebec election
stories.summary: CAQ Leader requests meeting with Carney after report said U.S. officials attempted direct negotiations with Quebec on tariffs
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
Quebec’s incumbent premier says she is “very concerned” about possible interference in the Oct. 5 provincial election by the United States.

Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette told journalists she reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney and requested a meeting with him to discuss the matter.

She was reacting to a news report published by Québecor media outlets that said American officials had attempted to negotiate directly with Quebec government officials regarding tariffs.

“I want to ensure that the full truth about this issue comes to light,” Fréchette said on the campaign trail. “[The election] must remain in the hands of and be decided by the people of Quebec.”

Canada’s Foreign Affairs Minister, Anita Anand, said at a news conference in Ottawa that the federal government is taking the issue very seriously.

“Protecting our democracy is of the utmost importance to our country,” she said.

She added that she will speak with her American counterpart, Marco Rubio, after reviewing evidence of the allegations.

“Right now I have not seen the evidence,” Anand said.

stories.title: Two people found in burning cars at opposite ends of Toronto were murdered, police say
stories.summary: Police haven’t confirmed a connection between the two deaths but that remains under investigation
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi
stories.content:
Toronto police say two people who were found in burning vehicles overnight on opposite ends of the city earlier this week were targeted and killed before they were burned.

Police say the first body was found in a burning vehicle in the city’s northeast corner around Rouge National Urban Park just before 11:30 p.m. on Monday.

Det.-Sgt. Henri Marsman says the victim has been identified as 32-year-old Marcus Charles, who was living in Toronto.

He says Charles was identified using his fingerprints.

The second body was found about 90 minutes after the first, in James Gardens Park in the city’s west end.

Marsman says the second victim has not been identified yet as the body was badly burned.

He says officers are investigating both homicides.

Police say they haven’t confirmed a connection between the two deaths but that remains under investigation.

They say the first vehicle was a rental and the second one was stolen from the Greater Toronto Area.

stories.title: Mississauga woman faces upgraded murder charge after stabbing victim dies
stories.summary: A Mississauga woman has been charged with second-degree murder after the victim of a stabbing died in hospital days later.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A Mississauga woman has been charged with second-degree murder after the victim of a stabbing died in hospital days later.

Peel Regional Police said they responded to reports of a stabbing in the area of Dixie Road and Dundas Street East on Sept. 6 around 5:30 p.m.

When officers arrived on scene, they found a man with a “serious stab wound to the neck.”

The man was transported to hospital in critical condition.

Officers immediately arrested a man who was involved in an altercation with the victim but determined he was not responsible and was released.

The next day, officers located and arrested 42-year-old Lorena Sanchez and charged her with attempted murder.

On Sept. 10, police say the man died in hospital and Sanchez’s charges were upgraded to second-degree murder.

The investigation is ongoing.

stories.title: Muslim schools across Canada on high alert after receiving e-mails threatening violence
stories.summary: Same anonymous e-mail was sent to schools in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec this week, association spokesperson says
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
The Muslim Association of Canada says nine schools it operates across Canada are on high alert after the schools each received an e-mail this week threatening violence against Muslims.

Spokesperson Nabil Sultan says the same anonymous e-mail was sent to schools in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec over a 24-hour period, and local police forces have been notified.

The email, shared with The Canadian Press and signed by a “Citizen Vigilante,” threatens the “slaughter” of Muslims and vows Canada will be “Islam free.”

Sultan, whose own child attends a MAC school, says he was devastated to read the letter, and that MAC has hired paid security to keep students safe.

He says the organization is used to receiving threatening and Islamophobic e-mails, but this is the first time the non-profit’s schools have been targeted in such a direct way.

Police in Ontario’s Peel region say they’re aware of a letter “containing hate-motivated threats” against Islamic institutions and increased police patrols overnight near mosques and schools, which will continue into the weekend.

The force says its hate crime unit is investigating.

Sultan says the threats against Mac’s schools come amid a backdrop of rising Islamophobia in Canada.

He pointed to recent atrocities against Muslim communities, including the 2021 killings of four members of the Afzaal family in London, Ont., which was ruled an act of terrorism, as well as a 2017 shooting at a Quebec City mosque that left six worshippers dead.

“These threats are real, and we know that they are real,” Sultan said. “The targeting of children, the targeting of schools, in that kind of way is something that shook us to our core.”

The latest data from Statistics Canada shows the number of police-reported hate crimes against Muslims rose by over 170 per cent between 2020 and 2024.

Sultan says students are feeling “scared and vulnerable” as they walk past security and police officers on their way to class, and that the threats have raised tough questions about who gets to be considered Canadian and who are labelled outsiders.

“All of the things that we try to teach our children in these schools is that they are equal to any other Canadian, that they have equal rights and responsibilities,” Sultan said. “Threats like this really make them question if they belong because of the way they pray and because of their faith.”

He argues Canada needs to address an “environment of Islamophobia and xenophobia” that breeds threats against Muslims and other visible minorities.

stories.title: ‘Zero chance’ U.S. attacks Canada, Alaska governor tells conference
stories.summary: Calgary — Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy says it would be shocking to the average American to see the United States invade Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, right, speaks on stage as Gary Mar, president and CEO of the Canada West Foundation, looks on during a talk at the Global Business Forum, in Banff, Alta., Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Lauren Krugel

By Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

Posted September 25, 2026 1:42 pm.

Last Updated September 25, 2026 1:49 pm.

Calgary — Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy says it would be shocking to the average American to see the United States invade Canada.

Dunleavy made his remarks in an onstage discussion at the Global Business Forum in Banff, Alta., days after Prime Minister Mark Carney told the New York Times that his government has studied the “extreme tail risk” of U.S.-led military action in Canada.

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly asserted he wants to make Canada the 51st state, but has said he would do so through economic coercion.

Jody Thomas, who was national security and intelligence adviser to former prime minister Justin Trudeau, calls a U.S. invasion “an improbable, slightly impossible” notion.

stories.title: Margaret Atwood donates $1M to Western University for avian research chair
stories.summary: The legacy of celebrated Canadian author and bird conservation advocate Graeme Gibson will continue through a $1-million gift to Western University from his longtime partner, acclaimed author Margaret Atwood.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The legacy of celebrated Canadian author and bird conservation advocate Graeme Gibson will continue through a $1-million gift to Western University from his longtime partner, acclaimed author Margaret Atwood.

The donation will establish the Graeme Gibson Chair in Avian Biology, a new research position at the London, Ont., school focused on understanding how birds move, behave and adapt to changing environmental conditions.

Western president Alan Shepard said the gift will help advance the university’s internationally recognized bird and migration research programs.

“In addition to their extraordinary leadership in Canadian writing and the arts, Margaret Atwood and Graeme Gibson have been lifelong champions for birds and nature conservation efforts across Canada and around the world,” Shepard said. “Western is deeply honoured to receive this gift in Graeme’s memory to advance world-leading bird and migration research.”

Atwood said the donation honours Gibson’s lifelong passion for birds and conservation. Gibson, a Western arts graduate, died in 2019 at the age of 85.

The chairholder will join Western’s biology department and become part of the Centre for Animals on the Move, an interdisciplinary research hub that studies the movement of birds, bats, fish and insects. The successful candidate will also have access to the university’s Advanced Facility for Avian Research (Afar), which Atwood described as one of the country’s leading bird biology programs.

Atwood said the new chair builds on an existing connection between Western researchers and the Pelee Island Bird Observatory, which she and Gibson co-founded in 2003.

“Graeme would be very pleased. He was devoted to birds, evidenced by his best-selling The Bedside Book of Birds ,” Atwood said.

“Birds are the canaries in the coal mine. They indicate the health of an ecosystem. Also, imagine a world without birds or birdsong. Birds have long been a symbol of hope, and hope is what we need more of right now.”

Atwood said the gift also reflects Gibson’s ties to Western, where his experiences as a student inspired his first novel, Five Legs .

“Graeme would have gotten a kick out of a chair in his name at Western because he went there, with mixed and hilarious though ultimately beneficial results,” she said.

stories.title: Landlord withdraws rent increase after tenant strike at Toronto apartment: organizers
stories.summary: Tenant organizers say they have successfully beat back a landlord's attempt to retroactively raise rents by over five per cent at a west-end Toronto apartment building.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Tenant organizers say they have successfully beat back a landlord’s attempt to retroactively raise rents by over five per cent at a west-end Toronto apartment building.

In March, tenants at 75 Spencer Avenue began withholding rent payments after their building’s property manager applied for an above guideline rent increase, or AGI.

After six months of the rent strike, tenant organizers say Metcap Living has withdrawn the application.

The maximum allowable increase for rent-controlled buildings in Ontario was 2.5 per cent in 2025, but landlords can apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board for AGIs to fund renovations and building improvements.

The tenants told The Canadian Press in February that the landlord had renovated the lobby and turned an office into a rental unit.

They argued that those projects hadn’t directly improved their living conditions so they shouldn’t have to cover the costs by way of a rent increase, and that a 5.4 per cent increase in their housing costs would be unaffordable.

Organizers say the building in Toronto’s Parkdale neighbourhood was sold to a new owner in May, and tenants travelled to Montreal last weekend to confront them over the rent increase.

“The rent strike won because our neighbours did the thing that everyone talks about but almost no one does: they formed an independent organization, stepped outside of legal and political convention, and directly confronted their landlord,” said Bryan Doherty of Parkdale Organize, a group that advocates for tenants.

stories.title: Quebec author dropped from Goncourt amid AI, plagiarism allegations
stories.summary: The Académie Goncourt has removed Quebec author Thélyson Orélien’s novel from a list of finalists for the prestigious French literary prize.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Quebec author Thélyson Orélien has lost his spot in the running for one of France’s most prestigious literary prizes over allegations that he used artificial intelligence to write his first book.

The Académie Goncourt announced Friday that it had removed Orélien’s novel, “C’était ça ou mourir,” which translates to “It was either that or dying” from the running for the Prix Goncourt amid allegations that the book was written using artificial intelligence, and separate plagiarism allegations involving his earlier work.

The decision marks the latest fallout from a controversy that has quickly spread through the French-language literary world, prompting Orélien’s Quebec publisher to suspend promotion of the novel, citing Orélien’s well-being, and a Quebec book fair to cancel his appearances.

Orélien, who earlier this week vehemently denied using AI to write the novel, declined on Friday to respond to the new allegations or provide further comment.

“I can’t talk about it. I want to focus on my physical and mental health,” he said in a WhatsApp message to The Canadian Press.

The Académie Goncourt, which awards an annual prize recognizing the best French-language novel, said it was removing the novel from its long list of 16 titles to “preserve the integrity of the Prix Goncourt” and recognize “literature written by women and men.”

The academy said its decision was informed by several analyses conducted by researchers and journalists it considers credible who had reached similar conclusions and alleged that the novel May have been largely written using artificial intelligence. It also cited plagiarism allegations involving Orélien’s previous work.

The academy’s president, Philippe Claudel, did not immediately respond to a request for details about the evidence used to reach the decision. The short list for the prize comes out on Oct. 6.

The academy’s decision comes days after allegations surfaced that Orélien used generative AI to write his novel.

The allegations were first raised by “Balance ton Claude,” a collective project that analyzed the book using AI-detection software Pangram.

In a post on X Friday, Samuel Fitoussi, a columnist for the French newspaper Le Figaro and one of the people behind the project, said the group had tested several other books and that “none reached such high AI scores.”

Fitoussi said the project grew out of broader concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence on writing and defended the decision to make its findings public.

“We obviously have compassion for the difficult days Orélien must be going through, and we hope he is being supported,” he wrote. “But we felt it was our duty to raise the alarm.”

He argued that readers should be able to know whether they are reading the work of a human or artificial intelligence so they can “choose with full knowledge of the facts.”

The controversy expanded Wednesday when La Presse reported separate allegations involving Orélien’s earlier work.

The newspaper said some articles attributed to him and published in Quebec and French media between 2012 and 2014 contained passages also found in previously published work by other authors.

La Presse said it used Pangram to identify a number of paragraphs that appeared to have been plagiarized.

The Canadian Press has not independently verified the AI or plagiarism allegations.

When CP put an excerpt of the novel through Pangram on Friday, a message on the platform alleged the text was “a mix of AI and human-written content.”

The British scientific journal Nature reported in August that Pangram has performed well in independent evaluations at differentiating AI-generated from human-written text, though researchers caution that its scores should not be treated as definitive proof of how much of a text was written by AI.

Les Éditions du Boréal, which published Orélien’s novel in Quebec, said Thursday it was concerned about the plagiarism allegations, saying they raise questions about copyright and editorial integrity.

“Plagiarism is an unacceptable practice,” the Montreal-based publisher said.

Boréal said it could neither confirm nor refute the allegations that artificial intelligence was used to write the novel. It said its editorial process began with a completed manuscript and included exchanges between the author and editor, language editing and proofreading, none of which involved the use of AI.

The book remains available for sale, the publisher said on Thursday.

The Salon du livre de l’Estrie, a book fair in Sherbrooke, Que., withdrew Orélien as a guest of honour Thursday and cancelled his participation in two activities.

The controversy follows a rapid rise for Orélien in the French literary world; the Goncourt recognition had marked a major literary breakthrough for him.

Michel Lacroix, a professor of literary studies at the Université du Québec à Montréal, told The Canadian Press earlier this month that it was extremely rare for a Quebec writer, particularly a debut novelist, to receive that level of recognition in France.

“C’était ça ou mourir” won France’s Prix du Roman Fnac earlier this week.

The novel remains in contention for several other major French literary prizes, including the Renaudot, Femina, Médicis and Prix Décembre.

The organizations behind the prizes did not immediately respond to questions about how they plan to respond to the controversy.

The Académie Goncourt awards its prize each fall to a work of French-language fiction. The winner receives a symbolic cheque for 10 euros, but the prestigious award typically brings significant attention and a major boost in book sales.

Orélien, who was born in Haiti and moved to Quebec after the 2010 earthquake, said he drew from his own experience as well as those of other migrants in writing the novel, which follows a Haitian man forced to flee his country and make a perilous journey through the Americas to Quebec.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

Michel Lacroix, a professor of literary studies at the Université du Québec à Montréal, told The Canadian Press earlier this month that it was extremely rare for a Quebec writer, particularly a debut novelist, to receive that level of recognition in France.
“C’était ça ou mourir” won France’s Prix du Roman Fnac earlier this week.
The novel remains in contention for several other major French literary prizes, including the Renaudot, Femina, Médicis and Prix Décembre.
The organizations behind the prizes did not immediately respond to questions about how they plan to respond to the controversy.

The Académie Goncourt awards its prize each fall to a work of French-language fiction. The winner receives a symbolic cheque for 10 euros, but the prestigious award typically brings significant attention and a major boost in book sales.

Orélien, who was born in Haiti and moved to Quebec after the 2010 earthquake, said he drew from his own experience as well as those of other migrants in writing the novel, which follows a Haitian man forced to flee his country and make a perilous journey through the Americas to Quebec.

stories.title: Flair Airlines ordered to pay B.C. passenger after jewelry goes missing from checked baggage: tribunal
stories.summary: A tribunal says Flair Airlines has been ordered to pay a woman more than $600 after she said jewelry disappeared from her checked baggage.
stories.author: Emma Crawford
stories.content:
Posted September 25, 2026 1:15 pm.

The BC Civil Resolution Tribunal (CRT) says Flair Airlines has been ordered to pay a woman more than $600 after she said jewelry disappeared from her checked baggage on a flight from Mexico to Vancouver.

According to the decision, the woman had just flown home from a trip on Flair in February 2024. The next morning, when she opened her luggage, she says she noticed her bag appeared to have been repacked. She says she then noticed a pouch containing jewelry was missing.

She says she reported the loss to the airline via text on Feb. 7, 2024, tribunal member Amanda Binnie wrote in her ruling this week. After not receiving a reply, she says she then reported the loss, via the airline’s website, ON April 10, 2024.

“On June 13, 2024, Flair acknowledged [the applicant’s] missing item claim, apologized for the missing items, and said it might contact her for additional information,” Binnie said. “Though neither party said when, they agree that Flair denied [her] claim because she did not provide an itemized list or receipts.”

The tribunal says the applicant provided a list of nine jewelry items, ranging in value from $15 to more than $535.24, for a total of $868.73. She didn’t provide receipts to support these amounts.

In the decision, the CRT says it found Flair was responsible for the loss.

However, the airline says jewelry should not be packed in checked baggage.

“Flair argues that under its international tariff, jewelry is unacceptable for transportation as checked baggage and can only be transported in a carry-on,” the ruling says.

Binnie says she acknowledges the airline’s argument that passengers shouldn’t put valuables in checked luggage.

“However … Flair did not provide any evidence, including its tariff,” she said.

“It also did not provide any evidence it told [the woman] she should only transport valuable items in carry-on luggage before her flight.”

Ultimately, the CRT found that under the Montreal Convention and the federal Carriage by Air Act (CAA), an airline can be liable for the loss of registered baggage while it is under the carrier’s care.

The tribunal didn’t award the woman the full amount claimed because she had no receipts, photos, or other evidence to show the condition or age of the jewelry.

Binnie ordered Flair to pay the applicant, within 30 days, $500 in damages, $38.68 in interest, and $67.50 toward her tribunal fees, for a total of $606.18.

stories.title: $680K raised for hero Belleville cop who prevented a Jewish massacre
stories.summary: The shooting described as hate-motivated by Police Chief Rodd occurred as a Yom Kippur service was being attended by roughly 25 congregants.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The GoFundMe campaign supported by the Canadian Jewish community for Belleville, Ont. police officer, Const. Jeff Smith has exceeded its initial goal of $18,000, raising more than $691,869 as of midday Friday.

The online campaign has garnered top donations from notable figures, including criminal defence lawyer Solomon Friedman.

Const. Smith prevented a mass shooting when he defended against multiple gunshots fired outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., by shooter Sean Ward , 29, ON Sunday night. Const. Smith sustained multiple gunshots wounds to his head and body. He was shot before he exited his vehicle, Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said in a press conference on Thursday afternoon. Const. Michael McCurdy, a second police officer assisting Const. Smith, was not harmed.

“Cons. Jeff Smith put himself in mortal danger to defend innocent men, women and children whose only crime was to gather as Jews,” Friedman told National Post. “Words are insufficient to describe the debt that is owed to both Cst. Smith and his fellow officer, Cst. McCurdy. They and their families are deserving of our endless gratitude and support.”

The shooting described as a hate-motivated crime by Police Chief Rodd occurred as a Yom Kippur service was being attended by roughly 25 congregants and Const. Smith was stationed outside the synagogue for security reasons.

“Jeff has a very long, difficult road ahead,” Smith’s wife Ashley Smith said on Tuesday in a Facebook post as she shared a photo of her holding her husband’s hand. “But he is not walking it alone,” she added, expressing her gratitude for the outpouring of support.

The 29-year-old gunman opened fire after shouting “you are going to die for the Jews,” as seen during a video the police played during the Thursday conference. Police Chief Rodd added that the attack was an “exclusive threat to our Jewish community.”

As for the success of the GoFundMe campaign, campaign organizer Derek Kreindler said in an online post, “I am astounded at the donations that have poured in, and never imagined we would raise over $500,000. My hope is that we are able to reach $1,000,000 by the time Constable Smith has been discharged from hospital.”

“Think about that for a second. Running toward gunfire while everyone else is trying to get away,” Williams wrote on Facebook . “We’ve spent the last few days talking about tragedy, fear and hate. We should also take a moment to recognize extraordinary courage when we see it,” he wrote.

“Some donors have asked about the second officer that assisted Constable Smith before more backup arrived,” wrote GoFundMe organizer Kreindler. “Constable McCurdy faced the same danger as Constable Smith while protecting the synagogue and those gathered inside, and assisting his fellow officer. We are deeply relieved that he is safe, and grateful to learn that he was physically unharmed.”

Meanwhile, Sons of Jacob have also launched a fundraiser to help rebuild the damage sustained by gunfire and aims to raise $90,000.

Smith sustained multiple gunshots wounds to his head and body. He was shot before he exited his vehicle, Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said in a press conference on Thursday afternoon. Const. Michael McCurdy, a second police officer assisting Const. Smith, was not harmed.

“Cons. Jeff Smith put himself in mortal danger to defend innocent men, women and children whose only crime was to gather as Jews,” Friedman told National Post. “Words are insufficient to describe the debt that is owed to both Cst. Smith and his fellow officer, Cst. McCurdy. They and their families are deserving of our endless gratitude and support.”

The shooting described as a hate-motivated crime by Police Chief Rodd occurred as a Yom Kippur service was being attended by roughly 25 congregants and Const. Smith was stationed outside the synagogue for security reasons.

“Jeff has a very long, difficult road ahead,” Smith’s wife Ashley Smith said on Tuesday in a Facebook post as she shared a photo of her holding her husband’s hand. “But he is not walking it alone,” she added, expressing her gratitude for the outpouring of support.

The 29-year-old gunman opened fire after shouting “you are going to die for the Jews,” as seen during a video the police played during the Thursday conference. Police Chief Rodd added that the attack was an “exclusive threat to our Jewish community.”

As for the success of the GoFundMe campaign, campaign organizer Derek Kreindler said in an online post, “I am astounded at the donations that have poured in, and never imagined we would raise over $500,000. My hope is that we are able to reach $1,000,000 by the time Constable Smith has been discharged from hospital.”

“Think about that for a second. Running toward gunfire while everyone else is trying to get away,” Williams wrote on Facebook . “We’ve spent the last few days talking about tragedy, fear and hate. We should also take a moment to recognize extraordinary courage when we see it,” he wrote.

“Some donors have asked about the second officer that assisted Constable Smith before more backup arrived,” wrote GoFundMe organizer Kreindler. “Constable McCurdy faced the same danger as Constable Smith while protecting the synagogue and those gathered inside, and assisting his fellow officer. We are deeply relieved that he is safe, and grateful to learn that he was physically unharmed.”
Meanwhile, Sons of Jacob have also launched a fundraiser to help rebuild the damage sustained by gunfire and aims to raise $90,000.

stories.title: Two year delay in EV battery plant construction “nothing but good news”: Ford government
stories.summary: On Thursday, PowerCo Canada, a subsidiary of German automaker Volkswagen, announced it would delay the production of the $7 billion giga factory in St. Thomas, Ont.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
On Thursday, PowerCo Canada, a subsidiary of German automaker Volkswagen, announced it would delay the production of the $7 billion giga factory in St. Thomas, Ont. where the company was planning to produce electric vehicle batteries.

The two-year construction delay comes in the wake of other electric vehicle manufacturing investments also pulling up stakes, leaving much of the Ford government’s EV supply chain strategy up in the air.

Ahead of the cabinet meeting, Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli — the architect of the EV strategy — called the construction delay “extremely exciting.”

“There are now shovels in the ground, a company has been hired and awarded contracts, there’s a $7 billion building and infrastructure being built there,” Fedeli said.

“To me, that’s nothing but good news.”

Fedeli added that full construction is expected to begin in a month, and that he expects the facility will be able to open ion 2029 as per the schedule.

Critics of the Ford government, however, argue that other plants have followed the same trajectory before eventually cancelling their investments altogether.

“We know Stellantis started with closing for retooling back in 2023 and then when 2025 came along and the tariffs hit, the retooling of that plant was delayed and a few months later we learned that the plant was being moved to Illinois,” said Liberal MPP Stephanie Smyth.

According to the government’s public accounts, Honda, NextStar, Toyota and General Motors received a combined $347 million over 2025-26 fiscal year, while the city of St. Thomas received $65 million for sewer and water connections for a new industrial park.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government should be more transparent about whether strings were attached to taxpayer funding.

“Especially when we are heavily subsidizing big companies — and I’m not saying it’s not the right thing to do — but I think it’s very clear that we should know what those strings are, that there are strings attached, there are conditions and we understand what they are,” Stiles said.

Fedeli said much of the promised provincial funding was based on future production and won’t be awarded if batteries or vehicles don’t come off a manufacturing line.

Still, Fedeli offered optimism about the state of Ontario auto manufacturing sector.

“Toyota invest a billion two this year in January. We’ve seen General Motors invest $1 billion in St. Catharines and more of it for Oshawa. We’ve seen Stellantis hire a third shift. Ford will be opening a multi-billion dollar facility in a couple of months here in Ontario,” he said.

“So we see great movement in the auto sector as well.”

stories.title: Volkswagen subsidiary delays opening of Ontario battery plant to 2029
stories.summary: The company behind the plan for a massive battery plant in southwestern Ontario says the facility is expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than initially planned.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The company behind the plan for a massive battery plant in southwestern Ontario says the facility is expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than initially planned.

PowerCo, founded by automaker Volkswagen, is currently building a gigafactory in St. Thomas, Ont., to produce batteries for its growing electric vehicle range.

On Thursday, the company announced the hiring of the construction firm EllisDon Corporation as the general contractor for the new plant.

In a news release, PowerCo said the appointment “enables work on-site to continue building on steady progress since groundbreaking in 2025.”

“Construction is now moving into core infrastructure and structural phases that will support future production.”

In an email statement to Global News, a spokesperson for PowerCo said the phased approach is not a sign of stepping back, but about ensuring each step of the project is completed efficiently and effectively.

“It preserves flexibility while supporting skilled trades, regional suppliers and economic activity in Southwestern Ontario,” the spokesperson said.

The first phase of development includes core building structures and site-wide infrastructure, the press release said. That includes mechanical, electrical and plumbing installations, energy and utility systems, and supporting site services.

The company said approximately 60 EllisDon workers are currently on site and that is expected to ramp up to 1,300 workers at peak.

The federal government previously said the company’s first battery plant outside of Europe will create 3,000 direct and 30,000 indirect jobs and contribute $200 billion to the Canadian economy in the coming decades.

In August 2025, PowerCo announced it had awarded two construction contracts for work on the new facility. Construction began in October.

The battery plant is being built under the cloud of tariffs and a changing vehicle market. Over the past year, Honda has postponed its plans for an EV plant in Canada and GM paused production of its electric vehicle vans.

These announcements came after the Trump administration levied tariffs on Canadian vehicles and removed subsidies to boost electric vehicles.

PowerCo said the project’s timeline is in line with “evolving market demands, technological advancements and Volkswagen Group’s long-term strategy.”

stories.title: Jewish CBC journalist faces discipline over comments about anti-Israel protest
stories.summary: CBC management "quietly pulled Herland off the air" and "hit him with disciplinary action."
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
CBC management 'quietly pulled Herland off the air' and 'hit him with disciplinary action'

A longtime CBC journalist and national newsreader has reportedly been removed from the air and is facing disciplinary action after posting video on social media showing pro-Palestinian protesters outside an event for Yom Kippur in north Toronto.

Neil Herland posted the video and his comments on Monday after attending a service at the Meridian Arts Centre at Yonge and Sheppard. The Song Shul holds annual events there to mark Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, and Yom Kippur, known as the Day of Atonement. The synagogue doesn’t have its own building but rents different locations to hold services.

“I’m a journalist. And I happen to be Jewish,” Herland wrote in the post. “On Yom Kippur I went to a synagogue service in Toronto and was met by protesters trying to taunt and intimidate me from entering the building.”

I'm a journalist. And I happen to be Jewish. On Yom Kippur I went to a synagogue service in Toronto and was met by protesters trying to taunt and intimidate me from entering the building. 1/5 pic.twitter.com/2eH3MaC9QB — Neil Herland (@NEWSneil) September 22, 2026

The video shows about 20 people, some blowing horns and waving large Palestinian flags and signs. As Herland moves through them, someone shouts in his face several times with a megaphone: “You’re going to hell!”

CBC journalist accosted outside Yom Kippur service and Americans are outraged: ‘Try this in Florida and you go to jail’

CBC journalist says protesters tried to 'taunt and intimidate' him from attending Yom Kippur service

At another point he turns to look behind him — some distance away are two individuals with a placard that says “Where’s your humanity?” One of them shouts “Zionist alert” through a megaphone before waving at the camera.

According to Toronto Sun’s Warren Kinsella , CBC management “quietly pulled Herland off the air” after the post became known, and “hit him with disciplinary action” over its content. He added that the first disciplinary hearing was held with Herland and his lawyer on Thursday.

Herland’s LinkedIn page notes that he has 30 years of on-air experience and says: “I’m heard nightly in Canada on every CBC Radio One station and across North America on Sirius XM Satellite Radio,” adding: “Canadian and EU passport holder.”

In his post on X, Herland says his late father was an Austrian Jew who survived the Holocaust in Romania before coming to Canada as a refugee. “This year I got an Austrian passport, in case Canada becomes unsafe for me as a Jew,” he added. “I fear that moment is approaching, here in Canada and elsewhere.”

A CBC spokesperson told National Post by email: “We respect the privacy rights of our employees and won’t comment on internal matters. However, we are aware of reporting on this matter that contains errors and mischaracterizations.”

The spokesperson did not say what those errors and mischaracterizations were, citing “the privacy of the situation.”

While the CBC has not commented on the reason for its action, a spokesperson for the group Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (Cjpme) told National Post: “We submitted complaints to CBC’s Ombud and the Values and Ethics Commissioner. In addition, we created a campaign for others to complain to the Commissioner.”

The group also shared its letter to the CBC, which says Herland’s post “was fundamentally misleading to an extent that it appears to be deliberate, resulting in disinformation that defames pro-Palestinian activists.”

It goes on to quote CBC’s Journalistic Standards and Practices , which says that reporting on riots and demonstrations “should avoid inflaming or aiding in any way the various sides in a confrontation.” It adds: “Mr. Herland clearly violates these practices.”

Aliza Spiro , creative director of The Song Shul and songwriter and singer, wrote a blog post this week titled: “Yup. That Was My Shul: How it feels after a Yom Kippur pro-Palestinian protest.”

stories.title: Canadian charged with fraud in the U.S. for allegedly voting in 3 elections
stories.summary: A Canadian has been charged in the United States with three counts of voter fraud for casting ballots in three elections without being a U.S. citizen.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Canadian has been charged in the United States with three counts of voter fraud for casting ballots in three elections without being a U.S. citizen.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for Florida says Christiane Vinette Young voted in the 2024 and 2022 general elections and the 2022 primary elections, despite knowing she was not a U.S. citizen.

The office says the 75-year-old was illegally present in the United States when she voted.

She faces a maximum penalty of three years in prison if she is convicted.

Vinette Young did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office says the case was investigated by Homeland Security and that she is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

stories.title: Fanshawe anime reflects growing trends in London
stories.summary: Fanshawe's anime club recently hosted an event where they watched the anime film Ghost in the Shell (1995). "I...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
Fanshawe’s anime club recently hosted an event where they watched the anime film Ghost in the Shell (1995).

“I got into loving anime by just finding it on vacation in Jamaica,” said Dejean Douglass, the vice president of the anime club at Fanshawe. “I’ve been watching it ever since.”

Douglass had been in the anime club for two years and has been the vice president starting only this year. He says that compared to last year, the anime club has been much popular.

“There’s more people showing up for events and it seems like everyone want’s to show up for more,” Douglass said. “I’m honestly so happy to see that.”

The growth of the anime club at Fanshawe reflects overall trends in London. According to Rob Chamberlain, owner of the Neo-Tokyo anime store in London, anime is becoming more mainstream.

“Traditionally, we would see someone and they’re like ‘oh I have a niece into that or something like that,” Chamberlain said. “But now it’s more of a ‘oh I saw this, that was really interesting.’ People are much more aware of it than they used to be.

Chamberlain attributes the rising popularity of anime in London due to adaptations of anime shows on live stream services introducing these shows to mainstream audiences.

“The One Piece live action, and other things … have really started to drive people who are not your traditional fans,”said Chamberlain. “It was traditionally more of an underground thing, but it’s become much more mainstream now.”

stories.title: Ontario sees negligible improvement in standardized test scores
stories.summary: French-language students fared relatively better in almost all areas, according to latest Eqao results for math, reading and writing
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
Students in Ontario saw hardly any improvement in math, reading and writing in the 2025-26 school year compared to the year before, according to the latest standardized test scores.

Only 52 per cent of Grade 6 students in English-language schools met the provincial standard for math, a slight increase of one percentage point over the 2024-25 school year. Meanwhile, the percentage of students who met the standard for reading and writing remained unchanged, at 86 per cent and 85 per cent, respectively.

Among Grade 3 students, 65 per cent met the provincial math standard and 75 per cent met the standard for reading, for increases of one per cent in both subjects. In writing, 67 per cent of students met the standard, an increase of two percentage points.

Niagara boards’ math strategies May be a lesson for Ontario

The data was released Friday by the province’s Education Quality and Accountability Office (Eqao), an arm’s length agency of the Ontario government. Students in Grades 3 and 6 are tested annually in reading, math and writing. Grade 9 students test in math, and Grade 10 students take a literacy test. The provincial standard is equivalent to a B grade.

This year’s results showed that Grade 9 students at English-language schools only saw an increase of one percentage point in math over the 2024-25 school year, to 59 per cent meeting standard.

Meanwhile, 86 per cent of Grade 10 students successfully passed the literacy test, up one per cent.

Ontario students faring poorly in math, standardized tests reveal

Students in French-language schools fared relatively better in almost all areas.

The results show students are making progress in math and literacy remains strong, Education Minister Paul Calandra said Friday in a statement.

“These results are encouraging, but they also make clear that there is more work to do. Too many students continue to struggle, achievement gaps persist and results remain uneven across the province,” he said.

In March, Ontario appointed an expert advisory body to review student assessment and achievement across the province, including Eqao testing.

A final report will be made public when its review is complete.

stories.title: ‘Unusual odour’ from sewer prompts late-night evacuations in Middle Sackville
stories.summary: HRM says the the smell, which originated at a catch basin, came from a petroleum-based substance. The municipality is warning people to dispose of hazardous materials properly.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
An “unusual odour” coming from the sewer system in Middle Sackville prompted the evacuation of around 70 households on Thursday night, municipal officials said.

Residents in the area of Claudia Crescent, Lucy Court, Flora Court, and Old Sackville Drive were reporting a chemical smell inside some homes, and from the sewers.

According to Halifax Regional Municipality (HRM), first responders went door to door to check on residents, who could evacuate from the area if they wanted.

About 15 residents spent the night at an evacuation centre at the Sackville Sports Stadium.

Halifax Regional Municipality said the issue was “resolved” around 3 a.m. Friday and that the smell, which originated at a catch basin, came from a “petroleum-based substance.” The exact substance is unknown, HRM added.

“Following standard response procedures, (Halifax Water) crews flushed additional water through the sewer system to isolate the material and then vacuumed the substance from the system for proper disposal,” the municipality said in a release.

HRM is reminding people not to discharge hazardous materials into the wastewater system.

“Improper disposal of these substances can create public safety risks, impact the environment and disrupt municipal infrastructure,” the municipality said in a release.

“Residents should always use approved hazardous waste disposal services for these materials.”

stories.title: Western faculty vote overwhelmingly in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: Faculty members represented by the University of Western Ontario Faculty Association (Uwofa) have voted overwhelmingly in favour of giving their bargaining team a strike mandate as contract negotiations with Western University continue.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
According to Uwofa, the parties have met 20 times since bargaining began in June. The association said negotiations have now moved into conciliation, with additional bargaining dates scheduled through the end of October.

Verwaayen added that the vote reflects faculty members’ desire to secure a fair agreement that recognizes their work. Western University has not publicly commented on the strike vote. Negotiations between the university and Uwofa are continuing.

Uwofa bargaining priorities Pay and benefits: Uwofa says it is seeking compensation that keeps pace with inflation and reflects the cost of living, as well as improvements to benefits that have not kept pace with the cost of care.

For example, the current benefit plan only provides $15 per visit toward physiotherapy, massage therapy, chiropractic care, and other paramedical services. Sustainable workloads: The Uwofa says faculty work extends well beyond time in the classroom.

At a research-intensive university like Western, faculty balance teaching with research, student supervision, and service. Uwofa is seeking workload provisions that clearly state responsibilities, including a clear list of duties that should not be assigned to faculty, helping ensure work is appropriately distributed across the university.

Security for contract faculty: According to Uwofa, contract faculty are an important part of teaching at Western, but many face uncertainty about whether they will continue to have work from one term or year to the next.

Uwofa says it is seeking greater job security and more predictable employment for contract faculty.

stories.title: U.S. not rushing to strike deal with Canada, Washington’s trade envoy says
stories.summary: Two sides continue to talk, but there are no formal negotiations right now, source says
stories.author: Steven Chase, Jeff Gray
stories.content:
The United States isn’t rushing to strike a deal with Canada that would end the trade war because it is still receiving what it needs, Washington’s point man on trade says.

United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer was asked during an interview with Cnbc on Friday about relations with Canada, given the damaging trade war that has escalated in recent weeks after Ottawa walked away from negotiations in August.

“We’re still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash, all of these things. We’re shipping [agricultural products] back and forth across the border, so there’s still a lot of strong trade between the two countries,” Greer told Cnbc. “We’re comfortable with where we are.”

A Canadian government official said there are continuing communications with Washington, but no formal negotiations right now. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

Mr. Greer said there are sporadic conversations with Canada, but stopped short of suggesting there are active negotiations taking place to resolve the dispute.

“There’s no urgency on our side, I would say.”

Speaking about the curtailed trade talks in August, Mr. Greer said “we gave them a deal. They left.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney at the time said the U.S. was offering a “bad deal” that “asked too much and offered too little” for this country.

Consumers and businesses on both sides are feeling the impact of the trade war.

The U.S. began collecting 50-per-cent duties on roughly $28-billion of Canadian goods on Aug. 22, and Canada matched the tariffs dollar for dollar the day after Labour Day. These retaliatory tariffs are on top of existing U.S. levies on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber that were imposed earlier.

Mr. Greer said Washington’s approach to Canada mirrors its policy toward China, the United Kingdom, Brazil and other countries.

He said the tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos are intended to prompt companies to “reshore,” or relocate their manufacturing to the U.S. and argued this policy is already reaping benefits for American steel and auto manufacturers.

Ontario’s representative in Washington, David Paterson, said Friday it was up to the federal government to decide when to return to the negotiating table and declined to say whether he was aware of any backchannel talks were under way. But he said he believed that negotiations would resume “in the long term.”

Speaking to reporters in Toronto, he said pressure is mounting on Washington from many U.S. businesses for a deal in the face of high diesel and gasoline prices and economic uncertainty.

He said he expects the coming midterm elections to reflect the shift he is seeing in U.S. opinion – but that no one should expect a completely tariff-free deal for Canada.

Ontario’s Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli said the province’s $30-billion package aimed at supporting tariff-hit businesses was helping the province weather the storm. He also touted the successes of Ontario’s recent efforts to attract investments and new jobs. But he said the province must adapt to a world where U.S. tariffs are permanent.

stories.title: The latest CPP and OAS payments hit bank accounts Friday
stories.summary: Most older Canadians who qualify will see more money in their bank accounts as of Friday, with the latest scheduled Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security benefit payments.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Most older Canadians who qualify will see more money in their bank accounts as of Friday, when scheduled Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and Old Age Security (OAS) benefit payments start rolling out from the federal government.

CPP and OAS payments are sent out every month to qualifying Canadians, and although both are designed to provide financial support for older Canadians, they differ in terms of how one qualifies and how much money can be received.

Payments will be sent electronically to bank accounts as soon as Friday for those who are signed up for direct deposit, while others could receive paper cheques, but May have to wait longer.

Here’s what to know and how much money to expect.

CPP payments are going out to qualifying Canadians on Friday, and are jointly administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Employment and Social Development Canada (Esdc).

CPP is a mandatory deduction Canadian workers pay into for their retirements, and usually through regular payroll deductions by employers, while those who are self employed must ensure they are paying into CPP regularly.

The amount one could see on their regular CPP payments, including on Friday, varies based on average lifetime earnings, total contributions and the age they start claiming the benefits.

To qualify for payments, a recipient must be at least 60 years old and have made at least one valid contribution to the program through their employment or self-employment.

The age one decides to start taking CPP payments determines how large their monthly payments will be.

The CRA says 65 years of age is the standard benchmark age it uses to estimate CPP payments, but those who qualify can start early at the age of 60 or as late as 70. Starting earlier means the monthly payments will be smaller, while taking CPP from a later age will see larger monthly payments, but the maximum monthly amount is reached once a recipient turns 70.

For the 2026 calendar year, and based on the Cra’s benchmark age of 65 years old, the maximum benefit amount is $1,507.65 per month, while the average benefit could be $877 per month for new recipients.

CPP payments are fully taxable as income, and must be declared when it comes to tax season. However, the payment amounts do not change based on a person’s income level, unlike with OAS.

OAS payments are also administered by Esdc, along with Service Canada, and although the CRA is not involved with administering the payouts, those OAS payments are still fully taxable as income.

While CPP provides a retirement income for Canadians that paid into it while they were working, Canadians do not need to be employed or previously employed to qualify for OAS payments.

To qualify for OAS, recipients must be at least 65 years old, a Canadian citizen or legal resident at the time of approval, and they must have been a resident of Canada for at least 10 years since the age of 18.

Although OAS qualifications are not based on employment or contributions, a person’s income in the most recent tax year is one of the main factors that determine how much a recipient will get.

Income, in this context, can be generated from employment, but also from EI benefits, rental property revenue, Rrsp withdrawals, taxable interest, dividends and capital gains, among other examples.

Canadians between the ages of 65 and 74 could receive up to a maximum monthly payment of $751.97, while those 75 years and older could see OAS payments of up to $827.17.

Those amounts could be reduced if an OAS recipient’s income exceeds certain thresholds, which is commonly known as OAS “clawbacks.”

This means the maximum monthly OAS payment will most likely be seen by Canadians who receive a net income in the 2025 tax year that falls below the income threshold, which is $93,454. The monthly payment will then be “clawed back” gradually for every dollar above that figure and up to the maximum income threshold.

Those maximum income thresholds are $152,062 for recipients aged 65 to 74 years old, while those aged 75 and over have a maximum of $157,923.

stories.title: Federal government posts $5.1-billion deficit for April-to-July period
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal government posted a deficit of $5.1 billion for the April-to-July period of its 2026-27 fiscal year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
People sit on benches in Major's Hill Park as the Peace Tower on Parliament Hill looms behind in Ottawa, ON Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Keito Newman The Canadian Press

By The Canadian Press

Posted September 25, 2026 11:13 am.

Last Updated September 25, 2026 11:49 am.

Ottawa — The federal government posted a deficit of $5.1 billion for the April-to-July period of its 2026-27 fiscal year.

In its monthly fiscal monitor report, the Finance Department says the result compared with a deficit of $7.8 billion for the same four-month period a year ago.

The deficit came as revenue totalled $175.5 billion for the period, up from $163.4 billion a year ago, boosted by increases in personal income tax revenue, other revenues and GST revenue.

Program expenses excluding net actuarial losses amounted to $159 billion, up from $151.3 billion, due to higher direct program expenses and major transfers to persons.

Public debt charges totalled $20 billion, up from $18.6 billion.

Net actuarial losses were $1.7 billion, up from $1.3 billion.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto police to hold update after finding 2 bodies in burnt-out vehicles
stories.summary: Toronto police will hold an update Friday afternoon after emergency crews found two bodies in two burnt-out vehicles earlier this week.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police say two people found in two burnt-out vehicles in opposite ends of the city this week are homicide victims.

Investigators announced the development Friday and identified one of the victims as 32-year-old Marcus Charles.

Police received calls for both incidents within hours of each other late Monday night and early Tuesday morning.

The first incident was reported to police around 11:24 p.m. Officers were called to a hydro field on Reesor Road, near Steeles Avenue East.

It was reported that there was a vehicle on fire. When crews arrived on scene, they found a body inside the vehicle. The victim in that case was identified Friday as Charles.

At 12:55 a.m., police were called to James Garden Park in Etobicoke for another vehicle on fire. Police said smoke was seen coming from the park, and there were reports of what sounded like an explosion.

After crews arrived, a body was found inside the car. Their identity is not yet known.

Anyone with information is asked to call police.

stories.title: Ready for the harvest moon this weekend? Here’s what you’ll see in the sky
stories.summary: The moon is named for the fall harvest because it provides extra evening moonlight during the fall harvest as the day gets shorter and the sun sets earlier.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Crank up that Neil Young playlist — a harvest moon is on its way this weekend.

Canadians will be treated to the 10 th full moon of the year this weekend, with the harvest moon appearing in the skies.

The term “harvest moon” refers to the full moon that occurs closest to the start of autumn, according to Nasa. The moon is named for the fall harvest because it provides extra evening moonlight during the fall harvest as the day gets shorter and the sun sets earlier.

The harvest moon typically occurs in September, although occasionally it happens in October. It is also referred to as the “corn moon,” in a reference to the main fall crop being harvested in the northern United States and parts of Canada during this time of year.

Unfortunately for Canadians, the moon will reach its exact full phase at 12:49 pm Eastern, when the moon is on the other side of the planet, according to the Old Farmers’ Almanac.

But that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy the sight of the moon “appearing” nearly full through Friday night to Sunday night.

The moon will appear “over 99 per cent illuminated,” according to the Weather Network.

“A Full Moon rises around sunset and sets at sunrise, since it sits opposite the Sun. You don’t need to observe it at the exact listed time. If clouds interfere one night, try again the night before or after— it will still appear full,” the Old Farmers’ Almanac says.

2026 is set to see 13 full moons, instead of the typical 12. This is because the month of May had two full moons.

The next moon that will reach its fullest will be the “hunter’s moon,” shortly after midnight on Monday, Oct. 26. This will be followed by two more full moons, ON Nov. 24 and Dec. 23.

stories.title: Trump ‘comfortable’ with pause in Canada trade talks, Greer says
stories.summary: Both sides have been having 'good conversations about potential deals,' but the U.S. felt 'no urgency' to make a trade deal, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump is “comfortable” with where things stand with trade talks with Canada and feels “no urgency” to make a deal, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview.

“President Trump is comfortable with where we are on Canada. Our trade policy is a global policy, it applies to Canada, China, the U.K., Brazil, all kinds of countries. He has his tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos to reshore,” Greer told Cnbc.

The U.S. still has “a lot of other trade” with Canada, he said.

“We’re still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash,” he added.

There was still a lot of “strong trade” between both countries, with Canada still looking for a trade deal, he said.

“The Canadians, periodically they come and they want to have a deal,” Greer said.

While both sides have been having “good conversations about potential deals,” the U.S. felt “no urgency” to make a trade deal anytime soon, he added.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc’s office told Global News, “Canada maintains ongoing communications with our American counterparts.”

Trade talks collapsed between Canada and the United States in August after Ottawa walked away from the negotiating table in response to last-minute terms that Prime Minister Mark Carney says the U.S. demanded, including restrictions on Canada entering into new trade deals with other countries.

Since then, Trump has escalated his economic attacks against Canada, imposing multiple rounds of tariffs as well as import restrictions.

With a file from Global News’ Reggie Cecchini

stories.title: Quebec City man charged with making threats against Carney
stories.summary: Forty-five-year-old suspect allegedly made threatening comments on his Facebook page
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
RCMP say a Quebec City man is facing charges after he allegedly threatened Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The 45-year-old suspect, Ousmane Bah, appeared in court on Thursday, where he was charged with uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm.

He also faces a charge of wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group.

The suspect will remain in custody until his next court appearance on Oct. 1.

Police say the suspect allegedly made the threatening comments on his Facebook page.

At least two other people have been arrested and charged with threatening Carney in recent months, including a 51-year-old Montreal man in August and a 31-year-old Calgary man earlier this month.

stories.title: How seeing a Tragically Hip show in the ’90s changed Raine Maida’s aspirations
stories.summary: Toronto — When Raine Maida was trying to break into the music scene more than 30 years ago, he says he bought tickets to the Toronto Music Awards at Massey Hall, in hopes he could use the event to network with industry folks.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

Posted September 25, 2026 10:58 am.

Last Updated September 25, 2026 11:49 am.

Toronto — When Raine Maida was trying to break into the music scene more than 30 years ago, he says he bought tickets to the Toronto Music Awards at Massey Hall, in hopes he could use the event to network with industry folks.

But the night didn’t unfold as expected. Rather, the Our Lady Peace frontman said he thought the performances weren’t great and left him uninspired. He was ready to leave, but decided to watch the final act.

That’s when the Tragically Hip stepped on stage.

Maida said he watched as lead singer Gord Downie and the band commanded the show with an authenticity and a nod to poetry that he hadn’t seen from the other artists that night.

The Hip’s 1988 performance at the awards show is part of the band’s lore, as members have described the night as “disastrous” but it led to them being signed.

At the time, Maida says he thought to himself: “That’s the connection I want to be able to make someday.” He left the concert venue and ripped up a potential record deal that he said now would have been “the worst deal in the world” and listened to more music by the Hip.

Today, the 56-year-old Toronto-born singer said that night remains a seminal moment that impacted the trajectory of his career, which spans more than three decades and includes over 10 albums with his band and as a solo artist.

“That performance by the Hip gave me enough stock to be like, OK, slow this down. We’re not just chasing getting a record deal, we are trying to chase the art first and then the things will come, hopefully. That’s how I started to think when I left there,” said Maida, who later wrote the song “Ballad Of A Poet” about watching Downie and the Hip perform that night.

Now, Maida will come full circle as Our Lady Peace will perform a tribute to the Tragically Hip when the Kingston band is inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame on Saturday during a gala held at Massey Hall.

Maida said he’s had many amazing career moments, but “this is up there.”

“Getting to honour literally one of my favourite bands and favourite singers, now that you’re making me, like, talk about it, actually I’m starting to get nervous,” he said.

Meanwhile, Hip guitarist Rob Baker has had months to absorb the news that the band will be inducted alongside Toronto indie pioneer Feist, Mike Reno and Paul Dean of Loverboy and French-Canadian singer-songwriter Roch Voisine.

But Baker still said it’s “surreal” to join a Hall of Fame that includes artists the band admired, including Neil Young, Joni Mitchell, Gordon Lightfoot and Rush.

The 64-year-old said it’s also special to go in as a band, since songwriting credits on the Hip’s music were shared among the group.

Of course, there is a bittersweet note to the festivities for Baker and his bandmates as well, because Downie, who died in 2017 after he was diagnosed with a rare and incurable form of brain cancer, won’t be there with them. But Baker said their songs remain the group’s “lasting testament.”

“We wrote these songs and we wrote them collectively and they go out there like our kids,” he said. “We have hundreds of little kids that went out. Some of them were ne’er do wells, never to be heard from again. And some of them have taken up residence with people and they’ve gone on to storied careers of their own. That’s really nice. It’s gratifying to sit back and watch what your kids go on and do.”

Baker said the Hip, whose hits include “Ahead by a Century,” “Bobcaygeon” and “Fifty-Mission Cap,” often wrote songs during jam sessions, passing a guitar around a circle, trying to impress someone else in the group.

“If they were impressed and maybe they got excited about the song, then someone else got excited and it would snowball,” he said.

Baker has fond memories of how their songs came together, he said, including one especially productive session at Convocation Hall at Queen’s University where they were rehearsing before recording their 1991 album “Road Apples.” In one day, the Hip wrote about four songs that all ended up on the record, Baker said, including “Long Time Running.”

Maida praised the Hip’s lyricism, which often includes references to history, Canadian landmarks and imagery, and unique turns of phrase. Maida said sometimes the phrasing felt “unfinished” which allowed a listener to make their own conclusions.

“It’s not just packaged so properly that it’s, like, ‘Oh, that’s what it is,'” Maida said. “Gord always allowed you to get inside those songs with him and see things.

“I think the idea of him putting you in a time and a place where it’s like, ‘Oh, I can smell where he is, I can feel that, I could see it,’ whether I’m sitting at a kitchen table. It’s those kind of nuances that Gord had that are truly special,” he said.

As Our Lady Peace’s success grew across Canada, Maida said they had the chance to play shows with the Hip, which shifted his relationship from strictly a fan to a peer.

“I love their music, but it’s so much deeper now being an artist and being a peer,” said Maida, who has covered his favourite Hip tune “Locked in the Trunk of a Car” with Our Lady Peace.

Baker said it’s an honour to know Maida was inspired by a Hip performance.

“These moments can mean a lot, if they hit at the right time,” Baker said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Toronto — When Raine Maida was trying to break into the music scene more than 30 years ago, he says he bought tickets to the Toronto Music Awards at Massey Hall, in hopes he could use the event to network with industry folks.

content_blocks.text: But the night didn’t unfold as expected. Rather, the Our Lady Peace frontman said he thought the performances weren’t great and left him uninspired. He was ready to leave, but decided to watch the final act.

content_blocks.text: Maida said he watched as lead singer Gord Downie and the band commanded the show with an authenticity and a nod to poetry that he hadn’t seen from the other artists that night.

content_blocks.text: The Hip’s 1988 performance at the awards show is part of the band’s lore, as members have described the night as “disastrous” but it led to them being signed.

content_blocks.text: At the time, Maida says he thought to himself: “That’s the connection I want to be able to make someday.” He left the concert venue and ripped up a potential record deal that he said now would have been “the worst deal in the world” and listened to more music by the Hip.

content_blocks.text: Today, the 56-year-old Toronto-born singer said that night remains a seminal moment that impacted the trajectory of his career, which spans more than three decades and includes over 10 albums with his band and as a solo artist.

content_blocks.text: “That performance by the Hip gave me enough stock to be like, OK, slow this down. We’re not just chasing getting a record deal, we are trying to chase the art first and then the things will come, hopefully. That’s how I started to think when I left there,” said Maida, who later wrote the song “Ballad Of A Poet” about watching Downie and the Hip perform that night.

content_blocks.text: Now, Maida will come full circle as Our Lady Peace will perform a tribute to the Tragically Hip when the Kingston band is inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame on Saturday during a gala held at Massey Hall.

content_blocks.text: Baker has fond memories of how their songs came together, he said, including one especially productive session at Convocation Hall at Queen’s University where they were rehearsing before recording their 1991 album “Road Apples.” In one day, the Hip wrote about four songs that all ended up on the record, Baker said, including “Long Time Running.”

stories.title: Canada’s foreign minister set to speak after German trade, security talks
stories.summary: Canada has deepened defence ties with Germany after selecting Tkms for massive contract to build new fleet of up to 12 submarines.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada has secured a new information-sharing deal with Germany to exchange classified and protected intelligence on both defence and security issues and economic files.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand announced the deal at a signing ceremony with her German counterpart, Johann Wadepuhl, in Ottawa Friday.

Anand referenced Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pitch for closer ties between Canada and the European Union last week, and said Germany is central to that partnership.

1:51 Canada, Germany sign agreement to share classified information

“This agreement will strengthen cooperation on trade, ON innovation and on advanced technologies,” Anand said.

“And it’s going to strengthen Canada’s position as a trusted partner in strategic sectors and support economic growth. It’s going to contribute to building a stronger, more competitive Canadian economy.”

While the text of the new General Security of Information Agreement between the two countries was not yet released early Friday afternoon, Anand said it would apply to information shared both by governments and by industry.

Without directly mentioning U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration, Wadepuhl noted that both Canada and Europe are living through “huge changes in the international order.”

“Where old dependencies are turning into new vulnerabilities, it is really important to know whom we can rely on,” Wadepuhl told reporters.

“Germany can rely on Canada and Canada can rely on Germany.”

Canada recently deepened both defence and economic ties with Germany by selecting Tkms for a massive, $80 billion contract to build a fleet of up to 12 new submarines over a rival South Korean bid.

But asked about negotiations between the Canadian government and Tkms on the deal Friday, Anand provided no details. She first handed the question, asked by a reporter from the Canadian Press, over to her German counterpart before saying she’s not involved in the negotiations.

“On the price response to your question, the negotiations are continuing now and they’re not continuing at the level of ministers,” Anand said.

“So our conversation this morning was very much about the implications of the further relationship on defence and security, the importance of that relationship.”

stories.title: Police charge Quebec City man accused of threatening to kill Mark Carney
stories.summary: A man who is accused of making death threats online directed at Prime Minister Mark Carney has been charged.
stories.author: Denio Lourenco
stories.content:
Posted September 25, 2026 10:34 am.

Police have charged a man who is accused of making death threats online directed at Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The RCMP said 45-year-old Ousmane Bah of Quebec City was charged with uttering threats that he posted on Facebook. He is also accused of promoting hatred against an identifiable group.

An investigation was launched on July 6 and Bah appeared in court on Sept. 24.

He remains in custody until his next court appearance on Oct. 1.

No other details were available.

stories.title: Nova Scotia government is cutting off funding to a homeless shelter in New Glasgow
stories.summary: The operator of a New Glasgow shelter says the provincial government owes local residents an explanation about why it is cutting off its funding.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
The operator of a Nova Scotia emergency shelter says the provincial government owes local residents an explanation about why it is cutting off its funding.

The Northstar shelter made the comment after the Nova Scotia government announced that within 90 days it would stop funding the facility in New Glasgow, a small community on the province’s north shore, about 150 kilometres northeast of Halifax.

“This decision places the future of our organization — and the safety of the hundreds of people who rely on us — in serious jeopardy,” reads the organization’s statement, posted Thursday night on social media.

Less than 10,000 people live in New Glasgow, according to Statistics Canada data collected for the 2021 census.

Income data from the previous year, the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, say more than 4,200 households in New Glasgow had a total income below $40,000. More than 1,700 of these households had a total income of less than $20,000 in 2020, which is the most recent figures available.

Premier Tim Houston’s Progressive Conservative government said this week it is seeking expressions of interest for new supportive housing projects in the area, and it will work with the shelter’s residents to identify alternative options for housing and other support.

The shelter is asking the province how the unhoused residents will survive this winter and who will be there to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses the effects of an opioid overdose, when needed.

“Who will provide over 1,000 meals a month to those experiencing poverty? Where will the next person experiencing homelessness turn when every supportive housing unit is occupied?” reads the statement.

A spokesperson for the Department of Social Development said detailed transition planning will happen this week.

The Town of New Glasgow passed a unanimous motion last month asking the province to shut down the emergency shelter, saying the facility was not addressing the needs of people experiencing homelessness and addiction.

New Glasgow Mayor Nancy Dicks said last week it is “no secret” the town is dealing with serious safety issues.

“We’re not going to hide behind that and we’re not going to ignore it,” Dicks told reporters after a news conference in Halifax announcing the province’s plans to use federal money to establish safety projects aimed at preventing crime in three communities.

Dicks said challenges related to the 20-bed shelter were behind the town’s decision to take part in the public safety pilot project organized by the province.

Multiple media reports say New Glasgow residents have complained about public drug use, vandalism, assaults, property damage and thefts near the downtown shelter.

The council’s motion in August said a health-focused approach was needed to provide people with a chance to “stabilize” and receive treatment. The council also said it wanted the province to develop a residential rehabilitation centre.

Dicks said people from across Pictou County go to New Glasgow for health care, housing and other support, which “gives us a close view” of how challenges involving mental health, addictions, housing and poverty affect residents.

“The nature of these challenges has changed significantly in recent years,” the mayor said last week. “They are becoming more complex. And the solutions often extend beyond what police or municipal government can provide on their own.”

Erica Parrill, a spokesperson with the Department of Social Development, said in an email Friday that work to strengthen housing support in Pictou County has been underway for “some time.”

“The decision to end the relationship with Northstar reflects that broader work and our goal of making sure people have the right supports for their needs, while helping more people move from homelessness toward stable housing,” she said in an emailed statement.

Northstar said it agrees the community needs additional support to help residents facing complex challenges, but that doesn’t mean the shelter should be shut down.

“Supportive housing is a critical part of the solution — but (an) emergency shelter remains the place people turn when every other option has failed,” the organization said.

Northstar said it will not quietly accept a plan that allows people to fall through gaps created by the provincial government.
