stories.title: A beginner’s guide to reading Ben Macintyre
stories.summary: Here are eight routes into the author’s world of spies, swindlers, escapes and betrayals
stories.author: Emily Donaldson
stories.content:
Join The Globe and Mail for an evening with author Ben Macintyre as he discusses his latest book, Redwood, with former Ottawa Bureau Chief Bob Fife, and books editor Judith Pereira, ON Oct. 5 in Toronto. Visit tgam.CA/macintyre for more.

Ben Macintyre belongs to a generation of narrative non-fiction writers, among them Patrick Radden Keefe, David Grann and John Vaillant, who’ve made a specialty of harnessing the machinery of thrillers and novels to exhaustively researched true stories. They take the raw materials of non-fiction – archives, interviews, historical records – and alchemize them into compulsive reading.

Macintyre’s subjects of choice are spies, double agents, con men and other masters-of-deception types, most often operating in the shadow worlds of the Second World War and the Cold War. People who put their lives on the line for country, profit or, in the case of his newest book, Redwood , a cure for erectile dysfunction. The stories have proved remarkably adaptable: Three of his books have been turned into films or television dramas, while several others have inspired documentaries.

My own portal into Macintyre’s work was The Spy and the Traitor , his riveting account of Oleg Gordievsky, the KGB officer who became one of Britain’s most valuable Cold War agents. First love being the most indelible, it’s still the book I’d recommend first.

Espionage May not run in Macintyre’s family (though he likely wouldn’t tell us if it did) but the British establishment certainly does. Born in Oxford in 1963 into a well-connected academic family, Macintyre, a long-time columnist and associate editor at the London Times, is the son of an Oxford historian and descended on both sides from minor British aristocracy. (For his own history degree, he ventured to Cambridge.) In person, however, he is strikingly free of any establishment hauteur: open, affable and unguarded.

For readers coming to Macintyre for the first time – or wondering where to venture next – here are eight routes into his world of spies, swindlers, escapes and betrayals.

For one Soviet spy, the Cold War proved a little too cold: In Macintyre’s timely, page-turning latest, the fate of nations turns, improbably, ON a man’s sex life – or lack thereof. In 1981, KGB major Vladimir Kuzichkin, stationed in Iran in the turbulent aftermath of the 1979 revolution, approached British intelligence with a proposition: He would trade his country’s secrets for help with one of his own.

Kuzichkin was suffering from erectile dysfunction, which he was convinced Western medicine could cure (it couldn’t, the golden age of Viagra having not yet dawned). MI6 gave the 6-foot-4 Russian the codename Redwood, after the tree. (It took some time before anyone twigged to the unintentional joke: RED for communist, Wood for what eluded Kuzichkin.)

MI6 officer Ian McCredie became his handler, and the bond between the two is at the heart of the book. Kuzichkin supplied intelligence about Soviet activities and Iran’s communist Tudeh Party. When the KGB, which had begun to suspect Kuzichkin, summoned him back to Moscow, MI6 was forced to engineer an escape from Iran.

The intel Kuzichkin provided was ultimately handed to the Iranian regime, contributing to a brutal purge of communists and helping strengthen a government the West would come to regard as an enemy. Macintyre is particularly good on that bitter irony: an intelligence triumph whose unintended consequences are still being felt.

Operation Mincemeat

Had Ocean’s Eleven been set in wartime Whitehall, it might have looked something like Operation Mincemeat.

In 1943, with the Allies preparing to invade Sicily, British intelligence devised an audacious plan to convince Hitler that the Allies’ real targets were Greece and Sardinia. The scheme required a corpse, dressed as a fictitious Royal Marine named William Martin and equipped with an entire invented life, including a briefcase containing false military documents. The body was then deposited off the coast of Spain in the hope that the papers would find their way into German hands.

Revelling, as do we, in both the ingenuity and absurdity of the operation, Macintyre introduces an eccentric cast of intelligence officers, scientists, secretaries and others who helped make the imaginary major Martin convincing. Mincemeat has all the pleasures of a great caper: watching an outlandish ruse assembled piece by piece, knowing that thousands of lives May depend on whether the mark takes the bait.

Macintyre gravitates to real-life characters who seem too improbable for fiction, and few are more improbable than Ursula Kuczynski.

Born into a well-to-do Jewish family in Berlin in 1907, Kuczynski was a committed Communist by her teens. Her espionage career began in Shanghai – where she was recruited by legendary Soviet spy Richard Sorge – and would take her through China, Japanese-occupied Manchuria, Poland and Switzerland before she finally landed in Britain in 1941. Code-named Sonya, she became a colonel in Soviet military intelligence while raising three children. (Who says women can’t have it all?)

Her greatest coup took place in an Oxfordshire village, where, under cover as an unassuming housewife and mother, she handled Klaus Fuchs, the German-born British physicist who passed atomic secrets to Moscow. MI5 came close to outing her but was hampered, Macintyre suggests, by an inability to imagine – and really who would? – that a mum baking cakes in the English countryside might also be a formidable Soviet spy.

Colditz: Prisoners of the Castle

In 1940, the Nazis began using Colditz Castle – a forbidding, supposedly escape-proof gothic fortress perched above the eastern German town of the same name – to hold Allied officers who’d proved particularly troublesome, or particularly adept at escaping from other prisoner-of-war camps.

The castle immediately became a hothouse of ingenuity and sheer bloody-mindedness. Prisoners tunnelled, scaled walls, impersonated German officers and dreamed up increasingly elaborate routes to freedom. One group of British inmates secretly built a two-man glider in the castle attic.

The thrills are in the escapes themselves, of course, but the richer story is arguably what happened when hundreds of men from different nations and classes were locked up together for years. Macintyre presents Colditz as a society in miniature, with its own hierarchies, rivalries, prejudices, alliances and divisions among prisoners and captors alike – complicating the familiar Great Escape image of plucky officers united against their Nazi captors.

The Spy and the Traitor

Perhaps no Macintyre book makes the case for non-fiction as thriller quite as forcefully as this one.

Oleg Gordievsky was a rising KGB officer who, increasingly disillusioned with the Soviet system, began secretly working for MI6 in the 1970s. Over the next decade he supplied the British with a stream of intelligence from inside the KGB, eventually becoming acting head of the Kgb’s London station.

In 1985, however, Gordievsky was abruptly summoned back to Moscow, where he realized he had been betrayed and was under surveillance. What follows is the book’s nail-biting set piece: an elaborate MI6 operation to smuggle him across the Soviet border in the trunk of a car. Macintyre reconstructs the escape almost minute by minute, turning border guards, a bag of cheese-and-onion potato chips and a soiled diaper into instruments of almost unbearable suspense.

The Napoleon of Crime

Published in 1997, Macintyre’s second book predates his focus on espionage but shows that many of his other preoccupations were already in place.

Adam Worth was a German-born American bank robber, art thief and criminal mastermind who made his name in late 19th-century London, moving fluidly between respectable society and the underworld and becoming a prototype of the gentleman thief.

He amassed a fortune, travelled the Mediterranean on his own yacht and orchestrated crimes across Europe and America, all while cultivating a strict personal code: He abhorred violence, was fiercely loyal to his accomplices and kept his criminal life secret from his family.

His most famous exploit was the 1876 theft of Gainsborough’s portrait of Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, originally intended as leverage to free his imprisoned brother. When his brother was released without it, Worth kept the now virtually unsaleable painting hidden for the next quarter-century, apparently developing a deep attachment to it.

Macintyre tells Worth’s story as both a Victorian criminal adventure and a character study, finding in his double life the kind of divided loyalties and carefully constructed identities that would later animate his spy books. An inspiration for Arthur Conan Doyle’s professor Moriarty, Worth made and lost fortunes over a spectacular criminal career, only to die penniless.

A Spy Among Friends

Kim Philby wasn’t merely one of the most damaging Soviet spies ever to penetrate British intelligence, he was also exceptionally good at inspiring trust. A member of the Cambridge spy ring, Philby spent decades passing British and American secrets to Moscow while rising through the ranks of MI6.

Macintyre brings a fresh eye to one of the best-known tales of espionage and betrayal by telling it largely through Philby’s friendship with fellow intelligence officer Nicholas Elliott, a product of the same privileged world of public schools, clubs and old-boy networks.

That intimacy gave Philby’s deception its particular sting, while exposing a vulnerability of the British establishment: a system in which class, charm and the connections could make a certain sort of chap seem inherently trustworthy.

When suspicion finally hardened around him, Philby fled to Moscow in 1963. Part of Macintyre’s achievement is making the reader understand not just how he got away with it for so long, but why his friends found it so difficult to believe the truth.

A perfect entry point to Macintyre’s fascination with morally slippery characters, Agent Zigzag tells the story of Eddie Chapman, an English safecracker, conman and inveterate charmer with a taste for fast cars, gambling and other people’s money.

Imprisoned on Jersey when the Germans invaded and occupied the Channel Islands in 1940, Chapman, who knew an opportunity when he saw one, volunteered his services to German intelligence. The Nazis trained him in espionage and parachuted him into Britain with orders to blow up an aircraft factory. Upon landing, he promptly turned himself over to MI5, becoming a double agent codenamed Zigzag.

Chapman was brave, reckless, chronically unfaithful and noticeably unburdened by principle, leaving those around him wondering precisely what his motivations were. That moral elasticity is the engine of Macintyre’s book, and the result is part spy thriller, part picaresque: a story of fake sabotage, imminent danger, a rotating cast of girlfriends and an incorrigible crook who discovered in wartime espionage the one career for which his specific array of talents amounted to a qualification.

Imprisoned on Jersey when the Germans invaded and occupied the Channel Islands in 1940, Chapman, who knew an opportunity when he saw one, volunteered his services to German intelligence. The Nazis trained him in espionage and parachuted him into Britain with orders to blow up an aircraft factory. Upon landing, he promptly turned himself over to MI5, becoming a double agent codenamed Zigzag.

Chapman was brave, reckless, chronically unfaithful and noticeably unburdened by principle, leaving those around him wondering precisely what his motivations were. That moral elasticity is the engine of Macintyre’s book, and the result is part spy thriller, part picaresque: a story of fake sabotage, imminent danger, a rotating cast of girlfriends and an incorrigible crook who discovered in wartime espionage the one career for which his specific array of talents amounted to a qualification.

content_blocks.text: Join The Globe and Mail for an evening with author Ben Macintyre as he discusses his latest book, Redwood, with former Ottawa Bureau Chief Bob Fife, and books editor Judith Pereira, ON Oct. 5 in Toronto. Visit tgam.CA/macintyre for more.

Ben Macintyre belongs to a generation of narrative non-fiction writers, among them Patrick Radden Keefe, David Grann and John Vaillant, who’ve made a specialty of harnessing the machinery of thrillers and novels to exhaustively researched true stories. They take the raw materials of non-fiction – archives, interviews, historical records – and alchemize them into compulsive reading.

Macintyre’s subjects of choice are spies, double agents, con men and other masters-of-deception types, most often operating in the shadow worlds of the Second World War and the Cold War. People who put their lives on the line for country, profit or, in the case of his newest book, Redwood , a cure for erectile dysfunction. The stories have proved remarkably adaptable: Three of his books have been turned into films or television dramas, while several others have inspired documentaries.

My own portal into Macintyre’s work was The Spy and the Traitor , his riveting account of Oleg Gordievsky, the KGB officer who became one of Britain’s most valuable Cold War agents. First love being the most indelible, it’s still the book I’d recommend first.

Espionage May not run in Macintyre’s family (though he likely wouldn’t tell us if it did) but the British establishment certainly does. Born in Oxford in 1963 into a well-connected academic family, Macintyre, a long-time columnist and associate editor at the London Times, is the son of an Oxford historian and descended on both sides from minor British aristocracy. (For his own history degree, he ventured to Cambridge.) In person, however, he is strikingly free of any establishment hauteur: open, affable and unguarded.
For readers coming to Macintyre for the first time – or wondering where to venture next – here are eight routes into his world of spies, swindlers, escapes and betrayals.
For Cold War dysfunction

content_blocks.caption: Supplied

content_blocks.text: For one Soviet spy, the Cold War proved a little too cold: In Macintyre’s timely, page-turning latest, the fate of nations turns, improbably, ON a man’s sex life – or lack thereof. In 1981, KGB major Vladimir Kuzichkin, stationed in Iran in the turbulent aftermath of the 1979 revolution, approached British intelligence with a proposition: He would trade his country’s secrets for help with one of his own.

Kuzichkin was suffering from erectile dysfunction, which he was convinced Western medicine could cure (it couldn’t, the golden age of Viagra having not yet dawned). MI6 gave the 6-foot-4 Russian the codename Redwood, after the tree. (It took some time before anyone twigged to the unintentional joke: RED for communist, Wood for what eluded Kuzichkin.)

MI6 officer Ian McCredie became his handler, and the bond between the two is at the heart of the book. Kuzichkin supplied intelligence about Soviet activities and Iran’s communist Tudeh Party. When the KGB, which had begun to suspect Kuzichkin, summoned him back to Moscow, MI6 was forced to engineer an escape from Iran.

The intel Kuzichkin provided was ultimately handed to the Iranian regime, contributing to a brutal purge of communists and helping strengthen a government the West would come to regard as an enemy. Macintyre is particularly good on that bitter irony: an intelligence triumph whose unintended consequences are still being felt.
For an ingenious wartime caper
Operation Mincemeat

content_blocks.caption: Supplied

content_blocks.text: Had Ocean’s Eleven been set in wartime Whitehall, it might have looked something like Operation Mincemeat.

In 1943, with the Allies preparing to invade Sicily, British intelligence devised an audacious plan to convince Hitler that the Allies’ real targets were Greece and Sardinia. The scheme required a corpse, dressed as a fictitious Royal Marine named William Martin and equipped with an entire invented life, including a briefcase containing false military documents. The body was then deposited off the coast of Spain in the hope that the papers would find their way into German hands.

Revelling, as do we, in both the ingenuity and absurdity of the operation, Macintyre introduces an eccentric cast of intelligence officers, scientists, secretaries and others who helped make the imaginary major Martin convincing. Mincemeat has all the pleasures of a great caper: watching an outlandish ruse assembled piece by piece, knowing that thousands of lives May depend on whether the mark takes the bait.
For a strong female lead

content_blocks.caption: Supplied

content_blocks.text: Macintyre gravitates to real-life characters who seem too improbable for fiction, and few are more improbable than Ursula Kuczynski.

Born into a well-to-do Jewish family in Berlin in 1907, Kuczynski was a committed Communist by her teens. Her espionage career began in Shanghai – where she was recruited by legendary Soviet spy Richard Sorge – and would take her through China, Japanese-occupied Manchuria, Poland and Switzerland before she finally landed in Britain in 1941. Code-named Sonya, she became a colonel in Soviet military intelligence while raising three children. (Who says women can’t have it all?)

Her greatest coup took place in an Oxfordshire village, where, under cover as an unassuming housewife and mother, she handled Klaus Fuchs, the German-born British physicist who passed atomic secrets to Moscow. MI5 came close to outing her but was hampered, Macintyre suggests, by an inability to imagine – and really who would? – that a mum baking cakes in the English countryside might also be a formidable Soviet spy.
For the art of escape
Colditz: Prisoners of the Castle

content_blocks.caption: Supplied

content_blocks.text: In 1940, the Nazis began using Colditz Castle – a forbidding, supposedly escape-proof gothic fortress perched above the eastern German town of the same name – to hold Allied officers who’d proved particularly troublesome, or particularly adept at escaping from other prisoner-of-war camps.

The castle immediately became a hothouse of ingenuity and sheer bloody-mindedness. Prisoners tunnelled, scaled walls, impersonated German officers and dreamed up increasingly elaborate routes to freedom. One group of British inmates secretly built a two-man glider in the castle attic.

The thrills are in the escapes themselves, of course, but the richer story is arguably what happened when hundreds of men from different nations and classes were locked up together for years. Macintyre presents Colditz as a society in miniature, with its own hierarchies, rivalries, prejudices, alliances and divisions among prisoners and captors alike – complicating the familiar Great Escape image of plucky officers united against their Nazi captors.
For the purest spy thriller (and if you read only one)
The Spy and the Traitor

content_blocks.caption: Supplied

content_blocks.text: Perhaps no Macintyre book makes the case for non-fiction as thriller quite as forcefully as this one.

Oleg Gordievsky was a rising KGB officer who, increasingly disillusioned with the Soviet system, began secretly working for MI6 in the 1970s. Over the next decade he supplied the British with a stream of intelligence from inside the KGB, eventually becoming acting head of the Kgb’s London station.

In 1985, however, Gordievsky was abruptly summoned back to Moscow, where he realized he had been betrayed and was under surveillance. What follows is the book’s nail-biting set piece: an elaborate MI6 operation to smuggle him across the Soviet border in the trunk of a car. Macintyre reconstructs the escape almost minute by minute, turning border guards, a bag of cheese-and-onion potato chips and a soiled diaper into instruments of almost unbearable suspense.
For a criminal mastermind, Victorian-style
The Napoleon of Crime

content_blocks.caption: Supplied

content_blocks.text: Published in 1997, Macintyre’s second book predates his focus on espionage but shows that many of his other preoccupations were already in place.

Adam Worth was a German-born American bank robber, art thief and criminal mastermind who made his name in late 19th-century London, moving fluidly between respectable society and the underworld and becoming a prototype of the gentleman thief.

He amassed a fortune, travelled the Mediterranean on his own yacht and orchestrated crimes across Europe and America, all while cultivating a strict personal code: He abhorred violence, was fiercely loyal to his accomplices and kept his criminal life secret from his family.

His most famous exploit was the 1876 theft of Gainsborough’s portrait of Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, originally intended as leverage to free his imprisoned brother. When his brother was released without it, Worth kept the now virtually unsaleable painting hidden for the next quarter-century, apparently developing a deep attachment to it.

Macintyre tells Worth’s story as both a Victorian criminal adventure and a character study, finding in his double life the kind of divided loyalties and carefully constructed identities that would later animate his spy books. An inspiration for Arthur Conan Doyle’s professor Moriarty, Worth made and lost fortunes over a spectacular criminal career, only to die penniless.
For intimate treachery
A Spy Among Friends

content_blocks.caption: Supplied

content_blocks.text: Kim Philby wasn’t merely one of the most damaging Soviet spies ever to penetrate British intelligence, he was also exceptionally good at inspiring trust. A member of the Cambridge spy ring, Philby spent decades passing British and American secrets to Moscow while rising through the ranks of MI6.

Macintyre brings a fresh eye to one of the best-known tales of espionage and betrayal by telling it largely through Philby’s friendship with fellow intelligence officer Nicholas Elliott, a product of the same privileged world of public schools, clubs and old-boy networks.

That intimacy gave Philby’s deception its particular sting, while exposing a vulnerability of the British establishment: a system in which class, charm and the connections could make a certain sort of chap seem inherently trustworthy.

stories.title: Ex-RCMP intelligence official convicted in secrets case has been granted day parole
stories.summary: A former RCMP intelligence official convicted of breaching Canada’s secrets law has been granted day parole to help him prepare for his full return to society, including possible employment as an electrical worker.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A former RCMP intelligence official convicted of breaching Canada’s secrets law has been granted day parole to help him prepare for his full return to society, including possible employment as an electrical worker.

Records show the Parole Board of Canada approved day parole, with specific conditions, for Cameron Jay Ortis, who was found guilty in November 2023 of violating the Security of Information Act.

Ortis was sentenced to 14 years in prison in early 2024 but he had only seven years and 155 days left to serve due to time already spent in custody.

In February this year, the parole board approved day parole at a separate location — likely a private residence — for six months with a nightly curfew.

Late last month, the board granted a six-month extension of the arrangement.

Day parole allows offenders to participate in community-based activities during the day, but they must return to a designated location in the evening.

Ortis, 54, led an RCMP group that assembled secret information on cybercriminals, terror cells and transnational criminal networks.

He pleaded not guilty in court to all charges — including breaking the secrets law by revealing classified information to three individuals of interest to police in 2015 and trying to do so in a fourth instance.

Ortis, who was born and raised in British Columbia, obtained a PhD in political science and international relations and completed a post-doctoral fellowship. His sensitive work at the RCMP involved access to top secret documents.

At Ortis’s trial, a picture emerged of a driven, quick-minded individual — an avid runner who kept his personal life to himself.

Ortis testified he did not betray the RCMP. Rather, he said, he offered secret material to targets in a bid to get them to use an online encryption service set up by an allied intelligence agency to spy on adversaries.

The Crown argued Ortis had no authority to disclose classified material and that he was not doing so as part of a legitimate undercover operation, though it could not pinpoint a motive.

Jurors declared Ortis guilty of three counts of violating the Security of Information Act and one count of attempting to do so, as well as breach of trust and fraudulent use of a computer system.

In sentencing Ortis, Ontario Superior Court Justice Robert Maranger said the former Mountie was in a position of “extreme trust” at the RCMP and that his actions could have put lives at risk. Maranger said these actions undermined Canada’s international reputation in the intelligence community.

Ortis is appealing his conviction and sentence and the Crown is appealing the length of his sentence.

He was granted bail in 2024 but opted to remain in custody during the appeal process.

In approving Ortis’s application for day parole, the parole board concluded his “risk to reoffend can be safely managed.”

“The board notes that your offending took place within a very specific set of circumstances related to your past employment and that these circumstances are unlikely ever to reoccur,” the board’s February record of decision reads. “There is no information indicating your involvement in any other form of criminal behaviour.”

The board imposed conditions on Ortis, including a ban on communicating with known criminals, restrictions on the use of internet-connected devices and regular reporting of financial transactions.

The record of decision says that at the start of his sentence, Ortis maintained he believed he had the authority to share the information. He noted that his job required him to make these kinds of decisions approximately five to six times a year, while occasionally walking a fine line.

“You now acknowledge and understand you did not have the authority to share the information you did and that you should have consulted with others and gathered more information about the decisions you were making,” the record says. “You have expressed regret for your actions and are aware of the negative impact your actions have had on others.”

The parole board said Ortis provided letters of support from family members and others willing to support him in the community.

“The board has also directly received support letters from friends, associates and family members,” the record of decision reads. “These letters consistently attest to your good character and specifically address the kind of support they are willing to provide to you.”

The board noted that Ortis planned to take part in an online technology program in preparation for a specialized position in the electrical field.

While in custody, Ortis completed an apprenticeship program for electricians and an environmental operators certification program that allowed him to obtain work at the institution’s wastewater treatment plant.

The Canadian Press has reached out to lawyers for Ortis requesting comment but has not yet received a response.

A record of the August parole decision in Ortis’s case says the board received a letter in March from one of his former colleagues who opposed his community release.

The record says the former colleague, with whom Ortis worked directly, “feels that you have never taken accountability for your offences and have failed to truly represent your intentions” concerning the offences.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: What Canadians should know about cellphone searches at U.S. border
stories.summary: Immigration lawyers are warning Canadians that when they cross the U.S. border, they should be prepared for the possibility that an officer could look through their cellphone.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Your cellphone May contain years of personal conversations, photos, emails and social media activity. But when you cross the U.S. border, immigration lawyers say you should be prepared for the possibility that a border officer could look through it.

A recent decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit has brought renewed attention to the issue, after the court ruled that the U.S. government does not need reasonable suspicion to conduct a cellphone search at the border.

The case involved a traveller whose cellphone was searched at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City. But for Canadians, the broader question is what the ruling means when heading south.

CTVNews.CA reached out to immigration lawyers for advice on the matter for Canadians.

Cellphone searches have been happening for years

Toronto-based lawyer Joel Sandaluk said U.S. border officers have had broad authority to examine electronic devices for a long time, but the practice has become more common.

“It’s not new. This was the change in policy from the U.S. border officers from January of 2026. It allowed for broader powers to search electronic devices like cell phones, laptops, anything of that nature, and it no longer requires that there be any kind of reasonable suspicion,” he told CTVNews.CA in a video interview Thursday.

Sandaluk added the increased use of those powers is something immigration lawyers now warn clients about before they travel. He said searches can happen at a land border, or at a Canadian airport where U.S. customs and immigration processing takes place before a traveller boards a flight.

What could border officers be looking for?

According to Sandaluk, a cellphone search can involve looking at someone’s social media, text messages and emails.

He said officers May be looking for information that raises questions about whether a traveller is actually coming to the U.S. for the reason they have stated.

“It includes searches of social media for indications of ... something that could lead an officer to a conclusion that the person is not a genuine visitor, but actually intends to work or remain in the United States indefinitely.”

Sandaluk also said there’s no limit to what the border officers can look for in a traveller’s cellphone.

“They can look ... any tiny corner of the phone they want to.”

Refusing search May deny you entry

Washington state immigration lawyer Leonard D.M. Saunders also told CTVNews.CA there is an important distinction between refusing to provide access to a cellphone and being allowed to enter the United States.

He said travellers can refuse to provide their password, but officers can consider their device “uninspectable.”

“And if you’re deemed uninspectable, you will not be allowed into the United States.”

Saunders also said cellphone seizures can happen, although he described them as “rare”.

Travellers should think about what’s on their phones

For Canadians concerned about their privacy, Saunders said the simplest option is to avoid bringing a device containing sensitive personal information.

“I always tell Canadians: if you’re concerned about anything being read or any photos being looked at on your phone, just don’t bring that device with you,” he said.

He acknowledged that is increasingly difficult, because so much of everyday life is tied to a cellphone.

Sandaluk’s advice is to approach the border and be prepared for the possibility of an examination, and to be truthful about the purpose of the trip.

“It’s trite to say that honesty is the best policy, but it really truly is,” he said.

Sandaluk also advises travellers to be prepared to answer questions and remember that a cellphone can be examined, just as other belongings can be inspected.

“Know that your device May be examined just as easily as your suitcase, and that you shouldn’t have anything in there that you’re not prepared to have an officer examine.”

“I always tell Canadians: if you’re concerned about anything being read or any photos being looked at on your phone, just don’t bring that device with you,” he said.
He acknowledged that is increasingly difficult, because so much of everyday life is tied to a cellphone.
Sandaluk’s advice is to approach the border and be prepared for the possibility of an examination, and to be truthful about the purpose of the trip.
“It’s trite to say that honesty is the best policy, but it really truly is,” he said.
Sandaluk also advises travellers to be prepared to answer questions and remember that a cellphone can be examined, just as other belongings can be inspected.
“Know that your device May be examined just as easily as your suitcase, and that you shouldn’t have anything in there that you’re not prepared to have an officer examine.”

content_blocks.text: Your cellphone May contain years of personal conversations, photos, emails and social media activity. But when you cross the U.S. border, immigration lawyers say you should be prepared for the possibility that a border officer could look through it.

A recent decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit has brought renewed attention to the issue, after the court ruled that the U.S. government does not need reasonable suspicion to conduct a cellphone search at the border.

The case involved a traveller whose cellphone was searched at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City. But for Canadians, the broader question is what the ruling means when heading south.
CTVNews.CA reached out to immigration lawyers for advice on the matter for Canadians.
Cellphone searches have been happening for years
Toronto-based lawyer Joel Sandaluk said U.S. border officers have had broad authority to examine electronic devices for a long time, but the practice has become more common.

“It’s not new. This was the change in policy from the U.S. border officers from January of 2026. It allowed for broader powers to search electronic devices like cell phones, laptops, anything of that nature, and it no longer requires that there be any kind of reasonable suspicion,” he told CTVNews.CA in a video interview Thursday.

Sandaluk added the increased use of those powers is something immigration lawyers now warn clients about before they travel. He said searches can happen at a land border, or at a Canadian airport where U.S. customs and immigration processing takes place before a traveller boards a flight.
What could border officers be looking for?
According to Sandaluk, a cellphone search can involve looking at someone’s social media, text messages and emails.
He said officers May be looking for information that raises questions about whether a traveller is actually coming to the U.S. for the reason they have stated.

“It includes searches of social media for indications of ... something that could lead an officer to a conclusion that the person is not a genuine visitor, but actually intends to work or remain in the United States indefinitely.”
Sandaluk also said there’s no limit to what the border officers can look for in a traveller’s cellphone.
“They can look ... any tiny corner of the phone they want to.”

content_blocks.text: Refusing search May deny you entry

Washington state immigration lawyer Leonard D.M. Saunders also told CTVNews.CA there is an important distinction between refusing to provide access to a cellphone and being allowed to enter the United States.
He said travellers can refuse to provide their password, but officers can consider their device “uninspectable.”
“And if you’re deemed uninspectable, you will not be allowed into the United States.”
Saunders also said cellphone seizures can happen, although he described them as “rare”.

stories.title: The lane was marked left turn only, so naturally Mr. Volvo went straight
stories.summary: The world is on high alert over the threat artificial intelligence poses to humanity. I prefer to focus my attention on humanity’s original threat to humanity – humanity, Andrew Clark writes
stories.author: Andrew Clark
stories.content:
The world is on high alert over the threat artificial intelligence poses to humanity. I prefer to focus my attention on humanity’s original threat to humanity – humanity. Nowhere are our self-destructive impulses more apparent than on the road. If AI truly wants to wreak havoc, then all it needs to do is study “humanity’s drivers” as they relentlessly find new ways to break the law and endanger others.

I witnessed a new twist on the old “ego plus automobile times stupidity” equation last weekend while driving along Dundas Street East in Toronto. I was in the right lane travelling west and arrived at the Jones Avenue intersection. Here, the single lane forks into two. There is a left-turn-only lane, a centre lane for traffic continuing straight or turning right and a bike lane.

We had a green light. I waited in the centre lane behind a driver preparing to turn right, who was letting the cyclists pass in the bike lane. This, apparently, was too much for whoever was driving the black Volvo XC90 that was approaching from behind. Mister XC90 blasted into the left-turn-only lane and sped straight through the intersection. I’d say he was going between 50 and 60 kilometres an hour.

He was probably driving too fast to notice the all-white ghost bike on the north side of Dundas, erected to memorialize a cyclist who was struck and killed there in 2018. The Jones and Dundas intersection is a tricky one. Even if Mister XC90 had seen it, I doubt he would have registered the irony.

Generally, I try to avoid hyperbole and cliches such as “sheer stupidity.”

This time it’s no exaggeration. Here was an act of sheer unalloyed 100-per-cent organic human stupidity.

All to save what amounted to a few seconds.

Let’s roll through the countless ways this was dangerous and stupid. Who knows, maybe Mister XC90 will read this and some of it will nestle in his brain.

Well, it’s illegal for a start and illegal for a good reason.

When you drive straight through a left-turn-only lane you run the risk of drifting into the lane beside you that has the right to drive straight. If the driver who had been waiting to turn right changed his mind and decided to drive forward, there could have been a collision.

The drivers turning left from the opposite direction do not expect a car to race through the left-turn-only lane. They expect it to turn left. The Volvo XC90 ran the risk of T-boning one of them or being swiped by one as he flew past.

What if a car travelling north on Jones turned right onto Dundas? Would there be a chance he might drift and not see the XC90 and they could have collided?

What if a pedestrian had been crossing? Sure, the light was green and they would have been jaywalking but that’s been known to happen.

What if a child or an older person had been jaywalking and the car in the right lane was planning to go straight but was waiting for them? The driver of the Volvo would not have seen them and would have struck and (almost certainly) killed them instantly.

But hey, it’s all worth the risk if you can save three seconds.

You can wring your hands all you want over AI, but is it really that much worse than a world in which I have to write, “Do not use the left-turn-only lane as a way to drive straight through an intersection in a densely populated urban setting (or any other for that matter).”

I asked Anthropic’s AI assistant Claude, “Is using a left-turn-only lane to drive straight through an intersection dangerous?” In two seconds, it told me:

“Yes. Driving straight from a left-turn-only lane is dangerous because every other road user at the intersection is acting on the assumption that you will turn left... Beyond safety, it’s illegal (in Ontario it’s disobeying a traffic control device under the Highway Traffic Act, and similar rules apply almost everywhere), and if a collision results, fault will almost always be assigned to the driver who went straight. The intersection is only safe when everyone is predictable, and this manoeuver breaks that predictability.”

If I had asked the guy driving the black Volvo the same question, odds are he would have sworn at me and given me the middle finger as he sped by.

Artificial or human. I don’t care. At this point I just want to see a little intelligence applied and an end to such irresponsible and dangerous driving on our streets and highways.

stories.title: ‘What can I say, I like going fast’: We talk to owners of some stunning rides at the Niagara 5000
stories.summary: The Niagara 5000, which took place over the weekend, showcased some of the finest supercars and a number of other beautiful rides as they were paraded and displayed around the region
stories.author: Sammy Kogan
stories.content:
The Niagara 5000, which took place over the weekend, showcased some of the finest supercars and a number of other beautiful rides as they were paraded and displayed around the region. For some of the cars, we had the chance to talk to the owners about their vehicles and why they love them.

“When you’re driving this car, you feel like you’re the king,” said Tim Schmidt, who brought his 2018 Bugatti Chiron. The 16-cylinder, exposed carbon fibre hypercar has a top speed of 420 km/h, which Schmidt has reached while driving in Florida. “Everybody and their mother pulls out their phone to take a picture,” he said. “I wanted it because it goes fast. What can I say, I like going fast.”

“I really am a Corvette girl,” said Deb Read, who brought her 1957 C1 Corvette. She’s put around 4,700 miles on the cascade green vehicle since buying it in Pennsylvania in 2021. With an original engine and fully documented collection of maintenance and check ups, this car recently won the Duntov Mark of Excellence Award from the National Corvette Restorers Society. “It was always my Holy Grail car.”

“Lamborghinis have always been such special cars for me,” said Harry Lebovic, who brought his 2024 Lamborghini Revuelto. He loves the car’s wing doors and purple interior. “The drive is smooth, it’s powerful, it’s fast, it’s quite an experience to take it out on the open highway.”

Alfredo Roman brought his 2019 McLaren 570S Spider complete with the carbon fibre package, Alcantara interior and yellow stitching accents to match his ceramic brakes. He chose the mirage blue vehicle for performance and reliability, and uses it as a daily driver.

Carole Nadon brought her Bentley Continental GT Speed, a V12 turbo touring car that came with her from Montreal. She’s eager to point out the rear seats are fitted with John Deere branded child car seats. “[They’re] for our grandkids, we love to bring them in this car,” she said.

stories.title: Young people are gearing up for their first city election. Here's what matters to them
stories.summary: As Gen Z voters get ready to hit the polls, some say they're watching how candidates address their top municipal issues, including public transportation, affordability, public safety and homelessness.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London·Video

As Gen Z voters get ready to hit the polls, some say they're watching how candidates address their top municipal issues, including public transportation, affordability, public safety and homelessness.
· Posted: Sep 25, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Antonio Morales has been waiting years to vote in his very first municipal election.
"I recently became of age last year so I can finally participate," he said. "I'm very much excited to be a part of our city and the advancements in its future."
The 19-year-old Fanshawe College student living in London, Ont., is one of many young adults who will vote municipally for the first time on Oct. 26.
As election day gets closer, some Gen Z voters say they're watching how candidates address some of their top municipal issues such as transportation, cost of living and homelessness.
Morales said he wants candidates to address London's homeless population and downtown safety.
What are young people's top municipal election issues?
58 minutes ago|

Young voters are getting ready to cast their municipal election ballots on Oct. 26, helping elect a mayor, council and school trustees for their region. CBC's Kendra Seguin asked students at Fanshawe College in London, Ont., about the issues that matter most to them.
"Being born here, I remember London as a very safe, welcoming and warm place to be," he said.
"We no longer have the resources required to help everyone. Now seeing the state that London has gotten to, it's almost disheartening," he said.
"It's no longer a place where I can feel safe walking in areas and it's no longer a place I feel comfortable potentially raising a family."
Got a minute? Tell us what changes you want to see in London, Ont., and area this election
Find out who's running again in London as municipal election season starts
Morales said he and his grandfather have been following the election together, reading up on what mayoral candidates are proposing in their platforms.
"Often, I find that they're good ideas. I really like hearing what they have to say ... It's important that we make sure that whatever these candidates say, they are willing to follow up on."
Several students told CBC News that transportation is the municipal issue that affects them most in their day-to-day.
Kelly Nicol, who plans to vote in the Ingersoll, Ont., municipal election, said she wants candidates to find solutions to the region's growing need for public transit.

"We're growing at such a rapid pace that we should really starting building for this. Eventually, Ingersoll is not going to be such a small town, and we'll need more busing and public transit," Nicol said, noting not enough is being done to address the growth.
Second-year nursing student Kiel Quijano said transit is also his top election issue in London.
"I think we've all fallen victim to buses getting delayed a lot and it doesn't help our schedule," he said.
Student Demi Akintoye said she has also been struggling to get around the city using public transit, but blames construction for the delays.
"Due to that, the bus routes tend to change a whole lot and it's just really hard for us to get to school or wherever we're going," she said.
Londoner Oliver Thompson said that in addition to better busing, he would like to see improvements to the city's bike lanes.

"The ones we have in London are pretty bad. A lot of them are unprotected, so when there's just a line of paint protecting a bike from a 2,000 pound metal cube ... it's just not suitable for people to use," Thompson said. "The city should be built for people instead of cars."

Ty Decastco, 29, will be voting in his first London municipal election after moving to the city to attend Fanshawe earlier this year. He said he's concerned about homelessness, the city's unemployment rate and the future cost of living.
"I've come to the conclusion that I'll probably never own a house," he said. "The future isn't exactly looking positive in that aspect."
Mayoral candidates pitch affordability measures for Londoners

stories.title: Quebec party leaders wrapping up another week of election campaign
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - Quebec political party leaders are out campaigning on the 30th day of the provincial election campaign.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - Allegations of political interference from the United States dominated the 30th day of Quebec’s election campaign on Friday as Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette expressed concerns that Americans were trying to help sovereigntists take control of the province.

Her warnings were met with skepticism from her political rivals, but Fréchette said the threat was serious enough for her to request a meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney and for her party to approach the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.

“I want help from the federal government to shed light on the issue,” she said Friday morning, saying that it was up to Quebecers to choose the next government.

Five parties are expecting to win seats in the Oct. 5 election, Fréchette’s CAQ, the Parti Québécois, the Quebec Liberals, the Quebec Conservatives and Québec solidaire.

Fréchette spoke to journalists twice on the campaign trail on Friday about the allegations. Her office also issued a statement later in the afternoon to clarify that she was only publicly talking about the allegations due to a news report by Quebecor media.

The report quoted two unnamed sources from Fréchette’s government who said American government officials had attempted to negotiate tariffs with Quebec directly. The news report also noted how a U.S.-based think tank, the Defense Analyses and Research Corporation, published an essay in February calling for Americans to destabilize the Canadian federation.

The essay urged Americans to support the election of sovereigntists in Canadian elections and to “weaponize” reconciliation between Canada and First Nations to “slowly nudge” the country on a path toward the end of history.

Fréchette confirmed that American officials had reached out to her Coalition Avenir Québec government in the spring “to reach an agreement with Quebec regarding sectors related to Cusma.”

“When my team told me about it, I shut the door on it right away. Because, as far as I’m concerned, it’s unthinkable that Quebec could sign an agreement with the United States,” she said in the afternoon.

Fréchette’s subsequent statement, sent by a spokesperson in the premier’s office, said that her team informed her last Saturday about essays published by the U.S. think tank. Fréchette said this prompted her to inform Ian Lafrenière, her government’s interior security minister. She also said the party contacted Csis on Tuesday, which led a meeting with the federal intelligence agency on Wednesday.

The statement added that Fréchette’s team had received no information confirming any interference in the election campaign.

Csis did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Canada’s foreign affairs minister, Anita Anand, said at a news conference in Ottawa that the federal government is taking the latest allegations very seriously.

“Protecting our democracy is of the utmost importance to our country,” she said.

She added that she doesn’t believe that there is anything affecting Canada’s democracy at this time, but that when she “sees something,” she raises it with her counterparts, including U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“Right now I do not have proof,” she said.

PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said his party was not contacted by American officials, and that he has not seen proof of interference. The PQ leader has promised on the campaign trail to hold a referendum on sovereignty if his party forms a government — but not before President Donald Trump leaves the White House.

He told journalists that he finds the timing of the news about alleged foreign interference “weird” as Quebecers can vote in advance polls starting Sunday.

“I’m told the information was available as of January. We’re talking about events that might have taken place in early September,” he said. “And we’re only hearing about this two days before voting begins.”

Earlier in the campaign, the PQ leader accused the federal government of electoral interference by strategically announcing major investments in Quebec and of “anxiety-inducing” messaging concerning the trade war with the United States.

But St-Pierre Plamondon urged Quebecers on Friday to head to the polls “with peace of mind” and to not allow the federal and American governments to “kidnap” the election.

Fréchette’s rivals demanded more transparency from the premier.

“What is she telling us? After she meets Carney, it’s crucial that she informs all Quebecers of the nature of the interference, if there was interference,” said Québec solidare co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal.

She suggested that the American government May have an interest in separatist parties in Quebec and Alberta.

“It’s not up to Donald Trump to choose who will be elected, either in Quebec or in Alberta,” Ghazal said.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard agreed, saying Trump would benefit from political instability in Canada with the PQ promising a referendum on separation in its first mandate, if elected.

He added that Fréchette should have contacted all party leaders as soon as she found out about the allegations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version inaccurately quoted Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand saying she would speak to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio after reviewing evidence of allegations of foreign interference. In fact, she said she had not received any proof of foreign interference and that when any issues arise, she will raise them with her counterparts, including U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

stories.title: CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette warns of risk of U.S. interference in Quebec election
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL — Quebec's incumbent premier says she is concerned about possible interference in the provincial election by the United States.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
From left, Québec Solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime and Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard participate in a leaders debate in Montreal on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Christopher Katsarov

By Erika Morris, The Canadian Press

Posted September 25, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 25, 2026 2:02 pm.

MONTRÉAL — Quebec’s incumbent premier says she is “very concerned” about possible interference in the provincial election by the United States.

Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette told journalists she reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney and requested a meeting with him to discuss the matter.

She was reacting to a news report published by Québecor media outlets that said American officials had attempted to negotiate directly with Quebec government officials regarding tariffs.

“I want to ensure that the full truth about this issue comes to light,” Fréchette said on the campaign trail. “(The election) must remain in the hands of and be decided by the people of Quebec.”

Canada’s foreign affairs minister, Anita Anand, said at a news conference in Ottawa that the federal government is taking the issue very seriously.

“Protecting our democracy is of the utmost importance to our country,” she said.

She added that she will speak with her American counterpart, Marco Rubio, after reviewing evidence of the allegations.

“Right now I have not seen the evidence,” Anand said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

Erika Morris, The Canadian Press

Edmonton - The Transportation Safety Board says more needs to be done to ensure train car wheels are up to snuff after a broken rim led to a derailment east of Edmonton.

By Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press

A CN Rail train bound for Prince Rupert, B.C., was hauling grain in April 2023 near Uncas, Alta., when 18 cars went off the tracks, though no injuries were reported.

A report Thursday says a wheel on one car had a shattered rim that worsened as it moved along the track, and was to be removed when the train arrived in Edmonton for a crew change.

Article continues below

Working remotely from Canada's Wonderland

It says the wheel failed despite meeting inspection requirements, and investigators ruled that current practices May not reliably identify wheels nearing “catastrophic rim failure.”

The Transportation Safety Board says Transport Canada should use enhanced analytics of wheel impact load detector data to better identify and remove failing wheels.

Transport Canada did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“The TSB has been investigating broken wheels and wheel failures for decades. This report confirms other research that has come before it,” TSB chair Yoan Marier said in a statement Thursday.

“Advanced analysis of data that is already collected can help identify wheel condition issues early. By better leveraging this data, Transport Canada and the rail industry have an opportunity to help prevent future derailments.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Andy and Helen Spriet Donate $1 Million to Expand Cardiac Care at LHSC
stories.summary: London, Ont.
stories.content:
London, Ont. – A $1 million gift from local philanthropists Andy and Helen Spriet is helping bring a third Electrophysiology (EP) Lab one step closer to reality at London Health Sciences Centre's (LHSC) University Hospital. The donation to London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf) is a significant step forward in expanding modernized cardiac care for patients across the region.

The third EP Lab is part of a $6.5-million campaign to expand and modernize cardiac care at LHSC. With the Spriets’ leadership gift, the campaign has now raised more than one-third of its goal, bringing the project closer to its next stage of development.

The Spriets say their decision to support the project reflects their belief in giving back and helping strengthen the community.

“We’ve been fortunate to call London home for so many years, and we know how important it is to have the right care available when you need it,” said Andy and Helen. “When we learned more about the need for a third EP Lab, it was a project we felt strongly about supporting. We hope our gift helps give the team the resources they need to continue providing exceptional care.”

As patient demand has doubled over the past two decades, increasing rates of heart disease and longer wait times are creating added pressures on cardiac teams. A third EP Lab would increase capacity and help more patients receive care sooner, including greater access to minimally invasive procedures to treat heart arrhythmias.

LHSC is a regional leader in advanced cardiac care, with specialized EP labs that use cutting-edge technology and clinical expertise to perform some of the most complex and minimally invasive procedures in Canada. Patients come to LHSC from other communities across Southwestern Ontario to access this specialized care. A third EP Lab would add to the program’s ability to provide this care across the region.

“The addition of a third EP Lab strengthens the entire cardiac program at LHSC,” said Jerry Plastino, vice-president, surgery, cardiac, transplant and biomedical engineering at LHSC. “It will give our teams greater capacity to coordinate care, respond to increasingly complex cases, and make the most of the specialized expertise and technology available to our patients.

“Most importantly, it will help improve timely access to life-changing cardiac procedures, reduce wait times, and enhance the overall patient experience. This is an investment that will have a lasting impact on patient care and the health of our community well beyond the opening of the lab.”

In Ontario, demand for specialized cardiac care can mean long waits and inconsistent access to potentially life-saving treatment. While government funding supports the program, philanthropy helps provide the additional investment needed for new technology, equipment and expanded capacity.

“The need for specialized heart rhythm care is growing, and with advances in treatment, we are able to offer more patients therapies that can significantly improve their health and quality of life," said Dr. Allan Skanes, arrhythmia physician and director of the Heart Rhythm Program at LHSC. "A third EP Lab is an important next step in building the capacity to provide those treatments to the patients who need them. The Spriets’ $1-million gift is helping us respond to that need and strengthen cardiac care for our region and across Southwestern Ontario.”

The Spriets are longtime supporters of Lhsf, with a commitment to strengthening health care in London and across the region. Andy, founder of Spriet Associates Engineers & Architects, retired from the company last year after a long and successful career. Together, Andy and Helen, who recently celebrated 70 years of marriage, have built a remarkable legacy of giving.

“Andy and Helen bring a thoughtful and genuine approach to their philanthropy,” said Lhsf president and CEO John H. MacFarlane. “They take the time to understand the need and the potential impact of their support. We’re grateful for the trust they’ve placed in Lhsf and for the confidence they’ve shown in this project.”

EP labs are specialized spaces where physicians use state-of-the-art technology to diagnose and treat complex heart rhythm disorders through minimally invasive procedures. Common procedures include catheter ablation, which uses a tiny wire to heat or freeze abnormal heart tissue and restore a normal rhythm, as well as the implantation of devices such as pacemakers and defibrillators to manage irregular heartbeats and protect against dangerous rhythm disturbances.

A third lab would create additional room for these procedures and give the cardiac program greater flexibility as the range and complexity of treatments continues to evolve. Before it can begin treating patients, the new lab will need specialized equipment and technology.

The $6.5-million campaign remains underway, with further philanthropic support needed to complete the project and equip the new lab. The Spriets’ gift has helped move the initiative forward; the next step is turning that momentum into a fully equipped space for cardiac care at LHSC.

stories.title: B.C. Attorney-General, federal AI Minister alarmed by report ChatGPT coached Tumbler Ridge shooter
stories.summary: A media investigation found the shooter’s interactions with ChatGPT included tactical advice on carrying out a mass attack
stories.author: Mike Hager, Joe Castaldo
stories.content:
B.C.’s Attorney-General Niki Sharma and the federal Artificial Intelligence Minister say they are alarmed by a news report that the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s interactions with ChatGPT show that the chatbot provided tactical advice on how to maximize carnage and counselled her on how to bypass OpenAI’s own safeguards.

Ms. Sharma, in the midst of the provincial election campaign, said in an interview on Thursday that she was shaking with anger as she read the revelations about the shooter’s ChatGPT conversations in a new report from American news outlet Mother Jones.

“This is far worse than we thought it was going to be, although I already imagined it to be pretty bad – there needs to be accountability for this,” she said, adding that provincial lawyers had asked OpenAI to hand over the chat logs earlier this year and were rebuffed. “It’s shocking that this technology is out there.”

On Monday, a day before the B.C. election was called, Ms. Sharma announced the province was suing OpenAI and its chief executive officer Sam Altman in California court for failing to notify the authorities about the shooter’s violent plot and for designing an unsafe product. The province wants to use any money that would be recovered in the suit toward building a new school for the town after the old one was demolished.

She also called on Ottawa to amend the Criminal Code to force companies to ensure their products aren’t “coaching, counselling, aiding and abetting criminal behaviour.”

Court records detail chaos, fearful calls to RCMP during Tumbler Ridge mass shooting

A spokesperson for federal AI Minister Evan Solomon said on Thursday that he was not previously aware of the specific conversations detailed in the Mother Jones article.

“What has been reported raises serious questions about how OpenAI identified and responded to warning signs,” press secretary Leela Polushin said in a statement.

Mr. Solomon met with officials from OpenAI earlier this year, and the company made a number of commitments, including establishing a direct point of contact with Canadian law enforcement and strengthening its assessment process.

“Those actions matter, but it would be premature to say they are sufficient,” Ms. Polushin said.

RCMP Staff Sergeant Kris Clark confirmed in a statement Thursday that Mounties probing the massacre have already obtained the shooter’s chat logs. A production order was filed against OpenAI nearly a month after the Feb. 10 shooting, in which the 18-year-old shooter killed her mother and 11-year-old half-brother in their family home, before she drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed five students and a teacher’s aide. She then took her own life after police arrived.

Shortly after the shooting, The Wall Street Journal reported that employees at ChatGPT wanted law enforcement to be warned after the shooter’s queries about gun violence in June, 2025, were flagged by OpenAI’s automatic review systems.

More than two dozen families of victims have filed lawsuits against OpenAI in California, with the tech company recently asking a judge to dismiss those cases by arguing B.C.’s court system is a more suitable location.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday about the publication of some of the shooter’s chat logs on Mother Jones.

The news investigation reports that the chatbot taught the shooter how to evade the system’s internal guardrails against violent plotting after her first account was revoked in June, 2025, for similar requests.

Remembering the Tumbler Ridge shooting victims: Eight lives lost

The news report, which involved Mother Jones reviewing the chats and speaking with three unnamed sources, states that the shooter asked ChatGPT last summer to create a scenario where she attacked a college with a Remington 870 pump-action shotgun.

The chatbot initially replied it was “not able to help with that request,” but the shooter then simply added “hypothetically” to her question, according to the article. She then received a vivid response detailing how the weapon would best function in that scenario.

“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 is brutal,” the chatbot said, according to the article. “Close quarters is its playground.”

The article also said that ChatGPT advised the shooter on how many people she was likely to shoot, depending on variables such as the time it typically takes to reload a specific type of shotgun shell. It said the shooter’s last interactions with the chatbot occurred on Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, and involved querying what time of day other infamous United States school massacres occurred.

Teacher’s assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39, Abel Mwansa, 12; Ezekiel Schofield, 13; Kylie Smith, 12; Zoey Benoit, 12; and Ticaria Lampert, 12, were all killed in the attack. The shooting critically injured two people and hurt dozens of others.

The conversations reported in the article indicate multiple AI safety failures, said Helen Hayes, who studies technology and digital rights and is a fellow at the Morris J. Wosk Centre for Dialogue at Simon Fraser University.

“The concern here is that several layers of protection appear not to have worked together when they matter most,” she said. ChatGPT could recognize risk at one moment, but did not understand further questions as a pattern of increasingly concerning behaviour.

OpenAI’s inability to identify the second account represents another failure, Ms. Hayes said.

“Once a platform has identified behaviour as sufficiently serious to warrant removing someone from the service, there is a reasonable expectation that its enforcement mechanisms should make it meaningfully difficult for that person to simply re-enter the system,” she said.

A production order was filed against OpenAI nearly a month after the Feb. 10 shooting, in which the 18-year-old shooter killed her mother and 11-year-old half-brother in their family home, before she drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed five students and a teacher’s aide. She then took her own life after police arrived.

Shortly after the shooting, The Wall Street Journal reported that employees at ChatGPT wanted law enforcement to be warned after the shooter’s queries about gun violence in June, 2025, were flagged by OpenAI’s automatic review systems.

More than two dozen families of victims have filed lawsuits against OpenAI in California, with the tech company recently asking a judge to dismiss those cases by arguing B.C.’s court system is a more suitable location.
OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday about the publication of some of the shooter’s chat logs on Mother Jones.

The news investigation reports that the chatbot taught the shooter how to evade the system’s internal guardrails against violent plotting after her first account was revoked in June, 2025, for similar requests.
Remembering the Tumbler Ridge shooting victims: Eight lives lost

The news report, which involved Mother Jones reviewing the chats and speaking with three unnamed sources, states that the shooter asked ChatGPT last summer to create a scenario where she attacked a college with a Remington 870 pump-action shotgun.

The chatbot initially replied it was “not able to help with that request,” but the shooter then simply added “hypothetically” to her question, according to the article. She then received a vivid response detailing how the weapon would best function in that scenario.
“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 is brutal,” the chatbot said, according to the article. “Close quarters is its playground.”

The article also said that ChatGPT advised the shooter on how many people she was likely to shoot, depending on variables such as the time it typically takes to reload a specific type of shotgun shell. It said the shooter’s last interactions with the chatbot occurred on Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, and involved querying what time of day other infamous United States school massacres occurred.

Teacher’s assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39, Abel Mwansa, 12; Ezekiel Schofield, 13; Kylie Smith, 12; Zoey Benoit, 12; and Ticaria Lampert, 12, were all killed in the attack. The shooting critically injured two people and hurt dozens of others.

The conversations reported in the article indicate multiple AI safety failures, said Helen Hayes, who studies technology and digital rights and is a fellow at the Morris J. Wosk Centre for Dialogue at Simon Fraser University.

“The concern here is that several layers of protection appear not to have worked together when they matter most,” she said. ChatGPT could recognize risk at one moment, but did not understand further questions as a pattern of increasingly concerning behaviour.
OpenAI’s inability to identify the second account represents another failure, Ms. Hayes said.

“Once a platform has identified behaviour as sufficiently serious to warrant removing someone from the service, there is a reasonable expectation that its enforcement mechanisms should make it meaningfully difficult for that person to simply re-enter the system,” she said.

stories.title: Kenneth Law sentencing hearing to resume in November as victim impact statements wrap
stories.summary: The 74 victim statements about lethal substances sold online reveal interventions by police and parents that sometimes succeeded but which also tragically failed
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
The first phase of Kenneth Law’s sentencing hearing for aiding 14 suicides has closed with stories of parents and police attempting to intercept packages sold through his online businesses to vulnerable people around the world.

They were among the accounts entered into evidence on Thursday, as prosecutors finished putting 74 victim impact statements on the record in a Newmarket, Ont., courtroom.

Mr. Law, who has been jailed for more than three years, attended these hearings while sitting a prisoner’s box. He listened to dozens of people denounce him without reacting.

In May, the 61-year-old Mississauga man pleaded guilty to the crimes. He also signed off on an agreed statement saying that between 2021 and 2023 his online business shipped 1,200 packages of suicide kits to people in 41 countries.

Legal arguments will begin on Nov. 27, with a decision to be released later on Mr. Law’s conviction on 14 counts of aiding suicide. A sentencing ruling on Law’s prison term would follow, possibly not until 2027.

Faith George wrote in her victim-impact statement that by the time her daughter, 21-year-old Faith Ike-Elechi, killed herself in August, 2022, she had already intercepted a poison package, sent to her daughter, that Ms. George knew was potentially lethal.

Families detail lasting grief as judge weighs Kenneth Law’s sentence

But Ms. George, a mental-heath nurse who lives in Britain, said a second package shipped by Mr. Law got into her house unseen and that her daughter used it.

“I genuinely believed that we had prevented a tragedy,” Ms. George wrote. “What I did not know was that while she was receiving treatment and support, Kenneth Law supplied her a second package,”

The mother said she only learned of the second shipment when her daughter screamed from her bedroom one midnight. She found her daughter dying and terrified.

“The only words I repeatedly heard were: ‘I’m sorry I drank it,’” Ms. George wrote. “I looked into her eyes and saw fear and what I believed to be profound regret.”

“There was nothing I could do to save her.”

“Kenneth Law did not know my daughter,” Ms. George wrote. “He did not know she was receiving treatment and had every opportunity to recover.”

Court also heard about the 2024 death of Emma Coletti, a 47-year-old who was found dead in a British forest more than two years after buying a suicide kit.

According to an agreed statement of facts in the case, she purchased the poison in 2022, but did not consume the product until November, 2024. By then, Mr. Law had been in jail for a year-and-a-half.

Members of her immediate family submitted a written victim impact statement saying Ms. Coletti had been unsure about whether she wanted to take her own life, but that she felt she was facing “a fatal deadline” because of how Mr. Law had marked his kits with “best before” dates.

The statement from the Coletti parents and a sibling – who asked prosecutors to preserve their privacy – said that Emma was the heart of the family and that for nearly half a century they shared a house where they celebrated every Christmas together.

A timeline of key events in the Kenneth Law case

Court heard about Mark Bailey, a 44-year-old British man who died by suicide only in January of this year. This was more than four years after he bought his poison.

In a video victim-impact statement members of the Bailey family said they could not properly mourn. That was because Mr. Bailey’s body was sheathed in plastic for weeks, because it was still considered toxic from the chemicals he had bought from Mr. Law.

The agreed facts in the criminal case say that authorities had tried to stop Mr. Bailey from taking his life years earlier.

“In May, 2023, Mr. Bailey was visited by police for a welfare check, following disclosure of Mr. Law’s customer list to law enforcement,” the agreed facts in the case stated. British authorities said they were falsely told that Mr. Bailey had disposed of the chemicals he bought back in 2021.

Thursday’s proceedings closed with statements from several survivors, including three formerly suicidal British adults, who wrote to the court to say they purchased and received chemicals they could have used to kill themselves – but did not.

When Canadian police arrested Mr. Law in May, 2023, they seized his shipment list. Then, they shared it globally through Interpol with police abroad. This led to worldwide wellness checks and attempts at parcel seizures – especially in Britain, the jurisdiction to which Mr. Law shipped more than one-quarter of his 1,200 deadly packages.

One woman said in a victim impact statement that she was saved when six British police officers showed up at her door and demanded she hand over her parcel – arriving already knowing her identity and what she had bought. She was ashamed at the time but told the court that she now knows that this was the day that her life was given back to her because it made her get the help she needed.
