stories.title: Justice Minister Fraser orders court to revisit Indigenous sisters’ 1994 murder convictions
stories.summary: Odelia and Neressa Quewezance have maintained their innocence and have spent almost three decades in prison
stories.author: Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
Two Indigenous sisters who have maintained their innocence since they were convicted of murder more than 30 years ago will have their case reviewed after federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser ordered a new appeal.

Mr. Fraser issued a statement that said an in-depth review had concluded that the 1994 convictions of Odelia and Neressa Quewezance were likely a “miscarriage of justice.”

The sisters have spent almost three decades in prison.

While Mr. Fraser cautioned that it is up to the courts, not him, to make findings of guilt or innocence, his department said new information was identified that had not been presented to the courts at the time of the sisters’ trial or appeal.

“Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts for new information to be considered,” Mr. Fraser said in his statement.

From the archives: Indigenous sisters struggle to undo a 1994 murder conviction and break a cycle of parole and punishment

James Lockyer, the lawyer who represents the sisters on behalf of Innocence Canada, an advocacy group against wrongful convictions, said the new information is contained in the disclosure that the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal had to hand over to the Attorney-General but refused to give to the defence in the 1995 appeal case that was dismissed.

“We already had a basis for challenging the convictions but the new information that was provided by the Saskatchewan Attorney-General’s Office enhanced the strength of the application,” Mr. Lockyer told The Globe and Mail.

Odelia Quewezance made a statement through Innocence Canada on Thursday.

“Neressa was 18 when she was arrested and is now 52. I was 21 and am now 55. But we have never stopped fighting. Today’s announcement by the Minister is encouraging and now we will continue the fight in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal. Thank you to all those who have kept the faith in us.”

Neressa and Odelia were arrested and charged in the stabbing death of 70-year-old Joseph Dolff, a janitor at the local residential school that the sisters attended in their home community of Keeseekoose First Nation, Sask.

From the archives: Case of Indigenous sisters serving life sentence underscores need to reform review process for miscarriages of justice, lawyer says

The sisters’ 15-year-old male cousin, whose identity remains protected because he was a youth at the time, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and confessed to the crime.

He later testified at the sisters’ trial that he was the one who ultimately caused Mr. Dolff’s death at his farmhouse northeast of Kamsack, Sask., by tying a phone cord around his neck, throwing a television on him and stabbing him. He said the sisters only participated in the initial assault.

On the night of Feb. 25, 1993, the sisters had been drinking heavily, consuming significant quantities of beer and whisky provided to them by Mr. Dolff, who himself was not drinking. The sisters and their cousin also took prescription sleeping pills, both orally and by injection.

Court would later hear that at some point in the evening, Odelia took money from Mr. Dolff’s bedroom, and the group decided to leave.

Mr. Dolff was driving the sisters and their cousin home when he discovered the money was missing and they returned to his property. There, a violent confrontation ensued, in which Mr. Dolff was beaten, hit with household items and then stabbed to death.

The sisters and their cousin were arrested later that day.

From the archives: Saskatchewan judge orders release of sisters jailed for 30 years for a murder they say they didn’t commit

The sisters pleaded not guilty, but a jury found them guilty and a judge sentenced them to life in prison with no chance of parole for 10 years, the shortest period of parole eligibility possible for a murder sentence.

A ministerial review of the sisters’ conviction was granted in June of 2022, several months after Mr. Lockyer applied in a last bid for his clients’ freedom. The sisters were granted bail in 2023 before returning to custody for breaching release conditions.

The sisters’ time in custody, particularly in the days after their arrest by the RCMP has long been questioned by Mr. Lockyer and advocates.

Mr. Lockyer said the women’s alleged incriminating statements were never recorded and that as residential school survivors, they were more vulnerable to the pressures of police and of being in an in-custody environment that could have likely resulted in false confessions.

Innocence Canada called this week’s order of appeal a step toward vindication for the sisters.

“They were held in the Kamsack RCMP Detachment for five days, despite a judge’s order that they be taken to a detention centre away from the detachment,” Innocence Canada wrote in a press release.

Mr. Lockyer has called the Quewezance case, and the fact the sisters are still in custody, an example of fundamental inequities in the justice and correctional systems, and the discrimination that Indigenous people, particularly women, face not only from police and the courts, but also in prison and on parole.

He said he will be applying sometime in the next month for the sisters’ release on bail pending the appeal hearing.

With a report from Jana G. Pruden

stories.title: Caroline Elliott's theory of culture war: persuasion, not anger
stories.summary: Analysis: Talk of “culture wars” makes people flinch. Elliott, likely candidate for the B.C. Conservatives, thinks that flinch is the point.
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
A week is a long time in politics. This one in British Columbia produced a party rupture and reconsolidation, a leadership resignation, and a snap election.

When I talked with Caroline Elliott last week, the official opposition B.C. Conservative Party was already fracturing. By Friday, more MLAs were peeling away and the upstart CentreBC was stocking itself with the defectors. On Sunday, Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned as leader, four months after her narrow win over Elliott. On Tuesday, Premier David Eby dropped the writ for an Oct. 24 election, casting it as a firebreak against Donald Trump — and seven of CentreBC’s eight legislators, including Peter Milobar, walked back to the Conservative fold. One stayed behind.

So much has changed since I first spoke to Elliott that the interview has aged in dog years.

Among other things, Elliott’s own situation has changed. She is no longer just the well-respected but recently failed runner-up for the leadership; she appears likely to run as a B.C. Conservative candidate on Oct. 24 (more later on that), and who knows what happens after that. The party is being led by an interim leader; the party is saying he gets to keep the job if the Conservatives win the election.

Amid all this, Elliott has been making a sharp case for her worldview in Without Diminishment, the publication she co-founded: any party promising “free enterprise and nothing else” will not fix British Columbia.

In that way, our original conversation is only more relevant.

stories.title: ‘We are ready for anything,’ federal minister says as Quebecers prepare to head to the polls
stories.summary: 'I am prepared for any eventuality. I have my own hopes, but we are ready for anything,' said Minister of Canadian Identity Marc Miller.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture Marc Miller said the federal government is prepared to work with whomever will win the trust of Quebecers in the election in early October — even if he has some personal beef with the frontrunner.

“I am prepared for any eventuality. I have my own hopes, but we are ready for anything,” said the outspoken minister on his way to a cabinet meeting on Thursday afternoon.

The separatist Parti Québécois seems well on its way to forming the next government, possibly with a majority, judging by the most recent polling. Quebec Liberals are poised to be the official Opposition, while the incumbent Coalition Avenir Québec is sliding in the polls.

Miller said the federal government will be working with the incoming government in Quebec, “whether it is a minority government or otherwise.”

“What we’re hearing from Quebecers is that they want different levels of government to work together,” he said.

Miller still threw a bit of shade.

“That is why (Quebecers) loathe referendums, because they are immensely divisive, highly emotional,” he added.

Miller has some recent history with PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Last year, St-Pierre Plamondon accused the cultural sector in Quebec of “intellectual vacuity and spineless subservience” to Ottawa after some groups had welcomed Miller’s nomination as the federal minister for culture and official languages.

The PQ leader lashed out after Miller said, right after his nomination, that he was tired of the politicization of the debate around the decline of French in Quebec.

St-Pierre Plamondon went even further by suggesting that some in the cultural sector lacked loyalty to Quebec, which caused a firestorm in the province. Miller accused him of going too far with his comments , and the PQ leader apologized a few days later.

St-Pierre Plamondon has slightly toned down his attacks in the lead-up to the election.

But he still has an axe to grind with the federal government, which he accused of “interference” near the start of the campaign given the many announcements Prime Minister Mark Carney made with Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette before the writ dropped.

No Quebec-Ottawa joint announcement has taken place during the campaign.

The PQ leader is again making headlines since Wednesday night’s third and last debate , during which he reiterated his promise to hold a referendum in the first term of a PQ government, once U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in 2029.

“Personally, I think we shouldn’t be afraid of democracy,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he wouldn’t back down on that promise, even if over 70 per cent of Quebecers currently say they would vote “No” to separate from Canada.

“I think it’s a secret to no one that we’re federalists,” said Carney’s Quebec lieutenant, Joël Lightbound, when asked if Ottawa should do more to advocate for a united Canada.

In terms of the Quebec campaign, he said “the election is not over, and we’ll be following closely.” He added there is still a large proportion of undecided or uncertain voters.

But Lightbound stuck his neck just a wee bit by saying he thinks “very highly” of Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, which he said is in his view “a strong candidate.”

Miller said he has no “intimate links” with the Quebec Liberal Party nor will he profess his love for the CAQ, a party which whom he has also had strained relationships.

But he said he has worked quite well with Fréchette on the immigration file in the past. He was the federal minister when she was his counterpart in Quebec.

“We didn’t always see eye to eye, but she is someone who is a very hard worker.”

Miller said Quebec voters — including him — must first go to the polls. Advance polling begins this weekend.

The election is on October 5.

“I am prepared for any eventuality. I have my own hopes, but we are ready for anything,” said the outspoken minister on his way to a cabinet meeting on Thursday afternoon.

The separatist Parti Québécois seems well on its way to forming the next government, possibly with a majority, judging by the most recent polling. Quebec Liberals are poised to be the official Opposition, while the incumbent Coalition Avenir Québec is sliding in the polls.
Miller said the federal government will be working with the incoming government in Quebec, “whether it is a minority government or otherwise.”
“What we’re hearing from Quebecers is that they want different levels of government to work together,” he said.
Miller still threw a bit of shade.
“That is why (Quebecers) loathe referendums, because they are immensely divisive, highly emotional,” he added.
Miller has some recent history with PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Last year, St-Pierre Plamondon accused the cultural sector in Quebec of “intellectual vacuity and spineless subservience” to Ottawa after some groups had welcomed Miller’s nomination as the federal minister for culture and official languages.

stories.title: Fifteen ER nurses leave Ontario hospital citing overcrowding, safety issues, union says
stories.summary: Resignations at Oakville Trafalgar Memorial Hospital highlight a health care system under pressure across the country
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
More than a dozen emergency room nurses have resigned from a hospital in the Greater Toronto Area over the past two months, owing to unmanageable patient volumes and an unsafe work environment, according to a provincial union.

Fifteen registered nurses have left their positions at the Oakville Trafalgar Memorial Hospital, and a number of other nurses have limited their hours or not returned from leave, the Ontario Nurses’ Association said. The Oakville emergency department, which sees roughly 80,000 patients yearly, is now scraping to bolster its work force, the union said.

ONA president Erin Ariss said the Oakville hospital has “turned its back” on its staff, who are experiencing burnout because of an unsustainable workload and frequent violence and abuse from patients. She said the hospital made matters worse by eliminating, earlier this month, unit assistants, who help with such tasks as transporting patients, cleaning equipment and stocking supplies.

“They are overcapacity. They are underwater. They are being assaulted. They are being psychologically harmed by the workplace and then they remove all the support staff,” Ms. Ariss said. “It is overwhelming everywhere in Ontario, but particularly there.”

The swath of resignations underscores a crisis playing out in EDs across the country, which are struggling to retain and attract staff because of severe exhaustion due to overcrowding and health-system dysfunction. Health care workers have stressed that bottlenecked EDs are putting patients at risk.

Burnout driving Canadian emergency room doctors to reduce hours or leave the field, new study finds

The Oakville hospital has been under scrutiny since 16-year-old Finlay van der Werken died in February, 2024, of sepsis and pneumonia after waiting more than eight hours for care. The van der Werken family filed a lawsuit last year against Halton Healthcare, which operates Oakville Trafalgar Memorial.

The Oakville ED had a 10 per cent resignation rate from June through early September, which is in line with industry standards, Adrienne Spafford, a spokesperson for Halton Healthcare, said in a statement on Friday.

“Our exit interviews show that the actual reasons for a majority of these departures are new opportunities, moving to a new community and personal reasons,” Ms. Spafford said.

Referring to unit assistants, she said Halton will introduce personal support workers, often referred to as health care aides, in their place. There were 28 unit assistants at the hospital, one of whom was assigned to the ED, she said.

Halton did not directly respond to a number of questions from The Globe and Mail, including the specific number of nurses in the Oakville ED who resigned or have limited their hours, how many RN positions are required to staff it or if any physicians have resigned.

Opinion: An urgent prescription for our ailing Canadian health care system

Ms. Spafford said there was an “unusual increase” in patient visits between April and mid-September. The Oakville ED recorded 11.4-per-cent growth – the sixth highest in Ontario. She added that there has been no spike in reported workplace violence.

Laurie Rogers, who is the ONA bargaining unit president for Halton Healthcare, said nurses are telling her frequently that they are distressed and looking to change jobs. She said, after the string of resignations, the hospital has been offering overtime and premium payments to maintain coverage, in addition to partial shifts.

“The problem is, when you work your work force continuously, it is going to come to an end because an individual will probably get injured or sick,” Ms. Rogers said. “You can’t run at top speed forever.”

Ms. Spafford said nursing staff are being moved between areas of the hospital to balance workloads, which the union does not agree with. The company is also relying on agency nurses when needed while trying to fill vacancies.

ONA is advocating that the hospital not only improve staffing and workloads but implement nurse-to-patient ratios.

Emergency physicians say this summer’s patient levels are unprecedented

“You never see a fire truck heading to a dangerous situation with one firefighter, nor do you see one police officer responding to a dangerous call on their own. They have ratios,” Ms. Ariss said. “We’re asking for the same protections.”

She is also calling on the province to better protect health care workers from violence, pointing to the death of two people in their 70s who were shot outside a Scarborough hospital earlier this week.

“It’s getting worse by the day and the Premier is aware of this,” she said, adding she recently showed him a photo of a duffel bag confiscated by a nurse in the northeastern Ontario city of Timmins, filled with guns, knives and ammunition.

“Who, in their right mind, would want to endure the type of abuse that nurses are enduring in this province and the lack of action by the government?”

Lily Barnes, press secretary to Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones, in a statement on Thursday, pushed back against critiques of the provincial government, pointing to several initiatives aimed at violence prevention and guidance for health care settings.

stories.title: Power restored for Hydro One customers in Huron, Perth Counties
stories.summary: Power has been restored for thousands of Hydro One customers in Huron and Perth Counties.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Power has been restored for thousands of Hydro One customers in Huron and Perth Counties.

Hydro One says at approximately 10 a.m. an outage occurred affecting 16,800 customers in parts of southwest Ontario.

Crews and the grid control centre worked to reroute power and restore customers in stages.

All customers were restored shortly after 3 p.m.

“Our helicopter is supporting crews with line patrols to try and determine the cause of the outage,” said Hydro One.

The power outage affected customers in Exeter, Zurich, Seaforth, Mitchell, and reached as far as St Marys.

stories.title: Synagogue attacker Sean Ward was embroiled in lawsuit against military's COVID-19 vaccine mandate that forced him out
stories.summary: The lawsuit claims Sean Ward refused to be vaccinated “on religious grounds” but his claim for an exemption was refused by the military.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Sean Ward, the gunman who died in a shootout during “a targeted attack against the Jewish community” at an Ontario synagogue, was one of dozens of Canadian soldiers and former soldiers suing the government over directives requiring COVID-19 vaccines.

Ward was involuntarily discharged from the Canadian Armed Forces when he was deemed “unsuitable for further service” after defying the military’s vaccine mandate during the pandemic, according to court documents. He was seeking $1,500,000 in general damages and additional compensation for a financial loss of $140,000.

The lawsuit claims Ward, 29, refused to be vaccinated “on religious grounds” but his claim for an exemption was refused by military officials.

“He has served honourably for almost 5 years. He was told no exemption to receiving the injections would be made. Mr. Ward did not accept the injections,” the lawsuit’s statement of claim says.

The lawsuit describes Sean Douglas Reginald Ward as holding the rank of Corporal in the infantry with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based at Canadian Forces Base Edmonton.

Ward’s military training as an infantry soldier becomes particularly important as police continue to probe Sunday’s shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., as about 25 people gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

On Thursday, Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said Ward came well-armed with a shotgun, other undisclosed weapons, a significant amount of ammunition, containers of gasoline and additional resources.

A Belleville police officer posted outside the synagogue, Const. Jeff Smith, was shot several times by Ward and remains in serious condition. Ward was killed in a subsequent firefight with Smith and a second officer, Const. Mike McCurdy, police said.

Rodd said a video of the attack, shown by police, reveals Ward calling out, presumably to Smith or McCurdy, saying: “You are going to die for the Jews.”

Rodd declared it a hate-motivated attack.

“This was a targeted attack against the Jewish community. The suspect had the means, the motive and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue,” Rodd said.

The original statement of claim in the vaccine lawsuit involving Ward was filed Sept. 27, 2023, with the Federal Court in Edmonton. It was sealed by the court and an amended claim was filed Feb. 25, 2026.

Originally named as defendants were several high-ranking military brass, other military officials and government ministers past and present.

The amended claim pared the defendants down to Wayne Eyre, the now-retired Chief of Defence Staff, the Minister of National Defence and the Attorney General of Canada.

In a statement of defence filed by Department of Justice lawyers, the government and military “deny each and every allegation” in the lawsuit.

The government defended the vaccine mandates as having a primary objective “to protect the readiness, health, and safety of the Force, the entire Defence Team, as well as members of the public they May be called upon to serve.” It says “a member’s failure to comply with the Directives demonstrates an unwillingness to obey and support lawful authority.”

Ward was plaintiff number 110 in a list of 128 members and former members of the Forces claiming they were adversely hit by the military’s COVID-19 vaccination mandate.

“This mandate, implemented through a series of Directives, coerced vaccination under threat of career-ending sanctions, bypassing statutory processes and infringing fundamental rights,” the lawsuit claims.

The plaintiffs seek damages of $1 million each for negligence, Charter breaches and misuse of authority, and another $500,000 each for bad faith conduct. They also seek individualized damages for future income loss, pension loss, medical expenses and other expenses.

Apart from money, they also seek declarations from the court that the Canadian military’s COVID-19 vaccine mandate violated the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms; and that Eyre issued an unlawful order; among others.

“The Directives prioritized demonstrating leadership to encourage public vaccination uptake, a role not legislated for the CAF and secondary to operational imperatives, constituting a misuse of military authority for non-military purposes,” the lawsuit claims.

The plaintiffs complained that the military granted exemptions for medical reasons but not for ethical or philosophical reasons.

“It was grossly disproportionate, with severe sanctions like career loss and stigma outweighing benefits, rendering the ‘choice’ illusory and shocking the conscience,” the suit complains.

The lawsuit also claims the military’s grievance system was rigged against those objecting to the mandate.

The lawyer representing the plaintiffs was not available to comment on the lawsuit or on the impact Ward’s attack might have on it.

The plaintiffs seek damages of $1 million each for negligence, Charter breaches and misuse of authority, and another $500,000 each for bad faith conduct. They also seek individualized damages for future income loss, pension loss, medical expenses and other expenses.

Apart from money, they also seek declarations from the court that the Canadian military’s COVID-19 vaccine mandate violated the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms; and that Eyre issued an unlawful order; among others.

“The Directives prioritized demonstrating leadership to encourage public vaccination uptake, a role not legislated for the CAF and secondary to operational imperatives, constituting a misuse of military authority for non-military purposes,” the lawsuit claims.
The plaintiffs complained that the military granted exemptions for medical reasons but not for ethical or philosophical reasons.
“It was grossly disproportionate, with severe sanctions like career loss and stigma outweighing benefits, rendering the ‘choice’ illusory and shocking the conscience,” the suit complains.
The lawsuit also claims the military’s grievance system was rigged against those objecting to the mandate.
The lawyer representing the plaintiffs was not available to comment on the lawsuit or on the impact Ward’s attack might have on it.

content_blocks.text: Sean Ward, the gunman who died in a shootout during “a targeted attack against the Jewish community” at an Ontario synagogue, was one of dozens of Canadian soldiers and former soldiers suing the government over directives requiring COVID-19 vaccines.

Ward was involuntarily discharged from the Canadian Armed Forces when he was deemed “unsuitable for further service” after defying the military’s vaccine mandate during the pandemic, according to court documents. He was seeking $1,500,000 in general damages and additional compensation for a financial loss of $140,000.
The lawsuit claims Ward, 29, refused to be vaccinated “on religious grounds” but his claim for an exemption was refused by military officials.
“He has served honourably for almost 5 years. He was told no exemption to receiving the injections would be made. Mr. Ward did not accept the injections,” the lawsuit’s statement of claim says.

The lawsuit describes Sean Douglas Reginald Ward as holding the rank of Corporal in the infantry with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based at Canadian Forces Base Edmonton.

Ward’s military training as an infantry soldier becomes particularly important as police continue to probe Sunday’s shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., as about 25 people gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

On Thursday, Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said Ward came well-armed with a shotgun, other undisclosed weapons, a significant amount of ammunition, containers of gasoline and additional resources.

A Belleville police officer posted outside the synagogue, Const. Jeff Smith, was shot several times by Ward and remains in serious condition. Ward was killed in a subsequent firefight with Smith and a second officer, Const. Mike McCurdy, police said.
Rodd said a video of the attack, shown by police, reveals Ward calling out, presumably to Smith or McCurdy, saying: “You are going to die for the Jews.”
Rodd declared it a hate-motivated attack.
“This was a targeted attack against the Jewish community. The suspect had the means, the motive and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue,” Rodd said.

The original statement of claim in the vaccine lawsuit involving Ward was filed Sept. 27, 2023, with the Federal Court in Edmonton. It was sealed by the court and an amended claim was filed Feb. 25, 2026.
Originally named as defendants were several high-ranking military brass, other military officials and government ministers past and present.
The amended claim pared the defendants down to Wayne Eyre, the now-retired Chief of Defence Staff, the Minister of National Defence and the Attorney General of Canada.
In a statement of defence filed by Department of Justice lawyers, the government and military “deny each and every allegation” in the lawsuit.

The government defended the vaccine mandates as having a primary objective “to protect the readiness, health, and safety of the Force, the entire Defence Team, as well as members of the public they May be called upon to serve.” It says “a member’s failure to comply with the Directives demonstrates an unwillingness to obey and support lawful authority.”

The plaintiffs seek damages of $1 million each for negligence, Charter breaches and misuse of authority, and another $500,000 each for bad faith conduct. They also seek individualized damages for future income loss, pension loss, medical expenses and other expenses.

stories.title: Lawyer Rory Nott skillfully navigated work and life as a man with quadriplegia
stories.summary: After an accident left him paralyzed from the shoulders down, Rory decided to live and live well
stories.author: Margaret Nott, Ron Beram
stories.content:
Harley (Rory) Nott: Father. Wheelchair user. Wordsmith. Stoic. Born June 21, 1962, in Montreal; died Oct. 25, 2025, in Toronto, of medical assistance in dying; aged 63.

Harley, or Rory as he was also known, lived two lives. His first life ended May 18, 1980, just before his 18 th birthday when he dove into the Macjack River on Vancouver Island and broke his neck. His second life, lived from a wheelchair, as a man with quadriplegia, ended six months after his 63 rd birthday.

A photograph of Rory taken on the day of his accident shows him striking an athletic pose, smiling at the camera, a vital, handsome teenager. Rory grew up a bit wild on Vancouver Island and his teenage years were filled with poor judgment and lessons learned. At 16, he was expelled from high school and worked in forestry and logging. After his accident, while paralyzed from the shoulders down and in rehab, he decided to live and live well.

He completed his education and pursued a career in law. He met Margaret Kralt in 1985, a fellow student at University of Victoria Law. Rory caught Margaret’s eye in class early on and when she smiled at him, it was the sweetest smile. They were first friends and later partners.

They married in 1988 and moved to Toronto for work. Rory litigated for the Department of Justice, a job he loved. His professionalism and competence were lauded by colleagues and judges.

Lawyers with quadriplegia are uncommon and he had help meeting the challenges he faced in his practice from Tonka, a black standard poodle and trained service dog. Tonka opened doors, picked up wallets and pulled Rory and his wheelchair navigating streets, hallways and courtrooms. On occasion, Tonka reminded agitated litigants who got too close, to stay back.

During his working years, Rory met weekly for lunch with friends, always at the same Greek place, telling stories, with maybe a bit of B.S. just for good measure. Tonka might have received food scraps during these lunches.

For years, Rory was deeply involved with the Canadian Paraplegic Association (now Spinal Cord Injury Canada) and later the Toronto Rehab Institute as a board member. In 2014, he acted in the play Borne, written by Judith Thompson, which explored the lives of people living with disabilities.

Rory and Margaret had two children, Evan and Margaret. When they were small, he was their happy charioteer, with his always available lap. He could, if he wasn’t stopped, go on and on about how great they were and their accomplishments. After his retirement in 2001, Rory became a stay-at-home parent, a role he grew into and relished as it meant time with his kids, being their chauffeur, hanging out and hearing their stories. What others were doing interested Rory and he was the repository for the stories of his kids and others.

Rory wrote beautiful congregational prayers for the First Christian Reformed Church of Toronto and songs with his friend John that they posted on YouTube. He and John had shared a room during rehab, and the songs reflected on their lives as men living with quadriplegia. They talked weekly about everything, from astrophysics and secular Buddhism to books, movies and family. Their bodies were limited but their minds ranged far and wide.

Rory loved his words. Why use one when you could use five? Why use one example when six really made the point? His family would listen, sometimes impatiently, with the odd eye roll. “Yeah, yeah, we get it,” was occasionally heard when Rory talked about something at length.

For most of his second life, Rory endured the many indignities, limitations, chronic pain and physical challenges that came with quadriplegia. Despite this, he lived with grace and determination. He did not complain. He was a man of calm reflection, kindness and self-effacing humour. His faith in God kept him company and was a support that he depended on throughout his life.

In 2025, Rory experienced significant increase in physical deterioration and pain, and he decided it was time to leave his second life. He didn’t want to go, but he couldn’t go on. He had lived well and it was enough.

Rory met death on his terms, as he had lived his life on his terms.

Margaret Nott is Rory Nott’s wife; Ron Beram is Rory Nott’s friend.

stories.title: ‘Aggressive protestors’ force Saskatoon to halt encampment clean-up, city says
stories.summary: The City of Saskatoon said it is pausing its encampment cleanup efforts at the sites at 19th Street and Avenue K, due to protests that it said are acting aggressively.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The planned cleanup of two encampments in Saskatoon has been paused due to aggressive protests, the city said.

Crews were set to clean two vacant lots at Avenue K between 19th Street and 20th Street Thursday morning when protesters tried to stop them from working, the City of Saskatoon said. It alleged that the demonstrators circled crews’ vehicles and climbed on top of the fencing, which was stacked on one of them.

“Saskatoon Fire Department, police officers and other partner agency staff were confronted by aggressive protestors, directing profane, derogatory and vulgar comments at them,” the city claimed in a news release.

Workers present at the site Thursday reported the majority of those involved did not appear to be encampment occupants, according to the City of Saskatoon.

The city acknowledged that its decision May frustrate people in the area, including the students, families of students and staff at the St. Mary’s Wellness and Education Centre, who have been requesting Saskatoon to step in for a year.

David Fineday lives in Saskatoon and is a member of the Sweetgrass First Nation. He spoke at a news conference at the encampment site Thursday, before the city announced it is pausing work.

“They want to displace all of these people; they want (them) to get out of here. And my question is, ‘where are they going to put them?'” Fineday told reporters, adding that “they want to take them down, so they have to re-place them somewhere.”

He said the city should have to provide people who would be displaced with alternative places to live after the site is cleaned up.

“There’s lots of people here that want help, that need help, that are on survival mode,” Fineday added.

“This tent city is just like any other neighbourhood in this city. The only thing is we don’t have affordable housing.”

The City of Saskatoon is planning its next steps for the encampments, it said.
paragraphs: The planned cleanup of two encampments in Saskatoon has been paused due to aggressive protests, the city said.

Crews were set to clean two vacant lots at Avenue K between 19th Street and 20th Street Thursday morning when protesters tried to stop them from working, the City of Saskatoon said. It alleged that the demonstrators circled crews’ vehicles and climbed on top of the fencing, which was stacked on one of them.

“Saskatoon Fire Department, police officers and other partner agency staff were confronted by aggressive protestors, directing profane, derogatory and vulgar comments at them,” the city claimed in a news release.
Workers present at the site Thursday reported the majority of those involved did not appear to be encampment occupants, according to the City of Saskatoon.

The city acknowledged that its decision May frustrate people in the area, including the students, families of students and staff at the St. Mary’s Wellness and Education Centre, who have been requesting Saskatoon to step in for a year.
David Fineday lives in Saskatoon and is a member of the Sweetgrass First Nation. He spoke at a news conference at the encampment site Thursday, before the city announced it is pausing work.

“They want to displace all of these people; they want (them) to get out of here. And my question is, ‘where are they going to put them?'” Fineday told reporters, adding that “they want to take them down, so they have to re-place them somewhere.”
He said the city should have to provide people who would be displaced with alternative places to live after the site is cleaned up.
“There’s lots of people here that want help, that need help, that are on survival mode,” Fineday added.
“This tent city is just like any other neighbourhood in this city. The only thing is we don’t have affordable housing.”
The City of Saskatoon is planning its next steps for the encampments, it said.

stories.title: Tackling antisemitism and hate should be a priority, Jewish leaders and MPs say
stories.summary: Small synagogues can’t afford to pay for government program to boost security: CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs
stories.author: Marie Woolf
stories.content:
Days after a shooting attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., the government faced calls, including from Jewish leaders, to boost federal funding for community security, noting that some small synagogues can’t afford it.

A federal rule requiring synagogues contribute almost a third of the cost of security improvements, such as reinforcing doors and windows, means that some small communities can’t access the government funding, said Noah Shack, CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, an advocacy group.

The Belleville synagogue targeted by a shooter on Yom Kippur, ON Sept. 20, had only rudimentary security, Mr. Shack said, adding that if a heroic police officer had not intervened to stop the shooter, the outcome would likely have been horrific.

The Cija CEO called on the government to be flexible with the funding rules saying that improving security at Jewish community buildings is an urgent matter.

In the spring, the federal government earmarked $75-million over five years, starting in 2026–27, for the Canada Community Security Program, which provides funding and support for communities at risk of hate-motivated incidents and hate-motivated crimes to boost security. But institutions that tap into the funding need to cover 30 per cent of the costs.

Belleville synagogue shooting was a ‘hate-motivated’ crime, police say

At a Thursday press conference in Ottawa, Mr. Shack and Liberal and Conservative MPs said that tackling antisemitism and hate should be a priority, including on university campuses.

Jewish students recounted how they have had to cope with open expressions of antisemitism including Hitler salutes.

Kate Blumberg, a student at McMaster University, said Jewish students were being singled out in tutorials, excluded from groups and finding that campus spaces no longer felt welcoming to them.

“Unfortunately, we live in a time when being recognizably Jewish on campus, whether by our names, the necklace you wear or the kippa that adorns your head, comes with repercussions,” she said at the press conference. “We are students that, when noticed, are cast on campus as the sole responders to a geopolitical crisis much older and larger than ourselves, forced to hold the answers or else be held accountable for it all.”

Liberal MP Anthony Housefather said in an interview the Belleville shooting illustrated the gravity of the security situation for Canadian Jews, which he and others have been warning about for some time.

Editorial: The courage needed to face down hatred

He said the federal government should step up to foot the bill to ensure that security upgrades needed to protect people at synagogues and other community buildings is completely covered. He said, despite welcome injections of cash by the federal government into improving security “there should be more federal and provincial funding.”

“While it’s totally unacceptable that Jewish institutions throughout the country require security that nobody else so requires, this shouldn’t come out of the pocket of the Jewish community. Governments should be paying for this, and both the federal and provincial government need to step up and make sure that, in combination, that we cover these costs,” he said.

In June, the new federal Combatting Hate Act made it a crime, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, to obstruct someone from accessing a place of worship or other sites where Jews, Muslims and other identifiable groups gather, including by blocking doors and driveways.

Mr. Housefather said the police and prosecutors and judges need to be “properly trained” on the new legal sanctions. Provincial attorney generals, he said, need to issue directions to ensure that the new law is properly enforced.

On Thursday, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree and Justice Minister Sean Fraser presented a progress report on commitments made to combat antisemitism.

Opinion: The Belleville attack was a warning shot for the antisemitic attacks Canada has let fester

“The Government of Canada recognizes that antisemitism can also be a matter of national security,” it said. “Beyond the direct harm it causes to Jewish individuals and communities, antisemitism is a core component of many violent extremist ideologies. It can contribute to radicalization and violence, and threatens social cohesion and democratic values.”

Synagogues are among the institutions that can apply to the government to cover 70 per cent of security upgrade costs, such as alarm systems and cameras and reinforced doors, with Public Safety Canada, the department which runs the community security program, funding up to $5-million per project.

But Mr. Shack said one Ontario synagogue recently had to decide between paying to upgrade their hot water system or paying the required 30 per cent to improve security.

He said Canada was lagging behind countries such as France and Britain in providing enhanced security for Jewish communities. The country also needs more counter-radicalization work, he said, adding social media is a source of antisemitic conspiracy theories, and that foreign regimes are responsible for disseminating some of it.

Mr. Anandasangaree, the Public Safety Minister, earlier this year announced $10-million in funding aimed at bolstering security in Canada’s Jewish communities, days after shootings directed at synagogues in the Toronto area.

stories.title: More than $3.6 million of contraband tobacco seized at Blue Water Bridge
stories.summary: The Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) has seized more than $3.6 million worth of contraband tobacco and nicotine products in Point Edward, Ont.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) has seized more than $3.6 million worth of contraband tobacco and nicotine products in Point Edward, Ont.

On Sept. 9, 16.147 kilograms of bulk tobacco was seized from a commercial driver coming from the U.S. at the Blue Water Bridge. This seizure was worth $2.9 million.

The next day, border officials seized 4,992 kilograms of tobacco products and 500 nicotine vapes from another commercial driver coming from the U.S. The second seicure was worth more than $620,000.

The two drivers are Canadian residents, the Cbsa confirmed.

The investigations are ongoing.

stories.title: ‘Better on a tractor than my feet’: Farmers turn their antique tractors into “square dancing” tractors at IPM
stories.summary: To the delight of crowds at this year’s International Plowing Match, Bruce County’s Square Dancing Tractors have come out of retirement, to swing, swivel, and square dance their way around a square dirt track near Walkerton.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Who knew tractors could dance?

To the delight of crowds at this year’s International Plowing Match, Bruce County’s Square Dancing Tractors have come out of retirement, to swing, swivel, and square dance their way around a square dirt track near Walkerton.

The squad of square dancers have had their tractors in storage since 2019.

The 12 drivers, and one square dance caller have been practicing since March perfecting their tight turns, and spinning wheels into a spectacle for all to see.

“Oh, it is a lot of fun. Hundred percent, both on the square and off the square it’s a lot of fun with the group. So that’s why we do it,” said one of the drivers/dancers, Jamie Gowland.

“Never say never, but if you want to see us, get here,” said Scott.

stories.title: Defence minister downplays PM’s comments on prospect of U.S. military action
stories.summary: Ottawa — A day after Prime Minister Mark Carney told a U.S. media outlet his government has studied the possibility of U.S.-led military action in Canada, Defence Minister David McGuinty says all militaries analyze such risks.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump hold a press conference at the White House in Washington, D.C., Tuesday, Oct. 7, 2025. THE Canadian Press/Adrian Wyld

By The Canadian Press

Posted September 24, 2026 5:24 pm.

Last Updated September 24, 2026 5:42 pm.

Ottawa — A day after Prime Minister Mark Carney told a U.S. media outlet his government has studied the possibility of U.S.-led military action in Canada, Defence Minister David McGuinty says all militaries analyze such risks.

McGuinty is downplaying the significance of comments Carney made to the New York Times on Wednesday indicating Ottawa has examined the possibility of American military action.

Carney told the New York Times he would not to discuss in detail what that examination involved, but suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called “extreme tail risk.”

McGuinty says it’s normal for a country to do that but the government would not be going into any detail about what such an analysis entails.

He says Canada and the United States have one of the most important military relationships in the world, having co-operated for decades to keep North America safe.

Conservative MP Ellis Ross says Carney’s comments were irresponsible, “uncalled for” and served to stoke division and fear, and wants to know what the United States has to say about this.

stories.title: B.C. a travel hotspot this season, Airbnb data reveals
stories.summary: According to data, travellers are especially drawn to the beautiful scenery across the province, with domestic destination searches up 40 per cent over the last year.
stories.author: Meghan Unadkat
stories.content:
New Airbnb data shows British Columbians are staying closer to home this fall.

B.C. rural destinations are gaining in popularity, including Haida Gwaii, Powell River on the Sunshine Coast and Colwood on Vancouver Island.

According to data compiled by Airbnb, travellers are especially drawn to the beautiful scenery across the province, with domestic destination searches up 40 per cent over the last year.

Airbnb says families are particularly eyeing villages and lake towns such as Parksville – a Vancouver Island beach town, as well as Invermere – a town on Lake Windermere that offers warm-water swimming and hot springs in Kootenay National Park.

All across Canada, stays in rural communities and small towns this year are gaining momentum, according to Airbnb; this means contribution and support for small, local businesses too.

The platform says that searches for domestic stays in Canada this season are up 25 per cent from 2025. Rural destinations also up 30 per cent.

stories.title: Two men switched at birth in Manitoba each compensated $250,000 by province
stories.summary: Edward Ambrose and Richard Beauvais were awarded payments in 2025, more than a year after Premier Wab Kinew apologized for the mistake
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
Two men who were switched at birth in a rural Manitoba hospital 71 years ago have each been compensated $250,000 by the provincial government for the “miscarriage of justice,” that altered their identities and deprived them of knowing their biological parents.

Edward Ambrose and Richard Beauvais were awarded the payments by the Manitoba government in June, 2025, more than a year after Premier Wab Kinew apologized for the mistake and promised to work toward compensation, said their lawyer Bill Gange, who negotiated the settlement. The men wished to keep the compensation confidential, according to their lawyer, but the amounts were made public when financial disclosure documents were released by the province this week.

“What happened was a miscarriage of justice,” Manitoba Minister of Justice and Attorney General Matt Wiebe wrote in a statement. “No one can give them back the years that were lost but we hope the settlement brings some closure.”

The Globe and Mail published an exclusive story in 2023 about the switch that led the men to be estranged from their biological families and heritage for 68 years. In 1955, the men were sent home as newborn babies from a small hospital in Arborg, Man. – about 100 kilometres north of Winnipeg – with the wrong parents, all of whom are now deceased.

A hospital’s mistake left two men estranged from their heritages. Now they fight for answers

Mr. Ambrose was raised by Ukrainian parents in the rural farming town of Rembrandt, just south of Arborg. Mr. Beauvais was raised by his mother and grandparents, alongside six siblings in the Métis community of St. Laurent, southwest of Arborg, attending residential day school for Indigenous children and forcibly separated from his family during the Sixties Scoop. The mixup was discovered in 2022 by a relative who started asking questions after obtaining genealogy results through an at-home DNA test kit.

Initially the Manitoba Progressive Conservative government said the mistake was not their fault and disputed the hospital was even under their purview, but when the NDP came to power, Mr. Kinew took a different tack. In a heartfelt apology at the legislature in 2024, he apologized to Mr. Ambrose and Mr. Beauvais and their families and ordered his government to work toward a settlement to acknowledge the government’s failure to care and protect them.

Mr. Gange, who has also been an outspoken advocate for two other switched at birth instances in the province in the community of Norway House, said Mr. Ambrose and Mr. Beauvais were grateful for the apology and the resolution of financial compensation. Neither responded to requests for comment.

“What do you pay somebody for something like this? And that was something that I wrestled with long and hard with the provincial government because it took a very, very long time after the apology. ... It was a lot of back and forth before I was finally able to get them to agree to the $250,000,” Mr. Gange said in an interview.

Premier Wab Kinew apologizes to two Manitoba men switched at birth in 1955

“The money is simply, in my view, an acknowledgment by the government of Manitoba that the government failed them. And so, whether it’s enough money or not enough money, doesn’t matter. It’s an acknowledgment of saying ‘You were affected by a mistake by our society and here’s something to acknowledge that.’”

The Manitoba government’s handling of the province’s failure is in contrast to Newfoundland and Labrador, where victims of two separate switched at birth cases that occurred in rural hospitals in the 1960s have been seeking apologies and acknowledgment of the mistakes from the government for years.

Craig Avery and Clarence Hynes were sent home with the wrong families at the Come by Chance Cottage hospital in 1962. Caroline Weir Greene and Arlene Lush, born at the Springdale Cottage hospital in 1969, also met the same fate. Their cases were also confirmed by DNA testing.

In 2022, then Progressive Conservative health critic Paul Dinn called on the then Liberal health and community services minister Tom Osborne to apologize and review what went wrong in both switched at birth cases in Newfoundland, saying it had been extremely tough on the families.

Manitoba men switched at birth to get official government apology

The Progressive Conservatives are now in power in Newfoundland and have not provided any apology or compensation.

Premier Tony Wakeham’s office did not respond to a request for comment. Instead, the province’s Department of Justice and Public Safety provided an unattributed statement saying the government of Newfoundland and Labrador is unable to provide any comment because it’s involved in litigation regarding the matter.

While Mr. Avery and Mr. Hynes have outstanding litigation with the provincial government dating back to 2019, the other victims do not.

“Neither one of us have a lawyer,” said Ms. Lush. Ms. Weir Greene also confirmed she doesn’t have a lawyer and is not involved in any litigation either.

“There’s no reason that they can’t say ‘Arlene, We’re sorry,’” Ms. Lush said. “We just want something to be acknowledged.”

stories.title: Volkswagen subsidiary delays opening of $7B St. Thomas, Ont., battery plant to 2029
stories.summary: PowerCo, the Volkswagen subsidiary building a $7-billion electric vehicle battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: PowerCo, the Volkswagen subsidiary building a $7-billion electric vehicle battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned.
· Posted: Sep 24, 2026 12:30 PM EDT | Last Updated: September 24

The Volkswagen subsidiary building an electric vehicle (EV) battery "gigafactory" in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned.
PowerCo Canada made the announcement in a news release about hiring Mississauga, Ont.-based EllisDon Corporation as the general contractor for construction of the factory.

"St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve," said a news release.
PowerCo declined to make a spokesperson available for an interview with CBC News about the delay.
Volkswagen to open its first North American EV battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont.

Originally scheduled for a 2027 opening, the $7-billion factory — with a promise of up to $13 billion in subsidies from the federal government — was first announced in 2023. It was estimated it would result in the creation of 3,000 direct jobs and tens of thousands of indirect jobs in the region.
Video Highway 3 expansion gets underway as St. Thomas prepares for battery plant boom
Construction has started on massive Volkswagen battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont.

To prepare for the arrival of the plant, surrounding municipalities and the provincial government have undertaken infrastructure projects to increase sewer and road capacity for the population boom that was expected in 2027.
Before the plant was announced, the province allowed St. Thomas to annex land from the neighbouring municipality of Central Elgin to make room for the development.
In August 2025, PowerCo Canada announced it had awarded two major construction contracts for the project. Construction began in October 2025, with work starting on the foundations for the facility.
St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston, who has championed the factory as a major driver of economic growth for his city, told CBC News he's unfazed by the two-year delay.
"They've picked a great local Canadian general contractor and in doing so, they had to adjust the [opening] date," said Preston.
PowerCo begins hiring blitz for positions at St. Thomas EV battery gigafactory
PowerCo has been hiring workers in the St. Thomas area since August 2025. Preston estimates roughly 500 people are currently employed by the company in the surrounding area.

He also cited "the number of employees they already have working and living in the city of St. Thomas, the amount of construction that's going on in that site each and every day" as reasons for maintaining confidence in the project.
Preston also pointed to Yarmouth Yards, a large industrial park developed by St. Thomas, which is being populated by industries that are complementary to battery production.
Provincial officials also welcomed EllisDon's selection as general contractor.

In a written statement to CBC News, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade said the contract "represents a major milestone as they work towards the start of production that will create thousands of direct and indirect jobs across the supply chain."
The ministry's statement didn't address the two-year delay.

"We look forward to continuing to work with PowerCo as they progress on their $7-billion gigafactory in St. Thomas that will position Ontario at the forefront of innovative battery and automotive production for decades to come," it said.
Andrew Lawton, the Conservative MP representing Elgin—St. Thomas—London South, called news of the delay disappointing and questioned Volkswagen's commitment to the plant.

“I realize that Volkswagen is saying it's just about pace and not about the overall commitment. But ultimately, it is about the commitment because we were expecting this to be moving forward at a speed that we're just not seeing,” Lawton said.
Lawton also said he wants to know what the federal government is doing to move things along and ensure Volkswagen remains committed.

"We saw $13 billion worth of federal subsidies put forward to this and the promise — the expectation — was 3,000 well-paid local jobs, not to mention the construction jobs. All of this has been thrown into jeopardy right now."
The market conditions cited by PowerCo come as automakers across Ontario have adjusted plans for electric vehicle production amid changes in EV demand.

In April 2025, General Motors cited lower-than-expected demand when it announced plans to halt production of the Chevrolet BrightDrop electric delivery van at its Cami Assembly plant in Ingersoll. Hundreds of workers were laid off.
Video Hundreds of workers laid off at Ingersoll, Ont., assembly plant as GM halts production
Honda more definitively halting $15B EV plant development in Ontario, according to reports
Honda also delayed plans for a $15-billion EV plant in Alliston in 2025 before ultimately cancelling the project. The company said it would continue to assess the EV market.
At the same time, Canadian EV sales have shown signs of growth.
Statistics Canada data released in June showed the number of new EVs purchased by Canadians had increased by more than 20 per cent compared with the same period a year earlier.
Canadians bought 8,672 new EVs in January, 12,547 in February and 21,574 in March before sales fell to 17,795 in April.

stories.title: The fix B.C. is in: An election without a reason, an opposition without a leader
stories.summary: Scofflaws – people who feel entitled to disregard the laws – exist in any country, but only in Canada do they include the governments that passed them
stories.author: Andrew Coyne
stories.content:
The province of British Columbia is having an election, barely two years after the last. There is, it is commonly acknowledged, no pressing matter in the public interest that obliged Premier David Eby to call it.

He has called the election now, two years before its scheduled date under the province’s fixed-election-date law, for one reason only: to take advantage of the disarray within the ranks of the opposition Conservative Party, culminating in the resignation of its leader, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, ON Sept. 20 – two days before the election call.

There is no precedent for this in Canadian history: No prime minister or premier in possession of a majority has ever called an election while its chief rival was without a permanent leader. The closest parallel is Alberta in 2015: Conservative premier Jim Prentice called an election 10 days after the Wildrose Party elected Brian Jean as its leader.

It is difficult, indeed, to find a precedent in any parliamentary democracy: Britain (Stanley Baldwin) in 1935, maybe Australia (Malcolm Fraser) in 1983, one or two others.

Much criticism has properly been directed at Mr. Eby for his crass opportunism, forcing British Columbians into a choice between his own tottering government and a leaderless opposition. It is certainly dirty pool. But rather than dwell on Mr. Eby’s motives, we would do well to consider how he came to possess the means, and the opportunity, to act as he did.

Editorial: Eby’s snap election snubs democracy

It is an extraordinary thing, that the head of any government should still, in 2026, be able to call an election at a time exactly suited to his own political interests. We do not allow one side in the Stanley Cup final to decide when the games will be played, and how long they will last. In most contests, we insist on an impartial set of rules set in advance by an independent authority.

Indeed, that was the point of the fixed-election-date law the province passed in 2001: the first in the country, soon to be emulated by all provinces and the federal government (Ontario and Nova Scotia have since rescinded theirs). But in B.C., as elsewhere, the law left a giant loophole, stipulating that nothing in it limited the discretion of the lieutenant-governor, in whose name elections are formally called.

At the time, this was presented as pro forma boilerplate, to avoid constitutional challenges. But given the record since then – one government after another, federal and provincial, calling a snap election; I count 17 in all – Canadians must wonder what the point was.

Scofflaws – people who feel entitled to disregard the laws – exist in any country, but only in Canada do they include the governments that passed them.

Mr. Eby should not have done what he did, but more important, he should not have had the power to do so. Even so, he might not have had the opportunity, had it not been for the implosion of the Conservative Party under Ms. Findlay. That Ms. Findlay’s short tenure was a disaster is universally acknowledged. But again, it is better to ask how she came to be leader in the first place.

The job of a party leader is, first and foremost, to lead the caucus of elected members in the legislature. (That is, if you think elected members or legislatures are central to our system of democracy.) Yet caucus members have next to no power in deciding who should lead them, even as party leaders have come to possess the power of life or death over their careers. Strange but true: The maxim “government with the consent of the governed” applies virtually everywhere in Canada, except to the people we elect.

The big B.C. reshuffle continues ahead of snap election

Classically, party leaders in Westminster democracies were chosen by caucus. They still are, elsewhere. But in Canada we long ago allowed the presidential model to take hold, in which the leader is elected by the party membership at large. Ms. Findlay had the support of only a handful of her party’s legislators in the leadership contest earlier this year. She was imposed on them by another body altogether.

Who was that body? The members? Not really. As of December, 2025, the B.C. Conservative Party had only 7,000 members. By the mid-campaign cutoff for membership sales, the party had grown to six times that number. It was those new members, with no history of involvement in the party before the vote and, most of them, no involvement after, that decided it.

It is good to see the Conservative caucus reasserting itself. They May even pull off an upset, free of Ms. Findlay and fuelled by popular revulsion at Mr. Eby’s cynicism. But if they are wise they will consider how to ensure neither they nor the province are ever put in this position again.

It is certainly dirty pool. But rather than dwell on Mr. Eby’s motives, we would do well to consider how he came to possess the means, and the opportunity, to act as he did.
Editorial: Eby’s snap election snubs democracy

It is an extraordinary thing, that the head of any government should still, in 2026, be able to call an election at a time exactly suited to his own political interests. We do not allow one side in the Stanley Cup final to decide when the games will be played, and how long they will last. In most contests, we insist on an impartial set of rules set in advance by an independent authority.

Indeed, that was the point of the fixed-election-date law the province passed in 2001: the first in the country, soon to be emulated by all provinces and the federal government (Ontario and Nova Scotia have since rescinded theirs). But in B.C., as elsewhere, the law left a giant loophole, stipulating that nothing in it limited the discretion of the lieutenant-governor, in whose name elections are formally called.

At the time, this was presented as pro forma boilerplate, to avoid constitutional challenges. But given the record since then – one government after another, federal and provincial, calling a snap election; I count 17 in all – Canadians must wonder what the point was.
Scofflaws – people who feel entitled to disregard the laws – exist in any country, but only in Canada do they include the governments that passed them.

Mr. Eby should not have done what he did, but more important, he should not have had the power to do so. Even so, he might not have had the opportunity, had it not been for the implosion of the Conservative Party under Ms. Findlay. That Ms. Findlay’s short tenure was a disaster is universally acknowledged. But again, it is better to ask how she came to be leader in the first place.

The job of a party leader is, first and foremost, to lead the caucus of elected members in the legislature. (That is, if you think elected members or legislatures are central to our system of democracy.) Yet caucus members have next to no power in deciding who should lead them, even as party leaders have come to possess the power of life or death over their careers. Strange but true: The maxim “government with the consent of the governed” applies virtually everywhere in Canada, except to the people we elect.
The big B.C. reshuffle continues ahead of snap election

Classically, party leaders in Westminster democracies were chosen by caucus. They still are, elsewhere. But in Canada we long ago allowed the presidential model to take hold, in which the leader is elected by the party membership at large. Ms. Findlay had the support of only a handful of her party’s legislators in the leadership contest earlier this year. She was imposed on them by another body altogether.

Who was that body? The members? Not really. As of December, 2025, the B.C. Conservative Party had only 7,000 members. By the mid-campaign cutoff for membership sales, the party had grown to six times that number. It was those new members, with no history of involvement in the party before the vote and, most of them, no involvement after, that decided it.

It is good to see the Conservative caucus reasserting itself. They May even pull off an upset, free of Ms. Findlay and fuelled by popular revulsion at Mr. Eby’s cynicism. But if they are wise they will consider how to ensure neither they nor the province are ever put in this position again.

stories.title: Volkswagen delays production at Ontario electric vehicle battery plant until 2029
stories.summary: The opening of a massive Volkswagen electric vehicle battery plant in southwestern Ontario has been pushed back two years until 2029.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The opening of a massive Volkswagen electric vehicle battery plant in southwestern Ontario has been pushed back two years until 2029.

PowerCo Canada, a subsidiary of the German automaker, says it is delaying production at the $7-billion factory in St. Thomas, Ont., in order to align the project’s timeline and product strategy with evolving market demand, technological advancements and the Volkswagen Group’s long-term strategy.

It says the later opening date will allow for next-generation battery technology while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve.

Latest updates on company news here

Joel Karlsberg, chief procurement officer for the battery company, says the move is “about getting the pacing right ... to protect our long-term investment (and) support regional jobs.”

PowerCo also announced Thursday it has selected Canadian construction firm EllisDon Corp. as general contractor for construction of the factory as it moves into its next phase, which will focus on core infrastructure and structural work.

The plant was announced in 2023, with the federal government committing $700 million in upfront capital costs to build the factory and Ontario kicking in $500 million.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

stories.title: Carney will miss target for balancing operating budget, PBO says
stories.summary: A new report by Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog raises questions about when the government will eliminate its operating deficit.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — A new report by Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog raises questions about when the government will eliminate its operating deficit, despite Prime Minister Mark Carney saying last week that the government now expects to balance its operating budget a year earlier than the original goal.

Based on the information that the government released in its 2025 budget and this spring’s economic update, the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) projects that Ottawa will miss its target of balancing the operating budget by 2028-29 by a year.

The PBO says Ottawa spent about $546.6-billion on operating expenses in 2025-26 and $34.5-billion on capital costs.

The report also says the Carney government’s treatment of some of its budget items is contradictory, raising further questions about the government’s decision last year to split its spending into two distinct ledgers.

The PBO said Thursday the federal government needs to do more to sort out its definitions for capital versus operating items, wiggle room that many economists say will tempt governments to lump as much spending as possible into the rosier-sounding capital side.

That temptation will be particularly alluring for the Carney government because it’s facing massive deficits for the foreseeable future and established a key fiscal target last year of eliminating the operating deficit by 2028-29.

In a document called The Government’s Operating Budget Fiscal Anchor, the PBO says it seems contradictory to classify the government’s Agricultural Clean Technology program as a capital cost, for example, while its Agricultural Climate Solutions program is on the operating side. Both programs, the PBO says, are designed to trigger farm investments.

“This makes it difficult to anticipate how future spending will be sorted,” the PBO report says.

The PBO points out that Canada is not the first country to split its operating and capital budgets. The United Kingdom, Norway and Singapore do similar things, but the PBO points out that the U.K. also paired the move with a rule that borrowing is only allowed to pay for capital costs. The UK also used a definition of capital spending that is internationally accepted.

Franco Terrazzano, federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, said the PBO report is further evidence that Ottawa has been expanding the definition of capital spending in a way that wouldn’t be allowed in the UK.

But the real problem, Terrazzano said, isn’t the government’s accounting methods but that Carney’s “credit card government” spends and borrows way too much.

The federal government is borrowing about $65-billlion a year, Terrazzano said, more than Ottawa sends to the provinces and territories for health transfers or collects from the GST.

“We’re paying way too much paying interest on the debt.”

John Fragos, spokesman for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said the government has already identified $60-billion in savings over the next five years, allowing Ottawa to eliminate the operating deficit a year ahead of schedule. Those savings, Fragos said, will allow the federal government to spend more on capital costs that will support economic growth.

The Carney government’s first budget last fall marked the first time that Ottawa had separated capital and operational or day-to-day spending. The key distinction, according to the government, is between regular, day-to-day expenses such as wages for federal public servants and social service payments, and those capital costs on such things as ports, military equipment and other infrastructure that should provide long-term benefit.

In its spring economic update, the government said it expected to post a deficit of $66.9 billion for the past year, slightly less than expected, due to improved fiscal outcomes. But Ottawa’s broader fiscal outlook remains dire. The federal government has now accumulated $1.27-trillion in total debt, almost half of which has been added over the last five years.

stories.title: London patient a Canadian first for ‘heart in a box’ transplant
stories.summary: A London man who survived cardiac arrest and received a life-saving heart transplant became the first patient in Canada to receive a donor heart preserved using new “heart-in-a-box” technology at London Health Sciences Centre.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Some of the images in this article May be sensitive to some readers

“It was really scary. You never plan for things like that.”

Raj Mittal recalls the first time doctors at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) saved his life.

In June 2025, the London man was working in his backyard when he began experiencing chest pain. His wife called 911 and he was rushed to hospital.

“When I came in, I had a cardiac arrest and they needed to give me 45 minutes of CPR to revive me,” Mittal said. “All three of my arteries were blocked, so they had to do a triple bypass.”

A series of health setbacks followed before Mittal was placed on the provincial wait list for a heart transplant. Earlier this year, a donor heart became available and he underwent transplant surgery.

But this was not a typical transplant, said London Health Sciences Centre cardiac surgeon Dr. Dave Nagpal.

“It’s technology that allows us to take a heart from a donor, place it on this machine with some of the donor’s blood and actually see the heart functioning,” Nagpal said. “We can make sure it’s suitable for the recipient.”

Traditionally, donor hearts are transported in coolers, giving surgeons a window of about four to six hours before transplantation. The new technology can extend that timeframe to as much as 12 hours, allowing hearts to be transported from much greater distances.

Nagpal said the technology could help shorten wait times and increase the number of available donor hearts.

“We expect it could increase the donor heart pool by up to 40 per cent,” he said. “Recipients like Raj and others waiting for a heart transplant will hopefully spend less time waiting and be less sick when they receive their donor heart.”

Mittal, 50, is still recovering but hopes to return to his job as an IT professional sometime next year.

“I would like to thank the doctors and nurses who took care of me,” he said. “With the grace of God and the support of my family and friends, I’m here. This is my second life.”

stories.title: Higher income households eating out less as consumer pain bites: survey
stories.summary: Canadians say they are dining out at restaurants less than last year amid the heightened cost of living, according to new data from Restaurants Canada.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canadians say they are dining out at restaurants less than last year amid the heightened cost of living , according to new data from Restaurants Canada, which shows higher income households with the sharpest change.

A retail analyst and consumer expert says the report is another example of the “K-shaped” economy writ large, which sees a growing divide between top earners in Canada and lower income brackets that is also showing strain among more middle and higher income earners.

The report was released Thursday and featured details of Restaurants Canada’s survey, which was conducted by Angus Reid in May and included 1,500 Canadian participants. When questions were asked about dining out at restaurants, it included both fast food (a.k.a. “quick-service restaurants”) and full-service restaurants.

Eighty per cent of all respondents said they have been eating out less often due to the rising cost of living, up from 75 per cent a year earlier.

That sentiment was also shared by 78 per cent of households that claimed to earn a combined income of $100,000 per year or more, up from 70 per cent in 2025.

Eighty-one per cent of households that said they earn between $50,000 and $100,000 annually said they were dining out less this year, up from 76 per cent last year.

Meanwhile, households that earned less than $50,000 were little changed, with 87 per cent saying they are dining out less than last year, up from 86 per cent a year earlier.

“You have this sort of divergence of consumers: You have people getting really rich — that’s the upward swing of the ‘K’ — and then you have people getting poorer, and that’s the downward swing of ‘K,'” says consumer and retail analyst Bruce Winder.
