stories.title: Live updates: Kenneth Law sentencing hearing enters second day with more grieving family members set to speak
stories.summary: Ontario man who sold lethal substances online pleaded guilty to aiding 14 suicides in Canada and admitted to role in dozens more in U.K.
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
A Toronto man whose son died by suicide after purchasing poison from Kenneth Law called for a public inquiry while speaking at a Wednesday sentencing hearing .

Stephen Mitchell called on the Ontario government to take action, as he and other relatives of Mr. Law’s victims delivered harrowing public victim-impact statements on the first day of the hearing. Mr. Mitchell’s son, Stephen Jr., died just weeks before Mr. Law’s arrest in 2023. Mr. Mitchell criticized Canadian law enforcement for not recognizing the threat that Mr. Law posed before a British newspaper exposed his business in the spring of 2023.

He said grieving families want to know why the 61-year-old Mississauga engineer was able to operate an online business selling toxic salts and other deadly paraphernalia for years before his arrest. By the time Mr. Law was stopped, he had shipped more than 1,200 deadly parcels, including 330 to Britain and 157 within Canada, mostly to young people at risk of suicide.

Mr. Mitchell said that earlier intervention could have saved lives, including his son’s. “Premier Ford, I respectfully ask you to authorize an independent third-party inquiry into what occurred,” he said outside the court.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected the idea of a public inquiry earlier this year. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Crown attorney Peter Westgate said the court will hear victim-impact statements from a total of 74 people this week.

In court documents filed ahead of his sentencing hearings earlier this month , Kenneth Law had told a psychiatrist that he considers himself a “pathfinder” and not a psychopath.

“I was just trying to serve a need that I thought was humane,” Mr. Law said during interviews with psychiatrist Jonathan Rootenberg conducted in a Lindsay, Ont., jail this July.

“I’m not a diabolical madman.”

In the post-conviction medical interviews, Mr. Law describes his upbringing and his crimes in his own words, while arguing that much of what he did was morally defensible even if it violated the law.

“Now I can look back and say that what I was doing was legally wrong ... that’s why I pled guilty. It’s about taking ownership and responsibility for your actions,” Mr. Law told the psychiatrist. “We all learn from our mistakes.”

Read the full story here.

- Colin Freeze, Mike Hager

The sentencing hearing is scheduled to run for several more days as the families of victims from Canada and the U.K. provide victim-impact statements.

Kenneth Law’s victims in Ontario included two 16-year-olds, a 21-year-old found dead by his brother and a 19-year-old honour-roll student, as well as dozens more in the U.K. whose deaths he has admitted a role in.

Here are five of their stories .

In May, Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in an Ontario court to aiding in the suicides of 14 people in Ontario, and also admitted to assisting in 79 other deaths in Britain by shipping toxic substances and suffocation equipment to people seeking to die.

Prior to pleading guilty to the 14 counts of aiding suicide, Mr. Law signed a lengthy agreed statement of facts, which was read aloud in court by prosecutors.

In the agreed facts, Law admits to shipping hundreds of packages of his products from a Canada Post office near his Mississauga home. Prosecutors named dozens of countries that received shipments but said most went to the United States (431 packages), Britain (330) and Canada (157).

- The Canadian Press

Nearly four years since a coroner’s report on woman’s death in the U.K. listed details police later linked to Kenneth Law in Ontario, the marathon criminal proceedings in Canada are nearing a close.

But the path to Law’s guilty pleas for aiding 14 suicides in Canada – and his admission of involvement in dozens more abroad – has not been a straight line.

Here is a timeline of key events in the case .

stories.title: What to watch this weekend: Binge this rich-people thriller The Perfect Lie
stories.summary: Or try a comedy about (rumoured) brothers Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey
stories.author: J. Kelly Nestruck
stories.content:
The Perfect Lie, Netflix

Netflix knows exactly what it’s doing. The streamer has retitled its Dutch miniseries De Eetclub – which directly translates to “The Dinner Club” – as The Perfect Lie in English, and it’s become a hit with subtitles.

The seven-part thriller, based on a novel popular in the Netherlands, does indeed feel like a cross between the narratives and tones of popular American beautiful-rich-people shows The Perfect Couple and Big Little Lies . (Singalongs during car rides to school? Check. A big choreographed number with the whole cast? Check.)

The Perfect Lie follows four wealthy, irresponsible couples living seaside in Bergen, whose kids go to the same Waldorf school. The show opens with a police interrogation of the main mom character Karen (Loes Haverkort) – and flashes back to the events leading up to and after a fire that left the group’s most handsome husband, Evert (Edwin Jonker), dead and that nearly consumed his wife Babette (Noortje Herlaar) and their two kids as well.

Drinking, drugs and games of truth or dare are all involved. This is bingeable pulp, elevated by a few excellent grounded performances by the European ensemble – especially Rifka Lodeizen as a wounded woman whose husband stops sleeping with her.

Brothers, Apple TV

This new stoner comedy, co-created by Canuck writer for screen and stage David West Read ( Schitt’s Creek , & Juliet ), is “based on a true rumour,” as the opening disclaimer proclaims.

Woody Harrelson, playing a fictionalized version of himself, shows up one day at his old True Detective co-star Matthew McConaughey’s Texas ranch with his wife and daughters in tow. There, he stumbles upon the possibility that his father May have been his friend’s father, too.

Woody keeps this a secret for no clear reason beyond needing a narrative arc for a season of TV. He settles in for a long visit to help manage Matthew’s run for Texas governor, and get on the nerves of his friend’s beautiful wife (played by McConaughey’s actual beautiful wife, and natural actor, the Brazilian model Camila Alves).

The first episode is a little rough in writing and execution, but the second settles into an Odd Couple rhythm. The gentle friction between Woody and Matthew over veganism versus hunting is easily resolved by getting blazed together. Harrelson is better at playing himself in an amusing manner, and at hitting comic beats; McConaughey does the Lincoln ad version of himself over and over.

Director Sophy Romvari’s deeply affecting feature debut (streaming Sept. 25) follows a large Hungarian-Canadian family as they figure out how to deal with the difficult behaviour of their teenage son Jeremy (Edik Beddoes, in a haunting performance).

The parents quickly hit the limits of social services and understanding of mental health in 1990s B.C.; the young kids try to ignore or observe from a distance. The moving third act of the movie shifts time frames – and, in another way, doesn’t – to follow sister Sasha (Amy Zimmer) still trying to understand and process what happened with her brother.

“Ultimately, Blue Heron is an epic exploring the power and fissures of memory,” The Globe and Mail’s Barry Hertz wrote in his Critic’s Pick review . “But there is no chance that audiences will ever forget what Romvari has accomplished here.”

I Used to Be Funny, CBC Gem

Another Globe Critic’s Pick film lands on another Canadian streamer on Sept. 25. Written and directed by Ally Pankiw, this dark dramedy follows stand-up comedian Sam ( I Love LA ’s Rachel Sennott) as she struggles with Ptsd after a sexual assault.

“I love how Pankiw drops important pieces of information in almost casual ways, because she knows that’s how people, especially funny people, talk,” Johanna Schneller wrote in her review . “Listen for the line that Sam’s ex, Noah (Ennis Esmer), said in the immediate aftermath of Sam’s assault – the one he wishes he could take back, the one she can’t get over. Huge traumas crash your life, but the smallest betrayals can break your heart.”

Perfect Storm, Disney+

Empathie , Florence Longpré’s wonderful drama about a prison psychologist, won 14 awards at the Prix Gémeaux last week, a record haul for a single season of a show at Canada’s awards for French-language television. This was something the whole country could celebrate: The Crave drama has a strong fan base among English-speaking Canadians because it has been distributed on the bilingual streaming service with subtitles right from its debut.

Readers of this column are less likely to have watched L’oeil du cyclone , the long-running, lighthearted Radio-Canada show about a single mother of three (Christine Beaulieu) that finally eked out Best Comedy at the Gémaux for its sixth season. That’s because CBC/Radio-Canada is a linguistically divided public broadcaster that thinks like a prestreaming private broadcaster, and rarely makes the content it commissions with your tax dollars available in both official languages.

But the first four seasons of L’oeil du cyclone are now available with English subtitles for the first time on Disney+ in Canada, under the title Perfect Storm . I sampled a few episodes and found it an enjoyably modern family sitcom, kind of a Quebec corollary to CTV’s Children Ruin Everything .

content_blocks.text: Director Sophy Romvari’s deeply affecting feature debut (streaming Sept. 25) follows a large Hungarian-Canadian family as they figure out how to deal with the difficult behaviour of their teenage son Jeremy (Edik Beddoes, in a haunting performance).

The parents quickly hit the limits of social services and understanding of mental health in 1990s B.C.; the young kids try to ignore or observe from a distance. The moving third act of the movie shifts time frames – and, in another way, doesn’t – to follow sister Sasha (Amy Zimmer) still trying to understand and process what happened with her brother.

“Ultimately, Blue Heron is an epic exploring the power and fissures of memory,” The Globe and Mail’s Barry Hertz wrote in his Critic’s Pick review . “But there is no chance that audiences will ever forget what Romvari has accomplished here.”
I Used to Be Funny, CBC Gem

content_blocks.caption: I Used to Be Funny examines the trauma of sexual assault from the perspective of stand-up comic Sam, played by Rachel Sennott. Janick Laurent/Supplied

content_blocks.text: Another Globe Critic’s Pick film lands on another Canadian streamer on Sept. 25. Written and directed by Ally Pankiw, this dark dramedy follows stand-up comedian Sam ( I Love LA ’s Rachel Sennott) as she struggles with Ptsd after a sexual assault.

“I love how Pankiw drops important pieces of information in almost casual ways, because she knows that’s how people, especially funny people, talk,” Johanna Schneller wrote in her review . “Listen for the line that Sam’s ex, Noah (Ennis Esmer), said in the immediate aftermath of Sam’s assault – the one he wishes he could take back, the one she can’t get over. Huge traumas crash your life, but the smallest betrayals can break your heart.”
Perfect Storm, Disney+

content_blocks.caption: Award-winning Quebec family sitcom L’oeil du cyclone gets an English audience (with subtitles) under the title Perfect Storm. Radio-Canada/Supplied

content_blocks.text: Empathie , Florence Longpré’s wonderful drama about a prison psychologist, won 14 awards at the Prix Gémeaux last week, a record haul for a single season of a show at Canada’s awards for French-language television. This was something the whole country could celebrate: The Crave drama has a strong fan base among English-speaking Canadians because it has been distributed on the bilingual streaming service with subtitles right from its debut.

Readers of this column are less likely to have watched L’oeil du cyclone , the long-running, lighthearted Radio-Canada show about a single mother of three (Christine Beaulieu) that finally eked out Best Comedy at the Gémaux for its sixth season. That’s because CBC/Radio-Canada is a linguistically divided public broadcaster that thinks like a prestreaming private broadcaster, and rarely makes the content it commissions with your tax dollars available in both official languages.

But the first four seasons of L’oeil du cyclone are now available with English subtitles for the first time on Disney+ in Canada, under the title Perfect Storm . I sampled a few episodes and found it an enjoyably modern family sitcom, kind of a Quebec corollary to CTV’s Children Ruin Everything .

stories.title: So Delicious Dairy Free dessert product recalled after small hard objects found
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has published a recall for a brand of dairy-free frozen desserts due to “plastic-like” and “gravel-like fragments.”
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) has published a recall for a brand of dairy-free frozen desserts due to “plastic-like” and “gravel-like fragments.”

The notice from Sept. 22 affects 500-ml products of So Delicious Dairy Free salted caramel with a cashew base.

The products have a best-before date of Sept. 8 2027, Oct. 15 and 16 in 2027, Feb. 3 and 25 in 2028, and March 30 and 31 in 2028.

Consumers are advised to not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected product.

Caitlin Gray, external communications adviser for Sobeys, confirmed on Thursday that the recalled products have been removed from all banner stores in all regions.

The banner stores include FreshCo, Safeway, IGA and Foodland. The products have also been removed from Voilà by Sobeys, an online grocery delivery service owned by Sobeys’ parent company, Empire Company Ltd.

Danone Inc., the company that produces the products, issued its own recall notice in the U.S. on Sept. 15.

The notice affects all pints with best-by dates on and before April 3, 2028, due to the presence of “foreign materials,” such as small stones and other hard objects within the cashew inclusions.

The U.S. notice stated that the issue had been identified via consumer complaints and that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has been informed of the recall. It added that unaffected product is still on shelves in retail stores and product shipped going forward is not affected by the recall.

A similar food recall notice was posted by the Cfia on Jan. 2, 2026, which applied to all pints with best-before dates from Feb. 13 of this year to July 10, 2027.

stories.title: $11.5M from Sturgeon Lake trust helped fund Rath firm’s Tallcree payment: receiver
stories.summary: Alberta separatist leader Jeffrey Rath’s firm took $11.5 million from one First Nation trust to help him make a court-ordered refund to another First Nation, court documents show.
stories.author: Ashleigh Stewart
stories.content:
A court-appointed receiver says Alberta separatist leader Jeffrey Rath’s firm moved $11.5 million from a First Nation trust it controlled to help cover a court-ordered payment it owed to another First Nation client, Global News has learned.

The receiver’s latest filings show that on Jan. 23, 2024, the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation Trust’s bank accounts issued two cheques totalling $11.5 million to RathPC. The next day, the firm moved the money into another RathPC account and commingled it with other funds.

Within a week, RathPC paid $8.5 million into the Alberta Court of King’s Bench, which was deciding whether the money belonged to Tallcree First Nation or its trust, filings show.

Both First Nations retained the Foothills lawyer and his firm, RathPC, to pursue claims against the federal government, resulting in settlements worth tens of millions of dollars. The firm then became trustee of the funds held for beneficiaries, including minors.

In 2017, Rath’s professional corporation, RathPC, collected $11.5 million under a contingency fee agreement with Tallcree after the band settled a $ 57.6 million claim with the federal government. A judge later ruled the payment unreasonable and ordered the firm to repay $8.5 million.

“At each step of this proceeding, our worst fears come true,” says Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake. saying the repayment was made by taking money from “the children of our Nation.”

“It is enraging that he is still being given a platform in this province, and this is hardly being mentioned,” Sunshine said. “This will have a generational impact.”

Rath did not respond to questions from Global News.

The revelation comes as Rath finds himself at the centre of a legal maelstrom. Sturgeon Lake and Tallcree First Nations are each suing Rath and his firm, alleging that RathPC improperly withdrew tens of millions of dollars from its trusts and withheld financial statements that would have revealed the withdrawals.

In July, Tallcree obtained an interim Mareva injunction, which is a court order that freezes a person’s or company’s assets and prohibits a defendant from hiding or moving funds that could otherwise satisfy a future judgment. A final determination of the order is pending.

That same month, the Alberta court also appointed a receiver, financial advisory firm AlixPartners, to trace the funds the First Nations claim are missing.

Global News reported that, around the same time, financial auditor Doane Grant Thornton raised concerns about several withdrawals from the Sturgeon Lake trust in 2024, including two in January, for $9.8 million and $1.7 million.

Rath said the payments were retroactive administrative fees covering 2017 to 2024, according to court documents.

Those two withdrawals, the receiver says, went towards Tallcree’s multi-million-dollar, court-ordered repayment.

Rath has filed four appeals challenging the trustee removal, the asset freeze, the receivership and the receiver’s access to the firm’s records.

Tallcree and Sturgeon Lake’s allegations remain contested and have not been finally adjudicated.

The $8.5-million refund involved a complicated path through RathPC’s accounts.

RathPC first paid the money into court, allegedly using the proceeds of millions transferred from Sturgeon Lake, while Tallcree and the firm disputed whether the refund belonged to the Nation or its settlement trust.

Eventually, ON Nov. 5, 2025, the court ordered RathPC to return the money to the Tallcree trust. Instead, 12 days later, court-filed banking records show that the money was quickly converted into $8 million in bullion, plus a $500,000 draft payable to Rath.

From there, the money trail widens. RathPC’s account at Bow Valley Credit Union became the hub for millions of dollars in precious-metals trading, according to the receiver.

Between November 2025 and March 2026, $11.4 million was transferred from the account to purchase bullion in a series of trades, according to the receiver’s court documents.

The sales yielded almost $8 million, resulting in an estimated net trading loss of about $3.25 million due to market fluctuations, the receiver states.

The receiver also identified another $200,971 in physical gold and silver purchases, but says it does not know where those coins are.

It says Rath’s lack of cooperation has hampered its investigation and that it has been unable to interview him about the disputed transactions.

When asked for comment, Rath said he would not respond.

Meanwhile, as the legal battles continue, Rath has remained active in Alberta separatist politics on social media and in interviews, calling for Premier Danielle Smith’s resignation and promoting separatism ahead of the province’s Oct. 19 referendum.

stories.title: David Eby’s BC election gamble
stories.summary: British Columbians will be heading to the polls two years ahead of schedule this fall.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
B.C. Premier David Eby speaks outside the new Stride Avenue Community School built to replace the former school that opened on the site in 1929, in Burnaby, B.C., ON Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Darryl Dyck

By Analysis by The Big Story podcast

Posted September 24, 2026 7:36 am.

British Columbians will be heading to the polls two years ahead of schedule this fall.

The snap call by Premier David Eby comes amid turmoil within the B.C. Conservative Party, his chief opponents, and at a sensitive time for the province, as the government has attempted to deal with controversy around Indigenous rights legislation.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks with Shannon Waters, a B.C. political and environmental reporter for The Narwhal, about the gamble Eby took by dropping the writ, the drama surrounding the B.C. Conservative Party, and how much of an election issue Indigenous rights and Dripa might be.

stories.title: Dolphin shipped out of Marineland dies in Spain after move
stories.summary: Echo is the fifth animal from the closed Niagara Falls tourist attraction to die after a massive movement of whales and dolphins over the summer
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
A dolphin shipped out of Marineland has died in Spain, making it the fifth animal from the closed Niagara Falls, Ont., tourist attraction to die after a massive movement of whales and dolphins over the summer.

Oceanografic Valencia said Echo, a blind Black Sea bottlenose dolphin believed to be 30 years old, died Wednesday.

“In recent hours, Echo began experiencing difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems and was transferred to the medical pool,” Oceanografic said in a statement.

“Her condition deteriorated rapidly throughout yesterday and, despite the care provided by Oceanografic’s animal care and veterinary teams, she passed away overnight.”

Echo, along with three other dolphins and two belugas, was sent to the Spanish aquarium on Aug. 26 in an epic 19-hour voyage from the shuttered Niagara Falls, Ont., tourist attraction.

One of those belugas, Jelly Bean, died last week .

Oceanografic is conducting necropsies on both animals along with an examination by pathology experts at CEU Cardenal Herrera University to try to understand the cause of death.

“The other four animals rescued from Canada are doing well and remain under the care and monitoring of Oceanografic’s professional teams,” Oceanografic said.

“Echo’s loss is an especially difficult moment for the Oceanografic team, who had been particularly dedicated to her care and well-being since her arrival due to her specific needs.”

Fourth Marineland whale dies after relocation from Niagara Falls park

Four belugas and one dolphin have now died since Marineland shipped out 30 belugas and four dolphins to five different parks over the summer.

Three of those belugas died at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago along with one of the park’s resident belugas.

Marineland closed in 2024 and had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its whales. If they were not moved, the park was set to euthanize them.

Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson nixed a deal Marineland had with Chimelong Ocean Kingdom in China, saying it was not in the whales’ best interest to send them there.

She said China did not have the same laws as Canada, which banned whale and dolphin captivity in 2019 but grandfathered in Marineland’s animals.

In response, Marineland said it would euthanize the whales if it did not get emergency funding, a threat that made international headlines.

Marineland pivoted to a consortium of American and Spanish aquariums for help. The move of its whales and dolphins began in mid-July and wrapped up by the end of August.

Both Shedd and Oceanografic are investigating to better understand what caused the animals’ deaths.

Veterinarians from all parks were at Marineland in the months leading up to the move and cleared the animals for transport, as did Thompson, who signed off on the moves after receiving updated health information.

stories.title: Western alumni support Toronto Tempo, Canada’s first Wnba team
stories.summary: Western University students and alumni are helping Toronto Tempo, Canada’s first Wnba team through leadership, legal, and business roles.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
The last year has brought milestones for women’s sports in Canada, paving the way for future generations of athletes. The Canadian women’s hockey team came head-to-head with the United States at the Winter Olympics in Milan, while the Professional Women’s Hockey League expanded to 12 teams and reached record-breaking attendance. The creation of the Toronto Tempo — the Wnba’s first Canadian franchise — represents a massive step.

As the Tempo season wraps up at the end of September, Western University students and alumni who have been part of the team since before the first ball was thrown are reflecting on what it means to be part of the fast-growing franchise.

Many Western graduates were embedded with the team or supporting its progress even before the inaugural season kicked off, from manager of human resources Karisma Sharma, Bmos’19, to the team’s chief financial officer Patrick Lee, Bmos’07, to Sukhinder Singh Cassidy, Hba’92, Lld’26, who’s part of the Tempo ownership group.

Esra Osman, a fourth-year student at Ivey Business School, was studying for exams when her roommate put on Running Point, a Netflix series about a businesswoman in charge of her family’s professional basketball team.

She was inspired to apply for a summer position with the Tempo – the team’s first-ever internship. Three rounds later, Osman landed what she calls the best summer of her life.

A business operations intern working to promote the Tempo in different communities, Osman delved deep into the history of women’s sports. She saw firsthand that not everyone has equal access to organized sports the way she did as a child, playing basketball and other sports alongside her brothers.

“I realized I had the privilege of access to sports. But that’s not the reality for everyone. The Tempo and all the community work they do was a really big wake-up call for me,” said Osman.

The hype around the Tempo is visible at every game and community event. Osman often met girls as young as five who told her they dreamed of playing for the team one day.

“A lot of our work was focused on connecting with our community, making sure people from different locations and with a variety of backgrounds are feeling heard and represented – it isn’t just Toronto’s team, but the country’s team,” she said.

The internship was also valuable to Osman as a young professional. Her leaders took time to be vulnerable about the challenges of working in a male-dominated industry, she said, sharing personal advice on an issue well-documented in research studies.

“They were very keen on protecting me and my experience within the sports industry – not everyone has the luxury of that support early in their career. My colleagues wanted me to have fun, but they were also honest about the struggles and did their best to make sure that I always felt safe and heard,” said Osman.

Amy Kong, Hba’24, Toronto Tempo account executive in premium sales and service, can relate to being inspired by the women around her. She sees all-stars like Marina Mabrey on the court at almost every game, but she’s equally inspired by the leaders walking through the team’s office, like coach Sandy Brondello and president Teresa Resch, a former senior leader with the Toronto Raptors.

Kong helps sell tickets and manage relationships with season ticketholders, primarily focusing on courtside seats and suites. But because the Tempo operates as a small, independent team, she does a little bit of everything – from helping set up before games, talking with various attendees and repping the team at the Pride parade in Toronto this year.

“We have a very different demographic than the traditional sports viewer. You need to have empathy, perspective and be able to listen to people, knowing it’s a unique audience of sports fans,” said Kong.

Although the Coca-Cola Coliseum fits a few more fans than Alumni Hall, Kong credits Western with helping her discover her future career path. After playing basketball in her youth, she became a varsity athlete on Western’s ultimate frisbee team and managed its social media.

“I never would have been able to understand my love for the sports world without that experience. Western taught me to be a strong communicator and teammate, whether it was in class or on a club or sports team,” Kong said.

Another Western alum who has been with the Tempo since the beginning is Aaron Barrett, JD’20, the Toronto Tempo’s general counsel and a graduate of Western Law. His work touches most of the organization, including negotiating deals involving players, sponsors and venues.

Before joining the Tempo directly, Barrett was part of the group that helped secure the expansion agreement in 2024.

“It’s been really cool because I was working for the team long before we actually started playing games; you honestly had to remind yourself that you were working for a basketball team at some points,” laughed Barrett.

But the job became very real very quickly, he says. It was only about six weeks before the start of the season that it was clear a team would hit the court. The roster was finalized 30 days before the first game.

Like Kong, Barrett loves to watch thousands of fans fill the stands.

“When you go to other sporting events, a lot of time the crowds are very reactive. But Tempo fans are so proactive. We could be down 20 points, and they’re still on their feet, cheering, supporting the players. It’s been really an incredible atmosphere to witness,” said Barrett.

Barrett had always dreamed of becoming a sports lawyer, but said Western Law helped broaden his skill set and refine his legal interests, including learning about the intersections between law and sports.

Barrett and Kong recognize many students who love sports will never compete professionally as athletes, but they encourage young people to consider building careers around the game.

It’s rarely a straightforward 9-to-5 gig. Kong’s advice is to be prepared to take on “side quests” outside a traditional job description, and to always show up for women’s sports as a fan.

“You have to attend games and be engaged with the teams if you’re a true fan. Never forget there are multiple ways to contribute to a team, even if it’s in a smaller capacity,” said Kong.

Working for the Tempo has its perks. She was there as members of Canadian rock band The Beaches took their seats courtside and had the chance to meet Canadian Olympic legends Andre DeGrasse and Christine Sinclair at the home opener.

But her favourite part is hearing from people who have waited their whole lives to support Wnba team in Canada. Kong was especially inspired to see the excitement among the 2SLGBTQIA+ community, including older queer couples who followed the league for years but never had a local team in which they could see themselves represented.

“People come from far and wide. It is really special to be able to bring something so meaningful to someone who’s waited for so long,” said Kong.

My colleagues wanted me to have fun, but they were also honest about the struggles and did their best to make sure that I always felt safe and heard,” said Osman.

Amy Kong, Hba’24, Toronto Tempo account executive in premium sales and service, can relate to being inspired by the women around her. She sees all-stars like Marina Mabrey on the court at almost every game, but she’s equally inspired by the leaders walking through the team’s office, like coach Sandy Brondello and president Teresa Resch, a former senior leader with the Toronto Raptors.

Kong helps sell tickets and manage relationships with season ticketholders, primarily focusing on courtside seats and suites. But because the Tempo operates as a small, independent team, she does a little bit of everything – from helping set up before games, talking with various attendees and repping the team at the Pride parade in Toronto this year.

“We have a very different demographic than the traditional sports viewer. You need to have empathy, perspective and be able to listen to people, knowing it’s a unique audience of sports fans,” said Kong.

Although the Coca-Cola Coliseum fits a few more fans than Alumni Hall, Kong credits Western with helping her discover her future career path. After playing basketball in her youth, she became a varsity athlete on Western’s ultimate frisbee team and managed its social media.

“I never would have been able to understand my love for the sports world without that experience. Western taught me to be a strong communicator and teammate, whether it was in class or on a club or sports team,” Kong said.

Another Western alum who has been with the Tempo since the beginning is Aaron Barrett, JD’20, the Toronto Tempo’s general counsel and a graduate of Western Law. His work touches most of the organization, including negotiating deals involving players, sponsors and venues.
Before joining the Tempo directly, Barrett was part of the group that helped secure the expansion agreement in 2024.

“It’s been really cool because I was working for the team long before we actually started playing games; you honestly had to remind yourself that you were working for a basketball team at some points,” laughed Barrett.

But the job became very real very quickly, he says. It was only about six weeks before the start of the season that it was clear a team would hit the court. The roster was finalized 30 days before the first game.
Like Kong, Barrett loves to watch thousands of fans fill the stands.

“When you go to other sporting events, a lot of time the crowds are very reactive. But Tempo fans are so proactive. We could be down 20 points, and they’re still on their feet, cheering, supporting the players. It’s been really an incredible atmosphere to witness,” said Barrett.

Barrett had always dreamed of becoming a sports lawyer, but said Western Law helped broaden his skill set and refine his legal interests, including learning about the intersections between law and sports.
Barrett and Kong recognize many students who love sports will never compete professionally as athletes, but they encourage young people to consider building careers around the game.
It’s rarely a straightforward 9-to-5 gig. Kong’s advice is to be prepared to take on “side quests” outside a traditional job description, and to always show up for women’s sports as a fan.
“You have to attend games and be engaged with the teams if you’re a true fan. Never forget there are multiple ways to contribute to a team, even if it’s in a smaller capacity,” said Kong.

Working for the Tempo has its perks. She was there as members of Canadian rock band The Beaches took their seats courtside and had the chance to meet Canadian Olympic legends Andre DeGrasse and Christine Sinclair at the home opener.

But her favourite part is hearing from people who have waited their whole lives to support Wnba team in Canada. Kong was especially inspired to see the excitement among the 2SLGBTQIA+ community, including older queer couples who followed the league for years but never had a local team in which they could see themselves represented.
“People come from far and wide. It is really special to be able to bring something so meaningful to someone who’s waited for so long,” said Kong.

stories.title: Belleville synagogue raising funds to rebuild as Jewish leaders remain committed to safety
stories.summary: Jewish leaders in Canada say they are committed to safety as several police services boost patrols near places of worship.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Jewish leaders across Canada remain committed to safety after a shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont. left a police officer injured.

The suspect of the Sept. 20 shooting — which occurred on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in Judaism — died Tuesday after succumbing to his injuries. He was identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward from Quinte West. The officer, Const. Jeff Smith, is in stable condition but “continues to face a significant road to recovery,” according to Belleville police’s Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks. A GoFundMe set up for Smith by Toronto’s Jewish community has reached more than $360,000.

None of the roughly 25 congregants inside the synagogue were injured.

Belleville police were only assigned to the synagogue because congregants had reported a suspicious vehicle parked outside a week earlier, according to Global News.

In an update from the Belleville synagogue, Sons of Jacob, shared with National Post on Wednesday, it referred to the shooting as a “targeted attack against Jews gathering together to pray and be in community.”

“Yom Kippur asks us to confront what is broken and consider how we can repair it,” the update said. “This week, our community is living that teaching in a very real way.”

A GoFundMe has been set up to raise money for repairs and security at the synagogue.

Rabbi Carnie Rose from the Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Winnipeg said what occurred in Belleville was a “very unfortunate situation” and he has been in talks with police.

Shaarey Zedek was the target of antisemitic graffiti in 2025 and in early 2026.

“The police have been outstanding, wonderful,” he said, as have local politicians. Many safety measures are being taken, he said, although he did not want to cite specific details out of caution.

He said it was sad that the community’s money had to be spent on security rather than education or charitable work, but it is a necessity at this time.

“The Islamic community has … reached out to tell us that we’re in this together,” he said, adding that other faith communities have also been supportive. “So, if there is a silver lining, it is a possibility of … coming together of people who have otherwise had some edges with one another, and maybe this will be the catalyst for a better day for us all.”

Rose said that past events have not dissuaded his congregation from attending synagogue.

“People are proud, and people are strong, and people are not going to be pushed around, not in a country that that is supposed to be about liberty and equality and democracy, and a cultural mosaic,” he said.

In a separate incident, Durham Regional Police arrested a 19-year-old Whitby man for allegedly making threats online about shooting up a synagogue one day before the Belleville shooting.

Koren Kassirer is the vice president of a small congregation in Oshawa called Beth Zion Congregation, located in the Durham Region. She told National Post that the recent events have been “very concerning.”

“Living outside the GTA, we felt that the likelihood of these incidents was far lower,” she said. However, she said she did notice antisemitic incidents in Bowmanville, where she lives, including swastikas being graffitied outside over the summer and antisemitic flyers on the shelves of a local store earlier in the year.

Kassirer said the synagogue is in talks with local police and two congregants are taking a course to learn how to better secure the facility.

Durham Regional Police will continue with enhanced patrols, Const. Nicholas Gluckstein told National Post in a written statement. He said this was a “proactive” measure that reflects the police service’s “ongoing commitment to community safety, crime prevention, and support for faith-based communities across Durham Region.”

“We recognize the significance of all religious observances and want members of the Jewish community to know that their safety remains a priority,” said Gluckstein.

In Toronto, which is home to Canada’s largest Jewish population, Toronto Police Services said in a post on X it would increase visibility and patrols at synagogues and other places of worship although there was no known threat or connection to the city at this time.

In March alone, there were three overnight shootings at Toronto-area synagogues. No one was injured.

Phil David, the executive director of Toronto synagogue Beth Tzedec, told National Post that the Belleville shooting “reinforces what Jewish institutions across Canada already know: security can no longer be treated as an occasional concern.”

David said the synagogue is in regular contact with Toronto police and the Jewish Security Network (JSN), dedicated to the security needs of our Greater Toronto Jewish community. “Security is an ongoing responsibility for us, not a response to any single incident,” said David.

A new security fence is being installed around parts of the property, he said.

The JSN continues to “monitor developments through its 24/7 Integrated Security Operations Centre and share information directly with community institutions,” said Yonatan Belete from the UJA Federation of Greater Toronto, a charitable organization dedicated to helping the Jewish community. The UJA launched the JSN in 2024.

The JSN has been working closely with police before and after the Belleville shooting.

“Synagogue is where our community gathers to pray, support one another and practise our faith,” said Belete.

“We want people to continue doing that with confidence, knowing that substantial work is being done to help keep them safe. Each person who stays aware, reports a concern or gets involved strengthens that effort.”

The Barrie Police Service told National Post in a statement that there was no “specific or immediate threat to Barrie,” but there would be an increase in patrols “around places of worship within the city out of an abundance of caution.”

Montreal police could not immediately respond to National Post’s request for comment about whether it would be increasing patrols near places of worship.

In June, a man was arrested after allegedly attempting to set a fire at a synagogue in the city’s Westmount neighbourhood.

stories.title: David Eby’s snap election in B.C. snubs democracy
stories.summary: NDP Leader makes a legal but unseemly attempt to capitalize on opposition disarray
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
David Eby wants to be very clear why he called a snap election , only two years after British Columbia went to the polls. It’s about Donald Trump and Saskatchewan potash, and Trump and culture wars, and Trump and health care, and Trump and chaos. Did we mention Trump? Because it’s mostly about Trump. The province needs to build a firebreak against the destructive U.S. President, he argued.

Of course, the fact that the Opposition is in a state of hapless disarray could not possibly be part of Mr. Eby’s calculations. It goes without saying, this is about the good of the province. As Mr. Eby argued, residents need the chance to choose between his excellent solutions and the awful vision of the Opposition.

B.C. Premier David Eby calls snap election

Outside the alternate reality of Mr. Eby, though, this is clearly about capitalizing on a wounded Opposition.

The election call is legal, in that the rules permit it, and also quite unseemly. In politics, sometimes the electoral ends don’t justify the cynical means. Calling this election tramples on democratic norms, ignoring that democracy is about more than winning elections.

This is not to say that Mr. Eby’s gambit won’t pay off. Ontario Premier Doug Ford made a (slightly less) opportunistic decision last year, citing the same threat posed by Mr. Trump, going to the polls more than a year early and securing a third majority. Had he waited until the scheduled election date this past June, he would have been facing the electorate with his popularity at a record low .

However, cynicism doesn’t always pay. In 1990, an Ontario premier named David Peterson was buoyant in the polls and called a snap election. The electorate was not amused and gave his Liberal Party a spanking, vaulting the NDP into government. Mr. Peterson lost his own seat.

Opinion: David Eby’s snap election call is cynical and self-serving

Mr. Eby already has a majority, and a long list of priorities – including amending Indigenous rights legislation that has muddied property rights in the province – that could fill his calendar. The hardest question for him May be justifying why he really called the election.

It was less than a month ago that Mr. Eby announced a by-election, which had been scheduled for this Saturday, that could have allowed the then-Conservative leader to enter the legislature. Although Mr. Eby argues that pivoting to a general election is about the trade war, what has really changed is the state of the Opposition.

The Conservative Party of British Columbia has been falling apart for weeks and its leader resigned on the weekend. The prospect of going to the polls has sharpened minds among the Opposition factions, though, and they seem to be re-coalescing into something cohesive enough to contest this election.

In his announcement Tuesday, Mr. Eby tried – rather unconvincingly – to blame Mr. Trump. While the U.S. trade war on Canada does indeed pose a threat to British Columbia, that is not a particularly new turn of events. And Mr. Eby is acting already to counter the impact of the trade war.

In fact, the B.C. government recently announced a pause on a planned expansion of provincial sales tax on professional services, citing the uncertainty caused the trade war, and also a $90-million support package for businesses affected by tariffs.

In the news release announcing the aid package, Mr. Eby was quoted saying that “we won’t let decisions made in Washington determine our future.” Ironically enough, given that he is also blaming those same decisions made in Washington for a vote that will, after all, determine the province’s future.

Ask us your questions about B.C.’s snap election

Regardless of how his party fares in this election, Mr. Eby will have succeeded in damaging democracy by ignoring its norms. Such norms grow organically over time, often unnoticed, and help ensure the success of democracy.

For evidence of the importance of such norms, one need look no further than the supposed reason Mr. Eby called this election. Mr. Trump has spent years spitting on traditional democratic norms. He has got away with this behaviour because his own party refuses to rein him in. By doing so, they have allowed him to create new norms, debased and undemocratic ones that May outlive his presidency.

Proper democracy is about the people speaking through an elected leader – and that leader respecting the people. That confers legitimacy. It is also about respect and reverence for the process, not just playing to win.

stories.title: Thursday’s analyst upgrades and downgrades
stories.summary: Inside the Market’s roundup of some of today’s key analyst actions
stories.author: David Leeder
stories.content:
Inside the Market’s roundup of some of today’s key analyst actions

TD Cowen analyst Steven Green predicts investors will punish shares of Kinross Gold Corp. ( KGC-N , K-T ) in response to the reduction to its 2026 and 2027 guidance due to underperformance at its La Coipa in Chile and Round Mountain in Nevada.

“The stock has underperformed the large caps by almost 11 per cent year-to-date, so we believe some of this operational under-performance was priced in, however H2/26 and 2027 are below prior expectations as well ... The ongoing share buyback should help support the stock,” he said.

After the bell on Wednesday, the Toronto-based miner announced it now expects production to come in at 1.84–1.86 million gold equivalent ounces, which is 7.5 per cent under its previous guidance of 2 million ounces for both years.

“The shortfall is concentrated at two of Kinross’ smaller operations, while Paracatu and Tasiast continue to perform well and are expected to deliver a combined 1.1 Moz in 2026,” said Mr. Green.

The reduction includes a third-quarter production of approximately 425,000 ounces, which is 16 per cent under Mr. Green’s prior estimate.

“K does however expect to continue generating strong FCF and has upped their capital return target to 50 per cent of FCF (from 40 per cent), which equates to $1.4-billion on our estimates,” he added. “They have returned $800-million to shareholders year-to-date, including $655-million through buybacks.

“We have decreased our 2026 and 2027 production forecasts by 7 per cent and 9 per cent respectively and reflected the new cost guidance. This decreases 2026 Ebitda by 10 per cent and 2027 Ebitda by 11 per cent. Our NAV/sh decreased by 3 per cent, to $28.36.

“Lower production drives cost guidance higher. K now expects 2026 cost of sales of $1,420– 1,460/oz and Aisc [all-in sustaining costs] of $1,850–1,900/oz, an increase of 6 per cent & 8 per cent respectively. We now model Aisc of $1,867/oz (prev. $1,778).”

Maintaining his “buy” rating for Kinross shares, Mr. Green reduced his target to US$35 from US$40. The average on the Street is US$38.43.

“Kinross has delivered very consistent and predictable results in recent years, is generating significant free cash flow and is and methodically advancing its development projects and mine-life extensions. Kinross has become a steady, predictable producer with upside potential as Great Bear continues to grow. We expect continued and growing share buybacks,” he concluded.

Elsewhere, other analysts making revisions include:

* Desjardins Securities’ Bryce Adams to $53 (Canadian) from $58 with a “buy” rating.

“The 2026–27 guidance revisions are concentrated at La Coipa and Round Mountain. At La Coipa, unprecedented winter weather impacted mining and milling rates through September, while higher copper grades and weaker recoveries from sulphide ore led to the deferral and stockpiling of copper-rich material. At Round Mountain, lower Phase S mining rates defer higher-grade ore, and weaker feed grade and recoveries result in a loss of ounces. Paracatu and Tasiast remain on guidance and are expected to deliver a combined 1moz annually. A production recovery is expected in 2028, with Phase X at Round Mountain and Curlew commencing production, and Tasiast moving into a higher grade orebody,” said Mr. Adams.

* Canaccord Genuity’s Carey MacRury to $47 (Canadian) from $52 with a “buy” rating.

* Scotia’s Tanya Jakusconek to US$39 from US$41 with a “sector outperform” rating.

Slate Grocery Reit ’s ( SGR.U-T , SGR.UN-T ) late Wednesday announcement of the suspension of its monthly cash distributions at the recommendation of its independent Special Committee is “a very negative development,” according to ATB Cormark analyst Sairam Srinivas.

Pointing to the timing of the news as well as its ongoing strategic review, he downgraded units of the Toronto-based Reit, which owns and operates U.S.-base grocery-anchored real estate, to “underperform” from “sector perform” previously.

“Given the timing of the news release, lack of commentary around the process, and the fact that the strategic review was initiated by a proposal from the third party asset manager, in combination with Sgr’s investment proposition as an income play, which is now fundamentally changed with the distribution suspension, we see this update as significant and negative,” said Mr. Srinivas.

“While the fundamental thesis around the real estate has not changed, this announcement changes our view on Slate as an income play. The lack of commentary around the review, mystery around the offer price (bid made by Slam), and the fact that this will add further pressure on the stock, makes us question the true rationale behind the announcement.”

He reduced his target to $8 from $13 “applying a 30-per-cent discount to last close in anticipation of a selloff).” The average is US$12.14.

ATB Cormark analyst Gavin Fairweather sees Thinkific Labs Inc. ’s ( Thnc-T ) late Wednesday announcement of a workforce reduction of 96 employees, or approximately one-third, as “transformative for the stock given the scale of the expected cash flow relative to the prevailing valuation.”

“Thinkific announced a cost structure reset that refocuses the organization toward its growing Plus business while turning its Self-Serve business into a meaningful cash cow. The size of the cost reductions will drive a step change in Ebitda beginning in Q4, with a 25-per-cent FCF margin target for C27,” he said.

In reaction to the news, Mr. Fairweather upgraded the Vancouver-based software company to “outperform” from “sector perform” previously, emphasizing its valuation was “at a modest premium to cash prior to the news.”

“The key question from our perspective relates to how the cuts will impact Self-Serve which accounts for 70 per cent of revenue,” he said. “Self-Serve can be disaggregated into two cohorts - customers which have found success on the platform and churn infrequently and earlier-stage ‘dreamers’ who churn at high rates if success is not achieved. Management noted that it has maintained certain low-cost CAC marketing channels (SEO & LLMs) while cutting brand marketing further. Support for self-serve customers has been imagined to be lighter touch, while R&D has been curtailed. Plus go-to-market and R&D are not impacted.

We now model self-serve subscription declining mid-single-digits in H2, 8 per cent in Q1 and high teens by late C27 (15 per cent on the year). This May prove too conservative if new logos are being attracted at lower CAC, pricing/packaging is revised, or the ‘mature’ cohort is larger than expected. Commerce declines are more moderate given they are tied to successful customers (down 8 per cent). We continue to model a modest Plus growth acceleration from mid-teens in recent quarters to high-teens through C27 (Q2 had strong bookings and an initial reacceleration for the business)."

Mr. Fairweather increased his target by $1 to $3.25. The average is $1.50.

“We view the ‘reset’ as necessary given the low CAC:LTV ratio in selfserve, which May limit the impact of early-stage churn on Ebitda,” he said. “With $47-million in cash post-restructuring fees, $18-million in FCF, and Plus growing and moving to profitability, the profile has dramatically changed vs. the prior business with immaterial growth and profitability. With SelfServe more than 65 per cent of revenue, we are taking a cautious view to the target multiple at 5.0 times C27 Ebitda as we wait for evidence of the churn rate and its impact on FCF.”

National Bank Financial analyst Mohamed Sidibé thinks “execution is now the key to realizing Casa Berardi’s value” for Orezone Gold Corp. ( ORE-T ) following a tour of the Quebec project and an update to its life-of-mine plan.

“The LOM plan requires the rebuilding of a previously demonstrated underground operating model,” he said. “Development is currently approximately 16 metres/day, with a near-term target of 20 m/day, compared with 26 m/day in the LOM plan and a planned peak of approximately 35 m/day in 2029. New equipment, contractor support and training should increase active stope inventory, supporting higher underground tonnes and grades and the planned East Mine restart.

“Plant performance provides upside beyond the current LOM plan. The plan assumes approximately 3.8 ktpd [thousand tons per day], compared with an average of approximately 4.0 ktpd since the acquisition and up to 4.8 ktpd on individual days. Average LOM recovery of approximately 84 per cent also compares with 86.8 per cent in Q2/26 and nearly 90 per cent historically. Increasing recovery to approximately 90 per cent and throughput to 4 ktpd would increase our Casa Berardi DCF5-per-cent by 32 per cent.”

Mr. Sidibé said the Sept. 17 tour, which came a day after the release of the new LOM, further reinforced his view that acquisition of Casa Berardi, which came in a deal for Hecla Quebec Inc., was “one that was accretive on all metrics, supports Ore’s objective to become a mid-tier producer with a potential to produce 350 koz per annum and that jurisdictionally should improve its multiples as the LOM plan is enacted and further optimizations are put in place.

“More upside remains within the current LOM plan through better underground grade dilution management, exploration, as well as leveraging the potential throughput upside at the plant,” he added. “Our model does not currently incorporate upside from higher throughput, improved recoveries, tighter dilution control or exploration success beyond the current resource base. The updated LOM plan exceeded our prior forecasts across most key operating metrics.”

The analyst increased his overall net asset value for Vancouver-based Orezone by 5 per cent to $5.65 per share from $5.40,while his 2027 Ebitda decreased by 1 per cent to $706-million from $715-million.

Reaffirming an “outperform” rating for the company’s shares, he increased his price target to $4.25 from $4.

“The plan exceeded our prior forecasts across key operating metrics and reinforced our view that the acquisition was accretive, improves Orezone’s jurisdictional exposure and supports its ambition to produce more than 350 koz annually,” he said.

Previewing third-quarter earnings season for North American railway companies, RBC Dominion Securities analyst Walter Spracklin sees Canadian National Railway Co. ( CNR-T ) “delivering the best earnings upside versus consensus given solid volumes and operating metrics, we believe this sets the stage for a Q3 beat and potential guidance raise.”

“We see a near-term neutral reaction to CSX and UNP where our unchanged estimates are right in line with consensus,” he added. “We could see negative sentiment in CP shares as we expect street earnings to move lower into earnings, although flag the reduction to our estimates is mostly fuel driven. In terms of valuation, we roll forward our valuation year to 2028 and adjust our target multiples across the group as a result - with price targets coming down reflecting recent macro uncertainty. From a longer-term perspective, we also continue to flag Cpkc and UNP on the back of their respective acquisitions.”

Mr. Spracklin increased his third-quarter earnings per share estimate to $2.12, exceeding the Street’s consensus of $2.10, from $2.07, citing “solid operating metric trends.”

“Our 2026 EPS growth estimate of 7.1 per cent (from 7.0 per cent) is ahead of consensus 6.7 per cent and compares to guidance for up mid-single-digits to high-single digits,” he added. “Given strong operating momentum exiting the quarter, we flag risk to the upside and could see management raise EPS guidance, which we believe would be well received.”

Keeping his “outperform” rating for CN shares, he trimmed his target to $198 from $205 based on a lower multiple. The average is currently $188.54.

“Our Outperform rating is based on favourable network dynamics as well as GDP plus growth opportunities and potential for margin improvement, in addition to discounted valuation in our view,” the analyst said.

For rival Canadian Pacific Kansas City Ltd. ( CP-T ), Mr. Spracklin cut his EPS to $1.30 from $1.36, falling under the consensus $1.34, to redlct higher fuel costs and compensation and benefits expense.

“Our 2026 EPS growth estimate decreases to 11.4 per cent (from 12.4 per cent), below consensus 12.5 per cent, but in line with guidance for EPS up low-double-digits,” he said. “Key focus on the call will be the extent to which CP specific opportunities can offset continued Coal headwinds in Q4 and tough Grain comps in 2027.”

With his “outperform” rating, Mr. Spracklin increased his target by $1 to $146, which exceeds the $138.11 average.

“Our positive view on CP centers on a best-in-class railroad ahead of a transformative acquisition, which we believe will set the stage for significant growth and a material upward valuation re-rate,” HE Said.

“NSC is trading highest in the group as a result of the proposed deal with UNP. Csx’s valuation is also higher, likely baking in a takeover premium,” he said. “Cpkc is trading in the middle of the pack and UNP toward the bottom despite both rails having exceptional longer-term opportunities in our view resulting from their respective acquisitions. Furthermore, CN appears to trade cheapest in the group, although closed the gap recently reflecting solid volumes and strong performance metrics. Turning to the group, ... Rails are now trading at a 9-per-cent premium to the index, up from a discount of 21 per cent in January, likely reflecting recovering volumes and indication pricing will inflect as intermodal contracts roll over into 2027″

The weaker-than-anticipated third-quarter results from AGF Management Ltd. ( AGF.B-T ) brought a “resetting” of expectations on alternative investments and fees alongside “strong” momentum from separately management accounts (SMAs) and exchange-traded funds, according to Desjardins Securities analyst Gary Ho.

Shares of the Toronto-based independent asset manager plummeted 9.7 per cent on Wednesday after it reported adjusted earnings per share of 49 cents, falling short of Mr. Ho’s 55-cent estimate and the Street’s 58-cent projection, due to a lower management fee rate and softer private alts contribution.

“GF lowered its near-term return outlook on long-term investments to 6–8 per cent from 8–10 per cent, as its legacy portfolio moves into harvest, and now guides to a 2–3 basis points decline in its net fee rate on mix shift toward SMAs and F-Series,” he said. “Investment performance remains solid. We lower our estimates and target.”

“Negatives. (1) Net fee rate of 67 basis points (down 1 bps quarter-over-quarter); AGF now guides to a 2–3 bps decline on mix shift to SMAs and F-Series. (2) Revenue from long-term investments of $3.9-million, vs our $7.9-million, was subdued by a $5-million markdown at a legacy venture capital partner. With the portfolio weighted to mature, later-stage assets now in harvest, AGF lowered its 1–5 year return outlook to 6–8 per cent (8–10-per-cent long-term target maintained) and expects only 1–2 per cent for 2026. A material portion of the book is expected to be monetized over 1– 5 years, recycling capital into new affiliates. (3) Segregated accounts and sub-advisory AUM [assets under management] declined 12 per cent year-over-year on a $650-million institutional redemption tied to asset allocation ($150-million pre-announced); no further redemptions are known in 4Q. (4) Kensington’s private equity fund is down 7.5 per cent year-to-date. (5) 4Q-to-date mutual fund net redemptions of $48-million reflect risk-off sentiment, though combined flows including SMA/ETF remain positive. Recall that AGF funds are more equity-tilted.”

Mr. Ho lowered his full-year 2026 EPS forecast to $1.99 from $2.13 with his 2027 and 2028 estimates falling to $2.05 and $2.19, respectively, from $2.22 and $2.27.

Keeping a “buy” rating for AGF shares, he cut his target to $21 from $23. The average target is $20.75.

“We foresee a few near/medium-term positive catalysts: (1) SMA/ETF flows momentum; (2) redeployment of capital for organic growth to seed new private alt strategies and for share buybacks; (3) M&A should be EPS-accretive,” said Mr. Ho.

Elsewhere, others making target revisions include:

* TD Cowen’s Graham Ryding to $20 from $23 with a “buy” rating.

“Our takeaways from the earnings call are mixed. FCF is solid (buybacks and dividends), as is the balance sheet. AUM growth for the SMA channel remains strong. However, mutual fund flows have stalled, AGF Capital Partners is mixed, and the earnings contribution from AGF Capital Partners is balance sheet heavy,” said Mr. Ryding.

* Rbc’s Bart Dziarski to $20 from $23 with a “sector perform” rating.

“AGF shares declined 10 per cent [Wednesday] following Q3/26 adjusted EPS missing consensus due to a $3.3-million FV [fair value] loss on private investments (which can be lumpy) and guide-downs on i) net fee compression to 2-3 bps/annum (previously 2 bps/annum) and ii) 6-8-per-cent return from private investments (previously 8-10 per cent). We lower our estimates reflecting lower guidance and lower net flow assumptions as net flows remain benign,” said Mr. Dziarski.

Following a tour of Cameco Corp. ’s ( CCO-T ) “highly strategic” conversion and fuel manufacturing facilities in Port Hope, Ont., TD Cowen analyst Craig Hutchison sees an “improving outlook” driven by “rising price dynamics.”

“The Port Hope facility is Canada’s only uranium conversion facility and one of just two in North America,” he said in a client note. “The facility produces both UF6 [uranium hexafluoride] for light water reactors and UO2 [uranium dioxide]for Candu reactors domestically. The UF6 plant has a design capacity of 12.5M kgU, and produced a record 11.2M kgU in 2025. The company is targeting 2026 output of 13–14M kgU from its Port Hope fuel services business, broadly in line with 2025 production. Its current priorities are improving operational efficiency, controlling costs, and ramping output toward full design capacity as the global outlook for light-water reactors strengthens.”

Mr. Hutchison said he expects an improvement in margins as legacy contracts roll off and new contracts are added.

“As at the end of 2025, Cameco has 83M kgU of UF6 under long-term contracts, with some contracts going out 10 to 12 years,” he explained. “Conversion prices have remained elevated since 2022, supported by stronger demand, declining secondary supplies, and market disruption following the U.S. ban on Russian uranium imports. Long-term conversion prices currently stand at US$53/kgU, compared with Cameco’s average realized fuel services price of C$44.62/kgU, or US$32/kgU, in H1/2026. As new long-term contracts replace legacy agreements, we expect fuel services margins to improve, supporting stronger overall financial performance.

“The fuel conversion business currently accounts for 7 per cent of our Cameco operational NAV estimate, with potential upside as new markets emerge and margins expand.”

He reaffirmed a “buy” rating and $190 target for Cameco shares. The average is $182.59.

“Cameco remains one of the very few ways to invest in a publicly traded producing uranium miner, and, in our view, it is the most attractive way for investors to add uranium leverage to their portfolios,” he said.

Elsewhere, Rbc’s Mohamed Sidibé kept an “outperform” rating and $184 target.

“While the flowsheet May seem simple, achieving nameplate is hard,” he said. “Management emphasized that conversion scarcity also reflects the difficulty of operating capacity reliably. Cameco operates a wet process conversion process vs. most other facilities around the world using a dry process. Managing highly corrosive hydrofluoric acid and fluorine chemistry requires specialized equipment and operating experience. Elemental fluorine is produced onsite and cannot be stored, requiring close alignment between fluorine generation and the downstream process.

“Cameco’s vertical integration provides it with additional commercial flexibility. Management indicated that this allows Cameco on the contracting front as it can offer a bundled supply arrangement, and it helps in better understanding the flow of deals and information across the fuel cycle.”

In other analyst actions :
