stories.title: The big B.C. reshuffle continues ahead of snap election
stories.summary: Parties have until Oct. 3 to file candidate applications
stories.author: Andrea Woo, Mike Hager
stories.content:
John Rustad, who resurrected the Conservative Party of B.C. and brought it within three seats of forming government two years ago, is not seeking re-election in next month’s early vote, while former Green leader Andrew Weaver will return under the banner of the fledgling CentreBC party.

The announcements Wednesday add to a frenetic reshuffling of the province’s political landscape that has seen candidates change allegiances, leaders come and go and parties scramble to assemble slates for an election arriving two years early. On Tuesday, NDP Leader David Eby announced a snap election to be held on Oct. 24.

Mr. Rustad has represented the riding of Nechako Lakes since 2009 and served as party leader from 2023 to 2025, resigning amid a party revolt. He was ousted from caucus last Friday by former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay and rejoined on Monday.

“Under his leadership, our party grew from less than 2 per cent of the vote to Official Opposition,” the party said in a statement. “The Conservative Party of B.C. would never have reached where it is today without his conviction, hard work and willingness to stand up when few others would.”

Every other Conservative MLA will run again, the party said. As well, its board will “pursue the appropriate means” under its constitution and bylaws to ensure interim leader Lorne Doerkson “will remain leader if elected.”

Opinion: Is David Eby about to gamble away his government?

Meanwhile, CentreBC announced its recruitment of climate scientist and University of Victoria professor Andrew Weaver to run in his old riding of Oak Bay-Gordon Head.

Mr. Weaver joined the Conservative Party of B.C. earlier this year to vote for Kamloops Centre MLA Peter Milobar in the party’s leadership race, cancelling his membership when the polarizing Ms. Findlay won. He then supported CentreBC from the sidelines and was dismayed when seven of the eight Conservative MLAs who had joined the more centrist party, including Mr. Milobar, returned to the Tories on Tuesday.

Even with Mr. Doerkson replacing Ms. Findlay, who resigned Sunday, Mr. Weaver said he could not back a party whose membership had chosen her as leader just months earlier.

He agreed to run moments after learning that Elenore Sturko would remain and become CentreBC’s new leader.

“I thought, ‘Oh, for heaven’s sake. Does anyone have any principles left?’” he said in an interview Wednesday. “So I thought, you know what, Elenore needs help. She’s sticking her neck out there. Good for her. I’ve always respected her. So I let them know.”

Ms. Sturko, an independent MLA and former RCMP officer who was booted from the Conservatives a year ago after a falling out with Mr. Rustad, said CentreBC is now vetting applicants who want to run in all of the province’s 93 ridings.

Mr. Weaver said he hopes CentreBC can win enough seats to deny the NDP a majority government, noting the province’s $13.8-billion deficit under Mr. Eby.

“My wish is that there’s a minority government and that nobody trusts anyone with the keys to the House by themselves, because they have not demonstrated their ability to act like adults in the legislature,” he said.

The Editorial Board: The crosswinds of Canadian conservatism

Stewart Prest, a political science lecturer at the University of British Columbia, said the upstart CentreBC faces a massive uphill battle for relevance compared to the Conservatives. But, he said, Mr. Weaver qualifies as a star candidate capable of breaking through in the tony region that houses his alma mater, the University of Victoria.

“He’s the kind of person who can create his own weather in that particular riding,” Prof. Prest said.

Mr. Weaver was elected to the riding in 2013, becoming the province’s first Green MLA, and re-elected in 2017, when he and his two fellow Green MLAs signed a cooperation agreement with the New Democrats that swung a hung Parliament and ended 16 years of successive BC Liberal governments.

As CentreBC announced Mr. Weaver’s candidacy, NDP Leader Mr. Eby held a campaign event at a B.C.-Washington State border crossing in Surrey, where he pledged a tripling of a government advertising campaign to lure U.S. health care workers to the province if re-elected.

A $5-million blitz that started in June, 2025 and targeted workers in Washington State, Oregon and California has resulted in about 800 doctors, nurses and other health care professionals accepting job offers in B.C., Mr. Eby said. A re-elected NDP government would commit an additional $10-million and expand the campaign to Republican-controlled states where such workers face restrictions on their ability to provide life-saving reproductive care, he said.

Opinion: David Eby’s snap election call is cynical and self-serving

Mr. Eby’s remarks repeated the messaging of his election address one day earlier, when he sought to link B.C.’s political right to U.S. President Donald Trump and position the NDP as the party to stand up to Maga-style policies.

He cited a February, 2025, social media post by Conservative MLA Heather Maahs, who said that “Eby needs to comply” with the Trump administration’s demand to stop the flow of illicit fentanyl into the U.S. from Canada in order to avoid tariffs. He argued that a B.C. Conservative government would create the same repressive conditions from which U.S. health care workers are fleeing.

“If we turn our province into America Jr., we put all of that at risk,” Mr. Eby said.

(The Globe and Mail has debunked Mr. Trump’s claim that the synthetic opioid was pouring south across the border.)

The NDP also announced Wednesday that former Global News and CBC legislative reporter Richard Zussman will be its candidate in Saanich South.

Meanwhile, Brenda Bailey became the fourth NDP cabinet minister to announce that she would not be seeking re-election, after Ravi Kahlon, Lana Popham and Kelly Greene.

B.C. Green Leader Emily Lowan, who does not have a seat in the legislature, announced Wednesday that she will run in the riding of Saanich North and the Islands, after Green MLA Rob Botterell announced his retirement.

stories.title: From meat to the saddle: B.C. rancher trains yaks to carry riders
stories.summary: “Our hope is that as we raise them from calves to be well handled that you can continue training them and then they would have a purpose aside from just being butchered,”
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
For Jamie Kamps, yaks have traditionally been raised for one main purpose: meat.

Kamps, who operates Black Yak Cattle Co., has about 30 Tibetan yaks on her farm close to Salmon Arm. The herd is primarily raised for grass-finished meat, while cows and calves can also be raised for their wool and fibre.

Kamps estimates there are only about 1,000 yaks in Canada, making them a relatively uncommon livestock animal.

But one of her younger yaks, Toro, could have a different future. To one day carry a rider.

Yaks have traditionally been used in parts of Central Asia to carry people and heavy loads. Their thick coats also help them withstand cold conditions, with their winter coats growing longer and providing insulation in low temperatures.

Kamps describes the roughly one-and-a-half-year-old Toro as a “chill dude” who is calm, tolerant and easy to handle. She says that temperament has her looking beyond the traditional meat market and toward training some of her animals to become riding or pack yaks.

“So our hope is that as we raise them from calves to be well handled, that you can continue training them and then they would have a purpose aside from just being butchered,” Kamps said.

Toro is already being trained, and Kamps says he could potentially carry a rider at around two years old. She says yaks can also be trained to pull a sleigh or carry loads.

The animals’ build makes them suited to riding, according to Kamps. She says their hump works well with a Western saddle and that they can be less “flighty” than horses.

For Kamps, the idea is about giving some of her animals another purpose.

“Well, we found that the stock we’re producing have such a nice temperament and such great trainability that if they can be utilised for something outside the meat market, people enjoy them, they’ll have a good life as a pleasure animal, not just a meat animal.”

Kamps says the long-term goal is to build up a group of mature, well-trained animals that could be sold for packing and other recreational uses.

She also hopes to eventually use some of the mature animals for petting zoos and similar experiences, but only once they are old enough, trained and ready to safely interact with the public.

For now, that means waiting for the animals to grow and continuing their training. Toro is just one of the first yaks Kamps hopes can help demonstrate what these animals can do beyond the meat market.

stories.title: How President Trump’s White House bans have left Fanshawe journalists feeling unsettled
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/7EffmiqaJsQ Journalists at Fanshawe College are concerned and unsure about the future of jour...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
Journalists at Fanshawe College are concerned and unsure about the future of journalism in politics because of the recent spat between U.S. President Donald Trump and American news media.

The uncertainty comes in the aftermath of President Trump banning CNN, Msnbc, and Politico from the White House, accusing them of being “fake news”. In retaliation, several news outlets have either boycotted the White House’s press releases or have declined to collect audio from Trump as he speaks.

“This has been taken to a whole different level,” said Steve Young, the former news and information director at CTV News London and current program coordinator of Fanshawe’s multimedia journalism program. He also said he was unsurprised that the journalistic community was acting in support of the banned publications.

A collection of logos for London-based news outlets. Journalists in the city believe their profession’s community would support each other if they and politicians became at odds like in the U.S. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

“It is very important from a journalistic standpoint that we all stand up and say ‘we have a right to be able to hold politicians accountable,'” said Young. “You don’t know if their media organization might be the next one to be banned from the White House.”

The concerns extend to those entering the journalistic community as well. When asked, several students in the multimedia journalism program shared many of the same feelings on the situation between President Trump and U.S. news media.

“I feel like he’s forcing other companies to have one opinion and one opinion only,” said Owen Schuller. “The whole point of a journalist is be [unopinionated] and to have just the facts right.”

Fellow student Georgia Chambers echoed Schuller’s concerns about President Trump’s relationship with news media, saying she feels he is “a little bit scared of the media” and that she believes it to be the reason for his actions.

Another concern raised was how the situation might change the relationship between politicians and journalists, who are traditionally referred to in politics as the “fourth estate”.

“I do think it’s going to create a big rift in the media and political landscape going forward,” said Ryan Baynton, another student in the journalism program.

The impact of the situation May not be limited to the U.S. Schuller, Chambers, and Baynton each expressed concern that a shift in how journalists deal with politics could affect their careers.

Young also commented on the possibility of politician/journalist relationships in Canada changing because of the situation, saying he hopes they will not. Him and Baynton both believe if it did happen though, the journalistic community would respond the same way it has to President Trump.

“We have to have that ability to be able to [hold politicians accountable] on this side of the border,” said Young.

As for what will happen next, Young believes that journalists will continue to be a part of politics, and that the banned outlets will get access to President Trump by going to other locations or by taking the bans to court to try to have them lifted.

“It will be very interesting to see how this ends,” said Young. “How that will happen is anybody’s guess.”

stories.title: Western university unveils indigenous themed mural
stories.summary: Western University unveiled a new mural depicting the creation story of the Anishinabek tribe. The mural, depi...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
Western University unveiled a new mural depicting the creation story of the Anishinabek tribe. The mural, depicting how the Earth was created on the back of a turtle shell according to the Anishinabek myth, was revealed on Sept 21 at the Thames Hall Jeff and Shelley Parr Family Atrium.

“T here are different versions of the creation story .” Said Jeanette Ladd, the painter of the mural. “O ther people that you know share the same story, b ut there might be a little bit of a tweak of something added. O ur language is spoken not written so things, May have changed along the way.”

Radd was able to create this mural for Western through a special program Western was hosting. “I t was an open proposal for any artist to apply,” Radd said. “ I love the creation story and so I wanted t o paint it. Yo u could have chosen like any of the walls within the atrium space you could do anything in the atrium space. I had to d o like a timeline of how long it would take, materials that I wanted to use, even the maintenance of the piece if I was the accepted artist.”

Radd hopes that her art brings comfort to Western students, both indigenous and otherwise. “F or the indigenous students I want them to see a little little piece of home like. F or the other students, I’m hoping that they feel a piece of calm when they look at the piece .”

Western’s students seem to really appreciate the new mural, and what it represents. “I think it’s a beutiful piece to add to Western,” said Jacklyn Bagley, a student at Western University. “I’ve honestly never seen anything that represents Indigenous identity and culture at Western, so I think it’s a great staple.”

stories.title: Politics Insider: Ottawa City Council votes to rename Trump Avenue
stories.summary: Residents of the street no longer want to be associated with the U.S. President
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Ottawa City Council today voted unanimously to rename Trump Avenue, a residential street named more than 20 years ago.

The street is a part of an Ottawa neighbourhood called Central Park, which is filled with New York-themed names such as Staten Way, Bloomingdale Street and Grammercy Park. The U.S. President was basically a Manhattan novelty act when the streets were first set out in the subdivision.

“I’m embarrassed that in the nation’s capital we have Donald Trump honoured in this respect,” Riley Brockington, the city councillor whose ward contains the street, told council when he initially brought up the rebranding idea in the heat of the trade war between Canada and the U.S.

Now that the motion has passed, the councillor said he’ll form a working group with a handful of residents to come up with new potential names to put to a vote.

Mr. Brockington said no other street in his ward generates anything near the “constant” volume of complaints that Trump Avenue does. This is the second attempt to change the street’s name, after a 2021 effort that was strategic in its timing, the councillor said.

“I said, I don’t want to do anything while he’s in office because I feared retribution – honest to goodness” he said. “So he came out of office January ’21, and that’s when I did the outreach.”

That process failed to get two-thirds of the residents of the street to vote in favour of the change. Mr. Brockington suspects that those who voted no at the time didn’t necessarily like the original name – they just didn’t want to be bothered changing their addresses.

Trump says Canada is ‘destroying itself’ with ‘unchecked’ immigration: Trump took aim at Canada again today, this time to claim that it is allowing millions of people into the country “essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

Amid shifting political winds, Canada gets more of the spotlight on the UN’s stage: Since a watershed speech to the World Economic Forum in January, Prime Minister Mark Carney has become a leading voice of what he and some others call “middle powers.”

Canada ratifies landmark High Seas Treaty and commits funding to ocean protection: Carney pledged $82-million over five years to a global ocean-monitoring alliance, highlighting Canada’s responsibilities as a country with the world’s longest coastline.

Prime Minister’s Day: Carney was in New York this morning, where he spoke at a United Nations event to support the OceanEye International Alliance before heading back to Ottawa. Party Leaders: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre attended his party’s caucus meeting on Parliament Hill. NDP Leader Avi Lewis hit the picket lines with striking Bank of Canada security guards. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May spoke to reporters about the government’s new economic legislation, Bill C-39, which she called “a monster, in every sense of the word.” Belleville synagogue shooting makes it into Parliament: Belleville residents are angry and looking for answers after a shooting on Sunday outside a synagogue in the Ontario city, said Liberal MP Chris Malette, who represents the area. Stephanie Levitz reports.

“Canada’s special envoy is here. Diana – make sure I get the last name right – Fox Carney, who’s working tirelessly on this.” – Prime Minister Mark Carney , at the United Nations OceanEye International Alliance event, speaking about his wife, who has been named Canada’s first Ocean Envoy.

With B.C. Premier David Eby officially calling a snap election, the province’s Conservative Party is scrambling to present a united front in the hopes of winning power from the NDP. How many leaders (or interim leaders) has the party had since becoming Official Opposition in March, 2023? (Bonus points for their names!)

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Mark Carney gets to work on the plumbing

In its first year, Mr. Carney’s government built a lot of workarounds and special powers that were supposed to cut through the thicket of bureaucracy. Now, it’s trying to clear away some of that underbrush. Now, it’s trying to clear away some of that underbrush. — Campbell Clark

David Eby’s snap election call is cynical and self-serving

In a stunning display of mind over matter, Mr. Eby didn’t even turn red as he uttered the ridiculous defence of his actions. — Gary Mason

Canadian airports can anchor a global infrastructure champion

Private airport owners would create more opportunities for travellers to drop stupid amounts of money on cucumber-lined Hendrick’s martinis or Rolex watches. That’s discretionary consumer spending. Want to curtail the cost of a trip? Avoid airport restaurants and retailers. stories.title: Students hit the stage for ‘School of Rock’ musical at London’s The Grand theatre
stories.summary: The Grand Theatre High School Project is blasting, bringing the tunes to downtown London this fall. Local students are hitting the stage with their own version of the 2003 blockbuster film, ‘School of Rock’.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The Grand Theatre High School Project is blasting, bringing the tunes to downtown London this fall. Local students are hitting the stage with their own version of the 2003 blockbuster film, ‘School of Rock’.

Professional theatre director Lezlie Wade says the students are putting on quite a show and highlighting their many talents.

“This performance is such a great chance for them to explore the rock and roll side of their personalities and slightly rebellious side as well,” said Wade.

“However, it’s very inspirational.”

H.B Beal Secondary School student Isaac De Melo plays the role of Dewey Finn in the musical, a fake substitute teacher who helps the kids get out of their shell.

“I would say it’s a group full of kids who just want to be heard and I’m trying to let them find their voice,” said De Melo.

Isabelle Parent is another Beal student who plays the part of the principal in the play, Rosalie Mullins.

“She kind of has this hardened exterior but she grew up loving rock music and that’s discovered later in the show,” said Parent.

“With Dewey’s help, she rediscovers her younger self.”

Wade says the group on stage performs like pros.

“It doesn’t look like they are students and that great and the greatest compliment you can pay them,” Wade said.

If you would like to catch the first production of the brand-new season at the Grand Theatre, School of Rock is on now until Oct. 3.

Professional theatre director Lezlie Wade says the students are putting on quite a show and highlighting their many talents.
“This performance is such a great chance for them to explore the rock and roll side of their personalities and slightly rebellious side as well,” said Wade.
“However, it’s very inspirational.”
H.B Beal Secondary School student Isaac De Melo plays the role of Dewey Finn in the musical, a fake substitute teacher who helps the kids get out of their shell.
“I would say it’s a group full of kids who just want to be heard and I’m trying to let them find their voice,” said De Melo.
Isabelle Parent is another Beal student who plays the part of the principal in the play, Rosalie Mullins.
“She kind of has this hardened exterior but she grew up loving rock music and that’s discovered later in the show,” said Parent.
“With Dewey’s help, she rediscovers her younger self.”
Wade says the group on stage performs like pros.
“It doesn’t look like they are students and that great and the greatest compliment you can pay them,” Wade said.
If you would like to catch the first production of the brand-new season at the Grand Theatre, School of Rock is on now until Oct. 3.

stories.title: Alberta activist convicted of promoting hatred at Toronto's Pride Parade
stories.summary: William Whatcott's “intention in handing out the flyers at the parade was to vilify gay men,” said the judge.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
An Albertan who, along with six of his followers, donned skin-tight, lime-green spandex body suits with matching green hooded masks and handed out anti-gay pamphlets disguised as condoms at Toronto’s Pride Parade a decade back has been convicted of wilfully promoting hatred.

William Whatcott, who accessorized his parade outfit with a tutu and a rainbow-striped cape, was originally acquitted of the charge, but the Crown appealed because the trial judge refused to hear from an expert on the history of anti-gay discrimination. Ontario’s top court saw that as an error and ordered a new trial. The Supreme Court of Canada declined to hear Whatcott’s appeal.

His new trial in Ontario’s Superior Court of Justice heard that, ON July 3, 2016, Whatcott marched with his followers in the parade after obtaining a permit by “falsely representing” the group as the “Gay Zombies Cannabis Consumers Association” using a fake name.

In his parade application, Whatcott “falsely told the organizers that his contingent consisted of ‘zombies who are gay and who smoke pot’ and that their message was ‘to have fun’ but to do so ‘responsibly and safely,’” said the recent decision. “He said they would provide ‘zombie safesex packets’ to ‘encourage zombies to be safe when having sex or when playing with blood sports.’”

Although Whatcott was “required to get advance approval for any handouts,” he didn’t provide a sample to parade organizers.

“Based on the evidence in the trial before me, I am satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the flyer distributed by Mr. Whatcott and his fellow Zombies promoted hatred of gay men, as defined in the case law, and also that Mr. Whatcott willfully distributed the flyer knowing this to be the case,” Justice Anne Molloy wrote in her Sept. 16 verdict.

Each of the people in Whatcott’s group “carried a large shoulder bag containing packages of what appeared to be condoms, but which instead contained a folded-up flyer printed on both sides with what is alleged in this case to be anti-gay messaging,” said the judge.

“As they continued along the parade route, the Gay Zombies handed out 3,000 of these packages.”

One recipient complained to the Toronto Police Service. Whatcott, whose name and contact information were on the flyer, was charged with inciting hatred against gay men.

“The content of the flyers is partly about the health risks associated with gay men, partly about their sinful ways and criminal conduct, and partly about government figures said to have been associated with the gay agenda in a negative way,” Molloy said.

“Gay men are portrayed as immoral and a danger to children. It is thinly disguised scare-mongering and loaded with toxic imagery. However, it also includes calls for sinners to repent and messages that God loves them.”

An expert on the history of anti-gay discrimination — Nick Mulé, a practising psychotherapist and an associate professor at York University — testified that Whatcott’s pamphlets include demeaning tropes that identify “gay men as carriers of disease,” and “references to the gay lifestyle as being sordid; the use of pejorative terms like sodomy and homosexual; references to pedophilia, recruiting children to become gay, and feeding false information to children who then change their genders; and repeated strong religiosity and references to sinful conduct.”

Whatcott, 58, who once worked as a registered nurse but now drives a school bus and cleans carpets part-time in Calgary, self-identified on the stand as a “‘conservative evangelical’ who believes the Bible to be the word of God and authoritative.” He said he believes that sex is “sinful unless between one man and one woman within a lifelong marriage.”

Whatcott “acknowledged he told lies in the course of getting permission for the Gay Zombies to participate in the 2016 Gay Pride parade,” said the decision.

When confronted with the statement “that there is a Christian duty not to engage in trickery and not to lie,” Whatcott responded: “It’s not an absolute prohibition, for a tactical purpose one can do it. Certainly in wartime, it’s used and I viewed this as a spiritual war and an act of activism.”

These were ‘commandos’ on the attack against gay culture, with hatred and mockery.

After the parade, Whatcott “gleefully posted photos of his group, with messaging to his followers that he conceded constituted gloating,” the judge said.

“Looking at the whole picture, Mr. Whatcott, by his actions, has demonstrated a deep animus towards members of the gay community, notwithstanding his testimony that he wants only to save their souls by having them repent their sins. He is far from a simple Christian missionary seeking to convert sinners. He is an activist and an attention-seeker. He loves the spectacle of what he did, he enjoyed the attention, and he continues to do so.”

Many of the “things included in his flyer, standing alone, are merely offensive and would not amount to hate,” said the judge.

“However, the combined effect of the whole flyer, the lengths to which Mr. Whatcott went to deliver his ‘message,’ the range of people he gave it to, and his gloating after the fact all support my ultimate finding that his intention in handing out the flyers at the parade was to vilify gay men. He knew that would be the effect of his actions.”

On top of that, “the carnival-like costumes he and his ‘commandos’ wore to conduct this ‘truth assault’ were a mockery rather than a genuine attempt to persuade sinners to repent,” Molloy said.

“These were not respectful Christians come to help guide people away from unhealthy sexual practices or to convince gay men to repent their sins and find God. These were ‘commandos’ on the attack against gay culture, with hatred and mockery.”

stories.title: End of the road coming for ‘End of the World’? Erosion impacts Edmonton viewpoint
stories.summary: Keillor Point — which for years was also known as “End of the World” — has been impacted by the record-setting rainfalls Edmonton experienced in June and July 2026.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
The end May be near for the “ End of the World ” as we know it.

Keillor Point — which for years was also known as “End of the World” — sits at the top of the riverbank in the Belgravia neighbourhood.

It’s above the remains of Keillor Road, which was closed to traffic in 1994 before crumbling into the river valley due to erosion.

Now, the City of Edmonton says what claimed the road three decades ago is now affecting the viewpoint below Saskatchewan Drive, between 74 Avenue and 76 Avenue.

This summer’s record-setting rainfalls in June and July worsened the slope instability at the Keillor Point viewing area, which the city built into an official spot after decades of people clandestinely visiting the lookout in the North Saskatchewan River valley.

The fenced-off area was restricted and regularly patrolled — but it didn’t deter those looking to take in the view and party at the secluded spot, where visitors got to by going down a steep section of embankment.

For years, the city tried to stop people from going to the scenic and remote spot offering a breathtaking view of the river valley and west Edmonton, but eventually conceded — adopting an “if you can’t beat them, join them” mentality when it became clear signs forbidding entry were doing little to deter visitors.

City council approved engineering work on the lookout in 2017 and a staircase, hand railing, formalized viewing area and granular trail opened in 2019 . The lookout was officially renamed Keillor Point.

The viewpoint was built to make the space safer and protect people from falling down the steep embankment or getting injured on exposed rebar and deteriorating concrete.

Before the city built the current lookout, large pillars of an old retaining wall formed a makeshift ledge to sit on.

On Wednesday, the city said since construction of the viewing platform about eight years ago, regular geotechnical inspections and monitoring have confirmed continued deterioration of the slopes due to erosion and localized instability.

The massive amount of rain this summer accelerated that deterioration, the city said.

The current viewing platform is supported by the remnants of a pile wall originally installed to stabilize a portion of Keillor Road.

“The extreme conditions this summer caused additional loss of support for the structure,” the city said.

No plan to fix the current issues has been released.

The city has installed barricades and temporary signs to prevent access to an extended portion of the viewing area and platform. Permanent signs with additional info will be installed soon, the city said.

The site will be regularly inspected to monitor conditions and public safety risks, and the city said further engineering work will “help inform longer-term options for the viewing area.”

In 2015, the city conducted a survey on “The End of the World .” A total of 2,568 citizens participated and 2,282 completed the survey, including nearly 600 Belgravia residents.

About half of the respondents had been to the site in the previous year and many came to enjoy the unrestricted view.

The main concerns for respondents were the height of the fence and whether the site would lose its “natural” feel.

stories.title: Pro wrestler Paul Leduc thrilled crowds as half of an axe-wielding tag team of faux lumberjacks
stories.summary: He and his fictional brother, Jos Leduc, attracted huge numbers of fans to their bouts, which often featured clashes with the Rougeau family and the notorious Vachon brothers
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
The brothers Paul and Jos Leduc wore tuques topped by a pompom, grew chinstrap beards and donned checked flannel shirts open to the navel.

Like any tough lumberjacks from the backwoods of Quebec, they also carried axes.

The fearsome tag team engaged in sweaty, bloody combat against other professional wrestlers, most notably feuding with the Rougeau family and the notorious brothers Maurice (Mad Dog) and Paul (The Butcher) Vachon.

Between Expo 67 and the 1976 Olympics, the Leduc brothers were an attraction on bills luring large crowds to the Forum in Montreal and Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto. The Leducs also built a dedicated Quebec fan base by performing in arenas and baseball parks in such cities as Sherbrooke, Trois-Rivières and Cap-de-la-Madeleine.

Paul Leduc, who has died at the age of 89, was the smaller of the pair, standing at 5 foot 10 (1.78 metres) and weighing 195 pounds (88.5 kilograms). His brother was a massive figure, carrying 280 pounds (127 kilograms) on a slighter taller frame.

On one notable occasion, Paul brought a foreign object into the wrestling ring – a wedding ring. In that match, he was less interested in a headlock than in wedlock. Paul married Pierrette Brault in what might be called a double-ring ceremony before either 5,000 (according to the Montreal Gazette) or 10,000 (Montréal-Matin) paying guests (top ticket $4) as the opening match of a wrestling card featuring 37 fighters at the Forum on Dec. 27, 1971.

The bride wore a white silk gown with a fur-trimmed hood. The groom wore a tuxedo and a toque. Father Paul Aquin, who had married the couple two hours earlier at the Mary, Queen of the World Cathedral, once again conducted the ceremony, only this time his invocation of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost was each cheered by the crowd. The Forum organist played such tunes as Strangers in the Night, I’m in the Mood for Love and (Where Do I Begin?) Love Story.

The newlyweds cut their wedding cake with a swift chop from a hatchet.

Jos Leduc, who had served as best man, then joined the other wrestlers – including football’s Angelo Mosca, Baron Scicluna, Little Brutus, Little Beaver, Sky Low Low, Pee Wee Adams, Frenchy Lamont, Sonny Boy Hayes, Farmer Boy Jerome and Abdullah the Butcher – for several hours of sweaty grappling.

The newlyweds avoided such entanglements by heading off to honeymoon at a motel in Florida.

Soon after, the Leduc brothers were wrestling throughout the Sunshine State as well as in Texas, avoiding their home province’s cruel winters.

While the Vachon brothers hailed from the same family, the Leducs’ backstory was fiction, a gimmick created to whet the appetite of wrestling crowds. The pair maintained the kayfabe (the pro wrestler code of staying in character in public and never acknowledging any scripted outcome) until Jos Leduc died in 1999. It was then revealed Jos was a former policeman who had legally changed his name, as Paul Leduc did in 1977.

Paul Leduc’s real-life story was as compelling as that of his fictional alter ego, if not more so. Orphaned at 13, he learned to wrestle in Mexico. After retiring from the ring, he became a central figure in a shocking incident of picket-line violence. He later ran a wrestling promotion known by the eyebrow-raising acronym FLQ.

Joseph Léodard Mimeault, as he was originally named, was born on Nov. 10, 1936, in Saint-Maxime-du-Mont-Louis, a fishing village on the northern Gaspé coast. He was the youngest of 15 children, not all of whom survived infancy, born to Hortense Lemieux and Edmond Mimeault, a farmer. His father died when the boy was four. When his mother died of a heart ailment nine years later, he went into foster care before elder siblings were able to take him in, according to Pat Laprade of TVA Sports.

He played hockey and trained as an amateur wrestler, a purely athletic endeavour unlike the scripted spectacle of the pro variety. After deciding to become a professional wrestler, he went south to Mexico to learn the trade. On his return to his native province, he adopted the character of a Roman gladiator. A contemporary photograph shows him in a toga with a helmet, while carrying a dog-topped sceptre in one hand and a leash attached to a drooling St. Bernard in the other.

Fighting under the name Del Leo Mimolt, the undersized (by wrestling standards) grappler struggled to build a following. It was only after he persuaded a friend named Michel Pigeon, a former constable with the provincial police, to join him in the ring that he found success.

They were introduced as the Leduc brothers from Godbout, a forestry town across the mouth of the St. Lawrence from Paul’s birthplace. The Vachon brothers had run a lumberjack gimmick before them, but only on the road. The Leducs would become heroes in their home province.

The early storyline debuted in 1968 had Paul being beaten in the ring before being rescued when his gargantuan, though awkward, brother Jos entered the fray.

The Leducs were marketable and they bounced between promotions, winning tag-team championships with Stampede Wrestling out of Calgary, as well as a Florida championship with the National Wrestling Alliance in 1973.

By jumping to the Vachon brothers’ Grand Prix Wrestling promotion in the early 1970s, the Leducs became the baby face (good guys) foils to the Vachon heels (bad guys). The brothers attracted massive crowds in Quebec, including one for a steel-cage match at the Colisée in Quebec City that was so successful the attendance, which was several thousand beyond legal capacity, could not be reported for fear the next show would be shut down.

“When the Mad Dog bit you,” Paul Leduc once said, “you felt it for two or three days.”

At a public memorial for Mr. Vachon, as reported by Mike Wyman for Slam Wrestling, Mr. Leduc recalled a dramatic bout during which Mad Dog fired his brother, the Butcher, mid-bout, vowing to defeat both Leducs on his own.

“The crowd started cheering him and booing us,” Mr. Leduc said. “At that moment Mad Dog Vachon became Good Dog Vachon. The crowd turned against us and the chairs started flying.”

Jos was the bigger attraction of the two faux brothers, and the pair often fought separately with Paul occupying bouts on the undercard. That was not always a disadvantage, as in Florida in 1974, Paul had the good fortune to be teamed with Haystacks Calhoun, who was billed as “the world’s biggest wrestler” at 601 pounds (273 kilograms). They won their match.

Heart troubles persuaded Mr. Leduc to abandon the ring and retire his tuque and flannel shirt.

Before doing so, he took a position as a vice-president with the Bureau des detectives industrielles, a private-security company.

On July 22, 1977, striking Robin Hood flour mill workers and their supporters protested at the mill, which stayed in production by hiring strikebreakers. As a small group of protesters advanced toward the mill, Mr. Leduc’s security guards fired shotguns, wounding eight protesters. The images of overweight men in shorts, T-shirts and mismatched helmets shooting at unarmed protesters shocked viewers of the nightly news.

It also overnight turned Mr. Leduc from a sporting hero to a villain.

“I was driving to work this morning and people on the street were shaking their fists at me,” he told Richard Cleroux of The Globe and Mail. “When I was wrestling, I was always the good guy. Suddenly, I’m a bad guy. I’ve become a licensed killer for hire. That’s not pleasant when that happens.

“I’ve been called a traitor and told that I’m not a true Quebecker. I’ve been told, ‘You work for Americans and live with the English’ and it’s going to affect me.

“I heard one woman say on an open-line radio show this morning that ‘the Leduc brothers lived off workers because workers went to their matches and cheered them and now they shoot workers down for the bosses.’ I don’t like that.”

The notorious incident added powerful momentum to demands for the Parti Québécois to ban the use of replacement workers, enacting what is known by unions as anti-scab legislation, which the provincial government did later that year.

Mr. Leduc’s new-found notoriety did not prevent him from finding lucrative work. One day, media magnate Pierre Péladeau saw him being interviewed on television. He called the studio and told him he wanted to hire him for Québecor. When Mr. Leduc arrived at the head office, he overheard a secretary on the phone pleading, “But Mr. Péladeau what do you want that I do with a former wrestler?!”

He worked as a travelling salesman for the company before becoming director-general of Messageries Dynamiques, a Québecor division that distributed such newspapers as Le Soleil and Le Journal de Montréal.

Mr. Leduc wrote a wrestling column in French titled, “1-2-3,” echoing a ring referee’s countdown to a clinch.

He also operated a wrestling school with his son and held weekly bouts in the hall of the St-Jean-Berchmans church in Montreal. He called his promotion the Fédération de Lutte Québécoise, which used as an acronym FLQ, the same as the violent revolutionary group responsible for bombings and the murder of a Quebec cabinet minister during the 1970 October Crisis. The crowd’s chant of “F-L-Q! F-L-Q!” gained some media attention.

Mr. Leduc died in Montreal on Aug. 30 following six weeks of hospitalization for cardiorenal syndrome. He leaves a daughter, Kim; sons Yan and Carl, the latter of whom followed his father into the ring as a pro wrestler; as well as two grandchildren by marriage. He was predeceased by his wife, Pierrette, his bride from the Forum, who died in 2011. He was also predeceased by all his siblings, the most recent being brother Denis Mimeault, who died in 2021, aged 88.

Mr. Leduc endured many travails before finding success in the wrestling ring. Eager to be accepted by the other pro wrestlers, as a rookie he agreed to drive promoter Larry (Babe) Kasaboski and wrestlers Killer Kowalski and Édouard Carpentier (né Weiczorkiewicz) on a trip from Montreal through a tour of Northern Ontario, he told wrestling writer Gary Howard. Once in the car, the other three men spoke solely in Polish for the entire journey.

To add injury to insult, they made the young wrestler grapple with Terrible Marcus, a 181-kilogram (400-pound) bear. The bruin pinned the human as part of a card at Memorial Gardens in North Bay. The beast’s trainer rewarded the animal with a jug of pop. The defeated wrestler then had to drive the others home. It is unknown if he learned along the way the meaning of the word niedźwiedź , Polish for bear.

That was not always a disadvantage, as in Florida in 1974, Paul had the good fortune to be teamed with Haystacks Calhoun, who was billed as “the world’s biggest wrestler” at 601 pounds (273 kilograms). They won their match.

content_blocks.caption: The fictional brothers would become heroes in their home province before heart troubles persuaded Paul Leduc to abandon the ring. Paul Leduc Collection/Supplied

content_blocks.text: Heart troubles persuaded Mr. Leduc to abandon the ring and retire his tuque and flannel shirt.
Before doing so, he took a position as a vice-president with the Bureau des detectives industrielles, a private-security company.

On July 22, 1977, striking Robin Hood flour mill workers and their supporters protested at the mill, which stayed in production by hiring strikebreakers. As a small group of protesters advanced toward the mill, Mr. Leduc’s security guards fired shotguns, wounding eight protesters. The images of overweight men in shorts, T-shirts and mismatched helmets shooting at unarmed protesters shocked viewers of the nightly news.
It also overnight turned Mr. Leduc from a sporting hero to a villain.

“I was driving to work this morning and people on the street were shaking their fists at me,” he told Richard Cleroux of The Globe and Mail. “When I was wrestling, I was always the good guy. Suddenly, I’m a bad guy. I’ve become a licensed killer for hire. That’s not pleasant when that happens.
“I’ve been called a traitor and told that I’m not a true Quebecker. I’ve been told, ‘You work for Americans and live with the English’ and it’s going to affect me.

“I heard one woman say on an open-line radio show this morning that ‘the Leduc brothers lived off workers because workers went to their matches and cheered them and now they shoot workers down for the bosses.’ I don’t like that.”

The notorious incident added powerful momentum to demands for the Parti Québécois to ban the use of replacement workers, enacting what is known by unions as anti-scab legislation, which the provincial government did later that year.

Mr. Leduc’s new-found notoriety did not prevent him from finding lucrative work. One day, media magnate Pierre Péladeau saw him being interviewed on television. He called the studio and told him he wanted to hire him for Québecor. When Mr. Leduc arrived at the head office, he overheard a secretary on the phone pleading, “But Mr. Péladeau what do you want that I do with a former wrestler?!”

content_blocks.caption: Paul Leduc during the TOW tv pilots in 2013. Paul Leduc Collection/Supplied

content_blocks.text: He worked as a travelling salesman for the company before becoming director-general of Messageries Dynamiques, a Québecor division that distributed such newspapers as Le Soleil and Le Journal de Montréal.
Mr. Leduc wrote a wrestling column in French titled, “1-2-3,” echoing a ring referee’s countdown to a clinch.

He also operated a wrestling school with his son and held weekly bouts in the hall of the St-Jean-Berchmans church in Montreal. He called his promotion the Fédération de Lutte Québécoise, which used as an acronym FLQ, the same as the violent revolutionary group responsible for bombings and the murder of a Quebec cabinet minister during the 1970 October Crisis. The crowd’s chant of “F-L-Q! F-L-Q!” gained some media attention.

Mr. Leduc died in Montreal on Aug. 30 following six weeks of hospitalization for cardiorenal syndrome. He leaves a daughter, Kim; sons Yan and Carl, the latter of whom followed his father into the ring as a pro wrestler; as well as two grandchildren by marriage. He was predeceased by his wife, Pierrette, his bride from the Forum, who died in 2011. He was also predeceased by all his siblings, the most recent being brother Denis Mimeault, who died in 2021, aged 88.

Mr. Leduc endured many travails before finding success in the wrestling ring. Eager to be accepted by the other pro wrestlers, as a rookie he agreed to drive promoter Larry (Babe) Kasaboski and wrestlers Killer Kowalski and Édouard Carpentier (né Weiczorkiewicz) on a trip from Montreal through a tour of Northern Ontario, he told wrestling writer Gary Howard. Once in the car, the other three men spoke solely in Polish for the entire journey.

To add injury to insult, they made the young wrestler grapple with Terrible Marcus, a 181-kilogram (400-pound) bear. The bruin pinned the human as part of a card at Memorial Gardens in North Bay. The beast’s trainer rewarded the animal with a jug of pop. The defeated wrestler then had to drive the others home. It is unknown if he learned along the way the meaning of the word niedźwiedź , Polish for bear.

stories.title: Entrepreneur restores, then donates property to charity fighting addiction, homelessness
stories.summary: Mandy Rennehan has spent her entire career renovating, restoring and transforming older properties. Now she’s gifted one of them, a multi-unit rental property, to a nonprofit organization in her hometown.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Yarmouth, N.S. – Mandy Rennehan has spent her entire career renovating, restoring and transforming older properties. Now she’s gifted one of them, a multi-unit rental property, to a non-profit organization in her hometown.

Rennehan, a Yarmouth, N.S., native who starred in the Hgtv show “Trading Up” and is nicknamed Canada’s “Blue Collar CEO,” restored a six-unit building and transformed it into a profitable rental property.

“For three years, we’ve been ‘the’ luxury Airbnb in town, and it’s done extremely well,” she said.

Rennehan has now donated the building to the Souls Harbour Rescue Mission, which supports people battling addiction, hunger and homelessness.

The facility has been renamed Souls Harbour South. It will continue to operate as a short-term rental business and the money raised will support hundreds of people living in the Yarmouth area who need assistance.

“I think it is awesome,” Rennehan said. “To be able to give them something like this, it allows them to have that income that can then give to more people.”

Souls Harbour CEO Michelle Porter said the donation came at a time when the need to help people living in Nova Scotia has never been greater. She added that one thing the organization does well is “that we don’t forget the smaller towns.”

“While we are receiving Souls Harbour South, the big thing in my heart is how many people that will help as a living legacy,” said Porter. “It is true, it is better to give than receive, and our level of gratitude over this incredible gift is difficult for all of us to express.”

Souls Harbour South will also create opportunities for local community members to gain work experience and hospitality skills while rebuilding their lives.

Rennehan inspired by personal experience

Rennehan, who was appointed to the Order of Canada in 2025 , said her own family has experienced addiction. She said she watched her brother Troy struggle with alcoholism.

“You hear people say when they had that first drink, that was it. He was that guy,” she said.

Troy, now sober, said he’s “very proud” of himself “for what I have accomplished and what I have turned out to be.” He added that his sister is a big reason for his sobriety.

“I’m thankful Mandy has been with me, every step of the way.”

While supporting her brother, Rennehan felt her hometown needed to do more to assist people battling addiction. She said she wanted to “build pride back through architecture,” which led to her idea of restoring the property.

“We need more places for people to go.”

stories.title: Fact File: Checks in place to prevent non-Albertans from mailing in referendum votes
stories.summary: Edmonton - A viral post on the social media platform X this week shared a claim that mail-in voting for Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum is “open to anybody” without verification of whether applicants live in the province. Other social media users posted screenshots suggesting they had been able to apply for a mail-in ballot using fake addresses outside the pro…
stories.author: Timon Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada

Edmonton - A viral post on the social media platform X this week shared a claim that mail-in voting for Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum is “open to anybody” without verification of whether applicants live in the province. Other social media users posted screenshots suggesting they had been able to apply for a mail-in ballot using fake addresses outside the province. But Elections Alberta says it checks all special ballot applications against its voter registration system to exclude any fraudulent ones, and proof of ID is also required to cast a ballot.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘Nothing can ever really bring justice’: Family speaks after guilty plea in Esther Jones homicide
stories.summary: The family of a Nova Scotia woman who was the victim of a homicide two years ago says the discovery of her remains still doesn't bring closure.
stories.author: Ella Macdonald, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
The family of a Nova Scotia woman who was the victim of a homicide two years ago says the discovery of her remains still doesn’t bring closure .

They face another long road ahead as they plan to fight to keep Esther Jones’ killer behind bars.

for a brutal murder of my little sister,” said Judy Uhlman.

Jones, 55, was reported missing from Torbrook, N.S., in Annapolis County, ON Sept. 2, 2024, and was last seen at the Kingston Bible College in Greenwood two days earlier.

On Sept. 13, 2024, RCMP revealed that their investigation into Jones’ disappearance had identified enough information to lay a charge of first-degree murder against Dale Allen Toole.

Earlier this month, Toole pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of second-degree murder.

Jones’ remains were found on Sept. 9 in a wooded area in Cloud Lake, south of Greenwood, N.S.

Now, Jones’ 13 brothers and sisters, as well as their families, are trying to keep her memory at the forefront.

“The older she got, I think the kinder she was in looking out for people,” said Uhlman.

For more on this story, watch the video above.

stories.title: Northwest Territories latest to stay on daylight time year-round
stories.summary: Clocks will not have to go back an hour on Nov. 1, the government says, when time change would occur in the Northwest Territories.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Northwest Territories government says it is officially ending seasonal time changes.

The territory’s new permanent time standard, known as Northwest Territories time, will be observed year-round.

Clocks will not have to go back an hour on Nov. 1, the government says, when time change would occur in the Northwest Territories.

The territory will now share a common time with Alberta and Saskatchewan.

The government says that for most residents, the transition is expected to be simple as devices running the latest software are to receive the time zone update once it is released by system providers.

It says the change comes after public feedback in 2022, when more than 3,500 residents participated in an online survey, with more than 87 per cent supporting ending the practice of changing the clocks twice a year.

The territory says respondents most commonly expressed a preference for maintaining mountain daylight time year-round, which is in line with the new time zone.

“Ending seasonal time change gives residents what they’ve asked us for,” Premier R.J. Simpson said in a news release Wednesday.

“This change provides greater consistency for people, families, organizations and businesses across the territory.”

stories.title: Former Montreal Canadiens owner George Gillett Jr. dies at 87
stories.summary: George Gillett Jr. bought the Bell Centre (then Molson Centre) and a majority stake in the Canadiens for $275 million on Jan. 31, 2001.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
George Gillett Jr., the former majority owner of the NHL’s Montreal Canadiens , has died at 87.

The Canadiens confirmed Gillett’s death in a release Thursday. A cause of death was not given.

Gillett bought the Bell Centre (then Molson Centre) and a majority stake in the Canadiens for $275 million on Jan. 31, 2001, with the help of $140 million in loans from two banks and the Caisse de depot et placement du Quebec, the province’s pension fund manager.

He owned the Original Six club until agreeing to sell the team and arena to the Molson family on June 20, 2009.

The sale was approved by the NHL’s board of governors in December of that year.

Gillett, along with fellow American Tom Hicks, also owned English soccer giant Liverpool FC from 2007 to 2010.

Born on Oct. 22, 1938, in Racine, Wis., Gillett rose to prominence as the founder of Brook Creek Management Corp., a portfolio management firm.

“On behalf of the entire Canadiens organization, I would like to extend my deepest condolences to George’s family,” Canadiens owner, president and chief executive officer Geoff Molson said in a statement.

“George immersed himself in the Montreal community and was appreciated by everyone in the organization. We sincerely appreciate his contributions to the Montreal Canadiens during his time as owner.”

stories.title: N.W.T. ends seasonal time changes, will stay on daylight time year-round
stories.summary: The Northwest Territories government says it is officially ending seasonal time changes. The territory’s new permanent time standard, known as Northwest Territories time, will be observed year-round.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Yellowknife — The Northwest Territories government says it is officially ending seasonal time changes.

The territory’s new permanent time standard, known as Northwest Territories time, will be observed year-round.

Clocks will not have to go back an hour on Nov. 1, the government says, when time change would occur in the Northwest Territories.

The territory will now share a common time with Alberta and Saskatchewan.

The government says that for most residents, the transition is expected to be simple as devices running the latest software are to receive the time zone update once it is released by system providers.

It says the change comes after public feedback in 2022, when more than 3,500 residents participated in an online survey, with more than 87 per cent supporting ending the practice of changing the clocks twice a year.

The territory says respondents most commonly expressed a preference for maintaining mountain daylight time year-round, which is in line with the new time zone.

“Ending seasonal time change gives residents what they’ve asked us for,” Premier R.J. Simpson said in a news release Wednesday.

“This change provides greater consistency for people, families, organizations and businesses across the territory.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026

stories.title: Saskatchewan mother calls for safer football helmets after son’s head injury
stories.summary: A Balgonie, Sask. family wants change after their son, a high school football player, collapsed and suffered a head injury during a game earlier this month.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The family of a Saskatchewan high school football player is calling on schools to use better helmets after he suffered a head injury during a game.

Hunter Gronick, a Grade 12 student at Greenall High School in Balgonie, Sask., experienced a head injury during his Sept. 10 football game. His Balgonie Greenall Griffins were away, facing the Swift Current Comprehensive High School Colts.

“He was doing awesome. He didn’t have any major hits that anybody could tell. Then, he just fell onto the field at one point and that was the last play,” Sabrina Gronick, Hunter’s mother said.

“The coach recalls him saying that he couldn’t see, he couldn’t hear and he collapsed, and then started vomiting.”

Hunter was rushed to hospital for a CT scan when paramedics arrived. He was then taken from the hospital in Swift Current to Regina via air ambulance. In Regina, he underwent an hours-long surgery to remove a major portion of his skull, Sabrina told Global News in an interview.

To protect other high school football players in Saskatchewan, and prevent their families from having to go through the same experience as Hunter’s, his family launched the Hunter’s Headstrong Initiative. It calls on Saskatchewan schools to provide better, safer helmets to football players in order to prevent head injuries.

“I understand that it’s not a fix,” Sabrina said, noting that the goal of the initiative is to minimize the chance of head injuries. She is waiting for the high schools athletic association to approve the equipment for use in Saskatchewan.

Patrick Neary, a University of Regina professor with the faculty of kinesiology and health studies, said the effects of brain injuries can be severe. He said options like the guardian cap, soft padding that can be attached to the outside of a helmet, May not always successfully prevent head injuries.

“I hope there’s not a false sense of security when people put the guardian cap on, “ the professor said, explaining that the pads May be ineffective because “something exterior to the brain is not necessarily going to prevent that concussion from happening.”

Hunter is now stable, despite the injury’s effects on his brain and brain stem, his mother said.

“He’s very, very, very slowly achieving milestones,” Sabrina said. “He’s still an extremely long ways away from recovery. He can open his eyes, but at the same time he’s not tracking us. Or when he looks at you, it’s almost like he’s looking past you.”

“Hunter will never be the same kind of guy that he was before,” she continued.

He played football at his high school for two years.

“Hunter is very much a go-getter and very much into camaraderie and that kind of stuff. He loves his team. He loves the game,” his mother said.

stories.title: Highschool students rock the stage and find their voice at the Grand Theatre
stories.summary: London teenagers are set to rock the stage with School of Rock, a musical based on the 2003 blockbuster film o...
stories.author: Kelly Nicol
stories.content:
London teenagers are set to rock the stage with School of Rock, a musical based on the 2003 blockbuster film of the same name.

“I think we’re all trying to find our voice,” said director Lezlie Wade. “If you see young people brave enough to get on stage and [perform] a play that is written by Julian Fellowes, and music by Andrew Lloyd Webber, I think you can sort of appreciate that if they can do it, anyone can.”

The show follows wannabe rockstar Dewey Finn, who pretends to be a substitute teacher at a prestigious prep-school. With his guidance, he turns a group of straight-A students into a rock band.

Wade says that coming from a professional background with limited budgets and crews something like this is a breath of fresh air. “If you get 15 people in a cast, that’s really huge. Here we have 34 young people on stage. I don’t often get to work with 34 people of any age, and this is really exciting and really a thrill to have that opportunity to work with them.”

“I’ve been in many productions, but this is bigger than anything I’ve ever done,” Marian Viancy Mamigo, who plays Summer Hathaway, said. “It makes me feel more professional, being in this area makes me do my best. I’m in an area I can grow and see how far I’ve come from a smaller theatre.”

The production runs until October 3rd. Tickets can be bought online, by phone, or at the box office at 471 Richmond Street.

stories.title: 'Broke all of our hearts': Families give testimony at Kenneth Law sentencing
stories.summary: “My son is dead, he is gone, I am empty, hollow,” Cindy MacMinn said in an angry voice through tears.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
No matter what prison sentence is ultimately imposed on the suicide poison merchant Kenneth Law, Thursday’s proceedings before Justice Michelle Fuerst had the deflated air of inadequate compromise.

No one will get what they want.

Rather, testimony from family members of people who died by suicide with Law’s poison during the pandemic was a heart-rending litany of grief and loss.

“My son is dead, he is gone, I am empty, hollow,” Cindy MacMinn said in an angry voice through tears. “If it hadn’t been for your offence, perhaps Clayton (Choquette, 32) May still be here … Your actions caused me to have no desire to live any longer, because Clayton is not there to share with. It is pointless. He was everything to me.”

“There are things you do not realize you are memorizing while your child is still alive,” like the sound of his “gallop” down the stairs to ask if the chicken and rice is ready, said Sarjit Kaur Rana, mother of Amrit Rana, 21. “Now it’s one of the most precious memories of my life.”

The Ontario Crown originally wanted Law to get life for murder, but a legal obstacle rose up unexpectedly in an unrelated case. So the plea deal agreed in May on assisting 14 suicides was the best the Crown could legally do.

Now, Law faces sentencing for a crime with a maximum sentence of 14 years, but the possibility that some penalties for his 14 admitted offences could be imposed consecutively. He is 60 years old.

Some of the people who delivered victim impact statements looked Law in the eye and said his name, with one man even warning Law that he would always be vigilant in case he ever tried to sell poison again. “He was ill and he needed help and I tried my best to give him that help,” said Stephen Mitchell, Sr., father of Stephen Mitchell, Jr., who died by suicide aged 21. “Mr. Law robbed my son of the chance to be healed.”

“Mr. Law broke all of our hearts,” said Greg Bryson, father of Tyler Bryson, 34, a professional commercial pilot. He “knowingly took actions to steal something so precious in all of our lives.”

Others determinedly did not say Law’s name, and walked past his prisoner’s box with their eyes on the back wall of the courtroom in Newmarket, Ont.

One dramatic moment came when a woman told court she had taken Law’s poison in an effort to end her life but survived thanks to medical care, and has been left guilt stricken as a survivor.

A striking commonality across the many victim impact statements on this first day of a hearing expected to last several weeks was how many people have taken stock of their own life through their grief, and found a new sense that it is broken into unfamiliar chapters, punctuated by absences.

Many took note of the numerical fact that some day will come when their loved one’s absence grows longer than their presence was.

Over and over again, people said there was a before, and now there is an after. Their health has changed, emotions, finances, values, responses to the stresses of life.

The loved ones of Maurizio Vadala, who dies aged 36 in 2023 spoke especially movingly. His sister Adrienne Dalli said she is left with not just his absence, but “the presence of a constant, unrelenting grief.” She is tormented by the words in his last letter to his family: “It’s time to face reality. I love and will miss you all. Goodbye.” In his emotional suffering, “he encountered guidance toward death instead of support, protection or intervention,” she said, and this has left her feeling “anger, confusion, and an overwhelming sense of injustice.”

Vadala’s long time close friend Daniel Calderone took the witness stand and unbuttoned his shirt to display a T-shirt with a picture of Maurizio, as he recalled camping trips and helping each other during difficult periods for both of them in the last months of his life. “I deeply wish I could have helped him more,” Calderone said. “I grieve the future experiences we will never have, the conversations we will never finish, the laughs we will never share.”

Law denied murder, but evidence suggests he was not personally bothered by the idea of assisting suicide, which he admitted in the plea deal. On a journalist’s secret recording that led to his downfall, he even seemed pleased with himself for offering this service to which he believed people had a right, even proud of himself for only profiting modestly.

His Ontario victims formally number 14, with details of 79 more shared by Britain to inform this sentencing hearing. But that does not include his American market, so the real number is likely higher, almost certainly more than 100.

He sent 431 packages to the U.S., 330 to the U.K., and 157 within Canada, all during the pandemic in 2021 until his arrest in 2023 sparked a panicked international search for packages already mailed. In addition to poison, he also sold more expensive kits for asphyxiation by gas.

One man who died by this manner made a donation before he died to a charity for first responders, and left cautionary notes to ensure those who found his body in a parked car were not injured or unduly traumatized.

Most of the suicides, however, were by poison ingested by dissolving it in water, purchased for less than $100 from Law online, who made $300,000 from his various schemes, roughly equally through PayPal and Shopify.

Thursday morning, Law sauntered slowly toward the central prisoner’s box in a black bomber jacket, khakis and brown leather shoes, making no eye contact with anyone. He sat impassively through all the proceedings as the Crown made its start on 74 victim impact statements, some read by their authors, others by prosecutors.

“I have no words for how cold the blood ran in my veins, the ice that dropped me to my knees and destroyed the world I lived in until that moment, to hear the words ‘He did it this time,’” said Kim Prosser, mother of Ashtyn Prosser-Blake, 19. He had just called her to say good night, and she thought he sounded tired. “I didn’t know he was making his last call goodbye,” she said. It lasted 38 minutes and 18 seconds.

She confessed that she has since made an attempt on her own life, not planned, after an unexpected emotional loss and the burden of the court process.

“I am still here and Ashtyn is not,” she said.

Her other son Drake Prosser, Ashtyn’s older brother, noted that Ashtyn spent 7274 days alive, and he knows there will be a day when he will have been gone longer than he was here.

He talked about the stages of grief, and how he was stuck in anger without feeling acceptance, but he has changed. “I wasn’t angry with him, I was sad that he would never do anything to anger me again,” he said.

“We are two people trying to survive the same loss while watching each other suffer,” said Leonardo Bedoya Forero, father of Jeshennia Bedoya-Lopez, 18, who gave a statement with his wife Maria Lopez, read out by a prosecutor due to language barriers. “It terrifies me to think what would happen if we both collapse at the same time.”

“We are two people clinging to each other because neither of us knows how to stand up on our own,” he said. “The future we had imagined as a family disappeared.”

He spoke of powerlessness, how could not protect his daughter, and now fears he cannot protect his wife.

“I saw my daughter, pale, bruised and cold,” a prosecutor read in Bedoya-Forero’s words. “That image became part of me.”

“The place she went for understanding led her to greater danger,” he said, to a man who “paves a path to death … How was I supposed to protect my daughter from something I didn’t even know I was supposed to protect her from?”

“There was a before, and then there is an after when we have gained membership in a club that nobody wants to be part of,” said Norson Harris, father of Ashley Harris, 26, who graduated in computer science and systems design.

“I still write to Ashley, message her, in the hopes there’s a small corner of the universe where she has written a system that is able to receive them,” he said. He said he leads a smaller life now and has become an introvert, and is not working at a similar level as in the past.

“We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashley’s death, or to intervene in a way that would have changed the course of events”

Before she died, Ashley had just got into a new therapy program. But Law “sold her a chemical that Ashley ultimately used to end her own life.”

Her father Norson said it is a “small consolation” that Law has admitted his responsibility, and he said he hopes Law recognizes the answer he should have given his customers is “that they were loved, they were not alone, and that help is available.”

The hearing continues with dozens more victim statements expected.

“There are things you do not realize you are memorizing while your child is still alive,” like the sound of his “gallop” down the stairs to ask if the chicken and rice is ready, said Sarjit Kaur Rana, mother of Amrit Rana, 21. “Now it’s one of the most precious memories of my life.”

The Ontario Crown originally wanted Law to get life for murder, but a legal obstacle rose up unexpectedly in an unrelated case. So the plea deal agreed in May on assisting 14 suicides was the best the Crown could legally do.
Now, Law faces sentencing for a crime with a maximum sentence of 14 years, but the possibility that some penalties for his 14 admitted offences could be imposed consecutively. He is 60 years old.

Some of the people who delivered victim impact statements looked Law in the eye and said his name, with one man even warning Law that he would always be vigilant in case he ever tried to sell poison again. “He was ill and he needed help and I tried my best to give him that help,” said Stephen Mitchell, Sr., father of Stephen Mitchell, Jr., who died by suicide aged 21. “Mr. Law robbed my son of the chance to be healed.”
“Mr. Law broke all of our hearts,” said Greg Bryson, father of Tyler Bryson, 34, a professional commercial pilot. He “knowingly took actions to steal something so precious in all of our lives.”
Others determinedly did not say Law’s name, and walked past his prisoner’s box with their eyes on the back wall of the courtroom in Newmarket, Ont.
One dramatic moment came when a woman told court she had taken Law’s poison in an effort to end her life but survived thanks to medical care, and has been left guilt stricken as a survivor.

A striking commonality across the many victim impact statements on this first day of a hearing expected to last several weeks was how many people have taken stock of their own life through their grief, and found a new sense that it is broken into unfamiliar chapters, punctuated by absences.
Many took note of the numerical fact that some day will come when their loved one’s absence grows longer than their presence was.
Over and over again, people said there was a before, and now there is an after. Their health has changed, emotions, finances, values, responses to the stresses of life.

The loved ones of Maurizio Vadala, who dies aged 36 in 2023 spoke especially movingly. His sister Adrienne Dalli said she is left with not just his absence, but “the presence of a constant, unrelenting grief.” She is tormented by the words in his last letter to his family: “It’s time to face reality. I love and will miss you all. Goodbye.” In his emotional suffering, “he encountered guidance toward death instead of support, protection or intervention,” she said, and this has left her feeling “anger, confusion, and an overwhelming sense of injustice.”

Vadala’s long time close friend Daniel Calderone took the witness stand and unbuttoned his shirt to display a T-shirt with a picture of Maurizio, as he recalled camping trips and helping each other during difficult periods for both of them in the last months of his life. “I deeply wish I could have helped him more,” Calderone said. “I grieve the future experiences we will never have, the conversations we will never finish, the laughs we will never share.”

Law denied murder, but evidence suggests he was not personally bothered by the idea of assisting suicide, which he admitted in the plea deal. On a journalist’s secret recording that led to his downfall, he even seemed pleased with himself for offering this service to which he believed people had a right, even proud of himself for only profiting modestly.

His Ontario victims formally number 14, with details of 79 more shared by Britain to inform this sentencing hearing. But that does not include his American market, so the real number is likely higher, almost certainly more than 100.

He sent 431 packages to the U.S., 330 to the U.K., and 157 within Canada, all during the pandemic in 2021 until his arrest in 2023 sparked a panicked international search for packages already mailed. In addition to poison, he also sold more expensive kits for asphyxiation by gas.

One man who died by this manner made a donation before he died to a charity for first responders, and left cautionary notes to ensure those who found his body in a parked car were not injured or unduly traumatized.

Most of the suicides, however, were by poison ingested by dissolving it in water, purchased for less than $100 from Law online, who made $300,000 from his various schemes, roughly equally through PayPal and Shopify.

Thursday morning, Law sauntered slowly toward the central prisoner’s box in a black bomber jacket, khakis and brown leather shoes, making no eye contact with anyone. He sat impassively through all the proceedings as the Crown made its start on 74 victim impact statements, some read by their authors, others by prosecutors.

“I have no words for how cold the blood ran in my veins, the ice that dropped me to my knees and destroyed the world I lived in until that moment, to hear the words ‘He did it this time,’” said Kim Prosser, mother of Ashtyn Prosser-Blake, 19. He had just called her to say good night, and she thought he sounded tired. “I didn’t know he was making his last call goodbye,” she said. It lasted 38 minutes and 18 seconds.
She confessed that she has since made an attempt on her own life, not planned, after an unexpected emotional loss and the burden of the court process.
“I am still here and Ashtyn is not,” she said.
Her other son Drake Prosser, Ashtyn’s older brother, noted that Ashtyn spent 7274 days alive, and he knows there will be a day when he will have been gone longer than he was here.

He talked about the stages of grief, and how he was stuck in anger without feeling acceptance, but he has changed. “I wasn’t angry with him, I was sad that he would never do anything to anger me again,” he said.

“We are two people trying to survive the same loss while watching each other suffer,” said Leonardo Bedoya Forero, father of Jeshennia Bedoya-Lopez, 18, who gave a statement with his wife Maria Lopez, read out by a prosecutor due to language barriers. “It terrifies me to think what would happen if we both collapse at the same time.”
“We are two people clinging to each other because neither of us knows how to stand up on our own,” he said. “The future we had imagined as a family disappeared.”
He spoke of powerlessness, how could not protect his daughter, and now fears he cannot protect his wife.
“I saw my daughter, pale, bruised and cold,” a prosecutor read in Bedoya-Forero’s words. “That image became part of me.”

“The place she went for understanding led her to greater danger,” he said, to a man who “paves a path to death … How was I supposed to protect my daughter from something I didn’t even know I was supposed to protect her from?”

“There was a before, and then there is an after when we have gained membership in a club that nobody wants to be part of,” said Norson Harris, father of Ashley Harris, 26, who graduated in computer science and systems design.

“I still write to Ashley, message her, in the hopes there’s a small corner of the universe where she has written a system that is able to receive them,” he said. He said he leads a smaller life now and has become an introvert, and is not working at a similar level as in the past.
“We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashley’s death, or to intervene in a way that would have changed the course of events”
Before she died, Ashley had just got into a new therapy program. But Law “sold her a chemical that Ashley ultimately used to end her own life.”

Her father Norson said it is a “small consolation” that Law has admitted his responsibility, and he said he hopes Law recognizes the answer he should have given his customers is “that they were loved, they were not alone, and that help is available.”
The hearing continues with dozens more victim statements expected.
