stories.title: Attempted kidnapping stopped by border officials at Blue Water Bridge
stories.summary: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has stopped an attempted kidnapping at the Blue Water Bridge in Point Edward, Ont.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) stopped an attempted kidnapping at the Blue Water Bridge in Point Edward, Ont.

The incident happened on Aug. 27. CBP Director of Field Operations, Marty Raybon, said a minor female passenger was reported missing and was with an unrelated male driver, who is a U.S. permanent resident deriving from Afghanistan.

The girl was reunited with her mother. The suspect was then arrested and turned over to Kalamazoo, Mich. police.

CTV News has reached out to CBP for further details.

stories.title: Homelessness Support Centre moves ahead in Oxford despite concerns over location and security
stories.summary: Oxford County is charging forward with a new Homelessness Support Centre at the former Ymca building on Dundas Street in Woodstock.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Oxford County is charging forward with a new Homelessness Support Centre at the former Ymca building on Dundas Street in Woodstock.

“Every time we delay this, we condemn someone else to another winter in the cold, another summer of pushing the shopping cart around with their belongings, another business coming to open in the morning and having someone asleep in their doorway,” exclaimed Warden Marcus Ryan.

In a vote of 9-1 Wednesday, Oxford County Council defeated a motion by Woodstock Councillor Deb Tait to put a pause on the centre at the Y building and find and alternate location. Tait says she believes the Y building would better serve as transitional housing for those leaving the province’s abstinence-based Hart Hub program.

“So, our whole mission of this was to help the homeless. So, what’s happening, they’re coming out of the Hart hub, nowhere to go, falling back into addiction, back into homelessness,” said Tait, speaking to CTV News after the council session.

Council also received a staff report outlining public input to date on the Homelessness Support Centre. Councillors further agreed to consider input into planning from a Y Neighbourhood Committee, along with the greater community.

Chief among concerns for both businesses and residents is security on and around the site, said Y Neighbourhood Committee representative Lee Ann VanWees in a delegation to council.

“The long-term economic survival of our local businesses, and the daily safety of our families cannot depend on a reactive ‘wait and see’ approach. Public trust is fragile. And once a neighbourhood fractures, it takes decades to rebuild,” said VanWees.

“What it means is our staff will specifically meet with that group, and other groups in the community. But they were going to do that anyway, that’s part of the engagement plan,” explained Warden Ryan.

The Homelessness Support Centre is set to open in the fall of 2028.

stories.title: Canada defender Cornelius hospitalized after suffering injury in training
stories.summary: Canada Soccer says Cornelius sustained a "non-contact lower body injury" and was transported to hospital, where he is being treated and assessed.
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
Canada defender Derek Cornelius (13) runs to the play during an international friendly soccer match against Ireland in Montreal, Friday, June 5, 2026. (Gary McCullough/AP).

By The Canadian Press

Posted September 23, 2026 4:38 pm.

Defender Derek Cornelius has been taken to a Toronto-area hospital after getting hurt while training with the men’s national soccer team on Wednesday.

Canada Soccer says Cornelius sustained a “non-contact lower body injury” and was transported to hospital, where he is being treated and assessed.

The national sports organization says medical staff are focused on supporting the 28-year-old left back, and further updates will be provided “as appropriate.”

News of the defender’s injury comes after Canada Soccer sent midfielder Jeevan Badwal back to Vancouver earlier on Wednesday after determining he had suffered a hamstring injury while playing for the Whitecaps on Saturday.

Cornelius, who plays for Olympique de Marseille, and Badwal were training with Canada ahead of the nation’s upcoming friendlies against Chile in Toronto in Sept. 26 and Peru in Montreal on Oct. 3. The country will also take on the United States in St. Paul, Minn., ON Oct. 6.

The three friendlies will mark the national team’s first games since Canada’s historic World Cup run this summer.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Premier Tim Houston softens stance on data centres operating in Nova Scotia
stories.summary: Houston said data centres are becoming increasingly critical pieces of infrastructure and Canada can’t rely on other countries to store its data.
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
Premier Tim Houston is softening his stance on the prospect of new data centres setting up in Nova Scotia.

The premier previously said it was premature to have a conversation about the issue before completing major energy projects such as the Wind West offshore wind proposal.

In a statement Wednesday, the premier said the situation has changed and data centres considering Nova Scotia should help create demand and investment cases for energy projects.

Data centres, used in artificial intelligence and other high-tech industries, are massive operations that require an immense amount of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

Houston said data centres are becoming increasingly critical pieces of infrastructure and Canada can’t rely on other countries to store its data.

The premier said he is also willing to consider proposals since Ottawa has rolled out new rules for the sector.

“If a company can protect our water, protect ratepayers, strengthen our communities, create economic opportunity and keep critical Canadian data in Canada, we will hear them out,” Houston said in the statement. “If they cannot meet that standard, they will not build here in Nova Scotia.”

stories.title: Former soldier's alleged role in synagogue shooting very concerning: defence minister
stories.summary: Defence Minister David McGuinty says it’s very concerning that the suspect in Sunday’s shooting outside a Belleville, Ont., synagogue was a former soldier.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Defence Minister David McGuinty says it’s very concerning that the suspect in Sunday’s shooting outside a Belleville, Ont., synagogue was a former soldier.

Sean Ward, who died in hospital after a shootout with police outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue, was a member of the Canadian Armed Forces for about five years before he was released in June 2022.

Citing anonymous military and National Defence sources, the Globe and Mail and Global News both reported that Ward was released from the army after refusing to be vaccinated against COVID-19.

One of the sources also told Global News that the shooting suspect voiced antisemitic conspiracies.

Belleville police have not spoken about a motive behind the shooting that occurred as people gathered inside the synagogue for Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

McGuinty says the government has been making “culture changes” in the Canadian Armed Forces for a decade, including changing recruitment standards and extending the probationary period for recruits.

“The situation is a serious one, and we’re taking it very seriously,” McGuinty said Wednesday in Ottawa.

He said there have been “improvements” to military culture, but “there’s always work to be done.”

McGuinty said his thoughts are with the Belleville police officer injured in the shootout and the city’s Jewish community.

“We’re obviously very concerned,” he added.

The Department of National Defence has confirmed that Ward joined CAF in July 2017 and had served with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry without being deployed.

Beyond identifying the 29-year-old as a resident of nearby Quinte West, Belleville police have not released any other details about Ward.

He died on Monday and the province’s police watchdog has said that an autopsy would be performed Wednesday.

The injured police officer, Const. Jeff Smith, was also taken to hospital in critical but stable condition. In a Facebook post shared by Belleville police, Smith’s wife said the officer has a long and difficult road ahead but the family is buoyed by an outpouring of support.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said Wednesday that antisemitism is “a scourge upon our communities” that highlights the need to fully implement anti-hate legislation passed earlier this year.

“We’re having conversations now about how we can bring together provinces and territories, so we’re going to have a hand in the implementation of those laws, making sure that there’s training for police officers on the ground, for prosecutors, for judges,” he said in Ottawa.

“We need to make sure that the laws that we have adopted are actually implemented with the full understanding of the importance of law enforcement on the ground and the justice system on the back end.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

--With files from David Baxter in Ottawa

Canadian Press Staff, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Controversial Kincardine monument destruction heading to court
stories.summary: The destruction of a century old monument in downtown Kincardine, will be heading to court.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The destruction of a century old monument in downtown Kincardine, will be heading to court.

“It wasn’t theirs to destroy. So, that that is the primary focus, and how they could make that decision,” said David Secord.

David Secord, a descendant of Dr. Solomon Secord, has filed legal action against the Municipality of Kincardine for destroying a monument bearing his family member’s name, Dr. Solomon Secord, in September 2024.

“Well, at first, it was very, very shocking. And then secondly, very disappointing,” said Secord, who hails from Calgary.

During downtown construction in the spring of 2023, Kincardine council took down the Dr. Solomon Secord monument, which was located outside the town’s library, ON Kincardine’s main street.

The monument had stood since 1915, erected by Dr. Secord’s friend and patients, marking his 50 years treating locals, as the town’s physician. But Dr. Secord also served as a surgeon for the Confederate Army in the American Civil War, prompting some to suggest he supported slavery.

A year long public discussion, ended with council deciding not to put the monument back up and ultimately destroy it on Sept. 17, 2024.

In his statement of claim, David Secord says he and other family members contacted Kincardine’s administration on multiple occasions, requesting the monument be returned to them at the family’s cost. Instead, it was destroyed. Secord maintaining that the monument, built and erected by locals, was not Kincardine’s to destroy.

“This wasn’t a story that should end this way, and with the way he was treated,” said Secord.

The Municipality would not comment on the legal action, but at the time of removing and destroying the document, said they were doing so in the public interest. Secord is seeking over $150,000 in damages in the family’s legal claim, including $23,000 to cover the cost of rebuilding the exact monument, in honour of their descendant Dr. Secord.

“They were determined that this wasn’t going to be the end of the story, and that we would we would remake the monument, in the same vein as the first one,” he said.

“Identical. And then, we would bring it out west, if we had to, and erect it again.”

Kincardine has until the end of September to respond to the lawsuit.

“It wasn’t theirs to take down,” said Secord.

stories.title: ’You’re not killing him’: Jewish mother tells how she shielded son during Belleville synagogue shooting
stories.summary: Sharlene Weitzman was inside the Sons of Jacob synagogue with her son and partner when a shooter arrived and opened fire.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
As the thunder of gunfire erupted outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue on Sunday evening, Sharlene Weitzman, one of roughly two dozen congregants inside, thought first of protecting her son, Finn Luke Weitzman, who had accompanied her to mark the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day for the Jewish community.

“I wasn’t going to let my child be killed at 19 years of age for being a Jew,” she told National Post in an exclusive interview three days after the shocking shooting near the modest shul in a quiet Belleville, Ont., neighbourhood.

“You can kill me, I’m 59, but you’re not killing him.”

Weitzman pushed her son down against concrete and used her body to shield him, with her arms wrapped around him. So determined was she to safeguard his life, she said if a shooter had come through the close-by doors of the synagogue at that moment, she was “ready to pounce.”

Thankfully, Weitzman, her partner Jennifer Aronson, nor any of the others sheltering from bullets hitting the stained glass of their synagogue that evening were forced to act.

Const. Jeff Smith of the Belleville Police Service was already on the scene and returned fire when suspected shooter Sean Ward of nearby Quinte West arrived and opened fire with a shotgun, according to the Ontario Special Investigations Unit (SIU). The 13-year veteran officer was struck during the shootout, but was joined by another responding officer not yet identified, and both were able to stop the shooter.

Smith remains in Kingston General Hospital in critical but stable condition while Ward, a 29-year-old former member of the Canadian Armed Forces, died there on Tuesday. Ward had been released from the CAF in 2022, with a source telling Global News it was over his refusal to receive the COVID-19 vaccine, adding that Ward also “spouted” antisemitic conspiracy theories, including one that blamed the Jewish community for the pandemic disease.

Weitzman said another jarring thought came to her mind amid the chaos, one that she’s not been able to shake: a vision of what it would look like if it turned out like the Hamas Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks on Israel.

“That ‘what if’ is the real killer, and that to me is what I need to fight against because there’s a literal war of hatred and I believe that the people, the institutions, the systems running that war want Jews to live fearfully and I refuse to,” she said.

Weitzman said it had been about 10 years since the family had attended a service at the Sons of Jacob and returned now because it seemed as if new life had been breathed into the assembly and they wanted to show their support.

But not without hesitation.

“I sensed it before we went. I asked my partner if we should go,” she said, highlighting an ever-present and yet intangible sense of danger they were inherently aware of as Jews.

“Every Jew who went to shul on Yom Kippur around the world, I tell you, was worried that it would be their shul that was shot at.”

Determined not to lose their faith and give in to fear, especially on Yom Kippur, they ventured out. At the synagogue, they were among the first arrivals and acted as unofficial greeters, re-introducing themselves as other congregants arrived.

As people began to make their way inside the sanctuary for Rabbi Oded Peles’s service, a few minutes later than anticipated, Weitzman said they heard “three enormous banging noises” that at first sounded like someone using a battering ram to gain access, but what she now believes was the first of the shotgun blasts.

Weitzman shielded her son, Aronson went to assist an elderly woman and everyone else lay down on the floor or found shelter somewhere else as a gunfight ensued for the next few minutes.

Someone inside called 911 and stayed on with dispatchers throughout the ordeal, but it did little to quell immediate fears inside the temple.

“I think what was most terrifying for everyone, beyond the fact that the gunfire was hitting the window, was that there was a shootout and we didn’t know if there was a shootout towards us and it was two or three shooters shooting at us and they were going to come in or if it was the police defending us,” she said. “We just didn’t know.”

Weitzman believes at least one bullet came through into the sanctuary because one of the candles on the Yahrzeit wall, a memorial installation honouring deceased congregants, was extinguished.

Photos from the scene shared by congregants Eva and Doug Lobel show well over a dozen bullet holes in the windows along one side of the sanctuary wall. Peles later told The Canadian Jewish News that 50-year-old stained glass behind the pulpit where he would have been leading prayer was hit with 23 bullets.

“Thank God we were a few minutes late and we took extra time lighting the Yontif candles,” he told the outlet. “We got extra candles and maybe by lighting the candles, extra four candles, saved our lives.”

Peles, the CJN reported, is from Israel and was visiting the synagogue for the second straight year. Asked if the incident would deter him from returning, Peles said it wouldn’t.

“It’s like almost asking, ‘Are you not going to come to the Holy Land because we have rockets?’”

After the cacophony of gunfire ended, synagogue president Norm Weddum bravely ventured to a window and saw a significant police presence, Weitzman said. It was another 25 minutes before they had contact with police, who kept them in the security of the sanctuary while sweeping the building and neighbourhood, during which time “they gathered around the table and held hands and prayed.”

They were soon bused to the local police station for interviews before being sent home.

Days later, with the adrenaline well out of her system, Weitzman said she believes that Ward came there to “massacre all of us” and would not have survived but for the “grace of God and the police.”

The investigation is being led, at this stage, by the SIU, which is mandated to look into the circumstances of a police shooting. Spokesperson Kristy Denette wouldn’t speculate on whether it was a targeted attack against Jewish people during a Monday press conference, but said “common sense would say that probably was the case.”

“Let me be very clear, hate and violence have no place in our community. Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones, or participating in community life,” added Belleville police deputy chief Sheri Meeks.

For Weitzman, however, there’s no doubt in her mind that “this was a premeditated, full-on terrorist attack.”

“Stop telling us Jews that we’re overreacting. Stop telling us it’s not antisemitism, ‘It’s not all about you. Oh, where there’s smoke, there must be fire. If people hate you, there’s a reason,’” she said.

“But I’m not Benjamin Netanyahu. I’m not the leader of the government. I’m not Mark Carney. I’m just a Jewish mom trying to raise my family in the community that we’ve been in for 25, 30 years.”

This wasn’t Aronson, Weitzman and her son’s first scary incident related to their Jewish roots. While in Jerusalem for an educational event with Israeli scholars last year, the couple were forced to briefly take cover in a bomb shelter as Houthi missiles were defeated by Israel’s Iron Dome. Her son had to do the same last year while visiting Eilat during his Reverse Shinshinim, a gap-year service that gives non-Israeli-born high school graduates a chance to immerse themselves in Israeli life.

“I don’t think he has any false beliefs about his safety anymore,” Weitzman said.

She commended police for their heroics Sunday, especially Smith, whose injuries she said “brought a great deal of attention” to the seriousness of the situation.

“I am hopeful that people, especially those who can protect us, as we just evidenced, do now understand the gravitas that this is a real threat and it’s everywhere.”

Weitzman said they plan to return to the synagogue in the future.

stories.title: Lions host Riders in important West Division clash
stories.summary: It's been a long way back for Nathan Rourke and the B.C. Lions.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
It’s been a long way back for Nathan Rourke and the B.C. Lions.

B.C. opened its season by losing its first three games and five-of-six overall. But since then, B.C. (7-6) has reeled off six wins in seven contests, including a 48-29 home decision versus the Montreal Alouettes on Sept. 12.

On Friday night, B.C. hosts the Saskatchewan Roughriders (8-5) in a battle for second in the West Division. The winner also claims the season series, which is the tiebreaker should the two finish with identical records.

B.C.’s offence leads the CFL in net yards (427.7 per game), rushing (121.3) and time of possession (31 minutes 44 seconds) and is second in passing (322.5). Rourke, last season’s top Canadian and outstanding player, is fifth among league quarterbacks (3,476 passing yards) with 16 touchdowns and 10 interceptions but his 71.1 per cent completion average is second only to Montreal’s Davis Alexander (71.4 per cent).

Rourke has only rushed 20 times this season, but sports a stellar 12.3-yard average per attempt with three TDs. However, the Lions don’t really needed Rourke to run with Zander Horvath (723 yards, 5.1-yard average, CFL-high 16 rushing TDs) and James Butler (393 yards, 4.6-yard average, four TDs) in the backfield.

Saskatchewan’s defence should present a good test, though. It has allowed a CFL-low 31 offensive TDs and is ranked second in fewest offensive points allowed (25.1 per game) despite a rash of injuries.

And the unit couldn’t really be faulted for Saskatchewan’s 19-6 loss to Winnipeg on Sept. 12. Bombers safety Redha Kramdi forced a first-half fumble then sealed the win with a fourth-quarter interception as the Riders’ offence managed just two field goals in the contest.

The good news, though, is help could be on the way. Running back A.J. Ouellette (knee) and receiver Kian Schaffer-Baker (knee) were both full participants in practice.

Veteran Riders quarterback Trevor Harris, 40, is enjoying another solid campaign, having completed 69.3 per cent of his passing for 4,124 yards, fourth-best in the CFL. He also has 24 TD tosses with 12 interceptions while Saskatchewan has allowed just 19 sacks, second only to Montreal (12).

But versus Winnipeg, Harris was 24-of-45 passing for 231 yards and an interception. The offence converted just four-of-22 second-down opportunities and had five giveaways (two fumbles, interception, twice on downs).

Both B.C. and Saskatchewan are 4-3 within the West Division. The Riders have dropped their last three road games but would clinch a playoff berth with a win and Winnipeg and Calgary losses this week.

Toronto Argonauts vs Winnipeg Blue Bombers (Friday night)

At Winnipeg, Dru Brown starts at quarterback ahead of Zach Collaros (head). Brown threw for 339 yards with a TD and pick in a 30-21 win over Toronto in July. The Argos (8-6) have won three straight and earned a home playoff game with last week’s 24-19 decision over Edmonton. Chad Kelly had 19 completions for 373 yards with two TDs and two interceptions but cornerback Tarvarus McFadden (hand) is out. The Bombers (7-6) boast CFL rushing leader Brady Oliveira (1,084 yards) while the Double Blue ranks eighth in rushing (76.1 yards per game). But Damonte Coxie (67 catches, 1,111 yards, six TDs) anchors a solid receiving corps for Kelly.

Calgary Stampeders vs Ottawa Redblacks (Saturday afternoon)

At Ottawa, Calgary (6-8) won 40-38 last week at McMahon Stadium on Rene Paredes’s walk off 62-yard field goal. Vernon Adams Jr. passed for 357 yards with two TDs and an interception while Deonta McMahon ran for 102 yards (6.8-yard average). Veteran McLeod Bethel-Thompson is expected to make a second straight start for the Redblacks (0-13) after throwing for 379 yards and five TDs last week. This could be another shootout as the two defences are the league’s worst in offensive yards, points and TDs allowed. However, the home team has committed a league-high 40 turnovers — the Stamps have 23 — and the visitors are third in points scored off opponents’ turnovers (100).

Hamilton Tiger-Cats vs Edmonton Elks (Saturday night)

At Edmonton, the Elks (10-4) look to rebound following last week’s loss in Toronto. Cody Fajardo completed 31-of-42 passes for 360 yards and scored the offence’s lone TD but also threw two interceptions. The defence intercepted Kelly twice but did allow 373 passing yards and the two TDs on 19 completions. Harrison Frost is expected to start again for Hamilton (4-10) after going the distance in last week’s 37-25 home loss to Montreal despite Canadian Tre Ford being available. The Ticats will be eliminated from playoff contention with a loss and Calgary win or a loss and Winnipeg and B.C. victories as both scenarios would confirm a crossover.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

stories.title: ‘We will fight with him’: Wife of Belleville police officer critically injured in shooting outside synagogue releases statement
stories.summary: The wife of a police officer who was critically injured in a shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont. on Sunday evening says that her husband has “very long, difficult road ahead.”
stories.author: Joanna Lavoie
stories.content:
The wife of a police officer who was critically injured in a shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Sunday evening says her husband has “very long, difficult road ahead.”

In a lengthy post on Facebook on Tuesday, Ashley Smith, who is married to Const. Jeff Smith, said he is “not walking it alone.”

“(Jeff) has an army of love behind him. And I know Jeff. He is the best man I know. He loves his family with his whole heart,” she wrote.

“He cares deeply. He gives freely. He shows up. He is a man of integrity. He is my safest place. And right now, he is fighting. So we will fight with him.”

Smith was stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue when a gunman armed with a shotgun opened fire on him.

Sources tell CP24 that the 13-year Belleville Police Service veteran was shot multiple times, including in the neck. He remained in hospital in stable condition, as of Tuesday.

The suspect, Sean Ward, a 29-year-old Quinte West resident, died on Sept. 21 in hospital, following an exchange of gunfire with police, the province’s Special Investigation Unit said.

In her statement, the officer’s wife expressed her appreciation “from the deepest part of my heart and soul” to all who have supported her husband and family since the shooting.

“I cannot begin to express what the outpouring of love and support has meant to us. I know there are things happening every day that I don’t even know about yet. Messages being sent. Prayers being said. People checking in. Hands reaching out,” Smith said.

“And I know that my gratitude will never be enough.”

She went on to say that she’s been “witnessing real-life miracles” in the wake of Sunday’s shooting, so many of which have happened “through human hands.”

She also offered “love and prayers” to the Jewish community, “and to every scared soul who was there on Sunday night.”

Premier Doug Ford has previously called Const. Smith a “hero,” saying that he “stopped a tragedy in its footsteps.”

Little known about suspect

At this point, few details are known about the gunman.

A spokesperson for the Canadian Armed Forces told CP24 on Tuesday that Ward enrolled in the military in July 2017 and was released in June 2022 at the rank of corporal. He served as an infantry soldier with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, they said, but did not deploy.

Speaking with reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday, federal Minister of National Defence David McGuinty called the shooting “very, very unfortunate.”

Asked about concerns it could point to wider issues within the military, McGuinty said that efforts have been underway for more than a decade to make “cultural changes.”

“We are making great progress. We have changed the standards for recruitment. We have changed the standard, for example, for probationary periods from nine weeks until the end of your basic training,” he said.

“There have been improvements. There is always work to be done. This is a very, very unfortunate situation. I feel very much for the Jewish community in Belleville. I have one of the largest synagogues in this region in my riding so we are obviously very concerned.”

With files from CP24’s Chris Fox

stories.title: ‘This is going to be the springboard’: More resident doctors coming to Oxford and Lambton Counties in 2027
stories.summary: A new partnership between Western’s Schulich School of Medicine and area hospitals will bring more family medicine to Lambton and Oxford counties.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A new partnership between Western’s Schulich School of Medicine and area hospitals will bring more family medicine to Lambton and Oxford counties.

Beginning in July 2027, medical centres including Bluewater Health and Woodstock Hospital will each welcome two new medical residents.

It will be the first time graduates have served in those communities, according to Scott McKay, the chair of family Medicine at Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry.

“They will complete most of their entire residency in these communities. Previously, residents would have had an opportunity to do, you know, maybe one or two months in these communities, sometimes just in the emergency room,” McKay said.

Dr. Ian Hons, chief of staff at Woodstock Hospital, said residents will serve in multiple areas of patient care.

“They’ll see a full spectrum of what family practice can look like. And, at the same time, they’ll be in our hospitals working directly with our specialists,” he said.

Hons predicts that waiting times in some areas of medicine will improve, especially as the residents move into their second year.

“There is benefit as they become increasingly skilled as physicians to do some of the work the supervising physician is doing any given day,” said Hons.

The goal for all parties is to encourage residents to become attached to the communities they serve.

With recently announced paid tuition incentives from the province, it is hoped more young family doctors will opt to stay in the region.

Ontario helps family doctors learn and stay in the province for them to set up a comprehensive family practice or a medical practice within these communities,” added McKay.

The new program comes just a year after medical students still in their initial training were placed at health care sites in Lambton County.

Both leaders are confident the program will expand to other areas in the coming years.

stories.title: Defence minister says it’s concerning that synagogue shooting suspect was ex-soldier
stories.summary: Sean Ward, who died in hospital after a shootout with police outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue, was a member of the Canadian Armed Forces for about five years before he was released in June 2022.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Bullet holes are pictured in the side of a pickup truck near the scene of a shooting that took place late Sunday evening near Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Ian MacAlpine

By Canadian Press Staff, The Canadian Press

Posted September 23, 2026 4:04 pm.

Last Updated September 23, 2026 6:00 pm.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says it’s very concerning that the suspect in Sunday’s shooting outside a Belleville, Ont., synagogue was a former soldier.

Sean Ward, who died in hospital after a shootout with police outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue, was a member of the Canadian Armed Forces for about five years before he was released in June 2022.

Citing anonymous military and National Defence sources, the Globe and Mail and Global News both reported that Ward was released from the army after refusing to be vaccinated against COVID-19.

One of the sources also told Global News that the shooting suspect voiced antisemitic conspiracies.

Belleville police have not spoken about a motive behind the shooting that occurred as people gathered inside the synagogue for Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

McGuinty says the government has been making “culture changes” in the Canadian Armed Forces for a decade, including changing recruitment standards and extending the probationary period for recruits.

“The situation is a serious one, and we’re taking it very seriously,” McGuinty said Wednesday in Ottawa.

He said there have been “improvements” to military culture, but “there’s always work to be done.”

McGuinty said his thoughts are with the Belleville police officer injured in the shootout and the city’s Jewish community.

“We’re obviously very concerned,” he added.

The Department of National Defence has confirmed that Ward joined CAF in July 2017 and had served with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry without being deployed.

Beyond identifying the 29-year-old as a resident of nearby Quinte West, Belleville police have not released any other details about Ward.

He died on Monday and the province’s police watchdog has said that an autopsy would be performed Wednesday.

The injured police officer, Const. Jeff Smith, was also taken to hospital in critical but stable condition. In a Facebook post shared by Belleville police, Smith’s wife said the officer has a long and difficult road ahead but the family is buoyed by an outpouring of support.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said Wednesday that antisemitism is “a scourge upon our communities” that highlights the need to fully implement anti-hate legislation passed earlier this year.

“We’re having conversations now about how we can bring together provinces and territories, so we’re going to have a hand in the implementation of those laws, making sure that there’s training for police officers on the ground, for prosecutors, for judges,” he said in Ottawa.

“We need to make sure that the laws that we have adopted are actually implemented with the full understanding of the importance of law enforcement on the ground and the justice system on the back end.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

–With files from David Baxter in Ottawa

stories.title: Alicia Keys immortalizes her childhood neighbourhood in Hell’s Kitchen, playing in Toronto this month
stories.summary: The semi-autobiographical jukebox musical runs at the CAA Ed Mirvish Theatre from Sept. 23 until Oct. 25
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Thirty years ago, a wunderkind burst onto the music scene in New York. A classically trained pianist with an ear for R&B, she graduated from high school at the age of 16 – at the top of her class, no less – and immediately started studying at Columbia University. When she dropped out of postsecondary studies, it wasn’t because she couldn’t handle the pressure, but because making music full-time was the obvious path forward.

It should come as no surprise that Alicia Keys has since gone on to create a Broadway musical heavily inspired by her own life. Known for hits such as Fallin ’, If I Ain’t Got You and No One , Keys is singular as an auteur: Her evocative lyrics, smoky voice and classical sensibilities combine to create a sound not quite in the world of hip-hop or soul, but instead a genre all its own.

Her biography, too, offers compelling stage fodder. In her 45 years she’s risen from Manhattan Plaza, the subsidized residential complex in Hell’s Kitchen where she spent much of her childhood, to stages and arenas around the world. With a book by Kristoffer Díaz and direction by Michael Greif ( Rent , Next to Normal, Dear Evan Hansen ), the musical largely takes place in the storied – and 46-storeyed – apartment building of Keys’s youth.

Ahead of Hell’s Kitchen ’s touring stop in Toronto, scheduled to play at the CAA Ed Mirvish Theatre until Oct. 25, The Globe and Mail spoke with Keys over Zoom to discuss her remarkable career – and the songs audiences might recognize in her jukebox musical.

Fall theatre season bets big on made-in-Canada productions

You served as BlackBerry’s global creative director for one year, helping to launch the BlackBerry 10 in 2013. Given that, have you seen Canadian director Matt Johnson’s satirical bio-dramedy BlackBerry ?

I haven’t. Should I see it?

That’s so funny. I was there for such a specific era of BlackBerry. I’ll have to check that out.

In a somewhat atypical move for a living artist with a jukebox musical, you were highly involved in the creation of Hell’s Kitchen , from the story and music to even being in the room for auditions. Why was it important for you to have your fingerprints on every part of the production?

This is 100 per cent my vision. No one came to me and was like, ‘Hey, let’s adapt this and that.’ It was a story I felt was an important one to tell. I wanted to capture the timelessness of Hell’s Kitchen, the spirit of it. You can’t write about this very specific place if you don’t understand it.

How did you feel about recontextualizing some of your own back catalogue into a new story? The show is semi-autobiographical – it follows a teenager named Ali through her coming-of-age as a musician in Hell’s Kitchen – but these songs tell a different story now than they did when you wrote them.

That’s one of my favourite parts of the show. The songs were really designed to propel the story forward, and to get a deeper understanding of these characters. You hear songs you know with voices you’ve never heard. If I Ain’t Got You becomes a duet between a father and a daughter. No one would have ever thought of that, myself included, when the song was written.

Fallin ’ is sung completely by the father, so it’s a male voice singing. I don’t know if I’ve ever heard a man sing Fallin ’ outside of this show. It’s not a normal occurrence. I find it’s really exciting for the audience when they hear it, because they don’t know it’s coming.

I sometimes ask myself if maybe this is why those songs were written – to eventually represent these deeper things. It’s really special to think about why a song comes to life, and what it’s meant to portray.

As an artist who partially rose to prominence for her skills as a pianist, what kind of piano do you keep in your home?

I love that question. It’s the same Steinway baby grand I was offered when I got signed to Columbia Records. At that time in my teenage life, it was the most beautiful piano I’d ever seen – I’d never seen anything more special. My manager was like, ‘No, you’re not signing for a piano.’ Thank God my manager had that good sense. I think my young mind was just overwhelmed by the fact that it was so gorgeous.

But eventually that piano did end up becoming something I owned, and it’s been with me ever since. My oldest son, Egypt, learned how to play on that piano. It’s still in my house today, and I really love it. It’s very special.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

It should come as no surprise that Alicia Keys has since gone on to create a Broadway musical heavily inspired by her own life. Known for hits such as Fallin ’, If I Ain’t Got You and No One , Keys is singular as an auteur: Her evocative lyrics, smoky voice and classical sensibilities combine to create a sound not quite in the world of hip-hop or soul, but instead a genre all its own.

content_blocks.caption: Maya Drake stars as Ali. Marc J. Frankin/Supplied

content_blocks.text: Her biography, too, offers compelling stage fodder. In her 45 years she’s risen from Manhattan Plaza, the subsidized residential complex in Hell’s Kitchen where she spent much of her childhood, to stages and arenas around the world. With a book by Kristoffer Díaz and direction by Michael Greif ( Rent , Next to Normal, Dear Evan Hansen ), the musical largely takes place in the storied – and 46-storeyed – apartment building of Keys’s youth.

Ahead of Hell’s Kitchen ’s touring stop in Toronto, scheduled to play at the CAA Ed Mirvish Theatre until Oct. 25, The Globe and Mail spoke with Keys over Zoom to discuss her remarkable career – and the songs audiences might recognize in her jukebox musical.
Fall theatre season bets big on made-in-Canada productions

You served as BlackBerry’s global creative director for one year, helping to launch the BlackBerry 10 in 2013. Given that, have you seen Canadian director Matt Johnson’s satirical bio-dramedy BlackBerry ?
I haven’t. Should I see it?
That’s so funny. I was there for such a specific era of BlackBerry. I’ll have to check that out.

content_blocks.caption: Keys receives a gift during rehearsals from the cast of the North American tour. Hell's Kitchen/Supplied

content_blocks.text: In a somewhat atypical move for a living artist with a jukebox musical, you were highly involved in the creation of Hell’s Kitchen , from the story and music to even being in the room for auditions. Why was it important for you to have your fingerprints on every part of the production?

This is 100 per cent my vision. No one came to me and was like, ‘Hey, let’s adapt this and that.’ It was a story I felt was an important one to tell. I wanted to capture the timelessness of Hell’s Kitchen, the spirit of it. You can’t write about this very specific place if you don’t understand it.

How did you feel about recontextualizing some of your own back catalogue into a new story? The show is semi-autobiographical – it follows a teenager named Ali through her coming-of-age as a musician in Hell’s Kitchen – but these songs tell a different story now than they did when you wrote them.

That’s one of my favourite parts of the show. The songs were really designed to propel the story forward, and to get a deeper understanding of these characters. You hear songs you know with voices you’ve never heard. If I Ain’t Got You becomes a duet between a father and a daughter. No one would have ever thought of that, myself included, when the song was written.

Fallin ’ is sung completely by the father, so it’s a male voice singing. I don’t know if I’ve ever heard a man sing Fallin ’ outside of this show. It’s not a normal occurrence. I find it’s really exciting for the audience when they hear it, because they don’t know it’s coming.

I sometimes ask myself if maybe this is why those songs were written – to eventually represent these deeper things. It’s really special to think about why a song comes to life, and what it’s meant to portray.

content_blocks.caption: Kennedy Caughell as Jersey and Desmond Sean Ellington as Davis. Marc J. Frankin/Supplied

content_blocks.text: As an artist who partially rose to prominence for her skills as a pianist, what kind of piano do you keep in your home?

I love that question. It’s the same Steinway baby grand I was offered when I got signed to Columbia Records. At that time in my teenage life, it was the most beautiful piano I’d ever seen – I’d never seen anything more special. My manager was like, ‘No, you’re not signing for a piano.’ Thank God my manager had that good sense. I think my young mind was just overwhelmed by the fact that it was so gorgeous.

But eventually that piano did end up becoming something I owned, and it’s been with me ever since. My oldest son, Egypt, learned how to play on that piano. It’s still in my house today, and I really love it. It’s very special.

stories.title: Fanshawe students face mixed experiences in search for jobs
stories.summary: Fanshawe College students are having mixed experiences finding part-time employment, with some facing months o...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
Fanshawe College students are having mixed experiences finding part-time employment, with some facing months of applications while others have found jobs through previous experience or personal connections.

A student on the Fanshawe College Parents Group made a post regarding the struggles they have been facing with landing a job, and is in search for help. The post mentions how they have applied everywhere but has had no bites.

Randabouz Arifa, who is a student at Fanshawe College, said she has been looking for a job for about two years.

“Probably ignoring,” she said when asked whether employers were responding to their applications.

Arifa said that balancing school, personal life, and employment can be difficult.

Randabouz Arifa, cyber security, year 1, photo: (Torey Joseph Legarrie)

“You need a lifestyle to have a balance between your lifestyle and your study” she said.

Arifa said not finding work has also been frustrating financially.

“I feel mad, I’m going to be honest,” she said.

Rebecca Summerfield, a Fanshawe career services consultant, said finding work that fits around a students school schedule is one of the biggest challenges.

“For the most part, the biggest challenge is finding a flexible employer that will work around a school schedule,” she said.

Summerfield said students who are not hearing back from employers should consider following up professionally after applying.

Rebecca Summerfield, career services Fanshawe, photo: (Career services Fanshawe Facebook)

“I always suggest that students try following up in person, as long as they’re doing it professionally,” she said.

Summerfield also recommended that students dress as if they are going to an interview when following up with an employer.

Fanshawe’s Career Opportunities Fair happens on Sept, 30, from 10a.m. to 2p.m. in both J gyms. The event is open to Fanshawe students and Alumini, with employers offering opportunities that include part-time positions.

Summerfield said students should look at social media and job postings.

“I find that Instagram seems to be a good place for students to find part-time jobs a lot of times right now,” she said.

According to Statistics Canada labour force data , London is the third highest unemployment rate for students across the country. Data shows for people aged 15 to 24 in London was 22.2 per cent in May 2026 . The overall unemployment rate is seven per cent when the Canadian average is 6.6 per cent.

While some students are struggling to find work, others have been able to secure employment after months of searching through previous experience and personal connections.

Fanshawe student Alexis Moore said it took several months of sending out resumes before finding a job.

“I probably applied to 30 plus” she said.

Alexis Moore, pre-health, year 2, photo: (Torey Joseph Legarrie)

Moore found their current job through Indeed and said previous supervisory experience helped her stand out.

“I think when I had the higher experience, like supervisor, that was what really got me a job quicker than most,” she said.

Moore recommended students include volunteer experience on their resumes when applying for jobs.

Fanshawe Career Services is located in room D1063 and provides students with assistance with their employment searches.

stories.title: Outraged reaction to news of protesters outside Yom Kippur service in Toronto
stories.summary: "Try this in Florida, and you go to prison for five years," says Florida congressman.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
'Try this in Florida, and you go to prison for five years,' says Florida congressman

A social media post by CBC National Radio News Reader Neil Herland has been widely shared, with some outraged responses from outside the country. Herland had recounted the intimidation he faced when trying to enter a building to attend a Yom Kippur service in Toronto on Monday night, adding that he May have to leave Canada amid rising antisemitism. “On Yom Kippur I went to a synagogue service in Toronto and was met by protesters trying to taunt and intimidate me from entering the building,” he wrote in a post on X, where he identifies himself as a journalist and a Jew. Florida Congressman Randy Fine, a Republican, responded yesterday, noting: “Try this in Florida, and you go to prison for five years.” He added: “Proud to have sponsored the bill to make that happen.”

He added: “Proud to have sponsored the bill to make that happen.”

Try this in Florida, and you go to prison for five years. Proud to have sponsored the bill to make that happen. Muslim terror is not welcome here. https://t.co/ma4ayUQY4v — Congressman Randy Fine (@RepFine) September 22, 2026

Meanwhile, Kyle Smith, a columnist, novelist and film critic for the Wall Street Journal, asked simply: “How did we let it get this bad for Jews?” And the X account of the U.S. Israel Education Association posted: “We have seen where unchecked hatred can lead. History has taught us that silence in the face of antisemitism comes at a terrible cost.” The group added: “On Yom Kippur, Jews should never have to face intimidation simply for walking into a synagogue to pray. We cannot normalize this. We cannot look away. And we cannot allow hatred of Jews to manifest itself in our communities unchecked. We stand with you!”

Herland’s post came a day after a synagogue came under attack in Belleville, Ont., a city about two hours to the east. Herland’s post shows a group of about 20 people milling about, blowing horns and waving Palestinian flags in front of the Meridian Arts Centre at Yonge and Sheppard, where The Song Shul holds annual events to mark Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, and Yom Kippur, known as the Day of Atonement. The synagogue doesn’t have its own building but rents different locations to hold services. “My late father was an Austrian Jew who survived the Holocaust in Romania,” Herland wrote. “And came to Canada as a refugee. This year I got an Austrian passport, in case Canada becomes unsafe for me as a Jew. I fear that moment is approaching, here in Canada and elsewhere.” The Belleville shooting happened Sunday night outside a synagogue in the city of 55,000, where worshipers had gathered to mark Yom Kippur. Const. Jeff Smith, a nearly 13-year veteran of the Belleville Police Service, was in critical but stable condition after exchanging gunfire with a shooter outside the building. No one else was injured in the attack. The gunman later died in a hospital. Police continue to investigate a shooting outside of Belleville’s Sons of Jacob Synagogue, Tuesday September 22, 2026. “Jewish Canadians are living in a parallel world,” Herland wrote in his post. “Where police stand guard with guns outside synagogues. And Jewish schools, religious sites and businesses are targeted with bullets. And most Canadians have no awareness or understanding.” Multiple synagogues in Ontario, and specifically the Greater Toronto Area, have been targeted in shooting attacks in recent years. In March, three GTA synagogues were struck by gunfire in the space of five days — Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto in Thornhill, and Temle Emanu-el and Shaarei Shomayim in North York. York Regional Police have charged three suspects in connection with two of the shootings.

stories.title: Advocates voicing concerns over rising drug overdoses in Manitoba
stories.summary: Drug overdoses and drug-related deaths appear to be rising again in Manitoba, according to advocates and data from the Winnipeg Fire Paramedic Service (Wfps).
stories.author: Marney Blunt
stories.content:
Drug overdoses and drug-related deaths appear to be rising again in Manitoba, according to advocates and data from the Winnipeg Fire Paramedic Service (Wfps).

Data from Wfps shows so far this year, from January until the end of August, paramedics have responded to 4,040 calls related to opioids; the highest number of calls related to opioids the service has seen, with four months left in the year. In all of 2025, Wfps responded to 3,270 calls related to opioids.

“The repetitive nature of the calls is what our staff is finding challenging,” said Tom Wallace, the deputy chief of paramedic operations, education and training for Wfps.

“That and the fact opioids have surpassed alcohol as the substance that we’re dealing with most frequently.”

From 2018 to 2025, alcohol-related calls always remained well above calls related to opioids. But so far this year, there have been 3,408 alcohol-related calls, compared to the 4,040 opioid calls.

Paramedics are also administering more doses of naloxone. So far this year, 5,712 doses of naloxone have been given, compared to 4,900 in all of last year.

“When they’re responding to the same call over and over again, sometimes for the same individual within a given shift, that can be challenging for staff,” Wallace said.

In an interview with Global News earlier this year, Dr. John Younes, the chief medical examiner for the province, said while there was no finalized data, it appeared drug-related deaths were rising in the province this year, following a decline in 2024 and 2025.

Preliminary data shows that between January and April of this year, 141 Manitobans lost their lives due to suspected substance-related deaths.

A grandmother’s message

Lorna Reykdal knows the impact additions can have. She keeps memories of her grandson, Brayden Crotty, close after losing him to addiction.

“He was really funny. He had a good sense of humour and he loved his clothes – dressed nice,” Reykdal told Global News.

“And we never thought we’d lose him, but we did.”

She says Brayden struggled with addiction for a number of years and sought help, attending the Bruce Oake Recovery Centre.

But nearly two years ago, in October 2024, Brayden’s battle with addiction came to a tragic end.

“We never expected to have him pass. But one day he got something quite bad and yeah, his sister found him,” she said.

At the age of 32, Brayden had overdosed on down – a potent mixture of dangerous drugs, often including fentanyl and methamphetamine.

“That was the saddest day of our life when we got this call.”

In her mid 80s, Reykdal still advocates on behalf of her grandson, participating in awareness walks and taking part in support groups. There is also an annual memorial golf tournament called Brayden’s Next Chapter, which raises funds for the Bruce Oake Recovery Centre.

Reykdal hopes sharing Brayden’s story will help keep others alive. She wants others to know help is available.

“Brayden’s story means a lot to me and Brayden meant a lot to me. So if I keep speaking Brayden’s name, it warms my heart,” Reykdal said.

“If my story can touch one person that has any kind of addiction, it will make my day.”

Advocates push for safe supply, public health emergency

Arlene Last-Kolb lost her son Jessie in 2014 when he accidentally overdosed on fentanyl. She continues to advocate in his memory.

“I know that he would want me to do this. That’s just who he was,” Last-Kolb told Global News.

“I want to help families to not have to go through what I am going through.”

Last-Kolb says she has concerns about rising drug overdoses in the community.

“Everything has gone up. Nothing has changed. And naloxone can’t be an answer to a toxic drug crisis,” she said.

“We can’t continue to let people overdose over and over and over again and just give them naloxone. That is unacceptable.”

She also wants to see the province declare a public health emergency over the toxic drug supply and better education on toxic drugs and administering naloxone in schools. She also wants to see safe supply offered, an option she feels could have helped her son.

“The hardest thing is to know your child has passed away from an overdose and to know that there is something out there that might have helped you. That regulation should have been a choice for you, that your child’s choice shouldn’t have been to go to the street and just die,” she said.

“When people access safe consumption sites, it would make more sense to me if they took a regulated supply with them.”

Kate Sjoberg, the executive director of Resource Assistance for Youth, says they have also witnessed a spike in overdose deaths, particularly during the month of April.

“We’re in a real crisis as a community right now,” Sjoberg said.

In June, the province announced $1 million to combat the overdose crisis, which included a mobile paramedic overdose response team for downtown, distributing 20 oxygen delivery devices to Main Street Project, and first-aid and overdose response training for community partners.

Like Last-Kolb, Sjoberg also wants to see the overdose and addictions crisis declared a public health emergency.

“We’ve been calling for attention to this matter of drug toxicity and for governments to pay attention to the possibility of making the drug supply safer,” she said.

“Right now, in particular, the coincidence of drug toxicity with the public health emergency on HIV means all of us are less safe.”

Global News has reached out to the minister of housing, addiction, and homelessness for a response.

stories.title: Ottawa ends ‘political accord’ with controversial Indigenous group
stories.summary: The Congress of Aboriginal Peoples (CAP) says they will challenge Ottawa’s decision to cut ties with the organization, which claims to represent off-reserve Indigenous people.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier, Melissa Ridgen
stories.content:
The federal government is cutting ties with a controversial group that claims to represent Indigenous peoples living off-reserve in Canada.

The Congress of Aboriginal Peoples (CAP) said Wednesday that Ottawa had “unilaterally” ended a political accord with the group, which had been signed in 2018 under then-prime minister Justin Trudeau.

CAP, an organization founded in the 1970s to represent the interests of Métis and non-status Indigenous peoples, has drawn criticism from some prominent Indigenous voices for their affiliation with groups claiming to be “Eastern Métis” and “Southern Inuit.”

But membership with the organization was enough for companies to gain access to billions of dollars worth of federal contracting opportunities through the Indigenous Procurement Program, a Global News investigation revealed in 2024.

CAP did not respond to Global News’ request for comment Wednesday. But in a public statement , the organization vowed to “challenge” the federal government’s decision to end their 2018 accord.

“Indigenous people do not stop being Indigenous because they live off reserve, lack federal registration, or fall outside the federal government’s preferred administrative structures,” CAP National Chief Brendan Moore said in the statement.

“Their rights do not depend on the existence of a political accord, and neither does their right to be heard.”

The organization said the federal government made the decision without offering an explanation, and demanded accountability.

First Nations, Inuit and Métis governments, meanwhile, have maintained they represent their people regardless of where in Canada they live, making a group like CAP moot.

Neither Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada (Cirnac) nor Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) immediately responded to Global News’ request for comment.

Crystal Semaganis, who has testified before parliamentary committees as an expert witness on Indigenous identity fraud, said non-Section 35 rights-holding groups who claim Indigeneity can divert needed resources and supports away from First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities.

“It’s become something very fraudulent, something very exploitative and damaging to people who are in need of those funds and that community support for nation building, for capacity building, for education, for economic diversity and growth,” Semaganis told Global in an interview.

A 2024 Global News investigation into the government’s Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business (Psib) and Indigenous Business Directory found that companies with unclear claims to Indigeneity had been granted access to billions in contracts meant for First Nations, Métis and Inuit-owned businesses.

The investigation found that the federal government, through Indigenous Services Canada (ISC), had little control or oversight in place to ensure the businesses qualifying for the Indigenous Procurement Program were, in fact, majority owned and operated by Indigenous people.

Global News also detailed the practice of companies hiring Indigenous businesses as a front to gain access to the contracts, and then giving them a percentage of the proceeds — a scheme known in the procurement world as “rent-a-feathers.”

Procurement Ombudsperson Alexander Jeglic told Global News in March that the program was the “ worst (he’s) ever seen ” in terms of his office’s systemic review.

Jeglic’s office’s report found that ISC showed a “systemic disregard” for the program’s principles, confirmed the department repeatedly failed to verify companies were Indigenous-owned, and failed to measure how the program benefited First Nations, Métis and Inuit communities.

The result, Jeglic’s found, was the federal government could not “credibly” say it was accomplishing its targets for economic reconciliation with Indigenous peoples in Canada.

The Congress of Aboriginal Peoples (CAP) said Wednesday that Ottawa had “unilaterally” ended a political accord with the group, which had been signed in 2018 under then-prime minister Justin Trudeau.

CAP, an organization founded in the 1970s to represent the interests of Métis and non-status Indigenous peoples, has drawn criticism from some prominent Indigenous voices for their affiliation with groups claiming to be “Eastern Métis” and “Southern Inuit.”

But membership with the organization was enough for companies to gain access to billions of dollars worth of federal contracting opportunities through the Indigenous Procurement Program, a Global News investigation revealed in 2024.
CAP did not respond to Global News’ request for comment Wednesday. But in a public statement , the organization vowed to “challenge” the federal government’s decision to end their 2018 accord.

“Their rights do not depend on the existence of a political accord, and neither does their right to be heard.”

stories.title: Belleville residents searching for answers after shooting outside synagogue, MP says
stories.summary: Liberal MP Chris Malette pays tribute in House to residents of his riding, saying his thoughts are with Jewish community
stories.author: Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Belleville residents are angry and looking for answers after a shooting outside a synagogue in the Ontario city on Sunday, the member of Parliament for the area said.

Liberal MP Chris Malette paid tribute in the House of Commons Wednesday to the residents of his riding, saying his thoughts are with the Jewish community, the police officer wounded in Sunday night’s incident and all those affected.

Members of the city’s Jewish community had gathered for services to mark Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar, when an assailant identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward allegedly opened fire. He began shooting at Constable Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue, and then at another police officer who arrived on the scene.

Const. Smith was wounded and remains in hospital. Mr. Ward died in hospital, according to Ontario’s Special Investigations Unit.

Mr. Malette said Belleville is hurting.

“The good people of my riding, the Bay of Quinte, are angry, confused, hurt, and looking for answers in the near tragedy that unfolded Sunday at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue, two blocks from my own home,” he told the House of Commons ahead of Question Period on Wednesday.

He offered his best wishes to Const. Smith and the officer’s family and also addressed the Jewish community.

“To the Jewish families across the Bay of Quinte and the members of the Congregation of Sons of Jacob, you deserve to gather, worship, and live openly without fear,” he said.

“There is no place for hatred or antisemitism in Belleville or across Canada.”

The Globe and Mail reported Tuesday, citing sources, that the suspect spent five years in the Canadian Army but was released because he was deemed unsuitable for further military service.

The Globe is not identifying the sources, who were not authorized to publicly discuss the matter.

A postmortem for Mr. Ward was scheduled to take place in Kingston on Wednesday, Kristy Denette, a spokesperson for the Special Investigations Unit, told The Globe and Mail.

The SIU handles cases involving Ontario police that result in death or serious injury.

stories.title: Nova Scotia selling off remaining U.S. booze inventory, liquor profits dip
stories.summary: During the first quarter, the Nslc sold more than $1.8 million in U.S. products, according to its latest financial results.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia Liquor Corp. (Nslc) says its net income decreased by 6.8 per cent in the first quarter, hitting $62 million, and that it has already sold off the bulk of its American inventory.

Total sales from April 1 to June 28 were $219.4 million, which is up by just 0.2 per cent from the same period last year.

Beverage alcohol sales were down 1.7 per cent, while cannabis sales were up 11.2 per cent. Alcohol made up more than 83 per cent of Nslc’s total sales.

During the first quarter, the Nslc sold more than $1.8 million in American products, according to its latest financial results.

“The Nslc continues to sell existing U.S. product inventory only and is not importing any additional products made, manufactured or produced in the United States,” the province added in a release.

The provincial government directed the Nslc to remove all U.S. alcohol from store shelves last spring as part of Nova Scotia’s response to sweeping tariffs brought in by U.S. President Donald Trump.

The province began selling off its supply of U.S. products in December 2025, an inventory estimated to be worth about $14 million.

An Nslc spokesperson says as of Aug. 17, the Crown corporation had about $1.5 million in U.S. product remaining.

— with a file from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sports notes: Western WR group ready for Homecoming, high school season begins
stories.summary: It’s a battle of the unbeatens during Homecoming Weekend at Western University.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
It’s a battle of the unbeatens during Homecoming Weekend at Western University.

The Western Mustangs (3-0) will host the McMaster Marauders (4-0) with first place in the OUA on the line at 1 p.m. Saturday at Alumni Stadium.

The Mustangs under new head coach Michael Faulds and starting quarterback Jerome Rancourt have been throwing the football all over the place through the first three games.

Rancourt is second in the league averaging 326 passing yards per game and it’s made easier by having what play-by-play commentator and former Mustangs wide receiver Tom McConnell is calling “the deepest receiving corps in recent program history.”

“This is a very talented group, and I think any one of us can play in any spot and we’re a very dangerous group,” said Jackson Taylor, a transfer from McMaster who has three touchdowns this season.

The foursome of Taylor, Nick Schewchuk, Dasani McIntosh, and Emmett Charles are a nightmare for opposing defensive backs and defensive coordinators.

“Whether it’s blocking, cancelling anything like that and I think we just have a bunch of talent over here.”

Having this group makes it much easier for offensive play caller Gaetan Richard.

“I think they’ve done a good job in training camp and through the season of building a rapport with Jerome,” said Richard.

“It’s been good in the sense the ball can go anywhere on any given play depending on what the defensive structure is giving us. So as a play caller, that’s always good, where you feel confident with wherever the coverage dictates, the ball should go.”

Fall high school sports season underway

The Tvra high school sports season is underway. The season began Tuesday at City Wide Field with girls’ field hockey action.

The Medway Cowgirls took the field as the defending Ofsaa champions, but players describe this year as a “rebuilding year.”

“We had a bunch of amazing seniors that brought us to that victory,” said Leah Veal, a defender who scored the opening goal of the season.

“They carried it on their backs pretty much but this year we are expecting a rebuilding year, but with the looks of it, it’s going to be pretty good.”

The girls opened the year with a 4-0 victory over West Elgin.

“We had a great group of seniors last year that had taught us all so much,” said Molly Hammond.

“They went off to do their own great things and this year we have a ton of new promising rookies that I’m excited to see how they grow and like teach them. Just kind of the same thing that our seniors did for us.”

On the gridiron, the season began with Beal taking on Westminster Wednesday morning in the Walzak Division. It’s a division which features many smaller or starting programs, many which include a mix of junior and senior players.

Cameron Proctor got the season started for Beal Raiders, recovering a fumble and then switching to offence where he pounded in the first touchdown of the season.

The top division tier contenders begin play Thursday and Friday.

Over at Kennedy Field, the Catholic Central Crusaders are ranked number one in Ontario in the coaches’ preseason poll.The two-time defending Ofsaa Bowl champions will face St. Joseph’s Friday.

“I think we don’t we don’t really mind the rankings,” said Christian De Bernardo, a Crusaders offensive lineman.

“We just do what we do every day during practice, and we just go play and get ready for Friday. We lot a couple of guys to the [United] States, but I think we just have younger grade 11 filling in for the positions, and they’re doing a pretty good job.”

Running Back Nathan Sims is going to be a workhorse this season. He believes the rankings won’t affect their mentality but does feel they deserve the praise.

“We’re recovering really well and at the end of the day, we’re just we’re just here to play our own game and we’ll show we’ll show everybody what we’re made of.”

Having this group makes it much easier for offensive play caller Gaetan Richard.
“I think they’ve done a good job in training camp and through the season of building a rapport with Jerome,” said Richard.

“It’s been good in the sense the ball can go anywhere on any given play depending on what the defensive structure is giving us. So as a play caller, that’s always good, where you feel confident with wherever the coverage dictates, the ball should go.”
Fall high school sports season underway
The Tvra high school sports season is underway. The season began Tuesday at City Wide Field with girls’ field hockey action.
The Medway Cowgirls took the field as the defending Ofsaa champions, but players describe this year as a “rebuilding year.”
“We had a bunch of amazing seniors that brought us to that victory,” said Leah Veal, a defender who scored the opening goal of the season.
“They carried it on their backs pretty much but this year we are expecting a rebuilding year, but with the looks of it, it’s going to be pretty good.”
The girls opened the year with a 4-0 victory over West Elgin.
“We had a great group of seniors last year that had taught us all so much,” said Molly Hammond.

“They went off to do their own great things and this year we have a ton of new promising rookies that I’m excited to see how they grow and like teach them. Just kind of the same thing that our seniors did for us.”

On the gridiron, the season began with Beal taking on Westminster Wednesday morning in the Walzak Division. It’s a division which features many smaller or starting programs, many which include a mix of junior and senior players.
Cameron Proctor got the season started for Beal Raiders, recovering a fumble and then switching to offence where he pounded in the first touchdown of the season.
The top division tier contenders begin play Thursday and Friday.
Over at Kennedy Field, the Catholic Central Crusaders are ranked number one in Ontario in the coaches’ preseason poll.The two-time defending Ofsaa Bowl champions will face St. Joseph’s Friday.
“I think we don’t we don’t really mind the rankings,” said Christian De Bernardo, a Crusaders offensive lineman.

“We just do what we do every day during practice, and we just go play and get ready for Friday. We lot a couple of guys to the [United] States, but I think we just have younger grade 11 filling in for the positions, and they’re doing a pretty good job.”
Running Back Nathan Sims is going to be a workhorse this season. He believes the rankings won’t affect their mentality but does feel they deserve the praise.
“We’re recovering really well and at the end of the day, we’re just we’re just here to play our own game and we’ll show we’ll show everybody what we’re made of.”

stories.title: NDP leader says Ottawa breaking labour law as Bank of Canada strike nears 100 days
stories.summary: NDP Leader Avi Lewis says the federal government is defying its own labour laws after the head of the Bank of Canada admitted to using replacement workers during a strike involving security officers.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

Posted September 23, 2026 3:02 pm.

Last Updated September 23, 2026 5:20 pm.

Ottawa — NDP Leader Avi Lewis said the federal government is defying its own labour laws after the head of the Bank of Canada admitted to using replacement workers during a strike involving security officers.

In 2024, Canada passed legislation to ban federally regulated workplaces from bringing in replacement workers during a legal strike, and the new rules took effect last year.

At a rally outside the Bank of Canada Wednesday, Lewis said this strike is the first test of that law.

“This government and this employer have made it absolutely clear that they are prepared to defy the law of this country,” he said.

Security officers at the Bank of Canada went on strike in June after talks failed to secure a new collective agreement between the central bank and the union.

The Canada Industrial Relations Board has released two decisions indicating the central bank contravened the Canada Labour Code by using contractors and the services of union members during the strike.

Tiff Macklem, governor of the Bank of Canada, said in July that some exceptions to the rules allow for the use of replacement workers when necessary to prevent threats to life, health or safety, or to prevent serious damage to property.

“Ahead of the Cirb’s first ruling, the Bank made representations regarding the minimum necessary arrangements to ensure the security of our facilities and people in light of the strike,” he said.

“The bank felt it necessary to put in place alternative arrangements that, in the bank’s view, adhered to the Canada Labour Code and the previous Cirb ruling. The Cirb subsequently ruled a second time. The bank has also complied with that decision.”

Dozens of union members gathered in downtown Ottawa Wednesday as the Bank of Canada strike reached 93 days. Also present was a giant inflatable rat wearing a necklace with a $20 bill with Macklem’s face.

Alex Silas, national executive vice-president of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, said at the rally that the union is asking the Crown corporation to come back to the bargaining table and to remove its concessions.

“It’s concerning how little they respect their security officers that they would replace us instead of settling on a fair deal,” he said. “And it’s also concerning that they have completely untrained, unqualified people doing security at the Bank of Canada right now.”

Labour leaders are denouncing what they call a direct attack on the right to strike in the sweeping economic bill the Liberal government tabled Monday.

The Liberals claim the bill would place “guardrails” around a minister’s power to end work stoppages in federally regulated industries. Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu argues the changes in Bill C-39 are aimed at improving labour relations and reducing the number of times negotiations hit a boiling point.

According to the proposed Building Canada Strong Act, a work stoppage must be affecting the “national interest” before the minister can trigger Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end a strike or lockout.

The government says it must balance threats to the national interest — which could include economic impacts or social disruptions — with the need to protect the right to free association and to strike.

Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday that the proposed amendments would formalize the government’s power to break strikes.

Bruske said labour leaders are considering legal avenues to address the proposed changes but suggested those conversations are still in the early stages.

Unifor National president Lana Payne also accused the government of compromising workers’ right to strike in a media statement on Tuesday.

Lewis said Wednesday the labour movement across the country is “on fire against what is being called a direct attack on the fundamental right of workers to withhold their labour.”

“The right to strike is under attack in Canada by the government, by the prime minister, who used to run this little shop at the Bank of Canada behind us,” he said while standing in front of the central bank’s head office.

“The 49 workers who protect the people inside this building are exercising their right to strike and the government agency is bringing in replacement workers. This is a bad sign. It’s a terrible message.”

A statement issued by the Bank of Canada Wednesday said the Crown corporation respects the security officers’ right to strike and remains committed to the collective bargaining process and to working with the union to negotiate a fair settlement.

“When the Canadian Industrial Relations Board issued its orders, the Bank stopped using the external security support as directed,” said the statement. “The Bank continues to comply with these orders and has not used that support since July 23.”

The statement said the Bank of Canada remains committed to “taking all necessary measures to ensure Canada’s central bank is secure.”

“The Bank will not, under any circumstances, compromise the safety and security of our employees, our buildings and the assets we protect on behalf of Canadians,” it said. “The Bank has put in place a strong temporary plan, led by our experienced security managers, to support our operations at head office.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press
